  `json_whitespace_is_space_tab_lf_and_cr_and_nothing_else` is the unit half.

- **~~138~~ · Closed — a binary jsonb payload's first byte is its version.** 18.6's `jsonb_recv`
  (`src/backend/utils/adt/jsonb.c`) reads that byte **unconditionally** —
  `int version = pq_getmsgint(buf, 1)` — and takes the JSON text to be everything after
  it (`pq_getmsgtext(buf, buf->len - buf->cursor, &nbytes)`), raising
  `elog(ERROR, "unsupported jsonb version number %d", version)` for anything but `1`.
  The SQLSTATE is `XX000` (`internal_error`) because nothing here calls `errcode()` and
  `errstart` picks a default from the elevel — `if (elevel >= ERROR) edata->sqlerrcode =
  ERRCODE_INTERNAL_ERROR` (`src/backend/utils/error/elog.c`). `elog` is not what decides
  that: it expands to `ereport(elevel, errmsg_internal(...))`, and an `ereport(ERROR, ...)`
  carrying no `errcode()` of its own lands on the same default. `pq_getmsgint(buf, 1)`
  yields an **unsigned** byte, so the printed number runs `0`–`255`.
  There is therefore no such thing as a payload sent *with no version byte*: whatever the
  sender meant by its first byte, that byte is the version.

  pglet's `TypeOid::Jsonb` arm in `pglet_core::types::binary` read the payload as
  `bytes.strip_prefix(&[1]).unwrap_or(bytes)` — so a first byte that was not `1` left the
  **whole** buffer, pseudo-version byte included, to be handed to the server-encoding scan
  and then to the jsonb reader. What a payload earned was therefore **whatever that
  unstripped buffer earned from those two**, decided by the byte *and the body behind it*
  together and not by the byte alone. Where the buffer still parsed as JSON — a payload
  written with no version byte at all, or one whose leading byte is JSON whitespace — the
  value was **accepted**, and written where the statement wrote (measured on a build of the
  pre-fix arm: a binary `$1` of `{"a":1}` through `INSERT INTO r138 VALUES ($1)` reported no
  error and `SELECT v::text` read back `{"a": 1}`). `0x00`, and a byte at or above `0x80`
  that the text behind it did not complete into a legal UTF-8 sequence, made the scan answer
  `22021` over a byte 18.6 never scans. And what the reader was handed, it judged as JSON
  text — under whichever of **its own** codes that text earned, which is the reader's whole
  verdict space and not one code: `22P02` for a body it cannot parse, but a body it parses
  and then refuses carries that refusal instead. Behind a leading `0x20` the reader is
  handed ` "\u0000"` and ` 1e200000`, which answer `22P05 unsupported Unicode escape
  sequence` and `22003` — measured on this build by handing the reader those same two texts
  behind a correct version byte, which is byte for byte what the pre-fix arm handed it. So
  no count of answers bounds the arm.

  The members, measured on both engines over a raw extended-protocol client binding
  `SELECT $1::jsonb` with parameter format `1` and declared OID 3802, and re-measured
  on this build:

  | payload | pglet before | 18.6 | here now |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | `01` + `{"a":1}` | `{"a": 1}` | `{"a": 1}` | `{"a": 1}` — the control |
  | `{"a":1}`, no version byte | accepted and stored as `{"a": 1}` | `XX000 unsupported jsonb version number 123` | 18.6's |
  | `123`, no version byte | `123` | `XX000 … number 49` | 18.6's |
  | `"hi"`, no version byte | `"hi"` | `XX000 … number 34` | 18.6's |
  | `20` + `{"a":1}`, a leading JSON space | `{"a": 1}` | `XX000 … number 32` | 18.6's |
  | `00` + `{"a":1}` | `22021 invalid byte sequence for encoding "UTF8": 0x00` | `XX000 … number 0` | 18.6's |
  | `ff` + `{"a":1}` | `22021 … : 0xff` | `XX000 … number 255` | 18.6's |
  | `02` + `{"a":1}` | `22P02 invalid input syntax for type json` | `XX000 … number 2` | 18.6's |
  | *(empty payload)* | `22P02` | `08P01 insufficient data left in message` | 18.6's, since row 139's repair — `22000 execution error: invalid binary jsonb parameter` before it |

  One sweep is exhaustive **in the leading byte, over one body**: all 256 leading bytes
  ahead of a complete `{"a":1}` body. On the pre-fix build that body accepted 5 (`01`, and
  `09`/`0a`/`0d`/`20`, JSON's own whitespace), answered `22021` at 129 (`0x00` and every
  byte at or above `0x80`) and `22P02` at the remaining 122 — a partition of *that body's*
  256 payloads, never of the bytes on their own: the four whitespace bytes were accepted
  because the JSON behind them was acceptable, and the 122 answered `22P02` because this
  body's text is what the reader was handed. On this build the same sweep accepts exactly
  `01` and answers `XX000` at the other 255 — **SQLSTATE and message compared byte for byte
  against 18.6 at every one of the 256, zero divergences**.

  The repair is the **order**: the version byte is split off before the encoding scan, as
  `pq_getmsgint` runs before `pq_getmsgtext`, and only the remainder is scanned and parsed.
  Splitting first is what makes the `0x00` and high-byte members fall out — they stop
  being bytes the scan sees at all. It mints pglet's first `XX000` producer
  (`Error::UnsupportedJsonbVersion`); the tree had none.

  **Everything measured downstream of a correct version byte already agreed, and still
  does** — on both engines, before the repair and after: `01` + a NUL inside a string (`22021` both),
  `01` + invalid UTF-8 (`22021 invalid byte sequence for encoding "UTF8": 0xe9 0x22` both,
  byte-identical), `01` + leading JSON whitespace (accepted both), `01` + trailing junk
  (`22P02` both), `01` alone (`22P02` both), `01 01` + json (`22P02` both). The **output**
  side agrees at the shape measured: a binary-format result for `'{"a":1}'::jsonb` is
  `01 7b 22 61 22 3a 20 31 7d` on both engines. This was an input-only edge.

  **Reach.** One door reaches `value_from_binary` from outside
  `pglet_core::types::binary` — `pglet_server::encoding`'s `decode_param`, on the
  `format.is_binary()` branch — so the arm is reachable only through the native server's
  extended protocol; inside the module `decode_binary_array` reaches the same arm again
  through `recv_binary`, once per array element. The wasm hosts bind from JS through the text path, and `COPY … BINARY`
  parses but fails loud `0A000` at execution without reaching a binary decoder. The
  **`jsonb[]` element** route does reach it, and was measured divergent identically (a
  single element `{"a":1}` with no version byte: accepted here, `XX000 … number 123`
  there) — but it carries a condition the scalar route does not. `decode_binary_array`
  takes the element type from the **wire array header**, so the gate runs on an element
  only where that header names `jsonb`, or names an OID pglet does not recognise and falls
  back to the parameter's own element type. **Where the header names `jsonb`**,
  re-measured on this build, a one-element `SELECT $1::jsonb[]` refuses at every payload
  of the table above but the control under the same SQLSTATE and message as the scalar
  route, on 18.6 and here, and accepts the control as a one-element array. The
  unrecognised-OID branch does **not** inherit that agreement, because 18.6 refuses a
  mismatched header only where **both** OIDs are below its built-in-OID floor of `10000`:
  measured at header OIDs `10000` and `20000`, 18.6 falls back as pglet does and answers
  that same table, while at `9999` it refuses the parameter `42804` at every payload of
  it, the control included, where pglet runs this gate and gives the scalar route's
  verdict. That split, and a header naming *another* scalar element type pglet recognises —
  which routes the element past this gate entirely — are row 140.

  **Why no fixture holds it.** `@param $N jsonb '<literal>'` binds through
  tokio-postgres, which constructs a well-formed payload with its version byte, and the
  directive grammar has no raw-bytes form — so the shape cannot be written as
  SQL-plus-directives at all. The guards are the two `binary.rs` unit tests and the
  `handlers.rs` Bind test named in the row, all three under `cargo test --workspace`,
  which is the gated `test:rust`; `test_binary` is in neither `deno task test` nor the
  gate set, so a case added there would enforce nothing. The rule's statement is
  `docs/param_binding.md` § A binary `jsonb` payload's first byte is its version.

- **~~139~~ · Closed — a binary parameter is consumed exactly.** 18.6's `exec_bind_message`
  (`src/backend/tcop/postgres.c`) calls the parameter type's `*recv` over the payload and
  then refuses a payload that reader did not consume to its last byte:
  `22P03 incorrect binary data format in bind parameter <n>`, `<n>` the parameter's
  1-based number. A read past the end inside the `*recv` is the **message reader's** own
  `08P01` (`src/backend/libpq/pqformat.c`): `pq_getmsgbyte` says
  `no data left in message`, and `pq_copymsgbytes` and `pq_getmsgbytes` — behind
  `pq_getmsgint` and `pq_getmsgint64` too — say `insufficient data left in message`. The
  sentence follows the reader the `*recv` calls, not the width it asks for: `boolrecv`
  reads through `pq_getmsgbyte`, while `jsonb_recv`'s one-byte `pq_getmsgint(buf, 1)`
  answers `insufficient`.

  **What pglet did.** It had no such reader. The fixed-width arms refused a wrong length
  under `22000 execution error: invalid binary <T> parameter` (the array header reader's
  `<T>` the word `array`), `numeric` answered `22P02` and `interval` `22007`, and where the
  excess or shortfall read as ordinary framing nothing refused at all. An over-long
  `numeric` was stored with its tail unread. An array's elements were read while bytes
  remained, the dimension length never consulted, so a tail after the declared elements
  was decoded as further elements — `text[]` `{a}` plus a zero length decoded as
  `{a,""}`, plus `ffffffff` as `{a,NULL}`, plus a second element as `{a,b}`, and `int4[]`
  `{5}` plus a second element as `{5,6}` — a payload short of its declared count decoded as the elements
  present, a dimension length `ArrayGetNItems` refuses (`-1`, `134217728`) was accepted,
  and `ndim = 0` returned before the body was looked at.

  **`numeric_recv` carried members no length probe reaches**, measured on the pre-repair
  build against 18.6: a display scale of `0x4000`, a bit outside `NUMERIC_DSCALE_MASK`
  but positive as the `i16` pglet read it, was accepted where 18.6 answers
  `22P03 invalid scale in external "numeric" value`; and a `NaN` header returned before
  its scale and digits were checked, so a `NaN` with a digit of `10000`, with a scale of
  `0x4000`, or with two digits declared and one present was accepted as `NaN` where 18.6
  answers `invalid digit`, `invalid scale` and `08P01`. A bad sign, a digit outside
  `0 ..= 9999`, and a digit count of `0xFFFF` — `-1` as pglet read it, 65535 as 18.6
  does — were `22P02` here where 18.6 answers `22P03` or `08P01`.

  **The repair.** `BinaryReader` stands in for 18.6's message buffer, each reader method
  with its 18.6 reader's refusal (`byte` is `pq_getmsgbyte`'s `08P01 no data left in
  message`, the multi-byte ones `08P01 insufficient data left in message`); `recv_binary`
  is the type's `*recv`, leaving the cursor where it stops; and
  `value_from_binary(bytes, oid, param_number)` refuses the leftover, the number reaching
  it from the Bind loop's own position through `decode_param`. `PgNumeric::recv` keeps
  `numeric_recv`'s order — digit count unsigned, weight, sign (refused before the scale or
  any digit is read), scale against the mask, each digit — and refuses a complete
  `Infinity` or `-Infinity`, which `PgNumeric` cannot represent, with its old `22P02`
  after those reads. `decode_binary_array` gates the dimension length where
  `ArrayGetNItems` gates it — `54000 array size exceeds the maximum allowed (134217727)`
  for a negative length or one above that — and then reads exactly that many elements
  under `ReadArrayBinary`'s rules: an element length below `-1` or past the bytes left is
  `22P03 insufficient data left in message`, and an element its type's reader did not
  consume is `22P03 improper binary format in array element <i>`, NULL elements counted.
  The `22P03` that carries the message reader's words is a variant of its own
  (`Error::ArrayElementLengthInvalid`, beside the `08P01` `Error::InsufficientDataLeft`),
  so the code is keyed on the raiser rather than on the sentence.

  **Measured on this build**, SQLSTATE and message against 18.6 over a raw
  extended-protocol client: `bool`, `int2`, `int4`, `int8`, `float4`, `float8`, `uuid`,
  `date`, `time`, `timestamp`, `timestamptz` and `interval` at their width less one, at
  zero bytes and at their width plus one; an empty `text`, `varchar`, `bytea` and
  `jsonb`; `numeric` short and over-long at a number and a `NaN`, a bad sign alone and
  against a 65535-digit shortfall, a tail and a bad scale, a bad scale alone and against
  a shortfall and a tail and at a `NaN` and an infinity, a bad digit alone, ahead of a
  later digit's shortfall and at a `NaN`, and an infinity short of a declared digit;
  arrays across `text[]`, `int4[]`, `numeric[]`, `bool[]`, `jsonb[]`, `bytea[]` and
  `interval[]` — not every type at every shape — over-long, short, at `ndim = 0`, at a
  dimension length of `-2147483648`, `-2`, `-1`, `0`, `2`, `134217727`, `134217728` and
  `2147483647`, at an element length of `-2` and past the end, and at an element its
  reader leaves bytes in or runs past, first, second and second after a NULL; and a
  refused second and third parameter behind well-formed ones. Each agrees but the
  residuals below.

  **Residuals.** A binary `numeric` `Infinity` or `-Infinity` is accepted by 18.6 and
  refused `22P02` here — `PgNumeric` has no infinity (`docs/compatibility.md`'s numeric row) — and an
  `Infinity` with bytes after it keeps that `22P02` where 18.6 answers the leftover `22P03`, the
  refusal standing inside the reader and so ahead of the leftover check. The binary
  `interval` sentinels `PgInterval` refuses (`docs/param_binding.md`) take the same
  position, measured: an `infinity` or `-infinity` payload with a trailing byte is
  `22P03 incorrect binary data format in bind parameter 1` on 18.6 and the sentinel's
  `22007` here, an `interval[]` element holding a sentinel and a byte more is
  `22P03 improper binary format in array element 1` there, and a sentinel element followed
  by a three-byte one is `08P01 insufficient data left in message` there — `22007` here at
  each. Outside the class,
  a reader's own verdict on a value it has read in full keeps pglet's code, and now comes
  ahead of any leftover as 18.6's does: an out-of-range `time`, with or without a tail, is
  `22000` here and `22008 time out of range` there, while a `timestamp` or `date` outside
  18.6's own range is `22008 timestamp out of range` / `date out of range` on both —
  measured without a tail at both ends of each, and with one below a `date`'s range and
  past a `timestamp`'s. More widely, 18.6 accepts a binary `timestamp` or `date` outside pglet's date
  domain — a year before 1, a `timestamp` in year 20029 and a `date` in year 20001, measured
  — where pglet's range verdict is that same `22008` (row 142); the text path refuses those
  years too (`'20029-01-01'::timestamp` and `'20001-01-01'::date` are both `22008` here). The
  `infinity` and `-infinity` sentinels of a `date` or timestamp are not among them: both
  engines read each as the value, and one given a trailing byte is the leftover's `22P03`
  on both, measured. The refusals here that 18.6 does not share are raised at `Bind`,
  so inside an open block each now fails the block where 18.6 leaves it healthy: measured
  with a numeric `Infinity`,
  an `interval` `infinity` and a `timestamp` in year 20029, each
  bound between two inserts and a `COMMIT` that keeps both rows on 18.6 and neither here.
  The `W` 18.6 sends with each is row 76's standing omission.
  `numeric_recv` also truncates the digits a display scale hides (`trunc_var`), which is
  a value the reader constructs rather than a length it reads; `PgNumeric::recv` did not,
  and now does (`docs/param_binding.md` § A binary parameter is consumed exactly).

  **Why no fixture holds it.** `@param` binds through tokio-postgres, which encodes each
  value at its own width, and the directive grammar has no raw-bytes form. The guards are
  the unit tests and the Bind test named below, all under `cargo test --workspace`,
  which is the gated `test:rust`: `binary.rs`'s
  `a_fixed_width_value_is_read_to_its_width_and_no_further`,
  `a_binary_numeric_is_read_in_numeric_recvs_order`,
  `a_binary_arrays_dimension_length_is_spent`,
  `a_binary_arrays_dimension_length_is_gated_before_it_is_spent` and
  `a_binary_array_element_is_read_to_its_own_length`, plus `handlers.rs`'s
  `a_binary_param_is_consumed_exactly_and_refused_at_bind_with_its_number`. The rule's
  statement is `docs/param_binding.md` § A binary parameter is consumed exactly.

- **140 · a binary array header is checked short of 18.6's checks.** `decode_binary_array` reads
  the header — `ndim`, the flags word, the element OID, then the dimension's length and
  lower bound, and then each element's own length — and what it does with each is its
  own: `_has_nulls` and `_lower_bound` are bound to `_`; the element OID decides how every
  element is decoded
  (`let elem_type = TypeOid::from_oid(header_elem_oid).unwrap_or(inferred_elem);`) unless
  it names an array type, which is refused; and
  every `ndim` outside `{0, 1}` falls to one `NotImplemented`, matched only once the flags
  word and the element OID have been read. Not one of those is the check 18.6 has for
  that field. The dimension length and each element's own length are no longer this
  row's: row 139's repair gates and spends the one and checks the other as 18.6 does, and
  the table and paragraphs below keep their pre-repair measurements, marked. 18.6's
  `array_recv`
  (`src/backend/utils/adt/arrayfuncs.c`) gates `ndim`, the flags word, the element OID
  and the dimension length; that last one it gates **and** spends, and the gate is the
  same call that produces the count. `ArrayGetNItems` — a thin forward to
  `ArrayGetNItemsSafe` (`src/backend/utils/adt/arrayutils.c`) — raises
  `ERRCODE_PROGRAM_LIMIT_EXCEEDED`,
  `array size exceeds the maximum allowed (%d)` with `MaxArraySize` printing as
  `134217727`, at a negative dimension, at a running product that overflows an `int32`,
  and at a final count above `MaxArraySize` — of those arms a one-dimensional header
  reaches the negative one and the final one. `array_recv` calls it immediately after the
  `dim[i]`/`lBound[i]` read loop and **before any element is read**, on the line above
  its `ArrayCheckBounds` call; the count it returns is then the spend, `ReadArrayBinary`
  reading exactly that many elements and gating each element's own length as it goes. And
  the lower bound 18.6 both gates and **keeps**: `ArrayCheckBounds`
  (`src/backend/utils/adt/arrayutils.c`) raises `ERRCODE_PROGRAM_LIMIT_EXCEEDED`,
  `array lower bound is too large: %d`, where `pg_add_s32_overflow(dims[i], lb[i])`
  overflows, and where it does not the bound rides on the value.

  **The element OID's gate is conditional, and reproducing it as an unconditional check
  would over-refuse.** `array_recv` complains only where **both** the header's OID and the
  expected one are below `FirstGenbkiObjectId` — `10000`, from
  `src/include/access/transam.h` — because, its own comment says, "only built-in types
  have OIDs that are stable enough to believe that a mismatch is a real issue"; otherwise
  it assigns `element_type = spec_element_type` and carries on, which is pglet's fallback
  exactly. So at or above that floor the two engines **agree**, measured below. Every OID
  `TypeOid::from_oid` recognises is under the floor, so pglet's recognised/unrecognised
  split is not 18.6's built-in/non-built-in one: an OID pglet does not recognise sits on
  either side of the floor, and which side it sits on is what decides whether this member
  diverges. The *expected* side never decides it here: `oid.array_element()` answers with
  a `TypeOid`, so a pglet array parameter's own element type is always below the floor and
  18.6's second conjunct is always satisfied.

  Measured on both engines over a raw extended-protocol client binding a one-element array
  with parameter format `1`:

  | parameter | header element OID | element bytes | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | `$1::jsonb[]` | 3802 (`jsonb`) | `{"a":1}` | `XX000 unsupported jsonb version number 123` | the same — row 138's rule, agreeing |
  | `$1::jsonb[]` | 25 (`text`) | `{"a":1}` | **accepted** — `{"{\"a\": 1}"}`, and `INSERT` writes it to a `jsonb[]` column | `42804 … element type 25 (text) instead of expected 3802 (jsonb)` |
  | `$1::jsonb[]` | 9999 (unrecognised, below the floor) | `01` + `{"a":1}` | **accepted** — the fallback makes it a `jsonb` element and the version byte satisfies the gate | `42804 … 9999 (???) instead of expected 3802 (jsonb)` |
  | `$1::jsonb[]` | 10000 and 20000 (unrecognised, at and above the floor) | `01` + `{"a":1}` | **accepted**, by that same fallback | the same — 18.6 falls back too, agreeing |
  | `$1::jsonb[]` | 23 (`int4`) | `00 00 00 07` | `42846 cannot cast type integer to jsonb` | `42804 … 23 (integer) instead of expected 3802 (jsonb)` |
  | `$1::text[]` | 3802 (`jsonb`) | `hi` | `XX000 unsupported jsonb version number 104` | `42804 … 3802 (jsonb) instead of expected 25 (text)` |
  | `$1::text[]` | 9999 | `hi` | **accepted** — `{hi}` | `42804 … 9999 (???) instead of expected 25 (text)` |
  | `$1::text[]` | 20000 | `hi` | **accepted** — `{hi}` | the same, agreeing |

  **A header OID naming an array type pglet recognises is refused, and agrees.** pglet
  used to decode with
  it as the element type, which recursed: each element was read as another array, so a
  `$1::text[]` headed `1009` over an element that is itself a `text[]` payload was accepted
  as `{"{x}"}`, its output growing with each level of nesting, and a payload nesting
  headers 5000 deep (about 120 KB) overflowed the server's stack and aborted the process,
  every connection with it. 18.6 answers the first header
  `42804 binary data has array element type 1009 (text[]) instead of expected 25 (text)`.
  Every array OID `TypeOid::from_oid` recognises and every element type a pglet array
  parameter carries is below the floor, so 18.6's condition holds for each, and
  `decode_binary_array` refuses such a header with that `42804`, names rendered by
  `type_oid_display_name`, as soon as the OID is read. The element type it decodes with is
  therefore never an array, and the decoder cannot recurse. Measured agreeing on `text[]`
  and `int4[]` parameters under their own array OID and another's, on `varchar[]`,
  `timestamptz[]`, `bool[]` and `jsonb[]` under their own, on `text[]` at `ndim = 0` and
  over a header that ends after the OID, and at nesting depths 1 and 3; the 5000-deep
  payload is that same `42804` here. An array type `TypeOid::from_oid` does **not**
  recognise takes the unrecognised-OID fallback in the table above — the parameter's own
  scalar element type, so no recursion — and so answers what that fallback answers: a
  `text[]` headed `1028` (`oid[]`), `1014` (`character[]`), `199` (`json[]`), `1017`
  (`point[]`), `1040` (`macaddr[]`), `2277` (`anyarray`) or `0` is accepted as `{x}` here,
  where 18.6 answers `42804`, measured, `0` printing its name as `-`. A *scalar* OID is
  still taken at face value, which is the table above too.

  **Where 18.6 refuses an earlier header field, pglet answers from a later check.** pglet
  has no flags-word, scalar-OID or lower-bound check, so where 18.6 refuses one of those
  fields, the refusal pglet does raise — or none — answers instead. Measured over
  `int4[]` parameters on 18.6 and this build:

  | header | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | flags `7`, dimension length `-1` | `54000 array size exceeds the maximum allowed (134217727)` | `22P03 invalid array flags` |
  | element OID `25`, dimension length `-1` | that same `54000` | `42804 … element type 25 (text) instead of expected 23 (integer)` |
  | lower bound `2147483647`, one element and a trailing byte | `22P03 incorrect binary data format in bind parameter 1` | `54000 array lower bound is too large: 2147483647` |
  | lower bound `2147483647`, dimension length `2`, one element | `08P01 insufficient data left in message` | that same `54000` |
  | `ndim = 0`, flags `7` | **accepted** — `{}` | `22P03 invalid array flags` |
  | `ndim = 0`, element OID `25` | **accepted** — `{}` | `42804 … element type 25 (text) instead of expected 23 (integer)` |

  And over `text[]`: element OID `1009` with `ndim = -1`, or with flags `7`, is the array
  OID's `42804` here where 18.6 answers `22P03 invalid number of dimensions: -1` and
  `22P03 invalid array flags` — `array_recv` checks `ndim` and the flags word before it
  reads the OID, and pglet checks `ndim` after the flags word and the OID are read.

  The header's other fields, each measured as `SELECT $1::text[]` over a well-formed
  one-element body with that one field changed:

  | header field | value | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | the flags word | `7` | **accepted** — `{hi}` | `22P03 invalid array flags` |
  | an element's length | `-2` | before row 139's repair **accepted** — `{NULL}`, a NULL element invented; now 18.6's | `22P03 insufficient data left in message` |
  | `ndim` | `-1` | `0A000 not implemented: multi-dimensional arrays are not supported` | `22P03 invalid number of dimensions: -1` |
  | `ndim` | `99999` | that same `0A000` | `54000 number of array dimensions (99999) exceeds the maximum allowed (6)` |
  | `ndim` | `2`, over a real two-dimensional payload | that same `0A000` | **accepted** — `{{a}}` |
  | the dimension length | `-1` | before row 139's repair **accepted** — `{hi}`; now 18.6's | `54000 array size exceeds the maximum allowed (134217727)` |
  | the dimension length | `134217728` | before row 139's repair **accepted** — `{hi}`; now 18.6's | that same `54000` |
  | the dimension length | `134217727` | before row 139's repair **accepted** — `{hi}`; now 18.6's | `08P01 insufficient data left in message` — past the gate, then the spend |
  | the lower bound | `5` | **accepted** — `{hi}`, the bound dropped | **accepted** — `[5:5]={hi}` |
  | the lower bound | `2147483647` | **accepted** — `{hi}` | `54000 array lower bound is too large: 2147483647` |

  The dimension length was read at `1` (the control), `-1`, `-2`, `134217727`,
  `134217728` and `2147483647`, each over that one-element body and again over a
  header-only payload carrying no element at all. Before row 139's repair pglet answered
  `{hi}` at every with-body member and `{}` at every header-only one, the field read and
  discarded. 18.6
  answered the `54000` at `-1`, `-2`, `134217728` and `2147483647` in **both** shapes, and
  `08P01 insufficient data left in message` where the gate passed and the spend then ran
  out of payload — at `134217727` in both shapes, and at `1` in the header-only one. The
  discriminator is `134217727` against `134217728` over one identical payload: the
  refusal moves with the field's value, not with what the payload carries, which is what
  makes this a gate on the field rather than the framing consequence below. Re-measured
  on this build over `int4[]` payloads, pglet answers 18.6's code and message at
  `-2147483648`, `-2`, `-1`, `134217728` and `2147483647` in both shapes and at
  `134217727` header-only.

  The lower bound was read at `1` (the control), `5`, `0`, `-3`, `-2147483648` and
  `2147483647`. pglet answered `{hi}` at each; 18.6 answered `{hi}` at `1`,
  `[<lb>:<lb>]={hi}` at `5`, `0`, `-3` and `-2147483648`, and the `54000` only at
  `2147483647` — because the gate is on `dim + lb` overflowing an `int32`, `dim` being
  `1` over this body, and not on the bound alone, which is why `-2147483648` passes. The
  **write** half was measured into a `TEXT[]` column over the same one-element body: at
  `lBound = 5` pglet stored a row reading `{hi}` where 18.6 stored `[5:5]={hi}`
  (`array_lower` 5), and at `lBound = 2147483647` pglet's `INSERT` succeeded where
  18.6's was refused `54000`, leaving 18.6's table a row short against pglet's. Reading
  the field is not enough to close the `lBound = 5` half: `ArrayValue` is
  `{element_type, elements}`, with nowhere to put a bound, so reproducing `[5:5]={hi}` is
  a change to the value type itself rather than a check added in this decoder — where
  refusing the `54000` is a gate `decode_binary_array` can add on its own.

  Before row 139's repair the element-length arm took `len < 0`, not `len == -1`, where
  `ReadArrayBinary` refuses `itemlen < -1` before the `-1` NULL arm — so every negative
  but `-1` was an invented NULL; it now refuses below `-1` as `ReadArrayBinary` does. The
  `ndim = 2` row is pglet's pinned one-dimensional limit answering on its own
  account, loud and deliberate — and raised at `Bind`, so it fails an open block, where
  18.6 decodes the value and a `COMMIT` keeps the block's rows (measured); it is in the
  table because the **message** the two
  out-of-range `ndim` members take is that limit's, and it is wrong for a negative count
  and wrong for an over-large one.

  Some of these fields had a consequence that showed up as a **payload** divergence rather
  than a field one, and those members were recorded as row 139's. **The split was by which
  of 18.6's readers answers, not by the code it answers with.** Where the raiser is the
  **message reader** — the `08P01 insufficient data left in message` `pq_getmsgint` raises
  on an exhausted buffer — or the bind path's own
  `22P03 incorrect binary data format in bind parameter <n>` over unread bytes, the member
  was row 139's; where the raiser is `array_recv` or a helper it calls, it was this row's,
  whatever code it carries — `42804`, `22P03 invalid array flags`,
  `22P03 invalid number of dimensions`, `ReadArrayBinary`'s element-length
  `22P03 insufficient data left in message`, which carries the reader's own words under a
  different code and is what makes the code the wrong key, and each of the `54000`s.

  The dimension length fell on both sides of that split and the element length on this
  one, and row 139's repair closed the dimension length on both sides and the element
  length with it: the count is gated and then
  spent, so a tail past the declared elements is the bind path's `22P03` and a payload
  short of them the reader's `08P01`; `ndim = 0` reads no dimension, so a body after its
  header is that `22P03` too; and an element length below `-1` or past the bytes left is
  `ReadArrayBinary`'s `22P03`. What stays here is the flags word, the element OID, the lower
  bound and `ndim`. One `ndim` member moved with it: a negative count over a payload that
  ends after it — `ndim = -1` alone, measured — was `22000` and is now the header read's
  `08P01 insufficient data left in message`, where 18.6 has already answered
  `22P03 invalid number of dimensions: -1`, because pglet still reads the flags word and
  the element OID before it looks at the count.

  The `jsonb`-headed `text[]` member's **code** is one the version-byte repair moved:
  `XX000` is the code that repair minted (`Error::UnsupportedJsonbVersion`) and the tree
  had no `XX000` producer before it, so a `text[]` sender whose header says `jsonb` sees a
  jsonb version error on a parameter that is not jsonb. The divergence from 18.6 is the
  older one either way — the header's scalar element OID is not checked.

  This row also bounds row 138's array claim, in both directions. That gate reaches a
  `jsonb[]` element only where the header names `jsonb` or an OID the fallback turns into
  `jsonb`; a header naming another scalar type pglet recognises routes the element past the gate
  entirely. And where the fallback *does* run it, 18.6 may not be running any jsonb logic
  at all — below the floor it has already refused the parameter — so 138's agreement claim
  holds for the `jsonb`-headed branch and for an unrecognised OID at or above the floor,
  and not for one below it.

  **Not fixed with row 138.** Validating the header is `decode_binary_array`'s contract
  with every array type — `text[]`, `int4[]`, every element type the codec carries — not
  something one type's arm holds. The element OID's half also needs the floor comparison
  above, or it refuses where 18.6 accepts, and 18.6's message names both OIDs *and* both
  type names, which this decoder can render only for an OID pglet recognises. It is separate work.

  **Why no fixture holds it.** `@param $N <type>[] '<literal>'` binds through
  tokio-postgres, which writes a well-formed array header for the type it is encoding, so
  the directive grammar cannot produce a malformed one, and it has no raw-bytes form
  either. Nor does a unit test pin any of the rows above: those in `binary.rs` that reach
  this decoder's header each assert a neighbouring **correct** half instead.
  `multi_dim_array_rejected` asserts only that `ndim = 2` is `is_err()`, not which message
  it earns, so the message being wrong for `-1` and `99999` is invisible to it;
  `empty_and_null_element_arrays_decode` asserts that an element length of `-1` is a NULL
  element, which is 18.6's own answer; `truncated_array_header_errors` pins the header
  read's `08P01` and `array_element_length_past_end_errors` only a refusal, neither of them
  a field this row holds; and the smoke fuzz discards every result it gets. The
  dimension-length and element-length guards are row 139's.
  The **encoder** side varies nothing either: `encode_array_binary` writes the bound as
  `1` on every array it emits one for, so no round trip through pglet's own encoder
  varies that field.

- **~~1~~ · Closed — Common-type folds carry their own invariant.** Postgres's
  `select_common_type` is the single fold behind `COALESCE`/`CASE`/`ARRAY`/`GREATEST`/
  `LEAST`, set-op columns, and multi-row `VALUES`. Its step never returns a target the candidate cannot
  implicitly convert to — sharing a `typcategory` is not enough, and `time` vs
  `timestamp` is the reachable pair that proves it. The invariant lives in the fold, not
  in a wrapper, because three callers folded it raw and a wrapper is a second place to
  forget: with the target invented rather than checked, `coerce_value(timestamp → time)`
  is a supported *truncating* cast, so `SELECT tm UNION ALL SELECT ts` quietly returned
  `10:00:00` from a timestamp instead of `42846`.
- **~~2~~ · Closed — Integer `SUM`/`AVG` return a different type *and* a different value.**
  Measured on 18.6 and pglet, both legs, over a three-row table, before the close:
  `sum(bigint)` of three `9223372036854775807`s was `22003 bigint out of range` here and
  `27670116110564327421` there (loud); `avg(bigint)` of three `9007199254740993`s was
  `9007199254740992` here and `9007199254740993.0000` there — off by one, **silently**,
  because pglet accumulated in `f64`; `avg(int4)` of `3, 4, 6` was `4.333333333333333`
  here and `4.3333333333333333` there. The declared types diverged for all three
  (`sum(bigint)` `int8` vs `numeric`; `avg` over `int2`/`int4`/`int8` `float8` vs
  `numeric`), so a faithful fixture was red on both instruments and none issued them.

  **The close.** `aggregate_result_type` answers 18.6's `pg_aggregate` types —
  `avg(int2|int4|int8)` and `sum(int8)` `numeric`, `sum(int2|int4)` `int8` — and the
  readers that type an aggregate ask it: both declared-type walks, the certain-type gate
  and the coercion pass's branch reader, so `COALESCE(SUM(b), 0)` over a `bigint` unifies
  its `0` to `numeric` as 18.6 does. `compute_aggregate` picks the exact `sum`/`avg`
  accumulators by the type that rule answers for the argument's walked type, so the value
  is the type the descriptor advertises: integers are added in an `i128` and `numeric`s in
  a `PgNumeric`, and `avg` divides the exact sum by the count through `PgNumeric::div`,
  whose scale is `select_div_scale`'s. The fixtures are `select/agg_avg_integer_*`,
  `select/agg_sum_avg_bigint_exact.sql`, `select/agg_coalesce_sum_bigint*`,
  `spine/fact/orphan_facts_summary*` (the spine's `COALESCE(SUM(size), 0)::bigint` over its
  own `size BIGINT`) and `arithmetic/sum_bigint_exact.sql`, whose declared-type waiver is
  gone.

  **An integer argument takes the `numeric` rows only where its type is certain**, and
  that verdict has **one producer**. The coercion pass records it on the node
  (`Expr::Aggregate`'s `certainty`, a `planner::ArgCertainty`, written by
  `planner::coercion`'s `aggregate_arg_certainty`) while the plan is built, and every
  reader of the aggregate's result type reads it through `aggregate_type_of`: both
  declared-type walks, the certain-type gate, the coercion pass's own branch reader and
  `compute_aggregate`'s accumulator. Certain is what the pass's computed-reach branch reader
  types in the argument **as written**: a column whose type is certain
  (`ColumnScope::column_type_certain` — a base table's, a derived relation's where its own
  definition is certain, below, or a `JOIN … USING` column merged from same-typed
  columns), a literal, a cast, a bound value, a scalar subquery whose own column is
  certain (below), and the computed and fold shapes over those. A `COALESCE`, `CASE` or `ARRAY[…]` that reader types is one every
  branch of which it types — the sets the pass reads at the computed reach and casts to
  their common type — so a certain fold is one the pass resolved, by construction. Elsewhere `avg` stays `float8`
  and `sum(bigint)` `int8`, the answers an argument of unknown type gets. That rule is what
  keeps a guessed `integer` from turning `avg` exact over values that are not integers:
  over `t(i INT, f FLOAT8)` holding `(1, 1.5), (NULL, 2.5), (3, NULL)`,
  `avg(COALESCE(i + 0, f + (SELECT 1))) … WHERE i IS NOT NULL` is `701` `2` and the
  derived-table spelling `701` `2.5`, as on 18.6
  (`select/agg_avg_guessed_integer_argument.sql`); before the rule they answered `1700`
  `2.0000000000000000` and `0A000`.

  **Readers that each derived the verdict disagreed, and a value went out under another
  type's declaration.** Measured before the one producer, each against 18.6 and against the
  answers pglet gave before `avg` over an integer became `numeric`:

  - A grouped query's column through a derived table — `SELECT sum(g) FROM (SELECT b AS g
    FROM t GROUP BY b) s`, and `avg`, `HAVING`, `GROUP BY 1`, a `WITH` query, a nesting —
    declared `numeric` on the simple leg and `bigint`/`double precision` on `Describe` over
    `numeric` bytes, because the planner's descriptor dropped the grouped column's base
    table (row 11) where the executor's kept it; the scalar-subquery wrapper declared
    `double precision` on both over `numeric` bytes. Now `numeric` on both, 18.6's, the
    planner describing a grouped column as the executor does
    (`select/agg_grouped_derived_column*.sql`).
  - A fold over a `date - date` branch — `avg(COALESCE(d - d2, f + 0))` — was `0A000`
    where 18.6 answers `float8` `2.625`, and `numeric` over integer rows: the verdict
    called the fold certain where the coercion pass had not unified it, the branch reader
    typing arithmetic over numeric-category operands only. Now `float8`, 18.6's
    (`select/agg_avg_fold_temporal_branch*.sql`).
  - A `JOIN … USING` merged column under a `COALESCE` default over no rows declared
    `double precision` over `numeric` bytes, the coercion pass calling `k` certain and the
    walkers not. Now `numeric`, 18.6's (`select/agg_avg_using_merged_column*.sql`).

  The guards are `engine_subqueries::every_aggregate_shape_declares_its_values_type_on_both_legs`
  — over a corpus of aggregate shapes, `Describe`'s declared type, the simple leg's, and
  each returned value's own type agree, which no fixture compares —
  `aggregate::sum_tests::the_executor_readers_read_the_recorded_certainty`, and the
  fixtures above.

  **A relation's column is certain where the expression defining it is.** The pass reads
  a `SELECT`'s target-list entries and a `VALUES` list's cells — the expressions that
  define a derived table's, a `WITH` query's, a set operation's and a `VALUES` list's
  columns — as it reads an aggregate's argument: as written, with the same reader
  (`planner::coercion`'s `certain_entry_type`), before it resolves the expression. The
  plan node carries the type it read (`planner::CertainTypes`), the plan describes the
  column certain where that is the type it declares for it (`ColumnDesc::type_certain`),
  and the scope a query builds over the relation reads that. So the one reader decides a
  column at any depth of derivation, and a fold the pass left at a guess is typed at none
  of them (`select/agg_avg_guessed_fold_derived_column.sql`, whose fold reads as typed
  once it is resolved). Until this, a derived relation's column was certain only where its descriptor
  carried a base table, which a projection gives a column it passes through and not one
  it computes. Measured against 18.6 on both legs — `avg` over each was `701` and is
  18.6's `1700`, and `sum` over a `bigint` one was `20` and is `1700`:

  - A derived table's or `WITH` query's column an expression computes or an aggregate
    defines — `(SELECT b + 0 AS x …)`, `(SELECT max(b) AS x … GROUP BY id)`, `count(*)`,
    `sum(i)` — under a column list, unaliased (`avg(max)`), and through a second
    derivation over the first (`select/agg_derived_*.sql`).
  - A `VALUES` column every cell of which the pass typed. An untyped cell — a string
    constant, a `NULL` — takes the column's type, as 18.6 gives it one
    (`select/agg_avg_integer_values.sql`, `select/agg_values_column_*.sql`).
  - A set operation's column where both sides' are certain, an untyped side taking the
    other's type (`select/agg_setop_column*.sql`); and a recursive `WITH` query's where
    both terms' are (`select/agg_recursive_cte_column.sql`).
  - A FROM `unnest` of an array a cast converts — `unnest('{1,4}'::int[])`,
    `unnest($1::int[])` (`select/agg_unnest_cast_array*.sql`).
  - A derived table or `WITH` query passing on a `USING` merge of same-typed columns
    (`select/agg_using_merged_column_derived.sql`).
  - A column a scalar subquery defines, where the subquery's own column is certain — the
    subquery as the entry itself, as an operand of arithmetic or of a function, as a
    branch of a `COALESCE`, a `CASE`, a `greatest`, a `nullif` or an `ARRAY[…]` or an
    operand under one, as a `VALUES` cell and as a set operation's side
    (`select/agg_scalar_subquery_column*.sql`,
    `select/coalesce_operand_subquery_*_sibling.sql`).
  - A column a `date` less a `date` defines, or arithmetic over one: the difference is
    an `integer`, and `avg` over it the exact `numeric`
    (`select/agg_avg_date_difference.sql`).
  - A fold with a `$N` branch: the parameter takes the fold's type
    (`select/agg_avg_param_branch.sql`). Arithmetic with a `$N` or an untyped `NULL` for
    an operand is not one — `avg(i + NULL)` is `701` against 18.6's `1700`, as it was.

  The values followed the type. Over `(VALUES (1), (4)) v(x)`, `round(avg(x))` was `2` and
  is `3`, `round(avg(x), 1)` was pglet's own `0A000` and is `2.5`, and a `HAVING
  round(avg(x)) > 2` kept no group and keeps 18.6's (`select/agg_values_column_round.sql`,
  `select/agg_values_column_having_round.sql`); `sum` over such a `bigint` column past the
  `bigint` range was `22003` and is the exact total; and a fold beside a computed branch
  reads such a column as a typed branch (row 54) — at its own level, in a correlated
  subquery's re-run and in an `UPDATE … FROM`
  (`select/coalesce_derived_column_correlated_sibling.sql`,
  `update/update_from_*_column_fold.sql`). Two verdicts moved with it, each to 18.6's: a
  simple `CASE`'s string label over such a column is typed against it where the
  comparison was `42883` (`select/case_simple_label_*.sql`), and a `text` such column
  beside a computed `integer` branch is `42804` where the fold answered the `text`
  (`select/coalesce_values_text_column_computed_sibling_loud.sql`). What makes a certain column's values
  the type declared for it: an entry the reader typed evaluates to that type, the casts
  the pass wrote into it included; a `VALUES` cell is of its column's type or cast to it;
  the executor casts a set operation's sides, and a recursive query's rows, to the
  column's type; a cast converts its array; and a scalar subquery's value is its
  sub-plan's column's. The guards beside the fixtures:
  `engine_subqueries::a_relations_column_is_certain_where_its_definition_was_typed_as_written`
  and `…::a_relations_column_stays_uncertain_where_its_definition_was_not_typed`, over
  values an exact accumulation and a `float8` one tell apart;
  `planner::tests::a_plans_columns_are_certain_where_the_pass_typed_their_definition`,
  which reads the descriptors; and the three-leg guard above, whose corpus reads each
  such column directly.

  **A scalar subquery is certain where its sub-plan's column is, and the pass's own cast
  over a branch is not read for it.** The verdict on a sub-plan's column is the
  sub-plan's: the record its own run left in its plan, read as the column's descriptor
  says it (`ColumnDesc::type_certain`). The entry reader asks that
  (`planner::coercion`'s `certain_scalar_subquery_type`) and takes no verdict of its own,
  so one taken on a sub-plan's first run — an argument over an enclosing query's column,
  below — is the one every enclosing level reads, however deep. It answers the same
  wherever the subquery stands, and what keeps that the reading the pass's own folds
  take:

  - **The entry is read before the pass types its branch subqueries.** A scalar subquery
    standing as a branch of a fold whose column is not certain is typed for that fold by
    a `Cast` the pass writes over it, to the type its column references resolve to (row
    152) — a guess over a sub-plan whose column is one. Read after that cast is written
    an entry reads the guess as a written cast, measured on that reading: `avg(x)` over
    `COALESCE((SELECT x FROM unnest(ARRAY[1, 2.5]) q0(x) ORDER BY 1 DESC LIMIT 1), 0)`
    is `1700` `3.0000000000000000` against `2.5000000000000000`, where it is `701` `3`,
    as it was before a relation's column could be certain. An aggregate's verdict is
    taken before that cast is written for the same reason, in a `HAVING` and a sort key
    as in the select list.
  - **Under a fold the pass casts every subquery whose column is certain, wherever it
    stands.** The pass resolves a fold with a reader that holds no catalog, to which a
    subquery is typed by a cast and by nothing else. So it writes one, to the certain
    column's type, over each such subquery under a `COALESCE`, a `CASE`, an `ARRAY[…]`
    or a variadic — a branch, an operand of a branch, an aggregate's argument there —
    and the fold the entry reader types is one the pass's own reader types too. It asks
    the sub-plan's record before the reader that types a branch from its column
    references, so a wildcard over a FROM `unnest` of a cast array, which that reader
    declines (row 152), is a typed branch. An enum's column and a `name` one are
    answered at no position, no cast naming either type.

  Before the operand was typed, a fold over one was left at the written reach whatever
  the subquery's column, and where that column had become an exact `numeric` the fold's
  declared type moved with it. Over `t(k, f)` holding `0.1234567890123456789`, `1e300`
  and `2.5`: `SELECT k, COALESCE(-(SELECT avg(x) FROM (VALUES (1), (4)) v(x) WHERE x >
  t.k * 2), t.f + 0) FROM t` was declared `1700` over a `numeric` `-4.0000000000000000`
  and two raw `double precision` values, and `sum` or `avg` over it as a derived column
  `0A000`, where 18.6 answers `701` `-4`, `1e+300`, `2.5` and `701` `-1.5`, `-0.75`; the
  `CASE` spelling with the `double precision` branch leading declared `701` over a
  `numeric` value. Each is 18.6's now, as it had been while that `avg` was `double
  precision` (`select/coalesce_operand_subquery_float_sibling.sql`,
  `select/agg_fold_operand_subquery_derived_column.sql`); and beside an exact sibling
  the fold moved to 18.6's — `COALESCE(i, f + (SELECT 1))` is `701` `3.5` where the
  branch was cast to `integer` and answered `4`, and `COALESCE(-(SELECT avg(x) FROM
  (VALUES (1), (4)) v(x)), b)` beside a `bigint` is `1700` `-2.5000000000000000` where
  it was `20` `-2` (`select/coalesce_operand_subquery_exact_sibling.sql`).

  The guards: `planner::tests::a_scalar_subquery_is_certain_where_its_sub_plans_column_is`
  (each position, over certain sub-plans and over guessed ones),
  `…::a_subquery_operand_under_a_fold_is_typed_where_its_column_is_certain`,
  `…::the_pass_casts_a_subquery_under_a_fold_and_nowhere_else`,
  `…::a_branch_subquery_is_typed_by_its_sub_plans_certain_column`,
  `…::an_aggregates_verdict_does_not_read_the_pass_own_branch_cast`,
  `…::a_scalar_subquery_nest_is_read_in_one_descent_a_level` and
  `…::a_fold_over_a_certain_subquery_nest_does_not_ask_the_branch_reader` (the reading's
  cost over a nest; row 310 is the reader it does not ask), the two engine
  tests above, `select/agg_avg_guessed_fold_scalar_subquery.sql` and
  `select/coalesce_wildcard_subquery_certain_column.sql`.

  **A correlated aggregate is decided on its sub-plan's own run.** The pass runs again over
  a sub-plan once the enclosing levels exist (`planner::correlation`), but the verdict is
  taken once, on the first run, from the argument as written, and kept. An argument over an
  enclosing query's column cannot be typed on that run, so it is decided not certain —
  `avg` `float8`, `sum(bigint)` `int8`, the answers pglet gave before `avg` over an integer
  became `numeric`. Deciding it on the re-run instead was measured to give **third**
  answers: the enclosing level reads the sub-plan's verdict as it chooses its own branch
  types, before that re-run, and a cast written there from the undecided reading stayed
  when the re-run decided otherwise. Over `t(b) = (0)` and `u(b) = (2^53), (1), (1)`,
  `COALESCE((SELECT avg(t.b + u.b) FROM u), 7)` answered `701` `3.0023997515803315e+15` —
  the exact quotient cast to `float8` — against 18.6's `1700` `3002399751580331.3333` and
  the `float8` accumulation's `3.0023997515803305e+15`; and over `u(b)` holding
  `9223372036854775807, 1, -10`, `COALESCE((SELECT sum(t.b + u.b) FROM u), 7)` answered
  `20` `9223372036854775798` where 18.6 answers `1700` and the `int8` accumulation it
  declares refuses `22003`. A re-run that
  re-decided from the argument the first run had resolved read a guess cast as certain too.
  Every correlated shape now answers the `float8`/`int8` accumulation's type and value — the
  bare subquery, a fold, `CASE`, `greatest`, `nullif` or `ARRAY[…]` over it, a set operation
  side — and an argument whose type does not turn on the enclosing column, `avg(length(t.tx)
  + u.i)`, is certain on the first run and `numeric` everywhere
  (`engine_subqueries::a_correlated_aggregate_is_decided_on_its_first_run`, and the guard's
  wrapped-against-bare pairs over that data). No reader may read an undecided verdict:
  `aggregate_type_of` asserts it in debug builds. A **nested** aggregate fired it from
  inside the pass — the producer, reading `avg(avg(i))`'s argument as written, asked the
  type of the inner aggregate the pass had not reached — and a debug build's connection
  died where 18.6 refuses `42803 aggregate function calls cannot be nested`. Now an
  argument holding an aggregate is recorded not certain without asking any reader, and
  the plan-time gate refuses the nesting with 18.6's code and message
  (`select/agg_nested_*`, which `@expect-message` keeps from scoring a dead connection as
  agreement; `coercion::tests::an_argument_holding_an_aggregate_is_not_certain_and_asks_no_reader`).
  It answered `0A000` before. In a top-level `SELECT`, where pglet binds every name the
  statement writes at plan time, the refusal comes after a missing column in the call's
  own argument and in earlier select-list entries, and before the clauses 18.6 transforms
  later, as 18.6 orders them. Elsewhere it outranks errors 18.6 raises first:
  - Over a `FROM` naming a missing relation it outranks 18.6's `42P01` (row 154).
  - Inside a sub-plan or a DML statement it outranks the sub-plan's own unresolved names,
    the enclosing level's errors and the DML target's (row 302).
  - Before trailing junk it outranks 18.6's `42601` (row 128).
  - Before an outer call's signature or an argument operator 18.6 cannot resolve it
    outranks 18.6's `42883` (the residual below).
  And pglet reads every aggregate inside a sub-plan as that sub-plan's, so a pair 18.6
  assigns to different query levels is refused where 18.6 answers (row 303).

  **The residuals, measured on both legs against 18.6:**

  - **An integer argument that is certain on 18.6 and not here — silent.** The measured
    members each answer `701` for `avg` where 18.6 answers `1700`, and `sum` of such a
    `bigint` is `20` against `1700` — `22003` past the `bigint` range, where 18.6 answers
    the exact total — the answers pglet gave before `avg` over an integer became
    `numeric`, so none moved:
    - A relation's column defined by an expression the reader does not type — a window
      function (`row_number() OVER (…)`) — and a `VALUES` column holding such a cell, a
      set operation with such a side.
    - A column a scalar subquery defines where the subquery's own column is a member of
      this list — `(SELECT max(x) FROM unnest(ARRAY[1, 4]) q0(x)) AS x`, `(SELECT max(k)
      FROM t JOIN u8 USING (k)) AS x`, `(SELECT max(t.i + u.i) FROM u) AS x`,
      `(SELECT t.i) AS x` — as the entry and as a branch of a fold
      (`COALESCE((SELECT t.i), 0) AS x`); and a fold with such a subquery for an operand
      under a branch, `COALESCE(i, (SELECT * FROM unnest(ARRAY[1])) + 1) AS x`, or for a
      branch neither reading types, `COALESCE((SELECT * FROM unnest(ARRAY[1, 4]) LIMIT 1),
      0) AS x` (row 152).
    - A catalog view's column: over a three-column table, `avg(ordinal_position)` over
      `information_schema.columns` is `701` `2` against `1700` `2.0000000000000000`,
      directly and through a derived table, and `avg(relnatts)` over `pg_class` `701` `3`
      against `1700`. No virtual relation's descriptor says its column is certain.
    - A FROM `unnest` of an `ARRAY[…]` constructor, `unnest(ARRAY[1, 4])`: no pass
      converts the constructor's elements in a statement's own `FROM`, and its column is
      declared at the first element's type (row 308). An array over an enclosing query's
      column is one too.
    - A bare reference to a `JOIN … USING` column merged from different integer types
      (`int4` beside `int8`), whose claimants disagree and which is declared at the left
      side's type (row 309), and a derived table naming it. The `*` spelling of the same
      merge expands to an expression the pass unifies, and is certain.
    - A recursive `WITH` query's column whose recursive term is an untyped `NULL`; a
      data-modifying `WITH` query's `RETURNING` column, whose descriptor the planner
      builds without a record (row 11); and a no-`FROM` select's set-returning `unnest`,
      `(SELECT unnest(ARRAY[1, 4]) AS x) q`, over a cast array too.
    - An argument over an enclosing query's column — `(SELECT avg(t.i + u.i) FROM u)`,
      and a fold, `CASE`, `greatest`, `nullif`, `ARRAY[…]` or set operation side over it,
      `(SELECT COALESCE(avg(t.i + u.i), 7) FROM u)` and `(SELECT avg(CASE WHEN u.k = '1'
      THEN t.i ELSE 0 END) FROM u)` among them — and a correlated reference to a derived
      relation's column, `(SELECT avg(q.k + u.i) FROM u)` over an outer `q`.

    A cast makes the argument certain whatever the column under it: `avg(x::int)` over
    the `unnest` column is 18.6's (`select/agg_avg_cast_uncertain_column.sql`). The
    members are pinned at these answers by
    `engine_subqueries::a_relations_column_stays_uncertain_where_its_definition_was_not_typed`.
  - **An aggregate the branch reader cannot type is cast to its sibling's type inside a
    fold — loud, and silent in type and in value.** Uncorrelated, the argument is one of
    the uncertain integers above: over `unnest(ARRAY[2000000000, 2000000000]) v(x)`,
    `SELECT CASE WHEN count(*) > 0 THEN sum(x + 0) ELSE max(x) END FROM …` and `SELECT
    greatest(sum(x + 0), max(x)) FROM …` take `max(x)`'s `integer` and are `22003` where
    18.6 answers `4000000000` (each was `0A000` while an aggregate under a `CASE` or a
    variadic was not evaluated, row 89), and the `COALESCE` spelling is `22003` as it was;
    over `unnest(ARRAY[2, 3]) v(x)` the three answer `5` declared `int4` against 18.6's
    `int8`. Over a `VALUES` list, whose column is certain, each is 18.6's `bigint`.
    Correlated, the sub-plan's own run cannot type
    `sum(t.b + u.b)` over the enclosing `t`, so `(SELECT COALESCE(sum(t.b + u.b), 7) FROM
    u)` takes the `7`'s `integer` and casts the aggregate to it: `22003 integer out of
    range` where 18.6 answers `1700` `27021597764223069`. `(SELECT COALESCE(sum(t.i + u.i),
    7) FROM u)` is declared `int4` against 18.6's `int8`, and `max(t.b + u.b)` in the same
    place is `22003`. Over a non-integer enclosing column the cast rounds:
    `(SELECT COALESCE(min(t.n + u.i), 7) FROM u)` over a `numeric` `t.n` answers `23` `11`
    where 18.6 answers `1700` `11.25`, and `max(t.f + u.i)` over a `float8` `t.f` `52`
    against `51.5`. The bare `(SELECT min(t.n + u.i) FROM u)` is declared `int4` over the
    value `11.25`, which a binary client decodes wrong. pglet answered each the same before
    `avg` over an integer became `numeric`; the `avg` spelling answers `float8`, its
    sibling cast to it. The root is the walks' `integer` guess for an operator over an
    enclosing column the sub-plan's scope cannot type.
  - **An exact aggregate beside an enclosing query's column declares its own type, the
    column's unread — silent, and moved over a relation whose column became certain.**
    The same root with the aggregate outside the operator: the walks read an operator
    with one operand they cannot type at the other's type, so `(SELECT avg(u.i) + t.f
    FROM u)` over a `float8` `t.f` is declared `1700` over `double precision` values
    where 18.6 declares `701`, on both legs, and a binary client reads eight bytes as a
    `numeric`. Over a table's column that is the answer pglet gave already. Over a
    `VALUES` list's column, a derived table's, a set operation's or a cast array's
    `unnest` it **moved**: `SELECT k, (SELECT avg(x) + t.f FROM (VALUES (1), (4)) v(x))
    FROM t` was `701`, 18.6's, while that `avg` was `double precision`, and is `1700`
    over the same values; the fold spelling `(SELECT COALESCE(avg(x) + t.f, max(x) + 0)
    FROM …)` likewise, the re-run casting its branches to `double precision` under a
    declaration read off the first one. Over an `integer` `t.i` the same statement
    moved the other way, `1700` `3.5000000000000000` where it was `701` `3.5`. No
    fixture: a faithful one is red.
  - **A correlated `sum` over a non-integer enclosing column is refused — loud, where it
    was silent.** The same guess declares `(SELECT sum(t.n + u.i) FROM u)` over a
    `numeric` `t.n` as `integer`, so `sum` takes the exact `int8` accumulator, which now
    refuses the `numeric` value `0A000` (`sum() argument declared as integer holds a value
    of type numeric`); it used to skip it, answering **NULL** on every row where 18.6
    answers `1700` `93.75`. `sum(t.f + u.i)` over a `float8` is the same (18.6 `94.5`), and
    the order-lines idiom `(SELECT COALESCE(sum(t.n * u.i), 0) FROM u WHERE u.k = t.k)`
    answered `0` where 18.6 answers `12.50` and is now `0A000`. No accumulator can answer
    18.6's value under the guessed `int8` declaration, so the refusal is the right close
    short of typing the enclosing column.
  - **A nested aggregate 18.6 refuses for its outer signature first — loud, wrong code.**
    18.6 resolves the outer call's function and its argument's operators before it checks
    the nesting, so `avg(avg(tx))`, `sum(max(tx))`, `avg(max(d))` and `avg(max(i) || 'x')`
    are `42883 function avg(text) does not exist` (or `sum(text)`, `avg(date)`) there, and
    `avg(max(i) + tx)` and `SELECT tx + 1, avg(avg(i)) FROM t` are `42883 operator does
    not exist`. Each is `42803 aggregate function calls cannot be nested` here, the
    plan-time gate checking no aggregate's operand types; they were the eval-time `0A000`
    before, and the last was the ungrouped column's `42803`.
  - **Row 152's bare branch under `sum` — loud.** An integer value of any width is read
    exactly by the exact accumulators, under an integer or a `numeric` declaration — a
    `numeric` column's stray integers sum to 18.6's total where they used to be skipped —
    and any other value is refused `0A000`. Over `x` in `(1), (NULL), (2)`,
    `sum(COALESCE(x, (SELECT * FROM unnest(ARRAY[1.5::numeric]))))` is declared `integer`
    here (a guess, so `int8` `sum`) and `numeric` on 18.6, which answers `4.5`; it answered
    `3` and is now `0A000`. Its `avg` is `float8` `1.5`, the value 18.6's `numeric` `avg`
    holds. Pinned by
    `aggregate::sum_tests::an_exact_accumulator_refuses_a_value_it_cannot_read_exactly` and
    `engine_subqueries::an_exact_aggregate_reads_or_refuses_an_unconverted_branch_value`.
  - **A function over an uncertain integer's `float8` `avg` — silent.** Where `avg` stays
    `float8` for an argument whose integer type is not certain, a function over it reads
    that `float8`, and one that rounds parts from 18.6's exact `numeric`: over
    `unnest(ARRAY[1, 4]) v(x)`, `round(avg(x))` is `2` here and `3` there (`2.5` rounds to
    even as a `float8`, away from zero as a `numeric`), a derived column over a scalar
    subquery likewise, `HAVING round(avg(x)) > 2` keeps no group where 18.6 keeps one, and
    `round(avg(x), 1)` is pglet's own `0A000` against `2.5`. `avg(x)::int` is the same pair
    by the cast's rounding. A comparison reads that `float8` too: over `unnest(ARRAY[1, 0,
    0]) v(x)`, `avg(x) = 0.3333333333333333`, and `avg(x) = $1` bound that text, are `t`
    here and `f` there, 18.6's `avg` being `0.33333333333333333333`; over the certain
    `unnest('{1,0,0}'::int[])` the `$1` spelling is `f` on both. Row 89's residuals carry
    the measured statements.
- **308 · The coercion pass does not resolve a FROM `unnest`'s array where its query is
  lowered.** 18.6 transforms a function-in-`FROM`'s argument as it transforms any
  expression: an `ARRAY[…]` constructor's elements take their common type, an untyped
  constant among them is converted to it in parse analysis, and the function's column is
  that element type. pglet's pass reaches the select list, the filters, the keys and a
  `VALUES` list's cells (`docs/coercion.md` § Where the plan-time coercion pass reaches),
  and a FROM `unnest`'s arrays only on the correlated re-run over a **sub-plan**. So in a
  statement's own `FROM` the constructor is evaluated as it was written, and its column
  is declared by the walkers' reading of it — the **first element's** type. Measured on
  both legs against 18.6:

  | statement | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT x FROM unnest(ARRAY[1, 2.5]) u(x)` | `23` over `1`, `2.5` | `1700` |
  | `SELECT x FROM unnest(ARRAY[1, 5000000000]) u(x)` | `23` over `5000000000` | `20` |
  | `SELECT x FROM unnest(ARRAY[1, 2.5::float8]) u(x)` | `23` over `2.5` | `701` |
  | `SELECT x FROM unnest(ARRAY[1::smallint, 2]) u(x)` | `21` | `23` |
  | `SELECT x FROM unnest(ARRAY['1', 2]) u(x)` | `25` | `23` |
  | `SELECT x + 1 FROM unnest(ARRAY[1, 2.5]) u(x)` | `23` over `2`, `3.5` | `1700` |
  | `SELECT avg(x) FROM unnest(ARRAY[NULL::int, '7']) u(x)` | `701` `NULL` | `1700` `7.0000000000000000` |
  | `SELECT x + 1 FROM unnest(ARRAY[NULL::int, '7']) u(x)` | `42804 operator + requires numeric operands` | `8` |
  | `SELECT sum(x) FROM unnest(ARRAY[1, 2.5]) u(x)` | `0A000 sum() argument declared as integer holds a value of type numeric` | `3.5` |
  | `SELECT avg(x) FROM unnest(ARRAY['1', 4]) u(x)` | `42883 function avg(text) does not exist` | `2.5000000000000000` |
  | `SELECT nosuch FROM unnest(ARRAY[1, 'x']) u(x)` | `42703` | `22P02`, the array's conversion |

  The value under another type's declaration is row 36's consequence, reached with no
  fold. The controls: a constructor whose elements are of one type (`unnest(ARRAY[1,
  4])`) and an array a cast converts (`unnest(ARRAY[1, 2.5]::numeric[])`) declare 18.6's
  types; and inside a sub-plan the re-run resolves the constructor — `SELECT (SELECT
  max(x) FROM unnest(ARRAY[1, 2.5]) u(x))` is `1700` `2.5` on both.

  **It is why such a column's type is not certain** (row 2): the reader that types the
  constructor answers the common type its elements would be converted to, and nothing
  converts them. `unnest` of an array a cast converts is certain.

  **An aggregate in the array was the loud end of the same gap, and is closed.** In a
  statement's own `FROM` no pass decided an aggregate standing there, so `SELECT * FROM
  unnest(ARRAY[count(*)]) u(x)` was
  pglet's own `0A000` (`aggregate function evaluated where no aggregation computes it`),
  and a debug build's connection died on the assertion that no reader reads an undecided
  verdict (row 2). It is 18.6's `42803 aggregate functions are not allowed in functions in
  FROM` now, raised where the FROM item is parsed — ahead of the item's alias-list count
  and of the select list, as 18.6 orders them
  (`select/unnest_from_aggregate_argument_loud.sql`). It outranks two errors 18.6 raises
  first: a missing relation written earlier in the same `FROM` (`FROM nosuch_t,
  unnest(ARRAY[count(*)]) AS u(x)` is `42P01` there, row 154's class) and an unresolvable
  name in the aggregate's own argument (`max(u.x)`, `42P01` there). And an aggregate 18.6
  assigns to an enclosing query — `SELECT (SELECT sum(x) FROM unnest(ARRAY[max(t.i)])
  u(x)) FROM t`, `3` there — is refused too (row 303).

  No fixture holds the silent members: a faithful one is red. Resolving the array where
  its FROM item is parsed, as a `VALUES` cell is, is the close; measured, it moves every
  row of the table to 18.6's answer, and a constructor holding an element the pass leaves
  at a guess (row 54's open band) from one wrong declaration to another.
- **309 · A `USING` merge of differently-typed columns is declared at the left side's
  type.** 18.6 merges the two columns at their common type, each side converted to it.
  pglet's descriptor for a bare reference to the merged name takes the **left** side's
  type, on both legs, and the merged value is the `COALESCE` of the two sides as they
  are. Over `u4(k INT)` holding `1, 4`, `u8(k BIGINT)` holding `1, 5000000000`, `un(k
  NUMERIC)` and `uf(k FLOAT8)` each holding `1, 2.5`, and `us(k SMALLINT)` holding `1, 7`,
  measured on both legs:

  | statement | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT k FROM u4 JOIN u8 USING (k)` | `23` | `20` |
  | `SELECT k FROM u4 FULL JOIN u8 USING (k)` | `23` over `1`, `4`, `5000000000` | `20` |
  | `SELECT k + 0 FROM u4 FULL JOIN u8 USING (k)` | `23` over `5000000000` | `20` |
  | `SELECT sum(k), avg(k), max(k) FROM u4 FULL JOIN u8 USING (k)` | `20`, `701`, `23` | `1700`, `1700`, `20` |
  | `SELECT k FROM u4 FULL JOIN un USING (k)` | `23` over `2.5` | `1700` |
  | `SELECT k FROM u4 FULL JOIN uf USING (k)` | `23` over `2.5` | `701` |
  | `SELECT k FROM us FULL JOIN u4 USING (k)` | `21` | `23` |
  | `SELECT k FROM (SELECT k FROM u4 FULL JOIN u8 USING (k)) q` | `23` | `20` |

  With the wider side on the left the declaration is 18.6's — `u8 JOIN u4` is `20`, `u4
  FULL JOIN us` `23` — and so is the `*` spelling's, whichever side is wider: `SELECT *
  FROM u4 FULL JOIN u8 USING (k)` declares `20`, the wildcard expanding to the merge's own
  `COALESCE`, which the coercion pass unifies. A value under another type's declaration
  is row 36's consequence, reached with no fold. It is why a bare reference to such a
  merge is not a certain integer (row 2). No fixture holds it: a faithful one is red.
- **3 · Over-rejection where the plan-time coercion pass does not reach.** The pass, the
  operand rulebook it feeds and the positions it covers are `docs/coercion.md`
  § Correct-or-loud and § Where the plan-time coercion pass reaches; the two positions
  this row holds are outside it and fail loud rather than wrong (a third, a FROM-clause
  `unnest`'s array in a statement's own `FROM`, is silent and is row 308's):
  - A **set-op** node or a plan node the walker has no model for — the relations that
    remain un-enumerable.
  - A **set-op's trailing `ORDER BY`**, which has only output columns to resolve
    against. Postgres rejects *any* expression there (`0A000 invalid UNION/INTERSECT/EXCEPT
    ORDER BY clause`, "Only result column names can be used"), so for every set-op
    `ORDER BY` Postgres accepts the pass would
    do nothing; the gap is live only in the region pglet **over-accepts** relative to
    Postgres (`… UNION … ORDER BY -x` sorts here and is rejected there), where it
    currently yields a loud `42883`.

  Both remain a **false rejection, not a wrong answer** (the error direction to
  prefer), and the workaround is an explicit cast: `o.id = '<uuid>'::uuid`.

  The set-op `ORDER BY`'s members, measured. 18.6 refuses a **computed** expression there
  (`0A000 invalid UNION/INTERSECT/EXCEPT ORDER BY clause`) where pglet sorts —
  `… UNION … ORDER BY -a`, `a+0` and `abs(a)` — which is this row's silent half; a
  parenthesized column `(a)` and a cast `a::int` resolve on 18.6, so neither is part of
  it; and the bare literal is refused by both engines. Nothing in the corpus holds either
  half: the loud one is a pglet-only refusal 18.6 answers with a row, and the silent one
  is an over-accept an `@expect-error` cannot express.
- **56 · A query-position `DEFAULT` or `$N` is refused where evaluation reaches it, so a
  statement whose evaluation never does is accepted — wherever the grammar admits the leaf
  as an expression at all.** Postgres refuses both leaves in parse analysis whatever the
  rows and whatever the position — `42601 DEFAULT is not allowed in this context` and
  `42P02 there is no parameter $1`. pglet gates neither at plan time: the `DEFAULT` refusal
  is `executor/expr/eval.rs`'s `Expr::Default` arm and the `$N` one is `EvalEnv::param`'s
  out-of-range error, so each is reached only where its expression is actually evaluated.

  **The clause in the title is load-bearing.** Where pglet's own grammar refuses the
  position outright there is no leaf left to starve, and the statement is loud on both
  engines by a *different* route: `SELECT v FROM e LIMIT DEFAULT` and the `OFFSET DEFAULT`
  spelling are `42601 syntax error: LIMIT must be a constant, parameter, ALL, or NULL`
  here against 18.6's `42601 DEFAULT is not allowed in this context`, and
  `INSERT INTO e (a, v) VALUES (1, DEFAULT || 'x')` is `42601 syntax error: expected ')',
  found '||'` — same class, same SQLSTATE, different fault named. The bound is **per
  leaf**, not per clause: the `$N` at that same `LIMIT` position *is* grammatical
  (`LIMIT $1`, `OFFSET $1`) and takes this row's loud-and-miscoded `22000` where 18.6 says
  `42P02`. And `INSERT INTO e (a, v) VALUES (1, DEFAULT)` is the position where a bare
  `DEFAULT` is legal, accepted by both.

  **Where evaluation goes is a property of the plan, not of the clause**, and *three*
  levels decide it. The first two are below; the third — *what a node scans* — is the one
  that makes this row a **build-profile divergence**, stated after the tables and in full
  in `docs/indexes.md` § The starved-leaf exception.

  Across the plan, an expression is evaluated by the node that owns it, as many times as
  that node iterates — and *what* a node iterates over differs by node. A `WHERE` predicate
  runs per **scanned** row; a `GROUP BY` key per **input** row, in the grouping pass; and
  everything an aggregating query computes above that grouping — its `HAVING`, its
  projection, and its `ORDER BY` keys, which ride the Aggregate's own expression list as
  junk columns (`planner::build_sort`) — runs once per **group**, in the per-group output
  loop, which evaluates `HAVING` first and `continue`s (`executor/query/aggregate.rs`), so
  a group that forms and is then discarded evaluates none of them. An aggregate's
  *argument* is one level further in, evaluated per row **of the group**: skipped both
  where the expression containing it is skipped and where the group is empty — which is how
  an aggregate over zero input rows projects a row and still never reaches the leaf. A
  subquery is a plan of its own, so its leaves follow the same rule against its **own**
  rows — and a correlated one only for the outer rows it is re-run for, so either side can
  starve it. Within an expression, a short-circuiting `CASE`/`COALESCE` evaluates only the
  branch it takes, so a leaf in an untaken branch is skipped over a row that *is*
  projected. `AND`/`OR` short-circuit too, since row 172's close: over `d (a INT)` holding
  `1`, unindexed, `WHERE a = -1 AND DEFAULT IS NULL`, `WHERE false AND DEFAULT IS NULL`
  and `WHERE a = 1 OR DEFAULT IS NULL` count `0`, `0` and `1` here with no error — `42601`
  on 18.6 and, before that close, here — while `WHERE DEFAULT IS NULL AND a = -1`, the leaf
  on the left, stays `42601` on both. **Which branch a short-circuiting cell
  takes can be the row's own value**, which is the one place this row's silence turns on
  the data rather than on a row count: the same `SELECT COALESCE(i, DEFAULT) FROM dt`
  answers over one row of `dt` and is `42601` over the next (the table's short-circuit
  entries). The starving is per *cell operand*, not per cell — a cell that evaluates
  every operand (`ARRAY[…]`, `greatest`/`least`/`nullif`) is loud wherever the leaf is
  **its own operand**, and is silent again as soon as any level on the path to the leaf
  fails to reach it — the cell itself starved from **above** (measured: each of those
  over `… WHERE false`, and one nested in an untaken `CASE` branch), and equally a
  short-circuiting cell **below** it, since a total cell does not make its operands'
  *interiors* total. Measured, each silent where the bare-operand spelling beside it is
  `42601`: `ARRAY[length('ab'), CASE WHEN false THEN DEFAULT ELSE 1 END]` answers
  `{2,1}`, the `greatest`/`least`/`nullif` spellings `2`/`1`/`2`, and
  `ARRAY[length('ab'), COALESCE(1, DEFAULT)]` `{2,1}` — 18.6 `42601` to every one. The
  levels compose along the whole path from the statement to the leaf, outermost first,
  and the leaf is loud only where **every** one of them is reached.

  Measured on both engines and, wherever a declared type is quoted, on **both** wire legs,
  over `t(a INT, v TEXT)` holding one row and an empty `e(a INT, v TEXT)`, neither carrying
  an index. 18.6 answers `42601` to every `DEFAULT` statement in the table, silent and
  control alike (`42P02` to the `$N` row's), and every control is `42601` here too except
  the `$N` one, whose code is wrong (below). Each `pglet` cell reads *result* — row count or
  command tag — then the declared OID. The position list is **not exhaustive** — it is
  every position a probe has been written for, not every one the two gate sites can be
  reached from.

  | position | statement (silent here) | pglet | control (loud on both) |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | projection | `SELECT DEFAULT AS d FROM t WHERE a = -1` | `(0 rows)`; `d` → `25` | `… WHERE a = 1` |

  | …other zero-row shapes | `… FROM e` (empty, no `WHERE`); and over `FROM t WHERE a = -1`, each of `LIMIT 0`, `OFFSET 1`, `ORDER BY 1`, `GROUP BY 1` | `(0 rows)`; `25` each | the same four over the unfiltered `FROM t` — where `LIMIT 0` and `OFFSET 1` project the row and *then* discard it |
  | scalar subquery | `SELECT (SELECT DEFAULT) AS d FROM t WHERE a = -1` | `(0 rows)`; `25` | the no-FROM `SELECT DEFAULT AS d`, and a `VALUES (DEFAULT)` derived table |
  | …correlated | `SELECT (SELECT DEFAULT FROM e WHERE e.a = t.a) AS d FROM t` — starved by the inner scan; `SELECT (SELECT DEFAULT FROM t WHERE t.a = 1) AS d FROM e` — starved by the outer | one row, NULL; `25` — and `(0 rows)`; `25` | the same inner subquery over `t` as the outer (`… AS d FROM t`), and its no-FROM spelling `SELECT (SELECT DEFAULT FROM t WHERE t.a = 1) AS d` |
  | `RETURNING` | `UPDATE t SET v = 'y' WHERE a = -1 RETURNING DEFAULT`; `DELETE FROM t WHERE a = -1 RETURNING DEFAULT` | `UPDATE 0` / `DELETE 0`; `25` | `DELETE FROM t WHERE a = 1 RETURNING DEFAULT` |
  | `WHERE` | `SELECT v FROM e WHERE DEFAULT IS NULL` | `(0 rows)`; `25` | `SELECT v FROM t WHERE DEFAULT IS NULL AND a = -1` — the scan reaches a row. **Only while `a` is unindexed**: under an index it is silent instead, and profile-divergent (below) |
  | `HAVING` | `SELECT count(v) AS c FROM t WHERE a = -1 GROUP BY a HAVING DEFAULT IS NULL` | `(0 rows)`; `20` | the no-`GROUP BY` `SELECT count(v) AS c FROM t WHERE a = -1 HAVING DEFAULT IS NULL`, whose implicit single group forms |
  | `GROUP BY` key | `SELECT count(v) AS c FROM t WHERE a = -1 GROUP BY DEFAULT` | `(0 rows)`; `20` | `SELECT count(v) AS c FROM t GROUP BY DEFAULT` |
  | `ORDER BY` key | `SELECT v FROM t WHERE a = -1 ORDER BY DEFAULT` | `(0 rows)`; `25` | `SELECT v FROM t ORDER BY DEFAULT` |

  | more shapes, same rule | over `FROM t WHERE a = -1`: a `JOIN … ON DEFAULT IS NULL` whose other side is the empty `e`; `DISTINCT ON (DEFAULT)`; a window `PARTITION BY DEFAULT`; the cast `DEFAULT::text`; a CTE or derived table wrapping the projection; `ARRAY[DEFAULT]` | `(0 rows)`; `25` / `25` / `20` / `25` / `25` / `25` / `1009` | each over the unfiltered `FROM t` — and for the join, `FROM t JOIN t AS u ON DEFAULT IS NULL` |
  | **a set-op arm** | `SELECT DEFAULT AS d FROM t WHERE a = -1 UNION SELECT 'q'`, and the `UNION ALL` spelling | **one row**, `'q'`; `25` — the *other* arm's row is returned, so this member is silent and **not** zero-row | `SELECT DEFAULT AS d FROM t UNION SELECT 'q'` |
  | aggregate argument, `count` | `SELECT count(DEFAULT) AS c FROM t WHERE a = -1` | one row, `0`; `20` — likewise `count(DEFAULT + 1)`, and likewise over the empty `e` | `… WHERE a = 1`, and the bare `SELECT count(DEFAULT) AS c FROM t` |
  | aggregate argument, `sum` / `max` | `SELECT sum(DEFAULT) AS s FROM t WHERE a = -1`, and the `max` spelling | one row, NULL; `25` | `… WHERE a = 1` |

This row's own rule at every level, outranking the cell's arms |
  | …decided by the row's own value | `SELECT COALESCE(i, DEFAULT) AS d FROM dt`, over `dt(i)` holding `(7)` and `(NULL)` | `7` filtered to the non-NULL row, `42601` filtered to the NULL one, `(0 rows)` over `WHERE false`, `42601` over both — one statement, three verdicts, decided by the values rather than the row count | `CASE WHEN i IS NULL THEN DEFAULT ELSE length('ab') END` is the polarity twin, silent over the `7` row and `42601` over the NULL one with the leaf **leading** |
  | `$N`, **simple leg only** | `SELECT $1 AS p FROM t WHERE a = -1`; `count($1)` in it; `… GROUP BY a HAVING a = -1` with `count($1)` projected or as the `ORDER BY` key | `(0 rows)`, `25` (and `23` for `$1 + 1`); one row, `0`, `20`; `(0 rows)`, `20` — 18.6 `42P02` to each | `SELECT $1 AS p FROM t WHERE a = 1`, loud but miscoded (below) |
