  The set-op row is the one to read twice, and it is what falsified the first draft of the
  sentence above it: an arm whose own rows are starved contributes no row, but the
  *statement* still answers one — the row the other arm supplies. "Silent" here does not
  mean "zero rows", it means "no error", and the two come apart at the first member that
  unions.

  **The write path starves too, and an `UPDATE … SET` right-hand side is the sharp one** —
  the silent form there is an `UPDATE` the user believes did work. Same rule, a fourth
  table, four more positions:

  | write position | statement (silent here) | pglet | control (loud on both) |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | `INSERT … SELECT` source list | `INSERT INTO e (a, v) SELECT 1, DEFAULT FROM t WHERE a = -1` | `INSERT 0 0` — the leaf sits in the row source rather than in `RETURNING` | `INSERT INTO e (a, v) SELECT 1, DEFAULT FROM t` |
  | **`UPDATE … SET` right-hand side** | `UPDATE t SET v = DEFAULT \|\| 'x' WHERE a = -1`; `UPDATE t SET v = (SELECT DEFAULT) WHERE a = -1` | `UPDATE 0` for both | `UPDATE t SET v = DEFAULT \|\| 'x' WHERE a = 1` |
  | DML `WHERE` over an empty table | `DELETE FROM e WHERE DEFAULT IS NULL`; `UPDATE e SET v = 'q' WHERE DEFAULT IS NULL` | `DELETE 0` / `UPDATE 0` | the same two over `t` |
  | `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`, **no conflict** | `INSERT INTO tk (a, v) VALUES (2, 'y') ON CONFLICT (a) DO UPDATE SET v = DEFAULT \|\| 'x'`, over `tk(a INT UNIQUE, v TEXT)` holding `(1, 'x')`; likewise `… DO UPDATE SET v = 'q' WHERE DEFAULT IS NULL` | `INSERT 0 1` for both — the row is inserted and the action never runs | the same statement with a **conflicting** key `(1, 'y')` |

  That last one adds a **further starvation axis** — an arbitration outcome rather than a
  row count: no conflict arose, so the action's plan node never iterates at all. (One neighbour is loud and unrelated:
  `UPDATE t SET v = (SELECT DEFAULT) WHERE a = 1` is pglet's
  `0A000 not implemented: scalar subquery requires execution context` against 18.6's
  `42601` — a different gap reached from the same spelling.)

  **What a node scans is itself a plan property — and index selection decides it, so this
  row is also a build-profile divergence**: over an ordinary `INT` key under a plain
  B-tree index, a probe that matches no row starves the leaf beside it, so the accelerated
  build answers where the stripped one raises — over `ti(a INT, v TEXT)` with
  `CREATE INDEX ti_a ON ti (a)` holding `(1, 'x')`,
  `SELECT v FROM ti WHERE DEFAULT IS NULL AND a = -1` is `(0 rows)` against `42601`
  stripped and on 18.6, and `42601` on both once the probe *matches*. The measurement — the six-statement table, the
  three routes that reach it (the third carrying no predicate at all), the negative controls
  that bound it, and why it involves no refused type — is `docs/indexes.md` § The
  starved-leaf exception. A simple `UPDATE` / `DELETE` takes an index probe too, but only
  where its residual cannot fail, so the write spelling `UPDATE ti SET v = 'q' WHERE
  DEFAULT IS NULL AND a = -1` is `42601` on both builds
  (`dml_probe/update_default_leaf_ahead_of_probe_loud.sql`; `docs/indexes.md` § A write's
  target rows).
  **An unbound `$N` that is the probe value itself diverges the other way**: over an empty
  `pe(k INT PRIMARY KEY, v TEXT)`, the simple-leg `SELECT v FROM pe WHERE k = $1` and its
  `k = $1::int` spelling are `22000` accelerated and `(0 rows)` stripped, against 18.6's
  `42P02` — there the stripped build is the silent one (same section).

  The polarity control is `SELECT $$x$$ AS p FROM t WHERE a = -1` — `(0 rows)` declaring
  `25` on both engines, so what is measured is the leaf and not the zero-row shape. The
  unbound-`$N` half is simple-query-only because the extended protocol has no spelling
  that leaves a parameter unbound: a `Bind` supplying no value for it is `08P01` on both.
  A `RETURNING` control needs **fresh state per leg**: under `--storage memory` the
  simple leg's own failure leaves the row deleted.

  **On the extended leg the loud half is loud only at `Execute`.** pglet's `Describe`
  answers a full `RowDescription` for every member above, the loud ones included —
  `SELECT DEFAULT AS d FROM t LIMIT 0` describes `d` as `25` and then raises `42601` at
  `Execute` — where 18.6 has already refused one phase earlier, at **`Parse`**. That
  phase is measured and not inferred: a `Parse` + `Sync` carrying **no** `Describe` is
  `42601` on 18.6 and bare `ParseComplete` here, for that statement, for the no-FROM
  `SELECT DEFAULT AS d`, and for `SELECT count(DEFAULT) AS c FROM t GROUP BY a`. So a
  client that only prepares sees no error at all. **This paragraph is one member of
  `EDGES.md` row 60**, which records the same `Execute`-rather-than-`Parse` placement as
  a class over the eval-time gates it enumerates — including the silent half this
  bullet's own *evaluation never reaches the leaf* mechanism produces.

  The loud halves are not both correctly coded: `DEFAULT` raises 18.6's own `42601`,
  while the unbound `$N` raises `22000 execution error: bind message supplies 0
  parameters, but statement requires $1` where 18.6 says `42P02` — a wrong-code
  divergence at every row count, silent only where evaluation misses the leaf.

  **The DDL-time twin of both leaves is gated and agrees**, which is the whole of the
  difference: `CHECK (DEFAULT > 0)` is `42601` and `CHECK (a > $1)` is `42P02` on both
  engines (the binding check in the operand-types bullet above) — refused once per
  statement there, and here by a gate that runs whether or not evaluation would ever
  reach the leaf, which is exactly what the query positions lack. That gate is
  deliberately a **structural walk** rather than a probe, and its own doc gives this
  bullet's reason: a probe reaches such a leaf only when evaluation visits it. The `text`
  OID above is not the declared-type walkers' doing — it is a `Text` substitution at each
  walk's own boundary, the executor walk's and `to_column_desc`'s on the planner side: a
  declared-type fallback, not a gate. (Not re-measured since the declared-type walkers were merged: a sweep
  over this family before and after the merge read byte-identical.) **Not pinnable by a fixture**: 18.6 errors and pglet answers,
  so a value expectation cannot be recorded and `@expect-error` is red — and the
  profile-divergent members (`docs/indexes.md` § The starved-leaf exception) cannot be
  pinned by the `@profile-lock` run either,
  since a fixture can hold one profile's answer or the other's, never both. The right
  close is a plan-time binding arm for both leaves, which reorders statement-level error
  precedence and is therefore its own change. It is the same row-count-dependent family as
  the two bullets below, one leaf-kind further out.


  The starving levels, named together, since the tables above are read one position at a
  time: no row reaching the node that holds the leaf; an untaken `CASE`/`COALESCE` branch
  over a row that *is* projected; a group that never forms, or that `HAVING` discards; an
  `ON CONFLICT` action no conflict reaches; and a scan that index selection shortened. The
  row's own values can decide any of them, so one statement is silent over one row and
  `42601` over the next.
- **4 · An aggregate in `RETURNING` is accepted, and whether it is loud depends on the row
  count.** Postgres rejects it at parse analysis (`42803`, *aggregate functions are not
  allowed in RETURNING*) regardless of rows. pglet has no such gate: measured on 18.6,
  `DELETE … WHERE id = 999 RETURNING count(*)` is accepted here and answers `(0 rows)`,
  while the same statement over a **matching** row raises `0A000 aggregate function
  evaluated where no aggregation computes it` from the evaluator. So the zero-row path is the
  silent one, and it is the reverse of the shape the plan-time `RETURNING` binding gate
  removed — that gate decides once per statement, this one is decided per row and only
  when there is a row. The two sit in the same clause and are different gates; do not
  read the binding rule's row-count independence as covering this.
- **5 · An ill-typed constant in an `UPDATE … SET` right-hand side is loud only when a row
  matches.** `lower_update` coerces each `SET` RHS with `coerce_to_type`, which inserts
  a cast node and does not fold it, so the `22P02` comes from evaluating that cast per
  row. Measured: `UPDATE amb_t SET id = 'notanint' WHERE id = 999` reports `UPDATE 0`
  here and `22P02` on 18.6; over a **matching** row both say `22P02`. The same shape in
  the neighbouring constant positions agrees at zero rows — `UPDATE … WHERE id =
  'notanint'`, `DELETE … WHERE id = 'notanint'`, `INSERT … VALUES ('notanint', …)` are
  all `22P02` on both with no row in sight — and so is the explicit-cast spelling
  `SET id = 'notanint'::int`, which is what identifies the unfolded implicit cast as the
  cause rather than the clause. It is the same row-count-dependent shape as the
  `RETURNING` aggregate above, in the other DML clause. **The boundary is the word
  *constant*, and the bullet below is what lies one step outside it** — a non-constant
  RHS of the wrong type is not a timing divergence at all.

  **A `SET` list that also repeats a target column answers that repeat's `42601`
  instead** — `UPDATE t SET a = 'notanint', a = 2` is `22P02` on 18.6 and `42601` here at
  either row count. The two gates stand a phase apart on each engine and in opposite
  directions: pglet's duplicate refusal sits where 18.6's rewriter does while this
  conversion sits later than 18.6's. What that gave up was itself row-count-dependent —
  over a matching row the repeat answered this same `22P02`, and over no row it reported
  `UPDATE 0` and wrote nothing (row 38).

  The `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET` route is **not** this row's subject, and what the
  `42601` replaced there depends on the key. `INSERT INTO u VALUES (…) ON CONFLICT (a) DO
  UPDATE SET b = 'notanint', b = 2` is the same `22P02`-there / `42601`-here pair over a
  free key and over a conflicting one, but the two arrived at it from opposite sides: over
  a **free** key the pre-gate build reported success and **inserted the row**, so the
  `42601` replaced a silent write; over a **conflicting** one it evaluated the action and
  answered `22P02`, so the `42601` replaced an **agreement**. Measured on both builds.
  That second half is the residual `docs/names.md` § What the refusals do not carry
  records, and it is wider than this route — the same `22P02` / `42601` pair stands
  where the ill-typed
  constant is a **row-source cell** rather than a `SET` right-hand side, and the `42703`
  pair stands where the cell is an unknown name.

  **The order the right-hand sides run in reaches it too.** 18.6 converts the constant in
  parse analysis, before any right-hand side is evaluated; pglet converts it when its
  column's turn comes in the column order it runs the list in (row 244), so an earlier
  column's evaluation error answers in its place. Measured on the native server over
  `a INT, b INT` holding `(1, 0)`: `UPDATE t SET a = a / b, b = 'notanint'` and `UPDATE t
  SET b = 'notanint', a = a / b` are both `22P02` on 18.6 and `22012` here, and `UPDATE t
  SET b = a / b, a = 'notanint'` is `22P02` on both. The same holds for a right-hand side
  18.6's planner folds, which is row 60's `1/0` mechanism rather than a conversion: `SET b
  = 2147483647 + 1, a = a / b` is `22003` there and `22012` here, and over no row `UPDATE t
  SET b = 2147483647 + 1` is `22003` there and `UPDATE 0` here — this row's zero-row
  shape, reached by the fold. Row 244's bullet carries the measured members of the
  mechanism and which of them the column order moved; the `ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET
  b = 'notanint', a = t.a / t.b` spelling over a conflicting key answers as the `UPDATE`
  does.
- **~~6~~ · Closed — An assignment now takes `pg_cast`'s castcontext, and what is left of the class is
  two residuals and one refuted prediction.** Postgres's `transformAssignedExpr`
  coerces every `INSERT` cell, `UPDATE … SET` right-hand side, `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET` right-hand side and
  `INSERT … SELECT` source column with `COERCION_ASSIGNMENT` and raises
  `42804 column "x" is of type A but expression is of type B` when
  `find_coercion_pathway` finds none. pglet had no castcontext at all — a non-`Column`
  right-hand side was wrapped in a plan-time `Cast` and a `Column` one passed through to
  the store finalizer, which coerced whatever it was handed — so the whole class was
  silent. All nine members recorded here are now `42804` on both engines, re-measured
  over the same tables (`ct(i INT, t TEXT, u UUID, j JSONB, b BOOL, n NUMERIC, d DATE,
  ts TIMESTAMP)` and friends): `UPDATE cw SET id = s` and its `INSERT INTO cw (id)
  SELECT s FROM cw` twin, `UPDATE ct SET i = b`, `UPDATE cv SET j = s` and
  `SET u = s` in **both** their parseable and unparseable spellings — the pair that used
  to make loudness depend on the data rather than the statement — `UPDATE ct SET u = t`,
  `UPDATE ct SET d = i`, and the zero-row `UPDATE cz SET id = s WHERE id = 999`. The
  controls still agree and are what identify castcontext rather than "different type":
  `SET t = i`, `SET t = u`, `SET t = j` (the string-target I/O fallback), `SET i = n`
  (a `numeric → int4` assignment cast, still rounding `9.5` to `10`) and `SET d = ts`
  all succeed on both engines with the same value.

  The rule lives in `planner::legality`'s `assignment_legality`, driven at the four
  lowering sites by two routes: `planner::coercion`'s `check_assignment` at three of them,
  and a direct call from `check_insert_select_assignments` for `INSERT … SELECT`. Its accepted set
  is four rules read off a measured 441-pair matrix (see the `int ↔ bool` bullet above
  and `the_four_rules_reproduce_the_measured_matrix`). What is left:

  - **Not left: a client-declared parameter type is compared with the target, and an
    undeclared one is not, and must not be.** The gate reads a bare `Expr::Parameter` as untyped and skips
    it: pglet infers an undeclared `$N`'s type **from** the assignment target, so it
    resolves to exactly the column type and is ordinary SQL on both engines (measured —
    `PREPARE p AS INSERT INTO t (b) VALUES ($1)` is accepted on 18.6, and the pglet
    spelling is an extended-protocol `Parse` with no parameter OIDs). A `$N` whose type the
    client declared at `Parse` is read as a cast to that type (row 146), so the gate sees
    it typed: over a `BOOL` `b`, `INSERT INTO t (b) VALUES ($1)`, `UPDATE t SET b = $1` and
    `INSERT INTO t (b) SELECT $1`, each with `$1` declared `int4`, are `42804` at `Parse` on
    both engines (measured over a raw extended-protocol client). pglet has no SQL-level
    `PREPARE` with a type list, so that `Parse` is the only route to the declared shape.
  - *(A predicted residual that measurement refuted, kept because the prediction is the
    obvious one.* `transformValuesClause` unifies each **column** across all rows before
    coercing, so a multi-row `VALUES` looked like it must report the leftmost bad column
    where pglet's cell-by-cell row-major walk reports the first bad cell. It does not:
    over `mz(b BOOL, i INT, u UUID)`, `VALUES ('t', 5, 5), (1, 5, 't')` is `"u"` on
    **both** engines — the arrangement that separates the two orders, since column `b`
    is also ill-typed and to the left — its exact reverse is `"b"` on both, and four
    neighbouring arrangements agree too. Re-measured independently; do not re-derive
    this one from the C source without measuring it.)* What the column-major unification
    **does** change is *which kind* of error wins when one column's unknown resolves to
    the target and fails its **input** function: `VALUES ('t', 5, 't'), (1, 5, 5)` is
    18.6's `22P02 invalid input syntax for type uuid: "t"` and pglet's
    `42804 column "b" …`, because there the `uuid` column's two cells unify to unknown
    and are parsed, while pglet reaches row 1 column 1 first. Loud on both, and a
    different divergence from the predicted one.
  - **An `ENUM` target, five evaluator-only pairs, and a right-hand side subquery over a
    missing relation** — the three residuals recorded in full under the `int ↔ bool`
    bullet in this file. The `INSERT … SELECT`-behind-a-wrapper residual
    that stood here is **closed**: the source-type walk descends the nodes that resolve
    no target-list entry (`Limit`, `Filter`, `JunkFilter`, `DistinctOn`) and marks the
    **positions** the claiming clauses name, which are recorded at the lowering
    (`Plan::ResolvedTargets`, on `Plan::Sort` and `Plan::Aggregate`) because both clauses
    rewrite the key into the entry it named and two entries can be equal. `Distinct`
    stays marked at the walk — it claims every entry, so no position question arises.
    Measured both ways over a dozen shapes and pinned by
    `tests/fixtures/insert/assignment_cast_select_{limit,group_by_*,having,distinct*,
    sort_*,window,set_op}*.sql`.

    Two things the first version of that walk got wrong, closed here, and they are not
    the same kind of defect. It read the claims off the finished plan by **expression
    equality**, which marks every entry equal to the substituted key: that is an
    over-**rejection** and only that — `INSERT INTO ir (t, b) SELECT 't', 't' FROM s
    GROUP BY 1` was `42804` where 18.6 accepts, while the `GROUP BY 2` mirror it also
    over-marked happens to be the answer 18.6 gives. (The *repair* is where the silent
    direction lives: a first-match scan fixes the first statement and accepts the
    second, writing a row 18.6 refuses. Only the position gets both, which is why the
    two fixtures are a pair.) The second is a silent write outright: its
    `Plan::Sort` arm never fired in the **sort-below-projection** layout `build_sort`
    chooses whenever a key reads a base column the output drops, because there the
    `Sort` sits *under* the `Project` the walk stops at: five spellings measured —
    `SELECT '5' FROM s ORDER BY 1, n` into an `INT`, `DISTINCT ON (1) 't' … ORDER BY 1,
    n`, `'t' AS z … ORDER BY z, n`, a join source with `ORDER BY 1, a.n`, and
    `ORDER BY n+0, 1` — each stored rows where 18.6 answers `42804`.

- **~~243~~ · Closed — Every right-hand side of one `SET` list reads the target row, never
  an earlier assignment's result.** 18.6 projects a `SET` list's right-hand sides from one
  input tuple, so each reads that tuple, and the new row is assembled from those values
  before it is checked, written and returned. pglet's assignment loop wrote each value into the row
  it went on reading, so a right-hand side read the result of any assignment to its left.
  Silent, and it wrote. Measured before the repair on the native server (default build,
  in-memory B+tree) against 18.6, each statement over a fresh table:

  | statement | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | over `(10, 0)`: `UPDATE r SET a = a + 1, b = a` | `11`, `11` | `11`, `10` |
  | over `(10, 11)`: `UPDATE r SET a = b, b = a` | `11`, `11` | `11`, `10` |
  | over `(1, 0)` under `a INT DEFAULT 7`: `SET a = DEFAULT, b = a` | `7`, `7` | `7`, `1` |
  | over `(10, 0)` under `CHECK (a <> b)`: `SET a = a + 1, b = a` | `23514` | `UPDATE 1`, `11`, `10` |
  | over `(1, 2)` under `CHECK (a <> b)`: `SET a = b, b = a + 1` | `UPDATE 1`, `2`, `3` | `23514` |
  | over `(1, 2, 3)`: `SET a = b, b = c, c = a` | `2`, `3`, `2` | `2`, `3`, `1` |
  | over `(1, 10, 0)` and a source `(1, 100)`: `UPDATE t SET a = s.v, b = a + s.v FROM s WHERE s.id = t.id` | `100`, `200` | `100`, `110` |
  | over `(1, 10, 0)`: `INSERT … VALUES (1, 50, 60) ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET a = t.a + 1, b = t.a`, with and without `WHERE t.a = 10` | `11`, `11` | `11`, `10` |
  | over `(1, 10, 0)`: `… DO UPDATE SET a = excluded.a, b = t.a + excluded.b`, inserting `(1, 50, 60)` | `50`, `110` | `50`, `70` |
  | over `(1, 2), (3, 4)`: `WITH u AS (UPDATE w SET a = b, b = a RETURNING *) SELECT * FROM u`, and the same `UPDATE` in a `DO` body | `(2, 2), (4, 4)` | `(2, 1), (4, 3)` |
  | over `k INT, k2 INT UNIQUE` holding `(1, 2), (3, 1)`: `UPDATE t SET k = k2, k2 = k` | `UPDATE 2` | `23505` on `k2` |
  | over `k INT PRIMARY KEY, k2 INT` holding `(1, 10), (2, 20)`: the same swap | `(10, 10), (20, 20)` | `(10, 1), (20, 2)` |

  The first key swap is one where the old-row reading decides a uniqueness verdict, and the
  second writes different values under a verdict both readings share. 18.6 checks a
  non-deferrable unique index as each row is written, so a swap's verdict depends on the
  order the statement visits the rows as well as on what the right-hand sides read. Every
  table in this bullet is freshly inserted, and over those the two engines' verdicts agree
  after the repair: a swap is refused where a new key collides with a row not yet updated
  and accepted where the earlier row has already moved off it. Over `k INT UNIQUE` holding
  `(1, 2), (2, 1)` the swap is `23505` on both engines, before the repair and after — the
  in-place reading collides at the same row — and over `(2, 3), (1, 2)` it is accepted on
  both, the values differing before. Where an earlier `UPDATE` has made the two engines
  visit the rows in different orders, their verdicts part whatever the right-hand sides
  read (row 246).

  **What closed it.** `executor::dml`'s `assign_row` (the `UPDATE` and `UPDATE … FROM`
  paths) and `apply_do_update` (the `DO UPDATE` path) evaluate every right-hand side against
  the target row the scan or the conflict probe returned and write each value into a
  separate copy, which is the row then checked, written and projected. For a `DO UPDATE`
  that target row is the row as it stood before the statement: a probe that lands on a row
  the statement itself inserted or updated is refused `21000` (row 247). A `DO UPDATE …
  WHERE` already read the existing row, ahead of the
  `SET` list, and still does (read from the code; a mutant evaluating it over the assembled
  row reddens `insert/on_conflict_do_update_where_reads_the_existing_row.sql`). Measured
  after the repair against 18.6 on the native server, with each statement above answering as
  18.6 does on the in-memory B+tree, a `--data-dir` store and `--storage memory` (default
  build), and the fixtures green on the default and `--no-default-features` builds; a `DO`
  body reaches the same executor (`update/set_do_block_reads_the_old_row.sql`). The swap's
  index and heap agree after it: a read through the key answers the swapped row
  (`update/set_swap_primary_key_index_read.sql`, `@profile-lock`). The wasm build was not
  measured.

  Not reachable through this rule: a scalar subquery correlated to the target row, which
  pglet refuses in a `SET` right-hand side (`0A000`, row 89); and a multiple-column or
  subscripted target, which it does not parse (row 245).

- **~~244~~ · Closed — 18.6's rewriter rebuilds a `SET` list in column order, and its
  right-hand sides run in that order.** `rewriteTargetListIU` (`rewrite/rewriteHandler.c`)
  re-forms an `UPDATE`'s target list, and an `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`'s `SET` list, in
  attribute order, so of two right-hand sides failing at evaluation the earlier *column*'s
  error answers, and two `DEFAULT`s drawing on one sequence draw in column order. pglet ran
  them in the order the list was written. Measured before the repair on the native server
  against 18.6: over `a INT, b INT` holding `(1, 0)`, `UPDATE t SET b = a / b, a = (a::text
  || 'x')::int` was `22012` here and is `22P02` there (the written-first order agrees:
  `22P02` on both); over `a` and `b` both `DEFAULT nextval('s')` with the sequence at `2`,
  `UPDATE t SET b = DEFAULT, a = DEFAULT` gave `a` `4` and `b` `3` here and `3` and `4`
  there — silent, and it writes.

  **What closed it.** `execute_update` and `apply_do_update` put the resolved assignments
  in column order before evaluating any right-hand side (`executor::dml`'s
  `in_column_order`), keeping written order among repeats of one column. Both statements
  above, and their `DO UPDATE`
  spellings, now answer as 18.6 does, pinned by `update/set_evaluates_in_column_order_loud.sql`,
  `update/set_default_draws_in_column_order.sql` and their two `insert/on_conflict_do_update_*`
  twins, measured on the native server with the `DO UPDATE` pair answering `22012` and
  `4`, `3` before the repair. What this orders is evaluation; a `SET` right-hand side's
  plan-time assignment errors are row 6's subject.

  **The residual: an error 18.6 raises before execution.** A right-hand side whose error
  18.6 raises before any right-hand side is evaluated — a literal's conversion to the
  column's type in parse analysis (row 5), or the planner's folding of an immutable
  expression over constants (row 60's `1/0` mechanism) — answers there whatever its column.
  Where pglet raises the same error at evaluation, it does so when that column's turn comes,
  so where an earlier column's right-hand side fails at evaluation, its error answers here
  and the constant's there. Not every such right-hand side waits for evaluation here: a string literal read directly by a cast to a scalar type — `'notanint'::int`, `CAST('notanint' AS int)`, `int4 'notanint'` — is converted before any row, and agrees; a cast of a cast's result (`'notanint'::varchar::int`, `'2147483648'::bigint::int`), a typmod (`'12345'::numeric(3,1)`) and an enum target (`'nope'::m`) wait, and diverge as the bare literal does. The written
  order diverged wherever the constant was written after the failing right-hand side; the
  column order diverges wherever its column comes after it, so the repair moved some members
  into agreement and others out of it. Where the earlier column fails, the order decides which of two errors answers, and both engines are loud. Where the earlier column is a `DEFAULT` drawing on a sequence, it decides whether the draw runs before the constant's error: 18.6 draws nothing, pglet draws, and both answer the same error — silent, the sequence advanced here and not there: over `a INT DEFAULT nextval('s'), b INT` holding `(1, 0)`, `UPDATE t SET b = 'notanint', a = DEFAULT` is `22P02` on both and the next `nextval('s')` is `2` here, `1` on 18.6; the written order agreed. Measured on the native server (default and
  `--no-default-features` builds answering alike) against 18.6, each statement over a fresh
  table holding `(1, 0)` in `a INT, b INT` unless the line says otherwise; the members are
  examples of the mechanism, not its list:

  | statement | written order, before the repair | column order | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SET b = 'notanint', a = a / b` | `22P02` | `22012` | `22P02` |
  | `SET b = 2147483647 + 1, a = a / b` | `22003` | `22012` | `22003` |
  | over `(2147483647, 1)`: `SET b = 1 / 0, a = a + b` | `22012` | `22003` | `22012` |
  | a `numeric(3,1)` `s` declared after `b`: `SET s = 12345, a = a / b` | `22003` | `22012` | `22003` |
  | a column `e` of an enum `m` (`'x'`, `'y'`) declared after `b`: `SET e = 'nope', a = a / b`, and the `e = 'nope'::m` spelling | `22P02` | `22012` | `22P02` |
  | a `varchar(2)` `s` declared after `b`: `SET s = 'long', a = a / b` | `22001` | `22012` | `22001` |
  | over `(1, 1, 0)` in `t (id INT PRIMARY KEY, a INT, b INT)`: `INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 5, 5) ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET b = 'notanint', a = t.a / t.b`, and the `b = 2147483647 + 1` spelling | `22P02`, `22003` | `22012`, `22012` | `22P02`, `22003` |
  | over `(1, 2147483647, 1)` in the same table: `… DO UPDATE SET b = 1 / 0, a = t.a + t.b` | `22012` | `22003` | `22012` |
  | `SET a = a / b, b = 'notanint'`, and `SET a = a / b, b = 2147483647 + 1` | `22012`, `22012` | `22012`, `22012` | `22P02`, `22003` |
  | `SET b = a / b, a = 'notanint'`, and `SET b = a / b, a = 2147483647 + 1` | `22012`, `22012` | `22P02`, `22003` | `22P02`, `22003` |
  | a cast of a cast's result or a typmod'd cast: `SET b = 'notanint'::varchar::int, a = a / b`, `SET b = '2147483648'::bigint::int, a = a / b`, and a `numeric(3,1)` `n` declared after `b`: `SET n = '12345'::numeric(3,1), a = a / b` | `22P02`, `22003`, `22003` | `22012`, `22012`, `22012` | `22P02`, `22003`, `22003` |
  | over `(1, 0)` in `a INT DEFAULT nextval('s'), b INT`: `SET b = 'notanint', a = DEFAULT`, then `SELECT nextval('s')` | `22P02`, `1` | `22P02`, `2` | `22P02`, `1` |

  The last two lines are the members the column order did not move away: the first diverges
  under either order, the second agrees only under the column order. The controls: `SET b =
  'notanint'::int, a = a / b` and `SET b = int4 'notanint', a = a / b` are `22P02` on both
  engines under either order, and `UPDATE t SET b = 'notanint'::int` over no row is `22P02`
  on both; and two right-hand sides both failing at evaluation on both engines: over `(1,
  1)`, `SET b = b + 2147483647, a = a / (b - 1)` is `22012` here and there, and was `22003`
  before the repair. Closing the residual means converting and folding constants before
  execution (rows 5 and 60).

- **246 · A per-row unique verdict follows the order a statement visits the rows, and the two engines' orders part once 18.6's heap order stops being insertion order — after an `UPDATE`, for one.** 18.6 checks a non-deferrable unique index
  as each row's new version is written, so a multi-row `UPDATE` whose new keys collide
  transiently is refused or accepted by the order the statement visits the rows. That order
  is 18.6's plan's: a sequential scan reads heap order, and an `UPDATE` writes a row's new
  version to a new slot — over `k INT UNIQUE` holding `(2), (1)`, after `UPDATE t SET k = k
  WHERE k = 2` the `ctid`s read `(0,2)` for `1` and `(0,3)` for `2`, so the updated row is
  read last. pglet's order was not moved by the prior `UPDATE` in any shape measured here:
  over `(1), (3)`, after `UPDATE t SET k = k WHERE k = 1`, `SELECT k FROM t` answers `1, 3`
  here and `3, 1` on 18.6. Measured on
  the native server, the default and `--no-default-features` builds answering alike, against
  18.6, each over a fresh table and the prior `UPDATE` the line names; the members are
  examples of the mechanism, not its list:

  | table, then the prior `UPDATE` | statement | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | `k INT UNIQUE` holding `(2), (1)`; `SET k = k WHERE k = 2` | `UPDATE t SET k = k + 1` | `UPDATE 2`, `2, 3` | `23505` |
  | the same under `k INT PRIMARY KEY` | the same | `UPDATE 2`, `2, 3` | `23505` |
  | `k INT UNIQUE, k2 INT` holding `(2, 3), (1, 2)`; `SET k2 = k2 WHERE k = 2` | `UPDATE t SET k = k2, k2 = k` | `UPDATE 2`, `(2, 1), (3, 2)` | `23505` |
  | `k INT UNIQUE` holding `(2), (1)`; `SET k = 20 WHERE k = 2`, then `SET k = 2 WHERE k = 20` | `UPDATE t SET k = k + 1 WHERE k > 0` — a bitmap heap scan on 18.6 | `UPDATE 2` | `23505` |
  | `k INT UNIQUE` holding `(1), (3)`; `SET k = k WHERE k = 1` | `UPDATE t SET k = k + 2` | `23505` | `UPDATE 2`, `3, 5` |
  | `k INT UNIQUE, k2 INT` holding `(1, 2), (2, 3)`; `SET k2 = k2 WHERE k = 1` | `UPDATE t SET k = k2, k2 = k` | `23505` | `UPDATE 2`, `(2, 1), (3, 2)` |

  **Silent, and it writes**, where pglet accepts: the table ends holding keys 18.6 refused
  to write. Loud where pglet refuses a statement 18.6 accepts. The build before the old-row
  repair (row 243) gives every verdict above as this one does; the accepted swap's values
  differ there, by that row.

  The controls. Over freshly inserted rows the two orders coincide and the verdicts agree:
  `(1), (2)` under `SET k = k + 1` is `23505` on both, `(2), (1)` is `UPDATE 2` on both, and
  the swap over `(2, 3), (1, 2)` is `UPDATE 2` on both with the same values. And a prior
  `UPDATE` does not always part them, because 18.6's plan decides its order: over `(2), (1)`
  after `SET k = k WHERE k = 2` — a heap-only update on 18.6 (`n_tup_hot_upd` `1`) —
  `UPDATE t SET k = k + 1 WHERE k > 0` runs as a bitmap heap scan there and is `UPDATE 2` on
  both, where the same statement without the `WHERE` is the table's first line. The fourth
  line's prior `UPDATE`s change the key and put it back instead (the row ends at `ctid`
  `(0,4)`), and there the bitmap heap scan is refused as the sequential scan is.

  An `UPDATE` is one way 18.6's heap order leaves insertion order, not the only one: over `k INT
  UNIQUE` holding `(1), (5)`, after `DELETE … WHERE k = 1`, a `VACUUM` and `INSERT … (2)`, 18.6 reads `2, 5` and
  refuses `UPDATE t SET k = k + 3` `23505`, where pglet reads `5, 2` and answers `UPDATE 2`. pglet refuses `VACUUM`
  itself; 18.6's autovacuum reaches the same state with no statement.

  Through the npm package the prior write need not touch the key, nor be an `UPDATE`: over
  `k INT UNIQUE, note TEXT` inserted `(3), (2), (1)`, after `UPDATE t SET note = 'b' WHERE k
  = 3`, or after `INSERT … VALUES (3, 'z') ON CONFLICT (k) DO UPDATE SET note = 'b'`,
  `UPDATE t SET k = k + 1` is `UPDATE 3` here, writing `2, 3, 4`, and `23505` on 18.6; over
  the same table fresh, both answer `UPDATE 3`.

  No fixture: a faithful one is red, pglet's verdict being the other one.

- **~~247~~ · Closed — One `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` statement meeting its own row a second time
  is refused.** 18.6 refuses a `DO UPDATE` whose conflicting row the same statement already
  inserted or updated — `21000 ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command cannot affect row a second
  time`, *Ensure that no rows proposed for insertion within the same command have duplicate
  constrained values* — and nothing the statement did stands. Here the second proposal of a
  key finds the row the first proposal inserted or updated, and its `SET` list reads that
  write: the right-hand sides below read `11` and `5`, the first proposal's values. Measured
  on the native server, the default and `--no-default-features` builds answering alike,
  against 18.6, each over a fresh `t (id INT PRIMARY KEY, a INT, b INT)` unless the line says
  otherwise; the members are examples, not a list:

  | statement | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | over `(1, 10, 0)`: `INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 0, 0), (1, 0, 0) ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET a = t.a + 1, b = t.a RETURNING *` | `(1, 11, 10), (1, 12, 11)`; the table holds `(1, 12, 11)` | `21000`; the table holds `(1, 10, 0)` |
  | empty: `INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 5, 0), (1, 0, 0) ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET a = t.a + 1, b = t.a RETURNING *` — the first proposal inserts | `(1, 5, 0), (1, 6, 5)`, `INSERT 0 2` | `21000`; the table is empty |
  | over `(1, 10, 0)` under `id INT UNIQUE`: `INSERT INTO t SELECT v, w, 0 FROM (VALUES (1, 1), (1, 2)) s(v, w) ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET a = t.a + excluded.a, b = t.a RETURNING *` | `(1, 11, 10), (1, 13, 11)` | `21000` |
  | over `(1, 10)` in `t (id INT PRIMARY KEY, a INT)`: `INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 1), (1, 2) ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET a = excluded.a WHERE excluded.a = 1` — the second proposal's `WHERE` is false | `INSERT 0 1`; the table holds `(1, 1)` | `21000`; the table holds `(1, 10)` |

  **Silent, and it writes.** The build before the old-row repair (row 243) writes twice as
  well, its right-hand sides reading in place. The controls agree: `(1, 1), (1, 2)` under
  `DO NOTHING`, into an empty `t (id INT PRIMARY KEY, a INT)`, insert the first and skip the
  second on both (`INSERT 0 1`, `(1, 1)`); and over `(1, 10)`, `INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 1),
  (1, 2) ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET a = excluded.a WHERE t.a < 0`, which neither
  proposal satisfies, is `INSERT 0 0` on both. The table above is the record before the
  repair.

  **What closed it.** `executor::dml`'s `execute_insert` keeps, for a `DO UPDATE` statement,
  the row ids it has inserted and rewritten, and a conflict probe that lands on one of them
  is `Error::OnConflictRowAffectedTwice` — 18.6's message and hint, no `s`/`t`/`n` — before
  the action's `WHERE` is read, as 18.6's `ExecOnConflictUpdate` (the PostgreSQL source's
  `ExecOnConflictLockRow`) refuses it on locking the row.
  The test is the row's identity, not its key, and the set is the statement's alone.
  Measured after the repair against 18.6 on the native server (in-memory B+tree), each
  answering as 18.6 does: the four members above are `21000` and write nothing; so is a
  second proposal whose `WHERE` would divide by zero (`21000`, not `22012`); a first
  proposal that moves the row from key 1 to key 11 and a second naming key 11 is `21000`,
  while a second naming key 1 again inserts beside the moved row; a first proposal whose
  `WHERE` is false leaves the row for the second to update; a row an earlier statement of
  the same block wrote is updated; and a second proposal's own `NULL` in a `NOT NULL`
  column is `23502` ahead of the `21000`. Inside a block the refusal aborts it (`25P02`
  after), and the `ROLLBACK` restores the block's start. The fixtures
  (`insert/on_conflict_do_update_same_row_twice*.sql`, `…_moved_row_*.sql`,
  `…_first_proposal_where_false_then_updates.sql`, `…_where_neither_proposal_holds.sql`,
  `…_row_an_earlier_statement_wrote.sql`) are `@profile-lock` and green on both build
  profiles; the state a refusal leaves is `crates/pglet/tests/on_conflict_row_affected_twice.rs`
  on the in-memory B+tree and a file store, and the npm package's refusal, its hint and the
  table it leaves are pinned in `tests-web/npm/dx_test.ts` and, through drizzle's
  `onConflictDoUpdate`, `tests-web/npm/drizzle_test.ts`. On `--storage memory` the refusal is
  the same `21000` and the statement's earlier writes stand — over `(1, 'a')`, `VALUES (1,
  'x'), (2, 'n'), (1, 'y')` leaves `(1, 'x')`, `(2, 'n')` — the partial effects of row 40.

- **245 · A `SET` target pglet's parser does not read.** The `UPDATE` and `DO UPDATE` `SET`
  grammars here take a bare column name before each `=`, so a target 18.6's grammar reads
  as more than that — a multiple-column target, a subscripted one, a dotted one — is a
  `42601` syntax error at the target. Measured on the native server against 18.6, the
  members examples rather than a list:

  | statement | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `UPDATE r SET (a, b) = (b, a)` | `42601` | `UPDATE 1`, the two values exchanged |
  | `UPDATE r SET (a, b) = (SELECT b, a)` | `42601` | `UPDATE 1` |
  | `UPDATE r SET (a) = ROW(b)` | `42601` | `UPDATE 1` |
  | `UPDATE r SET (a) = (b)` | `42601` | `0A000 source for a multiple-column UPDATE item must be a sub-SELECT or ROW() expression` |
  | over `x INT[]` holding `{1,2,3}`: `UPDATE r SET x[1] = 10, x[2] = 20` | `42601` | `{10,20,3}` |
  | `UPDATE r SET x[1] = 5, x = '{9}'` | `42601` (syntax error at `[`) | `42601 multiple assignments to same column "x"` |
  | `INSERT … ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET (a, b) = (t.b, t.a)`, and `… DO UPDATE SET x[1] = 9` | `42601` | `INSERT 0 1`, the row updated |
  | over `r (id INT PRIMARY KEY, a INT)`: `UPDATE r SET r.a = 5`, `UPDATE r AS q SET q.a = 5`, and `… ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET r.a = 7` | `42601` | `42703 column "r" of relation "r" does not exist` (`"q"` for the alias) |
  | `UPDATE r SET a.x = 5` | `42601` | `42804 cannot assign to field "x" of column "a" because its type integer is not a composite type` |

  Loud: nothing is written. `SET x[1] = 5, x = '{9}'` agrees on the code alone — 18.6's is
  the rewriter's repeat refusal, pglet's the parser's. No fixture: an `@expect-error` whose
  recorded shape is 18.6's success passes on any pglet error, so a faithful fixture for the
  members 18.6 answers is red; the dotted members 18.6 refuses under another code, so an
  `@expect-error` fixture for them compares `42601` against that code and is red too.

- **7 · A `RETURNING` claimant count over a catalog view counts pglet's columns, not
  Postgres's.** The `UPDATE … FROM` namespace registers each source with the columns
  pglet knows it by, and for a synthesized
  `pg_catalog` / `information_schema` view that is the list `CatalogTable::columns()`
  emits. Against 18.6's lists, nine of the 17 relations pglet models are **strict**
  subsets — `information_schema.columns` 17 of 44, `pg_class` 9 of 34, `pg_attribute` 12
  of 25, `pg_type` 10 of 32, `information_schema.tables` 4 of 12, `table_constraints` 9 of
  11, `pg_namespace` 3 of 4, `pg_constraint` 22 of 28, `pg_index` 15 of 21 (pglet's side
  counted from `CatalogTable::column_specs`; 18.6's carried, not re-measured) — and the
  remaining eight agree name-for-name. Every
  name in the difference is a claimant Postgres counts and pglet does not, and under-counting
  is the silent direction: with `vg(character_octet_length TEXT, table_name TEXT, x INT)`,
  `UPDATE vg SET x=1 FROM information_schema.columns c WHERE c.table_name='vg' RETURNING
  character_octet_length` answers the target's row here and is `42702` there, while the
  same statement `RETURNING table_name` — a name pglet's view *does* emit — is `42702` on
  both. That control is what identifies the column list rather than the gate as the cause.
  It is not a `RETURNING`-scope defect either: `SELECT character_octet_length FROM vg,
  information_schema.columns c WHERE c.table_name='vg'` answers here and is `42702` there,
  and so does `SELECT relacl FROM vg3, pg_class c` over `vg3(relacl TEXT, x INT)`. (A
  member of this class closes whenever `virtual_tables.rs` gains a name, and nothing ties
  the two: `udt_name` was one until `information_schema.columns` gained it.) **The fix was priced and
  declined**: registering 18.6's real lists would need a hand-maintained mirror of ~168
  column names across the 14 relations with **no gate able to keep it true** (pglet cannot
  project those columns, so no differential fixture compares them), and it would make a
  relation claim names it refuses to resolve — a name the view lacks does not resolve
  here under either registration — which is the same
  one-fact-two-derivations split the `RETURNING` namespace work spent itself removing. So
  the rule is stated instead: **a claimant is a name the source would resolve here**, and
  where pglet's view is narrower than Postgres's the verdict is narrower with it. No
  fixture can guard the divergence — pglet answers where 18.6 errors, and `@expect-error`
  requires pglet to error — so the guard is the control fixture
  (`update/returning_from_virtual_source_column_ambiguous.sql`) and this record.
  **Widening the `RETURNING` namespace to Postgres's did not change this gap and did not
  narrow it** (re-measured: both statements above answer as recorded). What it changed is
  the *qualified* spelling of a column pglet's view does not model, measured with
  `udt_name` while the view lacked it: `RETURNING c.udt_name` was `42P01` (the source was
  in no namespace at all) and became `42703` — still loud, still a divergence from 18.6's
  `int4`, and consistent with `SELECT c.udt_name FROM information_schema.columns c` then
  being `42703` here. The view has since gained `udt_name`; the qualified spelling is not
  re-measured with a column it still lacks.
- **8 · A `FROM`-clause `unnest(…)` is addressable by its alias in a value position and not
  in a wildcard.** Its relation name now reaches both walks that decide a *value*: the
  planner's `plan_relations` and the executor's `get_table_name_from_plan`, the latter
  keying `execute_join`'s column map and the `UPDATE … FROM` namespace alike. One
  neighbouring walk over the same leaf kinds still has no arm for an `unnest` item —
  `collect_nonbase_into` (which registers a non-base relation's columns under its FROM
  name); `leaf_qualifier` (which names a leaf for wildcard expansion) has one for every
  FROM function item, which closed the join member below. (`push_level_relations`
  is a third and *seals* on one deliberately, which is a different decision and recorded
  above.) Re-measured after the `RETURNING` widening added the executor arm, with
  `jn(q INT, y TEXT)` holding `(9, 'a')` and `jm(z INT)`:

  | statement | 18.6 | pglet |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT u.q FROM jm, unnest(ARRAY[1,2]) AS u(q)` | `1, 2` | `1, 2` |
  | `SELECT u.q FROM jn JOIN unnest(ARRAY[1,2]) AS u(q) ON true` | `1, 2` | `1, 2` |
  | `SELECT 1 FROM jn, unnest(ARRAY[1,2]) AS t(q) WHERE t.q = 1` | 1 row | 1 row |
  | `SELECT 1 FROM jn, unnest(ARRAY[1,2]) AS t(q) WHERE q = 1` | `42702` | `42702` |
  | `SELECT v.* FROM unnest(ARRAY[1,2]) AS v` | `1, 2` | `0A000` |
  | `SELECT * FROM jn JOIN unnest(ARRAY[1,2]) AS u(q) ON true` | 3 cols, 2 rows | closed — 3 cols, 2 rows |
  | `UPDATE t SET … FROM unnest(ARRAY['x','y']) AS u WHERE u.u = 'x'` | 1 row | 1 row |

  **Rows 2 and 3 were the silent wrongs and are closed** — they answered `9, 9` and zero
  rows, because with no relation name the qualifier was dropped and the reference fell
  through to a bare-name lookup over the executor's merged join row, which found `jn`'s
  `q`. Row 1 is why that stayed invisible for so long: with no competing name the wrong
  lookup finds the right column. Row 7 was `42P01 "u"` and is the same arm. What is left
  is the **wildcard** pair, rows 5 and 6, loud *as spelled here* — see the paragraph
  below, where a base table sharing the alias makes row 5's spelling silent — and both
  reaching a different walk from the value rows (row 6's was
  `leaf_qualifier`, then with no arm for the item, so `star_exprs` emitted an *unqualified*
  reference for that side; row 5's is `expand_qualified_wildcard`). They are one missing
  `Unnest` arm in each of **two** readers, not one arm in two spellings — which is why
  their SQLSTATEs differ, the qualified `v.*` refusing outright while the **bare** `*`
  emits a bare `q` that two relations then claim. **"Only one of them has a silent
  polarity" was that pair read as the whole class, and it is bounded to these two
  spellings**: a bare `*` reaches `leaf_qualifier` only over a **join**, and the same bare
  `*` over a *non*-join `FROM` — whenever it is not the sole projection item — reaches
  `expand_qualified_wildcard` instead, which is row 5's reader and carries row 5's silent
  polarity with it. Its members and the sole-`*` control are the two-call-sites paragraph
  closing this bullet. Two controls identify that as the mechanism rather
  than the shape: `AS u(zzz)` (no collision) answers on both, and so does the same bare
  `*` over a left side carrying no `q` at all (`FROM jm JOIN unnest(…) AS u(q)`), which
  is the reading where the unqualified reference has exactly one claimant. A
  `RETURNING u.*` shares neither, since the
  `RETURNING` expansion reads `plan_relations` rather than `leaf_qualifier`. The bare-`*`
  row is **not** something the executor's new `Unnest` arm introduced: with that arm
  reverted, the same statement is `42702` still, while row 2 goes back to answering
  `9, 9` — measured, which is what separates "the arm did not move this verdict" from
  "the mutation did not land". **Row 6 is closed**: `leaf_qualifier`'s arm for a FROM
  function item qualifies that side's columns by its effective name, and the statement,
  `SELECT *, 1 FROM uu, unnest(ARRAY[1,2], ARRAY[3,4]) AS zz(q,r)` and `SELECT * FROM jt,
  generate_series(1, 2) g` beside a `jt.g` answer as 18.6 answers (measured on the native
  server; `generate_series/star_over_a_join.sql`, `select/unnest_star_over_a_join.sql`,
  `select/unnest_star_non_sole_over_a_join.sql`). What remains of the row is row 5's
  reader.

  **"Both loud" was the table's own reading of a two-row sample, and a third spelling of
  row 5 is silent.** The qualified `v.*` does not reach `leaf_qualifier` at all — it
  reaches `expand_qualified_wildcard`, which is keyed on the **name**: it asks the
  `nonbase` map, then the FROM item list, then `schema.get_table`, and only a miss in all
  three is the `0A000`. `collect_nonbase_into` has no arm for an `unnest` item, so an unnest
  item's effective name is not in that map and a **base table of the same spelling
  answers for it** — the expansion emits *that table's* column names, which the binding
  gate then resolves against the *unnest's* columns. So the polarity is decided by whether
  the base table's names are a subset of the alias list's, and nothing else. Measured on
  three builds — before the `unnest` gate, before the FROM-kind flip, and after
  both:

  | statement | 18.6 | pre-gate | pre-flip | now |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT uu.* FROM unnest(ARRAY[1,2], ARRAY[3,4]) AS uu(q, r)`, base `uu(q INT)` | `q \| r` = `1\|3, 2\|4` | `q` = `1, 2` | same | same |
  | the same over `ARRAY[]::int[]` twice | two columns, no rows | one column, no rows | same | same |
  | the same beside a base `uu2(r INT, q INT)`, alias `uu2(q, r)` | `q \| r` = `1\|3, 2\|4` | `r \| q` = `3\|1, 4\|2` | same | same |
  | `SELECT u.* FROM unnest(ARRAY[1,2]) AS u(q)`, base `u(x, y)` | `q` = `1, 2` | `42703 column "u.x"` | same | same |
  | the same over `ARRAY[]::int[]` | `q`, no rows | `x \| y`, no rows | `x \| y`, no rows | `42703 column "u.x"` |
  | line 1's statement beside a base `uu3(q INT, r INT)` | `q \| r` = `1\|3, 2\|4` | conforms | same | same |
  | any of them under a name no table holds | expands | `0A000` (the statement table's row 5) | same | same |

  (Line numbers below are that table's, not the statement table's above it.) Lines 1–3 are
  the **silent** polarity, live on every build; line 4 is the loud one; line 6 is the
  **conformance** control that explains why the defect is invisible in the common case — a
  base table whose column names and order happen to match the alias list expands
  correctly, so only a table that *disagrees* with the alias list shows anything, and it
  is the disagreement rather than the collision that is observable. A partial overlap
  takes the loud side (base `uv(q, x)`, alias `uv(q, r)` is `42703 column "uv.x"`), which
  is the boundary: **all** the table's names in the alias list is silent, any one outside
  it is `42703`. Line 7 is the control that identifies the catalog as the route
  rather than the shape, since it is the recorded refusal reached by removing only the
  collision. Line 3 is the
  one worth reading twice: the values are the unnest's own, so nothing is lost or
  invented — they arrive under another relation's column names, in that relation's order,
  which is a shape no client can detect. **Line 5 is the one the FROM-kind flip moved, and
  it moved a silent member to a loud one**: with the base table's names out of the scope,
  `u.x` now fails the plan-time binding gate instead of being bound and merely never
  evaluated — so the flip closed the zero-row half of the loud spelling and left lines
  1–3 exactly where they were. That was also the only row-count sensitivity in the class,
  and only before the flip: after it every line above reads the same whatever the row
  count, so this is not row 56's mechanism. Recorded as a
  **residual of the flip** rather than a new row, the class's other remaining dimension
  being the `42712` duplicate-alias gate. Its repair is
  **not** the `leaf_qualifier` arm the paragraph above names but the one
  `collect_nonbase_into` deliberately lacks — or a `function_scan_columns` lookup beside it in
  `expand_qualified_wildcard` — and either **closes the statement table's row 5 with it**, which is exactly the
  neighbour change `function_scan_columns`'s own doc comment declines to take as a side effect of
  a declared-type fix and is fine to take deliberately. Three kinds are proved by
  `nonbase` today, each measured beside a base table of its name: a derived table
  (`SELECT d.* FROM (SELECT 1 AS z) AS d` → `z` = `1`, not the base `d(a)`'s `9`), a CTE
  (the `WITH d AS …` spelling, same), and a catalog view (`SELECT t.* FROM
  information_schema.tables t` beside a base `t(zzcol)` → the view's columns, not
  `zzcol`; that it emits four of them where 18.6 emits twelve is the separate
  modeled-subset divergence, not this one). `unnest` is the fourth.

  **That reader has two call sites, and the second is a bare `*`** —
  `planner::query`'s `expand_wildcards` calls `expand_qualified_wildcard` once for a
  `<qual>.*` and once more, inside its per-FROM-item loop, for a bare `*` over a
  **non-join** `FROM`. Only a **sole** bare `*` misses both: `expand_wildcards`
  short-circuits a single-item projection over a non-join `FROM` and returns it untouched
  (the `Plan::Project` fast path), which is why the defect has read as `alias.*`-only. So
  every polarity of the table above repeats under `SELECT *, 1 FROM …`, measured
  on the current build against 18.6 with the same base tables: subset base `uu(q INT)` answers
  `q \| ?column?` = `1\|1, 2\|1` where 18.6 sends `q \| r \| ?column?` = `1\|3\|1, 2\|4\|1`
  (silent, and `SELECT 1, *` is the same, so it is the *sole*-ness and not the position
  that decides); the reordering base `uu2(r INT, q INT)` answers `r \| q \| ?column?` =
  `3\|1\|1, 4\|2\|1` under 18.6's `q \| r \| ?column?` (silent); the matching base
  `uu3(q INT, r INT)` conforms; the partial overlap `uv(q INT, x INT)` is
  `42703 column "uv.x"` (loud); and with no base table of the name it is
  `` 0A000 `nosuchname.*` over a non-base relation `` — the message naming a qualified
  wildcard the statement never wrote, which is the route's own fingerprint. The subset
  member over two empty arrays reads the same — `q \| ?column?` against 18.6's
  `q \| r \| ?column?`, no rows on either — so this half is row-count-independent too.
  Two controls: the **sole** `*` — `SELECT * FROM unnest(ARRAY[1,2], ARRAY[3,4]) AS
  uu(q,r)` and `SELECT * FROM unnest(ARRAY[1,2]) AS u(q)` beside their colliding base
  tables — is correct on both engines, the short-circuit; and the same non-sole `*` over a
  **join** (`SELECT *, 1 FROM uu, unnest(ARRAY[1,2], ARRAY[3,4]) AS zz(q,r)`) takes
  the `leaf_qualifier` route, which is the statement table's row 6 and not this one, and
  answers as 18.6 does since that row closed. The
  repair is the same `collect_nonbase_into` arm — one arm closing both call sites.

  The two spellings the row names are `SELECT v.*` — the qualified wildcard, which is
  `expand_qualified_wildcard`'s route — and the non-sole bare `*` over a non-join `FROM`, which
  reaches that same reader through `expand_wildcards`' per-FROM-item loop:
  `SELECT *, 1 FROM unnest(…) AS uu(q,r)` is its short spelling and
  `SELECT *, 1 FROM unnest(ARRAY[1,2], ARRAY[3,4]) AS uu(q,r)` the measured one, beside a base
  `uu(q INT)`. A **sole** `*` over a non-join `FROM` short-circuits ahead of both readers and
  is the control, correct on both engines over every collision above. The loud verdict is
  told by its message: `expand_qualified_wildcard` refuses a qualifier neither the
  non-base map nor the catalog holds with `` 0A000 `<alias>.*` over a non-base relation `` — a
  `0A000 … over a non-base relation` naming a qualified wildcard the statement never wrote —
  while over a join `star_exprs`'s `leaf_qualifier` qualifies each side's columns by the
  item's name, so the join spellings answer.
- **~~9~~ · Closed — a bare outer reference into a multi-relation scope.** The executor's
  outer-frame chain (`EvalEnv::resolve_outer_slot`) addressed a multi-relation scope by
  *qualified* name only — such a scope's columns were named `relation.column` and the
  bare-name tier matched those exactly, so nothing was ever spelled `k` and the reference
  was `42703` where 18.6 counts one claimant and binds it. Both spellings measured on both
  engines, with the inner relation deliberately not carrying the name (`rcs_y(yk)`, and `k`
  a column of the outer `rcs_s`): `SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM rcs_y WHERE rcs_y.yk = k)
  FROM rcs_t t JOIN rcs_s s ON s.id = t.id` and the `UPDATE … FROM … RETURNING` spelling
  were `42703 "k"` against 18.6's `1`, while the qualified `s.k` answered on both
  throughout — the control that made it loud rather than wrong.

  A frame now carries its scope's `(relation, column)` pairs, so a bare name counts
  claimants the way `scanRTEForColumn` does: one resolves, two are `42702`, and a
  `USING` merge is the single bare-visible claimant its sides' own copies stand behind.
  If the inner relation *does* carry the name, both engines bind the bare reference to the
  inner one (SQL's innermost-wins rule) and agree — which is what makes an inner relation
  lacking the name the discriminating shape, and a probe written with a colliding name a
  degenerate control that reports agreement.
- **~~10~~ · Closed — a quoted user column with a dot in its name, read in a join scope or in a
  multi-relation outer frame.** The executor's join scope *encoded* each column's
  `(relation, column)` pair in the column's own name and every consumer re-parsed it, so a
  column a user quoted a dot into was byte-identical to a name the join synthesized — and the
  forgery ran both ways: a relation the query never named became addressable, while the pair
  the scan's own alias spells was never registered at all. The pairs come from the plan now
  (`executor::query::plan_scope`), which no spelling can forge. The mechanism — the two
  readers and two producers of a dotted `col_names` entry, `register_input_columns`,
  `SimpleColumns`, the correlated `OuterFrame`, the `RETURNING` frame handed the same
  namespace its clause already resolved through, and the near-misses that pass some of the
  rows below and not all — is `docs/scope.md`.

  Measured against 18.6 on the default in-memory B+tree backend (a `pglet_server` with
  no `--data-dir`), accelerated profile, simple-query text leg, with `wt(id, v)` holding
  `(1,'a'),(2,'b')` and `sd(id, "wt.v")` holding `(1,'srcval'),(2,'srcval2')`; every row
  now answers 18.6's column:

  | statement | 18.6 | pglet before |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT * FROM wt JOIN sd s ON s.id=wt.id` | `1,a,1,srcval` | `1,a,1,a` |
  | `SELECT s."wt.v" FROM wt JOIN sd s ON s.id=wt.id` | `srcval` | `a` |
  | `SELECT "wt.v" FROM wt JOIN sd s ON s.id=wt.id` | `srcval` | `42702` |
  | `SELECT wt.id FROM wt JOIN sd s ON s."wt.v" = 'srcval'` | 2 rows | `column "s.wt.v" does not exist` |
  | `SELECT wt.id FROM wt JOIN sd s ON s.id=wt.id WHERE s."wt.v" = 'srcval'` | 1 row | `(0 rows)` |
  | `SELECT "wt.v" FROM sd` (single-relation control) | `srcval` | `srcval` |

  Rows 1, 2 and 5 were **silent**. The single-relation control is what identifies the
  synthesis rather than the column name: a scan's names are the user's own, so nothing
  collides. Two more shapes are part of the same closure and neither is derivable from
  the rows above: with the *left* relation carrying a quoted `"zz.v"` too,
  `SELECT s."zz.v" FROM zw2 JOIN zs2 s ON s.id = zw2.id` answered `left`, `left2` against
  18.6's `srcval`, `srcval2` — silent, both engines accepting, and what puts the
  resolution in the descriptor *list* rather than in the spelling, since the
  left-naming spelling agreed on both throughout; and the `ON`-position reads resolve
  through `JoinColumnMap` rather than `SimpleColumns`, so a change confined to one could
  not reach the other. The **manufactured-relation** half (`ON zz.v = 'srcval'`,
  `SELECT zz.v`, `WHERE zz.v = 'srcval'`, all three silent) had already been closed by the
  plan-time binding gate, which refuses a qualifier the FROM namespace does not name
  before the executor is reached; it was recorded here as live and was not.

  **The correlated outer frame is the flat-string half.** Measured on the
  default in-memory B+tree backend (a `pglet_server` with no `--data-dir`), accelerated
  profile, simple-query text leg, against 18.6, with `q1(id, "a.b")` holding
  `(1,'hit'),(2,'miss')` and `q2(yv)` holding `('hit')`:

  | statement | 18.6 | pglet before | pglet now |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | `DELETE FROM q1 WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM q2 WHERE q2.yv = a.b)` | `42P01 "a"`, both rows survive | `DELETE 1`, **row 1 destroyed** | `42P01 "a"` |
  | `SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM q2 WHERE q2.yv = a.b) AS n, q1.id FROM q1` | `42P01 "a"` | `n` = `1`, `0` | `42P01 "a"` |
  | the same over `FROM q1 z` | `42P01 "a"` | `n` = `1`, `0` | `42P01 "a"` |
  | `UPDATE q1 SET id = q1.id RETURNING (SELECT … a.b) AS n, q1.id` | `42P01 "a"` | `n` = `1`, `0` | `42P01 "a"` |
  | the quoted-*alias* spelling: `SELECT s.z FROM (SELECT id, v AS "ta.v", v AS z FROM ta) s WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM tc WHERE tc.k = ta.v)` | `42P01 "ta"` | the row | `42P01 "ta"` |
  | over `tex(id PRIMARY KEY, "excluded.x")`: `INSERT … ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET "excluded.x" = EXCLUDED.x` | `42703 excluded.x` | stores the excluded row's `"excluded.x"` | `42703 "excluded.x"` |

  Three controls, each agreeing on both engines and unmoved by the gate: `SELECT a.b FROM
  q1` is `42P01` (the top-level gate was never the missing one — this was outer-frame-only),
  `q2.yv = zzz.nosuch` is `42P01` (so it is not the qualifier-blind path below, which
  searches for a bare `nosuch` and finds none), and `q2.yv = "a.b"` — the column under its
  own quoted name — answers. The `UPDATE` row is the one that shows a single-relation frame
  already *has* the pair the multi-relation one lacks: `relations.len() == 1`, so
  `returning_input_columns` takes its early return and renames nothing, and the frame
  carries `table: Some("q1")` beside bare names.

  The last row's SQLSTATE was the only one that did not land on 18.6's, and it does now.
  The gap was **pre-existing rather than the gate's**: a qualified correlated reference
  whose qualifier names a frame but whose column that frame lacks answered `42P01` here
  where 18.6 says `42703` — measured on `SELECT a2.id FROM ta a2 WHERE
  EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM tc WHERE tc.k = a2.nosuch)` and on `… DO UPDATE SET v =
  EXCLUDED.nosuch`, while the top-level `SELECT a2.nosuch FROM ta a2` was `42703` on both.

  **The refusal was the dotted tier's and not the class's**, and the escape used to
  re-open the row destruction the table's first row records: give the frame a **bare**
  column of the same name beside the quoted one and the reference fell past this gate into
  the qualifier-blind fallback, which never read the qualifier. Over `q4(id, b, "a.b")`
  holding `(1,'hit','dotted'),(2,'miss','dotted2')` and a one-row `q2b(yv)` = `('hit')`,
  `DELETE FROM q4 WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM q2b WHERE q2b.yv = a.b)` was `DELETE 1` here
  — row 1 gone — against 18.6's `42P01 "a"`. Which column answered is identified by the
  two-seed read control, since the `DELETE`'s own seed cannot distinguish "bound the bare
  `b`" from "bound nothing and matched by accident": over `q5(id, b, "a.b")` holding
  `(1,'bare','dotted')`, `SELECT q5.id, (SELECT count(*) FROM q2b WHERE q2b.yv = a.b) AS n
  FROM q5` answered `n=1` when `q2b` held `'bare'` and `n=0` when it held `'dotted'` — so
  it bound `q5`'s **bare `b`**. Both statements are `42P01 "a"` here now, and the fallback
  they escaped into is gone: `resolve_outer_slot` declines a qualifier no frame owns
  instead of matching a bare name (see *Qualifier-blind name resolution*).

  **The dotted tier's own gate was at eval time, which bounded what it reached — and the
  plan-time binding gate closed both halves of that boundary.** A statement whose target
  matches **no row** never evaluated the reference: over an *empty* `q1e(id, "a.b")`,
  `DELETE FROM q1e WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM q2 WHERE q2.yv = a.b)` was `DELETE 0` here
  against 18.6's `42P01`, and is `42P01` on both engines now, primary message
  byte-identical. A `RETURNING`-position reference is projected **after** the row writes,
  so a write error used to precede it: `UPDATE qpk SET id = 1 WHERE id = 2 RETURNING
  (SELECT … a.b) AS n, qpk.id` was `23505` here against `42P01` there, and the
  `NOT NULL` spelling `23502` against the same `42P01`; both are `42P01` on both engines
  now. Those write errors are
  still real and the `42P01` genuinely outranks them, which is what the same statements
  without the reference say: `UPDATE qpk SET id = 1 WHERE id = 2` is `23505` and
  `UPDATE qnn SET v = NULL WHERE id = 2` is `23502`, on both engines.

  **What the enumeration does not reach is the order of the `WHERE`'s own conjuncts, and
  that pair is live.** `DELETE FROM q1 WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM q2 WHERE q2.yv = a.b)
  AND nosuchw = 1` is `42703 "nosuchw"` here against 18.6's `42P01 "a"` — loud on both
  engines under different codes, which a fixture would score red. The reverse spelling
  (`… WHERE nosuchw = 1 AND EXISTS (…)`) is `42703 "nosuchw"` on both, and that control
  puts the divergence in *which* conjunct answers rather than in either conjunct alone.
  Nothing pins it: the shape is in no fixture. The neighbouring shapes split. A missing
  **target** relation is `42P01 relation "nosuchtable_q" does not exist` on both engines,
  and a bogus qualifier written **ahead** of the `EXISTS` is `42P01 "bogusrel"` on both.
  A missing **inner** relation is not: 18.6 answers `42P01 relation "nosuchinner_q" does
  not exist` where the dotted tier here answers `42P01 "a"` — one code naming two
  different things — and the same bogus qualifier moved **after** the `EXISTS` splits the
  same way, `42P01 "a"` there against `42P01 "bogusrel"` here. An ill-typed neighbour
  splits by *code*: written after the `EXISTS`, `… AND id = 'notanint'` is 18.6's
  `42P01 "a"` against `22P02` here, which a fixture would score red exactly as the
  conjunct pair would; written before it, both answer `22P02`. The divergent shapes are
  the conjunct pair's own precedence class — which reference answers first, some under
  18.6's code and some not — which is what the table's `silent?` cell states, so they
  need no cell of their own.

  **The multi-relation frame closed with it**, having been the last reader addressed by
  synthesized strings with no relation identity to gate on. Measured on the same legs,
  both engines accepting each statement, with `wt` / `sd` as above and `oy(yv)` holding
  `('srcval')`; the base statement is
  `UPDATE wt SET v = wt.v FROM sd s WHERE s.id = wt.id`, and the answers are the two
  returned rows in `wt.id` order:

  | `RETURNING` clause | 18.6 | pglet before |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `(SELECT count(*) FROM oy WHERE oy.yv = "wt.v") AS n, wt.id` | `n` = `1`, `0` | `n` = `0`, `0` |
  | the same with `s."wt.v"` in the subquery | `n` = `1`, `0` | `n` = `1`, `0` |
  | `"wt.v" AS n, wt.id` — the same reference at the clause's top level | `n` = `srcval`, `srcval2` | `n` = `srcval`, `srcval2` |

  It was silent, and the two controls are what put it in the frame rather than in the
  clause: the clause itself resolves by `(relation, column)` pair
  (`returning_column_map`) and got the top-level spelling right, and the qualified
  spelling inside the subquery was right on both engines. The row reaches the frame by the
  **unqualified** path, which no qualifier gate can touch — the frame reads the clause's
  own pairs now.

  **A frame lacking an identity is not the same fact as a frame being multi-relation**, and
  two single-relation scopes carried `table: None`, on statements both engines accept as SQL
  and 18.6 answers `42P01`. Both are closed, each at its own
  call site, and each was reached by two resolvers — the dotted tier above and
  `SimpleColumns`'s loose last tier. Measured on the default in-memory B+tree backend,
  accelerated profile, simple-query text leg, against 18.6:

  | statement | 18.6 | pglet before | pglet now |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | over `u1(id, "a.b")` + `u2(yv)`: `UPDATE u1 SET id = 99 WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM u2 WHERE u2.yv = a.b)` | `42P01 "a"`, both rows unchanged | `UPDATE 1`, **the wrong row written** | `42P01 "a"` |
  | `UPDATE ex1 SET v = 42 WHERE bogusrel.n = 1` | `42P01 "bogusrel"` | `UPDATE 1`, `v` is `42` | `42P01 "bogusrel"` |
  | `UPDATE ex1 SET v = bogusrel.n + 100` | `42P01 "bogusrel"` | `UPDATE 1`, `v` is `101` | `42P01 "bogusrel"` |
  | `SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM u2 WHERE u2.yv = a.b) AS n FROM unnest(ARRAY['hit','miss']) AS v("a.b")` | `42P01 "a"` | `n` = `1`, `0` | `42P01 "a"` |
  | `SELECT zzz.b FROM unnest(ARRAY['x','y']) AS v(b)` | `42P01 "zzz"` | `x`, `y` | `42P01 "zzz"` |

  The **aliased** spelling of the first row (`UPDATE u1 x SET id = 77 WHERE …`) is
  `42P01` on both engines and was so before, which is the control that identifies the
  identity rather than the statement kind: `execute_update` passed the statement's FROM
  *alias* as the scope's name, so only an unaliased target reached the resolvers with
  nothing. It passes Postgres's `eref` now, so `UPDATE hw x SET v = 'z' WHERE hw.id = 1`
  stays `42P01` on both, the alias still hiding the name. The second site is
  `single_table_name`, which
  had no `Plan::FunctionScan` arm; the accept controls `SELECT v.b FROM unnest(…) AS v(b)`,
  the same reference correlated, `SELECT unnest.unnest FROM unnest(ARRAY['x','y'])`, and
  the bare correlated `b` all answer on both engines before and after.

  **What the identity does not reach, measured on the same legs.** The qualifier-blind
  bare fallback beneath the dotted tier was untouched by the identity work — over the same
  unnest item `… WHERE u2.yv = zzz.b` still answered here against 18.6's `42P01` — and
  that fallback is what the accept control `v.b` used to resolve through, which is why
  removing it and giving these frames identities were one change and not two; it is gone
  now and both statements agree with 18.6. The zero-row boundary these frames shared with
  the dotted tier closed with it: over an empty table
  `UPDATE re SET id = 5 WHERE bogusrel.id = 1` was `UPDATE 0` here against 18.6's `42P01`
  and `SELECT zzz.b FROM unnest(ARRAY[]::text[]) AS v(b)` was `(0 rows)` against the same,
  and both are `42P01` on both engines now. The `Plan::Join` shape that used to stand
  beside them agrees as well: the fourth row's shape with the `unnest` item replaced by
  `FROM u1 JOIN u2 ON true` is `42P01 "a"` on both engines. And an identity is not an ambiguity
  check: a **multi-array** `unnest` aliased without a column list carries two columns both
  named `unnest`, so `SELECT t.unnest FROM unnest(ARRAY['x'], ARRAY[1]) AS t` answers `x`
  here against 18.6's `42702 column reference "unnest" is ambiguous`. Measured before and
  after — the identity moved which tier answers it and not the answer, since the loose
  tier it used to reach also took the first match. The controls agree on both engines: the
  same statement with a column list (`AS t(a, b)`), the unaliased form's two `unnest`
  columns, and a bogus qualifier over either spelling (`42P01`, closed on the multi-array
  form too).

  **The gates moved error precedence, in both directions**, and the direction that is still
  a divergence is the **target list**. Where a *reverted* answer is quoted below it comes
  from a scratch build with the `Plan::FunctionScan` arm of `single_table_name` — and nothing
  else — removed, so a row where that build differs from `pglet` is one this change moved.
  18.6 resolves the target list first (`transformTargetList` runs before
  `transformWhereClause`) while pglet's `Filter` evaluates below its `Project`, so a `WHERE`
  qualifier that now refuses gets there first. Four spellings measured, one mechanism; every
  row below is `… FROM unnest(ARRAY['x']) AS v(b) WHERE zzz.b = 'x'` with the target-list
  item varied:

  | target-list item | 18.6 | `Unnest` arm reverted | pglet |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | `(SELECT 1 FROM nosuchinner)` — a missing inner relation | `42P01 "nosuchinner"` | `42P01 "nosuchinner"` | `42P01 "zzz"` |
  | `nosuchcol` — a missing bare column | `42703 "nosuchcol"` | `42703 "nosuchcol"` | `42P01 "zzz"` |
  | `v.nosuch` — a missing column of the level's own relation | `42703 v.nosuch` | `42703 "v.nosuch"` | `42P01 "zzz"` |
  | `b + 1` — an ill-typed expression | `42883` | `42804` | `42P01 "zzz"` |

  Only the first row shares 18.6's SQLSTATE, which is what the sentence that used to
  close this paragraph — *the SQLSTATE matches either way, so only the relation named
  differs* — was true of, and false of the two beneath it: that is the difference between a
  fixture that would pass and one that would be red. The fourth row diverged before the
  change as well, and its answer moved anyway. Its old explanation is also wrong and worth
  replacing rather than dropping: the `+` operand gate is **not** plan-time here.
  Measured, an empty input reaches no row and raises nothing —
  `SELECT b + 1 FROM unnest(ARRAY[]::text[]) AS v(b)` is `(0 rows)` here against 18.6's
  `42883`, and `SELECT v + 1 FROM rz` over an **empty** `rz(id INT, v TEXT)` is the same
  pair — so the base-table spelling is eval-time too, and this is not an `unnest` property.
  The eval-time arithmetic error is `42804`, and it loses to the `WHERE` for the same
  `Filter`-below-`Project` reason as the three rows above it. Which pairs moved *into*
  agreement, and the `WHERE`-position precedence walk behind them, are `docs/scope.md`.

  **New members of a class the engine already had rather than a new class**, and the
  base-table controls say so. Over `r1(id INT, v TEXT)`, both
  `SELECT (SELECT 1 FROM nosuchinner) FROM r1 WHERE zzz.id = 1` and
  `SELECT nosuchcol FROM r1 WHERE zzz.id = 1` answer `42P01 "zzz"` here — against 18.6's
  `42P01 "nosuchinner"` and `42703` — and answer the same on the reverted build, which
  does not reach a base table's identity. The identity-less regime the unnest level left
  is still observable at this revision: `SELECT nosuchcol FROM r1 JOIN u2d ON true WHERE
  zzz.id = 1` is `42703` on both engines, the qualifier waved through and the target list
  answering.

  Unmoved and still diverging: a missing `SET` target column outranks the `WHERE`
  qualifier here (`UPDATE r2 SET nosuchset = 1 WHERE zzz.id = 1` is `42703` here against
  18.6's `42P01 "zzz"`), and a bogus qualifier in `RETURNING` outranks one in the `WHERE`
  (`UPDATE r2 SET id = 1 WHERE zzz.id = 1 RETURNING qqq.id` is `42P01 "qqq"` here against
  `42P01 "zzz"` there — same SQLSTATE, different relation named). Unmoved and agreeing: a
  missing target relation (`42P01`, naming it, on both), and a missing relation inside the
  `WHERE`'s own subquery (`42P01 "zzz"` on both).
- **~~30~~ · Closed — Qualifier-blind name resolution, by a plan-time binding gate.** A cluster of
  resolvers compared column references by **bare** name, so a qualified `pb.x` collided
  with a projected `pa.x` from a different relation, and a qualifier naming *no* relation
  answered whatever bare column the loose tier found. What decided a shape's fate was
  never the clause but **whether the resolver was handed a relation identity**: a
  `SimpleColumns` built with `None` for its table drops the qualifier and matches the bare
  name (`executor::expr::eval::resolve_column`'s last tier), and the call site chooses.
  Sort placement, the simple-query declared types, `Describe`'s output columns, the
  coercion pass and `DISTINCT ON` key canonicalization each carried an instance and are
  qualifier-aware; the DML scans and the FROM-clause `unnest(…)` item were given their
  names; and the correlated outer-scope chain was made to stop at the frame that owns a
  qualifier. Each of those fixed a *site*. What closes the class is a **binding gate at
  plan time**, because the planner knows the FROM namespace even where the executor's
  post-projection node does not. Where that gate can close, and where each of the sort-key
  positions below is judged, are `docs/scope.md`.

  Measured against 18.6, each of these answered a row here and is now identical on both
  engines. Over `ka(id, x)`, `kb(id, y)`, `srt(n, v)`, `gi2(ikey, tag)`, `ob1(a, b)`:
  `SELECT n, v FROM srt ORDER BY bogusrel.v`; `SELECT ka.x, kb.y FROM ka JOIN kb ON … ORDER
  BY bogusrel.y` and the `bogusrel.id` spelling a name **both** sides carry (which was
  `42703` — loud under the wrong code); `SELECT bogusrel.y FROM ka JOIN kb ON …` and
  `… WHERE bogusrel.y = 'by'`; `SELECT ka.y FROM ka JOIN kb ON …`, which answered
  **`kb`'s column**; `GROUP BY bogusrel.ikey` (`42803` here, wrong code), `SELECT
  bogusrel.ikey … GROUP BY ikey`, `HAVING bogusrel.tag = 'z'` and the no-`GROUP BY`
  `HAVING`; `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY zzz.v)` and its window `ORDER BY` twin; and
  `SELECT b AS x FROM ob1 ORDER BY ob1.x`, where the qualifier is real and the column is
  output-only.

  That removed the class's row-count dependence, which is what the eval-time rules could
  not do: `SELECT 1 FROM <empty> WHERE zzz.id = 1`, `UPDATE t SET v = zzz.v WHERE 1 = 0`,
  `DELETE FROM <empty> WHERE zzz.id = 1`, `DELETE FROM t WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM
  <empty> WHERE u.k = zzz.v)` and `SELECT (SELECT 1 FROM <empty> WHERE zzz.k = 1)` each
  reported success where 18.6 refuses, and `DELETE FROM t WHERE ikey IN (SELECT ikey FROM t
  GROUP BY ikey HAVING bogusrel.ikey = 7)` **removed a row**.

  **Three declines keep the gate from refusing what Postgres runs**, and each is a
  measured shape rather than caution. Postgres lets a **bare single-field** `ORDER BY` /
  `DISTINCT ON` key name a target-list entry (`findTargetlistEntrySQL92`), so such a key is
  matched against the level's target list before the range table is consulted — dropping
  that claimant set reddens **22** fixtures, `SELECT b AS x FROM ob1 ORDER BY x` among them,
  while `ORDER BY ob1.x` still refuses. (These clauses used to resolve *before* the
  projection existed, where the set cannot be built and the gate could only decline
  outright; they resolve after it now — see the sort-key member below.) A `JOIN …
  USING (c)` **merges** `c` into one
  column, so its claimants are counted once and not once per side (`SELECT num FROM a JOIN
  b USING (num)` is ordinary SQL), and that fact shifts outward with its level so a
  correlated subquery sees it too. And a relation the scope can name but not fully
  enumerate — a **catalog view**, where pglet models a strict subset of 18.6's columns for
  nine of its 17 relations and binds seven of them non-exhaustively — answers its own
  qualifier while a name absent from its list stays *unknown*: `SELECT udt_name FROM
  information_schema.columns WHERE table_name = '<absent>'` was `(0 rows)` on both while
  the view lacked `udt_name`, where an exhaustive gate makes it `42703`.

  **Residuals, all measured and all recorded here rather than closed.**
  - ~~A set-op's **trailing `ORDER BY`** has no `ColumnScope` at all.~~ **Closed**, at that
    clause's own lowering (`plan_set_op_order_limit`) — see the set-op member below for the
    rule. A **computed** key was once left open on a
    falsified argument, and the falsification is the transferable half: gating a computed
    key's leaves was said to refuse `… ORDER BY -a` "with a `42703` naming a column that
    *is* an output column", which is only true of the naive routing that sends every leaf
    to the empty base scope. 18.6 resolves a set-op key's names against the **output
    names** — `transformSetOperationStmt` adds them to the namespace as a join RTE
    precisely "so that `ORDER BY upper(foo)` will draw the right error message rather than
    `foo not found`" — so a leaf routed the way `scope_for_key` already routes a whole key
    binds `-a` and refuses `bogus+1`. Both now hold, measured. The leaves are judged
    (`bogus+1`, `bogus::int`, `a + bogus` → `42703`; `bogusrel.a+1` → `42P01`; and
    `SELECT x AS lbl … UNION … ORDER BY x+0` → `42703`, since an arm's own column name is
    not an output name and 18.6's DETAIL says so), while the `0A000` itself stays lenient:
    a computed key whose leaves all bind still **sorts** here (`-a`, `a+1`, `abs(a)`,
    `COALESCE(a,0)`, each `0A000` on 18.6 — but not `count(*)` or `(SELECT 1)`, which are
    `0A000` on both engines from different causes, pglet's own eval-context refusals, and
    are fixture-pinned for exactly that agreement). What the closure
