    introduces is one clause of the same wrong-code class the whole-key form already
    carries: a **correlated** leaf is `42P01` here qualified (`… IN (SELECT x FROM sa
    UNION … ORDER BY x + tgt.a)`) and `42703` bare (`… ORDER BY x + a`), against 18.6's
    `0A000` for either — loud on both engines, so no wrong answer. Guarded by the
    `select/set_op_order_by_computed_key_*` and
    `select/set_op_order_by_bogus_computed_key_before_a_bad_position_loud.sql` fixtures
    and the `a_set_op_computed_sort_key_*` row-survival tests. **The row-count
    characterisation this bullet used to carry was also wrong**, and in the direction that
    understates: emptiness was load-bearing for the **bare** read spellings only
    (`… ORDER BY bogus+1` was already `42703` from the eval-time resolver with a row in
    each arm), while the unreferenced-CTE **write** — `WITH c AS (SELECT a FROM sa UNION
    SELECT a FROM sb ORDER BY bogus+1) DELETE FROM t`, whose body never executes — and the
    **qualified** computed read were row-count independent.
  - `q.*` **expands before the gate**, so `SELECT bogusrel.* FROM t` is `0A000` here
    against `42P01` — loud, wrong code.
  - Inside a correlated subquery a **legality** error over the inner level's own column
    fires at that level's first lowering, before the re-run can bind: `… WHERE zzz.v = 'y'
    AND i.n LIKE 'x'` is `42883` here against 18.6's `42P01`. Closable by deferring
    `check_expr_semantics` at a nested level's first lowering and letting the re-run do
    binding and legality in one interleaved walk.
  - A **qualified** reference into a derived table whose select list carries the name twice
    answers the first rather than refusing — `SELECT d.id FROM (SELECT * FROM ka JOIN kb ON
    …) d` is `42702` on 18.6 — and the gate structurally cannot see it: a scope relation's
    columns are a `HashMap`, in which the two `id`s are one entry. The **bare** spelling is
    `42702` on both, which is the control that puts it in the qualified path.
  - A name pglet's catalog views do not model is a **decline**, so `SELECT nosuchcol_at_all
    FROM information_schema.columns` is `(0 rows)` here and `42703` there — the price of
    the non-exhaustive registration above, and the safe direction.
  - `SELECT a, a FROM ob1 ORDER BY a` is `42702` here over a **non-empty** `ob1` and
    accepted there (Postgres's `equal()` targets rule), a separate over-rejection this
    gate neither caused nor closes: the plan-time gate compares expressions rather than counting
    names (with the residual causes below), and what
    is left raising is the **eval-time** resolver, so over an empty `ob1` both engines
    answer `(0 rows)`. See the SELECT row of `docs/compatibility.md`.
  - **Four measured causes make the plan-time output-entry comparison refuse what 18.6
    resolves** — four is what has been measured, not a claim that a fifth cannot exist —
    each spelling `(0 rows)` there and `42702` here, each measured nested inside an
    `EXISTS` so the plan-time gate (and not the eval-time resolver) is the judge. Each
    carries two entries under one name, so the name *count* that preceded the comparison
    refused them too — none is a regression of the change that spelled the comparison.
    **Causes and not a count, deliberately.** This was recorded as "five
    shapes", and the number was an undercount the day it was written: further spellings
    reproduce over two causes that list did not name at all (unary minus, and an
    unknown-typed literal's cast), and one more is a fresh spelling of a cause it did
    name. A count is the form of a claim that goes stale silently (see the enumeration
    rule in `docs/scope.md`) — another spelling of a cause already listed reads as a falsified
    number rather than as the nothing it is; a cause list does not have that failure mode.
    It went the other way too: the **unary-minus** cause is now *closed* — the parser folds
    `-` over a numeric constant into the constant, as `doNegate` does, so `0` and `-0` are
    one entry again — which took the list from five to four and is why a number written
    here needs re-deriving rather than reading. All four are **row-count-independent at a
    level's own lowering** as well as inside a nested one, since the sort-key member below
    moved the keys to plan time.

    - **A no-op cast on an already-typed expression.** 18.6 has **no cast node to
      compare** — `coerce_type` returns the input unchanged when it already has the target
      type (`parse_coerce.c`) — while pglet keeps the `Cast`, so the two entries differ
      structurally. Measured: `SELECT c::int AS q, c AS q FROM ja2 …` and
      `SELECT 1::int AS q, 1 AS q FROM ja2 …`.
    - **An unknown-typed literal's cast is not folded to a constant.** Postgres resolves
      `'t'::bool` and `'{"a":1,"b":2}'::jsonb` during parse analysis into a `Const`, which
      then compares `equal()` to the same value written any other way; pglet keeps a
      `Cast` over the text literal, so the bytes differ. Measured:
      `SELECT true AS q, 't'::bool AS q FROM ja2 …` and
      `SELECT '{"a":1,"b":2}'::jsonb AS q, '{"b":2,"a":1}'::jsonb AS q FROM ja2 …` (the
      second needs the canonical jsonb key order too, which pglet already applies at value
      construction — so folding the cast is the whole of it here).
    - ~~**Unary `-` over a numeric constant is not folded into the constant.**~~ **Closed.**
      `parser::expr`'s `negate` folds `-` over a `Literal::Int` / `Literal::Numeric` into
      the constant, which is `doNegate`'s two `A_Const` kinds (`Integer`, `Float`), so `-0`
      *is* the constant `0` and the two entries are one repeated entry again;
      `nested_sort_key_negated_zero_is_one_entry.sql` is the value fixture for both numeric
      families and `nested_sort_key_negated_literal_is_a_distinct_entry_loud.sql` the
      control that keeps `1`/`-1` two entries. It is kept in the list struck through
      because its **independent observable** is the reason the fold shipped at all, and
      that observable was a silent write, not an over-rejection:
      `SELECT c FROM oa ORDER BY -1` is `42P10 ORDER BY position -1 is not in select list`
      on 18.6 and *returned rows* here, so `DELETE FROM wt WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM ws
      ORDER BY -1)` removed a row against an error — row-count-independent, and in every
      position measured (top level, derived table, CTE, all four set-op forms,
      `WHERE … IN`, `WHERE EXISTS`, a scalar subquery). The clause spellings are pinned by
      `select/order_by_negative_position_loud.sql` and its neighbours; the row survival by
      `crates/pglet/tests/scope_relation_identity.rs`.
    - **`IN` over a list is not normalized to the array form.** `transformAExprIn`
      rewrites `x IN (a, b)` into the same `ScalarArrayOpExpr` over an `ArrayExpr` that
      `x = ANY (ARRAY[a,b])` produces, and degenerates a one-element list into a plain
      `=`, so on 18.6 the two spellings are one expression; pglet keeps a distinct
      `Expr::InList`, so the bytes differ. Measured `(0 rows)` there and `42702` here:
      `SELECT c IN (1,2) AS q, c = ANY(ARRAY[1,2]) AS q FROM ja2 …`,
      `SELECT c NOT IN (1,2) AS q, c <> ALL(ARRAY[1,2]) AS q FROM ja2 …`, and
      `SELECT c IN (1) AS q, c = 1 AS q FROM ja2 …`. Three controls put the mechanism on
      18.6's `ArrayExpr` normalization rather than on array-constant folding: each
      spelling paired with **itself** (`c IN (1,2)` twice, `c = ANY(ARRAY[1,2])` twice) is
      `(0 rows)` on both engines, while
      `SELECT c IN (1,2) AS q, c = ANY('{1,2}'::int[]) AS q FROM ja2 …` is `42702` on
      **both** — an array *literal* is not the `ArrayExpr` the rewrite builds, so 18.6
      refuses that pair too. On the build that introduced the expression comparison, these
      three were `42703` like the other alias-keyed spellings, so this cause is a residual against both baselines.
    - **`ColumnScope::sole_relation_carrying`'s three declines.** It binds a bare
      target-list column to the relation carrying it before the entries are compared, and
      answers `None` on three — leaving the reference bare, so two spellings of one column
      no longer match. Its ≥2-claimant decline: `SELECT *, c FROM ua JOIN ub USING (c) …
      ORDER BY c` and `SELECT ua.c, c FROM ua JOIN ub USING (c) … ORDER BY c` (the `USING`
      merge makes one column, but both sides claim the name). Its uncertain-level decline:
      `SELECT t.table_name, table_name FROM information_schema.tables t … ORDER BY
      table_name` (pglet models a strict subset of the view's columns, so the level is not
      columns-exhaustive). And its 0-claimant decline: `SELECT ot2.k AS q, k AS q FROM ja2
      … ORDER BY q`, where `k` belongs to the enclosing level and no level-0 relation
      claims it.

    Every spelling above is **loud**, so none is a silent wrong and none writes. Which
    **baseline** they are read against is the discriminator, and the two baselines answer
    differently. Re-measured on the build predating the expression comparison,
    every spelling above answers the same `42702`, so none is a regression of *that*
    change. Re-measured on the build that introduced the expression comparison, the spellings
    keyed by an `AS q` alias were already `42703` — before the plan-time sort-key binding, a nested sort key
    bound to nothing — while three answered `(0 rows)`, matching 18.6, and refuse now:
    `SELECT *, c FROM ua JOIN ub USING (c) … ORDER BY c`,
    `SELECT ua.c, c FROM ua JOIN ub USING (c) … ORDER BY c`, and
    `SELECT t.table_name, table_name FROM information_schema.tables t … ORDER BY
    table_name`. Those three are exactly the ones whose sort key names a **base column**
    rather than an `AS` alias, which is why the alias-keyed spellings read as untouched and
    these do not: a base-column key resolved against the FROM relations at that baseline
    and is judged by the output-entry comparison now. **Accepted SQL narrowed there**,
    trading those three for the row-destroying binds the plan-time binding gate closed — a
    price, recorded here plainly, and those three are the members to re-check if it is ever
    re-opened. They are recorded here because the sentence above them used to cover them.
  - **The plan-time sort-key `42702` names the column where 18.6 names the clause** —
    `column reference "q" is ambiguous` against `ORDER BY "q" is ambiguous`
    (`DISTINCT ON "q" …` for that clause). It is a routing gap and not a missing shape:
    `Error::AmbiguousClauseKey` already renders Postgres's sentence and `GROUP BY` raises
    it, agreeing word-for-word with 18.6 (measured); the sort-key gate raises
    `Error::AmbiguousColumn` instead. The SQLSTATE matches, so `@expect-error` is green
    and no fixture is red; the consequence is that every such fixture's recorded
    `.expected.json` carries a sentence pglet does not emit on that path.

  **Closed: the correlated outer-scope chain.** The half of this class that ran through
  `EvalEnv::resolve_outer_slot` is gone. That resolver had two rules wrong at once, and
  both **wrote**: a qualified reference no frame owned fell into a bare loop that never
  read the qualifier, and an ambiguity at the inner level escalated outward instead of
  raising. Measured against 18.6 and now identical on both engines, each with the rows
  intact: `DELETE FROM hw WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM u2b WHERE u2b.yv = zzz.v)` (`42P01`,
  was `DELETE 1`); the same over a target carrying a bare `b` beside a quoted `"a.b"`
  (`42P01`, was `DELETE 1` — so the dotted-tier fixtures' "add a bare column and it
  destroys a row again" caveat no longer holds); `UPDATE hw x … u2b.yv = hw.v` (`42P01`,
  was `UPDATE 1` writing `99`); `INSERT … SELECT … zzz.v` (`42P01`, was a row stored);
  `DELETE FROM a WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM b WHERE EXISTS (… k.k = a.v))` where `a` owns
  the qualifier and `b` carries the column (`42703`, was every row removed — the
  stop-at-owner rule); `DELETE FROM o WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM c JOIN d ON … WHERE
  v = 1)` (`42702`, was the outer row deleted); and the three `ON CONFLICT … DO UPDATE`
  spellings that **stored the excluded value** — `SET v = zzz.v`, `SET v = "EXCLUDED".v`,
  and `SET v = 'x' WHERE zzz.v = <the excluded value>`. The SQLSTATE half moved with it:
  a frame that owns the qualifier and lacks the column is `42703 "t.name"` where pglet
  said `42P01` (`h.nosuch` over a single-relation outer, `o.nosuch` over a join outer,
  `excluded.nosuch`). Guards: eleven fixtures under `select/correlated_outer_ref_*`,
  `delete/correlated_outer_ref_*`, `insert/on_conflict_do_update_*` and
  `update/correlated_outer_ref_alias_hides_the_table_name.sql` for the SQLSTATEs, and five
  row-survival tests in `crates/pglet/tests/scope_relation_identity.rs` for the writes,
  since `@expect-error` is green for a refusal raised after them.

  **One residual of that half.** The executor's rule is at eval, so it was
  **row-count-dependent** — with either relation empty the headline `DELETE` was
  `DELETE 0`, silent — and the plan-time binding gate above is what closed that.
  The **false rejection** the rule introduced is closed with the pair-keyed scope: an
  outer frame used to own a qualifier by the synthesized `"t."` prefix, which a user's
  quoted `"a.b"` column forges, so over `f3i("a.c", "b.c")` a bare `c` had two suffix
  claimants at the inner resolver and `SELECT c FROM f3o WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM f3i,
  f3z WHERE c = 1)` was `42702` where both engines answer the row. `"a.c"` and `"b.c"` are
  ordinary column names to a pair-keyed scope, so neither claims a bare `c`
  (`select/correlated_outer_ref_dotted_columns_*`).

  **A clause-level instance closed with the grouping check.** `validate_grouped_expr` /
  `validate_grouped_columns` destructured `Expr::Column { name, .. }` and compared the bare
  name against the grouped relation's columns, so an outer-correlated reference was judged as
  if it were a local grouping key: with an overlapping column name, `SELECT okey FROM go WHERE
  EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM gi GROUP BY gi.ikey HAVING go.tag = '<uuid>')` raised `42803` where
  Postgres returns the row. Both sides now test the reference's qualifier against the
  relation's *effective* name (its FROM alias if it has one) through one shared rule, so a key
  or a projected column naming another level's relation neither grounds nor trips the grouping
  check. That is the direction the shared rule decides; a qualifier naming **no** relation
  clears the same test and is the sub-bullet above.

  **Four more items under this number**, each addressable here rather than as a top-level
  block of its own: three positions the gate above did not judge at all, closed at their own
  sites, and one live over-rejection the gates' placement causes. Where a plan-time gate on
  a sort key runs, and why each position needed its own, are `docs/scope.md`.

  - ~~**A top-level `ORDER BY` / `DISTINCT ON` key is exempt from the binding gate
    outright, and it destroys rows.**~~ **Closed** by resolving those keys *after* the
    projection, which is where the claimant set `findTargetlistEntrySQL92` names finally
    exists. **Read "only the qualified spellings" as a statement about the blanket
    exemption and not about this member's own list**: the set-op member below left the
    *qualified* spelling ungated too, by a different mechanism in a different file, and it
    destroyed rows until it was closed at its own site. Members measured on 18.6 and on
    pglet at the default B+tree backend, simple-query text leg, each before and after:

    - An **unreferenced CTE** — `WITH c AS (SELECT a FROM ru2 ORDER BY bogus) DELETE FROM
      rt2` over a two-row `rt2` is `42703` on 18.6 with both rows surviving, and was
      `DELETE 2` here; the `UPDATE` polarity wrote `99` over every row. **Emptiness is not
      load-bearing for this one** — `ru2` was seeded with a row and the answer is the same,
      because the CTE is unreferenced, so its body never executes and the key is never
      evaluated on any data. This member was the blanket's, and its **qualified** spelling
      identifies that: `WITH c AS (SELECT a FROM ru5 ORDER BY bogusrel.a) DELETE FROM rt5`
      is `42P01` on **both** engines with both rows surviving (measured), because the
      blanket exempted bare names only. Three more projecting nodes reached the same
      blanket and a fix aimed at one would have left the others: an **aggregate**'s and a
      **window**'s junk column (`WITH c AS (SELECT count(*) FROM ag GROUP BY a ORDER BY
      bogus) DELETE FROM t`, and its `row_number() OVER ()` twin, both `DELETE 2` here at
      *either* row count) and a **`SELECT DISTINCT`**, which was the one member that never
      wrote — it was already loud with the wrong code, `42P10 for SELECT DISTINCT, ORDER BY
      expressions must appear in select list` for 18.6's `42703`, because a key binding to
      nothing failed the select-list rule before any name check ran. Guarded by
      `select/order_by_key_binds_to_nothing_*` and, for the row survival,
      `crates/pglet/tests/scope_relation_identity.rs`'s `a_sort_key_binding_to_nothing_*`.
    - ~~A **set operation** inside a subquery.~~ **Closed**, and not by the blanket's fix:
      that member had its own two sites — `planner/query.rs`'s `plan_set_op_order_limit`
      resolved the trailing keys with **no `ColumnScope` at all**, and at the correlated
      re-walk `planner/correlation.rs`'s
      `Plan::SetOp { .. } => scope.push_opaque_relation()` makes the level name-unknown, so
      a qualified key answered `Uncertain` and a bare one stopped at the same relation. It
      is closed at the **first** site, hard, because that namespace is complete by
      construction. Guarded by the `select/set_op_order_by_*` fixtures and the
      `a_set_op_sort_key_*` / `a_paren_leading_*` row-survival tests in
      `crates/pglet/tests/scope_relation_identity.rs`. **The divergences the closure leaves
      or introduces**, all measured, and both of the first two are the same wrong-code
      class. A *correlated* key is now loud where it used to answer rows, with 18.6's
      `0A000` spelled as a binding error: `42P01` for the qualified spelling (`… IN (SELECT
      x FROM sa UNION SELECT x FROM sb ORDER BY tgt.a)`) and — the clause this record first
      omitted — `42703` for the **bare** one (`… ORDER BY a`, where `a` is the enclosing
      table's column and the output name is `x`). The computed-key member on the residual
      bullet above rides the same class one level down, and is now closed. And a
      parenthesized operand carrying its **own** `ORDER BY`
      (`(… UNION … ORDER BY a) ORDER BY bogus`) is 18.6's `42601 multiple ORDER BY clauses
      not allowed` — which was once read as a reason *not* to peel a `Plan::Sort`
      in the tree test, and that left the gate's whole subject out of reach: `WITH c AS
      ((SELECT a FROM sa UNION SELECT a FROM sb ORDER BY a) ORDER BY bogus) DELETE FROM tgt`
      destroyed every row, at either row count, in both key polarities, with a `LIMIT` on
      the operand too. The `Sort` was peeled, which made those spellings `42703` / `42P01`;
      the parse now refuses a clause a parenthesized query already carries, `42601` as on
      18.6 and ahead of the peel, and with them the *valid*-key spelling `(… UNION … ORDER
      BY a) ORDER BY a`, which no binding gate could reach and whose unreferenced-CTE
      `DELETE` removed every row (`select/paren_query_order_by_repeated_loud`,
      `cte/paren_query_limit_repeated_in_a_cte_body_loud`). The
      `a_paren_leading_set_op_carrying_*` row-survival tests hold that nothing is written.
      The check runs once the clauses after the parentheses are read, so an error pglet
      raises before that — an analysis error inside the parenthesized query, `(SELECT nosuch
      FROM t LIMIT 1) LIMIT 2`, or under a plain `WITH` in an earlier item (row 80) — is
      reported where 18.6's raw parse reports the `42601`: `42703` here, loud both ways.
      **Still open, and it writes:** a parenthesized **plain** select under a trailing
      `ORDER BY` it does not already carry leaves the key ungated — nothing below the
      operand's `Plan::Limit` is a `Plan::SetOp`, so the walk stops — and `WITH c AS
      ((SELECT a FROM t LIMIT 5) ORDER BY bogus) DELETE FROM tgt WHERE a = 1` deletes its
      row here where 18.6, which merges the key into the plain select, refuses `42703`
      (measured). `a_sort_over_a_bounded_plain_select_stays_ungated` holds that accept side,
      the peel's safety condition, until a gate for this spelling lands.
    - ~~A **no-FROM `SELECT`**, whose parse arm consumed and discarded its whole trailing
      tail.~~ **Closed** — the tail routes through `plan_no_from_order_limit`, which binds
      its keys as well as applying them, and the arm makes the `parse_for_locking()` call
      its siblings make. It was **three divergences in one arm and they are not one
      repair**, and a record naming only the first would have let a reader fix the loud
      member and ship the silent ones.

      *The sort key.* `DELETE FROM n1 WHERE a NOT IN (SELECT 1 AS q ORDER BY zzz)` over a
      three-row `n1` was `DELETE 2` here against 18.6's `42703` and every row surviving; the
      read polarity is the same shape one level up (`… WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 AS q ORDER BY
      zzz)`), and the qualified spelling wrote identically against 18.6's `42P01`, since
      what was dropped is the whole clause. **Routing the tail does not by itself close
      that**, which this record previously predicted it would (*"expected, not measured"* —
      and the measurement says no): a `Plan::Sort` over a `Plan::Values` judges its key only
      where a row reaches the eval-time resolver, so the empty-projection read
      (`SELECT unnest(ARRAY[]::int[]) AS q ORDER BY zzz`) and the unreferenced-CTE write
      (`WITH c AS (SELECT 1 AS q ORDER BY zzz) DELETE FROM n8`, whose body never runs) would
      both still be silent.

      *The bound, which is the worse half because it is silent on **both** engines.*
      Measured with `w1`/`w2` holding three rows each and `w3` empty: `SELECT 1 AS q LIMIT 0`
      and `SELECT 1 AS q OFFSET 1` each answered a row against `(0 rows)` there;
      `DELETE FROM w1 WHERE a IN (SELECT 1 AS q LIMIT 0)` removed a row 18.6 keeps,
      `UPDATE w2 SET a=99 WHERE a IN (SELECT 1 AS q OFFSET 1)` overwrote one, and
      `INSERT INTO w3 SELECT 7 AS q LIMIT 0` invented one. No statement in that list raises on
      either engine. What made the discard read as `ORDER BY`-only from outside is that
      `parse_limit_offset` still *validated* what it threw away (`LIMIT -1` is `2201W`,
      `OFFSET -1` is `2201X`, identically on both).

      *The locking clause, never reached rather than discarded.* `SELECT 1 FOR UPDATE` /
      `FOR SHARE` / `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` were `42601` here against one row each there, as was
      `SELECT 1 AS q ORDER BY 1 LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE`. Two controls put it on the arm rather
      than the clause and both already answered on both engines: `SELECT a FROM lk FOR
      UPDATE` (the `FromParts` arm) and `(SELECT 1 AS q) FOR UPDATE` (the paren-leading arm,
      whose `(SELECT 1 AS q) LIMIT 0` likewise already answered `(0 rows)`).

      Guarded by the `select/no_from_*` fixtures (the two bounds and their `DELETE`/`UPDATE`/
      `INSERT … SELECT` polarities, the four refusal spellings, the two interleave halves,
      the correlated accept, the two locking spellings, and the composed
      direction/bound/offset — over an array chosen so the two `Sort`/`Limit` nestings
      disagree) and by the `a_no_from_*` row-survival tests in
      `crates/pglet/tests/scope_relation_identity.rs`.

      **Three things stay open on this arm**, each measured. A **sequence
      projection** keeps the discard: the executor dispatches
      `SELECT nextval/currval/setval(…)` on `Plan::is_sequence_projection`, which matches a
      bare `Plan::Values`, so wrapping one routes it to the read-only eval path where a
      `SequenceFn` is `0A000` — the gates run over it, but the `Sort`/`Limit` is not built, so
      `SELECT nextval('s') LIMIT 0` answers a row against 18.6's `(0 rows)` (18.6 also leaves
      the counter unadvanced there, where each pglet spelling measured — `LIMIT 0`,
      `OFFSET 1`, `ORDER BY 1`, `DISTINCT` — advances it) while `OFFSET 1` is `(0 rows)`
      there **with** the counter advanced. Two things about that member's *extent*, because
      "top level" was how it was first written and is narrower than what it reaches. It is
      not confined to the outermost select: a **referenced CTE body** carries it too, so
      `WITH c AS (SELECT nextval('s') AS n LIMIT 0) SELECT * FROM c` answers a row and
      advances the counter here against `(0 rows)` and no advance there — silent on both
      engines, which is the worse polarity and the one the top-level spelling shares. And it
      is not confined to a *sole* sequence expression, `is_sequence_projection` matching on
      `any` projected expression: `SELECT nextval('s') AS n, 1 AS q LIMIT 0` is a row here
      against `(0 rows)` there. What bounds it, on the polarities measured, is that each
      **write** spelling is loud here, so none of them carries the wrong row count into a
      table — `INSERT INTO n8 SELECT nextval('s') LIMIT 0` and
      `DELETE FROM n8 WHERE a IN (SELECT nextval('s') LIMIT 0)` are `0A000` (a `nextval`
      outside a top-level projection at all) against `INSERT 0 0` / `DELETE 0` there, and
      `WITH c AS (SELECT nextval('s') AS n LIMIT 0) DELETE FROM n8` is `0A000` against
      `DELETE 2` there, with the plain `WITH c AS (SELECT 1 AS q) DELETE FROM n8` answering
      `DELETE 2` on both as the control that puts that one on the sequence rather than on the
      unreferenced CTE. The quantifier clauses take the same exclusion and it is **sound**
      there rather than open — a dedup over the single projected row returns that row — so
      `SELECT DISTINCT nextval('s')` and `SELECT DISTINCT ON (1) nextval('s')` answer
      identically on both engines. The
      **`LIMIT`-outranks-the-key** precedence now reaches this arm too, the pre-existing
      parse-time/plan-time split: `SELECT 1 AS q ORDER BY zzz LIMIT -1` is `2201W` here and
      18.6's `42703`, loud both ways. And the `42702` **over-rejection** widens by one
      spelling: `SELECT 1 AS q, 1 AS q ORDER BY q` is `42702` here against 18.6's row — the
      `ORDER BY` member of `correlation::target_list_exprs`' recorded `Plan::Values` gap,
      whose `DISTINCT ON` member was already open, with `SELECT 1 AS q, 2 AS q ORDER BY q`
      (`42702` on both) as the control that identifies the gap rather than the gate. **That
      one has a write polarity**, and it is row-count-**independent**:
      `WITH c AS (SELECT 1 AS q, 1 AS q ORDER BY q) DELETE FROM n8` is `42702` here with both
      rows surviving against 18.6's `DELETE 2`, and over an empty target it is the same
      `42702` here against `DELETE 0` there. Loud in both, so it refuses a statement rather
      than mis-writing one — but a `DELETE` refused is still a `DELETE` that did not happen.
      Two adjacent shapes are **not** members of anything new: a scalar-subquery sort key
      (`ORDER BY (SELECT 1)`) is `0A000` engine-wide — `SELECT a FROM ct ORDER BY (SELECT 1)`
      and the paren-leading `(SELECT 1 AS q) ORDER BY (SELECT 1)` are both `0A000` here and
      rows on 18.6, and neither goes through this arm — so the no-FROM arm has joined that
      pre-existing class rather than answering by dropping the clause; and the locking
      clause's own **semantic** refusals are accepted here, `parse_for_locking`'s recorded
      leniency, newly *reachable* from this arm rather than newly wrong. That leniency is
      wider than the one `OF` member it was recorded as. **Read the members below as the
      clause's *semantic* refusals only** — the wait policy is no longer among them, both
      spellings having moved to a `0A000` refusal of pglet's own (`docs/compatibility.md`'s `FOR UPDATE`
      row); every member here is a case where 18.6 refuses a clause pglet honours as a
      no-op, and refusing them would reject spine SQL that runs correctly here. Postgres's
      `CheckSelectLocking`
      raises `0A000` on seven grounds — a set operation, `DISTINCT` (which `DISTINCT ON`
      shares), `GROUP BY`, `HAVING`, an aggregate, a window function, and a set-returning
      function in the target list — and each has a spelling measured accepted here.
      **`HAVING` has a message of its own** (`FOR UPDATE is not allowed with HAVING
      clause`), re-derived from `analyze.c` and measured: the reason a `GROUP BY … HAVING`
      spelling reports the `GROUP BY` message is only that `groupClause` is tested first,
      and `SELECT 1 FROM lk HAVING true FOR UPDATE` reaches the HAVING one (rows here). Six
      of them in the FROM-bearing form over a
      two-row `lk(a)`:
      `SELECT a FROM lk UNION SELECT a FROM lk FOR UPDATE`, `SELECT DISTINCT a FROM lk FOR
      UPDATE`, `SELECT DISTINCT ON (a) a FROM lk FOR UPDATE`, `SELECT a FROM lk GROUP BY a
      FOR UPDATE`, its `HAVING a > 0` spelling, `SELECT count(*) FROM lk FOR UPDATE` and
      `SELECT row_number() OVER () FROM lk FOR UPDATE` each answer rows. The seventh has no
      FROM-bearing spelling to measure — `SELECT unnest(ARRAY[1,2]) AS q, a FROM lk FOR
      UPDATE` is `0A000` here for an unrelated reason, a set-returning `unnest` being
      supported only in a projection — and its no-FROM form is one of the three this arm
      newly reaches. Those three are `SELECT DISTINCT 1 AS q FOR UPDATE`, `SELECT DISTINCT
      ON (1) 1 AS q FOR UPDATE` and `SELECT unnest(ARRAY[1,2]) AS q FOR UPDATE`, each a row
      here and `0A000` there, against the plain `SELECT 1 AS q FOR UPDATE` that answers on
      both. `FOR UPDATE OF <a relation not in FROM>` is an eighth of a different code,
      `transformLockingClause`'s `42P01`, accepted here the same way — as is
      `FROM lt AS q … FOR UPDATE OF lt`, the alias-hidden spelling of the same refusal. A
      **ninth**: `FOR UPDATE OF <a CTE>` is `0A000 FOR UPDATE cannot be applied to a WITH
      query` there and rows here, with `FOR UPDATE OF <a derived table>` as the control
      that identifies the RTE kind rather than the `OF` list — 18.6 **accepts** that one
      (`applyLockingClause` recurses into the subquery), and so does pglet. Read those as
      the members, not as a closed enumeration of what a no-op locking clause lets through.
      The **wait policy is no longer among them** — see the note above.
    - An **`INSERT … SELECT`** whose source carries the key — `INSERT INTO rt5 SELECT a, 1
      FROM ru5 ORDER BY bogus` over an empty `ru5` reported `INSERT 0 0` here and is `42703`
      on 18.6. It inserts nothing, so this member was a silent *success* rather than a write,
      and unlike the unreferenced-CTE member it **is** row-count-dependent: seed one row into
      `ru5` and pglet raised `42703` too (measured). Its qualified spelling
      (`… ORDER BY bogusrel.a`) is `42P01` on both at either row count, so this member was the
      blanket's like the CTE one.
    - The **read** polarity of the ambiguous spelling — `SELECT sjq1.x FROM sjq1 JOIN sjq2
      ON false ORDER BY n` over a `sjq1(n, x)` and a `sjq2(n, y)` answered here and is
      `42702` on 18.6. Its *nested* spelling was refused on both
      (`select/subquery_sort_key_ambiguous_output_name_loud.sql`), which is what identified
      the first lowering rather than the shape. The target-list half of the same rule was a
      member too: `SELECT c AS q, x AS q FROM ja2 ORDER BY q` over an empty `ja2` answered
      here and is `42702` there.

    Guarded, and named as members rather than as a class: the four projecting nodes'
    reads and the write polarities (`select/order_by_key_binds_to_nothing_*` plus
    `a_sort_key_binding_to_nothing_*` for row survival), the ambiguity in both its join and
    its target-list spellings (`select/order_by_ambiguous_*`, `an_ambiguous_sort_key_does_not_
    delete`), the accept half the claimant set must keep
    (`select/order_by_star_and_bare_duplicate_resolve.sql`, its `AS`-label twin, and
    `a_sort_key_may_name_an_output_alias_or_a_dropped_base_column`), the three precedence pairs
    with their `GROUP BY` control, and the two interleave pairs. Their nested twins stay: a
    nested key binding to nothing (`select/subquery_sort_key_binds_to_nothing_loud.sql`), a
    nested key two of a join's columns claim
    (`select/subquery_sort_key_ambiguous_output_name_loud.sql` and four row-survival tests),
    and two matching target-list entries under one name
    (`select/nested_sort_key_duplicate_output_entries_resolve.sql` and its `_loud.sql` twin) —
    two phases, two derivations, either able to regress alone. A level whose own scope cannot
    enumerate a relation is in none of them — a catalog view, which registers
    non-exhaustively.

  - ~~**A no-FROM set-op leaf re-reads nothing it encloses, and where no enclosing level
    does either, a write through it destroys every row.**~~ **Closed** by the one
    `resolve_correlated_subplans` call `finalize_leaf` did not make, handed the same
    `scope_is_complete()` its twin passes. Measured on 18.6 and on pglet at the default
    B+tree backend, simple-query text leg, over a two-row `n8` and an empty `et`:

    - `WITH c AS (SELECT 1 AS z UNION ALL SELECT (SELECT DISTINCT ON (bogusdon) 1 AS q))
      DELETE FROM n8` is `DELETE 2` here, leaving none, against 18.6's
      `42703 column "bogusdon" does not exist` and both rows.
    - **The class is not the `DISTINCT ON` gate's and needs no key at all**: `SELECT 1 AS z
      UNION ALL SELECT (SELECT 1 FROM et WHERE zzz.k = 1)` answers two rows here (`1` and
      NULL) against 18.6's `42P01 missing FROM-clause entry for table "zzz"`, so an ordinary
      correlated reference rides it too.

    Two controls put it on the leaf rather than on the key or on the `WITH`. **Drop the
    `UNION ALL`** and both statements refuse with 18.6's own SQLSTATEs, both rows surviving
    (`WITH c AS (SELECT (SELECT DISTINCT ON (bogusdon) 1 AS q)) DELETE FROM n8` is `42703`
    here, and the `zzz.k` twin `42P01`) — that leaf lowers through `parse_select_inner`'s arm,
    which makes the call. **Wrap the set op in an `IN (…)`** instead — `DELETE FROM n8 WHERE a
    IN (SELECT 1 AS z UNION ALL SELECT …)` — and the *enclosing* statement's re-walk reaches
    it, likewise refusing with both rows surviving. The write polarity is row-count
    independent (the CTE is unreferenced, so its body never executes), and the no-FROM
    `DISTINCT ON` binding gate neither opened nor closed any of this: it declines at
    expression-subquery depth by design, and the second member carries no key for it to
    judge. A **third** member the record above missed: the leaf on the **left** of the set op
    reaches `finalize_leaf` through the other call site (`parse_select_inner`'s own rather
    than `parse_setop_operand`'s) and wrote identically, so the repair belongs in the shared
    function and not at one caller. Guarded by the `select/set_op_no_from_*` fixtures and the
    `a_set_op_no_from_*` row-survival tests in
    `crates/pglet/tests/scope_relation_identity.rs`.

  - ~~**Plain `DISTINCT` over a no-FROM projection `unnest` is a complete no-op, and one
    polarity of it writes an extra row.**~~ **Closed** — `parser::select`'s no-FROM arm
    builds a real `Plan::Distinct` where it discarded the flag. The discard was sound over
    the one-row `Plan::Values` that arm was written for and a complete no-op over
    `Plan::ProjectUnnest`, which row-expands. Measured before:

    - `SELECT DISTINCT unnest(ARRAY[2,1,2,1]) AS q` answered `2 1 2 1` against 18.6's two
      rows, and the projection's arity did not change it (`…, 7 AS r` was four rows here and
      two there);
    - `INSERT INTO n8 SELECT DISTINCT unnest(ARRAY[1,1,2])` was **`INSERT 0 3`** against
      18.6's `INSERT 0 2` — an extra row, with no error on either engine.

    Three controls narrowed it to this arm and this clause and are the shape of the guards:
    the same dedup over a **FROM**-clause `unnest` was two rows on both; `SELECT DISTINCT 1
    AS q` — the one-row `Values` the elision is true of — was one row on both; and
    `DISTINCT ON` over the identical no-FROM shape was correct at every measured spelling,
    because that clause built a real `Plan::DistinctOn` where this one was dropped. The one
    exclusion is the sequence projection the member above names, which is a single row and
    so the case the elision is sound for.

    **A dedup's output order is unspecified and 18.6's is not pglet's**: over
    `ARRAY[2,1,2,1]` 18.6's hash aggregate answers `1 2` and pglet's first-seen dedup `2 1`,
    and over `ARRAY[3,1,4,2]` an `OFFSET 1` splits them further. Both are correct; a fixture
    over the bare spelling would pin an order neither engine promises, so the read guard
    carries an `ORDER BY` and the row *count* is pinned separately by the `INSERT` polarity.
    Guarded by `select/no_from_distinct_dedups_an_unnest.sql`, its one-row control,
    `select/no_from_distinct_as_a_set_op_operand.sql`,
    `insert/select_distinct_no_from_unnest_dedups.sql`, and
    `a_no_from_distinct_does_not_write_an_extra_row`.

    **Left open beside it**, measured and unchanged in polarity by that fix: Postgres's rule
    that a `SELECT DISTINCT`'s `ORDER BY` expressions appear in the select list is not
    enforced for this shape, so `SELECT DISTINCT unnest(ARRAY[2,1]) AS q ORDER BY 1+1`
    answers here against 18.6's `42P10`. What reaches it is **any key naming no column**, not
    only a constant one — `ORDER BY abs(-1)`, `ORDER BY length('ab')` and `ORDER BY now()`
    each answer here against the same `42P10`, and a key naming no column *beside* one that
    does reaches it too (`ORDER BY q, 1+1`). The bound is the binding gate rather than
    constant-ness: a key that names something is judged there first, and over a no-FROM
    select the only names are its own target list, so a bare one resolves (and then satisfies
    the rule) while a nested one is an ordinary column reference against an empty FROM scope
    — `… ORDER BY q+0` is `42703` on both engines. The FROM-bearing spellings of the same
    keys are `42P10` on both (`SELECT DISTINCT q FROM t ORDER BY 1+1`, `… ORDER BY abs(-1)`),
    which is the control that puts the residual on this shape rather than on the rule.

  - **A derived table or CTE resets the chain-completeness depth, so a plan-time gate inside
    one refuses ordinary correlated SQL.** A **loud over-rejection**, live, and the price
    paid for the gates above firing at those positions at all. `Parser::in_from_item` resets
    `expr_subquery_depth` to `0` for a derived table's or a CTE's body, on the reasoning that
    a `LATERAL`-less FROM item cannot see the enclosing query's relations — which is **half
    of Postgres's rule**, so a FROM item nested inside an `EXISTS`/`IN`/scalar subquery is
    handed a closed scope missing every enclosing relation and any gate reading it invents a
    `42P01`. The members measured, each rows on 18.6 and
    `42P01 missing FROM-clause entry for table "ct"` here, over `ct(a)` and `ct2(b)`:

    - `SELECT * FROM ct WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM (SELECT 1 AS q ORDER BY ct.a) x)` — the
      most ordinary member and the one that routing **opened**, since the no-FROM `ORDER BY`
      key had no plan-time gate before the tail was routed. Measured red-on-revert: with
      `plan_no_from_order_limit`'s `check_key_bindings` call removed it answers both rows,
      and the FROM-bearing pair below is unchanged by that same mutation — which is what puts
      this one on the new gate and that pair on the pre-existing scope.
    - `SELECT * FROM ct WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM (SELECT b FROM ct2 ORDER BY ct.a) x)` and
      `… (SELECT b FROM ct2 WHERE b = ct.a) x` — the FROM-bearing spellings, both
      pre-existing.
    - `SELECT * FROM ct WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM (SELECT DISTINCT ON (ct.a) 1 AS q) x)` —
      the no-FROM `DISTINCT ON` spelling. It carries no `ORDER BY`, so
      `plan_no_from_order_limit` gates nothing on it and the refusal is
      `plan_no_from_distinct_on`'s own key gate, which predates that routing.

    Two controls narrow it to the clauses a plan-time gate reads, rather than to a nested
    FROM item's correlated references in general — both answer on both engines. The
    **projection** spelling puts the outer reference in the derived table's target list
    instead of in a key, at both positions measured (`… EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM (SELECT ct.a AS
    q) x)` and `SELECT (SELECT * FROM (SELECT ct.a AS q) x) FROM ct`). The projection
    spelling **with a FROM** is a member, not a control: over a non-empty `ct2`, `… EXISTS
    (SELECT 1 FROM (SELECT ct.a AS q FROM ct2) x)` and `SELECT (SELECT max(x.q) FROM (SELECT
    ct.a AS q FROM ct2) x) FROM ct` are `42P01` here and both rows on 18.6. The **gate-free tail**
    spelling `… EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM (SELECT 1 AS q LIMIT 1) x)` routes through the very arm
    the first member does and carries no key for the gate to judge.

    **What the repair waits on is measured, not estimated.** The rule it has to satisfy —
    a FROM item may be left provisional only where some `resolve_correlated_subplans`
    re-walk will reach it with a complete chain and a decidable namespace — is
    `docs/scope.md`; the one-line spelling of it (*reset only when the depth is already
    `0`*) was probed and carries two routes, of which **route one is now closed and route
    two is measured open**. With `lower_insert` running the pass and `walk_level`'s
    `Plan::Insert` arm visiting all three clause positions, every one of the seven `INSERT`
    members (`RETURNING` scalar/`EXISTS`/`IN`, its bogus-qualifier spelling, the
    `ON CONFLICT` `SET` and action `WHERE`, and the data-modifying-CTE spelling) refuses
    identically to 18.6 **with the one-line change applied**. The `Uncertain` route is
    untouched by it and still writes: over `n8(v)` = {1, 2},
    `DELETE FROM n8 WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM information_schema.columns c WHERE NOT
    EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM (SELECT b AS q FROM et ORDER BY zzz) x))` is `42703` with both
    rows surviving here, and `DELETE 2` under the change against 18.6's refusal. So what the
    repair still needs is a decision about a provisional FROM item beneath a
    non-exhaustively-registered relation — a change to `ColumnScope::check_binding`'s
    three-way verdict, not to `in_from_item` — and until then the change stays unshipped.
    **The `unnest` arm's flip narrowed which relations can be that blocker without
    touching the blocker itself**: a FROM-clause `unnest(…)` is columns-exhaustive at both
    scope builders now, so it is no longer one of them, and the substituted spelling
    (`… EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM unnest(ARRAY[1]) AS u(k) WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM
    (SELECT b AS q FROM et ORDER BY zzz) x))`) is `42703` on both engines — measured, and
    it was already `42703` before the flip, since the inner derived table resets the depth
    and closes at its own lowering. The member above stands as written: its relation is a
    catalog view, and a scan of a table the catalog lacks is the other.

  - **The four output-entry causes are row-count-independent at a level's own lowering as
    well as inside a nested one**, and that widening is what moving the keys behind the
    projection cost. Measured before and after over an empty `ja2(c, x)` and a two-row
    one, each `42702` here at the seeded row count before and `42702` at either row count
    after, against 18.6's rows throughout — the no-op cast
    `SELECT c::int AS q, c AS q … ORDER BY q`, the un-normalized list
    `c IN (1,2) AS q, c = ANY(ARRAY[1,2]) AS q`, the unknown-typed literal's cast
    `true AS q, 't'::bool AS q`, and two of `sole_relation_carrying`'s declines,
    `SELECT *, c FROM ua JOIN ub USING (c) ORDER BY c` and the
    `information_schema.tables` self-pair. No accept shape measured changed and no
    existing fixture did; the causes themselves are the residual list above.
  - **The no-FROM `DISTINCT` node is built in the leaf, so the set-op-operand route
    carries the quantifier too — measured, not assumed**:
    `SELECT DISTINCT unnest(ARRAY[2,1,2]) AS q UNION ALL SELECT 9` is three rows on 18.6
    and three here, which is what `select/no_from_distinct_as_a_set_op_operand.sql` pins.
- **46 · A FROM-clause `unnest(…)` registered non-exhaustively — closed, and the row is
  live for the residual it left: a name nested inside a sort key still binds the output
  column where 18.6 binds the FROM column.** The class (a bogus name into such an item
  judged only where a row reached the eval-time resolver, and a write through it
  destroying rows at any row count) closed in two steps, the *columns* first and the
  *exhaustive bit* second, each closing a different half and neither reachable from the
  other: `build_column_scope` registered such a FROM item with `push_partial_relation` —
  the name known, the columns known, **not** columns-exhaustive — and uses `push_relation`
  now, which is Postgres's own reading (a function RTE has exactly its declared columns)
  and, here, literally the node's `output_columns`. Registering *nothing* was never the
  alternative — a closed scope would then answer `42P01` for a qualifier the statement
  plainly writes. Why one relation kind had three registration routes, and which readers
  of the exhaustive bit can move with it, are `docs/scope.md`.

  **Step one, the columns**, moved exactly one `Binding` arm: the **claimant count**.
  `binding_bare` counts every relation whose
  `columns` map holds the name, exhaustive or not, and tests `claimants >= 2` **ahead** of
  the uncertainty check, so a bare name a sibling relation also carries went from one
  claimant to two and became a plan-time `42702`. Measured over `amb_un(id, x)`:
  `SELECT id FROM amb_un, unnest(ARRAY[]::int[]) AS u(id)` answered `(0 rows)` here and is
  `42702` at **Parse** — raw v3 `Parse` + `Sync`, error before `ParseComplete`, which is
  exactly where 18.6's `colNameToVar` raises it. The `x` spelling likewise. The **empty**
  array is what makes that a closure and not a no-op: the `ARRAY[7]` spelling was already
  `42702` on both engines, from the eval-time resolver a row reaches. Pinned by
  `select/unnest_ambiguous_bare_name.sql`. The other two arms did **not** move with the
  columns — a name the relation carries was `Uncertain` and became `Bound` (both `Ok(())`),
  and a name it lacks stayed `Uncertain`, because non-exhaustive is what
  `level_columns_uncertain` reads, not the map.

  **Step two, the exhaustive bit**, which is the arm the columns could not reach and where
  every silent member of this bullet lived. Measured over a two-row `n8`, each `(0 rows)`
  or `DELETE 2` before and `42703` on both engines after:

  - `SELECT v.bogus FROM unnest(ARRAY[]::int[]) AS v(q)` and the bare
    `SELECT bogus FROM unnest(ARRAY[]::int[]) AS u(x)`;
  - `WITH c AS (SELECT v.q FROM unnest(ARRAY[1,2]) AS v(q) WHERE v.bogus = 1) DELETE FROM
    n8` — `DELETE 2` here, leaving none, against 18.6's `42703` and both rows — and the
    same statement over `unnest(ARRAY[]::int[])` and in the bare spelling, all three
    writing identically, so **emptiness was not load-bearing for the write** (the CTE is
    unreferenced; its body never runs);
  - the clause positions, none of which follows from the others: `GROUP BY bogus`,
    `ORDER BY bogus`, `HAVING bogus > 1`;
  - a name **nested** inside a sort key, which was the *silent* member and needed rows to
    be visible at all: `SELECT lbl AS q FROM unnest(ARRAY[3,1,2]) AS u(lbl) ORDER BY q + 0`
    answered its rows, sorted, against 18.6's `42703` (row 46);
  - a `DISTINCT ON` key naming nothing over a bare `*` projection:
    `SELECT DISTINCT ON (nosuch) * FROM unnest(ARRAY[1,2,2]) AS u ORDER BY nosuch` was
    `0A000` here (the third member of `docs/compatibility.md`'s `DISTINCT ON` row).

  **The phase moved with it and the non-empty spellings are the control that says so.**
  With elements, the eval-time resolver reaches the reference and raises the same `42703`,
  so `SELECT bogus FROM unnest(ARRAY[1,2]) AS u(x)` was already green on both engines —
  what changed there is only *where*: raw `Parse` + `Sync` now errors before
  `ParseComplete` on pglet as it does on 18.6, where it used to answer `ParseComplete` and
  raise at `Execute`. That is why every reject fixture in the family carries
  `ARRAY[]::int[]` and the nested-sort-key one does not.

  Two controls fix the mechanism. The same CTE `DELETE` over a plain table
  (`FROM pt p WHERE p.bogus = 1`) was `42703` here with both rows surviving throughout, so
  it was the relation *kind* and not the statement shape. And the same bogus name **one
  level down** (`… WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM unnest(ARRAY[]::int[]) AS u(q) WHERE nosuch
  = 1)`) was `42703` on both engines throughout, because `push_level_relations` — the walk
  that builds a *correlated* sub-plan's scope — always registered an `Unnest` with
  `push_relation`. A **third** builder never had the split either: `push_plan_relations`
  has only `push_relation`, which is why `UPDATE pt SET v='x' FROM unnest(…) u(x) WHERE
  bogus = 1` was `42703` on both engines before the flip. Three builders, one relation
  kind, and the answer differed by route — `select/unnest_bogus_bare_name_one_level_down_loud.sql`
  and `update/unnest_from_source_bogus_bare_name_loud.sql` are those two controls, green on
  either side of the flip and there to keep the routes distinguishable.

  **No gate could see the flip**, which is why the fixtures came first: the whole gate
  corpus was green with the arm already exhaustive (1756/0/8 fixtures, 1431/0
  `cargo test --workspace`, both declared-type legs unmoved with 0 divergent), so the split
  measured on the revert is the whole of the evidence. **Eight redden**, and one of the
  eight is not an error fixture: the six `_loud` rejects
  (`select/unnest_bogus_bare_name_own_level_loud.sql`, `…_qualified_name_own_level_loud`,
  `…_group_by_key_loud`, `…_order_by_key_loud`, `…_having_name_loud`,
  `select/unnest_nested_order_by_name_loud.sql`), the write closure
  `select/unnest_bogus_bare_name_in_a_cte_delete_loud.sql` (the unreferenced-CTE `DELETE`
  above — measured on the pre-flip build removing both rows with no error, the one shape in
  the family where the flip stops a data loss; the harness pins its code, not the
  survival), plus
  `select/unnest_duplicate_output_entries_bind_to_the_unnest.sql`, whose pre-flip answer
  was a false `42702` — an accept-shaped fixture guarding a reader that answers no
  `Binding` at all. **Six stay green either way**: the four accepts
  (`…_real_column_over_an_empty_array_answers`, `…_sibling_relations_bare_name_binds`,
  `…_output_alias_sort_key_answers`, `…_correlated_outer_bare_name_answers`) and the two
  route controls named in the paragraph above. Shapes the flip closes that no fixture names
  — a window `ORDER BY` key, both `UNION` and `EXCEPT` branches (pre-flip a misleading `UNION types
  text and integer cannot be matched`), `INSERT … SELECT bogus`, a data-modifying CTE's
  tail, a `JOIN … USING` level, a recursive-CTE level, `ON CONFLICT DO
  UPDATE`'s `WHERE` and `SET` subqueries, and `IN (SELECT bogus …)` — are each `42703` on
  both engines now, and are recorded so the fixture list is not read as the closure's
  extent.

  **One reader moved that is not `check_binding`, and it closed a false
  rejection nothing in this bullet predicted** — while two more read the same field and
  *cannot* move, for a reason about this scope rather than about their rules.
  `bare_candidates` and `qualified` consult `level_columns_uncertain` only to decide
  whether to keep walking **outward**, and `build_column_scope` has nowhere outward to go,
  so both readers answer identically either way: the "the coercion pass could not walk
  *past* an unnest level to type an enclosing relation's column" this paragraph used to
  claim has no reachable member — it was a mechanism story attributed to an unmeasured
  widening, and the reading that produced it (a reader consults the field, therefore the
  field's flip moves it) is the one to distrust. The three genuine movers are
  `binding_qualified`, `binding_bare` and the one below.
  `ColumnScope::sole_relation_carrying` declines outright on an uncertain level, so no
  `ORDER BY` key over an unnest level could be bound to its relation when
  `output_name_binding` decides whether two same-named target entries are one expression or
  two: `SELECT u.x AS q, x AS q FROM unnest(ARRAY[]::int[]) AS u(x) ORDER BY q` was `42702`
  here against 18.6's `(0 rows)` and now agrees
  (`select/unnest_duplicate_output_entries_bind_to_the_unnest.sql`). Its non-empty spelling
  is **still** `42702` here (the eval-time resolver flags the collision on the row it is
  handed) and its `GROUP BY q` spelling likewise, from a resolver that does not read this
  binding — both open, both loud.

  **Three false rejections beside the bogus spellings were closed by the columns half**,
  and the first was recorded here as one the repair "may not reach, because it is eval-time
  in the sort-below path rather than a scope fact" — a mechanism claim, and wrong: it was a
  scope fact. A *real* `unnest` column the projection drops can be sorted by
  (`SELECT q * 10 AS x FROM unnest(ARRAY[3,1,2]) AS v(q) ORDER BY v.q, q`, both spellings,
  `42703` before and `10, 20, 30` on both engines now —
  `select/unnest_dropped_column_sort_key.sql`, red on the revert of the registration). The
  second is the `DISTINCT ON` **qualified**-key member
  (`select/distinct_on_unnest_qualified_key_over_star.sql`; its bogus-key twin needed the
  exhaustive bit, above). The third is the **comparison gate**, which typed the column from
  the same scope, so `SELECT v FROM unnest(ARRAY[1,2]) AS u(v) WHERE v = '2'` was
  `42883 operator does not exist: integer = text` — bare and qualified spellings alike, `>`
  as well as `=`, and the `LEFT JOIN` spelling too — where both engines answer. Pinned by
  `select/unnest_column_compared_with_literal.sql` (the `LEFT JOIN` spelling left unpinned:
  it reaches the same registration through the same `collect_function_scan_into` join arm).

  **Row-count dependence splits two-to-one among those three, and this bullet used to say
  "both", of the first two, wrongly.** Re-measured against the pre-fix build at both array
  lengths: the dropped sort key is row-count dependent (empty answers `(0 rows)` on both
  engines, non-empty was `42703` here) and so is the comparison gate (empty `(0 rows)` on
  both, non-empty `42883`) — for the same reason, that the *gate* is eval-time
  (`planner/legality.rs`'s rulebook, per row for a `WHERE` predicate) even though the
  coercion feeding it is plan-time, which is the inference worth resisting. The
  `DISTINCT ON` member is **not**: it is a plan-time `0A000` at any row count, raised over
  `unnest(ARRAY[]::int[])` as readily as over `ARRAY[1,2,2]`, against 18.6's `(0 rows)` and
  two rows respectively. All three fixtures carry a non-empty array regardless — for the
  first two because an empty one reaches no defect, for the third because the rows *are*
  the comparison.

  **What the flip did not touch, re-measured on both engines**, so a reader does not read
  this closure as wider than it is: `SELECT u.*` over an unnest is still `0A000` here
  against 18.6's rows **where no base table shares the alias's spelling** — it reads
  `expand_qualified_wildcard`, a name-keyed walk whose `nonbase` map has no `Unnest` arm,
  which is why widening this scope never widened it, and where a base table *does* carry
  the name that same miss falls to the catalog and expands *its* columns — silently, or
  `42703`, by that collision's own polarity (row 8); a
  column-alias list longer than the relation
  (`SELECT * FROM unnest(ARRAY[1,2]) AS u(a,b)`) is still accepted here against 18.6's
  `42P10`; and a bare `unnest($1)` is still pglet's `0A000` against 18.6's `42725 function
  unnest(unknown) is not unique`.

  **One recorded divergence *moved*, and the move is a silent-to-loud one worth naming.**
  Two FROM items sharing an alias are 18.6's `42712 table name "u" specified more than
  once`, a gate pglet does not have; `function_scan_columns` keys its map by effective name, so
  the two collapse into one entry and both scope relations get the **second** one's
  columns. Non-exhaustive, a name only the *first* carries was `Uncertain` and fell through
  to the executor's own row resolver, which answered it: over
  `unnest(ARRAY[1]) u(x), unnest(ARRAY[2]) u(y)`, `SELECT x` and `SELECT u.x` each answered
  `1` — **no error on either engine's side of the wire**, a wrong answer to a statement
  18.6 refuses outright. Both are `42703` now, and the `SELECT *` spelling moved from
  `42702` to the same `42703`; `SELECT y` was and remains `42702`. Those four are wrong
  *codes* against `42712`, so for them the flip traded two silent wrongs for a loud one —
  **but the collapse still answers rows through the spellings the second relation's
  columns serve**: `SELECT u.y` answers `2` (and `3, 4, 3, 4` over two-element arrays),
  and over `u(x), u(x)` the `SELECT u.x` spelling answers rows too, both before and after
  the flip, each a wrong answer to a statement 18.6 refuses. No fixture can hold any of
  it — an `@expect-error` compares SQLSTATEs and these differ, and the silent members
  answer — and the real repair is the `42712` gate, which closes every spelling at once.

  **The flip also reordered the gate ahead of a parser error, visible only through
  unparsed syntax.** `SELECT x, n FROM unnest(ARRAY[10,20]) WITH ORDINALITY AS u(x, n)` was
  `42601` at the `WITH` and is `42703 column "x" does not exist` now, where 18.6 answers
  `10|1, 20|2` — `WITH ORDINALITY` is unparsed here either way, so no accepted statement
  regressed, but the message now names as missing a column the user wrote as the alias.
  The control that identifies it as ordering rather than a parse change: a name that
  *does* resolve (`SELECT unnest FROM unnest(…) WITH ORDINALITY`) still gets the syntax
  error on both sides of the flip.

  **A pre-existing member the flip neither opened nor closed, found beside it — since
  CLOSED, and it was never an unnest defect at all: a FROM item whose name collides with a
  base table's bound to the *table*.** The recorded scope
  ("a FROM-clause `unnest(…) AS <name>`") was the narrowest spelling of it; the widest is
  `WITH t AS (SELECT … FROM t) SELECT … FROM t`, a CTE named for its own source, which is
  ordinary SQL. The two recorded members, re-measured, conform now:
  over a real `rv_u(x, y)`, `SELECT z
  FROM unnest(ARRAY[1,2]) rv_u(z)` answers `1, 2` (it was `42703` here — a **false
  rejection** at any row count) and `SELECT rv_u.x FROM unnest(ARRAY[]::int[]) rv_u(z)` is
  `42703` (it was `(0 rows)`, the silent polarity). The control identifying the mechanism —
  an alias matching a table that happens to carry the referenced column — answered on both
  engines throughout. The wider class, its members across both polarities, the two readers
  (`build_column_scope`, and a column check that refused only over a **one-column**
  relation, so the arity of a table the query never reads decided whether the statement
  was refused — that check is gone, row 159), and what the repair does **not** reach are
  `docs/scope.md` § A FROM name is
  resolved by the item's kind; the fixtures are `select/derived_table_alias_*`,
  `select/cte_named_for_its_base_table_binds.sql`,
  `select/one_column_table_shadowed_by_a_{derived_table,cte}.sql` and
  `select/unnest_{over_a_derived_table_shadowing_its_source,over_a_cte_shadowing_its_source,shadowed_arg_type_refused}.sql`.
  What that closure cost, in the class 18.6 refuses outright with `42712`, is stated there
  too — five spellings that trade one silent member for another, three more that show why a
  count is the wrong instrument, and `SELECT t.*` splitting by the second FROM item's kind.

  **A residual of the same reader split, its silent polarity live on every build: an
  `alias.*` over a FROM-clause `unnest(…)` still reaches the catalog, and there it is
  silent.** `collect_nonbase_into` has no arm for an `unnest` item, so an unnest
  item's name falls to a base table of the same spelling and the wildcard expands *that
  table's* column names, which the binding gate then resolves against the unnest's
  columns. Whether that is silent or loud is decided by one thing: whether the table's
  names are a subset of the alias list's. With a base `uu(q INT)` present and measured
  identical on every build back to before the `unnest` gate, `SELECT uu.* FROM unnest(ARRAY[1,2],
  ARRAY[3,4]) AS uu(q, r)` answers a **one**-column `q` = `1, 2` against 18.6's `q | r`
  = `1|3, 2|4`, silently dropping the column the alias list names; over `ARRAY[]::int[]`
  it still describes one column where 18.6 describes two, and with the base table's
  columns *reordered* (`uu2(r INT, q INT)`) it is `r | q` = `3|1, 4|2` — the right values
  under the wrong labels in the wrong order, the shape a client cannot detect. The loud
  polarity is a base-table name the unnest lacks (`SELECT u.* FROM unnest(ARRAY[1,2]) AS
  u(q)` beside a `u(x, y)` is `42703 column "u.x"` against 18.6's `q` = `1, 2`), and its
  **zero-row spelling is what this flip closed** — over `ARRAY[]::int[]` the same
  statement was a silent two-column `x | y` before and is that `42703` now, the binding
  gate refusing what the old scope bound and never evaluated. The control identifying the
  catalog as the route is the same statement under a name no table holds — pglet's
  `0A000`, the recorded refusal. The full statement, the three-build table and the bare-`*`
  half are the **addressable by its alias in a value position and not** bullet above; the
  remaining dimensions of this class are that missing `Unnest` arm and the `42712` gate,
  one repair each.

  **The `unnest` member of that sort-key residual is closed, and it is the row's own worked
  example of the rule the row states.** Filling the unnest's column map did **not** move it,
  because `level_columns_uncertain` reads the exhaustive bit and not the map; flipping that bit
  did, and `SELECT lbl AS q FROM unnest(ARRAY[3,1,2]) AS u(lbl) ORDER BY q+0` is `42703` on
  both engines now (`select/unnest_nested_order_by_name_loud.sql`). What is left under the
  number is the relation kind the scope still cannot prove columns-exhaustive: a catalog view,
  or a scan of a table the catalog lacks.
- **11 · A base column the planner re-describes reports no base-table provenance — or
  typmod — on the extended protocol: `RETURNING`, and — closed — a grouped query.** A `RowDescription` for a `RETURNING` column carries `table_oid = 0` /
  `attnum = 0` on the `Describe` leg, where the simple-query leg carries the real pair and
  18.6 carries it on both. Measured with `wt(id, v)`: `UPDATE wt SET v=wt.v RETURNING *`
  and `RETURNING id` are `0|0` on `Describe`, while `SELECT * FROM wt` on the same
  connection is `16384|1` — so it is `RETURNING`-wide and not an `UPDATE … FROM` effect.
  The cause is `Plan::returning_output_columns` → `Expr::to_column_desc` →
  `ColumnDesc::new`, which mints a descriptor with type and name and no provenance —
  every item takes that path, the wildcard's expansions included, since `lower_returning`
  has already replaced the `*` with per-column references. The executor's own walk
  propagates provenance for a passthrough column, which is why the two legs differ.
  Invisible to the fixture harness by construction: it compares the declared **type** OID
  on both legs and not `table_oid`/`attnum`, so no fixture can redden.

  **`ColumnDesc::new` drops a third field, and it is the same three sites.** The
  `Describe` leg reports `atttypmod = -1` for every `RETURNING` item as well, where the
  simple-query leg reports the column's own. Measured over `rr(id INT, v VARCHAR(5), n
  NUMERIC(6,2), ts TIMESTAMP(3))`, reading both legs off the raw wire on one connection:
  `INSERT … RETURNING id, v, n, ts`, `UPDATE … RETURNING id, v`, `DELETE … RETURNING v, n`
  and `INSERT … RETURNING *` are `-1 · -1 · -1 · -1` on `Describe` against
  `-1 · 9 · 393222 · 3` on the simple leg, while 18.6 sends `-1 · 9 · 393222 · 3` on both
  and the plain `SELECT id, v, n, ts FROM rr` control agrees on both legs here too. This
  is `ResultShape`'s two producers with nothing comparing them — the pair `CLAUDE.md`
  names — and here it is the *executor* leg that is right, which is not the direction
  rows 54 and 58 run in; no claim is made about which leg leads in general.

  **`RETURNING` is one member, and the repair is not one arm.** The mechanism is any arm
  of `Plan::output_columns_scoped` that builds a *base column*'s descriptor through
  `Expr::to_column_desc`, which mints one with `ColumnDesc::new` and so drops all three
  fields; `project_output_columns` looks a projected column up and keeps its descriptor
  whole, for a `Project` and — since it describes its items the same way — a `Window`.
  Measured over `t(v VARCHAR(5), n NUMERIC(6,2), ts TIMESTAMP(3))` reading both legs off
  the raw wire against 18.6, a **grouped query**, the `Aggregate` arm, described the base
  column with `-1` and no provenance on `Describe`, and with its own modifier (`9` for
  `v`) and `t`'s oid and attnum on the simple leg and on both 18.6 legs:
  `SELECT v FROM t GROUP BY v`, the three columns grouped together (`-1 · -1 · -1`
  against `9 · 393222 · 3`), `GROUP BY 1`, `v AS x`, a qualified `x.v` over an aliased
  `t x`, a grouped `HAVING count(*) > 0` or `HAVING n > 0`, an `ORDER BY` over it, and a
  derived table or a CTE over the grouped query (`SELECT * FROM (SELECT v FROM t GROUP BY
  v) d`, `WITH c AS (…) SELECT * FROM c`), as well as a grouped query **over** a derived
  table or a CTE.

  The controls agree on both legs of both engines: the plain projection, a derived table
  over it, `DISTINCT`, `DISTINCT ON`, `ORDER BY … LIMIT`, and a bare, qualified or aliased
  column beside a window call. `GROUP BY v` and a `RETURNING` measured the same on a build
  before the enum-identity gates. The arm list is the thing to re-derive, since a repair
  built from the members would miss what no probe here reached: `to_column_desc`'s call
  sites in `output_columns_scoped`'s tree are `ProjectUnnest` (no `FROM`, so no base
  column arrives), `returning_output_columns` (every item), and `project_output_columns`'s
  fallback, which a projected column reaches only when the lookup misses — the
  `Aggregate` arm, which called it for every item, reaching it now through that fallback.

  **The grouped query is closed.** The `Aggregate` arm describes its items through
  `project_output_columns`, as `Project` and `Window` do and as the executor's walk does
  for all three, so a grouped column passes its input descriptor through. Every grouped
  spelling above — the three columns together, `GROUP BY 1`, an alias, a qualified column,
  `HAVING`, `ORDER BY`, a derived table or a CTE over the grouped query, and a grouped
  query over one — now carries 18.6's base table, attribute number and modifier on both
  legs, measured off the raw wire (`9 · 393222 · 3` for the three columns); the
  aggregate's own column keeps `0`/`0`/`-1` on both engines. Guarded by
  `engine_subqueries::a_grouped_column_is_described_alike_on_both_legs`, since no fixture
  compares the three. **It moved declared types too**, which is why it closed here: the
  coercion pass read a derived relation's column as certain where its descriptor carried
  a base table, so `avg` over a grouped query's column through a derived table became
  18.6's `numeric` (row 2) and a computed `float8` sibling beside it in a
  `COALESCE`/`greatest` unified at 18.6's `double precision` rather than being cast to
  `integer` (`select/coalesce_grouped_derived_column_computed_sibling.sql`). A column's
  certainty no longer rides on its provenance — the plan records it where the pass reads
  the column's definition (row 2) — and those answers stand.
- **~~158~~ · Closed — a window query's column lookup took another relation's column, and so
  did a qualified `unnest` column.** Two readers of `Plan::output_columns_scoped`, the
  planner's descriptor walk, handed a projected column the descriptor of the **first**
  input column carrying its name, where two `FROM` relations carried it. The `Window` arm
  looked a projected `Expr::Column` up by bare name, the pattern discarding the qualifier;
  it now describes its items through `project_output_columns`, the lookup a `Project`
  uses, which reads the qualifier through `find_projected_column` and passes an aliased
  column through whole as well. And the `Unnest` arm put no relation in scope, so a
  qualified `u.k` fell through `find_projected_column` to the flat input list; it now
  registers the `unnest` under its effective name, as `plan_relations` already did.
  Measured on the native server against 18.6 over `t(v VARCHAR(5), n NUMERIC(6,2), k INT)`
  and `t3(v VARCHAR(8), n NUMERIC(10,5), k TEXT)`, reading both legs off the raw wire, the
  `Describe` leg declared:

  | statement | pglet `Describe` | pglet simple leg and 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT b.k, row_number() OVER () FROM t a, t3 b` | `int4` | `text` |
  | `SELECT b.v, b.n, row_number() OVER () FROM t a, t3 b` | `9 · 393222` | `12 · 655369` |
  | `SELECT x.v FROM (SELECT b.v, row_number() OVER () AS rn FROM t a, t3 b) x` | `9` | `12` |
  | `SELECT u.k FROM t, unnest(ARRAY['a']) AS u(k)` | `int4`, with `t`'s provenance | `text` |

  and the same `int4` for `u.k` through a grouped query and a window query over the
  `unnest`. Each now declares what the simple leg and 18.6 send, provenance included.

  **The identity reached answers as well as descriptors**, because a derived table's
  descriptors are what the operator and common-type gates read. Over `wte(m mood)` and
  `wtt(m text)`, a derived table over `SELECT b.m, row_number() OVER () … FROM wte a,
  wtt b` exported `wte`'s enum for `wtt`'s text column, so `x.m > 'zzz'` was refused
  `22P02` where 18.6 compares two strings, and a `UNION` with an enum column answered both
  rows where 18.6 refuses `42804`. Both now answer as 18.6 does; the `UNION` is a refusal
  this repair added, at 18.6's own code.

  **The answers it moved did not all move toward 18.6, and some of those that moved away
  are writes.** The descriptor the lookup lent was sometimes the only enum identity a
  statement's column had, and then it was right by accident. Measured on the native
  server's default build, in-memory storage, simple-query leg, against 18.6, over
  `te(m mood, k INT)` holding `('happy', 1)`, `tt(m TEXT, k TEXT)` holding one row and
  `te2(m mood)` holding `ok`:

  | statement | before the closure | after | 18.6 | moved |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | `DELETE FROM te WHERE (SELECT u.m FROM te t2, unnest(ARRAY['ok'::mood]) AS u(m)) > 'sad'` | deletes the row | deletes nothing | deletes the row | away |
  | `UPDATE te SET k = 2 WHERE` the same predicate | sets `k = 2` | changes nothing | sets `k = 2` | away |
  | `DELETE FROM te WHERE (SELECT x.m FROM (SELECT b.m, row_number() OVER () FROM te a, (SELECT 'ok'::mood AS m) b) x) > 'sad'` | deletes the row | deletes nothing | deletes the row | away |
  | `DELETE FROM te WHERE (SELECT x.m FROM (SELECT u.m FROM te a, unnest(ARRAY['ok'::mood]) AS u(m)) x) > 'sad'` | deletes the row | deletes nothing | deletes the row | away |
  | `SELECT (SELECT u.m FROM te t2, unnest(ARRAY['ok'::mood]) AS u(m)) > 'zzz'` | `22P02` | `f` | `22P02` | away |
  | `SELECT (SELECT u.m FROM te t2, unnest(ARRAY['zzz']) AS u(m)) > 'aaa'` | `22P02` | `t` | `t` | toward |
  | `DELETE FROM te WHERE (SELECT x.m FROM (SELECT b.m, row_number() OVER () FROM tt a, te2 b) x) > 'sad'` | deletes nothing | deletes the row | deletes the row | toward |
  | `SELECT x.m > 'zzz' FROM (SELECT b.m, row_number() OVER () FROM tt a, te2 b) x` | `f` | `22P02` | `22P02` | toward |

  In the pairs measured, the referenced column decides the direction. Where it is `text`
  on 18.6 as well (the `'aaa'` row, and the `UNION` above), the enum the lookup lent was
  wrong, and dropping it moved the answer to 18.6's. Where it carries an enum pglet reads
  (the `te2` rows), the lookup used to lend a `text` column's descriptor, with no enum, in
  its place, and reading its own moved the answer to 18.6's too. And where its values come
  from a **cast** — `unnest(ARRAY['ok'::mood])`, `(SELECT 'ok'::mood AS m)` — 18.6 types it
  by the cast and pglet's column carries no enum (row 104), so the lent `te.m` gave 18.6's
  member positions, and reading the column's own identity gives the label bytes. Those
  statements are row 104's, writes included. The same comparison outside a scalar
  subquery — `SELECT u.m > 'sad' FROM te, unnest(ARRAY['ok'::mood]) AS u(m)` is `f` against
  18.6's `t` — answered by the label bytes before the closure too; the closure brought the
  scalar-subquery spellings into line with it rather than with 18.6. The rows that moved
  away have no fixture, a faithful one being red; the `unnest` and `te2` directions that
  moved toward 18.6 are pinned on spellings of their own by
  `enum/unnest_derived_table_repeated_name_non_enum_literal.sql` and
  `enum/window_derived_table_repeated_name_enum_column.sql`.

  **It reached a recursive CTE's declared modifier.** `check_recursive_shape` folds the
  recursive term's modifier as the planner reads it, so a term reading `x.v` from that
  derived table — or `u.v` from `unnest(ARRAY['abcdefgh']) AS u(v)` beside `t` — carried
  `t.v`'s `9` into the fold, and beside a `VARCHAR(5)` seed the CTE declared `character
  varying(5)` on both legs over the rows `ab` and `abcdefgh`, where 18.6 refuses `42804`.
  A **seed** spelled through the `unnest` was typed `varchar(5)` the same way, where 18.6
  types it `text`. Beside a `VARCHAR(8)` seed the window term reads `12` and the CTE
  declares `12`, as 18.6 does; what 18.6 refuses there stays the recursive CTE's recorded
  over-acceptance (row 155 and `docs/declared_types.md`).

  `crates/pglet/tests/descriptor_column_identity.rs` compares both producers field for
  field against the type OID and modifier 18.6 sends and the provenance pglet's planner
  gives a plain projection of the column 18.6 names, `cte_column_list.rs`'s
  `a_recursive_terms_column_read_through_a_window_or_an_unnest_folds_its_own_modifier`
  holds the fold, and fixtures hold what the corpus can see — the declared type OIDs
  (`select/window_qualified_column_repeated_name_declared_type.sql`,
  `select/unnest_qualified_column_repeated_name_declared_type.sql`) and the answers
  (`enum/window_derived_table_repeated_name_*`,
  `enum/unnest_derived_table_repeated_name_non_enum_literal.sql`). The modifier and
  provenance halves are invisible to the corpus by construction (row 155's harness note). What still reaches
  `find_projected_column`'s flat fallback is a qualifier naming an enclosing level, which
  is row 159.
- **303 · pglet has no outer-level aggregates.** 18.6 assigns an aggregate to the lowest
  query level its arguments reference (`check_agg_arguments`, `parse_agg.c`): in
  `SELECT (SELECT max(t.tx) FROM u) FROM t`, `max(t.tx)` names only the outer `t`, so it
  is an aggregate of the **outer** query, which becomes an aggregate query of one row.
  pglet evaluates every aggregate at the level it is written in, over that level's rows,
  with the outer column bound from the current outer row. Measured, `t` holding four rows
  and `u` three:
  - `SELECT (SELECT max(t.tx) FROM u LIMIT 1) FROM t` is one row, `cccc`, on 18.6, and
    four rows here (`a`, `bb`, NULL, `cccc`).
  - `SELECT (SELECT max(t.i) + count(*) FROM u) FROM t` is one row, `8`, on 18.6, and four
    here (`4`, NULL, `8`, `5`).

  Both are **silent**, and the same before and after `avg` over an integer became
  `numeric`.

  **Its loud consequence.** The nested-aggregate gate (`Error::NestedAggregate`) reads
  every aggregate inside a sub-plan as that sub-plan's, so it refuses a **different-level**
  pair 18.6 accepts:
  - `SELECT (SELECT max(u.i + avg(t.i)) FROM u) FROM t` (18.6 `1700` `52.6666666666666667`).
  - `SELECT (SELECT sum(u.i + max(t.i)) FROM u) FROM t` (18.6 `20` `105`).
  - `SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM u HAVING sum(u.i + max(t.i)) > 0) FROM t` (18.6 `3`).

  Each is `42803 aggregate function calls cannot be nested` here; before that gate they
  were the eval-time `0A000`. A same-level pair inside a sub-plan agrees with 18.6's
  `42803` on both: `(SELECT max(avg(t.i)) FROM u)` is refused there too — both
  aggregates reference only `t`, so 18.6 assigns both to the outer query, one nested in
  the other. Modelling the
  level assignment is the close; a faithful fixture is red.

  An outer-level aggregate under an **expression** of the sub-plan's select list is the
  silent half reached by one more route, the expression being evaluated now (row 89):
  over `o (id, a, t)`, `SELECT id, (SELECT CASE WHEN count(*) > 1 THEN upper(max(o2.t))
  ELSE lower(min(o.t)) END FROM o o2 WHERE o2.a = o.a) FROM o` answers a row per outer
  row here and is `42803` there — `min(o.t)` is the outer query's aggregate, which makes
  the outer query a grouping one over an ungrouped `id`. It was `0A000` before.

  The misread level reaches the grouping's operand-type check too (row 89): the
  qualified argument of an outer-level aggregate resolves to the inner relation's column
  of the same name, so over `x (a INT, v INT)` holding a row and an empty `ye (a INT, v
  TEXT)`, `SELECT (SELECT sum(x.v) FROM ye GROUP BY ye.a) FROM x` is `42883 function
  sum(text) does not exist` here and `NULL` there; it answered `NULL` here while the
  check ran only for a group that was computed. Loud.

  And an outer-level aggregate in a FROM function's argument is refused with the
  sub-plan's own: `SELECT (SELECT sum(x) FROM unnest(ARRAY[max(t.i)]) u(x)) FROM t` is
  `42803 aggregate functions are not allowed in functions in FROM` here and `3` there
  (row 308). Loud.

  `count` over the outer column, compared with an integer, is the silent half too: over `o
  (y INT, z FLOAT8)` holding two rows and `ev` three, `SELECT (SELECT count(o.z) = 2 FROM
  ev LIMIT 1) FROM o` is one row, `t`, on 18.6 and two here, `f`, `f`. With the `2` written
  as a string, `= '2'`, it stays the base's `42883 operator does not exist: bigint =
  text`: a string literal is read at an aggregate's type only where every column its
  argument names binds at the aggregate's own level (`docs/coercion.md` § Where the
  plan-time coercion pass reaches).
- **159 · A correlated column in a sub-plan's target list takes a local column's
  identity — closed for the sub-plan's own descriptor; open where a projection that is
  itself a scalar subquery stands between.** A target-list reference binds the column
  18.6's level walk binds it to, and the sub-plan's output descriptor says so: the
  correlated re-run, the first point the enclosing levels exist, records on the level's
  projecting node (`Project`, `Aggregate`, `Window`, and a no-FROM `Values`) the type and
