  enum of each reference an enclosing level binds (`EnclosingColumns`, written by
  `correlation::record_enclosing`), and `Plan::find_projected_column` reads it for a
  reference the input does not bind, declining where nothing is recorded rather than
  reading a same-named local column. The executor's descriptors for the same nodes read
  the same record (`ProjectionScope::with_enclosing`) — a set operation inside a sub-plan
  unifies its executed sides' — and the record is shared with the copy
  `judge_nested_level` re-runs at the statement's own clause walk, so a reader between
  that walk and the statement's re-run, an `UPDATE`'s assignment gate, reads it too. A
  set-op arm naming an enclosing column carries that column's type and enum into the
  unification, through the record the statement's second parse builds the node with
  (`SetOpOuterTypes`), as does a nested set operation's unified column.
  Measured agreeing with 18.6 on the native server's default build, in-memory storage,
  over `te(m mood, k INT)` holding `('happy', 1), ('sad', 2)`, `tt(m TEXT, k TEXT)`, a
  one-column `tz(z TEXT)` and `ti(z INT)`, `p(a INT, b INT)` holding `(1, 10), (2, 20)`,
  a one-column `q(c INT)`, `q3(c INT, b TEXT)` and `tx(m TEXT, k INT)` beside `tm2(m
  mood2, k INT)`: the declared type (`(SELECT p.b FROM q)`, `(SELECT b FROM q)`, over an
  empty table, over `q3`'s `text` `b`, computed, over a FROM `unnest`, and a `RETURNING`
  sub-plan — `int4` on both legs), a comparison's member order and `BETWEEN`, a fold,
  `ORDER BY` and `DISTINCT`, a derived table's and a CTE's `> 'ok'`, `x.v > 9`, `sum(v)`
  and `max(m)`, a set operation's unification and dedupe (`… UNION SELECT '9'` is two

  (`[23]`), the inner `mood2` column not read for `tx.m` (`= 'qqq'`, `IN`, a fold,

  LIMIT 1`, under another sub-plan's `WHERE`, the `UPDATE` over `ti`, the `> $1` spelling
  bound to `ok`, and the no-FROM `(SELECT te.m) > 'ok'` (a row 107 shape); and over
  `ja(x INT, m mood)` and `jb(x INT, m mood)`, a sub-plan's set-op arm naming `ja.m` —
  `UNION`, `UNION ALL`, `EXCEPT`, `INTERSECT`, a no-FROM arm, an arm over a table lacking

  `UPDATE`'s predicate. A type modifier is not recorded
  (`-1`); no reader of the sub-plan's column reads one, the scalar subquery's pass-up

  **What stays open is the projection that is itself a scalar subquery.** Its descriptor
  is built by `Expr::to_column_desc`, whose subquery leaf declines for row 107's cost
  reason, so the enclosing enum the inner sub-plan carries does not reach it — the
  same answer its uncorrelated spelling gives. Measured, against 18.6: `SELECT k, (SELECT
  (SELECT o.m FROM tz c) FROM tz b) > 'ok' FROM te o` is `f`, `t` against `t`, `f`, and
  `DELETE FROM te WHERE (SELECT (SELECT te.m FROM tz c) FROM tz b) > 'ok'` deletes row `2`
  against `1`; `SELECT (SELECT o.m FROM tz b) AS v FROM te o UNION SELECT 'zzz'` answers
  three rows against `22P02`, and its `UNION ALL SELECT m FROM te` is `42804` against
  rows; a derived table's `x.v > 'zzz'` over that column answers against `22P02`, while

  Other rows' members met on the way: `ORDER BY`/`max`/`HAVING` over the subquery and

  a sub-plan's `FROM` naming the level outside it is `42P01`; a set-op arm `'sad'::mood`
  beside the enclosing enum is row 104's `42804`, as its uncorrelated spelling is.

  **The judgement's position is the enclosing level's binding gate**, which runs after

  ahead of the `WHERE` (`SELECT (SELECT bogus FROM q) FROM p WHERE a = 'x'`, `42703`) and
  an earlier literal ahead of a later sub-plan in one expression (`WHERE a = 'x' AND
  EXISTS (SELECT bogus FROM q)`, `22P02`) agree, over a one-column and a two-column inner

  Not members: `EXISTS (SELECT o.m FROM tt b)`, a reference in the sub-plan's `WHERE`, a

  from that are `42601` here — `op ANY (SELECT …)`, `ARRAY(SELECT …)` and a `LATERAL`
  derived table — reach no member. `*/correlated_target_list_*.sql` pin the binding, the
  conversions, the precedence pair, the controls and the closed members
  (`*_enclosing_identity_*`), `*/correlated_set_op_arm_enclosing_enum*.sql` the set-op
  arms, and `crates/pglet/tests/enclosing_column_identity.rs` the
  record, the `$N` type and the assignment gate's read.
- **12 · A `$N` compared with an outer level's *aliased* column reports OID 0 on
  `ParameterDescription`.** Parameter inference opens a fresh scope per subquery
  (`param_types.rs`'s `walk_scoped` **replaces** `from_scope` rather than chaining it),
  so inside a subquery the enclosing level's alias→table map is gone; a qualified outer
  reference then falls back to reading the qualifier as a relation name, which resolves
  when the outer relation is unaliased and reports nothing when it is aliased. Measured
  on the **extended protocol** — a raw v3 `Parse` + `Describe(S)` + `Sync`, so the phases
  are not collapsed — against 18.6, over `dt(id INT, b BIGINT)`, `ds(id INT, b INT,
  k INT)` and `dz(k TEXT)`, reading the reported OID list for `$1`:

  | statement | 18.6 | pglet |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM dz x WHERE t.b = $1) FROM dt t` | `[20]` | `[0]` |
  | `SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM dz x WHERE s.b = $1) FROM dt JOIN ds s ON s.id = dt.id` | `[23]` | `[0]` |
  | `UPDATE dt SET id=dt.id FROM ds s WHERE s.id=dt.id RETURNING (SELECT count(*) FROM dz x WHERE s.b = $1)` | `[23]` | `[0]` |
  | the same spelled `RETURNING EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM dz x WHERE s.b = $1)` | `[23]` | `[0]` |
  | the same with an extra inner predicate (`WHERE x.k = 'q' AND s.b = $1`) | `[23]` | `[0]` |
  | `SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM dz x WHERE dt.b = $1) FROM dt JOIN ds s ON s.id = dt.id` | `[20]` | `[20]` |
  | `UPDATE dt … RETURNING (s.b = $1)` (no subquery) | `[23]` | `[23]` |
  | `UPDATE dt … RETURNING (SELECT count(*) FROM dz x WHERE x.k = $1)` (inner column) | `[25]` | `[25]` |

  The single-table first row is what makes this a general correlated-outer-reference gap
  rather than a `RETURNING` or a join one, and the last three are the controls: an
  **unaliased** outer relation agrees (the qualifier is a real table name), a reference
  outside any subquery agrees **when its alias names no real relation** (see the next
  paragraph, which is where that control fails), and a reference to the subquery's own
  relation agrees.
  OID `0` is the value `param_types.rs`'s module doc records a binary-protocol client's
  type introspection tripping over — and it is not confined to the report. A **text**-format
  bind through the extended protocol runs the statement here, and the untyped `$1` arrives
  as `text` against a numeric outer column, so **the divergence reaches the values, loudly**:
  measured twice on the same seed, once with psql `\bind` and once with a raw v3
  `Parse` (no declared types) + text `Bind` + `Execute` + `Sync`, row 1 with `$1='111'` is
  a row on 18.6 and `42883 operator does not exist: bigint = text` here, and row 2 with
  `$1='7'` is a row there and `42883 … integer = text` here, while row 6 (the unaliased
  control) answers on both and the instrument's own sanity probe `SELECT $1::int8 + 1`
  answers `112` on both.

  **The reported OID is not a two-valued choice between the right type and `0`; the third
  outcome is another relation's type**, which is worse than `0` because it tells a binary
  client a definite width. It needs no subquery at all — a FROM **alias** that collides
  with a real relation's name is enough, because `infer_col_type` tries
  `expr.infer_type(&PlannerScope::catalog(schema, table))` *before* consulting the `from_scope`
  alias map, so the catalog wins whenever the alias resolves there. Measured the same way,
  with the same three tables:

  | statement | 18.6 | pglet |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT ds.b = $1 FROM dt ds` (top level, no subquery, one table) | `params=[20]` | `params=[23]` |
  | the same, text bind `5000000000` | `f` | `22P02 invalid input syntax for type integer` |
  | the same, text bind `111` | `t` | `t` |
  | `SELECT zq.b = $1 FROM dt zq` (alias names no real relation) | `[20]` | `[20]` |
  | `UPDATE dt ds SET id = ds.id RETURNING (ds.b = $1)` (already on `TypeScope::Input`) | `[20]` | `[20]` |

  The in-range value is what hides it — a client that only ever binds small integers sees
  agreement — and the last two rows are the controls that name the cause as the *collision*
  rather than the alias: rename the alias to something no relation is called and both
  engines agree, and the `RETURNING` spelling agrees because that clause already resolves
  through `TypeScope::Input` rather than the catalog. Two claims elsewhere are narrower
  than they read because of this: the *Real prepared statements / param type inference*
  row's "Column context is alias-aware across a JOIN" and the same sentence in
  `docs/param_binding.md` both hold only while the alias names no real relation. Closing it
  is the same `TypeScope::Catalog` class closed for `RETURNING`.

  **Why there is no fixture, measured rather than assumed.** Not harness blindness — the
  opposite: a throwaway `@param` fixture over the first row's shape (one table aliased
  `t`, `@param $1 int8`, one row expected) was written, run and discarded, and it is
  **red** on pglet. The control that attributes the redness to the binding is the same
  fixture with the literal `111` in place of `$1`, which **passes**. So a faithful fixture
  here is red while the engine is wrong, which is a different thing from the harness being
  unable to see it, and it is what leaves the shape recorded rather than pinned. The
  measured `42883` pair above is the simple reason it is red: the bound statement fails on
  pglet whatever the client, so no choice of driver leg reaches a passing fixture.
- **~~57~~ · Closed — where 18.6 cannot determine a parameter's type it refuses the
  statement at `Parse`; pglet parsed, described and ran it.** Postgres resolves each
  `$N` during parse analysis and gives a parameter reference the type the parameter has
  **when that reference is analysed**. A position that coerces nothing leaves an
  `unknown` reference as it found it, and nothing later revisits the node, so there are
  two refusals with one sentence, `could not determine data type of parameter $N`:
  `42P08`, from `check_variable_parameters` inside parse analysis, where some other
  occurrence does type the parameter and this reference disagrees with it; and `42P18`,
  from the sweep of the parameter array that follows
  (`pg_analyze_and_rewrite_varparams`, `tcop/postgres.c`), where nothing types it at
  all. pglet had neither: its `ParameterDescription` reported OID `0` for every slot it
  could not type, and the statement then ran on whatever type the client's `Bind` — or,
  through the wasm binding, the JS value's own runtime type — supplied.

  **The verdict is a property of the order of a parameter's occurrences**, and not of
  whether this engine's inference typed the slot, which is what makes the optional-filter
  idiom two statements rather than one. Measured through node-postgres with untyped
  parameters, and over a raw v3 `Parse` + `Describe(S)` + `Sync`:

  | statement | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT v FROM t WHERE $1 IS NULL` | `42P18` |
  | `SELECT count($1) FROM t` | `42P18` |
  | `SELECT count(DISTINCT $1) FROM t` | answers, `$1` is `text` |
  | `… WHERE ($1 IS NULL OR name = $1)` | `42P08` |
  | `… WHERE (name = $1 OR $1 IS NULL)` | answers |
  | `… WHERE ($1::text IS NULL OR name = $1)` | answers |
  | `SELECT $1 IS NULL, $1::text` | `42P08` |
  | `SELECT $1 AS p, $1 IS NULL` | `42P08` — the bare entry is `text` only once its query level is analysed |
  | `SELECT (SELECT $1), $1 IS NULL` | answers — the subquery's level is done first |
  | `UPDATE t SET v = $1 WHERE $1 IS NULL` | `42P08` — `WHERE`, then `RETURNING`, then the `SET` list |
  | `INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, $1) RETURNING $1 IS NULL` | answers |
  | `… WHERE $1 OR $1 IS NULL` | answers — a boolean operand is typed as it is read |
  | `jsonb_build_object('k', $1, 'j', $1::text)` | `42P08`; the two arguments swapped, answers |

  **What closed it.** The parameter-inference walk already timed each `$N`'s first
  type-fixing occurrence in parse-analysis order (`Inference::first_fix`, kept for the
  enum-cast rule). It now times the first occurrence that fixes **nothing** the same way
  (`first_unresolved`) and compares the two per parameter: an unresolved occurrence with
  no fix anywhere is `42P18`, one ahead of the first fix is `42P08`, and `42P08` outranks
  `42P18` as the check inside parse analysis outranks the sweep after it. The positions
  timed as fixing nothing, each measured to leave the parameter `unknown` on 18.6, are
  an `IS [NOT] NULL` operand, `IS [NOT] DISTINCT FROM NULL` (a null test to 18.6's
  parser), and an argument declared `"any"` — `count`'s without `DISTINCT`, `concat`'s,
  `concat_ws`'s past the separator, `jsonb_build_object`'s. The refusal is raised from
  `infer_param_targets`, where it is called: `Parse` on the native server (no
  `ParseComplete`), and `Database::execute_bound` ahead of its binding callback, so the
  wasm binding decodes no value for a refused statement. A parameter the client
  declared at `Parse` as a type this engine models is a typed reference from its first
  occurrence and is not refused. The walk's own order was corrected where it timed a
  fix away from 18.6's: a join's sides ahead of its condition, an `IN (SELECT …)`'s
  subquery ahead of its left operand, and a `VALUES` list's bare entries after its last
  row. A bare select-list or `RETURNING` entry is reported as `text` (`25`) rather than
  OID `0`, which is the control the old record measured; a bare entry of an `INSERT …
  SELECT` source is reported as its target column's type, as 18.6's `transformInsertRow`
  coerces it (`INSERT INTO kv (k, v, n) SELECT $1, $2, $3` describes
  `{text,jsonb,integer}` on both), where nothing in the source resolves it first: a
  sort, grouping, `DISTINCT` or window key naming the entry resolves it to `text` (row
  150), as does a set operation whose sides leave the column unknown. The refusal is not
  raised over a statement whose `FROM` clause or
  DML target names a relation the catalog lacks: that is `42P01` on 18.6, ahead of any
  parameter, and the executor's to raise here (row 276 has the errors the refusal does
  outrank).

  Guards: `tests/fixtures/params/undetermined_param_*`, recorded from 18.6, the refusals
  beside neighbours 18.6 answers; `crates/pglet/tests/undetermined_param.rs` for the
  in-process host (the callback is not asked, the block fails) and for accepted
  statements a binary client cannot bind here; `handlers.rs`'s
  `parse_refuses_a_parameter_left_without_a_type_unless_the_client_declared_it`; and the
  wasm and npm suites, which bind a number, a string, a boolean and a null alike.

  **What it did not close** is row 276 (the shapes still accepted, and the ones newly
  refused), row 148 (a parameter deduced two *types* — `SELECT $1 AS p FROM t WHERE id =
  $1` is 18.6's `42P08 inconsistent types deduced for parameter $1` and answers here),
  the `42725` family (`-$1`, `$1 + $1`, `unnest($1)`, `date_trunc('day', $1)` — `operator
  is not unique` / `function … is not unique` there, accepted here), a statement whose
  only untyped slot is a number it never writes (`SELECT $2::int` bound two values
  answers here where 18.6 is `42P18` naming `$1`), and the
  unbound-parameter half of row 56, which the in-process host now answers differently
  for these statements: run through the npm adapter with **no** values, `SELECT v FROM t
  WHERE $1 IS NULL AND a = -1` is `42P18` where node-postgres against 18.6 sends a
  simple query and gets `42P02 there is no parameter $1`; the native server's simple leg
  infers nothing and is as row 56 records it. Where two parameters both earn `42P08`,
  the one named differs: 18.6 names the first its walk of the finished tree meets (the select
  list ahead of `FROM`), this engine the first in analysis order — `SELECT $2 IS NULL,
  $2::text, a.name = $1 FROM t a JOIN t b ON $1 IS NULL` names `$2` there and `$1` here.

  **What a driver does with an OID pglet cannot name** — still live, for a parameter
  18.6 *does* type and this engine reports OID `0` for (rows 12 and 183; the
  accepted statements `undetermined_param.rs` holds off-corpus, `count(DISTINCT $1)` and
  a simple `CASE`'s operand, are members). Every step below is loud, and the damage is
  what the *next* statement gets. The `@param` path prepares through tokio-postgres
  `client.prepare`, which sends **no** declared parameter types (`fixture_params_owned`
  builds only the values). On pglet an OID-`0` `ParameterDescription` names no type
  tokio-postgres knows, so the driver runs its typeinfo lookup, and that lookup needs
  **one absent relation plus two absent columns on a present one**:

  | probe | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT 1 FROM pg_catalog.pg_range LIMIT 1` | `42P01 table "pg_catalog.pg_range" does not exist` | one row |
  | `SELECT typbasetype FROM pg_catalog.pg_type LIMIT 1` — likewise `typrelid` | `42703 column "typbasetype" does not exist` | one row, declared `26` |
  | `typname` / `typtype` / `typelem` (the controls) | one row each | one row each |
  | the driver's `TYPEINFO_QUERY` with the `pg_range` join **deleted** | `42703 column "t.typbasetype" does not exist` | one row |
  | the driver's `UNDEFINED_TABLE` fallback's own `SELECT NULL::OID` | `42704 type "oid" is not supported` | one row, declared `26` |

  So the `pg_range` half is not the whole gap, and the driver's fallback would never be
  *reached* even if it were: the fallback is keyed on `UNDEFINED_TABLE`, and `42703` is
  not that code. This is a different sub-shape from row 43's closed member (5) — there
  `pg_constraint`/`pg_index` accepted **any** column name and answered `(0 rows)` before
  both were populated, where `pg_type` refuses one it does not hold; the two catalog
  relations were wrong in opposite directions, and the corrected statement of the pair is
  row 43's member (7).

  The fallback rescues nothing for a second, independent measured reason: inside the
  harness's isolating `BEGIN … ROLLBACK` (`crates/pglet_tests/src/lib.rs`'s `run_query`)
  the first `42P01` has already aborted the block, so the fallback's own `Parse` and
  every statement after it report `25P02`. A client that meets an OID pglet cannot name
  therefore gets a `25P02` cascade for the rest of the transaction block, whatever the
  statement that follows — the loud edge whose blast radius, not whose silence, is the
  point.
- **276 · The order of two occurrences is not always kept — a parameter's null test
  ahead of the occurrence that types it is accepted where the plan cannot time the two,
  a parameter typed only where the walk cannot see is refused, and the refusal's rank
  among a statement's other errors is not 18.6's.** Row 57's verdict
  compares where two occurrences of a `$N` fall in 18.6's parse-analysis order. The
  walk reads a **plan**, and a plan does not always say. Measured against 18.6, over
  `g(id INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, tags TEXT[])`:

  | statement | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT name FROM g WHERE $1 IS NOT NULL AND id = $1` | answers on the accelerated build; `42P08` stripped | `42P08` |
  | `SELECT name FROM g WHERE $1 IS NOT NULL AND id > $1` | likewise | `42P08` |
  | `SELECT $1 UNION SELECT $1 IS NULL` | answers | `42P08` |
  | `SELECT * FROM (VALUES ($1, $1 IS NULL)) v` | answers | `42P08` |
  | `SELECT $1 AS p ORDER BY ($1 IS NULL)` | answers | `42P08` |
  | `WITH c AS (SELECT 1 FROM e WHERE v = $1) SELECT $1 IS NULL` | `42P18` | answers, `$1` is `text` |
  | `SELECT $1 IS NULL`, `Parse` declaring `$1` as `point` (OID `600`) | `42P18` | answers, `$1` is `point` |

  The index members are one mechanism: B-tree index selection lifts the comparison out of
  the `WHERE` into the scan node, and the conjunct's place among its siblings goes with
  it. A fix inside a lifted conjunct is therefore timed at the clause's start
  (`Inference::lifted`), which accepts the statement wherever *some* source order
  would — the controls with the comparison written first are accepted on both builds and
  held by `params/undetermined_param_indexed_*`. Timing it where the walk happens to
  reach it instead refused those controls. The stripped build keeps the conjuncts in
  one `Filter` and answers as 18.6 does, so these members are a **build-profile
  divergence**, beside rows 56 and 126. A GIN containment is not a member: its
  conjunct stays in the recheck `Filter` above the scan, in source order, and
  `($1 IS NULL OR tags @> $1)` is `42P08` on both builds. Other measured members of the
  lifted class, each answering on the accelerated build and `42P08` stripped and on 18.6,
  over `users(id INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, email TEXT UNIQUE)` and `posts` with a plain
  index on `user_id`: the same conjunction over the `UNIQUE` constraint's index
  (`$1 IS NOT NULL AND email = $1`) and over the secondary one, the probe cast
  (`id = $1::int`), a disjunction ahead of the probe (`($1 IS NOT NULL OR name = 'x') AND
  id = $1`), a two-bound range naming either parameter, and the conjunction inside an
  `IN (SELECT …)`. An `UPDATE`'s or a `DELETE`'s `WHERE $1 IS NOT NULL AND id = $1` is
  not a member, and neither is the same `WHERE` over a join: each is `42P08` on both
  builds. The set-operation and `VALUES`
  members are bare entries the lowering has already wrapped in a cast to the column's
  resolved type (`Cast { Parameter, Bool }` and `Cast { Parameter, Text }` in their plans), and
  a cast types its parameter where it stands — which a written `$1::text` in the same
  position does on 18.6 too, so the plan cannot tell the two apart; 18.6 types the bare
  entry only once the sides are unified or the list's last row is read. The `ORDER BY`
  member is the no-FROM select list, which lowers to a `VALUES` row under the `Sort` and
  is timed at that row's end rather than its query level's.

  **An `INSERT` row's and a `SET` list's bare entry** is a member by the mechanism of
  the set-operation one: the lowering wraps it in the assignment cast to its column, and
  the walk times a cast where it is **written** — a row's cells in the row's written
  order (`InsertRows::Values`' `written`, kept where the column list departs from the
  table's order, which is the order the lowered row is in), a `SET` list's in the list's. 18.6 coerces a row's entries to their
  columns once the whole row is analysed (`transformInsertRow` after
  `transformExpressionList`), and a `SET` list's likewise, so a null test or an `"any"`
  argument later in the same row or list is ahead of the entry's typing there. Measured
  over `kv(k TEXT PRIMARY KEY, v JSONB, n INT)`, the same on both build profiles:

  | statement | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `INSERT INTO kv (k, n) VALUES ($1, CASE WHEN $1 IS NULL THEN 0 ELSE 1 END)` | answers | `42P08` |
  | `INSERT INTO kv (k, v) VALUES ($1, jsonb_build_object('a', $1))` | answers | `42P08` |
  | `UPDATE kv SET k = $1, v = jsonb_build_object('a', $1) WHERE k = 'a'` | answers | `42P08` |
  | `UPDATE kv SET n = $1, k = CASE WHEN $1 IS NULL THEN k ELSE k \|\| 'x' END WHERE k = 'a'` | answers | `42P08` |
  | `INSERT … ON CONFLICT (k) DO UPDATE SET n = $3, v = jsonb_build_object('n', $3)` | answers | `42P08` naming `$3` |

  A column list in another order than the table's is the same member: over
  `t2(n INT, k TEXT, v JSONB)`, `INSERT INTO t2 (k, n) VALUES ($1, CASE WHEN $1 IS NULL
  THEN 0 ELSE 1 END)` answers here and is `42P08` there, single-row and as the first row
  of two. The written order moves a loud member too: a cast outranks a function argument's typing wherever
  it is written, and of two casts the first written is the parameter's type, so `INSERT INTO kv (n, v, k) VALUES
  (length($1), $1::jsonb, $1)` is `42883` here (`length` handed a `jsonb`) and answers on 18.6, which types `$1` at `length`.

  The controls agree on both engines: the two entries written in the other order
  (`INSERT INTO kv (n, k) VALUES (CASE WHEN $1 IS NULL …, $1)`, `SET v =
  jsonb_build_object('a', $1), k = $1`) are `42P08`; a later row of a multi-row `VALUES`
  reading an earlier row's parameter answers, the rows being coerced one at a time; and
  the entry written with its own cast (`VALUES ($1::text, CASE WHEN $1 IS NULL …)`, `SET
  k = $1::text, v = jsonb_build_object('a', $1)`) answers. That last control is why the
  entry is not timed at the row's end: a written `$1::text` into a `text` column and the
  lowered bare `$1` are one plan node, and timing it late refuses the written spelling
  18.6 answers. The written-cast and null-test-first controls are held with the column
  list against the table's order by `params/undetermined_param_insert_row_written_order_*`
  and `…_insert_rows_written_order_cast_first`, and in both orders (`kv (k, n)` and
  `t2 (k, n)`; `kv (n, k)` and `t2 (n, k)`) by `param_types.rs`'s
  `an_insert_row_is_timed_in_its_written_order`.

  The first `WITH` member is the other direction and **loud**: a `WITH` query no reference in
  the plan reaches is not in the plan, so its occurrences are not walked — a parameter
  written only there is already `08P01` at `Bind` (the count is short) — and here the
  body's null test finds nothing that typed the parameter. A `WITH` query read through
  another unread one (`…, d AS (SELECT * FROM c) SELECT $1 IS NULL`) is the same, and so
  is a `DELETE`, an `UPDATE` or an `INSERT` body (`WITH x AS (SELECT id FROM users WHERE
  name = $1) DELETE FROM kv WHERE $1 IS NOT NULL` is `42P18` here and deletes there), and
  a second, read `WITH` query holding the null test (`…, y AS (SELECT id FROM users WHERE
  $1 IS NULL) SELECT * FROM y`). A data-modifying `WITH` query is in the plan whether
  read or not, and is walked: `WITH x AS (UPDATE users SET age = 1 WHERE name = $1
  RETURNING id) SELECT $1 IS NULL` answers on both engines. The unread query can hold
  the null test instead, and that member is **silent**: `WITH y AS (SELECT id FROM users
  WHERE $1 IS NULL), x AS (SELECT id FROM users WHERE name = $1) SELECT * FROM x` answers
  here and is `42P08` on 18.6. The
  declared-`point` member is loud too and the native server's alone: a declared OID this
  engine does not model reaches it as "infer this one" (`docs/param_binding.md`
  § Deferred / known gaps), so the declaration that types the parameter on 18.6 is gone
  before the walk; before row 57's close `Parse` completed and described the parameter
  as OID `0`.

  **The refusal's rank among a statement's errors.** 18.6 raises it once parse analysis
  is done (`check_variable_parameters`), behind every error parse analysis raises. Here
  it is raised once the statement is planned, ahead of what this engine raises at
  execution. A relation the catalog lacks, named in a `FROM` clause or as a DML target,
  is the execution-time error it is made to yield to — `SELECT id FROM nope WHERE $1 IS
  NULL` is `42P01` on both engines (`params/undetermined_param_missing_relation_*`), on
  the native server from `Execute` after a `Parse` that completes — so a relation
  created between that `Parse` and its `Execute` lets the statement answer with its
  parameter untyped, as before row 57's close (18.6: `42P01` at `Parse`). "Lacks" is by
  the relation's kind: a name no relation carries and an enum type's name are `42P01`
  on both engines and an index's name `42809` on both
  (`params/undetermined_param_index_relation_outranks_null_test_loud`), while a
  sequence's name does not stand the refusal down — 18.6 reads the sequence and refuses
  the parameter, `SELECT last_value FROM sq WHERE $1 IS NULL` being `42P18` on both
  (`params/undetermined_param_sequence_relation_null_test_loud`). The executor raises
  the missing relation's error whatever the data — measured over empty tables under a
  `WHERE false`, a
  `LIMIT 0`, either side of a join, a derived table and a `WITH` query the plan holds.
  A relation named inside an expression's subquery it raises for a row that evaluates
  the expression and not over an empty table, so there the refusal stands rather than
  let the statement answer. Measured pairs it still outranks, each loud on both engines:

  | statement | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT id FROM users WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM nope) AND $1 IS NULL` | `42P18` | `42P01` |
  | `UPDATE kv SET n = 'x' WHERE $1 IS NULL` | `42P18` | `22P02` |
  | `INSERT INTO kv (k, n) VALUES ('q', 'x') RETURNING $1 IS NULL` | `42P18` | `22P02` |
  | `SELECT id FROM users WHERE count($1) > 0` | `42P18` | `42803` |
  | `UPDATE sq SET t = 'x' WHERE $1 IS NULL`, `sq` a sequence | `42P18` | `42703` |
  | `SELECT id FROM users WHERE $1 IS NULL LIMIT -1` | `2201W` | `42P18` |

  The last is the reverse: a `LIMIT` this engine refuses at parse is the executor's on
  18.6, behind the parameter's refusal.

  **Silent** for the accepted members: a test passes here and its statement is refused
  on Postgres. No fixture: pglet answers where 18.6 errors, so `@expect-error` cannot
  hold it, and the index members disagree across the two profiles.
- **13 · Statement-level error order — the clauses follow `analyze.c`, four guards still
  don't.** When two clauses of one statement are independently ill-typed, the error
  reported is the one Postgres reports, because each statement lowers its clauses in
  Postgres's own transform order: an INSERT resolves its **row source, then
  `ON CONFLICT`, then `RETURNING`** (which is why `ON CONFLICT` is lowered in the planner
  rather than where it is parsed), and an UPDATE resolves **`WHERE`, then `RETURNING`,
  then the `SET` list** — the target list last, as `transformUpdateStmt` does it. Inside
  the row source the **target column list** resolves before the cells, matching
  `checkInsertTargets` ahead of `transformInsertRow`. Ahead of all of it, a statement
  naming a missing **target** relation reports `42P01` and no clause is lowered at all,
  since `setTargetTable` runs before every `transform*Clause`. A missing relation
  *elsewhere* in the statement is not covered by that: an `UPDATE … FROM nosuchsrc s`
  is 18.6's `42P01 relation "nosuchsrc"` and, when the `RETURNING` carries a **name**
  pglet binds at plan time, pglet's `RETURNING` error (below). Spelled `RETURNING *` or
  `RETURNING <target>.*` the two engines agree on `42P01`.

  **Divergence (loud, wrong order) — a `RETURNING` name error outranks a neighbour's
  *value* or *relation* error.** `RETURNING`'s `Column` leaves are bound at **plan** time;
  since the chain-wide plan-time binding gate a neighbour clause's **name** error is bound
  there too and wins as on 18.6 — `DELETE … WHERE nosuchw=1 RETURNING nosuchr`,
  its `UPDATE` twin and the `RETURNING zzz.x` spelling all name `nosuchw` on both engines
  now — but a row-source *value* error and a `FROM` *relation* error are still reached at
  eval, after the `RETURNING` binding. Measured against 18.6, pglet naming the
  `RETURNING` column in every row:

  | statement | 18.6 | pglet |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `INSERT … VALUES ('notanint', …) RETURNING nosuchr` | `22P02` | `42703 "nosuchr"` |
  | `UPDATE … FROM nosuchsrc s … RETURNING nosuchr` | `42P01 "nosuchsrc"` | `42703 "nosuchr"` |
  | `INSERT … ON CONFLICT (nosuchcol) DO NOTHING RETURNING nosuchr` | `42703 "nosuchcol"` | `42703 "nosuchr"` |

  Controls that still agree, and they are what make this a statement about *plan-time
  binding* rather than a `RETURNING`-beats-everything one: `UPDATE … SET nosuchcol=1
  RETURNING nosuchr` is `42703 "nosuchr"` on both (the `SET` list resolves last on both
  sides), the INSERT **column list** (`INSERT … (nosuchcol) …`) beats it on both, an
  ill-typed cast in the `WHERE` (`WHERE id='notanint'`) is `22P02` on both, and the
  missing-source case's **other two** `RETURNING` members agree — `UPDATE … FROM
  nosuchsrc s … RETURNING *` and `… RETURNING <target>.*` are both `42P01 "nosuchsrc"`
  here and there, so it is the bare *name* member alone that diverges.

  It is **not** a clean type-axis-holds / name-axis-fails split, and reading it as one
  is wrong twice over. The table's INSERT row is a *type* error losing to a name error —
  `INSERT … VALUES ('notanint', …) RETURNING nosuchr` is `22P02` there and `42703` here,
  because pglet coerces an INSERT cell per row at eval while Postgres transforms the row
  source before `transformReturningClause`. What the `WHERE` control shows is narrower:
  a cast in a clause pglet *also* lowers at plan time is ordered correctly. Closing the
  class means moving the neighbour clauses' name resolution to plan time, which is a
  posture change and not a reordering — it is *not* a fifth guard sitting outside the
  clause order.

  **Divergence (loud, wrong order):** four guards still run ahead of the clause order.
  The `GENERATED ALWAYS` identity check (`428C9`) fires at four sites before any clause
  is typed, where Postgres raises it in the **rewriter** — after all of parse analysis —
  so `UPDATE t SET always_id = 5 WHERE <ill-typed>` is `42804` there and `428C9` here.
  And an `INSERT` **arity** mismatch outranks an ill-typed cell whose error pglet reaches
  only at execution (`VALUES (1 + '1x', 2, 3)` is `22P02` there and `42601` here); a cell
  pglet gates at plan time wins, as Postgres transforms the value list first (row 226's
  residual). Both report a real problem with the statement; only
  which of two real problems is named differs. Related: the `ON CONFLICT` **arbiter
  target** (`ON CONFLICT (<expr>)`) is never resolved or gated, so an ill-typed one is
  `42P10`/`42883` rather than Postgres's `42804`/`42703` — and where the statement also
  carries a `RETURNING`, the arbiter's error is not reported at all: `INSERT … ON
  CONFLICT (nosuchcol) DO NOTHING RETURNING nosuchr` is 18.6's `42703 "nosuchcol"` and
  pglet's `42703 "nosuchr"`, a member of the name-axis table above rather than of this
  guard. Resolving the arbiter would change how it matches an expression index, so it is
  deliberately left alone.
- **14 · Sequences model no `MINVALUE`/`MAXVALUE`, so every value-range check is missing.**
  Postgres range-checks a sequence's `START WITH`, its `RESTART` target, and every
  `setval` against the sequence's bounds — for an ascending sequence with `NO MINVALUE`
  the floor is `1` — so `CREATE SEQUENCE s START WITH 0` is `22023`, `ALTER SEQUENCE s
  RESTART WITH 0` is `22023`, `CREATE SEQUENCE s START WITH 3 RESTART -5` is `22023`
  (`RESTART` is a `CREATE` option too, so the gap has a `CREATE`-time door as well as
  an `ALTER`-time one), and `setval(s, 0)` is `22003`. pglet accepts all four and
  stores the out-of-range counter, whose next `nextval` then returns a value Postgres
  could never issue. This is one gap, not three: pglet's `nextval` is unconditionally
  `last_value + 1` with no bounds to check against, so closing it means modeling the
  bounds. Closing it *at the source* would also need the bounds, not just a `< 1`
  test: an explicit `MINVALUE n` (which pglet parses and ignores) makes a low
  `START WITH`/`RESTART`/`setval` perfectly legal on Postgres, so an unconditional
  rejection over-rejects. Only absence and `NO MINVALUE` mean `1` (measured on 18.6).
  The **dump is closed regardless**: a sequence whose start or resume point sits below
  `1` emits the explicit `MINVALUE` that floor needs (and, with it, an explicit
  `START WITH`, since `init_params` otherwise seeds `seqstart` from the minimum), so
  the acceptance gap no longer costs portability.

- **15 · The tolerated-no-op family never reaches the kind gate.** A statement the parser
  turns into a whole-statement no-op has no target resolution at all, so no amount of
  work on the wrong-kind gate can reach it — which is what keeps it outside the
  otherwise-closed `42809` class, and why it is a *parser* item rather than a gate one.
  `COMMENT ON`, `GRANT` and `REVOKE` are the open members; `ALTER TABLE IF EXISTS` was the
  other, and is closed with the residuals its sub-bullet names.
  - **`ALTER TABLE IF EXISTS …` — closed, with residuals.** The parser read
    `ALTER TABLE [ONLY] <name>` and dispatched on the token *after* it, so `IF` landed in
    the **name** slot and `EXISTS` was an action it did not know, and the statement fell
    through to the catch-all that tolerates a `pg_dump` clause as a no-op: `ALTER TABLE IF
    EXISTS t DROP COLUMN b` reported `ALTER TABLE` and left `b` in place on a real table,
    and over an existing `t15 (a int)` the actions' own verdicts — `ADD COLUMN a int`,
    `DROP COLUMN nosuch`, `ALTER COLUMN a TYPE nosuchtype`, 18.6's `42701`, `42703` and
    `42704` — and a sequence target's `42809` all reported success.

    **What closed it.** `parser::ddl`'s `parse_alter_table_body` reads the clause where
    `IF` is followed by `EXISTS` — `IF` is an unreserved keyword, so `ALTER TABLE if DROP
    COLUMN b` still drops `b` from a table called `if`, on both engines — and every
    `ALTER TABLE` plan carries it (`table_if_exists`). The executor answers 18.6's skip, a
    `NOTICE` `relation "…" does not exist, skipping` and the `ALTER TABLE` tag, when no
    relation holds the name, and runs the action otherwise — over an index or a sequence
    as well, which then meets the wrong-kind refusal it meets without `IF EXISTS`. The
    test is made where the statement runs, not where it is planned: a `DO` body's
    statements are planned before any of them runs, and `ALTER TABLE IF EXISTS` over a
    table the body itself creates adds the column. An operation pglet does not perform is
    a plan too, `Plan::AlterTableUnperformed`: a tolerated clause (`OWNER TO`, `SET
    STATISTICS`, …) reports `ALTER TABLE`, and a refused one (`RENAME`, `DROP
    CONSTRAINT`, `ALTER COLUMN … TYPE`, `DROP NOT NULL`, …) answers its `0A000` only over a
    relation that exists — so under `IF EXISTS` it is the skip, and without it a missing
    relation is `42P01`, as on 18.6, where the parser used to answer `0A000` (and
    `42601` for `DROP CONSTRAINT`, whose `CONSTRAINT` it read as a column name).
    `pg_dump --clean --if-exists` writes `ALTER TABLE IF EXISTS ONLY t DROP CONSTRAINT IF
    EXISTS c` for every constraint; over a missing table it is the skip, and over one that
    exists it is now `0A000` where it was a silent no-op — 18.6 drops the constraint, or,
    with it absent, notices and skips. A two-part name whose qualifier is neither `public`
    nor a system schema (`information_schema`, or a `pg_` name — the prefix 18.6 reserves,
    `42939` at `CREATE SCHEMA`) is the skip too, decided where the statement is parsed:
    pglet creates no other schema, so no relation can be there, and in a database
    pglet's own statements build 18.6 skips it as a missing schema's relation
    (`qualifier_holds_no_relation`). The operation is read first, so a grammar error in
    it is still `42601`, and the notice names the relation's own name, `relation "t" does
    not exist, skipping`, as 18.6's does. A `public` table of that name is not touched,
    `"Public"` being such a qualifier too (measured).

    Measured residuals, each under `IF EXISTS` over a name no relation holds, against
    18.6's skip. An action whose refusal the parser raises while reading it answers that
    refusal: `ADD CHECK ((SELECT 1) > 0)` is `0A000`, `ADD COLUMN s SERIAL DEFAULT 5` and
    the comma-separated action list `ADD COLUMN b INT, ADD COLUMN c INT` are `42601` — the
    list being `42601` over a table that exists too, where 18.6 performs both actions.
    Loud. The other direction is silent: the tail of a tolerated or refused operation is
    consumed unread, so `ALTER TABLE IF EXISTS nosuch RENAME garbage garbage` and `…
    OWNER TO x y z` skip where 18.6 answers `42601`, as `ALTER TABLE <a table> OWNER TO
    x y z` reports success. A tolerated clause without `IF
    EXISTS` does not look its relation up, so `ALTER TABLE <a missing table> OWNER TO x`
    reports success where 18.6 answers `42P01`. The parser's refusal of the *name* wins
    over the skip as well: a system-schema qualifier keeps `reduce_qualified_name`'s
    `42P01` — `pg_catalog.<a missing name>`, `information_schema.<a missing name>`,
    `pg_temp.t` and `pg_toast.t` are 18.6's skip, and over a catalog relation 18.6 answers
    `42501` (`pg_catalog.pg_class`) or `42809` (`information_schema.tables`), an answer
    that turns on catalog relations pglet has no list of — and a `pg_`-prefixed qualifier
    naming no schema at all keeps it too, `pg_nosuch.t` and `"pg_Catalog".t`, which 18.6
    skips; and a three-part name is
    `reduce_qualified_name`'s `42601`, where the current database's `db.public.t` is
    18.6's skip. Loud; each measured.
  - **`COMMENT ON …` — every object form.** `NoopCommand::Comment` swallows the whole
    statement, so `COMMENT ON TABLE <a sequence>` / `<an index>`,
    `COMMENT ON SEQUENCE <a table>`, `COMMENT ON INDEX <a table>` and
    `COMMENT ON COLUMN <a sequence-or-index>.<an existing column>` all report `COMMENT`
    where Postgres raises `42809` — and a missing relation reports `COMMENT` where
    Postgres raises `42P01` (all measured on 18.6). The column form splits the same way
    the sequence row's `42703`-vs-`42809` note describes: a column the sequence's
    `(last_value, log_cnt, is_called)` descriptor lacks is `42703` there, while
    `last_value` itself reaches `42809`. pglet stores no comments, so for a *correct*
    target the no-op answers as 18.6 does, and what it drops is visible to one reader:
    after `COMMENT ON COLUMN cdt2.a IS 'hello'`, `col_description(a.attrelid, a.attnum)`
    over `cdt2.a`'s `pg_attribute` row is `hello` on 18.6 and NULL here (measured) —
    silent; the `col_description('cdt2'::regclass, 1)` spelling is `42883` here (row 250). The wrong-kind and
    missing-relation cases are the other divergence.
  - **`GRANT` / `REVOKE` — every object form.** `NoopCommand::Grant` and `NoopCommand::Revoke`
    swallow the statement the same way (`parser/mod.rs`), so neither the privilege's target
    nor its grantee is resolved. Measured through the npm package against 18.6: `GRANT SELECT
    ON nosuch TO public`, `GRANT SELECT ON TABLE nosuch TO public`, `GRANT ALL ON SEQUENCE
    nosuch TO public` and `REVOKE SELECT ON nosuch FROM public` answer `GRANT` / `REVOKE` here
    and `42P01 relation "nosuch" does not exist` there, and `GRANT SELECT ON tt TO
    nosuchrole`, over an existing `tt`, answers `GRANT` against `42704 role "nosuchrole" does
    not exist`. The other object forms tried answer `GRANT` / `REVOKE` here and each its
    own code on 18.6: `ON SCHEMA nosuch` and `ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA nosuch` `3F000`, `ON
    FUNCTION nosuchfn()` `42883`, `ON DATABASE nosuchdb` `3D000`, `ON TYPE nosuchtype`
    `42704`, `ON SEQUENCE <a table>` `42809`, a column privilege over a missing column
    (`SELECT (zz) ON tt`) `42703`, and the role form `GRANT nosuchrole TO postgres`
    `42704`. In the same run `ALTER TABLE nosuch OWNER TO postgres` is the sub-bullet
    above's tolerated-clause member (`ALTER` here, `42P01` there), while `ALTER SEQUENCE
    nosuch OWNER TO postgres` is `42P01` on both. pglet models no privileges, so over a real
    target and grantee the no-op answers as 18.6 does. Reach: ordinary — a migration's
    `GRANT` naming a table it has not created, or one a later migration renamed.

  Closing `COMMENT ON` means the real implementation — parse the form and resolve its
  target — not a refusal: the tolerated no-op is deliberate for the inert `COMMENT ON`
  statements a `pg_dump` script carries, and failing loud instead would break that
  tolerance. A smaller sibling
  on the same theme, and the members are **five**, not two: a statement that
  *legitimately* skips emits no `NOTICE`
  where Postgres says `… already exists, skipping` / `… does not exist, skipping`.
  Measured on 18.6 one statement per connection, so no outcome can be mis-attributed to
  a neighbour: `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` and `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS` over an
  existing relation, `CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS public`, `ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN IF
  NOT EXISTS` over an existing column, and `ALTER TABLE … DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS` over a
  missing one. The last two really do skip — the column is neither duplicated nor
  dropped, and the same `DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS` drops a column that *is* there — they
  just say nothing. Seven spellings notice, with Postgres's wording: `CREATE SEQUENCE IF
  NOT EXISTS`, `ALTER SEQUENCE IF EXISTS`, `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS`, `DROP INDEX IF
  EXISTS`, `DROP SEQUENCE IF EXISTS`, `DROP SCHEMA IF EXISTS` and `DROP TYPE IF
  EXISTS`; of these, `CREATE SEQUENCE IF NOT EXISTS` sends SQLSTATE `00000` where 18.6
  sends `42P07`, and the six does-not-exist notices send `00000` on both (measured, psql
  `VERBOSITY verbose`). A third group is **loud**
  rather than silent, so it is a different divergence — the statement's *outcome*
  differs, not just its diagnostic: `ALTER TABLE … DROP CONSTRAINT IF EXISTS` over a
  table that exists is `0A000` (the drop is refused, the sub-bullet above), and `ALTER
  INDEX IF EXISTS …` and `ALTER VIEW IF EXISTS …` are `42601` (the parser has neither
  statement), while
  `DROP VIEW IF EXISTS` and the `MATERIALIZED VIEW` /
  `FUNCTION` / `TRIGGER` spellings are `0A000` — every one of them a
  `NOTICE` + skip on Postgres (the object-dispatch arm behind them is row 99). `DROP EXTENSION IF EXISTS` used to be in that list
  and is not any more: it skips, as Postgres does ([ddl.md](docs/ddl.md)
  § Extensions are a name check, not a catalog). `CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS <any name but public>` is
  `0A000` for a second reason (pglet models one implicit schema), so Postgres either
  creates it or notices and skips. For the five, the outcome is right and only the
  diagnostic is missing; the fixture harness compares rows and errors, not notices, so nothing there
  can hold any of it.

- **~~248~~ · Closed — A table carries a row type of its own name, and the type namespace
  holds it.** 18.6's `pg_type` holds each enum and each table's row type, and two routines
  ask it for a new name. `heap_create_with_catalog` asks it of every relation it creates —
  a sequence too, though a sequence gets no row type — behind the relation name's own
  `42P07`, answering `42710 type "…" already exists` with the hint `A relation has an
  associated type of the same name, so you must use a name that doesn't conflict with any
  existing type.`; `DefineEnum` asks it of an enum, `42710` with no hint. `index_create`
  never asks. Measured with `reltype <> 0` over `pg_class`: true of a table and a view,
  false of an index and a sequence — so an enum over an index's or a sequence's name is
  accepted, and an index over an enum's. pglet asked the relation namespace alone, so
  `CREATE TYPE ty8 AS ENUM ('a'); CREATE TABLE ty8 (x INT)` built both, and so did an
  enum over a table, a sequence over an enum, a declared identity `SEQUENCE NAME` over
  one, and a `SERIAL`'s minted `<table>_<column>_seq` — `ChooseRelationName` steps around
  `pg_class` alone, so 18.6 keeps the minted name and refuses it rather than picking
  `…_seq1`. Silent, and it wrote: `pglet_server dump` of a `--data-dir` store holding
  `ty8` as both, with a row, exited `0`, and `psql -f` into a fresh 18.6 database refused
  the `CREATE TABLE`, then answered `relation "ty8" does not exist` at the `COPY` and a
  syntax error at its row — the table and its row lost, `psql` exiting `0`.

  **What closed it.** `Schema::type_name_taken` is the type namespace pglet models — the
  enums and the tables' names. `execute_create_table` asks it directly behind the table's
  `42P07`, `execute_create_sequence` behind the sequence's and past its `IF NOT EXISTS`
  skip (which reads the relation namespace only, on both engines), and
  `resolve_implicit_sequence_name` of every `SERIAL` or identity sequence, minted or
  declared, at all three routes — each `Error::RelationTypeAlreadyExists`, carrying the
  hint. `execute_create_type` asks it of the folded key the enum is stored under, and asks
  the tables for the name as written, 18.6's own collision (`Error::DuplicateType`, no
  hint). `DROP TYPE` of a table's name finds the row type and is `2BP01 cannot drop type
  … because table … requires it`, `IF EXISTS` and `CASCADE` included, where it answered
  `22000` does-not-exist, or skipped. `execute_drop_type` looks the row type up by the
  name as written **ahead of** the enum lookup, which reads the folded key: `DROP TYPE
  "Rd"` beside a table `"Rd"` and an enum `rd` is the `2BP01` on both engines and the
  enum stays, the message and hint quoting the name as 18.6's do (`cannot drop type "Rd"
  because table "Rd" requires it`, measured). The one enum it reaches first is one
  holding that name byte for byte beside a table of it — a pair the gates above refuse to
  build, which a store written before them can hold — so such a pair is parted by dropping the enum where no
  column declares it (the paragraph on the refusal, below). A `DEFAULT nextval('<an enum>')` is `42P01` at the
  default's cook, as on 18.6, whose `'x'::regclass` finds no relation — where the name
  would otherwise be registered as a new sequence beside the type. Positions measured on
  both engines: a table's `42710` loses to a column type's `42704` and a repeated
  column's `42701`, and beats a missing foreign-key parent's `42P01`, a constraint index
  name a relation already holds (`42P07`) and a default's own `22P02`; a sequence's beats
  its `OWNED BY` table's `42P01`. A refused `CREATE TABLE` or `ADD COLUMN … SERIAL` leaves
  the catalog as it was on the autocommit path — no sequence, index or column it had
  claimed. A table and an enum of different names still dump, and restore into 18.6 under
  `ON_ERROR_STOP`.

  **A pair that stays legal, and the dump.** An enum over a sequence's name is accepted
  on both engines, so a sequence and an enum of one name — the sequence first — is a state
  pglet's own statements build, and a `DEFAULT nextval('<that name>')` names the sequence
  on both (`ddl/type_namespace_default_nextval_over_a_sequence_sharing_an_enum_name.sql`).
  `dump_sql` emits every `CREATE SEQUENCE` ahead of every `CREATE TYPE`
  (`emit_create_sequence`'s order note), since a `CREATE SEQUENCE` after the enum is
  `42710` on the reload. Measured on a
  `--data-dir` store holding a sequence `sq9` beside an enum `sq9`, a table drawing from
  the one with a column of the other, and a `SERIAL`'s `sr_id_seq` beside an enum
  `sr_id_seq` that a later column of the owning table declares: dumped with exit `0`,
  then run under `psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1` into a fresh pglet and a fresh 18.6, each exit
  `0`, and the rows, `pg_type` and the next draws agree on both and with an 18.6
  database the same statements built. The dump
  that created the types first was refused at its first `CREATE SEQUENCE` on both, exit
  `3`. An identity column's sequence cannot go first — its `ADD GENERATED` follows its
  table, and the table may declare the enum — so for an identity sequence and an enum of
  one name, also a state both engines build, `dump_sql` refuses the database, `0A000`
  naming the sequence (`refuse_identity_sequence_named_like_an_enum`): loud, and it costs
  the whole database's export. It emitted a script whose `ADD GENERATED` both engines
  refuse, and which `psql` without `ON_ERROR_STOP` ran to exit `0` with the column no
  longer an identity (measured into 18.6). 18.6's own `pg_dump` of that state is refused
  at the same statement (measured, exit `3`). `test_dump` round-trips the sequence-first
  pairs into both engines; `crates/pglet`'s `type_namespace` holds the order and the
  refusal.

  **A pair only a store written before the gates holds.** The gates close the producers,
  and a `--data-dir` store an earlier build wrote can hold a table and an enum of one
  name and still opens, its persisted shape unchanged. Whichever of the two `CREATE`s a
  restore runs second is `42710` on both engines, so `dump_sql` refuses the database,
  `0A000` naming the table (`refuse_table_named_like_an_enum`), as it refuses a legacy
  stored expression it cannot render (row 49). Its test is the enum's catalog key
  against the table's name, byte for byte — the reload's own collision, since the script
  spells the enum by that key, bare, and the table through `quote_ident` — so a table
  `"IdQ"` beside an enum created as `"IdQ"` (key `idq`) is not refused, and reloads.
  Measured on stores the build before the gates wrote: an enum then a table `ty8` with
  rows, a table then an enum `tb2`, a table `yc` beside an enum created as `"Yc"`, and an
  enum created as `"Ab5"` beside a table `ab5` — each dump exits `1` with nothing
  emitted, where that build's exited `0`, and its `ty8` script restored into 18.6 without
  the table, `psql` exiting `0`. A store holding `"IdQ"` beside `idq`, `"Ty9"` beside
  `ty9` and a pair of different names dumps with exit `0` and reloads under
  `ON_ERROR_STOP` into 18.6 and into pglet, the rows agreeing with the source. The refusal costs the whole database's export until the pair is parted: `DROP TYPE ty8` drops the
  enum, and the store then dumps and reloads into 18.6 with the table's rows. That parting is safe only where no column
  declares the enum: under one — the `"Ab5"` member's shape — `DROP TYPE` is accepted as well (row 261), the column left declaring
  a type the dump never creates, and the store then dumps with exit `0` to a script whose `CREATE TABLE` 18.6 refuses
  `42704`, the table and its rows lost, `psql` exiting `0` (measured).
  `dump.rs`'s `a_legacy_table_named_like_an_enum_fails_the_dump_loudly` holds it.

  Residuals, measured. An enum is stored under its ASCII-folded key (`execute_create_type`'s
  fold), which a quoted name does not share: `CREATE TYPE "YB"` over a table `yb` is
  refused `42710` here and accepted there — an over-rejection kept because the catalog
  would otherwise hold an enum and a table under one name — while over an enum created as
  `"Yc"`, `CREATE TABLE "Yc"` is accepted here (18.6 `42710`) and `CREATE TABLE yc` refused
  (18.6 accepts). At `CREATE` the fold is loud both ways; at `DROP TYPE` it is silent, and
  it writes: with no table holding the name as written, `DROP TYPE "Rd"` drops an enum
  created as `rd`, and `DROP TYPE rd` one created as `"Rd"` — 18.6 answers `42704` to both
  (measured). A name no type holds is `22000` does-not-exist here and `42704` there. A
  table's row type is in the namespace and nowhere else: `pg_type` lists
  no row for it (row 42), and it is no column type or cast target — `CREATE TABLE t2 (a
  zc1)` and `NULL::zc1` over a table `zc1` are `42704` here, and 18.6 accepts both. Across
  two connections the cross-kind `CREATE` is row 240's.

- **16 · Divergences no fixture reaches, and one of them still loses a write: an outside `query()`
  joining a raw-`BEGIN` transaction on the npm adapter, and a concurrent top-level
  `db.transaction()`.** The adapter's public
  `query()` queues behind an open `transaction()`, so the audit-log shape — a telemetry write
  that must outlive a failed business transaction — survives a rollback there, and
  `tests-web/npm/` plus `scripts/test_npm_node.mjs` pin it. But the queue is `transaction()`'s
  boundary and a raw `query('BEGIN')` has none: from the adapter's side the transaction's own
  statements and an outside one are the same call on the same lane, so `PgletDb.query` cannot
  tell them apart at all. Measured on the built package,
  `BEGIN; <write>; <an outside write>; ROLLBACK` loses the outside write — the reference here is a
  driver, not 18.6, since the shape is an adapter contract rather than a SQL answer.
  **That reference is a connection pool, and "`pg` and PGlite keep it", which this entry used to
  say, is measurably false.** On the identical raw-`BEGIN` spelling PGlite loses the write too
  (measured on 0.4.5 and 0.5.4) and so does a single `pg.Client`; a `pg` **Pool** keeps it by
  running it on a second connection. PGlite's boundary is `transaction()`'s, exactly as pglet's
  now is — its managed `transaction()` keeps the write on both versions. So the member is not
  "pglet diverges from its two references": of the four configurations measured, the three
  one-connection ones (pglet, PGlite, `pg.Client`) all lose this spelling and the pool keeps it,
  and what the pool has that they do not is a second connection to run the statement on.
  It stays recorded because it is silent and it loses a write a consumer following the
  `transaction()` documentation would keep, not because a comparable engine does better.
  Narrowed, not closed. One layer up the deferral is real but its **recorded reason was wrong**:
  kysely's driver seam hands `PgletDriver` explicit
  `beginTransaction`/`commitTransaction`/`rollbackTransaction` calls, and holding the lane across
  them needs no new API — `PgletDb.transaction()` is a lane-holding primitive once a deferred
  promise converts its callback scope into a controlled one. Prototyped against the public
  package: the shipped dialect loses the outside write (0 rows), the lane-holding driver keeps it
  (1 row), with the rollback still correct and the connection reusable. Two edits carry it, both
  inside `kysely.js` — a fresh `PgletConnection` per `acquireConnection` (it is a shared singleton
  today, and that aliasing is what makes the limitation look inherent) and routing the
  transactional connection through the held `tx` handle. What the prototype did **not** cover, and
  a real pass owes: kysely's savepoint hooks, the concurrent-transaction error changing from
  `25001` to `transaction()`'s nested rejection, and running `kysely_test.ts` against it. A
  hand-rolled
  raw-`BEGIN` consumer has no boundary either way. Beside it and **loud**
  rather than silent: a second `db.transaction()` called while a callback is running is rejected
  as *nested* whatever its lexical position, because the flag is read at call time and a browser
  has no `AsyncLocalStorage` to separate the readings — so a genuinely top-level concurrent
  transaction does not run at all, where a `pg` pool would give it its own connection and PGlite
  serializes it (measured: both callbacks fulfil and both rows land, while a genuinely *nested*
  PGlite `transaction()` does not settle at all). The undecidability is shared; the resolution
  is pglet's own choice, taken because the deadlock it declines to risk is largely silent — an
  ordinary `main()`-at-module-bottom entry exits **0** with no output at all, on node, deno and
  bun alike. Both are
  documented on `PgletDb` and in the package README, and `dx_test.ts` pins both as divergences.
  The same undecidability reaches `fork()` and `close()`: called while a `transaction()` callback
  is running, each is refused rather than queued, since awaiting it inside that callback would
  deadlock and a call from outside it cannot be told apart — so a teardown `close()` racing a
  running callback is refused and changes nothing (the db stays as it was: open, or draining
  toward an earlier `close()`).

- **~~17~~ · Closed — `fork()` branches the committed tree and clones the live catalog, so it refuses while a
  block is open (`25001`).** `Database::fork` takes `schema.clone()` while the storage fork
  takes the committed root, and no backend rolls the catalog back — so serving a fork across
  that split hands it two halves that disagree, silently in both directions: a pending
  `DROP TABLE` hid a committed table *and its committed rows* (`42P01`), a pending
  `ADD COLUMN` gave a wider descriptor than the rows carry (the wire-breaking phantom, made
  by `fork()` alone). On the advertised seed-once/fork-per-test workflow that yields
  well-formed empty fixtures, so the gate is the right answer rather than a catalog
  snapshot at the `Database` layer. Sequence counters ride the same `schema.clone()`, so
  sibling forks emit the same `SERIAL` ids — correct per-test behaviour, but a suite
  asserting id uniqueness across databases would fail.
- **18 · The aborted block is gated at Postgres's five phases now — and the two answers still
  divergent are both the *simple-query* gate's, not a missing phase.** `postgres.c` gates on
  `IsAbortedTransactionBlockState()` at five statement-processing phases (six tests, since
  Describe is two functions), and each reads a **different** discriminator, which is why they
  are five gates and not one applied five times:

  | phase | its test |
  | --- | --- |
  | `exec_simple_query`, per parse tree | `!IsTransactionExitStmt(parsetree->stmt)` |
  | `exec_parse_message`, inside `if (parsetree_list != NIL)` | `!IsTransactionExitStmt(raw_parse_tree->stmt)` |
  | `exec_bind_message` | `!(raw_parse_tree && IsTransactionExitStmt(…)) \|\| numParams != 0` |
  | `exec_describe_statement_message` | `psrc->resultDesc` — *does it return data* |
  | `exec_describe_portal_message` | `portal->tupDesc` — the same fact, other function |
  | `exec_execute_message` | `!IsTransactionExitStmtList(portal->stmts)` |

  pglet has all six. `Bind`'s is the **whole** condition and not its headline: disjunct 1 refuses
  a comment-only statement too (a NULL `raw_parse_tree` fails the exit test rather than being
  exempted — there is no `parsetree_list != NIL` exemption here, that test is
  `exec_parse_message`'s alone), and disjunct 2 **un-exempts** an exit statement that declared
  parameters, which one can only acquire at `Parse` since there is no `$N` to write in
  `ROLLBACK`. `Describe`'s reads the result descriptor rather than the statement kind, so an
  `INSERT` with no `RETURNING` is still described in a failed block on both engines — Postgres's
  comment gives the reason, in both functions: refusing every Describe *"might break the ability
  of some clients to issue COMMIT or ROLLBACK commands, if they use code that blindly Describes
  whatever it does"*.

  Re-measured with a raw v3 client that syncs and reads each phase separately (psql's `\bind`
  flushes Bind/Describe/Execute in one round trip and cannot separate them), against 18.6 and
  against the in-memory B+tree server: **28 of 30 shapes byte-identical**, including every
  `Bind` / `Describe` / `Execute` row and the parameterized-exit shape. The two that are not:

  | shape, in an aborted block | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | a **comment-only** simple query (`/* x */`) | `25P02` | `EmptyQueryResponse`, block still `[E]` |
  | a **parse-analysis** error (`SELEC 1`) | `25P02` | `42601` |

  Both belong to the simple-query gate. The first is a splitter difference:
  `exec_simple_query` loops over parse *trees*, so a comment-only message never reaches its test
  (`parsetree_list` is NIL), while pglet's `split_statements` slices raw **text** and hands such
  a piece to the gate. Skipping it there would trade one divergence for another, because pglet
  answers a comment-only simple query `CommandComplete "ALTER TABLE"` outside any transaction —
  `Plan::Empty`'s placeholder tag reaching the wire, measured on both engines (18.6:
  `EmptyQueryResponse`), and a divergence of its own that has nothing to do with transactions.
  The second is the same SQLSTATE-shaped approximation of the grammar/analysis stage split that
  the `Parse` arm documents: `pg_parse_query` runs ahead of the abort test there, so a grammar
  error surfaces as itself, and pglet's front end is one pass. A **lex** error (`SELECT 'abc`)
  now agrees at `42601` on both, because `split_statements` raises before the gate is reached.

  The **admitted set** diverges too, and that half is the parser's: pglet admits `COMMIT`/`END`
  (with the `TRANSACTION`/`WORK` noise word, excluding an `AND [NO] CHAIN` tail) and any
  statement whose first token is the `ROLLBACK` keyword, while `IsTransactionExitStmt` also
  admits `ABORT` and `PREPARE TRANSACTION` — which pglet's grammar does not model, so admitting
  them here would only move their `42601` from the gate to the parser. Pinned as such in
  `pglet`'s `exit_answers_that_diverge_from_the_reference`.

  **No fixture can hold any of this**, and for two independent reasons. A fixture is SQL text
  plus directives, so it can address a statement but not a phase — the recorded reason. And the
  harness cannot reach the aborted state at all: it propagates the first error from every
  statement it runs (`run_setup` with `?`, `execute_test` by returning), so the statement that
  *creates* the aborted state and the statement that *observes* it cannot sit on opposite sides
  of the compared boundary. The guards are accordingly raw-frame unit tests in `pglet_server`'s
  `handlers.rs` and `execute.rs`, an embed test in `crates/pglet`, and — for a real client over
  a real socket — two cases in `test_concurrent`.

- **19 · A portal's `RowDescription` reports result format code `0` for every column, whatever
  format the `Bind` asked for; 18.6 reports the format it will actually send.** The v3
  `RowDescription` field carries a per-column format code, and `Describe(portal)` is the
  reply that can fill it — a statement's `Describe` cannot, since no `Bind` has chosen a
  format yet, and `0` is the right answer there on both engines. After an all-binary
  `Bind`, pglet still says `0` and then sends binary bytes. Measured with a raw v3 client
  (`Parse`/`Bind`/`Describe(portal)`/`Execute`/`Sync`, one message per phase), against a
  scratch 18.6 database, on the in-memory B+tree backend of the accelerated build:

  | `Bind` result format | pglet `Describe(portal)` | 18.6 `Describe(portal)` | bytes both send |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | binary (`0001 0001`) | `[{oid:23, fmt:0}]` | `[{oid:23, fmt:1}]` | `len=4 00015f90` |
  | text (`0001 0000`) | `[{oid:23, fmt:0}]` | `[{oid:23, fmt:0}]` | `len=5 3930303030` |

  The query was the **control** `SELECT s + i FROM mw` — no alias, no derived table — so
  this is not the input-scope class the `alias_*_declared_types` fixtures cover; the field
  is simply never populated from the `Bind`. Whether a real client breaks on it is
  **inferred, not measured**: a client that trusts the field over its own `Bind` request
  would misparse, and none has been run against it here. The harness is structurally blind
  — tokio-postgres reads `Describe(statement)`, where `0` is correct — so no fixture and no
  declared-type leg can see it. Not fixed: populating it is a server change in the
  `Describe(portal)` path, a different seam from the walker scope that moved.

- **20 · A portal outlives the transaction that created it here and does not there, and the
  unnamed prepared statement outlives a simple query.** Postgres destroys portals at every
  transaction end — `PreCommit_Portals` removes the non-holdable ones created in the
  transaction, `AtCleanup_Portals` deletes them on abort — and `exec_simple_query`
  additionally drops the unnamed statement. pglet's `conn.portals` and `conn.prepared`
  (`handlers.rs`) are inserted at `Bind` / `Parse` and removed at `Close`, and at no other
  site in the crate; nothing reads transaction state. Note the width: this is **not** the
  aborted block, and it needs no failed statement. Measured with the same raw v3 client,
  byte-identical on the in-memory B+tree, `--storage memory` and stripped-B+tree legs:

  | after | phase | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | autocommit `Parse ''`/`Bind ''`/`Sync`, no simple query anywhere | `Describe` the portal | `RowDescription(1)` | `34000` |
  | ” | `Execute` the portal | `DataRow` + `SELECT 1` | `34000` |
  | an explicit `COMMIT` (unnamed portal) | `Describe` / `Execute` | rows | `34000` |
  | an explicit `ROLLBACK` (**named** portal) | `Describe` / `Execute` | rows | `34000` |
  | a **successful** simple query inside a block | `Describe` the unnamed **statement** | `ParameterDescription(0)` + `RowDescription(1)` | `26000` |
  | ” | `Describe` the unnamed **portal** | `RowDescription(1)` | `34000` |

  The first row is the one that bounds the class: an autocommit `Bind` followed by `Sync`
  already ends Postgres's implicit transaction, so the portal is gone before the client's
  next message — no explicit transaction, no simple query, no failure. Two consequences, and
  the second is the sharp one. An `Execute` after `COMMIT` returns rows from a portal 18.6
  destroyed. And a `SELECT *` portal bound before `ALTER TABLE un2 DROP COLUMN b`
  **silently re-shapes**: `RowDescription(2)['a','b']` at bind time, then `RowDescription(1)
  ['a']` and a one-field `DataRow` after the DDL, so a client decoding by the `RowDescription`
  it already read mis-reads the row — the declared-type-vs-wire class reached through portal
  staleness. **Row 62 is the statement-level twin of that member**, reached with no portal
  and no transaction boundary at all: there 18.6 keeps the object and refuses with its
  plancache's `0A000 cached plan must not change result type`, so the re-shape has an
  oracle comparison this member does not — 18.6 having already destroyed the portal here.
  The loud corner, for contrast: `Execute` over a portal whose table was `DROP`ped
  is `42P01` here and `34000` there — loud on both, different code.
  **Nothing guards any of it, and the two halves are unguarded for different reasons.** A
  fixture cannot express it *by construction* — a fixture is SQL text plus directives, so it
  can neither address a phase nor hold a portal across a transaction boundary, the same
  blindness the `Bind`/`Describe` gates above have. A raw-frame unit test *can*, as those two
  are, and none exists: this half is simply unwritten, not unwritable. Not fixed — dropping
  portals at transaction end and the unnamed statement at simple query is a server behaviour
  change, and adding or moving a gate changes error precedence every time.

- **169 · An `Execute` runs its portal's statement again, and ignores its row limit.** The
  native server's `Execute` handler (`handlers.rs`) runs the portal's query over its bound
  values through `execute_query_core` each time it is called, sends every row and a
  `CommandComplete`, and drops the message's row limit (`docs/param_binding.md` records the
  dropped limit). 18.6 runs a portal once and fetches from it: at most the limit's rows, then
  `PortalSuspended`, a further `Execute` resuming where the last stopped, and a finished
  portal answering no row — `SELECT 0`, `INSERT 0 0`, `UPDATE 0` — or `55000 portal "…"
  cannot be run` for a data-modifying statement with no `RETURNING`. Measured with a raw v3
  client, on the default storage, over `p(id INT PRIMARY KEY, v INT)` holding three rows
  and `s(x INT)` holding three, each statement `Parse`d, bound to a named portal and
  `Execute`d:

  | inside a `BEGIN` block | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT id FROM p ORDER BY id`, `Execute` limit 1, `Sync`, `Execute` limit 1 | three rows and `SELECT 3`, twice | `1`, `PortalSuspended`; `2`, `PortalSuspended` |
  | `UPDATE p SET v = v + 100 RETURNING id, v`, the same two `Execute`s, then `COMMIT` | three rows and `UPDATE 3`, twice; `sum(v)` `606` | a row and `PortalSuspended`, twice; `sum(v)` `306` |
  | `INSERT INTO s SELECT id + 10 FROM p RETURNING x`, the same | `s` holds nine rows | `s` holds six |
  | the `UPDATE`, `Execute` limit 0 twice | `UPDATE 3` twice, `sum(v)` `606` | `UPDATE 3`, then no row and `UPDATE 0` |
  | `INSERT INTO s SELECT id + 10 FROM p`, `Execute` limit 0 twice | `INSERT 0 3` twice, nine rows | `INSERT 0 3`, then `55000`; the block aborted |
  | the `SELECT`, `Execute` limit 1, then a simple `INSERT INTO p VALUES (4, 4)`, then `Execute` limit 0 | `1, 2, 3` and `SELECT 3`, then `1, 2, 3, 4` and `SELECT 4` | `1`, `PortalSuspended`, then `2, 3` and `SELECT 2` |

  A limit equal to the rows the portal returns is a member too — the `SELECT` with limit 3
  is its three rows and `PortalSuspended` there, and `SELECT 3` here. Two controls agree on
  both engines: a limit above that count (`5`) is every row and the command tag, for the
  `SELECT` and the `UPDATE` alike, and `SELECT id FROM p WHERE false` executed twice is
  `SELECT 0` twice.

  The same two `Execute`s before one `Sync`, outside a block, measure the same pairs, and
  the `INSERT` with no `RETURNING` leaves nine rows in `s` here where 18.6's `55000` aborts
  the implicit transaction and leaves three. A client that sends a row limit and fetches the
  rest with further `Execute`s — a cursor-style reader — receives the whole result each time,
  and a data-modifying statement read that way writes once per `Execute`. The limit is not
  needed to reach the write: a second `Execute` with limit 0 repeats it too. A portal used
  after its transaction has ended is row 20's; there too the `Execute` runs the statement
  again, where 18.6 answers `34000`. Neither the wasm host nor the embed `Database` has a
  portal: the wasm host's `query` / `query_params` and the `Database`'s `execute` /
  `execute_bound` run a statement once per call. No fixture can reach this — a fixture's
  extended leg sends each statement one `Execute` with limit 0 — and no test in the tree
  sends a non-zero row limit.

- **~~21~~ · Closed — Expression-key and partial-predicate index maintenance is evaluated at `COMMIT` on the
  B+tree backend, so a row that would poison it and is deleted before that `COMMIT` raises
  nowhere at all.** Measured before the repair on the native server (B+tree, in-memory) against 18.6, after
  `CREATE TABLE w (a INT); CREATE INDEX w_ix ON w ((10 / a)); INSERT INTO w VALUES (5);` —
  `BEGIN; INSERT INTO w VALUES (0); INSERT INTO w VALUES (9); DELETE FROM w WHERE a = 0;
  COMMIT;` reports success at every step here, tag `COMMIT`, and `SELECT a FROM w ORDER BY a`
  then answers `5, 9`; 18.6 raises `22012` at the first `INSERT`, answers `25P02` for the next
  two, converts the `COMMIT` to tag `ROLLBACK`, and answers `5`. A partial-index predicate
  carrying the same expression (`CREATE INDEX p_ix ON p (a) WHERE (10 / a) > 1`) measures the
  same pair. Dropping the `DELETE` moves the divergence rather than removing it — the
  in-block `SELECT` answers `0, 5`, a row that will never exist; the `COMMIT` then raises
  `22012` and leaves the block
  aborted (the next statement is `25P02`) until an explicit `ROLLBACK`, after which both
  engines hold `5`. **The aborted-block state does not close this**, which is worth stating
  because the shape looks like the aborted-block bullet above: every leg *has* that state, and
  the native server is where this bullet's rows were measured. Nothing raises until the `COMMIT`, so
  there is no failure for the state to latch — what would move the divergence is evaluating
  maintenance inside the statement. Not fixed here. **No fixture pins it, and the harness's
  wrapper is not why:** run as a fixture would run it — the whole setup plus a `SELECT`
  inside `BEGIN … ROLLBACK` — the two engines part at the poison `INSERT`, accepted here and
  `22012` there, and the `SELECT` answers `5, 9` here against `25P02` there. So a faithful
  fixture is red, not blind. On `--storage memory` the same script raises `22012` at the `INSERT` and ends at
  `5`, so the axis is the storage implementation and the B+tree side is the divergent one —
  the opposite polarity from the autocommit-atomicity edge below, where memory is the leaking
  one.

  **Mechanism** (source-read): `commit_transaction`
  (`crates/pglet_storage/src/btree/wrapper/transaction.rs`) builds the batch from
  `tx.pending`, which carries one final-state `PendingRow` per row id, and calls
  `emit_index_ops` per row with the old value read at the transaction's snapshot root — so a
  row inserted and then deleted inside the block arrives as `PendingRow::Deleted` with no old
  value, and nothing evaluates its key expression. What decides whether that batch is built
  once per statement or once per block is `run_one_locked`
  (`crates/pglet_server/src/execute.rs`): an autocommit statement that mutates storage runs
  inside a `storage.begin` / `commit` of its own, so under autocommit the evaluation happens
  within the statement and the error lands there. Inside an open block the statement runs
  unbracketed and the evaluation defers to the real `COMMIT`. That bracket is **not** what
  makes the memory backend agree with 18.6 here: `StorageBackend`'s `begin` and `commit` are
  no-ops for `Self::Memory` (`crates/pglet/src/backend.rs`) — it agrees because
  `MemoryStorage::insert` maintains the index inside the write itself.

  **A key the encoder refused reached the same deferral, and no longer does.** While the
  B-tree key encoder refused a float and a container key, a composite index over one
  (`CREATE INDEX fd_ix ON fd (id, j)` over `j JSONB`) accepted an in-block `INSERT` and
  raised the encoder's `0A000` at the `COMMIT`, where 18.6 commits the row. Both families
  have a key now (row 25), and re-measured on both build profiles against 18.6: `BEGIN;
  INSERT INTO fe9 VALUES (1, '{"a":1}'); INSERT INTO fe9 VALUES (2, '{"a":2}'); DELETE FROM
  fe9 WHERE id = 1; COMMIT;` under `CREATE INDEX fe9_ix ON fe9 (id, j)` commits the
  surviving row on each.

  **What closed it.** Every index entry is sized as 18.6 sizes it at every door that
  enters one (`executor::index_row`), and sizing an entry evaluates its key expressions and
  its partial predicate where the entry enters — at the write, inside the statement — so the
  poison row's error lands at its `INSERT`. Re-measured on the native server (B+tree,
  in-memory) against 18.6: the headline script answers `22012` at the first in-block
  `INSERT`, `25P02` for the next two, tags the `COMMIT` `ROLLBACK` and ends at `5`, as 18.6
  does; the partial-predicate spelling raises `22012` at its in-block `INSERT` on both. A
  build from just before the entry-sizing change answers the script as the first paragraph
  records; one from just after it answers as 18.6. Nothing pins the closure: no fixture or
  test drives the headline script.

  script. The rows the block writes itself are seen: a table created in the same block,
  and two in-block `INSERT INTO r VALUES (2)` after the `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX`, are `23505`

  own. An index committed before the `BEGIN` enforces the in-block duplicate (`23505` on

  could not create unique index` on both — so the build does read the committed rows — and
  an in-block `SELECT count(*) FROM r WHERE a > 0` counts the committed row.

  **The repair a reader would build** is to make the readers of the block's new index
  inside the block read the entries the block's own index build derived from the committed
  rows — the entries `COMMIT` publishes, which the post-`COMMIT` `23505` shows exist — so
  that the in-block statements see what 18.6's do; not a re-validation at `COMMIT`, which
  would leave the in-block read wrong and turn the `23505` into a `COMMIT`-time failure 18.6
  does not raise. The statements above reach four such readers: the unique probe an
  `INSERT` and an `UPDATE` make, the `ON CONFLICT` arbiter's probe, a foreign key's
  referenced-key probe, and the indexed read. Read from the
  code, not measured: those probes are `enforce_index_entries`, `probe_conflict` and
  `parent_tuple_exists`, each reaching the index through `occupancy_of` or directly
  through `Storage::index_lookup`, the method the equality read calls too.
