  action used to resolve *names* at eval, while its *types* were gated at plan time — so
  an INSERT that hit **no conflict** never evaluated the action and wrote its row where
  18.6 raises. Measured over `oc3 (n INT PRIMARY KEY, v TEXT)` holding `(1,'a')`, each
  statement inserting a **new** key: `… DO UPDATE SET nosuchcol = 'z'`, `… SET v =
  nosuchcol`, `… SET v = 'z' WHERE nosuchcol > 0` and `… SET v = excluded.nosuchcol` each
  wrote their row; the bogus-qualifier spellings (`SET v = zzz.v`, `SET v = "EXCLUDED".v`,
  `… WHERE zzz.v = <the excluded value>`) wrote too, and on a *conflicting* row stored the
  excluded value. The discriminator was plain: **the same statement errored or wrote
  depending on whether the row already existed.** The action's namespace is complete by
  construction — the target plus `excluded`, no enclosing level — so `lower_on_conflict`
  closes its `ColumnScope` and `check_binding` fires before any row is looked at; the
  `SET` **target** names are checked against the target's columns in the same pass
  structure. The executor's own outer-frame rule refuses the qualified spellings at eval
  time as well, and both are wanted, since neither row count covers the other.
  **The four checks run in Postgres's order**, which no per-assignment loop produces:
  every right-hand side (so `SET nosuchcol = 'y', v = zzz.v` is `42P01`, the *second*
  RHS beating the *first* target), then every target name (so `SET nosuchcol = 'z' WHERE
  zzz.v = 'b'` is `42703`), then the action's `WHERE`, then the `GENERATED ALWAYS` guard
  (a rewriter check: `SET n = 5 WHERE nosuchcol = 1` is `42703`, not `428C9`). Five
  fixtures pin the four positions and `insert/on_conflict_missing_target_stays_a_table_error.sql`
  is the false-rejection control — a target the catalog lacks must keep its own `42P01`,
  which `lower_insert`'s `lowers_clauses` gate is what guarantees. The *typing* gate was
  already plan-time and is unchanged:
  `… DO UPDATE SET v = CASE WHEN oc3.n LIKE 'x%' THEN 'a' ELSE 'b' END` is
  `42883 operator does not exist: integer ~~ …` on both engines with no conflict and no
  row written. Still open on this clause: the **arbiter target** is neither resolved nor
  gated, so `ON CONFLICT (nosucharbiter)` is `42P10` here against 18.6's
  `42703 column "nosucharbiter" does not exist` (§ *Statement-level error order*) — and
  it diverges in **phase** as well as in code, a fact of this clause's own, stated
  here rather than in the two rows that carry the code. Measured with a raw v3 client over
  `oc1 (a INT UNIQUE, b TEXT)` holding `(1,'x')`:
  `INSERT INTO oc1 VALUES (2,'y') ON CONFLICT (nosuchcol) DO NOTHING` completes `Parse`
  and answers `NoData` to both `Describe`s (`1 t n 2 n E Z`, the statement carrying no
  `RETURNING`), the `42P10` arriving at **`Execute`**, where 18.6 raises its `42703` at
  `Parse` and fails the client's prepare outright; the `DO UPDATE` and
  `ON CONFLICT (a) WHERE nosuchcol > 0` spellings measure identically. That makes the
  arbiter the **one missing-column spelling that defers** — the measured exception to
  row 29's otherwise-closed column half — and the three **column-resolution** checks above
  are what keep it alone (the fourth, the `GENERATED ALWAYS` guard, is not a
  name-resolution check and has no missing-column spelling to probe):
  `DO UPDATE SET nosuchcol = 1`, `… SET b = excluded.nosuchcol` and
  `… SET b = 'z' WHERE nosuchcol > 0` are each `42703` at `Parse` on **both** engines,
  re-measured beside it.
- **32 · An accepted `CREATE TYPE` can make the whole database unexportable.** `dump`'s
  `bare_type_ident` refuses a type name it cannot emit as a bare identifier, and that
  refusal fails the *export*, not the statement: `pglet_server dump --data-dir` exits `1`
  having emitted nothing, so the unrelated tables and their rows go with it.
  Measured on a `--data-dir` store also holding `keepme2 (a INT)` with two rows:
  `CREATE TYPE "Mood-X" AS ENUM ('x','y')` (the catalog key folds to `mood-x`, and `-` is
  not a bare-identifier character), `CREATE TYPE Sequence AS ENUM ('c','d')` — unquoted
  ordinary DDL, whose folded key `sequence` the lexer reads as a keyword — and
  `CREATE TYPE MÖÖD AS ENUM ('x','y')`, likewise unquoted, whose key is `mÖÖd`
  (`is_safe_bare_ident` accepts ASCII lowercase only, so no fold width rescues a
  non-ASCII letter: `mööd` is refused too). 18.6 accepts all three, and `pg_dump` emits
  `CREATE TYPE public."Mood-X"` / `CREATE TYPE public.sequence` /
  `CREATE TYPE public."mÖÖd"`. This is the catalog part of `docs/sequences.md`'s dump
  invariant, *any catalog pglet's own accepted statements build must dump*, broken from the
  type-name side; the enum fold in
  `execute_create_type` narrows the set of names that reach it and does not close it.
- **~~33~~ · Closed — A CTE column-rename list was silently ignored; the residual is a
  name.** `WITH c(v) AS (SELECT 2 AS zz) SELECT v FROM c` was `42703` and, inside a
  correlated subquery, a wrong answer with no error (0 rows where Postgres returns 1).
  The list now rides beside the plan and is applied by `alias_relation_columns` at every
  reader (`docs/scope.md` § A relation's column names are one object); both spellings
  answer `2` on both engines. What remains is the correlated spelling's output column
  **name**: `WITH c2(v) AS (SELECT 2 AS zz) SELECT (SELECT v) FROM c2` is headed
  `?column?` here and `v` there — a scalar subquery's output name is the inner column's
  on 18.6 and the generic one here, which is not this row's mechanism but was measured
  through it.
- **34/54/55 · Declared types across the two protocols — a differentially tested seam.**
  pglet computes a result's declared column types through **different code** per protocol
  — the extended protocol's `Describe` from the planner's `Plan::result_shape`, the simple
  protocol's `RowDescription` from the executor's `QueryResult::shape` — and the harness
  compares each column's declared OID on both legs, live against Postgres. The mechanism,
  the four walks behind those two and the `LeafScope` unification state are
  `docs/declared_types.md`'s; what this row records is what still diverges. **One
  divergence stands at row 34 itself, named in each fixture it reaches via
  `-- @no-declared-types:`**, which waives **both** legs: an `information_schema`
  identifier or character-data column reports `text` where 18.6 reports a **domain** whose
  `RowDescription` carries the base type — `name` (OID 19) for `sql_identifier`, `varchar`
  (1043) for `character_data`. (`SUM(bigint)`, which stayed `bigint` where Postgres widens
  to `numeric`, closed with row 2.) It is not a missing type: `TypeOid::Name` and
  `TypeOid::NameArray` (19/1003) are modelled, and what has not moved is `catalog/virtual_tables.rs`'s column
  specs, which still declare those columns `TypeOid::Text`.

  **A second member stands beside it, unwaived because no fixture reaches it: `min` and
  `max` over a `varchar`.** 18.6 has no `varchar` form of either — `pg_proc` carries
  `min`/`max` over `text`, `bpchar`, `anyarray` and `anyenum` among the string-shaped
  ones — so a `varchar` argument resolves to the `text` form and the result is `text`.
  pglet types the result as its argument. Measured on the raw wire, both legs, over
  `varchar(5)` and `varchar(3)` columns: `SELECT min(v), max(v) FROM t`, `max(v), min(c3)`
  and a grouped `min(v) … GROUP BY n` declare `1043` here and `25` on 18.6, the values
  identical; `min(n)` over a `numeric(6,2)` is the control, `1700` on both. `min(v)`
  measured the same on a build before the enum-identity gates.

  **The `MathFn` carve-out closed `abs(NULL)` and not the class it belongs to. So the
  cell is not closed, and three residual members are measured.** An argument that
  is only *transitively* untyped still splits the two declared-type walkers, on statements
  18.6 refuses outright: `abs(-NULL)` (18.6 `42725 operator is not unique: - unknown`),
  `abs(CASE WHEN true THEN NULL END)` and `abs(COALESCE(NULL, NULL))` (both 18.6
  `42883 function abs(text) does not exist`) each declare **25** on the simple-query
  `RowDescription` against `Describe`'s **701**. Loud on 18.6, silent here — the value is
  NULL, so a client sees only the OID, and it sees a different one per protocol. All three
  are pinned by `executor::walker_pins`, which compares the two walks over a raw `Expr`
  corpus because no fixture can assert a pair 18.6 refuses.
  `abs('5')` is the fourth and belongs to the literal-typing gap instead (`0A000` here,
  `701` answering `5` there); `abs(NULL::int)` is the control, `23` on both legs and both
  engines. **The general question — which of the four answers each rule should read, and
  whether the executor walk should stop being total — is open**, and the way to
  approach it is per rule against the oracle rather than by unifying the walks first: the
  duplicated-rules hazard here is not only drift but *agreement on being wrong*, which no
  pair-comparison can see. The same carve-out has since been made a **second** time, at
  the multi-operand cells (`COALESCE`/`CASE`/`greatest`/`least`/`nullif`/`ARRAY[…]` — see
  below), where it also declines for a bound NULL, an unbound `$N` and a bare `DEFAULT`;
  that instance leaves the identical transitively-untyped residual, so the two closes are
  the same shape and neither settles the general question.

  **The arithmetic unknown-operand fallback splits three ways, and two of the three are
  live on statements both engines accept and answer.** The two walks spell their fallback
  differently — the executor's `.unwrap_or(if left == Text { right } else { left })`
  against the planner's `(Some, Some) ⇒ .or(Some(l))`, else `lt.or(rt)` — and the seam map
  recorded them as coinciding on every constructed shape. They do not. Three spellings
  split, by three *different* mechanisms, which is why the covering sentence that stood in
  for them ("they coincide whenever exactly one operand is un-inferable") is false in both
  directions: members 2 and 3 are exactly that shape and split, and member 1 has no
  un-inferable operand at all.

  1. **A genuinely `text` left operand.** The executor walk cannot tell a real `text` from
     its own placeholder, so its fallback diverts to the right operand. Over
     `t(b BIGINT, tx TEXT)` **empty**, `SELECT tx + 1 FROM t` declares `23` on the
     simple-query `RowDescription` against `Describe`'s `25`, and `SELECT tx + b FROM t`
     `20` against `25`, where 18.6 refuses `42883 operator does not exist: text + integer`
     / `text + bigint`. With a row whose `tx` is not `NULL` pglet raises its own `42804`
     (loud, wrong code), so the member needs a statement that evaluates the operator over
     no such value — and an empty table is one way to that, not the only one: `SELECT a +
     1 FROM n` over `n (a TEXT)` holding one `NULL` row, and an aggregate over no row,
     `SELECT max(t) + 1 FROM e` and its `- 1` spelling over an empty `e (t TEXT)`, each
     declare `23` against `25` under a `NULL` value, where 18.6 is `42883`. The **order**
     is the control: `1 + tx` and
     `b + tx` declare `23` and `20` on both of pglet's legs — 18.6 refuses those
     spellings too, so what the control identifies is the divert and not the operator —
     because it only fires when the *left* operand is `Text`.
  2. **A `float4` operand beside an un-inferable one** — nothing to do with `text`, and
     **not** bounded to zero rows. `numeric_family_result` promotes `float4` mixed with
     anything else to `float8`, and the executor walk's placeholder `Text` is that
     "anything else"; the planner walk keeps `float4`. Over `t(f4 REAL)` **with a row**,
     `SELECT f4 + NULL FROM t` declares `701` on the simple leg against `Describe`'s `700`,
     where 18.6 says `700` on both. It is **eight** members, not one — re-measured
     operator by operator and position by position: `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`, with the
     `float4` on either side (`f4 + NULL` and `NULL + f4` alike), each `701` against `700`
     against 18.6's `700`. `f4 + COALESCE(NULL, NULL)` is a ninth spelling of the same
     mechanism, where 18.6 is `42883 real + text`. `float4` is the
     only type this reaches: `f8 + NULL` is `701` on both legs and both engines,
     `n + NULL` `1700`, `i + NULL` `23`, `s + NULL` `21`, and `f4 + f4` `700`.

     **`%` is not a ninth member of this class, and reading it as one got 18.6's answer
     wrong.** 18.6 registers no float `%` operator at all, so `f4 % NULL` is
     `42883 operator does not exist: real % unknown` there and `NULL % f4` is
     `unknown % real` — not `700`, and not one message for the pair. pglet answers
     `701` on the simple leg and `700` on `Describe`, so **both** walks are wrong and the
     divergence is an over-acceptance rather than a split one walk gets right. The band is
     wider than the split, and stays **open**: `f8 % NULL` is `701` on *both* pglet legs
     against the same `42883 double precision % unknown`, so it is an agree-wrong with no
     split to notice it by — and it holds **in both operand positions**, `NULL % f8`
     being `701` on both legs against `42883 unknown % double precision`, the same
     position pair the `float4` members are counted in. What lets any of them through is the operand gate's NULL
     short-circuit — `f8 % f8`, `f8 % i`, `i % f8` and `f8 % n` all raise pglet's own
     `42883` at eval, matching 18.6's refusal, and only a NULL operand skips that check.
     (Their `Describe` still answers a `RowDescription` on the extended leg, the gate
     being eval-time; that is a separate pre-existing seam, not this row's.) The integer
     forms are the controls and conform: `i % NULL` and `NULL % i` are `23` on both legs
     and both engines, `n % NULL` `1700`, `b % NULL` `20`.
  3. **`^` against a `numeric` operand** — a third spelling, and here the *executor* walk
     is the one that is right, by accident. It always folds through
     `numeric_family_result`, and `numeric_family_result(Text, Numeric)` is `numeric`; the
     planner walk short-circuits any `(None, Some)` or `(Some, None)` pair to `float8`.
     Over `t(n NUMERIC)` with a row, `SELECT NULL ^ n FROM t` and `SELECT n ^ NULL FROM t`
     both declare `1700` on the simple leg against `Describe`'s `701`, where 18.6 says
     `1700` on both, and `COALESCE(NULL, NULL) ^ n` splits identically where 18.6 is
     `42883 text ^ numeric`. `numeric` is the only type this reaches, because
     `pow_result_type` flattens every other promotion to `float8`: `NULL ^ 1`,
     `NULL ^ f8` and `f4 ^ NULL` are `701` everywhere.

  Members 2 and 3 point **opposite ways** — the executor walk is wrong in one and the
  planner walk in the other — so no unification may adopt one walker's cell wholesale;
  either choice ships a divergence that is correct today on the other leg. The artifact is
  the OID alone, `abs(-NULL)`-class: every spelling that reaches the split carries a NULL
  value, and a **non-NULL** bind through a bare `$N` is refused (`f4 + $1` bound `2` is
  `42804` here, `n ^ $1` bound `2` is `42883`, where 18.6 infers the parameter from the
  operator and answers) — so no non-NULL value ever arrives under the wrong width. A `$N`
  bound **NULL**, though, is *accepted* (the operand gates short-circuit on the NULL
  value), and that spelling is a further member measured against 18.6 on the one leg the
  route has: `SELECT $1 ^ n` and `n ^ $1` bound NULL declare **701** here against 18.6's
  `1700` (one NULL row on both), while `f4 + $1` bound NULL **agrees** at `700` — members
  2 and 3 on a single route, one diverging and one agreeing. Pre-existing, and **not pinnable by a
  fixture** — measured rather than argued: a candidate `SELECT f4 + NULL` fixture is red on
  the text declared leg (`Postgres oid=700 vs pglet oid=701`) and a candidate
  `SELECT NULL ^ n` one on the extended leg (`Postgres oid=1700 vs pglet oid=701`), each
  green on the other, and `-- @no-declared-types:` waives both legs by design. All three
  members and their controls are pinned by `executor::walker_pins`. The right close is
  18.6's own answer per member — a `42883` for the first, the surviving operand's type for
  the other two.

  **A fourth split at the same seam was live the whole time under a note saying it was
  not, and it is now closed.** The multi-operand cells — `COALESCE`, `CASE`,
  `greatest`/`least`/`nullif` and `ARRAY[…]` — pick one operand's type out of several, and
  the executor walk's totality made it always the *first* where the planner walk and 18.6
  take the first **inferable** one. What both readers *do* share is that every
  **computed** expression is `None`
  to them, so `{a bare NULL} ∪ {a computed branch}` reached both
  walkers raw. Measured on 18.6 and both pglet legs: `COALESCE(NULL, length('ab'))`,
  `CASE WHEN true THEN NULL ELSE length('ab') END`,
  `CASE WHEN false THEN NULL WHEN true THEN length('ab') END`,
  `greatest`/`least`/`nullif` of the same pair, `COALESCE(NULL, n + 1)` and
  `COALESCE(NULL, (SELECT i FROM …))` each declared `25` on the simple leg against
  `Describe`'s `23`/`1700`, and `ARRAY[NULL, length('ab')]` `1009` against `1007` — 18.6
  agreeing with `Describe` at every one of the twenty-four spellings tried, in every
  projecting position: a plain projection, `RETURNING`, a `GROUP BY`/`ORDER BY` ordinal, a
  derived table, a `VALUES` row, a scalar-subquery operand, an `unnest` wrapper, a nested
  `COALESCE`, an empty relation and `LIMIT 0`. Over a `timestamptz` operand it stopped
  being an OID-only artifact: the text encoder is column-type-aware, so
  `COALESCE(NULL, date_trunc('day', ts))` sent `2024-01-15 00:00:00` where 18.6 sends
  `2024-01-15 00:00:00+00` — a shifted instant to any driver that reparses in its own
  zone; the table-free spelling `COALESCE(NULL, now())` was the same corrupted value
  with no setup at all — `25` and offset-less on the simple leg **before the close**,
  `1184` with its `+00` on both legs and both engines after. **And the consequences were not all silent**: the
  executor walk's answer becomes the projecting node's `ColumnDesc`, which an enclosing
  aggregate's operand gate reads (row 58's mechanism), so
  `SELECT sum(c) FROM (SELECT COALESCE(NULL, length('ab')) AS c) s` was
  `42883 function sum(text) does not exist` on both legs where 18.6 answers `2` — a
  refused statement rather than a mislabelled column, and the shape the bound-`$N`
  fixture below is built on, a refusal against a row being comparable on either leg.
  Closed by handing the shared rule a real
  `None` for the four **typeless leaves**
  (a bare `NULL` literal, a bound NULL, an unbound `$N`, a bare `DEFAULT`), the same
  carve-out shape as `abs`'s; the guards are
  `select/{coalesce,case,variadic,array}_untyped_first_*`,
  `select/coalesce_untyped_first_branch_timestamptz.sql` and
  `select/coalesce_bound_param_null_aggregate_operand.sql`. That last one is the
  **bound-`$N`** leaf's, and it holds the *loud* consequence rather than the OID for a
  harness reason worth recording: the leaf's own divergence is text-format-only
  (`Bind($1=NULL)` + `COALESCE($1, date_trunc('day', ts))` sent `2024-01-15 00:00:00`
  under a correct `timestamptz` `RowDescription`), while `@param` binds through
  tokio-postgres and requests **binary** results, where `timestamp` and `timestamptz`
  share one 8-byte encoding — so the direct spelling is green on the defect exactly as
  `coalesce_untyped_first_branch_timestamptz.sql`'s binary leg was. **The residual is the
  `abs(-NULL)` family's**: an operand only *transitively* untyped keeps the total answer,
  so `COALESCE(-NULL, length('ab'))`, `COALESCE(CASE WHEN true THEN NULL END, length('ab'))`
  and `COALESCE(COALESCE(NULL, NULL), length('ab'))` still declare `25` against
  `Describe`'s `23` — and 18.6 refuses all three rather than answering the other branch
  (`42725` for the first, `42804 COALESCE types text and integer cannot be matched` for
  the two whose untyped branch resolves to `text`), so their right close is a refusal.
  The all-untyped shapes are the controls and did not move: `COALESCE(NULL, NULL)`,
  `greatest(NULL, NULL)`, `nullif(NULL, NULL)` and `CASE WHEN true THEN NULL END` are `25`
  on both legs and on 18.6, `ARRAY[NULL, NULL]` `1009`, and a genuinely `text` branch
  (`COALESCE(NULL, upper('ab'))`, `greatest(NULL, 'abc')`) stays `25` everywhere.

  **The fold band beside that close — closed for the numeric-category computed shapes.**
  18.6's rule is the common type of *all* the known branches, and `COALESCE`/`CASE`/`ARRAY`
  took the first inferable one on **both** walks, so two computed branches of different
  types left the two walks agreeing and both wrong, which no pair-comparison can see.
  Measured before the close: `COALESCE(NULL, length('ab'), n + 1)` and
  `CASE WHEN true THEN NULL WHEN false THEN length('ab') ELSE n + 1 END` declared `23` on
  both legs against 18.6's `1700`, `ARRAY[NULL, length('ab'), n + 1]` `1007` against
  `1231`, `COALESCE(NULL, i + 0, b + 0)` `23` against `20`, and `COALESCE(length('ab'),
  n + 1)` `23` against `1700` with no untyped branch at all. It reached a **value width**
  (`COALESCE(i + 0, b + 0)` over a NULL `i` declared `int4` over `5000000000`, row 36) and,
  through an aggregate, an answer: `avg(COALESCE(i + 0, f + 0))` was refused `0A000` once
  `avg` over an integer became `numeric` (row 2), the fold declaring `integer` over
  `float8` values.

  A walker-only fold would have **moved** the defect rather than closed it, because the
  binary encoder is **value**-driven (row 36): `SELECT COALESCE(i + 0, b + 0) FROM w`
  streamed eight bytes when `i` is NULL and four when it is `7`. The close is the coercion
  pass's: its branch readers (`concrete_branch_type`, and `arg_known_type` for
  `greatest`/`least`/`nullif`) now type the computed shapes whose result is in the numeric
  category and certain once their operands' are — `+ - * / %` and `^`, unary `-`/`+`, a
  math function, `length`/`strpos`/`position`, `EXTRACT`/`date_part`, a `date` less a
  `date`, and a nested `COALESCE`/`CASE` — so the pass resolves 18.6's target and inserts
  the coercing casts, and the walkers read the casts. Every spelling above now declares 18.6's OID on both
  legs — `ARRAY[NULL, length('ab'), n + 1]` declared `integer[]` over `{NULL,2,2.5}` and
  is `numeric[]` now; `COALESCE(i, f + 0)` answers `2.5` where the computed branch was cast to
  its `integer` sibling's type and answered `2`, and `COALESCE(i + 0, tx)` is 18.6's
  `42804` where it answered the `text`. The fixtures are
  `select/coalesce_computed_branch_*`, `select/variadic_computed_arg_common_type.sql` and
  `select/agg_avg_fold_*`.

  **The computed reach builds only on certain types.** A column operand is typed there
  only where its type is certain (`ColumnScope::column_type_certain` — a base table's, or
  a derived relation's whose defining expression this reader typed as written — and what
  that reader types is also what makes an aggregate's argument certain, row 2):
  a derived table's or CTE's column whose declared type is itself this band's guess would
  otherwise choose an outer target and be cast at it — `COALESCE(x * 1, b * 1)` over a CTE
  `x` of `COALESCE(i + 0, f + g.y)` holding `3.5`, `g.y` a column whose type is a guess,
  answered `4`. An `ARRAY[…]` branch
  is typed there only where every element is, the `text[]` of an all-unknown list being a
  guess too. The no-op test before a cast, and the gate, read the reach the set's target
  was chosen at (`select/coalesce_derived_guessed_column_not_cast.sql`,
  `select/coalesce_array_branch_partly_typed.sql`).

  **A set the readers type only in part keeps the target it had before** (`set_reach`):
  typing one computed branch and not its sibling would choose the target from the typed
  one and cast the other to it — read at the computed reach, `COALESCE(i + 0, f + g.y)`
  over a column `g.y` whose type is a guess casts `3.5` to `4`. So the band is **open**
  where a branch is outside them: a computed branch whose result is not in the numeric
  category (a string function but the three above, temporal arithmetic but a `date` less
  a `date`, `now()`), or one over a column or a scalar subquery whose type is a guess.
  `SELECT COALESCE(i + 0, b + (SELECT * FROM unnest(ARRAY[0]))) FROM w`, the subquery's
  column a constructor's `unnest`, still declares `23` over `5000000000` on both legs
  against 18.6's `20`. Members of the open band measured on both legs, each answering as
  it did before the close but those marked **moved**:

  - **A guessed column read at the written reach is cast at its guessed type — silent.**
    Over a derived `y` of `COALESCE(i + 0, f + (SELECT * FROM unnest(ARRAY[1])))` holding
    `3.5` beside a `bigint` `b`, `COALESCE(y, b)` and `COALESCE(y * 1, b)` are `20` `4`
    against 18.6's `701` `3.5`: the written reading types `y` by its declared `integer`
    and the target `bigint` casts it.
  - **A column whose type is right but not certain is read at the written reach, beside
    a computed branch of an exact type — silent.** Over `unnest(ARRAY[NULL::int]) u(x)`,
    whose column is declared `integer`, `COALESCE(u.x, t.n * 1)` over a `numeric` `t.n`
    holding `1.25` and `2.5` is `23` `1`, `3` against 18.6's `1700` `1.25`, `2.5`, and
    `COALESCE(u.x, t.b * 1)` over a `bigint` `5000000000` `22003` against `20`: the
    computed reader does not vouch for `u.x` (row 2's residuals), the set falls back to
    its written reading, and the target `integer` is cast onto the computed branch. The
    closure above holds for a column whose type is certain — a grouped query's column
    through a derived table
    (`select/coalesce_grouped_derived_column_computed_sibling.sql`), a `VALUES` list's
    column, a derived table's aggregate column and a set operation's
    (`select/coalesce_values_column_computed_sibling.sql`), and a column a scalar
    subquery defines (`select/coalesce_scalar_subquery_column_computed_sibling.sql`).
    Beside a computed `double precision` branch such a column's set takes that type,
    below; beside a computed `real` one it keeps the `integer`, `COALESCE(u.x,
    -(t.f::real))` answering `23` `-2` against 18.6's `700` `-1.5`.
  - **A branch over an operand whose type is a guess is cast to its sibling's type —
    silent.** `COALESCE(-(SELECT avg(x) FROM unnest(ARRAY[1, 4]) v(x)), b)` beside a
    `bigint` `b` is `20` `-2` against 18.6's `1700` `-2.5000000000000000`, the `avg`
    over a constructor's `unnest` being `double precision` here. Over a subquery whose
    column is certain the operand is typed and the fold 18.6's (row 2).
  - **An exact branch beside a branch neither reach types, that branch a `double
    precision` — silent, and moved.** The written target is the exact type and the
    untyped branch is cast to it, where 18.6's type for the set is the untyped branch's
    `double precision`. Over a `t(f, …)` row and `unnest(ARRAY[2]) g(z)`, whose column
    is a guess: `SELECT COALESCE(x, y + 0) FROM (SELECT (SELECT avg(v) FROM (VALUES (1),
    (4)) q(v)) + g.z AS x, f + g.z AS y FROM t, unnest(ARRAY[2]) g(z)) s` is `1700`
    `4.5000000000000000` against 18.6's `701` `4.5`; over `q.a` an exact `avg` of a
    `VALUES` column that is NULL and `unnest(ARRAY[0.1234567890123456789::float8])
    g(y)`, `COALESCE(q.a, g.y * 1)` and `greatest(q.a, g.y * 1)` are `1700`
    `0.123456789012346` against `701` `0.12345678901234568`, and `COALESCE((SELECT
    avg(x) FROM (VALUES (1), (4)) v(x) WHERE x > 9), (SELECT y FROM
    unnest(ARRAY[0.1234567890123456789::float8]) g(y)) * 1)` likewise. Each answered
    18.6's `701` while an `avg` over such a relation's column was `double precision` —
    the written target was then `double precision` for another reason than 18.6's — and
    the base-table spelling, `avg(i)` over a table's column, answered `1700` already.
    Reading the untyped branch at the walkers' `double precision` instead was measured
    and not taken: over a column a guessed integer's `avg` defines — `double precision`
    here, `numeric` on 18.6 — it turned statements that agree with 18.6 `double
    precision`, the exact sibling's digits lost past the fifteenth.
  - **A fold a bare branch defers, beside an exact aggregate — silent, and moved.** A
    scalar subquery branch no reading types — a wildcard over a constructor's `unnest`
    (row 152) — defers its whole fold, which is then declared by its first branch:
    `SELECT COALESCE(avg(v.x), (SELECT * FROM unnest(ARRAY[1, 4]) LIMIT 1), max(f) + 0)
    FROM (VALUES (1), (4)) v(x), t` is `1700` `2.5000000000000000` against 18.6's `701`
    `2.5`, which it answered while that `avg` was `double precision`. Without the float
    branch the same fold is 18.6's `1700` where it was `701`.
  - **A computed branch over an enclosing query's column is not typed on the sub-plan's
    own run — silent.** `SELECT k, (SELECT greatest(u.i, t.f + 0) FROM u WHERE u.k = 1)
    FROM t` over a `float8` `t.f` is `23` `2` against 18.6's `701` `1.5`, and the
    `COALESCE` spelling likewise: the run that lowers the sub-plan cannot type `t.f`,
    reads the set at the written reach and casts the branch to `u.i`'s `integer`, and
    the re-run over the enclosing levels finds that cast already written. The bare-column
    spelling `COALESCE(u.i, t.f)` defers to the re-run and agrees.
  - **A `$N` used more than once is unknown at each use.** A set holding a `$N` reads
    it as the unknown it is and converts it to the set's target, as 18.6 converts an
    unknown parameter: `COALESCE(i + 0, $1)` bound `'abc'` is `22P02` where it declared
    `23` and answered `abc`; `COALESCE($1, i * 1, f * 1)` bound `'2.5'` is `701` where it
    was `23`; `greatest(i + 0, $1)` answers where it was `42804`; and the parameter is
    described at the target, where it was described with no type
    (`select/coalesce_param_computed_sibling.sql`). 18.6 fixes a parameter's type at its
    first use and reads every later one at that type; here each use is unknown again.
    `SELECT COALESCE(n + 0, $1), COALESCE(b + 0, $1)` bound `'7.5'` is `1700` and `20`
    over `7.5` and `8` against 18.6's `1700` and `1700` over `7.5` and `7.5`, the second
    use being a `numeric` there; and `SELECT COALESCE($1, tx), COALESCE($1, i + 0)`
    answers where 18.6 refuses `42804`. Two folds whose targets no one type satisfies
    were loud and are **silent**: `SELECT COALESCE(e, $1), COALESCE(f + 0, $1)` over an
    enum `e`, bound `'7'`, is `42804` on 18.6 and was `22P02 invalid input value for
    enum`; it answers now, the row whose `e` is NULL holding `7` in the enum's column.
  - **An unknown operand of arithmetic is typed by no reader — silent, and moved beside
    an exact aggregate.** 18.6 converts a `$N` or an untyped `NULL` under `+ - * /` to
    its sibling operand's type; nothing here converts it, and the parameter is described
    with no type. Over the wire a bound value arrives as text and the operator is
    `42804 operator + requires numeric operands` where 18.6 answers, and bound NULL it
    answers NULL. Through the embed and the npm package a JS number binds as its own
    type — whole, a `bigint`; fractional, a `double precision` — and the operator
    returns that type's value: `price * $1` over a `numeric` `price` bound `0.1` is a
    `double precision`. So the readers do not type the operator at its sibling's type: a
    branch read so matched its fold's target and was left uncast, `COALESCE(price * $1,
    price)` handing a JS number under a `numeric` declaration where the cast to the
    target answers `0.15`
    (`undetermined_param::a_fold_over_an_unknown_operand_declares_the_type_its_values_have`).
    `nullif` with that operator as its second argument is not held together so: the
    first argument comes back as a `double precision` under its own declared type
    (row 288). Beside an integer constant the branch is cast to `integer` — row 65's
    cast of a branch the pass cannot type, taken here from the answers and not traced —
    so the product is rounded, and it writes. Through the npm package, over a `numeric`
    `price` holding `1.5`, `19.99` and `0.1234567890123456789`: `COALESCE(price * $1,
    0)` bound `0.1` is `23` `0`, `2`, `0`
    against 18.6's `1700` `0.15`, `1.999`, `0.01234567890123456789`, and bound the whole
    number `2` it is `23` `3`, `40`, `0` against `1700` `3.0`, `39.98`,
    `0.2469135780246913578`; `greatest(price * $1, 0)` and `CASE WHEN true THEN price *
    $1 ELSE 0 END` bound `0.1` are the same `23` `0`, `2`, `0`; `UPDATE p SET price =
    COALESCE(price * $1, 0)` bound `0.9` stores `1`, `18`, `0` where 18.6 stores `1.35`,
    `17.991`, `0.11111111011111111101`; and over an `integer` `qty` holding `3`, `7`, `9`,
    `COALESCE(qty * $1, 0)` bound `0.5` is `2`, `4`, `4` where 18.6 refuses the fraction
    (`22P02`). Beside a `numeric` sibling the type is kept and the digits are a float's:
    `COALESCE(price * $1, 0.0)` bound `0.1` is `1700` `0.15`, `1.999`,
    `0.0123456789012346`. The cast parameter (`price * $1::numeric`) answers as 18.6
    does in the `SELECT` and the `UPDATE` spellings. Over the wire each uncast spelling
    is `42804 operator * requires numeric operands`, and `COALESCE(price * $1, 0)` bound
    `NULL` answers `0` under `23` against `1700`.
    The branch is one no reach types, with that class's members: `SELECT
    COALESCE(avg(x), max(f) + $1) FROM (VALUES (1), (4)) v(x), t` bound NULL, and its
    `max(f) + NULL` spelling, are `1700` `2.5000000000000000` against 18.6's `701`
    `2.5`, which each answered while that `avg` was `double precision`; over a table's
    column, `COALESCE(avg(i), max(f) + $1)` answered `1700` already.

  The `numeric`-category restriction is a scope, not a measured bound: the other
  categories' members were not swept.

  **A `double precision` branch decides a written-reach set's target.** Where the
  branches the written reach types are all in the numeric category and a branch the
  computed reader types is `double precision`, the set's target is `double precision`
  (`planner::coercion`'s `set_types`; `COALESCE`, `CASE`, `ARRAY[…]`, `greatest`/`least`
  and both arguments of `nullif`). 18.6 chooses `double precision` for a set holding one
  whatever numeric types stand beside it, so that target does not turn on which type
  the written reading holds for another branch, nor on whether it holds one, and a value
  of any numeric type converts to it as 18.6 converts one. Over
  `unnest(ARRAY[NULL::int]) u(x)`, `COALESCE(u.x, t.f + 0)`, `greatest(u.x, t.f + 0)` and
  `CASE WHEN u.x IS NULL THEN t.f * 1 ELSE u.x END` were `23` `2` — the `float8` branch
  cast to the column's `integer` — and are `701` `1.5`, 18.6's; `COALESCE(u.x, t.f + 0,
  u.x * 1)`, a branch neither reach types beside them, likewise; `COALESCE(u.x * 1, t.f
  + 0)`, with no branch typed at the written reach, was left unresolved and declared
  `23` over the `double precision` value and is `701`; and over a column whose
  definition holds an exact `avg` beside an operand the reader does not type, `x` of
  `avg(v) + max(g.y)` over a constructor's `unnest` `g`, `COALESCE(x, t.f + 0)` over a
  `t.f` of `0.1234567890123456789` is `701` `0.12345678901234568`, where the written
  target `numeric` cast the branch to `0.123456789012346`
  (`select/coalesce_uncertain_column_float_sibling.sql`,
  `engine_subqueries::a_double_precision_branch_decides_the_target_of_a_set_read_at_the_written_reach`).
  The set must be of the numeric category: every branch the written reach types is, and
  every branch neither reach types is by the declared-type walkers' reading or is of
  unknown type. A branch they read as `text` leaves the set as it was, and the gates
  that refuse such a set read its branches uncast — `greatest(upper(tx), f + 0)` is
  `42804` and `nullif(upper(tx), f + 0)` `42883`, as on 18.6
  (`functions/greatest_untyped_text_float_operand_loud.sql`,
  `functions/nullif_untyped_text_float_operand_loud.sql`); cast to the float they
  answered `22P02`, or a row. What it does not do, each the answer the set gave before:
  a `real` branch does not decide the target — 18.6's type for it beside an exact
  branch is `real` and beside a `double precision` one `double precision`, so it turns
  on the type the written reading does not vouch for, and converted to `real` a column
  declared `integer` and holding the `double precision` `0.24691358024691357` answered
  `0.24691358`, and one holding `1.5e+300` was `22003 real out of range`; an **exact**
  computed branch does not join, since a guessed `integer` column holding `3.5` cast to
  a wider exact target answers `4`; and a written reading outside the numeric category
  is not touched — `COALESCE(u.tx, t.f + 0)` over a `text` `unnest(ARRAY['a']) u(tx)`
  answers the `text` where 18.6 refuses `42804` (row 65). Where the column's own value
  was already rounded by a fold inside its definition, the set's type is 18.6's and the
  value is not: over `x` of `COALESCE((SELECT avg(z) FROM unnest(ARRAY[1, 2, 4]) g(z)) +
  1, 7)`, an operand-subquery branch whose column is a guess cast to `integer`,
  `COALESCE(x, w.f + 0)` is `701` `3` against `3.3333333333333335`.

  **A second band sits beside the fold, from the same policy read the other way: a bare
  string literal is `unknown` to 18.6 and `text` to both walks here — where no sibling is
  typed.** Its measured members were the literal beside a `length` call:
  `COALESCE('7', length('ab'))` was `25` here against 18.6's `23` (the `ARRAY` spelling
  `1009` against `1007`, the `CASE` spelling `25` against `23`), `COALESCE('abc',
  length('ab'))` the **silent wrong answer**, `abc` as `text` where 18.6 is
  `22P02 invalid input syntax for type integer: "abc"`, and the variadic cells refused
  (`42804`, `42804`, `42883`) where 18.6 answers `7`/`2`/`7`. With `length` typed by the
  fold band's close, the literal adopts `integer` as 18.6's does and every one of those
  spellings agrees on both legs (`select/coalesce_computed_branch_literal_band*.sql`). The
  band is **open** beside a branch the readers still do not type — `COALESCE('7', 1 +
  (SELECT 1))` answers `7` on both engines, but as `text` here — and its right close is
  the one `docs/compatibility.md`'s `COALESCE`/`CASE` row names: resolving a bare literal
  against the surrounding claimant set rather than typing it `text` where it is read.

  **A query-position `unnest` of a non-array was the same seam under a different arm, and
  it is closed by refusal rather than by choosing between the two answers.** Over an empty
  table, `SELECT unnest(<column>)` answered zero rows and declared the argument's *own*
  type on the simple-query `RowDescription` — `21`, `23`, `20`, `1700`, `700` for
  smallint / int / bigint / numeric / real — against `Describe`'s `25`, where 18.6 refuses
  `42883 function unnest(<type>) does not exist` for every one of them. The executor arm
  is `array_element().unwrap_or(<the inner type itself>)` and the planner's is
  `.and_then(array_element)`, so neither answer was right; `unnest(tx)` is the control
  that identifies what was being measured, since the executor's fallback is `text` too and
  the two legs then agreed at `25` over the same refusal. **An agreeing pair is not a
  conforming one**, which is why no pair-comparison could have found this member and why
  it is the one the fixture family names.

  **The close is 18.6's `42883`, raised at plan time where signature resolution sits** —
  `planner::legality`'s `unnest_legality`. The gate's placement and everything that
  follows from it — why it is row-independent, why the refusal arrives at `Parse`, why
  the position is the expression's rather than the projection clause's, and which error
  wins at the two scales — is `docs/declared_types.md`'s.

  **Four residuals, and the first is what keeps cell F's arms alive. The first three share
  the row-count rule the gate took the closed half out of**: each leaves an `Expr::Unnest`
  for the gate to decline, so each is silent at `(0 rows)` and `0A000` — the
  scalar-position refusal, row 56's mechanism — once a row reaches the leaf. Where one is
  recorded below as "loud" that is a property of the *spelling measured*, not of the
  residual: a **no-FROM** projection has a row by construction, and putting the same
  argument under a `FROM` over an empty table makes it silent. The fourth is the exception
  and is row-independent for a reason of its own — neither the arity spelling nor a DDL
  position ever reaches the gate, the parser and the DDL walk both running before a row
  exists.

  - **An argument the gate's reader does not type stays silent over zero rows**, because
    the gate reads `arg_known_type` and that reader is deliberately narrow — an argument
    whose type is a *guess* defers rather than be refused on it, and refusing on a guess is
    how an over-rejection gets built out of the walkers' known agree-wrong band (row 54).
    Measured post-gate over an empty six-column `mw (s SMALLINT, i INT, b BIGINT, n
    NUMERIC, f4 REAL, tx TEXT)` — spelled out because the column *positions* decide a
    neighbouring pair below — each `(0 rows)` against
    18.6's `42883` and each declaring `23` on the simple leg against `Describe`'s `25`:
    `unnest(i + 0)`, `unnest(length(tx))`, `unnest(abs(i))`, `unnest(COALESCE(i, 1))`,
    `unnest((SELECT i FROM mw))`, `unnest(CASE WHEN true THEN i ELSE i END)`,
    `unnest(NULLIF(i, 1))`, `unnest(GREATEST(i, 1))`, `unnest(LEAST(i, 1))` and
    `unnest(-i)` — the last five added by re-deriving the list from the `Expr` variants
    `arg_known_type`'s `_` arm swallows rather than from the four expressions first
    written down. A member of that same reader class that is loud over the empty table:
    `unnest(sum(i))` is `0A000` there against 18.6's `42883 function unnest(bigint) does
    not exist`, the aggregate manufacturing a row for the leaf to be evaluated over.
    **"Computed" is the wrong name for the class**, which is why the two
    residuals below belong to it: what the members share is being invisible to *this*
    reader, and two of them are perfectly visible to `certain_operand_type`. So **the two
    `Expr::Unnest` arms are kept rather than merged**: they are still reachable, they
    still disagree, and there is no right answer to merge them onto. The right close is
    the reader's — widening `arg_known_type`/`concrete_branch_type` past these arms,
    which is row 65's close and takes this with it.

    **An untaken branch is a member with a row in the table, and it falsified the
    consequence this residual's two other homes had drawn from it** — `docs/declared_types.md`
    and `executor::walker_pins`'s cell F each read the row-count rule above as "what these
    two arms declare is only ever observable over a relation with no rows"; both now carry
    the leaf rule instead. The rule is row 56's and it is about
    *evaluation reaching the leaf*, not about the row count, so any spelling that keeps a
    row away from the leaf exposes the declaration with the table full: over a **one-row**
    six-column `mw`, `SELECT CASE WHEN false THEN unnest(i + 0) ELSE 'x' END FROM mw`
    answers `x` here against 18.6's `42883 function unnest(integer) does not exist`,
    declaring `case` **23** on the simple leg against `Describe`'s **25** — and the
    simple leg's `DataRow` is the text `x` under that `23`, an int4 declaration over a
    payload no int4 client can decode, while the extended leg's `25` and its binary
    `78` agree with each other. So this one spelling is **three** recorded
    things at once: this residual's (an `i + 0` argument `arg_known_type` will not type),
    a **row 36** route (a value under a declared type it is not), and cell F's two-arm
    split. Three controls bound it: taking the branch (`WHEN true`) is the `0A000`
    scalar-position refusal, so the leaf is what decides; `… WHERE false` is the same
    `23`/`25` split with no rows, so the row is not doing the work; and casting the same
    branch (`… THEN unnest(i + 0)::text ELSE 'x' END`) collapses both legs to `25` over
    the same `x`, so what splits them is the *uncast* `unnest` leaf. The residual list
    above is unaffected: those spellings are bare, and the one re-measured with a row here
    (`unnest(i + 0)`) is the `0A000` it is recorded as.
  - **An `unknown` argument takes 18.6's *other* code.** A bare `NULL` or a bare string
    literal is `unknown` at this position and 18.6 answers `42725 function unnest(unknown)
    is not unique`, not `42883`. pglet has no `42725`, so the gate deliberately declines
    both (`arg_known_type` answers `None` for them) rather than trade a recorded
    divergence for a differently-wrong one. `SELECT unnest(NULL)`, `unnest('{}')` and
    `unnest('abc')` are the no-FROM spellings — the first `(0 rows)`, the other two
    `0A000` — and the split is the *evaluated value*, not the code: under a `FROM` over an
    empty table all three are `(0 rows)`, and with a row all three are `0A000`.
  - **An `Expr::Bound` constant and an `Expr::Alias` are invisible to that same reader
    while `certain_operand_type` types them both**, which is row 65's boundary rather than
    any decision here — the gate's own comment records the pair. `SELECT unnest(INTERVAL
    '1 day')` is pglet's `0A000` against 18.6's `42883`, and
    `SELECT unnest(set_config('x', tx, false))` — `set_config` lowers to an
    `Expr::Alias` over its `value` argument — is `(0 rows)` against 18.6's
    `42883 function unnest(text) does not exist`. **The `INTERVAL` member's "loud" was the
    no-FROM spelling talking**: `SELECT unnest(INTERVAL '1 day') FROM <empty>` is
    `(0 rows)` here, so this residual has the silent polarity too and is not a miscode-only
    one. Both move when that reader does.
  - **Arity and the DDL positions are loud under `0A000`, and the DDL half is two routes
    at four sites rather than one arm at two.** `unnest()`, `unnest(a, b)` and the
    projection spelling of the FROM-clause zip (`SELECT unnest(arr, arr)`) are the
    parser's `single_arg` refusal, before an `Expr::Unnest` exists. The **stored-expression**
    sites are **four**, and the enumeration has to be re-derived rather than taken from a
    `CHECK`-and-`DEFAULT` memory: a column `DEFAULT`, a `CHECK`, an **index key
    expression** and an **index predicate** — the last three the ones `CLAUDE.md`'s
    stored-expression rule names as sharing `validate_stored_expr`, the `DEFAULT` running
    `cook_column_default` beside them. Each is `42883` on 18.6 for a non-array argument
    and `0A000` here.
    Which `0A000` splits by route, and only the `DEFAULT` one is a node arm:
    `executor::ddl`'s `check_default_expr_nodes` has the blanket `Expr::Unnest` arm, so
    `CREATE TABLE df (i INT, j INT DEFAULT unnest(1))` is `set-returning functions are
    not allowed in DEFAULT expressions` (18.6's own wording for its *array* refusal); the
    other three carry no `Expr::Unnest` arm at all and reach `validate_stored_expr`'s
    **representative-row probe**, whose `eval_expr` surfaces `executor::expr`'s
    scalar-position refusal — `CHECK (unnest(i) > 0)`, `CREATE INDEX … ((unnest(i)))` and
    `… WHERE unnest(i) > 0` are each `set-returning unnest() is only supported in a
    SELECT projection`, which is the same message a query-position leaf raises and names
    the wrong site. All four refuse an *array* argument too, correctly in code (18.6 is
    `0A000` there as well) and with 18.6 naming each site — `not allowed in check
    constraints` / `in DEFAULT expressions` / `in index expressions` / `in index
    predicates` — where pglet has two messages for the four. Neither route is this gate's,
    so neither can simply adopt its rule without an ordering of its own: the probe route
    is not even a rulebook consumer, which is the drift `docs/coercion.md` records under
    the signature family.

  **A neighbour this row's measurement surfaced, loud and pre-existing and not a member:
  a projection-position `unnest` over a `FROM` that yields rows is `0A000` here for an
  *array* argument too.** pglet row-expands a projection `unnest` only in the **no-FROM**
  shape (`Plan::ProjectUnnest`); with a `FROM` the expression sits in a plain
  `Plan::Project` and reaches the scalar-position refusal as soon as a row does. Measured
  over `mwa(arr INT[])`: empty, both engines answer `(0 rows)`; after
  `INSERT INTO mwa VALUES (ARRAY[1,2])`, 18.6 answers `1`/`2` for both
  `SELECT unnest(arr) FROM mwa` and `SELECT unnest(ARRAY[1,2]) FROM mwa` while pglet is
  `0A000 set-returning unnest() is only supported in a SELECT projection` for each. The
  same shape reached through a CTE or a `VALUES` derived table is the same refusal
  (`WITH c AS (SELECT ARRAY[1,2] AS a) SELECT unnest(a) FROM c`,
  `SELECT unnest(v) FROM (VALUES (ARRAY[1,2])) AS t(v)`). Loud, so no fixture is red over
  it and `docs/compatibility.md`'s `unnest($N)` row's parenthetical *(no-FROM)* is the only place the
  limit was written down. Nothing above moved it: the gate here raises `42883` and only
  for a **non**-array, so it never reaches this path.

  This is **different code** from the FROM-clause `unnest` below (the walkers' own
  `Expr::Unnest` arms and now this gate, not `function_scan_column_types`), which is why work on
  that derivation left these arms untouched — and why `SELECT * FROM unnest(1) AS u(v)`
  is unmoved at `0A000` against 18.6's `42883`: a FROM-position argument is never wrapped
  in an `Expr::Unnest`, so it never reaches the gate. One more neighbour is unmoved and
  worth naming beside the four that moved: `SELECT unnest(i), 1::nosuchtype FROM t` is
  `42704` here against 18.6's `42883`, because an unknown **type name** is refused in the
  parser — before an `Expr` exists for any item — where an unparseable **constant** cast
  (`'abc'::int`) is folded per projection item and so does yield to item one's gate.

  **A second parser-refused neighbour, and the gate's own pre-emption of a third** —
  both members of row 51's inherited *later-syntax-error* class, in opposite directions.
  A `LIMIT`/`OFFSET` argument pglet's grammar will not take beats the gate: `SELECT
  unnest(i) FROM mw LIMIT 'x'` is `42601 LIMIT must be a constant, parameter, ALL, or
  NULL` here against 18.6's `42883`, the `OFFSET` spelling likewise, and the control that
  separates the pre-emption from the underlying divergence is the same clause with no
  `unnest` in it — `SELECT i FROM mw LIMIT 'x'` is that same `42601` here against 18.6's
  `22P02 invalid input syntax for type bigint: "x"`. Measured identical on the builds
  either side of the gate, so it is a neighbour and not a cost. The other direction *is*
  the gate's: `SELECT unnest(i) FROM mw AS t1(a)` moved `42601` → `42883` with it, because
  `parser::parse` builds each statement's `Plan` — the coercion pass and this gate
  included — inside the loop that only afterwards checks for a trailing token, so a
  plan-time verdict on statement one arrives before pglet's own syntax error on what
  follows it. That lands on 18.6's code by coincidence rather than by agreement: an alias
  column list over a base table is ordinary SQL there, and the control `SELECT i FROM mw
  AS t1(a)` answers on 18.6 (zero rows, header `i`) while staying `42601` here.

  **Which `mw` the pair was measured over.** The six-column `mw (s SMALLINT, i INT,
  b BIGINT, n NUMERIC, f4 REAL, tx TEXT)`, the table `executor::walker_pins`'s cell F
  names — and re-measured over the three-column `mw (s SMALLINT, i INT, b BIGINT)`, the
  only `mw` the repo itself defines (eight fixtures plus `planner/tests.rs`),
  `SELECT unnest(i) FROM mw AS t1(a)`, its control `SELECT i FROM mw AS t1(a)` and
  `SELECT unnest(a) FROM mw AS t1(a)` each answer the same as under the six-column one,
  on both engines. 18.6's alias column list renames **positionally and only as far as it lists**
  (`doc/src/sgml/queries.sgml`: fewer aliases than columns leaves the rest unrenamed), so
  `AS t1(a)` renames `s` and leaves `i` under its own name; that is why `unnest(i)` still
  resolves there and reaches `42883`, and why the control answers. Re-measured on a
  two-column `mw (i INT, tx TEXT)`, where `i` is the column the list renames, both flip on
  18.6 and neither flips here:
  `SELECT unnest(i) FROM … AS t1(a)` is `42703 column "i" does not exist` there against
  pglet's unchanged `42883`, and the control is `42703` there rather than an answer. So
  the recorded code agreement is a property of `i`'s **position** in the table, not of the
  statement, and a reader who rebuilds `mw` with two columns will measure the opposite
  pair. A third member of the same ordering makes the asymmetry legible and holds under
  either table, because it names the renamed column: `SELECT unnest(a) FROM mw AS t1(a)`
  is 18.6's `42883 function unnest(smallint) does not exist` (`unnest(integer)` over the
  two-column table, `a` being `i` there) against pglet's `42703 column "a" does not
  exist` — the binding gate's verdict on statement one likewise arriving before the
  trailing-token check, and `a` binding to nothing here because pglet never applies the
  alias column list at all. That is the whole of pglet's side of this pair, and it is
  narrower than "the alias is ignored": the **table** alias lands and only the column list
  is left as a trailing token the grammar refuses, so every verdict pglet reaches here is
  one taken over `mw AS t1` with that list dropped. Two measurements say that and no more
  — `SELECT unnest(t1.i) FROM mw AS t1(a)` is `42883` here, so `t1` is in scope where an
  unapplied table alias would be `42P01`, while `SELECT t1.i FROM mw AS t1(a)`, which the
  plan-time gates accept, falls through to the trailing-token `42601`.

  Two controls place the ordering in
  `parser::parse` rather than in anything the gate did: `SELECT 'abc'::int FROM mw AS
  t1(a)` is `22P02` on **both** sides of the gate — a pre-existing member of the same
  ordering — while `SELECT i FROM nosuchtbl AS t1(a)` is the trailing-token `42601` on
  both sides of it, a relation being resolved at execute time and so *after* the loop.
  Both of those are pglet-side across builds and not engine agreements: 18.6 answers
  `22P02` to the first (agreeing by the same coincidence) and `42P01 relation "nosuchtbl"
  does not exist` to the second. Everything
  `parse_statement` decides, plan-time gates included, is decided before the loop looks
  for a trailing token; everything the executor decides is not.

  The residual is pinned by `executor::walker_pins`'s cell F; the array case, where the two
  arms must keep agreeing, is `select/unnest_projection_int_declared_type.sql` plus five
  incidental fixtures its header names.

  **A FROM-clause `unnest` whose array expression is untypable is the same seam one layer
  down, and its two readers disagree by construction.** `function_scan_column_types` answers
  `None` there, and the two readers fall back differently on purpose — the planner takes
  `text`, the executor takes the evaluated `Value::Array`'s own `element_type`. A bound
  `$N` the client **declared** at `Parse` does not reach it: it arrives as a typed operand
  (row 146), so `SELECT * FROM unnest($1) AS u(v)` declared `int4[]` (1007) or
  `timestamptz[]` (1185) describes 23 / 1184 at `Describe`, as 18.6 does, and renders the
  `+00` — measured on both engines over raw v3, in both result formats. An **undeclared**
  `$N` does: that spelling parses here where 18.6 answers `42725 function unnest(unknown) is
  not unique`, and the text-decoded value is then pglet's own `0A000 … unnest requires array
  arguments` at execution. `unnest(NULL)` reaches the fallback too — pglet answers 0 rows,
  18.6 is `42725 function unnest(unknown) is not unique`. Neither is pinnable by a passing
  fixture, pglet's answer being the one that differs.

  **An unnest alias column list longer than the array count is silently truncated.**
  `SELECT * FROM unnest(ARRAY[1,2]) AS u(a, b)` answers one column here where 18.6 is
  `42P10 table "u" has 1 columns available but 2 columns specified`; the `SELECT b`
  spelling of the same statement is a loud `42703` here, which is what leaves only the
  `*` spelling silent. The derivation is one-pair-per-*array* and the unused alias tail
  is exactly where 18.6 raises. pglet already implements the alias-arity `42P10` for
  `FROM (VALUES …) AS t(a, b)`, so the rule exists and this route lacks it. Measured on
  both engines; pre-existing (the earlier code dropped the tail identically).

  **The residual, and what the closed half replaced.** The closed half replaced `(0 rows)`
  under two disagreeing walkers and, where evaluation reached the leaf, one of two wrong
  codes — the scalar-position refusal and `unnest requires an array argument`. The residual
  is an argument the gate's reader does not type: over an empty `mw`, `unnest(b + 0)`
  answers `(0 rows)` declaring `20` against `Describe`'s `25`, while
  `unnest(set_config('x', tx, false))` and `unnest(tx || 'a')` answer `(0 rows)` at `25` on
  both legs, and with a row every one of them is `0A000`. Row-independence is the closed
  half's property alone: a residual recorded as loud is one whose no-FROM spelling has a row
  by construction, so `SELECT unnest(INTERVAL '1 day')` and `SELECT unnest('abc')` are
  `0A000` while the `… FROM <empty>` spelling of each is `(0 rows)`. 18.6's other code,
  `42725 function unnest(unknown) is not unique`, is the one pglet does not raise, which is
  why the `unknown` spellings are declined rather than refused; `set_config(…)` is the
  `Expr::Alias` member of the same reader gap. The nine guards are
  `select/unnest_projection_non_array_{column,text_column,column_with_rows,cast,literal}_loud.sql`,
  `select/unnest_non_array_{returning,order_by}_loud.sql`,
  `select/unnest_projection_non_array_beats_where_binding.sql` and
  `…_binding_beats_signature.sql`.

  **The three arithmetic members, the one bound-`$N` route, and why none is fixturable.**
  Each is an OID-only divergence — the simple leg against `Describe`, `23`/`20` against
  `25`, `701` against `700`, `1700` against `701` — and the `^` member has a second route
  the others do not, a bound-NULL `$N`: `$1 ^ n` declares `701` against 18.6's `1700` on the
  extended leg, the only leg that route has. Beside them the `%` band is the one where
  **both** walks are wrong rather than one, 18.6 registering no float `%` operator at all
  (`42883 real % unknown`). No fixture can hold any of it: a candidate `NULL ^ n` fixture is
  red on the extended leg and a candidate `f4 + NULL` one on the text leg, each green on the
  other, and a `@no-declared-types:` opt-out waives both legs. All three members and their
  agreeing controls are pinned by `executor::walker_pins`'s
  `arithmetic_over_an_unknown_operand_splits_on_a_text_left_a_float4_and_a_numeric_pow`.

  **The `pg_catalog` half of that residual is closed, and the `information_schema` half is
  closeable the same way.** `pg_catalog`'s identifier columns are declared `name` (19), its
  OID columns `oid` (26) and its code columns `"char"` (18), so `pg_tables` and `pg_indexes`
  no longer need a waiver. 18.6 declares the `information_schema` columns as **domains** —
  `sql_identifier`, `character_data`, `cardinal_number` — and a domain's `RowDescription`
  carries its **base** type's OID: `sql_identifier` is `name` (19), `character_data` is
  `varchar` (1043) and `cardinal_number` is `int4` (23), measured against a user
  `CREATE DOMAIN dom AS INT` control whose column describes as `integer`. So what is left is
  a `Text` to `Name`/`Varchar` change over `catalog/virtual_tables.rs`'s column specs —
  the `cardinal_number` columns already declare `Int4` and agree — not a per-cluster
  obstruction.
- **65 · The `42804` gate compares only what its own reader resolves in the post-pass tree.**
  Row 54's `Ok(None)` has a third consequence, and it is not a declared type at
  all: `planner::coercion`'s `check_branch_unification_node` — pglet's stand-in for
  18.6's "types X and Y cannot be matched" — resolves each branch through
  `concrete_branch_type`, the reader the coercion pass folds with, widened by the one arm
  the pass cannot use (a bare scalar subquery, whose type the pass would have to *cast*
  to — `docs/coercion.md` § What the gate reads), and `select_common_type` folds
  `types.iter().flatten()`. So a
  branch that reader answers `None` for is dropped from the fold **and** from the
  closing re-check that follows it, and is never compared against a sibling. **The
  condition is therefore per branch, not per set** — "no concrete member" is the
  narrower sub-case, and reading it as the boundary hid the ordinary spellings below.
  And it is per branch of **the tree the gate is handed**, which is not the tree the
  parser built: `resolve_expr_types_gated` runs the coercion pass and *then* the gate, so
  a branch the pass rewrote is the branch compared — the third sub-case below. That is
  why "a branch the coercion pass cannot resolve" is the wrong reading of this row: where
  the pass rewrites nothing and the gate's own reader types the pair, the gate fires and
  pglet conforms. `greatest(ARRAY[1,2], set_config('x', tx, false))` — neither argument
  concrete to `arg_known_type`, so `variadic_common_type` answers `None` and
  `unify_variadic_args` returns its arguments untouched — is
  `42804 GREATEST types integer[] and text cannot be matched` on both engines, with a row
  and over `WHERE false` alike.

  **Not over a branch set that names an enum.** There a branch `concrete_branch_type`
  cannot type is read through the complete type walk instead, so it is typed and compared:
  `COALESCE(n + 0, lower(s), COALESCE(m,'ok'))`, `greatest(n + 0, lower(s), m)` and their
  `least` / `ARRAY` / `UPDATE … WHERE` spellings answered on a build before the
  enum-identity gates and are now 18.6's `42804`. A set with no enum in it — and a set
  whose untyped branches the coercion pass has already cast to a bare column's type — is
  judged as below. Row 114's bullet carries the measurement.

  **The first two sub-cases differ in what else goes wrong, because only one of them
  casts** (the third casts too, and is below).
  With **no** concrete member the fold is `[None, None]`, `select_common_type` answers
  `Ok(None)`, nothing is raised *and* no coercing cast is inserted — so the branch sets
  that reach the two declared-type walkers raw are exactly these, and the declaration
  and the value can come from different branches. With **a** concrete member the
  siblings resolve a target and the pass casts the invisible branch to it: the
  declaration and the value stay together and the only thing missing is the refusal.
  Measured on both pglet legs and on 18.6, identical before and after the row-54 close
  except where noted. First the no-concrete-member members:

  - `COALESCE(length('ab'), upper('7'))` → int4 `2`; `COALESCE(upper('x'), length('ab'))`
    → text `X`. Which branch leads decides the answer, over a pair 18.6 will not match at
    all (`42804 COALESCE types integer and text cannot be matched`, and the reverse
    spelling's `text and integer`).
  - `CASE WHEN true THEN length('ab') ELSE upper('7') END` → int4 `2`, against
    `42804 CASE types text and integer cannot be matched`.
  - **The declaration and the value come from different branches, and one `WHEN false`
    parts them.** Both walkers declare the first *inferable* branch; evaluation returns
    the branch it takes; nothing casts one to the other, so the pair only agrees while
    the same branch wins both. `CASE WHEN false THEN length('ab') ELSE upper('x') END`
    declares `23` and streams **one** byte (`58`, the `X`); the
    `ELSE INTERVAL '1 day'` spelling declares `23` over **16**; and
    `COALESCE(nullif(length('ab'), 2), upper('x'))` reaches it with no `CASE` at all,
    `23` over one byte. 18.6 refuses all three `42804`. This is row 36's shape by its
    **untaken-branch** route, the more reachable of its two: no client-declared `$N`, no NULL
    column, no bound parameter — two computed branches and a condition. The simple leg
    reaches it too: it renders the surviving branch as its own type under the leading
    branch's OID — `X`, `1 day` and `X`, in the order above, each under `23`. **That is
    not what separates it from row 54's fold band**, which reaches the simple leg
    outright, so neither of row 36's live multi-operand routes is binary-only (row 36's
    bullet).
  - `COALESCE(INTERVAL '1 day', length('ab'))` → `1186` and `1 day`; the reverse
    spelling → int4 `2`, its declaration and value agreeing. An `INTERVAL` literal is
    parsed to an `Expr::Bound` (`parser::expr`'s `parse_interval_literal`), which
    `concrete_branch_type` answers `None` for at its `_` arm, so this sub-case's
    condition is not "every branch computed" — it is every branch **invisible to that
    reader**, and a constant can be one.
  - `ARRAY[length('ab'), upper('7')]` → `_int4` **`{2,7}`**, and this is the sharpest
    member: the gate's absence does not merely mislabel a column, it lets the `text` `'7'`
    be parsed **into** an integer array, so what the client reads is a row 18.6 declines
    to compute at all with the text operand silently reinterpreted. 18.6 is
    `42804 ARRAY types integer and text cannot be matched`.
  - `COALESCE(length('ab'), date_trunc('day', ts))` → int4 `2` against
    `42804 … integer and timestamp with time zone`, so the class is not confined to the
    string/number pair.
  - `COALESCE(NULL, length('ab'), upper('7'))` → int4 `2`. This is the one spelling the
    row-54 close **moved**: it declared `text` on the simple leg before and `int4` on both
    legs after, which changes the label on an answer 18.6 still refuses.
  - **Loud but late** where the surviving value will not parse:
    `ARRAY[length('ab'), upper('x')]` is `22P02 invalid input syntax for type integer:
    "X"` — at `Execute`, after a `Describe` that already declared `_int4` — against 18.6's
    `42804` at `Parse`. The refusal exists here, but it is the element cast's and it comes
    a phase later, so a client that only prepared the statement is told the wrong thing.
  - Through a **client-declared parameter type**, which is no longer a no-concrete-member
    spelling: a declared `$N` is read as a cast to its type (row 146), which
    `concrete_branch_type` answers for, so it joins the some-concrete-member sub-case below.
    `Parse` declaring `$1` as `text` (OID 25) plus `COALESCE($1, length('ab'))` bound
    `'zz'` declares `text` and streams `7a7a` in both result formats, and so do the
    `COALESCE($1, date_trunc('day', now()))` spelling and, over an empty `w(ts
    TIMESTAMPTZ)`, `COALESCE($1, date_trunc('day', ts))`'s descriptor — the declaration and
    the value agree, and what is left is the missing refusal: 18.6 refuses each `42804` at
    `Parse`. Measured over a raw extended-protocol client; a fixture reaches the shape
    through `-- @param-declared` (`tests/README.md`), and a faithful one is red.

  **And the some-concrete-member sub-case, which the "no concrete member" reading
  excluded and which is where the ordinary spellings live.** One invisible branch is
  enough; the other branch can be a plain column or a plain literal, so none of these
  needs a computed expression on both sides. The pass resolves the concrete siblings'
  target and casts the invisible branch to it, so the declaration and the value agree
  and the divergence is the missing refusal alone — which makes each of these a
  **silent wrong answer** wherever the cast succeeds, and 18.6's `42804` in every case:

  - `COALESCE(i, upper(tx))` over `t(i INT, tx TEXT)` holding `(7, '7')` → int4 `7`
    (`42804 COALESCE types integer and text cannot be matched`), and
    `CASE WHEN true THEN i ELSE upper(tx) END` → int4 `7` the same way. A column and a
    function call: the whole apparatus this row used to require is gone.
  - `COALESCE(upper('7'), 1)` → int4 `7` with **no table at all**, the invisible branch
    leading and the concrete literal behind it. `ARRAY[1, upper('7')]` → `_int4`
    `{1,7}`, `greatest(i, upper('7'))` → int4 `7`, `least(i, upper('7'))` → int4 `7`.
  - **Short-circuiting hides an unparseable one entirely**: `COALESCE(1, upper('x'))`
    → `1` and `CASE WHEN false THEN upper('x') ELSE 1 END` → `1`, the cast never run.
  - **`22P02` at eval where the cast is run and cannot parse**:
    `COALESCE(upper('x'), 1)`, `ARRAY[1, upper('x')]` and `greatest(i, upper('x'))` are
    each `22P02 invalid input syntax for type integer: "X"` — pglet's own code, a phase
    later than 18.6's `42804`, exactly as the `ARRAY[length('ab'), upper('x')]` member
    above. `nullif(i, upper('x'))` is the one spelling that **agrees**, `42883 operator
    does not exist: integer = text` on both engines, because 18.6 resolves `nullif`
    through the `=` operator rather than through `select_common_type`.

  **And the third sub-case, where the branch is invisible to the *pass* and visible to
  the *gate*.** The two are not the same reader: `check_branch_unification_node` hands one
  reader — `concrete_branch_type` and its scalar-subquery arm — to all five constructs the
  gate covers, while the coercion pass
  reads `concrete_branch_type` only for `COALESCE`/`CASE`/`ARRAY` — `greatest`/`least` go
  through `unify_variadic_args` and `nullif` through `coerce_nullif_args`, both over
  `arg_known_type`, which lacks the `Array` and `Alias` arms the other carries (its
  `Aggregate` arm is the other's, below). So over a variadic those two arms invert the
  usual order: `arg_known_type`
  cannot see the argument, `variadic_common_type` folds the concrete sibling alone, the
  pass wraps the invisible one in a `Cast` to that target — and the gate, which would
  have typed that argument and refused the pair, now reads a `Cast` at an agreeing type.
  The pass erases the evidence before the gate looks — **but only when it has a concrete
  sibling to fold**. With none, `variadic_common_type` answers `None`,
  `unify_variadic_args` returns its arguments untouched, and the gate types the raw pair
  itself: `greatest(ARRAY[1,2], set_config('x', tx, false))` and its `least` spelling are
  `42804` on both engines with a row and over `WHERE false` alike, and
  `greatest(ARRAY[1,2], ARRAY['a','b'])` is `42846 GREATEST could not convert type text[]
  to integer[]` on both. Two pass-visible arguments that *disagree* reach the same place,
  the fold having no target either: `greatest(ARRAY[1,2], tx, i)` is `42804` on both. So
  what blinds the gate is the pass's **cast**, not the pass's reader — the members below
  are the shapes where that cast is inserted. The `nullif` spelling of the
  no-concrete-sibling cell is *not* one of these conforming shapes: it is outside the gate
  entirely, so what bounds it is the eval-time `=` operand gate —
  `nullif(ARRAY[1,2], set_config('x', tx, false))` is `42883` with a row and `(0 rows)`
  over `WHERE false`, against 18.6's `42883` either way. Over
  `r5t(i INT, tx TEXT, a INT[], d DATE)` holding `(7, '7', {1,2}, '2024-01-15')`, each
  identical on both legs:

  - `greatest(ARRAY[1,2], tx)` → `25` over `{1,2}`; `least(ARRAY[1,2], tx)` → `25` over
    `7`; `nullif(ARRAY[1,2], tx)` → `25` over `{1,2}`. 18.6 refuses the first two
    `42804 GREATEST|LEAST types integer[] and text cannot be matched` and the third
    `42883 operator does not exist: integer[] = text`. The argument order does not
    matter: `greatest(tx, ARRAY[1,2])` is `25` over `{1,2}` too, against 18.6's
    `42804 GREATEST types text and integer[] cannot be matched`.
  - `greatest(set_config('x', tx, false), i)` and its `least` spelling → `23` over `7`;
    `nullif(set_config('x', tx, false), i)` → `23` over **NULL**, the cast having made
    `'7' = 7` true. 18.6 refuses all three, `42804 … types text and integer` for the
    first two and `42883 operator does not exist: text = integer` for the third. This is
    the `Alias` arm's first measured *divergence* — it was on record as reachable and
    carrying none, which was a claim about declared types only.
  - **The bound is whether the pass's cast succeeds**, and it runs per arm. An `ARRAY[…]`
    argument casts only to the **string family**, so any other sibling type is
    loud-but-miscoded: `greatest(ARRAY[1,2], d)` is pglet's
    `42846 cannot cast type Some(Int4Array) to Date`, and the `i`, `numeric`, `bool` and
    `timestamptz` siblings are the `… to Int4` / `Numeric` / `Bool` / `Timestamptz`
    spellings of it, every one against 18.6's `42804` (the `Some(…)` in that message is
    a separately-tracked rendering defect, not this row's). *Both* string types are on
    the silent side, not just `text`: `greatest(ARRAY[1,2], 'x'::varchar)` answers
    `1043` over `{1,2}`. Nor does the element type matter —
    `greatest(ARRAY['a','b'], tx)` answers `25` over `{a,b}` and
    `greatest(ARRAY['a','b'], i)` is `42846 … Some(TextArray) to Int4`. An `Alias`
    argument casts wherever its inner value converts to the sibling's target — `'7'`
    into `int4` above — and is loud at eval where it does not:
    `greatest(set_config('x', tx, false), d)` is
    `22007 invalid input syntax for type date: "7"`.
  - **The `Aggregate` arm is closed.** `arg_known_type` types an aggregate argument as
    `concrete_branch_type` does, so the pass folds it into the target instead of casting
    it to its sibling's: `greatest(sum(i), tx) FROM r5t GROUP BY tx` reaches the gate
    uncast and is 18.6's `42804`, `nullif(sum(i), tx)` its `42883`, and the `HAVING`
    spelling (`… GROUP BY tx HAVING greatest(sum(i), tx) IS NOT NULL`) its `42804`
    (`select/agg_expr_greatest_text_sibling_loud.sql`,
    `select/agg_expr_nullif_text_sibling_loud.sql`). These were pglet's own `0A000` while
    an aggregate under a variadic was not evaluated (row 89), and would have answered once
    it was. That leaves `Array` and `Alias` as this sub-case's live silent arms today.
  - **The row-count axis is the same as the other two sub-cases'**: over
    `… FROM r5t WHERE false` every member here answers `(0 rows)` under a full
    `RowDescription` — the six silent ones, and the `42846`, `22007` and `0A000` ones
    too, none of which is raised before evaluation.

  Which sub-case a statement is in decides whether row 36 is reachable through it: the
  no-concrete-member one parts the declaration from the value, and neither of the other
  two can, both having cast the declaration and the value back together.

  **`greatest`/`least` fold an invisible branch out of the same gate; `nullif` is not
  covered by it at all — and what catches either below it is the *data*, when it
  catches anything.** `branch_unification_legality`'s match names
  `Coalesce`, `Array`, `Case` and `VariadicFunc::Greatest | Least`, and the gate passes
  it one closure for all four, so `greatest`/`least` drop an
  invisible branch from the fold exactly as the other three do — `[None, None]` over
  the no-concrete-member sets below; `VariadicFunc::NullIf` falls to that
  match's `_ => Ok(())` and reaches no branch-unification check on any branch set. What
  makes all three look conforming in the first two sub-cases is their *eval-time* fold
  (and `nullif`'s eval-time `=` operand gate), which sees the runtime values and
  raises `42804`/`42883` — at `Execute`, so the extended leg still describes a row type
  first. **That is a property of the operands evaluation is handed, not of the
  construct**, which is the whole of the third sub-case below. Remove the rows and the
  first two sub-cases are silent at all six cells: over
  `… FROM w54 WHERE false`, `COALESCE`, `CASE`, `ARRAY`, `greatest`, `least` and `nullif`
  of `(length('ab'), upper('7'))` each answer `(0 rows)` under a full `RowDescription`
  where 18.6 refuses every one at parse analysis — the row-4/row-5 shape, on this gate.
  The `22P02` member goes with them: `ARRAY[length('ab'), upper('x')] FROM w54 WHERE
  false` is `(0 rows)` under a `_int4` descriptor, so **every** loud answer this class has
  is a property of the data rather than of the statement. **The some-concrete-member
  members obey the same rule**, reaching it through the cast rather than the eval fold:
  `COALESCE(upper('x'), 1)`, `ARRAY[1, upper('x')]` and `greatest(i, upper('x'))` over
  `WHERE false` are each `(0 rows)` under a full `RowDescription`.

  **Controls. The second pins the condition to the branch rather than the set, the next
  two pin the third sub-case to the arm list rather than to the argument, and the last
  pins it to the pass's *cast* rather than to the pass's reader.**
  `COALESCE(i, tx)` over ordinary columns says the gate is there and works:
  `42804` on both engines, on both legs. `COALESCE(i, tx, upper('7'))` says it *still*
  fires when an invisible branch stands beside a concrete pair — `42804` on both — so
  what is skipped is the comparison of the invisible branch, not the gate.
  `COALESCE(i, 1, upper('x'))` has two concrete branches that agree and an invisible one
  that does not, and answers int4 `7` against 18.6's `42804`. Then the same `int[]`
  argument, reached through an arm **both** readers carry, is refused as it should be:
  `greatest(a, tx)` over the `INT[]` column (the `Column` arm) and `greatest(a::int[], tx)`
  (the `Cast` arm) are `42804` on both engines. And the `COALESCE`/`CASE`/`ARRAY` family,
  where the pass and the gate fold the same reader over every arm but the subquery one, is
  untouched by the arms the two readers do not share: `COALESCE(i, ARRAY[1,2])`, `COALESCE(set_config('x', tx, false), i)`,
  `ARRAY[1, set_config('x', tx, false)]`,
  `CASE WHEN true THEN set_config('x', tx, false) ELSE i END` and
  `COALESCE(sum(i), tx) … GROUP BY tx` are each `42804` on both — so what the third
  sub-case names is the *reader split* at the point the pass casts, not the argument
  shape. Last, the same reader split with **nothing for the pass to fold**:
  `greatest(ARRAY[1,2], set_config('x', tx, false))` and its `least` spelling are `42804`
  on both engines and `greatest(ARRAY[1,2], ARRAY['a','b'])` `42846` on both, because a
  fold with no known argument answers `None` and leaves the gate the raw pair —
  `greatest(ARRAY[1,2], tx, i)`, whose two known arguments disagree, is `42804` on both
  for the same reason. What the third sub-case needs is the pass's cast, not merely its
  narrower reader.

  The condition those six together describe is a property of the tree the gate walks,
  which is the **post-pass** tree: over the five constructs it covers, the `42804` gate's
  **common-type fold**, where the branch set reaches it, reports no error exactly when
  that tree holds no disagreeing pair both of whose halves the gate's reader
  resolves. Only the disagreeing-pair qualification is an answer of the gate's own;
  *where the branch set reaches it* is wider than one arm: a branch set holding a branch
  this scope cannot type yet defers ahead of the fold — pair or no pair — leaving the
  verdict to the enclosing level's re-resolution, and, beside that defer arm, a clause
  the gated walk does not run over at all — measured, one: a set-op's trailing
  `ORDER BY` (`plan_set_op_order_limit` never calls `resolve_expr_types_gated`; row 3's
