  verdict three ways for that reason (`Castable` / `Uncastable` / `Deferred`,
  `docs/coercion.md` § What the gate reads), and each of the two non-`Castable` verdicts
  leaves the branch bare in the tree the declared-type walkers and the executor then read.
  Three measured members, over `q1 (i INT, tx TEXT, m qmood)` holding `(1, 'postgres',
  'ok')` and `t2 (i INT)` holding `(7), (8)`:

    enum's identity is not one — it is `ColumnDesc::enum_type` beside a `type_oid` of

    categories (`SELECT COALESCE((SELECT m FROM q1), i) FROM q1` was `42804` on both) and
    the **message** did not, pglet's sentence reading `COALESCE types text and integer`
    against 18.6's `types qmood and integer`. `SubqueryType::Uncastable` now carries a
    `ResolvedType`, so the **type name** agrees, and
    `select/scalar_subquery_enum_branch_mismatch_loud.sql` records it. The sentence still

    which is the whole `42804` family's and not the enum's. The
    pairs 18.6 refuses *because* the branch is an enum are row 114's and closed with it.
  - **(b) A `name` or `name[]`.** The gate types it and judges the set as 18.6 does — the

    `shared_multi_operand_type`, which takes a `COALESCE`'s first inferable branch and a
    `CASE`'s first inferable *result*, where
    18.6's `select_common_type` folds in its own order (`transformCaseExpr` prepends
    `defresult`, and an `unknown` literal contributes no type at all). Measured over `q1`
    widened with `vc VARCHAR(9)` holding `pg` and `ta TEXT[]` holding `{a,b}`, in both
    wire formats, over the subquery `(SELECT current_user)` beside each of a `text`
    column, a `varchar` column and a `text` literal, in both orders, in each of
    `COALESCE`, `CASE`, `ARRAY[…]`, `greatest` and `least`, plus `COALESCE` over
    `name[]` beside `text[]` in both orders — thirty-two spellings, of which **ten**

    written **first** is `25`, `25`, `1009`, `25`, `25` across the five against `19`,

    order at every constructor but `CASE`, whose `text`-column spelling is the first

    **What a binary client sees is the array half.** `name` and `text` share their text
    encoding and their binary encoding, so a scalar member's value bytes are the same on

  - **(c) A branch the gate cannot type at all.** `wildcard_column_type` answers for a

    `SELECT CASE WHEN t2.i = 7 THEN (SELECT current_schemas(true)) ELSE 'zz' END FROM t2`
    is `22P02 malformed array literal: "zz"` on 18.6 and answers here, the `'zz'` row's
    binary payload being `7a7a` under `1003`.

  (b) is the member with a wide accepting direction — the same thirty-two spellings — and

- **58/59/63/64 · A zero-column relation reached an arm recorded dead — 58 and 59 closed, 63 and 64 open.** The
  executor walk's `Expr::Aggregate` arm carried a rule the planner walk has no
  counterpart for: it
  returned `TypeOid::Float8` when the argument typed `text`, the function was
  `Sum`/`Min`/`Max`, **and the projection scope had no input columns**. The arm's own
  comment justified that last condition by "a subquery without schema", and that route
  never fired it — measured on both builds, `SELECT (SELECT max('abc') FROM zc)`,
  `SELECT (SELECT max(tx) FROM t2)` and `SELECT (SELECT max('abc') FROM t2)` each declare
  `25` on both legs. What *did* build a scope with no input columns is ordinary SQL:

  ```sql
  CREATE TABLE zc (x INT);
  INSERT INTO zc VALUES (1), (2);
  ALTER TABLE zc DROP COLUMN x;   -- both engines accept a zero-column relation
  ```

  **That spelling is one of two measured routes, and "which both engines accept" is a
  property of *it*, not of the class.** The second is a `RETURNING`-less data-modifying
  CTE that the outer query then references — a route pglet's own parser documents
  (`crates/pglet_sql/src/parser/select.rs`, `parse_cte_body`) — and 18.6 **refuses the
  whole statement**: `WITH c AS (INSERT INTO t3 VALUES (9)) SELECT max('abc') FROM c`
  declared `701` on the simple leg against `Describe`'s `25` on the pre-deletion build and
  `25` on both legs after, where 18.6 is `0A000 WITH query "c" does not have a RETURNING
  clause` on both legs. The `UPDATE` and `DELETE` body spellings behave identically, and
  so does the writing arm: `WITH c AS (INSERT INTO t3 VALUES (9)) SELECT sum(m) FROM
  (SELECT max('abc') AS m FROM c) s` answered one NULL row pre-deletion and is `42883`
  now. That pglet accepts and *writes* where 18.6 refuses is its own edge — **row 61**.
  The negative controls are worth naming so a re-derivation does not reach for them: the
  three further shapes that reach a zero-column relation on 18.6 are **not** pglet routes
  at all — `CREATE TABLE zc2 ()` (a construction), a bare `SELECT FROM t2` (a projection)
  and `TABLE zc` (a reference) are each `42601` here and each accepted there.

  **Measured before, on the two legs and the two engines.** `SELECT max('abc') AS a FROM
  zc` declared `701` on pglet's simple-query `RowDescription` and `25` on its `Describe`,
  against `25` on both of 18.6's legs — over a value that is the text `abc` on all four.
  The same for `min`, and for the alias (`FROM zc z`), derived-table
  (`FROM (SELECT * FROM zc) s`), CTE, join and `WHERE`-bearing spellings of the same
  FROM: seven shapes, one answer. **The join member is the all-zero-column one** —
  `FROM zc a, zc b` (and its `JOIN … ON true` and three-way spellings) declared `701`,
  while `FROM zc, t2` and `FROM zc LEFT JOIN t2 ON true` declared `25` on the same
  pre-deletion build. `scope.columns.is_empty()` is a property of the projecting node's
  *whole input*, not of any one relation in it, so one columned relation anywhere in the
  FROM defeats the guard — which is exactly the spelling a re-derivation reaching for
  "a join" is most likely to write, and it does not reproduce.

  **And it wrote a wrong answer, not only a wrong label.** The guessed descriptor is what
  an enclosing aggregate's operand gate reads through `certain_expr_type_oid`, and
  `aggregate_legality(Sum, Float8)` accepts what `aggregate_legality(Sum, Text)` refuses:
  `SELECT sum(m) FROM (SELECT max('abc') AS m FROM zc) s` answered **one NULL row** where
  18.6 raises `42883 function sum(text) does not exist` — the `avg(m)` spelling and the
  `WITH c AS (…) SELECT sum(m) FROM c` spelling likewise.

  **After.** All ten of those shapes take 18.6's answer: seven byte-and-OID-identical on
  both legs, three raising 18.6's own `42883` (on pglet's extended leg the refusal lands
  at `Execute` rather than at `Parse` — a separate, pre-existing phase divergence,
  recorded as **row 60**).
  The arm is deleted and the seam's "rules the other walk has no counterpart for" is four
  rather than five (`docs/declared_types.md`).

  **The residual, so this row is not read as the class fully closed.** `SELECT sum(NULL)
  FROM zc` and `SELECT avg(NULL) FROM zc` still answer a NULL row where 18.6 is
  `42725 function sum(unknown) is not unique`; that is the fenced unknown-argument
  leniency and not this arm's — measured, the same two statements over an *ordinary*
  table answer identically on both builds. Only the **row** is unmoved for the first:
  `sum(NULL)`'s simple-leg `RowDescription` did move, `701` → `25`, the guess having
  typed it, while `avg(NULL)` declares `701` on both sides for an independent reason
  (`aggregate_result_type(Avg, Some(Text))` is `Float8`). `SELECT sum('abc') FROM zc` is
  `42883` here against that same `42725`, unchanged. And `SELECT *` over such a relation
  was its own divergence, row 59, now closed; the `Execute`-rather-than-`Parse` phase the three
  newly-loud shapes raise at is row 60's, pre-existing and not this close's.

  **Why nothing caught it: no fixture in the corpus built a zero-column relation.** The
  **text** leg compares live against 18.6 and would have failed on the first shape above
  the moment any fixture issued it — the extended leg would have passed, since `Describe`
  already said `25`, which is the pair-only class these two legs exist for. They simply
  never saw one, which is the "it checks the corpus, not the
  dialect" limit doing exactly what `tests/README.md` says it does. Re-derived by corpus
  scan rather than inherited, **over the corpus as it stood before the two fixtures below
  were added** (a later scan counts those two as well): fourteen
  `ALTER TABLE … DROP COLUMN` statements, one per fixture, across fourteen fixtures (two
  further files mention the clause in prose only).
  Twelve of the fourteen target a **table**, and every one of those twelve declares at
  least two columns, so none can reach zero; the other two target an index and a sequence
  and are refusals. **Which spellings that scan covered is part of the derivation**, since
  the conclusion is only as wide as the search: `ALTER TABLE … DROP COLUMN` and
  `CREATE TABLE <t> ()`, the latter appearing nowhere in it. It did **not** cover the
  second live route — a `RETURNING`-less data-modifying CTE — and the conclusion survives
  re-derivation over that one anyway: the corpus holds **nine** data-modifying CTE bodies
  (`cte/insert_returning.sql`, `cte/update_returning_join.sql`, `cte/delete_returning.sql`,
  `cte/zero_match.sql`, `cte/update_returning_wildcard.sql`,
  `update/from_returning_wildcard.sql`,
  `update/returning_from_unambiguous_names_answer.sql`,
  `spine/grant/role_grant_offer_supersede.sql`, `spine/grant/role_grant_revoke_for_scope.sql`)
  and **every one of them carries `RETURNING`**, so none yields a zero-column relation. A
  bare `SELECT FROM` appears nowhere either, and would be `42601` here if it did.
  `select/zero_column_relation_aggregate_declared_types.sql`
  and `select/zero_column_relation_sum_over_text_loud.sql` are the guards, and both were
  written and shown **red** against the pre-deletion tree (the first as
  `m: Postgres oid=25 vs pglet oid=701, n: Postgres oid=25 vs pglet oid=701` on the text
  leg, the second as `expected error but got success`). The unit-level guard is
  `executor::walker_pins`'s cell C, which is now a merged cell asserting `text` under
  **both** scopes — the shape of the old scope-keyed assertion kept deliberately, so a
  later reader can see what the cell used to be.

  The transferable half: **a claim that an arm is dead is a claim about the callers that
  reach it**, and this one was falsified by a caller the arm's own comment does not name.
  The comment named the route someone had checked; the route that mattered was one nobody
  had asked about.

  **Closed: the zero-column result set is not described.** Over the same relation
  row 58 builds, `SELECT * FROM zc` diverged on the wire and in two different ways per
  leg. Measured with a raw v3 client against both engines, before and after the fix:

  | | 18.6 | pglet, before | pglet, after |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | simple `Query` | `T(0)`, two `D(0)`, `C(SELECT 2)` | **no `T`, no `D`s**, `C(SELECT 2)` | `T(0)`, two `D(0)`, `C(SELECT 2)` |
  | extended `Parse`/`Describe`/`Bind`/`Describe`/`Execute` | `1 t T(0) 2 T(0) D(0) D(0) C(SELECT 2)` | `1 t` **`n`** `2` **`n`** `D(0) D(0) C(SELECT 2)` | `1 t T(0) 2 T(0) D(0) D(0) C(SELECT 2)` |

  So a simple-query client saw **zero rows under a tag claiming two**, and an extended
  client was told the statement returns nothing and then handed two rows. Both were
  silent — no error on either leg — and the row loss was the simple leg's alone.

  **A second silent divergence closed with it, and it was not predicted.** Postgres's
  aborted-block `Describe` gate reads `psrc->resultDesc` / `portal->tupDesc` — a
  **pointer**, so a zero-column result set trips it. Measured on 18.6 with both statements
  prepared and bound while the block was healthy: `Describe` of the zero-column
  `SELECT *` is `25P02`, `Describe` of a `RETURNING`-less `INSERT` is
  `t n Z(E)`. pglet answered `t n Z(E)` to **both**; it now answers 18.6's pair. The
  column-count reading had made the gate's own doc comment — *does this statement return
  data* — true of the code only where the two questions happened to coincide.

  **What the fixture harness can and cannot hold**, measured rather than assumed:
  `select/zero_column_relation_star.sql` is the guard, and only its **text** leg is one.
  A zero-column row is `{}` in the recorded JSON and two of them are `[{}, {}]`, so both
  legs *hold* the shape; but the binary leg decodes the `DataRow`s that arrived after a
  `NoData` exactly as it decodes the ones after a `RowDescription(0)`, so it was **green
  on the pre-fix build**. Only the text leg went red there (`rows: [], row_count: 0`
  against 18.6's two), and that is the leg the row loss was on. The extended `Describe`
  half and the aborted-block gate therefore have no fixture at all and are pinned by three
  raw-frame tests in `crates/pglet_server`'s `handlers::tests`, each verified red against
  the pre-fix build.

  **The extended leg's `NoData` was never this row's own rule but the engine's one
  descriptor rule**, whose criterion and the spellings that moved with it are
  `docs/declared_types.md`'s. Read the rule at `row_description`, not from whichever
  record you reached first.

  **Two residuals, neither of them this rule's**, both surfaced by closing it: 18.6's
  two at-least-one-column clauses, accepted empty here (row **63** — the `SELECT DISTINCT`
  member was found by running this row's own checklist against the new rule, not by
  looking for it), and the undumpable catalog (row **64**).

  **18.6's at-least-one-column clauses are accepted empty.** 18.6 has exactly
  **two** clauses that refuse an empty column list, and the pair is an enumeration read
  off its source rather than a guess: `analyze.c`'s
  `errmsg("RETURNING must have at least one column")` and `parse_clause.c`'s
  `errmsg("SELECT DISTINCT must have at least one column")` are the only two
  `must have at least one column` sites in the backend. Over the zero-column relation row
  58 builds, both fire and pglet has neither. Measured with a raw v3 client against both
  engines:

  | statement | 18.6 | pglet |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `INSERT INTO zc DEFAULT VALUES RETURNING *` | `E[42601]` | `1 t n 2 n C[INSERT 0 1] Z` |
  | `DELETE FROM zc RETURNING *` (simple leg) | `E[42601]` | `C[DELETE 3] Z` |
  | `UPDATE zc SET … RETURNING *` | `E[42601]` | `E[42703]` — refused on the `SET` target, so the clause is never reached |
  | `SELECT DISTINCT * FROM zc` | `E[42601]` | `1 t T[] 2 T[] D[] C[SELECT 1] Z` |

  **The two members fail differently, and only the first is about a lost clause.** The
  `DISTINCT` one answers a zero-column result set with one row — the dedup ran, over rows
  that are all equal because they have no columns — which is a coherent reply to a query
  18.6 will not accept. The `RETURNING` one answers **no result set at all**, so a client
  that asked for `RETURNING` cannot tell the statement apart from one that wrote no such
  clause.

  **And the `RETURNING` member is not one shape but two, only one of which is silent.**
  The `INSERT` and `DELETE` spellings are the silent pair. The `UPDATE` spelling has no
  accepted form at all over a zero-column relation, because there is no column to assign
  to: `UPDATE zc SET x = 1 RETURNING *` is `42703` here against 18.6's `42601` — **loud on
  both engines under different codes**, which is a different bucket from this row's silent
  headline. Two clauses of the one statement are independently wrong and the engines name
  different ones, so it is an error-order divergence, the family row 13 records. The
  control that keeps it off the `SET` target is the spelling with no `RETURNING` at all:
  `UPDATE zc SET x = 1` is `42703` on **both**.

  **The `RETURNING` member's mechanism is a fact lost at lowering, and it is what stops
  row 59's rule from covering it.** `Plan::Insert`/`Update`/`Delete` carry a
  `returning: Vec<Expr>` that `lower_returning` has already expanded, so a written
  `RETURNING *` over a relation with no columns arrives as an **empty list** —
  indistinguishable, in the plan, from a statement that wrote no clause.
  `returning_result_shape` therefore answers `NoResultSet` and is right to, given what it
  can see: a plan that cannot see the clause cannot decide it. The gate that could belongs
  at lowering, where the wildcard is still a wildcard.

  **Not fixed here, and the obvious placement is wrong.** Raising `42601` on any empty
  expansion would also fire on `DELETE FROM nosuchtable RETURNING *`, whose expansion is
  empty because the *target* does not exist — 18.6 answers `42P01` there, and pglet
  answers it at `Execute` (row 29). So the gate has to distinguish "the target resolved
  and has no columns" from "the target did not resolve", which is row 29's territory, and
  it is a new refusal with its own statement-level error-precedence consequences
  (`docs/ddl.md` § which error wins).

  **The controls, measured in the same run**, which bound this to the two clauses rather
  than to zero-column relations generally: `SELECT *`,
  `SELECT * FROM zc HAVING count(*) > 0`, `UNION ALL`, `EXCEPT`, a cross join of two
  zero-column relations, and `LIMIT 0` over one are **byte-identical** on the two engines
  (row 59's close), `ORDER BY 1` and
  `GROUP BY 1` are `42P10` on both, and `VALUES ()` is loud on both under different codes
  (18.6's `42601` syntax error against pglet's `0A000` not-implemented — a pre-existing
  parser gap, neither silent nor this row's).

  The accepted spellings, on the wire: `INSERT … DEFAULT VALUES RETURNING *` and
  `DELETE … RETURNING *` report `C(INSERT 0 1)` and `C(DELETE n)` with `n` to both `Describe`s,
  so nothing the client reads distinguishes them from a statement that wrote no such clause,
  while `SELECT DISTINCT *` answers `1 t T[] 2 T[] D[] C(SELECT 1)` — a zero-column result set
  carrying its one deduped row. The relation itself is built by `ALTER TABLE … DROP COLUMN`
  down to nothing, which is why `INSERT … DEFAULT VALUES` is the only `INSERT` spelling that
  reaches it. 18.6's two refusals arrive at parse analysis on both legs.

  **A zero-column relation dumps to something nothing can load.** Built through the
  engine's own accepted DDL over a `--data-dir` database —
  `CREATE TABLE zc (x INT, y TEXT)`, two rows, `DROP COLUMN` both — the relation is
  durable: after a restart `SELECT * FROM zc` answers two zero-column rows and
  `count(*)` answers `2`. The dump is not:

  ```
  CREATE TABLE zc (
  );

  COPY zc () FROM stdin;
  <blank>
  <blank>
  \.
  ```

  Loading it into **stock 18.6** accepts the `CREATE TABLE` — 18.6 allows an empty column
  list — and then fails on `COPY zc () FROM stdin;` with `syntax error at or near ")"`.
  Loading it back into **pglet** fails one statement earlier, on `CREATE TABLE zc (\n);`
  with `42601 syntax error: expected a column name, found end of input`, pglet's parser
  requiring at least one column. So the dump invariant is violated in **both**
  directions, by two independent defects, and each leg at the part of it whose statement
  fails. Into 18.6 it is the rows' part — `docs/sequences.md`'s property A, the `COPY`
  framing refused after the `CREATE TABLE` lands — through an emitter that renders an
  empty `COPY` column list. Back into pglet it is the catalog part, *any catalog pglet's
  own accepted statements build must dump to something that loads into stock Postgres and
  back into pglet*, the `CREATE TABLE` refused — through a parser that will not read what
  the emitter writes.

  **The oracle says what the emitter should write.** `pg_dump` of the same catalog emits
  `COPY zcprobe.zc  FROM stdin;` — no parenthesized list at all, two spaces where one
  would go — followed by one **blank** data line per row, so the rows survive. The fix on
  the emitter side is that narrow; the parser side is `CREATE TABLE t ()`, an independent
  gap (18.6 accepts it, pglet is `42601` — the reason the second engine leg fails).

  **Not fixed here**, and not row 59's residual either: row 59's rule is about describing
  a result set on the wire, and nothing about the dump path reads it. What connects them
  is only the object. **No guard**: `test:dump` and `test:pg-dump` build no zero-column
  relation — the same corpus blind spot row 58 named, one directory over.

  The header pglet's own parser refuses is `CREATE TABLE zc ()` once its newline is
  closed up — the statement 18.6 accepts and pglet is `42601` over, which is why the two
  engines fail one statement apart on the same file.

- **60 · A refusal lands at `Execute`, not `Parse` — or nowhere.** 18.6 resolves operators,
  functions and relations during parse analysis, so a statement it will refuse is refused
  by `exec_parse_message` — before any `Describe`, `Bind` or `Execute`. pglet's parser and
  plan-time binder refuse their own share there, but everything an **eval-time** gate
  decides survives `Parse`, is described with a full `RowDescription`, and — *where
  evaluation reaches the gate* — errors at `Execute`. That qualifier is load-bearing and
  is the second half of this bullet: where evaluation does not reach it, there is no error
  at all. Measured with a raw v3 client (`Parse`/`Describe(S)`/`Bind`/`Describe(P)`/
  `Execute`/`Sync`) against both engines over `t2(tx TEXT)` **holding one row** — the row
  count is part of the measurement, not scenery. The message
  streams say the phase without inference: pglet answers `1 t T 2 T E Z` for every member
  of the table below — `ParseComplete`, `ParameterDescription`, `RowDescription`,
  `BindComplete`, the portal's `RowDescription`, then the error — where 18.6 answers a
  bare `E Z` (and, for the `1/0` member alone, `1 t T E Z`, its error landing one message
  later, at `Bind`, because *18.6's* planner folds the division and pglet's does not —
  below):

  | statement | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT sum(tx) FROM t2` | `42883` at **`Execute`** | `42883` at `Parse` |
  | `SELECT sum(tx) FROM t2 WHERE false` | `42883` at **`Execute`** | `42883` at `Parse` |
  | `SELECT sum(tx) FROM t2 GROUP BY tx` | `42883` at **`Execute`** | `42883` at `Parse` |
  | `SELECT avg(tx) FROM t2` | `42883` at **`Execute`** | `42883` at `Parse` |
  | `SELECT sum('abc') FROM t2` | `42883` at **`Execute`** | `42725` at `Parse` |
  | `SELECT tx + 1 FROM t2` | `42804` at **`Execute`** | `42883` at `Parse` |
  | `SELECT tx FROM t2 WHERE sum(tx) > 1` | `0A000` at **`Execute`** | `42883` at `Parse` |
  | `SELECT 1 FROM nosuchtable` | `42P01` at **`Execute`** | `42P01` at `Parse` |
  | `SELECT 1/0` | `22012` at **`Execute`** | `22012` at `Bind` |

  **The other side of the divide is what keeps this a bounded row rather than "pglet
  refuses late".** Measured in the same run, these are `Parse` on *both* engines:
  `SELEC 1` (`42601`), `SELECT 'x'::int` (`22P02`), `SELECT nosuchcol FROM t2` (`42703`),
  `SELECT tx FROM t2 a, t2 b` (`42702`), `SELECT tx::nosuchtype FROM t2` (`42704`),
  `SELECT tx, count(*) FROM t2` (`42803`), and `SELECT nosuchfn(tx) FROM t2` (pglet's own
  `0A000`). **No derivation of *which* gate decides survives, so the divide is stated as
  membership and nothing else.** Five general sentences have now been falsified in this
  row — the four that tried to summarize *which spellings are silenced* (below), and one
  here that tried to summarize *which gate decides*, putting the operand/legality gates
  wholesale on the `Execute` side. `planner/legality.rs` has members on **both**. Five of
  its gates are `42883` at `Parse` on both engines — `SELECT a LIKE 'x' FROM r1`
  (`like_legality`), `SELECT tx @> tx FROM t2` (`containment_legality`),
  `SELECT a || a FROM r1` (`concat_legality`), `SELECT a -> 'k' FROM r1`
  (`json_get_legality`) and `SELECT starts_with(a,'x') FROM r1`
  (`starts_with_legality`), which `check_expr_semantics` moved to plan time (`docs/compatibility.md`,
  the `COALESCE`/`CASE` common-types row) — while the same file's `aggregate_legality` is
  an `Execute`-side member this row records, and the `tx + 1` control's `42804` is raised
  by neither, at a per-row arithmetic gate in `executor/expr/arithmetic.rs`. The divide
  tracks neither the rulebook nor any one file. Nor do the row's silencers reach the plan-time
  five: the `LIKE` member is `42883` at `Parse` on both engines under every axis probed
  — an empty table, `WHERE false`, `LIMIT 0`, a never-taken `CASE` arm, a NULL operand,
  an unreferenced CTE, an empty inner relation, a subquery an empty outer scan never runs,
  and the `WHERE false AND (…)` reverse spelling. So the row's claim is the measured
  membership of the two tables above, member by member, and a gate neither names is
  unprobed rather than placed.

  **A plan-time refusal elsewhere in the statement outranks an eval-time one — loud,
  wrong code.** 18.6 transforms a target list in order, so the first entry's error is
  the statement's. Here an entry whose gate waits for a row loses to a later entry whose
  gate does not: over `t(tx TEXT)` and `w(f FLOAT8, i INT)`, `SELECT nullif(tx, w.f +
  0), least(tx, w.i * 1) FROM t, w` is `42804 LEAST types text and integer cannot be
  matched` here and `42883 operator does not exist: text = double precision` there —
  `nullif`'s operand gate reads no computed operand, so its refusal is the evaluation's,
  and `least`'s is the fold gate's at plan time. The same pair over a derived relation's
  column — `(SELECT i::text AS x FROM t) q`, a `boolean` constant's, a `max(tx)`'s — was
  `42883` on both while such a column's type could not be certain, the fold then being
  read at the written reach and raising nothing (rows 2 and 54), and is the `42804` now.
  The same holds inside one expression, and beside an aggregate whose literal is converted:
  over `k (i INT, tx TEXT)`, `SELECT (tx + 1) IS NULL OR i > 'x' FROM k`, `SELECT
  count(tx + 1) > 'x' FROM k` and `SELECT count(-tx) > 'x' FROM k` are `22P02 invalid input
  syntax for type …: "x"` here and `42883 operator does not exist: text + integer`
  (`- text`) there — the literal read at the column's or the aggregate's type at plan time,
  the operand's own refusal waiting for a row.

  **Not row 58's.** Every line in both tables reproduces identically — same code, same
  message, same phase — on the pre- and post-deletion builds of that row, and **none** of
  them involves a zero-column relation. What row 58's close changed is only the
  **membership**: three shapes that used to answer a silent NULL row now raise `42883`,
  and a newly-loud refusal inherits this phase placement rather than introducing it.

  **Where evaluation never reaches the gate, the divergence is not late but *absent* —
  no error at all, on either leg.** This is the headline category of this file. Two of the
  ways in are stated first, because they were measured first and on the pre-deletion build
  as well as the current one — over `r1 (a INT)` and `t2 (tx TEXT)`, on **both** legs,
  every silent line below being `T C Z` on the simple leg too. **More ways in follow them**
  — the enumeration after this pair names each; what is listed is what has been probed,
  never a bound:

  - **A subquery the outer scan never runs.** With `r1` **empty**, every gate family in
    the table above answers `1 t T 2 T C Z` — `CommandComplete(SELECT 0)`, no `E` — when
    it sits inside one: `a IN (SELECT 1 FROM no_such_table)`,
    `a::text IN (SELECT sum(tx) FROM t2)`, `a IN (SELECT tx + 1 FROM t2)`,
    `a IN (SELECT 1/0)`, `EXISTS (SELECT sum(tx) FROM t2)`, the scalar-subquery spelling
    `SELECT (SELECT sum(tx) FROM t2) FROM r1`, and the three remaining families
    (`IN (SELECT sum('abc') FROM t2)`, `EXISTS (SELECT tx FROM t2 WHERE sum(tx) > 1)`,
    `IN (SELECT sum(tx) FROM t2 GROUP BY tx)`). Nine for nine. Put **one** row in `r1` and
    each becomes the table's own `1 t T 2 T E Z` at `Execute` — `42P01`, `42883`, `42804`,
    `22012`, `42883`, `42883`, `42883`, `0A000`, `42883` — while 18.6 refuses all nine at
    `Parse` (the `1/0` member at `Bind`, `1 t T E Z`) whatever `r1` holds, under the same
    codes bar `sum('abc')`'s, which is `42725` there as in the table above. Row 56 already
    records this mechanism for a different leaf — *a statement whose evaluation never
    reaches the leaf* — so the counterexample was one row away.
  - **An empty table under the gate's own statement.** Two of the table's own lines go
    silent too, with `t2` holding **zero** rows: `SELECT tx + 1 FROM t2` and `SELECT tx
    FROM t2 WHERE sum(tx) > 1` each answer `SELECT 0` with no error, where 18.6 is `42883`
    at `Parse` at every row count. The table's other lines stay loud over an empty `t2` —
    `SELECT sum(tx) FROM t2 GROUP BY tx` among them, which answered `SELECT 0` too until an
    aggregate's operand type was checked for the statement rather than for each group
    (row 89). A function the argument's type has no
    signature for is a member too, through the npm package's plain `query` (the simple
    path): over an empty `t (id INT, name TEXT)`, `SELECT lower(id) FROM t` answers no row
    here where 18.6 is `42883 function lower(integer) does not exist`; with a row in `t`
    pglet raises `42883` too.

  **What decides which is which is row 56's rule, and this row does not re-derive it.**
  *Evaluation reaches the expression, or it does not* — row 56 states that in full, down
  to which plan node evaluates what and how often, and its query-position `DEFAULT`/`$N`
  leaf is the same mechanism under a different gate. Every general sentence written *here* to
  summarize that rule over this row's members has been falsified by a later
  measurement, so what follows is an **enumeration of measured silencers** rather
  than another.

  Each line is silent on **both** pglet legs — the extended stream is `1 t T 2 T C Z`, or
  the same with `D` rows before the `C` where a row is projected, and the simple leg
  answers those rows or `SELECT 0` with no `ERROR` — against 18.6's refusal, whose phase
  column is the extended leg's as everywhere in this row. Over `t2 (tx TEXT)` holding
  **one** row, `r1 (a INT)` holding three, and `e2 (ex TEXT)` empty, unless the line says
  otherwise.

  | silencer | statement (silent here) | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | the gate's own table is **empty** | `SELECT tx + 1 FROM t2`, `SELECT tx FROM t2 WHERE sum(tx) > 1`, `SELECT 1/0 FROM t2` | `42883`, `42883` at `Parse`; `22012` at `Bind` |
  | `WHERE false` | `SELECT tx + 1 FROM t2 WHERE false`, `SELECT 1/0 FROM t2 WHERE false` | `42883` at `Parse`; `22012` at `Bind` |
  | a **`HAVING`** that rejects the group | `SELECT 1/0 FROM t2 HAVING false` | `22012` at `Bind` |
  | a **NULL** operand, the row still projected | `SELECT tx + 1 FROM t2`, with the single row's `tx` **IS NULL** | `42883` at `Parse` |
  | a never-taken **`CASE`** arm, or a `COALESCE` that short-circuits | `SELECT CASE WHEN false THEN tx + 1 ELSE 0 END FROM t2`; `SELECT COALESCE(0, tx + 1) FROM t2`; the arm holding `(SELECT sum(tx) FROM t2)::int`, or `(SELECT 1 FROM nosuchtable)` | `42883`, `42883`, `42883`, `42P01` at `Parse` |
  | …the same, with an outer column deciding the arm | `SELECT CASE WHEN a < 0 THEN (SELECT sum(tx) FROM t2) ELSE NULL END FROM r1` — three rows here | `42883` at `Parse` |
  | an **`AND` / `OR`** whose left operand decides it | `SELECT count(*) FROM t2 WHERE false AND tx + 1 > 0`; over `WHERE tx = 'y' AND …`, each of `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM nosuchtable)`, `sum(1) > 0`, `sum(tx) > 0`, `1/0 = 0`; over `WHERE tx = 'x' OR …`, `lower(1) = 'a'` and `(SELECT tx + 1 FROM t2) > 0` | `42883`, `42P01`, `42803`, `42883` at `Parse`; `22012` at `Bind`; `42883`, `42883` at `Parse` |
  | an **unreferenced CTE** | `WITH c AS (SELECT 1 FROM nosuchtable) SELECT 1`, and the same with a `SELECT sum(tx) FROM t2` or `SELECT tx + 1 FROM t2` body | `42P01`, `42883`, `42883` at `Parse` |
  | an **empty inner** relation under a subquery the outer scan *does* run | `SELECT (SELECT ex + 1 FROM e2 LIMIT 1) FROM r1` and `SELECT (SELECT 1/0 FROM e2 LIMIT 1) FROM r1` — three rows each here; `SELECT 1 FROM r1 WHERE EXISTS (SELECT ex + 1 FROM e2)` | `42883` at `Parse`; `22012` at `Bind`; `42883` at `Parse` |
  | an **empty outer** scan over a subquery | the nine families in the bullet above, nine for nine | as recorded there |

  **An aggregate's operand type left the row-count lines, for a column or literal
  operand.** A grouping checks such an aggregate's operand type once for the statement,
  ahead of every group (row 89), so
  `SELECT sum(tx) FROM t2 GROUP BY tx` over an empty `t2`, `SELECT sum(tx) FROM t2 HAVING
  false` and its `avg(tx)` spelling are `42883` here as there — at `Execute` here — and
  the `sum('abc')` spelling is `42883` against 18.6's `42725`; each answered `SELECT 0`
  before. The check reads a type that needs no evaluation, so an argument whose type or
  refusal only evaluation shows is still silent over no group: over an empty `e (a INT,
  t TEXT)`, `SELECT sum(upper(a)) FROM e GROUP BY a` and `SELECT max(t::jsonb) FROM e
  GROUP BY a` answer no row where 18.6 is `42883` — and so does a kept aggregate over a
  typed constant, which is a cast: `SELECT sum(date '2020-01-01') FROM e GROUP BY a` and
  its `sum(text 'abc')` spelling (row 89 has the rest).

  **The controls that bound it**, measured in the same run and loud here as well as
  there. `LIMIT 0` silences **nothing** it was tried on — `SELECT sum(tx) FROM t2 LIMIT 0`
  is `42883`, `SELECT tx + 1 FROM t2 LIMIT 0` is `42804` and `SELECT 1/0 FROM t2 LIMIT 0`
  is `22012`, each at `Execute` — and the `OFFSET 5` spelling of all three is loud too, as
  is `SELECT sum(tx) FROM t2 HAVING true`.
  The `AND` / `OR` line was a control here, `42804` for `WHERE false AND tx + 1 > 0` and
  its `OR` spelling, until row 172's close made the connectives stop at a deciding left
  operand; each statement on that line was loud before it (`42804`, `42P01`, `0A000`,
  `0A000`, `22012`, `42883`, `42804` in the line's order), and each is silent on both
  legs now — the extended one measured through psql's `\bind`, without the stream
  letters. The same stop reaches a `HAVING`: over `sa (id INT, g INT)` holding two rows of
  one group, `HAVING count(*) = 99 AND max(id) + 'x' > 0` keeps no group, **silently**,
  against 18.6's `22P02`, where it was `42804` here. The line holds members, not the
  family's bound — any refusal pglet defers to evaluation joins it under a deciding left
  operand: `WHERE id = 99 AND 'nosuch'::regclass IS NOT NULL` (`42P01` on both engines
  before, so a matching answer went silent) and `WHERE id = 99 AND row_number() OVER () >
  0` (18.6's `42P20`) count `0` here too, measured over an unindexed `id` (row 172's *What
  it cost*).
  The **relation lookup** survives the row-count silencers over its own statement —
  `SELECT 1 FROM nosuchtable` under `WHERE false`, `LIMIT 0` or `HAVING false` is `42P01`
  at `Execute` (all three re-measured) — and goes silent under **five** of the
  reachability ones: a never-taken `CASE` arm, an unreferenced CTE, a `COALESCE` that
  short-circuits, an `AND` / `OR` its left operand decides, and a subquery an empty outer
  scan never runs (over a **non**-empty
  `r1`, `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM nosuchtable2)` is loud, `42P01` at `Execute`). Which of
  this table's rows reach a missing relation and which do not is enumerated in row 29,
  member by member, together with the `HAVING`-subquery spelling that takes a pglet gate's
  own `0A000` in place of the lookup; that enumeration is not derivable from this table
  and is not repeated here. A CTE that
  *is* referenced is loud: `WITH c AS (SELECT sum(tx) AS s FROM t2) SELECT s FROM c` is
  `42883`, at `Execute` here and `Parse` there. And two neighbouring spellings are **not**
  divergences at all, because 18.6 is silent too —
  `SELECT CASE WHEN false THEN 1/0 ELSE 0 END FROM t2` and `WITH c AS (SELECT 1/0)
  SELECT 1` project a row on both engines, since 18.6's fold does not reach into an
  untaken arm or an unreferenced body either.

  **`1/0` is not folded here**, only on 18.6.
  The fold is 18.6's, performed during planning — which is the whole reason that one
  member lands at 18.6's `Bind` rather than its `Parse`. pglet evaluates the division as
  an ordinary **per-row projection gate**, so it behaves like every other per-row member:
  the three row-count silencers in the table reach it (an empty `t2`, `WHERE false`, a
  `HAVING` that rejects the group) and the controls do not (`SELECT 1/0 FROM t2 LIMIT 0`
  and the `OFFSET 5` spelling are `22012` at `Execute`). The table's `SELECT 1/0` is loud
  only because a FROM-less select has exactly one row: `SELECT 1/0 FROM t2` over an empty
  `t2` is `SELECT 0` under the same `int4` `RowDescription`.

  **A constant in a branch evaluation does not take is a member too, in a grouping query
  as in any other.** 18.6's planner folds the constants of every branch it keeps, so a
  failing one raises there though no row reaches it; here it is evaluated where the walk
  reaches it and nowhere else. Over `u (a, b)` holding `(1, 10)` and `(2,
  0)`: `SELECT CASE WHEN a > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 1/0 END FROM u`, `SELECT coalesce(a, 1/0) FROM
  u`, `SELECT a > 0 OR 1/0 > 0 FROM u` and `SELECT a FROM u WHERE a > 0 OR 1/0 > 0` answer
  here and are `22012` there, **silently**. A grouping query's expressions take the same
  walk (row 89) and are the same members: `SELECT a, CASE WHEN a > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 1/0 END
  FROM u GROUP BY a`, `SELECT coalesce(count(*), 1/0) FROM u`, `SELECT count(*) > 0 OR 1/0
  > 0 FROM u` and `SELECT CASE WHEN count(*) > 0 THEN 2 WHEN 1/0 > 0 THEN 3 END FROM u`
  answer here and are `22012` there, and so does a constant in an aggregate's argument
  that no row reaches — `SELECT sum(1/0) FROM u WHERE false` is `NULL` here. A failing
  constant item after a matching one in an `IN` list, which 18.6 folds with its sibling
  constants, is one more: `SELECT 1 IN (1, 1/0)` and `SELECT max(a) IN (2, 1/0) FROM u`
  are `t` here and `22012` there. The neighbours 18.6 answers too are not members: `SELECT
  a, CASE WHEN length('abc') = 3 THEN 1 ELSE 1/0 END FROM u GROUP BY a` is `1` per group on
  both, its planner having folded the `CASE`, and `SELECT EXISTS (SELECT 1/0 FROM e GROUP
  BY a)` over an empty `e` is `f` on both (`select/agg_expr_constant_in_unreached_branch.sql`,
  `select/agg_expr_constant_in_empty_grouping.sql`).

  **The member that ran the other way closed with row 172.**
  `SELECT 1 FROM t2 WHERE false AND (SELECT 1/0) > 0` was `22012` at `Execute` here and
  **no error at all** on 18.6, which answers `1 t T 2 T C Z`, `SELECT 0`: 18.6's
  `simplify_and_arguments` walks the conjunction left to right and returns as soon as an
  argument const-simplifies to `false`, so the division is never const-simplified at all,
  while `simplify_or_arguments` *drops* a constant `false` and keeps scanning, which is
  why the `OR` spelling is loud there (`22012`, at `Bind`). pglet's `AND` now stops at the
  `false` too, so both engines answer no row, and the un-parenthesized `WHERE false AND
  1/0 > 0` with it; the `OR` spelling is `22012` on both (each measured on both legs, the
  extended one through psql's `\bind`). The row records no other member running that way.

  The same posture as the divide above: what is stated is which spellings were probed and
  what each answered, so a spelling none of these lists names is **unprobed** rather than
  covered.

  **Six prose homes carry members of this row, not one — the enumeration has gone stale
  three times, so re-run it rather than inheriting it.** The criterion that makes a re-run
  repeatable: a passage is a **home** when it asserts this row's phase placement for
  members of its own, so that a change to the measurement would leave it stating a false
  phase; a passage that only names row 60 as the record is a cross-reference. Three are in
  this file. **Row 56's** § *On the extended leg the loud half is loud only at `Execute`*
  is one, stated there for the query-position `DEFAULT`/`$N` leaf alone; **row 29's**
  relation half is a second — this row's `FROM nosuchtable` member under a wider
  projection, and both of this row's directions for it: the `SELECT * FROM no_such_table`
  sentence for the late half, and its enumeration of reachability-silenced spellings
  (an unreferenced CTE, a never-taken `CASE` arm, a short-circuiting `COALESCE`, an `AND`
  / `OR` its left operand decides, a subquery an empty outer scan never runs — the
  silencers of this row's that reach a
  missing relation, and not all of them, which is why that passage enumerates rather than
  delegating here) for the absent half (its ``UPDATE … SET nosuchcol`` sentence *used* to
  be a
  third before that split closed; see row 29 for the re-measurement); and **row 58's**
  close is a third, asserting `Execute`-rather-than-`Parse` for three newly-loud shapes of
  its own — re-measured `1 t T 2 T E Z`, `42883` at `Execute` here against `Parse` there,
  for the `sum(m)`, `avg(m)` and `WITH` spellings alike. Three are outside it:
  `docs/ddl.md` § *Which error wins is part of the contract* states the divide under
  **Between protocol phases**; `dispatch`'s `FrontendMessage::Parse` arm in
  `crates/pglet_server/src/handlers.rs` states which resolution failures raise there and
  which defer, at the handler that raises them; and the header of
  `tests/fixtures/select/zero_column_relation_sum_over_text_loud.sql` states the phase its
  own `@expect-error` cannot compare. **Row 59 is not a home**, though it was counted as
  one: its subject is a `NoData` descriptor over a statement that *succeeds* on both legs,
  so nothing in it goes stale if this row's placement moves — a neighbour on the `NoData`
  shape, cited as such below. Row 57 was the twin in the other direction until its close:
  the phase 18.6 refuses at is `Parse`, and the verdict pglet lacked was `42P18`. The consequence a
  driver sees is the same in all six homes: a prepare-only client is told the statement is
  fine.

  **The stream is `1 t T 2 T E Z` for the members that describe a row**, and the shape
  cell is that narrow deliberately: a member that returns **no result set** answers
  `1 t n 2 n E Z` instead — **`NoData`** to both `Describe`s, which a driver reads as
  *returns no rows*. That is `row_description`'s
  one rule and not a property of the missing relation. **Re-measured after row 59's
  close**, which moved that rule off the column count: what answers `n` here is a DML
  with no `RETURNING` clause — `INSERT INTO nosuchtable VALUES (1)`,
  `UPDATE nosuchtable SET x = 1`, `DELETE FROM nosuchtable` — and bare
  `SELECT * FROM nosuchtable`, once the other spelling of it, is now an **empty**
  `RowDescription`, `1 t T[] 2 T[] E Z`. Put a relation whose columns
  the `*` can expand into the same `FROM` and the descriptor fills rather than appears —
  `SELECT * FROM rz, nosuchtable` over `rz (a INT, b TEXT)` is `1 t T 2 T E Z`, describing
  `rz`'s own columns, while the same statement over a **zero-column** `rz` describes
  `T[]`, the missing relation unchanged; the two differ in width and not in kind, which
  is the sentence this paragraph used to get wrong. Row 29 enumerates the spellings and
  the routes; row 59 recorded the same rule over a relation that **exists** and nothing
  missing at all, and is closed.
  `SELECT 1 FROM nosuchtable`, the spelling the table names, is `1 t T 2 T E Z`.

  Not fixed here — moving these gates to plan time is an engine change with its own error
  precedence consequences (`docs/ddl.md` § which error wins), and this row is the record
  that the phase is measured.

  **Two spellings this row's tables hold only in longer form.** The aggregate-operand gate
  reaches it through its derived-table and `GROUP BY` spellings as well as the bare one, and
  the third direction — pglet loud where 18.6 is silent — is the single member
  `WHERE false AND (SELECT 1/0) > 0`, `22012` at `Execute` here against no error there.
- **61 · A `RETURNING`-less data-modifying CTE is referenced.** Postgres treats a
  `WITH c AS (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE …)` body with no `RETURNING` as producing **no
  relation the outer query may name**: referencing `c` is `0A000 WITH query "c" does not
  have a RETURNING clause`, raised during parse analysis, and the statement — write
  included — never runs. pglet accepts it, runs the write, and hands the reference a
  **zero-column** relation. Measured with a raw v3 client over `t3 (v INT)`, on both legs
  and against both engines; the phase column is the **extended** leg's — 18.6 answers a
  bare `E Z` with no `ParseComplete`, and the simple leg is one phase and so says nothing
  about placement:

  | statement | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `WITH c AS (INSERT INTO t3 VALUES (9)) SELECT max('abc') FROM c` | one row, `max` = NULL; `t3` then holds `(9)` | `0A000` at `Parse`; `t3` unchanged |
  | `WITH c AS (UPDATE t3 SET v = v) SELECT max('abc') FROM c` | one row, `max` = NULL | `0A000` at `Parse` |
  | `WITH c AS (DELETE FROM t3 WHERE false) SELECT max('abc') FROM c` | one row, `max` = NULL | `0A000` at `Parse` |

  The write is the part worth stating plainly: after the first statement `SELECT count(*),
  sum(v) FROM t3` is `1, 9` here and `0, NULL` there. So this is not only an
  over-acceptance of a query shape — it is a **write 18.6 does not perform**, with no
  error on either side of the wire to say so.

  **The `SELECT *` spelling of the outer query moved with row 59's close**, so the table's
  `max('abc')` evidence no longer shows the whole of what the wire carries: the zero-column
  relation is now *described* as one. Re-measured, `WITH c AS (INSERT INTO t3 VALUES (8))
  SELECT * FROM c` is `1 t T[] 2 T[] C(SELECT 0) Z` here — an empty `RowDescription` and a
  zero-row `SELECT 0` — where it was a bare `C(SELECT 0)` under `NoData` before, and the
  `UPDATE` and `DELETE` body spellings measure identically. 18.6 refuses all three with the
  same `0A000` at `Parse` it refuses the `max('abc')` spellings with, so the divergence's
  polarity is unchanged and only pglet's descriptor moved.

  The engine's own parser comment names this as Postgres's behavior
  (`crates/pglet_sql/src/parser/select.rs`, `parse_cte_body`), which is where the
  acceptance came from; that comment is corrected in place rather than left as the
  justification. **Not fixed here** — the fix is a plan-time refusal with its own error
  precedence consequences, and this row is the record that it is measured.

  This is the second of row 58's two routes to a zero-column relation, and it is how that
  route was found: row 58's prose defined the shape as `ALTER TABLE … DROP COLUMN` down to
  nothing, "which both engines accept", in six places at once — a bound belonging to that
  one spelling, written as though it bounded the class. The transferable half is the same
  one row 58 already carries in the other direction: **a claim about what builds a shape
  is only as wide as the spellings someone enumerated**, and here the widening turned up an
  edge of its own.

  No fixture holds it: pglet answers where 18.6 errors, so `@expect-error` cannot hold it
  and a value expectation would be red. Nothing in the corpus issues the shape either —
  all nine data-modifying CTE bodies in `tests/fixtures/` carry `RETURNING` (the scan is
  in row 58's bullet).
- **62 · A prepared statement's result type is not revalidated against the DDL that
  changed it.** Postgres's plancache re-analyzes a statement whose schema moved under it
  and then **compares the result descriptor to the one it already published**:
  `RevalidateCachedQuery` runs `PlanCacheComputeResultDesc` over the new target list and,
  where a `fixed_result` source's new descriptor is not `equalRowTypes` with the old,
  raises `0A000 cached plan must not change result type` — at the `Describe` and again at
  the `Bind`, so a client can never decode rows against a descriptor that no longer
  describes them. The branch just above that comparison is the one this row's agreeing
  control lands in: two descriptors that are both absent are "OK, doesn't return tuples",
  which is why a statement that returns **no result set** is exempt on both engines. pglet
  has no such comparison at all. `describe_result_shape` either reuses a cached plan
  whose generation still matches or re-plans the SQL, and **nothing compares the new shape
  to the old**: a re-plan that fails answers `NoResultSet`, and a re-plan that succeeds
  against a different shape is simply answered. Measured with a raw v3 client, extended
  protocol only, over `k (a INT, c INT)` holding `(1,10),(2,20)`, with
  `ALTER TABLE k DROP COLUMN a` run between the `Parse` and the row below. Both engines
  pass `Parse` and describe the original shape first, which is what makes this its own row
  rather than a member of 29, 43 or 60:

  | after the DDL | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | re-`Describe` the prepared `SELECT a FROM k` | `t n Z` — **`NoData`** | `42703` at the `Describe` |
  | `Bind` + `Execute` it | `BindComplete`, then `42703` at **`Execute`** | `42703` at `Bind` |
  | re-`Describe` the prepared `SELECT * FROM k` | `T[c:int4]` — the **new** shape | `0A000 cached plan must not change result type` |
  | `Bind` + `Execute` it, **no re-`Describe`** | `BindComplete`, two one-field `DataRow`s, `SELECT 2` | `0A000` at `Bind` |

  The two kinds are the two halves of that table. The `SELECT a FROM k` half is **loud but
  late** — the right SQLSTATE, one or two phases after 18.6's — and it is
  `describe_result_shape`'s swallowed `Err` seen from the client's side. *Late* bounds
  when the code arrives and not what the lateness costs: inside a transaction block this
  same half leaves the block **live** where 18.6 has already aborted it, so the statements
  the client sends in the gap run here and commit, and are discarded there — the
  transaction-block member below. The
  `SELECT *` half is **silent**, and the last row is why it is worth a row of its own:
  **no re-`Describe` is needed to reach it.** A client that prepared a two-column
  statement, read its two-column `RowDescription`, and then merely `Bind`s and `Execute`s
  is handed `DataRow`s carrying **one** field — verified by decoding the field count off
  the wire: `2` in the descriptor the client holds, `1` in each row it receives, no
  `ErrorResponse` anywhere. Whatever that client does with the second column is its own
  affair; the protocol gave it no signal.

  **The class bounds, measured in the same runs.** `DROP COLUMN` is not the only DDL that
  reaches it: `ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN z TEXT` under a prepared `SELECT *` re-describes
  `T[c:int4, z:text]` and answers two rows here against 18.6's `0A000`, and a
  `DROP TABLE` followed by re-`CREATE` of the **same name** with a different shape
  re-describes the new columns under the **new** relation OID and answers the new table's
  rows, again against `0A000` — pglet's prepared statement follows the name, and the OID
  in the `RowDescription` changes underneath a client that never re-read it. Two of
  18.6's other routes into the same refusal are **unreachable** here: `ALTER TABLE …
  RENAME COLUMN` and `ALTER COLUMN … TYPE` are both `0A000 not implemented` in pglet, so
  no prepared statement can be aged by either. A DDL, arrangement or protocol phase none
  of the paragraphs here names is **unprobed rather than converging** — these are the
  measured members, not the class's edge.

  **Inside a transaction block the divergence upgrades from a wire shape to a divergent
  commit.** Everything above is autocommit, where the divergence is confined to what the
  client is handed. In a block 18.6's refusal is also an **abort**, and pglet's non-refusal also
  leaves the block **live** — so the two engines end the block having kept different work.
  Measured over `r4w (a INT, cc INT)` holding `(1,10),(2,20)`, prepared
  `SELECT * FROM r4w`, then in **one** connection, with
  `ALTER TABLE r4w DROP COLUMN a` run in-block (both engines accept it, `C[ALTER TABLE]`,
  block still live):

  | next, in the same block | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | re-`Describe` the prepared `SELECT * FROM r4w` | `t T[cc:int4]` — the new shape — and `Z[T]`, still in-transaction | `t E[0A000] Z[E]` — the block is **aborted** |
  | `Bind` + `Execute` it | `2 D(1) D(1) C[SELECT 2] Z[T]` | `E[25P02] Z[E]` |
  | `INSERT INTO r4w VALUES (777)` | `C[INSERT 0 1] Z[T]` | `E[25P02] Z[E]` |
  | `COMMIT` | `C[COMMIT]` | **`C[ROLLBACK]`** |
  | the table afterwards | one column, `10`, `20`, `777` | two columns, `(1,10)`, `(2,20)` |

  The DDL **and** the `INSERT` survive here and are both discarded there, so what the gap
  admits is **arbitrary committed work** and not only mis-decoded `DataRow`s. The `INSERT`
  is not what carries it: the shortest spelling — `BEGIN`, the drop, the re-`Describe`,
  `COMMIT`, nothing else — still commits the column drop here against 18.6's `C[ROLLBACK]`
  and an untouched two-column table. The **loud** half has the same twin: prepared
  `SELECT a FROM r4w` re-`Describe`d in the block is `t n Z[T]` here against
  `t E[42703] Z[E]` there, and the `INSERT` after it commits here where 18.6 is already
  `25P02`.

  **No `Describe` is needed to reach it, which is the autocommit headline's property over
  again.** Dropping the re-`Describe` and merely `Bind`ing and `Execute`ing the silent
  half in the block measures the whole divergence: `2 D(1) D(1) C[SELECT 2] Z[T]` and a
  committed block here, `E[0A000] Z[E]` and `C[ROLLBACK]` there. A bare `Bind` — no
  `Execute`, no `Describe` — is enough on its own: `2 Z[T]` and a committed block here,
  `E[0A000] Z[E]` and `C[ROLLBACK]` there. So the re-`Describe` is not what 18.6's abort
  needs — a re-`Describe`, a `Bind` and a `Bind` + `Execute` each reach it, and a use of
  the statement none of those three names is unprobed. What the abort **does** need is
  some use of the statement: the DDL alone aborts nothing, and the
  control that runs the same block without touching the statement at all commits on both
  engines and leaves the same one-column three-row table. **The loud half reaches it
  without a `Describe` too, and what bounds it there is stopping short of `Execute`.**
  Over `r5u (a INT, cc INT)` under prepared `SELECT a FROM r5u`, the drop run in-block: a
  bare `Bind` is `2 Z[T]` here — block live, the following `INSERT` committed,
  `C[COMMIT]`, a one-column `10, 20, 777` — against `E[42703] Z[E]`, `25P02`,
  `C[ROLLBACK]` and an untouched two-column table there, and a bare `Bind` then a portal
  `Describe` (`n Z[T]`) commits the same way. Any route that reaches `Execute` converges
  the two instead, pglet's own `42703` aborting this block as well: `Bind` + `Execute`
  (`2 E[42703] Z[E]`), `Bind` + portal `Describe` + `Execute` (`2 n E[42703] Z[E]`), and a
  bare `Bind` whose `Execute` arrives in a later exchange each end `C[ROLLBACK]` on both
  with the same post-state. So the loud half diverges on all three of those routes, not
  on the `Describe` route alone, and the `Execute` is what ends it.

  **An empty result silences nothing, and a two-to-zero-column transition is not the
  exempt one.** `SELECT * FROM r4q LIMIT 0` over an **empty** two-column table, the drop
  run under it, re-describes the new one-column shape and answers `C[SELECT 0]` here with
  the block live and the following `INSERT` committed, against 18.6's `0A000` and
  `C[ROLLBACK]` — no row ever crosses the wire and the committed states still diverge.
  And dropping a table's **last** column ages the statement into a **zero-column result
  set**, which is *not* `RevalidateCachedQuery`'s "both absent" exemption (only two absent
  descriptors are): 18.6 raises `0A000` and aborts, while pglet re-describes the new shape
  and then answers two **zero-field** `DataRow`s, committing an `INSERT … DEFAULT VALUES`
  after them. **Re-measured after row 59's close**, over `k2 (a INT, c INT)` holding one
  row with both columns dropped under prepared `SELECT * FROM k2`: the re-`Describe` is
  `t(0) T(0) Z` here (it was `t(0)` **`n`** `Z`) against 18.6's `t(0) E[0A000] Z`, and the
  `Bind` + portal `Describe` + `Execute` is `2 T(0) D(0) C[SELECT 1] Z` (it was
  `2 n D(0) …`) against 18.6's bare `E[0A000] Z`. **The divergence did not move — its
  shape did**, and the sentence it falsifies is this row's own: this spelling used to be
  "the silent kind wearing the loud kind's `NoData`", and it no longer wears it. Across
  the DDL shapes measured here the two halves are told apart by whether the re-plan
  failed, and never by the `Describe` reply — which is now true for a second reason as
  well, the reply having stopped depending on the surviving column count at all. A shape outside them
  parts the two the other way: a `DROP TABLE` with no re-`CREATE`, under prepared
  `SELECT * FROM k5, j5`, re-plans **successfully** — pglet re-describes the surviving
  `T[a:int4, c:int4]`, the silent criterion — and is then loud at `Execute` with `42P01`,
  where 18.6 raises that `42P01` at the re-`Describe` already. In a block it is a divergent
  commit of its own, bounded the way the loud half is — by stopping short of `Execute`.
  Over a re-`Describe` or a bare `Bind`, pglet keeps the `DROP TABLE` and commits an
  `INSERT` after it while 18.6 raises its `42P01` at that first use and `C[ROLLBACK]`s
  both, leaving `j5` standing; add the `Execute` and the two converge instead, pglet's own
  `42P01` (`2 E[42P01] Z[E]`) aborting this block as well — `25P02`, `C[ROLLBACK]`, and
  `j5` standing on both. Row 59 is the record for a zero-column relation that exists
  already.

  **What the member does and does not need.** Rolling the block back converges the two —
  `ROLLBACK` in place of `COMMIT` discards
  everything on both, leaving the divergence on the wire only, and so does a `SAVEPOINT`
  taken before the DDL and rolled back to, after which **both** engines re-describe the
  original two-column shape again — 18.6's aborted block recovers with it — and commit the
  same rows. The prepared statement need not predate the block (preparing it inside,
  before the DDL, measures the same), and the DDL need not be on the same connection,
  though what diverges there is **narrower**: the second connection's DDL autocommits and
  stands on **both** engines, so the drop survives either way and only the block's own
  work splits — pglet's block stays live through the re-`Describe` and commits its
  `INSERT` (three rows), where 18.6's re-`Describe` is `0A000`, the `INSERT` `25P02` and
  the `COMMIT` `C[ROLLBACK]` (two rows), each over the same one-column table. That
  arrangement is reachable on 18.6 only while the block has not yet read the table, since
  the DDL otherwise waits on the block's lock, one pglet takes none of. Each DDL the bounds
  above **reach** carries the member — `ADD COLUMN z TEXT` re-describes `T[a, cc, z]` and
  answers three-field rows in-block, and a `DROP TABLE` + re-`CREATE` inside the block
  re-describes and answers the **new** table's rows, each against `0A000` and an aborted
  block — and the two the bounds call unreachable stay unreachable in a block too, pglet's
  `0A000 not implemented` for `RENAME COLUMN` aborting its own block while 18.6 accepts
  the rename and then aborts *its* block on the re-`Describe`, so that arrangement ends
  `C[ROLLBACK]` with the same post-state on both. The cross-connection arrangement adds a
  disagreement of pglet's **with itself**:
  there the re-`Describe` reports the new one-column shape while `Bind` + `Execute` in the
  same block answers two-field rows off the block's pre-DDL read snapshot, so the
  descriptor and the rows one statement returns do not agree either.

  **Three agreeing controls bound it — and the second carries its own boundary.** An explicit
  projection the DDL does not touch is unaffected in **name, type and rows**: prepared
  `SELECT c FROM k`, after the
  same drop of `a`, is `c:int4` plus the same two rows on both engines. Its `attnum` is
  **not** among what agrees — pglet re-describes it at `rel.1` where 18.6 keeps `rel.2` —
  and that is outside this row's subject in both directions: a **fresh** parse after the
  drop renumbers identically here, so it is the pre-existing no-tombstone model gap
  rather than anything a prepared statement did (a table created one-column is `rel.1` on
  both). That gap is now **visible through two complete relations** and did not shrink:
  `pg_attribute` models `attisdropped` as a constant `false` — truthful, since a dropped
  column leaves no catalog entry here at all — and `pg_constraint.conkey` reports the
  renumbered positions, so an introspecting client reads a consistent catalog that
  disagrees with 18.6's about every position after a mid-table drop. And `attnum` is not
  in 18.6's revalidation criterion either
  (`equalRowTypes`, PostgreSQL's `src/backend/access/common/tupdesc.c`, compares the
  column count and type id plus each column's `attname`, `atttypid`, `atttypmod`,
  `attcollation` and `attisdropped`), so no renumbering could reach the `0A000` this row
  is about. Next, a statement whose reading of the aged table never reaches its output
  columns is a control **only while that reading still analyzes** — `RevalidateCachedQuery`
  re-analyzes before it compares descriptors (PostgreSQL's
  `src/backend/utils/cache/plancache.c`, `pg_analyze_and_rewrite_*` ahead of the
  `equalRowTypes` test), so a reading that fails analysis raises no matter what the result
  type does: prepared `WITH c AS (SELECT * FROM r4v) SELECT 1`, the drop run under it
  inside a block, re-describes `?column?:int4` and answers its row with
  the block live on **both** engines, and both `COMMIT` to the same state — the star
  re-expands, nothing fails, and the unreferenced CTE reaches neither engine's descriptor.
  Name the dropped column in that same unreferenced CTE and it is a **member** instead:
  prepared `WITH c AS (SELECT a FROM r5w) SELECT 1`, whose result type never moves,
  re-`Describe`s `t n Z[T]` here with the block live and the following `INSERT` committed
  (`C[COMMIT]`, one column, `10, 20, 777`), against `t E[42703] Z[E]`, `25P02`,
  `C[ROLLBACK]` and an untouched two-column table there — the loud kind, over a statement
  whose descriptor the aged relation never reaches. And a statement that returns
  **no result set has no result type to revalidate**, so the whole class is absent
  from it: prepared `UPDATE k2 SET a = 1` and `INSERT INTO k2 (a) VALUES (5)`, after `a`
  is dropped, are `t n Z` at the `Describe` on **both** engines and then `42703` on both —
  pglet one message later, after `BindComplete`, which is row 60's placement rather than
  this row's — and 18.6's exemption there is `RevalidateCachedQuery`'s "doesn't return
  tuples" branch rather than a lenience. Both `Describe` legs agree on both headline
  shapes, statement and portal reading the one `describe_result_shape`. The class is
  **extended-protocol-only**: SQL `PREPARE p AS SELECT 1` is `42601` here, so no
  simple-query route leaves a statement standing across a DDL at all.

  **Not row 20's, though row 20 records a re-shape too.** That row's subject is a *portal*
  (or the unnamed statement) surviving a boundary 18.6 destroys it at, so 18.6's answer
  there is `34000`/`26000` and the re-shape it names is unobservable on the oracle at all.
  Here nothing is destroyed on either side: a **named** prepared statement, no transaction
  boundary, and 18.6 answering a specific plancache refusal that pglet has no counterpart
  for. Row 20 is the portal-lifetime twin, and its own re-shape member runs on **this
  row's** mechanism — nothing compares a new shape against a published one — reached
  through an object 18.6 had already destroyed, which is what costs it an oracle
  comparison.

  **No guard, and the harness cannot hold one.** The fixture harness prepares each `@test`
  statement and executes it in the same exchange, and `@setup` runs to completion before
  any of that, so no arrangement of directives leaves a prepared statement standing across
  a DDL — the shape cannot be written at all, let alone written green: on the silent half
  pglet *answers* where 18.6 errors, which `@expect-error` cannot hold either. A
  raw-frame unit test can express it, as row 20's half can, and none exists.
  **Not fixed** — revalidating
  a result type means holding the described shape on the prepared statement and comparing
  it on every re-plan, which is a new refusal with its own error-precedence consequences
  (`docs/ddl.md` § which error wins). The prose home outside this file is
  `describe_result_shape`'s doc comment in `crates/pglet_server/src/handlers.rs`.

  The two-to-**zero**-column member is the silent kind and no longer looks like the loud one:
  it re-describes `T(0)` and then sends its zero-field rows, where before row 59's close it
  answered `NoData` there and so read as a failed re-plan.
- **35 · Duplicate output column names are untestable by the harness.** `row_to_json`
  (`crates/pglet_tests/src/lib.rs`) keys a `serde_json::Map` by column name, so a
  `@test` projecting two columns named `x` collapses them into one — in the compared
  values *and* in the declared-type list. Any divergence that shows up only on the
  second of two same-named columns is invisible; a fixture must give them distinct
  `AS` labels to be testable at all.
- **36 · Plan-declared type ≠ runtime value.** The encoder streams
  off the runtime value with no target-OID coercion, so a place the planner declares
  one type but eval produces another corrupts any client that decodes by the declared
  OID. Past the `RowDescription`, the native server's result encoders read the declared
  OID at two points, and neither changes which value is sent: a `timestamptz` column's text
  carries `+00`, and a binary array's header names the column's element type only where
  every non-NULL element is sent as that type — otherwise the element type the value
  records (`value_to_binary_with_oid`). So a wrong column type does not put its element
  type over elements it does not describe: `ARRAY[COALESCE(i + 0, b + 0)]` over the fold
  band's NULL row was column `1007` over a header of `20` and eight-byte elements, as it
  was before the header read the column at all, where 18.6 is `1016` over `20` — and is
  declared `1016` now that row 54's close casts its branches. **Where two types share a representation, the
  elements cannot contradict a wrong column type, and the header follows it**: a `text`
  element is sent as `name` too (`value_sends_as`), so
  `SELECT CASE WHEN false THEN ARRAY[current_user] ELSE ARRAY['a'] END`, typed `name[]`
  (`1003`) here and `text[]` (`1009`) on 18.6, sends a binary header of `19` over the byte
  `61` where 18.6 sends `25` over the same byte — and where the header read the value's
  record alone it was `25`. The text leg is `{a}` on both. This row was filed as a **binary-wire** class with
  **`float4` arithmetic** as its one confirmed member and a `COALESCE`/`CASE` over
  differently-typed **column** branches and a nested `ARRAY[ARRAY[…]]` constructor as
  "suspected but unverified", with `GREATEST`/`LEAST`/`NULLIF` and `UNION` named as the
  reference fix that already unifies declared == actual. **Two of those claims no longer
  hold**: the class is not binary-only, and the `float4` member is closed.

  **The `COALESCE`/`CASE` half is confirmed now — row 54's fold band and row 65's untaken
  branch (row 65's `Parse`-declared `$N` is not a route, below); the nested
  `ARRAY` half
  stays unreachable** (`ARRAY[ARRAY[…]]` is `0A000` here, so no value reaches the wire).
  Every one of them is a branch set the coercion pass leaves un-rewritten, so no unifying
  `Cast` was inserted and the declaration came from a walker rather than from the fold:

  - **Row 54's fold band.** `SELECT COALESCE(i + 0, b + 0) FROM w` over a row whose `i`
    was NULL declared `int4` on both legs and streamed **eight** bytes
    (`000000012a05f200`, `5000000000`); over a row whose `i` is `7` the same statement
    streamed **four** (`00000007`). 18.6 declares `int8` and streams eight either way.
    Row 54's close casts that spelling's branches to `int8`; the route stays live where
    a branch is outside the readers' arms — `COALESCE(i + 0, b + (SELECT 0))` declares
    `23` over the text `5000000000` on both legs, measured, its binary stream unmeasured.
    **It is not binary-only either**: on the simple leg the same NULL row is `oid=23`
    over the text `5000000000` against 18.6's `oid=20`, a value no int4 holds — so a
    text client that decodes by declared OID overflows there too.
    That pair is why row 54's right close cannot be "fold the walkers to `int8`": this
    encoder is **value**-driven, so a walker-only fold repairs the NULL row and breaks
    the other. The close has to insert the coercing casts.
  - **Row 65's gate skip, through a client-declared parameter type — no longer a member.**
    A declared `$N` is read as a cast to its type (row 146), so `Parse` declaring `$1` as
    `text` plus `COALESCE($1, length('ab'))` bound `'zz'` now declares `text` over `7a7a`
    in both result formats, as does the `COALESCE($1, date_trunc('day', now()))` spelling:
    declaration and value agree. 18.6 still refuses both `42804` at `Parse`, so the
    missing refusal is row 65's and stays there; it no longer puts a value under a
    declaration that contradicts it. Measured over a raw extended-protocol client.
  - **Row 65's untaken branch** — the same missing refusal, reached with none of the
    apparatus the other two need: no client-declared parameter type, no NULL column, no
    bound value, so an ordinary `Query` builds it. The walkers declare the first
    *inferable* branch while evaluation returns the branch it takes, and nothing casts
    between them: `CASE WHEN false THEN length('ab') ELSE upper('x') END` declares `23`
    and streams the single byte `58`, the `ELSE INTERVAL '1 day'` spelling declares `23`
    and streams **16**, and `COALESCE(nullif(length('ab'), 2), upper('x'))` declares `23`
    over one byte with no `CASE` in it at all. A binary client decodes each as an `int4`
    of the wrong width; 18.6 refuses all three `42804`. On the simple leg the surviving
    branch renders as its own type under the other's OID — `X`, `1 day` and `X` under
    `23`, in the order above — so a driver that decodes by declared OID reads a
    malformed integer rather than a plausible one.

  **Neither live multi-operand route stops at the binary wire**: the fold band diverges on
  the simple leg outright, and the untaken branch on both legs. **There is no remainder to
  hand the distinction to — the member list is the whole statement**: fold band, both
  legs; untaken branch, both legs. **The `float4` arithmetic member the distinction
  was last parked on is closed**, and a closed member cannot carry it. `real <op> real`
  was declared `real` over an eight-byte f64 value; it is f32 throughout now, so
  `0.1::real + 0.2::real` is `700` over the four bytes `3e99999a` (text `0.3`) and
  `sum(f4)` is `700` over four, byte-identical to 18.6 on both legs
  (`arithmetic/float4_same_width.sql`, `arithmetic/sum_float4_accumulator.sql`).

  What is still live under the `float4` name belongs to **row 54**, not here.
  `f4 + NULL` over `r36(f4 REAL, f8 DOUBLE PRECISION, i INT, n NUMERIC)` with a row
  declares `701` on the simple leg against 18.6's `700`, and `700` on the extended leg on
  **both** engines — cell K's member 2, an OID-only walker split — while the value is
  **NULL** on every spelling that reaches it (`f4 + - * / NULL` and the NULL-leading
  forms alike; `f4 ^ NULL` and `NULL ^ f4` agree at `701` everywhere). Nothing is
  streamed under either OID, so it cannot be a declared-vs-value member, and its text is
  not "a valid number either way" — there is no text. Row 54's consequence cell has said
  the value is NULL on every arithmetic spelling that reaches it all along; this row now
  agrees with it. Every float4 spelling that *does* produce a value declares and streams
  consistently on both engines: `f4`, `-f4`, `abs(f4)`, `f4 - f4`, `f4 * f4`, `f4 / f4`,
  `sum(f4)`, `min(f4)`, `max(f4)` are `700` over four bytes, and `f4 + 1`, `f4 - 1`,
  `f4 + i`, `f4 + n`, `f4 + f8`, `avg(f4)` are `701` over eight. Across that sweep no
  float4 spelling parts pglet's own declaration from its own value.

  **Two routes, one shorthand for each.** Row 54's fold band is
  `COALESCE(i + 0, b + (SELECT 0))`; row 65's untaken branch needs neither a declared parameter
  type nor a NULL column. The `float4` name is live only under row 54
  now — `f4 + NULL` and its `- * /` and NULL-leading forms are an OID-only split whose value
  is NULL on every spelling that reaches it, so nothing is streamed under either OID and no
  member of this row hides there.

  **Outside a `COALESCE`/`CASE`, two more routes put a value under another type's
  declaration**, each with a row of its own: a FROM-clause `unnest`'s `ARRAY[…]`
  constructor (row 308) and a bare reference to a `USING` merge of differently-typed
  columns (row 309).
- **~~37~~ · Closed — JSONB containment / equality / build.** `@>`/`<@` was object-vs-object
  only, falling back to structural equality for every other pair (a wrong boolean, not
  fail-loud, on array-subset / scalar / nested-array containment, with the GIN recheck
  sharing it); `jsonb_build_object` didn't dedup duplicate keys, and its first-match
  readers then disagreed with the text path's last-wins; and equality was
  key-**order**-sensitive, so `DISTINCT`/`GROUP BY`/join dedup split one logical value
  into several. All three are fixed together: containment is a port of
  `JsonbDeepContains`, and every jsonb value is now built in Postgres's **canonical
  form** (keys deduplicated last-wins, then sorted length-then-bytewise), which makes
  key order insignificant for equality, ordering, *and* rendering. Canonical order
  changed the persisted form without changing its postcard shape — the store magic
  bumped **PGMD** so an old store fails loud on reopen instead of comparing wrong.
- **~~38~~ · Closed — DROP-side dependencies.** `DROP TABLE` / `ALTER TABLE … DROP COLUMN` now
  resolve their dependents through one function reproducing Postgres's `pg_depend` edge
  kinds (`executor/dependencies.rs`), and `DROP INDEX` refuses a constraint's index. The
  three integrity-loss shapes are gone: a referenced-*table* drop no longer dangles the
  child's FK (`2BP01`, or `CASCADE` sheds just the constraint), a referenced-*column*
  drop no longer silently disables it (`2BP01`), and the two **accepted-then-unwritable**
  shapes — a left-behind `CHECK` or FK over a dropped column, which failed every later
  write `42703` and made the table's dump unreloadable — are auto-dropped as Postgres
  does. The zombie-resurrection that followed (re-adding the column revived the CHECK)
  went with them. Two second-order holes closed with the same pass: a **duplicate
  *declared* constraint name** on one table (accepted on every inline / `ADD CONSTRAINT …
  FOREIGN KEY` path, so an AUTO-edge drop of one silently shed its same-named sibling and
  un-enforced it) is now `42710` — the gate applies to a name the *user* wrote; an
  engine-generated one is disambiguated instead, never refused, and reading the two as one
  rule is what later gated `ALTER TABLE t ADD FOREIGN KEY (a) REFERENCES p(id)` issued
  twice. And a **declared** `CONSTRAINT <n> PRIMARY KEY|UNIQUE`
  keeps its name instead of being reported to introspection under a fabricated
  `<table>_pkey` — a plausible-but-wrong value a client cannot detect.

  Keeping the declared name **opened a third hole in the same place**, which is the
  lesson worth carrying: with the name no longer dropped, a second `PRIMARY KEY` under a
  different name stopped replacing the first and started *coexisting* with it — two
  PRIMARY KEY rows in `information_schema`, and `Schema::primary_key_index` (a `find`
  over a name-sorted map) answering by index-name order, so `REFERENCES t` bound to
  whichever key sorted first. One silent-wrong traded for another. It is now `42P16`,
  checked at all three mint sites, and the name-order dependence is unreachable. The
  two name pools — CHECK/FK on the table, PK/UNIQUE on
  the index — also never consulted each other, so every cross-kind duplicate was accepted;
  they are one pool now, spanning all four kinds as `pg_constraint` does.

  And a **fourth** hole in the same place, from the same cause read one level up: the gate
  was applied to names the *engine* generates, which Postgres never refuses. The fix is not
  another gate but moving the decision — a constraint's name is now minted once, at execute
  time, by one function, and persisted (see `docs/compatibility.md`'s `ALTER TABLE … ADD CONSTRAINT` row).
  Three defect classes collapse into that one move. An **auto-name gated** where Postgres
  disambiguates: a repeated unnamed `ADD FOREIGN KEY` was `42710` instead of `t_a_fkey` +
  `t_a_fkey1`. A route that **claimed nothing**: `ADD COLUMN … REFERENCES` and every
  unnamed CHECK, each able to land a second row under an existing `(table, name)`. And a
  name **synthesized lazily at display time**, which unnamed CHECKs did three
  incompatible ways at once — the violation message said `t_a_check`,
  `information_schema` omitted the constraint entirely, and the dump called it
  `t_check`, so a dump/restore renamed every unnamed CHECK and a table carrying both a
  declared `t_check` and an unnamed one emitted two `ADD CONSTRAINT t_check` statements
  that neither engine will reload. What that
  leaves in this bullet: a target-less `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` is accepted where PG is
  `42601` at parse (silently when no row conflicts; on a conflict it is a loud `23505` —
  the wrong code, not a silent write); `ALTER TABLE IF EXISTS` no-ops the whole
  statement.

  **The duplicate target column and duplicate `SET` target members are closed** — a
  statement's target column list is a set, at the `INSERT` column list (`42701`), the
  `COPY` column list in both directions (`42701`), the `UPDATE` `SET` list and the
  `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` `SET` list (`42601`), each raised where 18.6 raises it
  (`docs/names.md` § A statement's target column list is a set), which is where the
  measured residuals are recorded — and not all of them are loud.
  The `ON CONFLICT` action's **own** `GENERATED ALWAYS` identity guard runs inside the
  clause's lowering here and after the target-list merge on 18.6, so `DO UPDATE SET id =
  1, id = 2` over such a column is `428C9` here against `42601` there — the identity
  guards' known position rather than the duplicate gate's. A `SET` list that both
  repeats a column and assigns it an ill-typed **constant** now answers `42601` where
  18.6 answers the constant's `22P02`: pglet defers an implicit assignment conversion to
  eval and 18.6 performs it in parse analysis, which is row 5's timing, reached here
  through the duplicate rather than created by it. An `INSERT … SELECT` whose **source
  query** errors reports that error where 18.6 reports the `42701`, because
  `checkInsertTargets` runs ahead of the source's `transformStmt` there and pglet lowers
  the source first — `INSERT INTO t (a, a) SELECT 1, nosuchcol FROM t` is `42703` here,
  and the `SELECT COALESCE(1, 'x'::text), 2` and `SELECT 1, 2 ORDER BY nosuchcol`
  spellings are `42804` and `42703`.

  **The `ON CONFLICT` gate cost an agreement, and the repair that looks obvious costs a
  different one.** Where 18.6 settles a **row-source cell** in parse analysis and pglet
