  settles it per row at execution, this gate answers first: over `u (a INT UNIQUE, b INT,
  bo BOOL)` holding `(1, 1, true)`, `INSERT INTO u VALUES (5, 'notanint', true) ON
  CONFLICT (a) DO UPDATE SET b = 1, b = 2` is `22P02` on 18.6 and `42601` here and the
  `nosuchcol`-in-the-cell spelling is `42703` there and `42601` here — at a free key and a
  conflicting one alike, where the pre-gate build answered 18.6's code at every one of
  them. The same pair stands on the `INSERT … SELECT` route's cell cast and on the
  `UPDATE` route's own right-hand side, which is row 5's second paragraph. Moving the
  gate below those verdicts is refused on a measurement rather than a preference: 18.6
  raises the `42601` before any row is evaluated, so `INSERT INTO u SELECT a, b FROM src
  WHERE false ON CONFLICT (a) DO UPDATE SET b = 1, b = 2` is `42601` there **and here**
  where the pre-gate build reported `INSERT 0 0`, and pglet's cell verdicts are per-row —
  a gate under them stops firing on that statement. Closing it properly is moving the cell
  verdicts to plan time, which is row 5's timing and row 13's error order. The divergent
  members cannot be fixtures (both engines error, the SQLSTATEs differ); what is pinned is
  the zero-row agreement and the repeat-free controls —
  `insert/on_conflict_duplicate_set_target_over_a_zero_row_source_loud.sql`, its
  `_writes_nothing` twin and `insert/on_conflict_single_set_target_yields_to_the_cell_*`.

  **The `UPDATE` gate's own skip is where the refusal goes silent** — a column assigned
  twice, and nothing saying so. A `WHERE` or `RETURNING` naming a relation the
  catalog lacks turns the gate off, and over an **empty** table pglet's `42P01` for that
  relation is never reached, so `UPDATE t SET a = 1, a = 2 WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM
  nosuchrel)` and its `RETURNING (SELECT 1 FROM nosuchrel)` spelling report `UPDATE 0`
  against 18.6's `42P01`. Over a matching row both are `42P01` on both engines, and
  nothing is written either way. The silence is row 29's zero-row reachability hole
  reached through this gate rather than opened by it — the single-assignment spelling is
  as silent — which is why the skip is the payable half. A `SET` **right-hand side**
  naming such a relation is outside the skip and the loud polarity of the same seam:
  `UPDATE t SET a = (SELECT 1 FROM nosuchrel), a = 2` is `42601` here against `42P01`
  there, at either row count.

  A **second `DEFAULT` on one column definition** is the same last-wins shape one level
  down, and it is `42601 multiple default values specified for column "a" of table "s4"` on
  18.6 (`transformColumnDefinition`, `parse_utilcmd.c:819` — it beats a duplicate
  constraint name and a missing FK parent and loses to the column type's `42704`, one more
  position of the error-order contract, each measured):
  `CREATE TABLE s4 (a INT DEFAULT 5 DEFAULT 7)` stores `7` here and inserts it,
  with `column_default` reading `7`. Where one of the two specifications is a `SERIAL` the
  *serial* wins instead of the last — `CREATE TABLE s3 (a SERIAL DEFAULT 5)` stores
  `nextval('s3_a_seq'::regclass)` and inserts `1` — so "last-wins" is not even a rule the
  route follows consistently, which is worth knowing before anyone leans on it. The site
  is the unconditional `default = self.parse_column_default(…)` in the column-constraint
  loop of `parser/ddl.rs`; pre-existing and independent of the `DEFAULT NULL` work above,
  which only changed what the *third* spelling stores (`DEFAULT 7 DEFAULT NULL` now leaves
  the column with no default where it used to leave a `Literal(Null)` — the same NULL
  either way, differing only in what `column_default` renders).
  The fixtures over the multiple-clause and `SERIAL` shapes are `ddl/default_multiple_clauses_on_one_column.sql`
  and `ddl/default_serial_is_itself_a_default_clause.sql`.
  **`ADD COLUMN … NOT NULL DEFAULT NULL` is closed**, and with it the
  build-profile-divergent `ORDER BY` that rode on it: the state it produced — NULLs in a
  `NOT NULL` column — is refused on this build by that statement and by the three
  neighbouring routes measured with it (`ADD COLUMN … NOT NULL` with no default,
  `ALTER COLUMN … SET NOT NULL` over NULL rows, `COPY` of a `\N`, each `23502`), and an
  index built over such a column then made an accelerated-profile `ORDER BY` elide its
  sort onto it and read **(0 rows)** on both storage backends (measured pre-fix; stripped
  answered both rows, as did the accelerated profile with no such index, and `count(*)`
  was right everywhere).
  Two independent changes close it and either would suffice — the `ADD COLUMN` gate now
  tests the **resolved backfill values** rather than whether a DEFAULT is present, and the
  parser normalizes `DEFAULT NULL` to *no* default, which is 18.6's own model
  (`AddRelationNewConstraints` stores no `pg_attrdef` row for a NULL constant, and
  `SET DEFAULT NULL` *removes* one — measured, 1 → 0). Measured as mutations, **each half
  is individually zero-red once the other stands**, in both directions: reverting the gate
  to the presence test reddens nothing, and reverting the normalization to the identity
  reddens no fixture either and only its own two unit tests
  (`crates/pglet/tests/column_default_verdicts.rs`'s `a_null_default_is_no_default_at_all`,
  `dump::column_default_round_trip::every_column_default_renders_back_to_the_same_variant`)
  — the belts that read a persisted `Literal(Null)` as no-default, in
  `information_schema` and in the dump, hold every other SQL observable. It is the
  **pair** the observables pin, not either member: removing the gate outright reddens three
  fixtures — `ddl/add_column_not_null_default_null_is_23502.sql`,
  `ddl/alter_addcol_notnull_no_default_loud.sql` and
  `ddl/add_column_not_null_backfill_beats_check.sql` (whose SQLSTATE goes `23502` → `23514`,
  the error-order half) — and three unit tests in
  `crates/pglet/tests/alter_add_column_backfill.rs`. The values gate is
  kept because it is the statement 18.6's `ATRewriteTable` actually makes (it inspects the
  rewritten tuples, not the catalog default) and it is what stays correct once a
  `DEFAULT <expr>` can evaluate to NULL.
  **That producer's legacy-store residual is closed, by the store magic rather than by a
  sweep.** Closing the producer said nothing about a database already holding the state, and the
  change that closed it did not move the magic — both sides read `PGMH` — so a
  `--data-dir` store written before that change reopened with no error at all, its two
  NULL rows under a `NOT NULL` column intact: `SELECT c FROM lg ORDER BY c` answered
  **(0 rows)** accelerated against the stripped build's two (the profile divergence,
  alive, in a store neither profile refused), and `pglet_server dump --data-dir`
  rendered `\N` under that column into a `COPY` stock 18.6 refuses mid-restore
  (`23502`, `CONTEXT: COPY lg, line 1`) — the table landing and the rows not. The
  `PGMH` → `PGMI` bump (`ColumnDefault::Expr`) refuses every such store **loud on
  reopen**, as every earlier break does, and takes this residual with it — which is
  the second of that bump's three recorded jobs, and the reason it is a bump rather
  than an append.

  **A fifth producer reached the state through the identity clause rather than through
  `NOT NULL`, and is closed.** `ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN x ADD GENERATED ALWAYS AS
  IDENTITY` over a column holding a NULL was **accepted** here — the column became an
  identity column, `information_schema.columns` reported `is_nullable = NO`, and the NULL
  row stood — where 18.6 refuses `55000 column "x" of relation "t" must be declared NOT
  NULL before identity can be added`. Measured on both. The four routes above were
  enumerated over the statements that *say* `NOT NULL`; this one set the flag as a side
  effect of adding the identity, which is why sweeping that enumeration missed it. It
  carried the family's read symptom in its milder form: over `x` holding `1, NULL, 1` with
  an index on it, `SELECT x FROM t` answered all three rows and `SELECT x FROM t ORDER BY
  x` answered **two** — the NULL row silently absent from the ordered read, on the
  accelerated profile. Under a `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` index, which holds an entry for the
  NULL key, the row was misplaced rather than absent — first ascending, where 18.6 sorts
  it last — until a range read stopped answering NULL keys (row 311), and absent after.

  **What closed it.** The clause reads the column's *declaration*, as 18.6's
  `ATExecAddIdentity` does, and no row: over a column not declared `NOT NULL` it is
  `55000` with 18.6's message — over rows holding a NULL, rows holding none and an empty
  table, `ALWAYS` and `BY DEFAULT`, each measured on both engines — and it no longer sets
  the flag. The refusal runs ahead of the statement's first catalog write, the
  sequence's registration, so a refused statement leaves no sequence behind, and behind
  the sequence's own refusals, which is where 18.6 raises it (`docs/ddl.md` § The mirror
  carries the measured pairs). `ALTER COLUMN … SET NOT NULL`, which reads the rows, is the
  way in. The statements that set the declaration over existing rows are then `SET NOT
  NULL`, `ADD PRIMARY KEY` and `ADD COLUMN`, and each reads the rows it declares over; no
  statement this build accepts is known to leave a NULL under a `NOT NULL` declaration.
  Guards: the `ddl/add_identity_*` fixtures, and
  `crates/pglet/tests/identity_declaration.rs`, which holds what a refused statement
  leaves behind — a fixture stops at the first statement that fails — and sweeps the
  statements that would declare `NOT NULL` over a NULL or write one under the
  declaration, comparing each indexed column's `ORDER BY` with a sort of the table's rows
  after each.

  **It reached the dump too**, which the read symptom does not say. On a `--data-dir`
  store holding `1, NULL, 1` under that identity column, `pglet_server dump --data-dir`
  emits `x integer NOT NULL`, an `ALTER TABLE … ADD GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY`, and a
  `COPY` carrying `1`, `\N`, `1`. Replayed into a fresh stock 18.6 database the table and
  the identity land and the `COPY` does not — `23502`,
  `CONTEXT: COPY gid, line 2: "\N"` — leaving `count(*) = 0`: all three rows gone, with
  **psql exiting 0**. Replaying the same dump back into pglet answers the same way,
  `23502` mid-`COPY` and an empty table, so this producer broke the dump invariant in both
  directions, and at its rows rather than its catalog — `docs/sequences.md`'s property C,
  *the stored rows satisfy the catalog the dump recreates*: the dump recreates `x` as
  `NOT NULL`, and the row holding the NULL fails it.

  **Its legacy store is the residual that remains, and no magic closes this one.** The
  refusal moved no store magic, so a `--data-dir` store in which an earlier build accepted
  the clause reopens with no error, the NULL still under `is_nullable = NO`. Measured on
  such a store, written before the refusal and read after it, holding `(NULL, 'null')`,
  `(1, 'one')` and `(2, 'two')`: `SELECT v … ORDER BY c` answers `one`, `two` on the
  accelerated build — under a `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` index as under a plain one — where the
  stripped build answers `one`, `two`, `null`; `count(*)` is `3` on both; `SET NOT NULL`
  over the column is `23502`; and its dump replays as above, `23502` mid-`COPY` into 18.6
  and into pglet, each table empty, psql exiting 0. Deleting the NULL rows repairs the
  read. **Silent**, a build-profile divergence, and known to be reached only through a
  store an earlier build wrote.

  **Some of those residuals are closed since**, and they are recorded here as a
  subtraction rather than as a fresh list. A negative-year timestamp or timestamptz
  literal is refused as malformed, and so is a `+`-signed one, which was accepted silently
  too (`'+2026-06-15 12:00:00'::timestamp` and `' +2026-06-15 12:00:00'::timestamptz` were
  values here, measured on a build before the date domain; 18.6 answers
  `22009 time zone displacement out of range`). The timestamp reader reads those digits as
  18.6 does, as an offset: `'-2026-06-15 00:00:00'` and `'+2026-06-15 12:00:00'`
  are `22009` on both, and `'-0001-01-01 00:00:00'`, whose offset field is in range and not
  read whole, is row 96's `22P02` against 18.6's `22007`, each measured. The `date` reader,
  which already refused both signs, answers `22007` — `'+2026-06-15'::date` against 18.6's
  `22009` (`docs/temporal.md` § The date and timestamp domain). A second `DEFAULT` on one column definition —
  including its `SERIAL DEFAULT 5` spelling, where a `SERIAL` type name *is* a default
  clause — is `42601 multiple default values specified for column …`. And a `--data-dir`
  store written before the `PGMH` → `PGMI` bump, holding NULLs in a `NOT NULL` column, no
  longer reopens at all: the bump refuses it loud. And `ALTER COLUMN … ADD GENERATED … AS
  IDENTITY` over a column not declared `NOT NULL` is `55000`, its legacy store remaining.
- **~~39~~ · Closed — CREATE-side atomicity, and it was a *durability* bug, not an ordering
  one.** `execute_create_table` now runs every fallible step ahead of
  `schema.create_table`. That is load-bearing because the autocommit path rolls back
  **storage** on an error and leaves `self.schema` mutated in place, and the next
  successful write serializes the catalog — so any error raised after the mutation left
  a **durable phantom table**: `information_schema.tables` listed it, `SELECT`/`INSERT`
  answered `42P01` (storage *had* been rolled back), and `CREATE TABLE <same name>` was
  `42P07` forever. Five routes reached it, all through the index-build loop: a
  `PRIMARY KEY`/`UNIQUE` naming a column the table lacks, the *second* such constraint
  after the first index had already built, a declared `CONSTRAINT <n>` equal to the
  table's own name, and — the two that took a second pass to find — a constraint index
  whose name a sequence *this same statement registers* already spoke for, once via a
  `SERIAL`'s implicit sequence and once via a user's own `DEFAULT nextval('x')`. The
  general shape is **a name this statement will register that a later gate cannot see**,
  and the gates that fix it seed those names into the namer as `catalog ∪ in-flight`.
  The `ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN` twin of the last one is worse than a phantom name: the
  column lands in the catalog while the widened rows roll back with storage, so every
  `SELECT *` on a populated table then fails at the wire (`unexpected field count in "D"
  message`) for every client, permanently. The differential harness is structurally blind
  to the whole class — every fixture runs inside `BEGIN … ROLLBACK`, which restores the
  catalog snapshot — so the guards are unit tests in `crates/pglet`
  (`*_leaves_no_phantom`, and `sequence_catalog.rs`'s two file-backed guards; the
  `ADD COLUMN` corruption needs the **B+tree** backend, since the plain in-memory storage
  double does not roll back and leaves the backfill applied).

  **`ADD COLUMN`'s own sequence registration is closed, and it is a *staging* fix rather
  than a reordering one.** The registration could not simply move after the checks: the
  backfill *draws* from the sequence, so it has to exist for `resolve_default` while the
  statement can still be refused. It is therefore computed into a local record —
  `executor::ddl`'s `staged_sequences` — that the backfill advances and that lands in
  `schema.sequences` only inside the mutation block. Before that, the registration ran
  ahead of the `23502` gate and of `validate_added_column_constraints`, so all three
  violations that gate can raise over such a column (`23514` / `23505` / `23503`) raised
  over a **durable phantom
  sequence carrying the failed backfill's advances**: `CREATE TABLE pht (id INT);` two
  rows; `ALTER TABLE pht ADD COLUMN c SERIAL CHECK (c > 100)` answered `23514` and then
  served `nextval('pht_c_seq')` → **3**, and `CREATE SEQUENCE pht_c_seq` was `42P07`
  forever, where 18.6 answers `42P01` and leaves the name free (measured, both engines).
  The user-written `DEFAULT nextval('x')` arm reached it too, through pglet's DDL-time
  auto-creation of `x`. **`23502` is a gate on this path and not a fourth violation**:
  `resolve_default`'s `NextVal` yields an `int8` and no coercion turns that into NULL, so
  `ADD COLUMN c SERIAL NOT NULL` over existing rows **succeeds** on both engines and a
  column type that cannot take the value fails as a cast error instead (18.6: `column "c"
  is of type boolean but default expression is of type bigint`) — measured both ways. The
  `23505` arm is reachable only through an exotic spelling, since the backfill's own draws
  are distinct: `NUMERIC(3,-1) DEFAULT nextval(…) UNIQUE`, whose `1, 2, 3` all round to
  `0` (`23505` on both engines). Unlike the phantom *column*, this half is
  **backend-independent** — it is a catalog residue with no storage counterpart, so the
  in-memory double reproduces it identically (measured) — and it is what
  the dump's dangling-owner branch had been seeded by. One asymmetry is load-bearing and
  is the reason the staging is conditional: a sequence the statement did **not** create
  is advanced in place, because `nextval` is non-transactional and is not rolled back
  (`Schema::restore_from`'s exception), so staging a copy of a live counter and
  discarding it would re-issue ids already handed out. Guarded by
  `a_failed_add_column_backfill_leaves_no_phantom_sequence` and
  `a_failed_add_column_leaves_no_phantom_user_named_sequence`, each red on the revert.
  **The sibling routes were swept and none shares the defect** (measured, not asserted):
  `ALTER TABLE … ALTER COLUMN … ADD GENERATED … AS IDENTITY` registers behind all five of
  its gates (`42P01` / `42703` / `55000` / `22023` / `42P07` — probed, each leaving no
  sequence), its only following `?` being a table re-lookup that the read-only resolve at
  the top of the same function has already answered; `ALTER COLUMN … SET DEFAULT` was
  fixed earlier and has its own guard; `CREATE SEQUENCE`'s insert is its last statement;
  and `CREATE TABLE`'s registration sits inside the mutation block by design, sharing the
  post-mutation backstop the paragraph above describes.

  Moving the checks up **changed statement-level error precedence**, as adding or
  hoisting a gate always does, and the new order is Postgres's parse-analysis order
  rather than an invention: column types resolve in the `tableElts` walk
  (`42704` outranks everything below), then `transformIndexConstraints` runs
  per constraint with the multiplicity test *above* the key-column resolution inside the
  same call — so `PRIMARY KEY (nosuch), PRIMARY KEY (a)` is `42703` and
  `PRIMARY KEY (a), PRIMARY KEY (nosuch)` is `42P16`, and no whole-list arrangement
  yields both. All of it outranks the execution-time errors (`42P07`, `42710`, `42883`,
  `42P01`), while `IF NOT EXISTS` still outranks all of it. Fixtures pin the
  arrangements.

  **The residual this row carried is closed: a repeated key column is `42701`, at both
  routes**, and it went in *inside* that key loop rather than beside it, because the
  repeat test sits **below** each key's own resolution in 18.6's loop body. That is
  observable and had to be reproduced rather than approximated:
  `PRIMARY KEY (a, a, nosuch)` is `42701` and `PRIMARY KEY (a, nosuch, a)` is `42703`,
  measured on 18.6, and no whole-list resolve-then-dedup yields both. On
  `ALTER TABLE … ADD CONSTRAINT` the resolution is not in that pass at all
  (`!cxt->isalter` defers it to `DefineIndex`), so **both** spellings are `42701` there
  — the route asymmetry is 18.6's, and `validate_key_columns` reproduces it by taking
  the column list as an `Option`. The gate's own precedence is pinned in both
  directions, and the arrangements are measured rather than derived from where the
  gate sits: it outranks the relation's `42P07`, the duplicate column, the system
  column name, a colliding declared `SEQUENCE NAME` and the column-default cook, and
  — on `ALTER` — a duplicate constraint name, a taken index name and the second
  primary key; it loses to the column types and, on `ALTER`, to the relation's
  `42P01`. The `SEQUENCE NAME` pair is the one that does **not** read off the two
  gates beside it: the duplicate column and the system column name each lose to it.
  The check is the **constraint's** and not its index's, which two accept-side controls
  bound: `CREATE INDEX t_i ON t (a, a)` and a foreign key's *referencing* list
  `FOREIGN KEY (a, a) REFERENCES p (x, y)` are accepted by both engines.

  **No unit test in the workspace constructs the repeat's `42701`** — nor the
  duplicate-column, system-column or FK-referenced refusals beside it: neither the
  variant names nor their message text appears in a Rust test, integration binary
  or `#[cfg(test)]` module alike. So the `*_leaves_no_phantom` family guards the routes above
  and not these. What pins the CREATE-side atomicity
  of the three `CREATE TABLE` gates is **transitive**, and it is the precedence
  fixtures doing it: each `*_beats_the_existing_relation` fixture asserts its gate
  outranks the table's own `42P07`, which itself sits above `schema.create_table`
  — so a placement low enough to leave a phantom is also below that `42P07` and
  answers it instead. Measured by moving all three below `schema.create_table`:
  `ddl/duplicate_column_beats_the_existing_relation.sql`,
  `ddl/system_column_name_beats_the_existing_relation.sql` and
  `ddl/key_column_repeat_beats_the_existing_relation.sql` each answered `42P07`
  against the oracle's `42701`, and each is green again on the restored tree.
  Which fixtures of this row's set also lock the *sentence* rather than only the
  code is `@expect-message`'s own grep over them — a list here would go stale
  without reddening anything.
- **40 · `MemoryStorage` has no per-statement atomicity under autocommit: a failed DML's partial
  effects stand — every row it wrote before the failure stays written and every row it
  removed stays removed, and when the failure lands *after* the heap write that holds for a
  single-row statement too.** Measured against 18.6 on `--storage memory`:
  `CREATE TABLE fu (a INT CHECK (a < 3)); INSERT INTO fu VALUES
  (1),(2),(99);` raises `23514` on both engines, then `count(*)` is **2** here and **0**
  there. The same on a `NOT NULL` violation, a `UNIQUE` violation, a mid-statement eval
  error (`VALUES (1),(2),(10/0)`), and an `INSERT … SELECT`; `UPDATE` is worse, since the
  half-applied rows are *visible* rather than merely extra — `UPDATE gb SET a = a * 50`
  over `(1),(2),(3)` under `CHECK (a < 100)` leaves `50, 2, 3`. It is
  **profile-independent** (both build profiles measured identical), and the comparison that
  isolates it to this backend is the same statements run **under autocommit** on the other:
  the **B+tree** backend — the default, and what every consumer that matters selects —
  answers Postgres's result on each of those shapes there, and so does `MemoryStorage` under
  the native server's explicit `BEGIN`. Read that as the two measured positions it is and no
  wider — inside an *open* transaction the B+tree backend keeps a failed statement's partial
  effects too, which is its own bullet in this ledger. The mechanism is a missing
  bracket, and it goes missing by a different route on each driver. On the **native server**,
  where these rows were measured, there is no bracket to collapse: `run_one` reaches its
  wrapping branch only when `read_snapshot()` returns a snapshot, and
  `StorageBackend::read_snapshot` is `None` for `Self::Memory`
  (`crates/pglet/src/backend.rs`), so an autocommit write takes the unbracketed "traditional
  path". On the **embed/wasm driver** the bracket is written and collapses: `run_planned_env`
  wraps an autocommit write in an implicit storage transaction *precisely* to buy
  per-statement atomicity, but `StorageBackend::begin`/`commit`/`rollback` are `Ok(())` on
  the memory arm and `has_transaction` is hardcoded `false`, so the wrap is a no-op. Either
  way each row is applied in place as it is produced. The explicit-transaction shapes are
  correct by an unrelated route: the transaction session every host drives clones the
  entire `MemoryStorage` into its outer frame at `BEGIN` and restores it on rollback
  (`crates/pglet/src/transaction.rs`, the frame's `storage` snapshot). That is also why the class is
  doubly invisible to the differential harness — it runs against the B+tree server, and its
  `BEGIN … ROLLBACK` isolation wrapper is exactly the path that works.
  A `DO` statement is the exception on this backend: its undo takes a whole-store copy at a
  savepoint before its first statement and puts it back when the `DO` fails (row 249), so a
  failed `DO`'s rows do not stand — measured on `--storage memory` and the embed's
  `Database::in_memory`.

  **The member that needs no second row is the easiest one to miss, and it is the same
  bug.** `MemoryStorage::insert` writes the row into `data.rows` and *then*
  calls `index_insert_row`, propagating its error with the row already in place
  (`crates/pglet_storage/src/memory.rs`), where the B+tree wrapper emits the index ops into
  the same uncommitted batch and so discards the row along with it. So the split is *where*
  the check runs, not what it checks — and the two sides are "before the heap write" and
  "after it", **not** two named features. A **pre-store** check is correct on memory even
  for a single row: `CHECK`, `NOT NULL`, an `INSERT`'s own foreign key, and the `UNIQUE`
  probe (which the executor runs against the index *before* the write) all answer
  identically on all four server shapes. Everything **after** the write leaks, and it needs
  neither an index nor a constraint to do it. **An `UPDATE`'s foreign-key work is after
  the write** — its actions and its rows' own key checks run as 18.6's after-row triggers
  do, once the statement's rows are written (`executor::dml`'s `FkTriggerQueue`) — and so is
  an `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`'s over a table some foreign key references: its actions and the
  queued checks of the rows it inserts and of the rows it rewrites. So every refusal they
  raise leaks here, a single row's included, and an action's conversion of the key it
  assigns is one of them. Measured on memory over `p (k int
  PRIMARY KEY)` holding `1`, `2` and `c (id int PRIMARY KEY, pk int REFERENCES p)` holding
  `(1, 1)`: `UPDATE c SET pk = 999` is `23503` everywhere and leaves `c` holding `(1, 999)`
  here, where the same key refused by `INSERT INTO c VALUES (2, 999)` leaves nothing; with
  `r (k int REFERENCES p ON UPDATE RESTRICT)` holding `2`, `UPDATE p SET k = 20 WHERE k = 2`
  is `23001` and leaves `p` holding `1, 20`; over `p2` holding `1, 2, 3`, an `ON UPDATE SET
  NULL` child whose column is `NOT NULL` makes `UPDATE p2 SET k = 10 WHERE k = 1` `23502`
  and leaves `10`, and an `ON UPDATE CASCADE` child whose `CHECK (pk < 100)` the repoint
  breaks makes `UPDATE p2 SET k = 200 WHERE k = 2` `23514` and leaves `200` beside a child
  still holding `2`, which references no row; and over `p3` holding `1` under an `ON UPDATE
  RESTRICT` child, `INSERT INTO p3 VALUES (1) ON CONFLICT (k) DO UPDATE SET k = 5` is
  `23001` and leaves `5`. The upsert's queued checks, over `u (id int PRIMARY KEY, par int
  REFERENCES u ON UPDATE CASCADE)`: holding `(1, NULL)`, `INSERT INTO u VALUES (4, 1), (1,
  NULL) ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET id = 10` is `23503` and leaves `(4, 1), (10, NULL)`,
  the inserted row's check refusing after the move; holding `(1, NULL), (2, NULL)`, `INSERT
  INTO u VALUES (1, 0), (2, 0) ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET par = CASE WHEN u.id = 1 THEN 2
  ELSE u.par END, id = CASE WHEN u.id = 2 THEN 20 ELSE u.id END` is `23503` and leaves `(1,
  2), (20, NULL)`, a rewritten row's check refusing. And the conversion: over `pv (k
  varchar(10) PRIMARY KEY)` holding `'a'`, referenced `ON UPDATE CASCADE` by a `varchar(3)`
  column holding `'a'`, `UPDATE pv SET k = 'abcdef'` is `22001` and leaves `pv` holding
  `'abcdef'` beside a child still holding `'a'`. Postgres and the B+tree backend leave each table as it was. Non-unique index maintenance is one member — measured
  on a plain `int` table with no unindexable type in sight: `CREATE TABLE w (a INT); CREATE
  INDEX w_ix ON w ((10 / a)); INSERT INTO w VALUES (0);` is `22012` on Postgres, on B+tree
  and on memory alike, and `count(*)` is then **0** on Postgres and B+tree and **1** on
  memory — the statement reports failure and the row is there. **`RETURNING` evaluation is
  another, and it needs none of that** — over bare single-column `int` tables carrying no
  index and no constraint, `INSERT INTO r1 VALUES (0) RETURNING 10/a` leaves the inserted
  row in place, `UPDATE r2 SET a = 7 RETURNING 10/(a-7)` (over a seeded `5`) leaves the
  update applied, and `DELETE FROM r3 RETURNING 10/0` (over one seeded row) leaves the row
  **gone** — every one reported as a failure, every one profile-independent, every one
  matching Postgres on B+tree. The `DELETE` is the direction a "keeps the rows it wrote"
  framing misses: there memory holds *fewer* rows than Postgres, not more.

  Not fixed: giving the memory arm real transaction semantics is an atomicity change that
  needs its own guards.
- **41 · `index not found: <oid>` reaches the wire as `22000` with a raw internal OID.** Not
  silent-wrong — it is loud — but it is an internal identifier escaping into a client-facing
  message, with no relation name, no SQLSTATE of its own, and nothing a client can act on.
  **The one producer this bullet used to name is gone, and the general statement about
  which paths produce it stands.** *Any* catalog index the storage cannot resolve makes
  the accelerated *read* paths answer it and makes **every write that probes a unique
  index** answer it on *both* build profiles, since that probe reads the index before the
  write and is not behind `index_acceleration`; what does not probe does not — a NULL key
  succeeds (NULL skips the probe) and so does `DELETE`, since removal iterates the indexes
  the storage *has*. What produced such a state was the failed back-fill on
  `MemoryStorage`: `CREATE TABLE oy (id INT, j JSONB); INSERT INTO oy VALUES
  (1,'{"a":1}'),(2,'{"b":2}'); ALTER TABLE oy ADD CONSTRAINT oy_u UNIQUE (j)` left a
  catalog index that backend had never registered, after which `INSERT`, `UPDATE`,
  `COPY … FROM STDIN` and `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` all answered
  `execution error: index not found: <oid>`. A failed build now writes no catalog entry at
  all (`docs/ddl.md` § A failed index build), so that script's `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and
  `DELETE` all succeed on both backends now, leaving the two rows the script implies. The known producer now is the
  catalog/storage index-OID desync `test_soak`'s Leg C regression-locks; the other one recorded, the
  concurrent-DDL tier's refused rollback of a block's `CREATE INDEX` (row 217), is gone with the tier. A catalog the
  planner can name but the storage cannot resolve is an internal invariant break; the
  message should say so.
- **42 · Catalog completeness — largely closed.** The per-view status is `docs/compatibility.md`'s
  *pg_catalog* and *information_schema* rows; what closed is worth stating because
  the gap used to drop whole columns from an ORM's introspection join.
  `pg_type` now carries every scalar `TypeOid` plus its array type and every user enum —
  it used to hold fourteen hand-written scalars and no arrays, so the
  `pg_attribute ⨝ pg_type` join **dropped** a `numeric` / `time` / `interval` / array
  column outright. `information_schema.check_constraints` and `sequences` are modelled,
  `pg_constraint` / `pg_index` / `pg_enum` are populated, and `table_constraints` /
  `constraint_column_usage` carry their PK/UNIQUE rows — under the user's declared
  constraint name where there is one — their `NOT NULL` rows, and every CHECK row, named
  or not.

  What survives: `pg_type` still omits `typispreferred` and the rest of 18.6's 32
  columns, `pg_class` has no `relkind = 'S'` row for a sequence (row 82), and the views
  pglet models at all are the ones `docs/compatibility.md` lists.
- **43 · Session-setup and introspection shapes a driver or ORM sends first, measured
  on a spawned server against 18.6.**
  (1) **`search_path` pointed at a schema pglet does not have — closed on every door that can
  name it — `SET`, `set_config` and the startup packet's key and `options` — and a computed
  `set_config` name is refused rather than echoed.**
  It used to be discarded like every other `SET` argument: a name no schema held was
  accepted and reads kept answering from `public` where 18.6 is `42P01`, so a
  schema-per-test harness read and wrote one shared schema believing itself isolated.
  The first repair gated the `SET` **statement** and left the **function** spelling —
  `SELECT pg_catalog.set_config('search_path', 'nosuch', false)`, which is the line
  modern `pg_dump` emits and the CVE-2018-1058 hardening idiom — walking straight past
  it; the gate is a property of the *request*, not of the statement that spelled it, and
  both routes now reach one decider (`catalog::check_search_path_elements`). The startup
  packet's two doors — a `search_path` key and a `-c search_path=…` in its `options`, the
  spelling `pg`'s `options` connection setting sends — reach it too, judged on the value the
  startup ends with and refused as a `FATAL`
  (`handlers::tests::startup_reads_its_settings_as_18_6_does`, and `test:pg`'s `options` test). Refused
  `0A000` — deliberately **stricter** than 18.6, which accepts any name here. The
  accepted set is exact and hard-coded, not "a schema pglet has": `public` in any
  spelling, `DEFAULT`, the two elements that select no schema of their own (`"$user"`,
  `pg_catalog`), and the empty list. `information_schema` is refused although pglet
  models it, and so are `pg_temp` / `pg_temp_N` — correctly, since an unqualified name
  under any of those resolves in `public` here and nowhere there, which is row 66's
  residual under another name. The `set_config` route reads its **setting name** as a
  literal and refuses a computed one rather than echoing it — row 70.
  Two readers feed the one decider because 18.6 has two as well —
  `SET search_path = 'a, b'` stores one schema literally named `a, b`
  (`flatten_set_variable_args` quotes each string element) while
  `set_config('search_path','a, b',false)` stores the string raw and it is two,
  measured. The residual is **row 66**.
  (2) **`SHOW server_version` and the startup `ParameterStatus` — closed.** Both claimed
  `16.0`, from two separately typed copies of the string, and `server_version_num` was
  `42704`. Both now render one table (`ShowVariable::report`, via
  `catalog::startup_parameters` for the startup block) and report `18.6` / `180006` — the
  release the differential corpus is asserted against, which names the **dialect target**
  and not feature completeness. `SHOW` also answers the other seven parameters the startup
  block asserts, which it used to answer `42704` while the same connection reported them.
  The residual is `SHOW server_version`'s exact string: 18.6 appends a packaging suffix
  (`18.6 (Debian 18.6-1.pgdg13+2)`) that pglet does not, which is why that one parameter
  is pinned by a unit test rather than by a differential fixture.

  The startup **list** was wrong too, and the comment justifying it stated the oracle
  backwards: it said `search_path` is not `GUC_REPORT`, where 18.6 sends it at connect
  *and* after every `SET`/`set_config` that moves it (it has carried the flag since
  PostgreSQL 14). Measured with a raw v3 client, 18.6's packet is `in_hot_standby`,
  `integer_datetimes`, `TimeZone`, `IntervalStyle`, `search_path`, `is_superuser`,
  `application_name`, `default_transaction_read_only`, `scram_iterations`, `DateStyle`,
  `standard_conforming_strings`, `session_authorization`, `client_encoding`,
  `server_version`, `server_encoding`. pglet now sends the ten of those it models a
  value for, and — the other half of `GUC_REPORT` — a `ParameterStatus` after a session
  command that **moves** one (on change only, which is 18.6's rule: a second identical
  `SET search_path TO public` sends nothing there, measured). `application_name` is what
  makes that rule non-vacuous: it is the one modelled parameter whose value is the
  session's, seeded from the startup packet and moved by `SET`/`RESET`/`DISCARD ALL`.
  The five it omits are `in_hot_standby`, `is_superuser`,
  `default_transaction_read_only`, `scram_iterations` and `session_authorization` —
  parameters pglet models no value for. (`transaction_isolation` and
  `server_version_num` are modelled and are correctly absent: 18.6 reports neither.)
  `search_path`'s own reported string never moves — row 66. (3) **Text compares in byte order** where the oracle's
  databases — the fixture harness's `postgres` included — are `en_US.UTF-8`: `'A' < 'a'` is
  `t` here and `f` there, `ORDER BY s` over `b, A, a, B, _x, Z` answers `A, B, Z, _x, a, b`
  against `a, A, b, B, _x, Z`, and `WHERE s BETWEEN 'A' AND 'b'` answers **6 rows against 2** —
  a different row set, not only an order. An index build over more than one oversized
  entry names the one first in byte order, where 18.6 names the first in its collation: over
  a `text` column holding `'B'` and `'a'` followed by 2 800 and 2 750 random characters,
  `CREATE INDEX` reports the `B` row's `2816` here and the `a` row's `2768` there, and a GIN
  index over one array of the two the same (measured). A grouping query lets no
  comparison of strings decide which branch's aggregates run — it keeps every branch,
  loud where 18.6 folds the comparison (row 89's residuals) — but the comparison itself
  is still evaluated by bytes, and a case mapping by Unicode's rule rather than the
  locale's: `upper('ß')` is `SS` here and `ß` there. ICU collation is a decided size cut
  (`TRADEOFFS.md`); pglet ≡ Postgres only at `LC_COLLATE=C`, and no fixture covers the
  difference because every fixture's data happens to sort the same both ways. (4) **closed** — **`json` was
  `jsonb`**: `'{"b":1,"a":2}'::json` rendered `{"a": 2, "b": 1}`, `'{"a":1,"a":2}'::json` dropped
  a key, and a `json` column reported wire OID 3802, not 114. The spelling answers `42704` now,
  at each position that resolves a type name, as any type pglet does not model does.
  **The residual is not the spelling but the wire**, and it sits at the width of the
  measurement — the general unmodelled-declared-OID gap, not a `json` one: `pglet_wire`'s
  `Parse` decoder maps a declared parameter OID through `TypeOid::from_oid` into an
  `Option`, so an OID pglet does not model is indistinguishable from an unspecified `0`.
  Measured with a raw v3 client — no SQL text can spell this — over `Parse "SELECT $1"`
  with `'1'` bound: `114` (json), `199` (json[]), `790` (money), `142` (xml), `2205`
  (regclass), `1042` (bpchar), `1014` (bpchar[]) and a wholly fictional `999999` all
  answer `ParameterDescription [0]` here, where 18.6 echoes the declared OID for the real
  ones and refuses `999999` outright — `XX000 cache lookup failed for type 999999`, with
  no `ParameterDescription` at all. pglet then runs the statement as `text` and returns
  the row rather than raising anything, `999999` included — and that row need not be 18.6's
  answer: `790` is `$1.00` there, `199` and `1014` `22P02`.
  The **controls agree at the description and not always past it**, which is a second gap
  the description alone cannot show: `3802`, `3807` and `26` are modelled, so their
  `ParameterDescription` echoes on both engines — but of those only `3802` and `3807` also
  agree at `Execute`. The same `'1'` under a declared `26` is
  `42846 cannot cast type text to oid` here against 18.6's row, and under `3807` it is the
  array reader's `22P02` on both. Closing the first is `TypeOid::from_oid`'s question
  rather than this member's.
  (5) **closed** — `pg_constraint` and
  `pg_index` were empty relations that accepted any column name (an ORM's FK/index discovery
  join read "no foreign keys, no indexes"); both are populated from the catalog now and an
  unmodelled column is `42703`. (6) **closed** — `ErrorResponse` carried only `S`, `C`, `M`,
  so node-postgres reported `err.constraint === undefined` where 18.6 names `t_pkey`; the
  structured fields `D`/`s`/`t`/`c`/`n`/`P` are sent now at 18.6's positions, and what is
  still omitted is row 76. (7) **`pg_type` is present but short of columns,
  and `pg_range` is absent entirely** — the opposite failure to (5), in the same catalog
  sweep a driver makes first: `SELECT typbasetype FROM pg_catalog.pg_type` is
  `42703 column "typbasetype" does not exist` here (likewise `typrelid`) against 18.6's
  `oid` column, while `typname`/`typtype`/`typelem` answer; `SELECT 1 FROM
  pg_catalog.pg_range` is `42P01`. Both are **loud**, and the blast radius is what makes
  them worth a row: tokio-postgres's `TYPEINFO_QUERY` joins `pg_range` *and* selects both
  of those columns, so removing the join still leaves `42703 column "t.typbasetype" does
  not exist` — and the driver's fallback query is keyed on `UNDEFINED_TABLE`, which
  `42703` is not, so it is never even tried (and is itself `42704 type "oid" is not
  supported` on its `NULL::OID`). Inside a transaction block the first refusal aborts it
  and every later statement is `25P02`. Measured on both engines; the chain in full is
  row 57's bullet. (8) **retired** — `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` double-claims: both wait-policy spellings are refused `0A000` now (`docs/compatibility.md`'s `FOR UPDATE` row, `select/for_update_{skip_locked,nowait}_loud.sql`), so the double-claim is unreachable rather than silent. What stays accepted is the rest of the clause, whose semantic refusals are row 30's. The open members are (3) text collation and (7) `pg_type`/`pg_range`, and of the two only (7) is actionable — (3)'s ICU collation is a decided size cut (`TRADEOFFS.md`). A closed member's residual, where it has one, is stated at that member.

  Row 76 holds what is left of the `ErrorResponse` fields.
- **66 · pglet's `search_path` is a value it reports, not a cell it keeps.** Every list
  the gate accepts (row 43) resolves the same way here — to the one `public` schema — so
  pglet keeps no session cell for the string and reports 18.6's own default,
  `"$user", public`, at connect, from `SHOW`, and after any accepted `SET`, `set_config` or
  startup `search_path` (a startup `pg_catalog`, `''` or `"$user"` included). 18.6 keeps the
  string: it echoes the accepted list from `SHOW` and announces it with a
  `ParameterStatus` (`GUC_REPORT`). Measured: `SET search_path TO public` is
  `CC SET, PS search_path=public, Ready` there and `CC SET, Ready` here; `SHOW search_path`
  after it is `public` there and `"$user", public` here. **Silent**, and it has a second
  observable with the same root: a list that names no schema at all — the empty one
  `pg_dump`'s preamble writes (`set_config('search_path', '', false)`), or a
  `pg_catalog`-only or `"$user"`-only list — makes every *unqualified* name `42P01` on
  18.6 and still resolves to `public` here. Accepting the empty list is deliberate
  (`test:pg-dump` is a gate and the preamble is that line), and it is invisible to the
  dump that motivates it because `pg_dump` schema-qualifies every name it writes. Closing
  it needs a resolution-time model of an empty `search_path` — a multi-schema feature, not
  a session cell — which is why it is a row and not a fix.

  Four spellings read that reported string and they agree here because none of them is a
  session cell: `SHOW search_path`, `current_setting('search_path')`,
  `current_schema`/`current_schema()` and `current_schemas(bool)`. `current_schema` answers the
  constant `public` and `current_schemas` the constants `{pg_catalog,public}` and `{public}`,
  one per polarity of its boolean argument — after a `SET`, after a `RESET`, and after the
  empty list `pg_dump` writes alike. 18.6's readers move with the list, measured:
  `SET search_path TO pg_catalog, public` puts `current_schema` at `pg_catalog`, and
  `SET search_path TO ''` makes it **NULL**. An unqualified name under a list that names no
  schema is `42P01` there and still resolves to `public` here, which is this row's second
  observable and not a second cause.
- **67 · The GUC-echo family accepts a name Postgres does not.** `SET nosuchguc = 1` and
  `RESET nosuchguc` report `SET` / `RESET` here against 18.6's
  `42704 unrecognized configuration parameter "nosuchguc"`. The accept is the family's
  posture and is deliberate: pglet models a dozen of the ~350 settings, and refusing every
  name outside that dozen would refuse `statement_timeout`, `lock_timeout` and the rest of
  a real pool's check-in list, which is the traffic this seam exists to pass. The two
  spellings agree with each other, which is what keeps it one row. Silent, and the error
  direction is the safe one only because a GUC pglet does not model is one it does not act
  on either.

  **One setting 18.6 has is refused on rather than echoed: `quote_all_identifiers`.** 18.6's
  `quote_identifier` reads it, so with it on `quote_ident('abc')` is `"abc"`,
  `pg_get_serial_sequence` answers quoted names and `pg_get_constraintdef` reads `CHECK
  (("a" > 0))` (measured); pglet honors it in none of those readers, so echoing the `SET` would
  leave each answering the unquoted spelling with no error. `SET quote_all_identifiers` to a
  value 18.6's Boolean reader takes as on (`on`, `true`, `1`, `'Yes'`, the prefix `'tr'`), and
  `set_config('quote_all_identifiers', 'on', …)`, are `0A000`; `off`, `0`, the prefix `'of'`,
  `DEFAULT` and `RESET` pass; a value that reader refuses (`'o'`, `' on'`, `2`, `'maybe'`) is
  18.6's own `22023 parameter "quote_all_identifiers" requires a Boolean value`. The value
  reaches that reader as 18.6's grammar builds it: a list (`on, off`) is `22023 SET
  quote_all_identifiers takes only one argument`, a signed number is read as `NumericOnly`
  (`-1` the Boolean `22023`, `- 0` off), and an integer literal is its integer (`01`, `0_1`,
  `+1` on, so `0A000`). The name is matched case-insensitively whatever its quoting, as 18.6's
  `find_option` matches it, so `SET "Quote_All_Identifiers" = on`, `SET LOCAL
  "QUOTE_ALL_IDENTIFIERS" TO true` and `set_config('Quote_All_Identifiers', 'on', false)` are
  the same `0A000` (all measured; `functions/quote_ident_quote_all_identifiers_*`,
  `functions/set_config_quote_all_identifiers_*`, `commands/set_guc_quoted_mixed_case_*`).
  The startup packet decides it at both of its doors — the key `quote_all_identifiers=on` (any
  case) and an assignment in its `options`, which pglet reads as 18.6 reads it: split by
  `pg_split_opts` (C `isspace`, the vertical tab included; backslash escapes) and read by
  `process_postgres_switches`' `getopt` (clustered switches, `-Ec quote_all_identifiers=on`; a
  switch's argument taken from the next word, so `-d -cquote_all_identifiers=on` sets nothing;
  `--`; `--quote-all-identifiers=on`). 18.6 applies `options` first, then the other keys in
  packet order, each checked as it is read, the last one the session's value — and pglet's
  refusal is judged on that last value: on is `FATAL 0A000` and the connection closes, a
  non-Boolean anywhere `FATAL 22023` as on 18.6, and `-c quote_all_identifiers=on
  -c quote_all_identifiers=off`, or `options` on with the key `off`, starts a session, as on
  18.6 (all measured; `handlers::tests::startup_reads_its_settings_as_18_6_does`, the `startup`
  module's tests). The `options` key is matched by its exact spelling, as 18.6's `strcmp` does;
  an `OPTIONS` key is a setting name 18.6 does not have — `FATAL 42704` there, ignored here, this
  row's posture, as are an `options` assignment of an unknown name (`-cx=1`), of a setting
  pglet does not model whose value 18.6 refuses (`-S -cquote_all_identifiers=on` is `work_mem`'s
  `22023` there), and of one 18.6 will not change in a session (`-p 5`, `-B 100`, `-F`,
  `-c server_version=1`: `55P02` there). Residuals: `SHOW
  quote_all_identifiers` is `42704` here against 18.6's `off`; `set_config(…, NULL, false)`
  answers NULL here and `off` there (row 69's echo); and `SET LOCAL quote_all_identifiers = on`
  outside a block is `0A000` here where 18.6 warns `25P01` and answers `SET`, changing nothing.
  That refusal is kept: in a multi-statement query's implicit block 18.6's `SET LOCAL` takes
  effect (`SET LOCAL quote_all_identifiers = on; SELECT quote_ident('abc')` answers `"abc"`,
  measured), and pglet has no implicit block (row 68) to tell the two apart.
- **224 · A `CancelRequest` and the timeout settings are accepted and not acted on.**
  Measured on the native server, in-memory B+tree backend, with npm `pg` 8.16.3 against
  18.6. pglet has no `pg_sleep` (row 44), so its long statement is `SELECT count(*) FROM big
  a, big b` over a 2 000-row `big`, which runs for seconds; 18.6's is `SELECT pg_sleep(2)`.
  - `Client#cancel` 300 ms into the statement: pglet answers the count when it finishes, and
    the connection serves on; 18.6 answers `57014 canceling statement due to user request`
    at once.
  - `SET statement_timeout = '500ms'`, then the statement: pglet answers `SET`, then the
    count; 18.6 answers `57014 canceling statement due to statement timeout` at about 500
    ms.
  - The settings at startup — pg's `statement_timeout` and
    `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` options, and `transaction_timeout` through
    `options=-c …`: pglet connects, and `SHOW` of each answers `42704 unrecognized
    configuration parameter`; 18.6 shows each value and times the statement out.
  - `SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '500ms'`, `BEGIN`, 1.5 s idle, `SELECT 1`:
    pglet answers; 18.6 ends the session `25P03 terminating connection due to
    idle-in-transaction timeout`, and the client's next query fails. `transaction_timeout`
    in its place: the same, `25P04 terminating connection due to transaction timeout` on
    18.6. That timeout is not an idle one there: `ProcessInterrupts` (`postgres.c`) ends
    the session whose transaction outlasts it, whether it is waiting for the client or
    running a statement; only the idle form was measured.
  - In psql, the `statement_timeout`, `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` and
    `transaction_timeout` `SET`s, and `SET LOCAL statement_timeout` inside a block, answer
    `SET`; `SHOW` of each and `current_setting('statement_timeout')` answer `42704`,
    where 18.6 answers the value.

  Read in the source: `connection.rs` answers a `CancelRequest` by closing that packet's own
  connection with no reply (its comment: pglet implements no query cancellation), and
  nothing reaches the backend the request names by `pid`/`secret`. Row 67 is the family's
  posture — pglet accepts a setting it does not model — but there 18.6 refuses the name;
  here 18.6 models each setting and acts on it. Silent: a statement the client cancelled or
  bounded runs and answers, and an idle block's session is not ended. No fixture sends a
  `CancelRequest` or waits; a spawned two-connection test would pin the cancel, and a
  session test the timeouts.

  **`lock_timeout` has left the row.** It bounds the one wait pglet has, a statement
  waiting for the writer, and answers `55P03 canceling statement due to lock timeout` past
  it — the code 18.6's `ProcessInterrupts` raises when a lock wait outlasts it
  (`ERRCODE_LOCK_NOT_AVAILABLE`), not the `57014` of a cancel or a statement timeout; `SET`, `SET LOCAL`, `RESET`, the startup parameter, `SHOW` and `current_setting` read
  it with 18.6's units and range (`catalog::parse_lock_timeout`), a list is `22023 SET
  lock_timeout takes only one argument`, and it is transactional as 18.6's GUCs are — a `SET`
  in a block is taken back by its `ROLLBACK`, a `SET` or `SET LOCAL` after a savepoint by a
  `ROLLBACK TO` it (`writer.rs`'s `the_settings_pglet_acts_on_are_transactional`, embedded;
  18.6's side read in `guc.c`, not run). The server's `--lock-timeout`
  and the embed's `Database::set_default_lock_timeout` move the default. `set_config`
  cannot set it at all: `set_config('lock_timeout', '5s', false)` is refused `0A000 not
  implemented: set_config cannot set lock_timeout; use SET` (row 69). The default is
  pglet's `1s`, where 18.6's `0` waits without a bound — deliberately, so a block left open
  by a client that went quiet fails the next writer loudly instead of hanging it. A
  `CancelRequest` during a writer wait is ignored like any other, and the cancelled write
  proceeds when the wait ends.

- **68 · A multi-statement simple `Query` is not one transaction.** Postgres wraps every
  statement of one `Query` message in a single implicit transaction; pglet runs them as
  per-statement autocommit (the transactions row in `docs/compatibility.md`). `DISCARD ALL` is the
  measured member: `Q "SELECT 1; DISCARD ALL; SELECT 2"` is
  `SELECT 1, ERROR 25001 DISCARD ALL cannot run inside a transaction block` on 18.6 and
  runs all three here. The **explicit** `BEGIN; DISCARD ALL` in one message is `25001` on
  both, which is what `commands/discard_all_in_transaction_block.sql` pins — so the guard
  covers the block pglet models and not the block it does not. Silent. The same root
  divergence has a heavier consequence the transactions row already carries: an error
  mid-batch rolls the whole message back on 18.6 and leaves the earlier statements
  committed here. A **setting** is one of them, whichever it is: `SET lock_timeout = '7s';
  SET default_transaction_isolation = 'serializable'; SET application_name = 'imp'; SELECT
  1/0` sent as one `Query` leaves `SHOW` answering `7s`, `serializable` and `imp`, and the
  connection's next `BEGIN` runs `SERIALIZABLE` (measured with psql on the in-memory B+tree
  and `--storage memory`; the `lock_timeout` one alone on `--data-dir` too), where 18.6's
  failed implicit block takes every `SET` back — `0`, `read committed`, `psql`, and the next
  block `READ COMMITTED` (measured) — silent: a later wait uses the value, and the next
  block runs `SERIALIZABLE`, under row 232's refusals. The settings are transactional
  only within an explicit block (`SessionSettings`), which a `Query` of its own does not
  open. A later statement that fails 18.6's **raw parse** is a different
  mechanism — 18.6 runs no statement of the message at all, an explicit `COMMIT` before it
  included — and is row 175.
- **141 · An extended-protocol pipeline is not one transaction.** pglet commits each
  `Execute` on its own; 18.6 (`exec_execute_message` and `start_xact_command`,
  `src/backend/tcop/postgres.c`) can leave a completed `Execute` uncommitted until `Sync`
  and treat what follows as an implicit block, with the results below. Measured on a raw v3 client over
  `CREATE TABLE rb (a int4)`, no block open, each pipeline ended by one `Sync` and then
  read back with `SELECT a FROM rb`; "a refused `Bind`" is a 5-byte binary `int4`:

  | pipeline | 18.6 | pglet |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `INSERT (1)`, `INSERT (2)`, a refused `Bind` | `22P03`; rows none | `22P03`; rows `1, 2` |
  | `INSERT (7)`, a `Parse` of `SELEC` | `42601`; the row not kept | `42601`; the row kept |
  | `INSERT (1)`, `BEGIN`, `INSERT (2)`, `ROLLBACK` | no error; rows none | no error; rows `1` |
  | `INSERT (1)`, `BEGIN`, `INSERT (2)`, a refused `Bind`; then `ROLLBACK` | `[E]`; rows none | `[E]`; rows `1` |
  | `BEGIN`, `INSERT (1)`, `COMMIT`, `INSERT (2)`, a refused `Bind` | rows `1` | rows `1, 2` |
  | `INSERT (1)`, `COMMIT`, a refused `Bind` | rows `1`, and a `NoticeResponse` at the `COMMIT` | rows `1`, no notice |
  | `INSERT (1)`, `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY rb_i ON rb (a)` | `25001 CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block`; rows none | accepted; rows `1` |
  | `INSERT (1)`, `DISCARD ALL` | `25001 DISCARD ALL cannot run inside a transaction block`; rows none | accepted; rows `1` |
  | `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY rb_j ON rb (a)`, then `INSERT (1)` | accepted; rows `1` | the same |
  | `DISCARD ALL`, then `INSERT (1)` | accepted; rows `1` | the same |

  So a `BEGIN` inside a pipeline takes the writes before it into its block, and its
  `ROLLBACK` undoes them. The `DISCARD ALL` member is row 68's `25001` reached through the
  extended protocol. A pipeline's `SELECT 1/0` also raises at a different phase on each
  engine, which is row 60's member.

- **69 · A parameter's value is fixed, and a `SET` that moves it is refused.**
  pglet has one session zone (`UTC`), one date style (`ISO, MDY`), one interval style
  (`postgres`) and one reading of a string literal (`standard_conforming_strings` on). 18.6
  moves each: after `SET TIME ZONE 'America/New_York'`, `SHOW TimeZone` is
  `America/New_York`, `'2024-01-01 03:00+00'::timestamptz::date` is `2023-12-31` and its
  `::text` `2023-12-31 22:00:00-05`; after `SET DateStyle = 'German'`, `DATE '2024-01-02'`
  renders `02.01.2024` (measured). pglet answered `SET` to each and went on answering in UTC
  and ISO — **that silent half is closed**: a value other than the one pglet has is
  `0A000 <name> "<value>" is not supported: pglet's is always "<fixed>"`, through one decider
  (`catalog::commands`' `check_fixed_guc`) reached by `SET <name> {TO|=}`, `SET [SESSION|LOCAL]
  TIME ZONE`, `set_config` and the native server's startup packet (its own key and an
  `options` assignment, `-e` included, judged on the value the startup ends with). **What
  stays open is the refusal itself** — real time zones and the other styles are not
  modelled, so a session that needs one cannot run here.

  The value pglet has is accepted, matched case-insensitively, and after each of these
  18.6's `SHOW` answers what pglet's does (measured): `TimeZone` `UTC` (as a string, a bare
  or a quoted identifier); `DateStyle` `ISO, MDY`, `ISO,MDY`, `ISO`, `MDY`, the two-word list
  `ISO, MDY` and the empty string; `IntervalStyle` `postgres`; `standard_conforming_strings`
  any Boolean that is on. `DEFAULT`, `SET TIME ZONE LOCAL`, `RESET` and `RESET ALL` are
  accepted as the resets they are, and `set_config` of an accepted spelling returns the
  fixed value, as 18.6 returns the setting as it stands (`UTC` for `'utc'`).

  **Loud where 18.6 accepts**, beyond a genuinely different value — each measured:

  | statement | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SET TIME ZONE 'GMT'`, `'Etc/UTC'`, `'UTC0'`, `0`, `'+00'` | `0A000` | `SET`; `SHOW` answers `GMT`, `Etc/UTC`, `UTC0`, `<+00>-00`, `<+00>-00` |
  | `SET TIME ZONE INTERVAL '0' HOUR TO MINUTE` | `42601` | `SET`; `SHOW` answers `<+00>-00` |
  | `SET timezone FROM CURRENT` | `42601` | `SET` |
  | `SET DateStyle = 'MDY, ISO'`, `'US'`, `'ISO, US'`, `'NonEuropean'`, `'DEFAULT'`, `' ISO , MDY '`, `'ISO, ISO'` | `0A000` | `SET`; `SHOW` answers `ISO, MDY` |
  | `SET DateStyle = 'ISO', 'MDY'` and `"ISO", "MDY"` (a list of quoted elements) | `0A000` | `SET`; `SHOW` answers `ISO, MDY` |
  | `set_config('timezone', 'U' \|\| 'TC', false)` (a value that is not a literal) | `0A000` | `UTC` |
  | `set_config('application_name', 'zz', false)`, `set_config('lock_timeout', '5s', false)` | `0A000 set_config cannot set <name>; use SET` | the setting moved, and `SHOW` answers it |

  The first row is deliberate rather than a missing spelling: 18.6 shows a zero-offset zone
  under its own name, pglet's `SHOW` answers `UTC`, and accepting one would put back the
  disagreement between a `SET` and the `SHOW` after it. The last row closes the other
  silent member this bullet carried — `set_config` lowers to an expression the session never
  sees, so it answered `zz` and `SHOW application_name` went on answering the value held
  before.

  **Loud under another code where 18.6 refuses too** — pglet has no list of zones or style
  words to tell a value 18.6 does not know from one it does, so each takes the refusal
  above: `SET TIME ZONE 'Nowhere/Nope'`, `'Z'`, `' UTC'` and `''` are `0A000` here and `22023
  invalid value for parameter "TimeZone"` there; `SET DateStyle = 'bogus'`, `'ISO, SQL'`
  (conflicting) and `'ISO,,MDY'`, and `SET IntervalStyle = 'bogus'`, likewise `0A000` against
  `22023`; `SET TIME ZONE INTERVAL '1 month'` is `42601` against `22023`, and `SET datestyle =
  iso,` `22023` against `42601`. `standard_conforming_strings` is the exception: a value that
  is no Boolean is 18.6's own `22023 … requires a Boolean value` here
  (`commands/set_standard_conforming_strings_not_boolean_loud.sql`).

  **On the native server** the same decider reads the startup packet, so a client that sends
  one of these parameters at connect with another value is refused `FATAL 0A000` where 18.6
  serves it (`handlers::tests::startup_reads_its_settings_as_18_6_does`); `TimeZone=UTC` and
  `DateStyle=ISO` are served. The refusal is judged on the value the startup ends with, and
  18.6's own check of `TimeZone`, `DateStyle` and `IntervalStyle` is not modelled, so an assignment 18.6 refuses
  where it is read is not refused here when a later one overrides it: `options` `-c
  timezone=Nowhere/Nope` with the key `timezone=UTC` is `FATAL 22023` there and served here
  (measured, libpq's `PGOPTIONS` and `PGTZ`).

  **Still silent**, each measured: `SET TIME 'UTC'`, `SET "time" zone 'UTC'` and `SET time
  "zone" 'UTC'` answer `SET` where 18.6 answers `42601` (row 67's shape — a `SET` naming no
  setting with no assignment is accepted); `SET server_version = '1'`, `SET integer_datetimes
  = on` and `RESET server_version` answer `SET` / `RESET` where 18.6 answers `55P02
  parameter "…" cannot be changed`, and `set_config('server_version', '18.6', false)` echoes
  its argument against the same `55P02` — nothing moves on either engine; and a parameter
  18.6 has that pglet does not model is accepted and not acted on — `SET bytea_output =
  'escape'` then `SELECT '\x616263'::bytea` answers `\x616263` here and `abc` there, and
  after `SET default_transaction_read_only = on`, or `SET transaction_read_only = on` in a
  block, an `INSERT` succeeds here and is `25006` there (`extra_float_digits` below `1` is
  row 255's residual, the timeouts row 224's).

  **`client_encoding` is refused on every route that can set it** (the startup packet's own key, matched case-insensitively, and an assignment in its `options` read as 18.6 reads one — row 67 — so `PGOPTIONS='-c client_encoding=LATIN1'`, which libpq forwards and JDBC's `options=` property also sends, and `-Ec client_encoding=LATIN1` are `FATAL 22023` here where 18.6 serves `LATIN1`. Each occurrence gets 18.6's own check where it is read — an encoding name 18.6 does not know is its `22023` even when a later one would override it — and pglet's UTF-8-only refusal is judged on the value the startup ends with, so `options` LATIN1 with the key `client_encoding=UTF8`, what psql sends under that `PGOPTIONS` on a UTF-8 terminal, is served, as on 18.6) — the `SET` statement,
  `SET NAMES`, `set_config`, **and the startup packet** — because an encoding decides
  whether bytes arrive intact, and pglet has no conversion layer. The packet is the route
  that matters, since libpq / JDBC / asyncpg set the parameter there: over a packet asking
  for `LATIN1`, 18.6 sends `63 61 66 e9` for `café` and pglet sends `63 61 66 c3 a9`,
  which that client renders `cafÃ©`. pglet now answers such a packet
  `FATAL 22023 invalid value for parameter "client_encoding": "…"` and closes, which is
  18.6's own shape for an encoding *it* cannot serve (`NOSUCHENC` — identical message and
  code); `LATIN1` is the pglet-stricter half, since 18.6 serves it by converting.
  Accepted: `UTF8`/`UTF-8`/`UNICODE` and **`SQL_ASCII`** in any of Postgres's spellings
  (its name match reads only a name's ASCII letters and digits, case folded —
  `clean_encoding_name` — after truncating it to 63 bytes, as every `GUC_IS_NAME` value is,
  without 18.6's `NOTICE 42622`: `SET client_encoding = 'utf8'` followed by 60 spaces sends
  `NOTICE 42622 identifier "…" will be truncated to "…"` there on every door, the startup
  packet's included, and no notice here, measured) —
  `SQL_ASCII` is "no conversion", which is
  what pglet does, and is what `pg_dump` of a `SQL_ASCII` database writes into its
  preamble. What is *not* closed is the echo: `SHOW client_encoding` answers `UTF8`
  whatever was accepted, where 18.6 echoes the request. The generic
  `set_config(<guc>, NULL, …)` is here too: 18.6 resets and returns the restored value
  (`set_config('statement_timeout', NULL, false)` answers `0`), pglet echoes the NULL —
  `search_path` and the fixed parameters above answer their value, a fixed string pglet
  can name. `default_transaction_isolation` is not moved by `set_config` either (row 232):
  a level that takes a transaction snapshot is `0A000` there, and `read committed` is
  answered and not recorded — after `SET default_transaction_isolation = 'serializable'`,
  `set_config('default_transaction_isolation', 'read committed', false)` answers `read
  committed` on both and `SHOW` is then `serializable` here and `read committed` there
  (measured), which is **silent**.
- **~~71~~ · Closed — an unparsed trailing word became an output alias, and the value was
  wrong.**
  `x ISNULL` and `x NOTNULL` are `gram.y` productions (`a_expr ISNULL` /
  `a_expr NOTNULL`, the historical spellings of `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL`) and were not
  in pglet's keyword table, so the word after the operand reads as an unaliased output
  label instead: `SELECT NULL ISNULL` answers NULL under a column named `isnull` where
  18.6 answers `t`, `SELECT 1 ISNULL` answers `1` against `f`, and `SELECT 1 NOTNULL`
  answers `1` against `t` — measured on both engines. Nothing is loud, and the shape is
  not exotic: an ORM emitting the short spelling gets a *column value* where it asked
  for a boolean, so a predicate over it (`WHERE x ISNULL`) filters on the operand rather
  than on its nullness.

  **The class is what matters here, not the two spellings.** Any postfix or trailing
  grammar word the parser does not consume lands in the same place — the alias reader —
  and the result is a wrong value rather than a syntax error. It is exactly the defect
  the `INTERVAL '…' <field>` qualifier had (`INTERVAL '90' MINUTE` answered ninety
  *seconds* under a column named `minute`) until that qualifier was parsed, and the
  repair there is the shape of the repair here: recognize the word in the production
  that owns it. What makes the class hard to see is that the corpus cannot: a faithful
  fixture is **red** (pglet's answer is the wrong one), so `@expect-error` cannot hold
  it and a value fixture cannot be recorded green. Re-deriving the class means sweeping
  `gram.y`'s postfix and trailing-word productions against this parser's, not extending
  a list of two.

  **What closed the two spellings.** `isnull` and `notnull` are keywords now, in
  `kwlist.h`'s class (`TYPE_FUNC_NAME_KEYWORD`), and the operator loop reads each at
  `IS`'s binding power (`%nonassoc IS ISNULL NOTNULL`) into the same `Expr::IsNull` /
  `Expr::IsNotNull` `IS [NOT] NULL` builds, so the output name (`?column?`), the stored
  rendering (`check_clause` `(a IS NOT NULL)`, as 18.6's) and the dump are that node's.
  The arm is `a_expr`'s only: `b_expr` has neither production, so `DEFAULT NULL ISNULL` is
  `42601` on both engines and `DEFAULT (NULL ISNULL)` is accepted on both. The class
  decides the bare-name positions too, measured on 18.6 and now here: `SELECT isnull FROM
  …`, `FROM t isnull` and `CREATE TABLE t (isnull int)` are `42601`, and `AS isnull` is a
  label on both; `test_keywords` sweeps the four positions for both words. Measured after
  the repair against 18.6, each agreeing: `SELECT NULL ISNULL, 1 NOTNULL` is `t | t`;
  `1 + NULL ISNULL` is `t`, `NULL = NULL ISNULL` `t`, `'a' LIKE 'a' ISNULL` `f`, `NOT NULL
  ISNULL` `f`, `NULL ISNULL ISNULL` `f`, `1 ISNULL IS FALSE` `t`; `WHERE a ISNULL` filters
  on nullness. Guards: the `operators/isnull_*` and `operators/notnull_*` fixtures, the
  precedence among them reddening under a mutation that binds the word as tightly as `::`.

  **What the two spellings inherit rather than open**, each measured and each `IS NULL`'s
  answer as well: `- NULL ISNULL` is `t` here against 18.6's `42725 operator is not
  unique: - unknown`. (`1 BETWEEN 0 AND 2 ISNULL`, `42883` here against `f`, was the
  `BETWEEN` bound's — row 299, closed.) `isnull(1)` is a call on both engines — a
  `TYPE_FUNC_NAME_KEYWORD` is a function name before `(` on 18.6, and pglet's primary
  reads it as one — and a call pglet does not build: `0A000 function not supported`
  against `42883 function isnull(integer) does not exist`, the loud
  *Wrong-SQLSTATE-class* member every unknown name is; `left('ab', 1)` answers `a` on both.

  **The class itself is open**, and its measured live member is silent: a single-field
  interval qualifier on a cast is still read as a label — `'1 year 2 mons'::interval year`
  answers `1 year 2 mons` under a column named `year` here against 18.6's `1 year`
  (`docs/temporal.md`). The struck number records the two spellings this row named, not
  the class.

- **~~299~~ · Closed — a `BETWEEN` read its upper bound at `AND`'s binding power.**
  `parser::expr`'s `parse_between` parsed the bound after `AND` with
  `parse_expr_bp(BP_AND + 1)`, so every operator binding tighter than `AND` — the
  comparisons, `IS …`, `ISNULL` / `NOTNULL` — is read into the bound. `gram.y`'s production
  is `a_expr BETWEEN opt_asymmetric b_expr AND a_expr %prec BETWEEN`, and `BETWEEN` binds
  tighter than the comparisons and `IS` (`%nonassoc BETWEEN IN_P LIKE …` above `%nonassoc
  '<' '>' '=' …` above `%nonassoc IS ISNULL NOTNULL`), so on 18.6 such an operator takes
  the whole `BETWEEN` as its left operand. Measured on both engines:
  `NULL::bool BETWEEN false AND true IS NULL` is NULL here — `NULL BETWEEN false AND (true
  IS NULL)` — against `t` there, and its `ISNULL` spelling the same; `1 BETWEEN 0 AND 2 =
  true` and `1 BETWEEN 0 AND 2 IS NOT DISTINCT FROM true` are `42883` here against `t`, and
  `1 BETWEEN 0 AND 2 ISNULL` `42883` against `f`. **Silent** where the bound and the
  operator's right side are both boolean, loud wherever the misread bound fails to type.
  The lower bound, a `b_expr` in `gram.y`, was read at the same binding power in full
  `a_expr` mode, so a word `b_expr` lacks was read into it: `true BETWEEN NULL IS NULL AND
  true` answered `t` here against `42601`, `1 BETWEEN NOT 0 AND 2` was `42804` against
  `42601`, and — once `ISNULL` / `NOTNULL` were read as postfix tests (row 71) —
  `true BETWEEN NULL NOTNULL AND true` answered `t` and `1 NOT BETWEEN NULL ISNULL AND 2`
  was `42883`, both `42601` on 18.6 and at the build before row 71's close.

  **What closed it.** `parse_between` reads the two bounds as the production does: the
  lower one in `b_expr` mode (so `AND` ends it and a postfix null test, an `IS [NOT] NULL`
  or a prefix `NOT` there is the syntax error 18.6 raises), the upper one at `BP_PRED + 1`
  (so only what binds tighter than `BETWEEN` — `||`, `+`, a cast — stays in it). And
  `BETWEEN` being `%nonassoc` with `IN`, `LIKE` and `ILIKE`, one of those — or its `NOT`
  spelling — directly after the bound is refused `42601`, where reading the upper bound at
  the new binding power alone would have chained it onto the `BETWEEN`'s result and
  answered. Measured after the repair against 18.6, each agreeing: every member above;
  `1 NOT BETWEEN 0 AND 2 = false` `t`; `1 BETWEEN 0 AND 2 BETWEEN false AND true`, `… IN
  (true)`, `… NOT IN (true)` and `… LIKE 't'` `42601`; and the controls `'b' BETWEEN 'a' AND
  'c' || 'x'`, `1 BETWEEN 0 AND 1 + 1`, `1 BETWEEN 0 AND 2 AND true`, `NOT 1 BETWEEN 0 AND
  2`, `1 BETWEEN (0 IS NOT NULL)::int AND 2`, `2 BETWEEN 1 + 0 AND 3`, and `1 BETWEEN 0 < 1
  AND 2` (`42883` on both, the lower bound keeping its comparison). Residual, loud and
  pre-existing: `opt_asymmetric` is not read, so `1 BETWEEN SYMMETRIC 2 AND 0` and `1
  BETWEEN ASYMMETRIC 0 AND 2` are `42601` here and `t` there. Guards: the
  `operators/between_*` fixtures and `operators/not_between_lower_bound_isnull_loud.sql`.

- **72 · Extensions are a name check, not a catalog.** `CREATE`/`DROP EXTENSION`
  parse with their full option tails and decide one thing — whether the **name** is
  one this engine provides — because there is nothing else to decide without
  installation state, and pglet keeps none: `gen_random_uuid()` and
  `uuid_generate_v4()` are builtins here, resolvable with or without the statement.
  That makes four of the six measured shapes exact, including the only one a
  migration actually writes (`CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS`), and leaves three
  **over-acceptances**, all in the same direction: a bare repeat succeeds where 18.6
  answers `42710 extension "pgcrypto" already exists`; the bare
  `CREATE EXTENSION plpgsql` succeeds where 18.6 refuses it from the very first
  statement, that extension being pre-installed there; and `DROP EXTENSION pgcrypto`
  with nothing created succeeds against 18.6's `42704`.

  A persisted set would close those three and **not** the fourth, which is why it is
  listed apart: the `VERSION` option is parsed and dropped, so
  `CREATE EXTENSION pgcrypto VERSION '99.9'` succeeds where 18.6 answers
  `22023 … has no installation script nor update path for version "99.9"`. Knowing
  that needs a per-extension version list, a different fact from *whether* an
  extension is installed. The `SCHEMA` option was a fifth and is closed rather than
  recorded — pglet models exactly one schema, so `SCHEMA nosuchschema` is `3F000`
  here as there, with no state needed to say so.

  This is **not** a member of the absent-but-fail-loud row above, and the difference
  is the column that matters: those are loud, these are silent. The cost of the trade
  is written out in [ddl.md](docs/ddl.md) § Extensions are a name check, not a
  catalog — a persisted set buys 18.6's `42710` and a truthful `pg_extension` for a
  store-magic bump and a ledger line, over a fact no query in the engine reads.

  The same missing state reaches statements outside the extension grammar. One is `DROP SCHEMA`: a
  `DROP SCHEMA public` without `CASCADE` refuses over the tables, enums and sequences
  `public` holds, and there is no extension to count, so over a `public` whose only
  object is an extension (`CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pgcrypto; DROP SCHEMA public`)
  it succeeds where 18.6 answers `2BP01` — `extension pgcrypto depends on schema public`
  (measured on both). A persisted set would close this one too.


  The over-accepting extension spellings, exactly: `CREATE EXTENSION <a known name>` repeated
  **without** `IF NOT EXISTS` — and the bare `CREATE EXTENSION plpgsql`, which 18.6 ships
  pre-installed — `DROP EXTENSION <a known name>` that is not installed (nothing created it, or a `DROP SCHEMA
  public CASCADE` removed it), and
  `CREATE EXTENSION … VERSION '<one that does not exist>'`.

- **~~116~~ · Closed — `FLOAT(n)` is `float8` here whatever `n` says.**
  `parser::type_name`'s `float` arm read the modifier and threw it away, returning the
  bare canonical `"float"`, which `type_oid_from_name` maps to `TypeOid::Float8`. 18.6's
  `opt_float` (`gram.y`) reads the same modifier as a **type selector**: `float4` for `n`
  in 1–24, `float8` for 25–53, and `22023` outside that range at both ends. So the
  modifier did not narrow a `float8` here — it was discarded, and the column was the
  wrong type.

  The divergence was a **value** one, which is what separated it from the display-name
  parting `type_oid_display_name` produces: over `t(f FLOAT(1))` holding
  `0.1234567890123456`,

  | probe | pglet, before | pglet + 18.6, now |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT f` | `0.1234567890123456` | `0.12345679` |
  | `information_schema.columns` `data_type` / `numeric_precision` | `double precision` / 53 | `real` / 24 |
  | `RowDescription` type OID / typlen of `SELECT f` | 701 / 8 | 700 / 4 |
  | `unnest(f)` | `function unnest(double precision) does not exist` | `function unnest(real) does not exist` |
  | the unaliased output column name of `SELECT 0.5::float(1)` | `float8` | `float4` |

  — the first row being the one that mattered: the stored value kept a precision the
  declared type did not have, so a client that reads the declared OID and a client that
  reads the bytes disagreed about the same column. The `42883` message is a *symptom* of
  the substitution rather than the divergence itself.

  **What closed it is a re-pointing, not a new type.** `Parser::float_type_name` returns
  the *selected* type's canonical spelling — `real` or `double precision`, the two
  strings the reader's own `real` and `double precision` arms already emit — so the
  modifier is spent on the decision and no canonical name a `FLOAT` spelling produces
  carries a `(…)` at all. A bare `FLOAT` takes `double precision` too, as `opt_float`'s
  `/*EMPTY*/` production takes `float8`. It reaches the positions that resolve a type
  name — measured at a `CREATE TABLE` column, `ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN`, `::`,
  `CAST(… AS …)`, the typed constant and under a `[]` suffix — and both edges of both
  halves are pinned (1, 2, 23, 24 and 25, 26, 52, 53, in
  `crates/pglet/tests/float_precision_selection.rs`), because an off-by-one at 24/25 is a
  silently wrong stored value rather than an error.

  **Where the refusal runs was the second decision, and it buys two more positions.**
  18.6 raises `opt_float`'s `22023` while *reducing the grammar*, ahead of any name
  resolution, so pglet raises it in the parser. That is why
  `CREATE SEQUENCE s AS FLOAT(0)` and `… GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY (AS FLOAT(0))` —
  positions that read a type name and **discard** it — now agree, at `22023` with 18.6's
  `P` byte for byte. Their *in-range* spellings are the residual and are still accepted
  here, where 18.6 refuses both under **different** codes for reasons of the position
  rather than the name: `22023 sequence type must be smallint, integer, or bigint` from
  `init_params`' kind check at the first, `42601 conflicting or redundant options` from
  the duplicate-option scan at the second, which never resolves the name. That split is
  the position's gap (row 260) and not this row's; it is stated on
  `json_is_refused_at_every_type_name_position`, whose doc records the same two positions
  over `json`, `point` and `nosuchtype` — where `nosuchtype` splits off at the sequence
  one, resolution failing `42704` ahead of the kind check that `FLOAT(1)` reaches.

  **The out-of-range spellings were an over-acceptance in the other direction, and silent
  as well**: `FLOAT(0)`, `FLOAT(54)`, `FLOAT(55)` and `FLOAT(1000)` were accepted here, at
  each of the resolving positions, against `22023 precision for type float must be at
  least 1 bit` / `… must be less than 54 bits` there. Both sentences are now pglet's own,
  byte for byte, from `Error::FloatPrecisionTooSmall`/`TooLarge` — the only error outside
  `42601` that fills `P` (`Error::position`'s arms are the enumeration). `FLOAT(1,2)`,
  `FLOAT(1.5)` and `FLOAT(2147483648)` were accepted here too — a `float(1,2)` column
  built as `double precision` and took the whole value, measured before the repair —
  and are now `42601` on both engines, for free: `opt_precision`'s window is one
  `Iconst`, which is `opt_float`'s own spelling.

  **The typed-constant speculation had to commit, and the commit is keyed on the `(`.**
  `parser::expr`'s `try_typed_constant` parses a multi-word type name from a checkpoint
