  and restores when no string literal follows, which swallowed the `22023` and demoted it
  to the function-call path's `0A000 function not supported: float` — the exact failure
  the phase split's own comment records for `time with time zone`'s `42704`. It now
  commits once `float` is followed by `(`, so `SELECT float(0)` is the `22023` and
  `SELECT float(1)`, `float(1) + 1`, `float(1.5)`, `float(1,2)` and `float(2147483648)`
  are `42601` on both engines. The control that fixes the key is bare `float`, an
  ordinary column reference on both (`42703 column "float" does not exist`), and the
  split is 18.6's own: `float` is a `COL_NAME_KEYWORD` (`kwlist.h`), excluded from
  `func_name`, so `float (` can begin nothing but `Numeric`.

  **The commit is scoped to `float`, and the lead words beside it are the second
  residual.** The membership test is `kwlist.h`'s category, and
  `is_multiword_type_lead`'s `character`, `numeric`, `char`, `varchar`, `bit`, `time`,
  `timestamp`, `dec` and `decimal` all pass it, so they commit on 18.6 the same way:
  `SELECT <word>(3)` is `42601 syntax error at end of input` there at each, measured,
  where pglet still answers its own `0A000 function not supported: <word>`. Loud both
  ways, and a different rule from this row's; closing it is a decision about those type
  names, not about `FLOAT(n)`. The five lead words that **fail** that same `kwlist.h` test —
  `bpchar`, `varbit`, `timestamptz`, `timetz` and the `UNRESERVED_KEYWORD` `double` — must
  never join the commit: `SELECT bpchar(3)` is `3` on 18.6 and the other four are
  `42883 function … does not exist`, all function-call answers, and `parser::expr`'s
  `a_float_open_paren_commits_where_the_bare_word_restores` pins them against a widening.

  **The *modifier-bearing* spelling of an uncommitted lead word is the same residual, and
  what decides its membership is whether the lead word's own `(…)` window refuses the
  number — not which word it is.** A refusal inside the speculation restores it, and the
  restored cursor answers: `0A000 function not supported: <word>` where the lead word is the
  whole spelling, a `42601` of `SELECT`'s own grammar where a tail is left over. Measured,
  at the literal-bearing spelling: `char(-1) 'ab'` and `char(5,2) 'ab'` are that `0A000`
  against 18.6's `42601 syntax error at or near "-"` / `… ","` (and so are their
  `character` / `varchar` spellings, while `character varying`'s leave `varying` behind and
  answer `42601` — the one spelling whose SQLSTATE agrees); `numeric(+5) '1'` is it against
  `42601 type modifiers must be simple constants or identifiers` — a **leading `+`** being
  the shape `numeric`'s reader refuses, where a leading `-` it reads and carries (which is
  how `numeric(5,-2)` works at all); and `timestamp(3.5) '…'`, `timestamp(-1) '…'`,
  `time(3.5) '…'` are it against `42601`, their `(p)` being the same one-`Iconst` window.
  **Row 124's close added three number shapes per character spelling** — `char(3.5) 'ab'`,
  `char(2147483648) 'ab'`, `char(99999999999999999999) 'ab'` and the same at `character`,
  `varchar` and `character varying` — which were a silent `ab` before the length window
  became that `Iconst`. The commit set is where all of this is decided, so the class is
  listed here as well as on row 124, whose bullet carries the table.

  **That lead-word set does not bound the class.** It is pglet's *speculation* list, and
  `kwlist.h`'s category is wider. Swept across all 64 `COL_NAME_KEYWORD`s at
  `SELECT <word>(3)`, eleven answer pglet's `0A000 function not supported: <word>` where
  18.6 answers `42601 syntax error at end of input`: every one of the nine
  `is_multiword_type_lead` words above, plus `interval` and `nchar`. Neither of those two is
  an `is_multiword_type_lead` word, so their *modifier-bearing* spelling never reaches the
  speculation — pglet reads `interval 'lit'` from its own `parse_primary_inner` arm ahead
  of it and `nchar 'ab'` through `try_typed_constant`'s single-word window, both keyed on
  the *next* token being a string, which a `(` is not. Thirty-one further
  `COL_NAME_KEYWORD`s take that same `0A000` against some *other* `42601` there —
  `SELECT int(3)` and `SELECT real(3)` are `42601 syntax error at or near "("`, those two
  type productions taking no modifier at all.

  **What separates those two from the lead words is the spelling with a literal after
  it.** For the lead words above the speculation does start, so
  `SELECT <word>(n) '<lit>'` reaches the type-name reader here rather than the
  function-call path, and where pglet models the type the modifier applies:
  `varchar(3) 'abcd'` is `abc`, `numeric(4,1) '1.55'` is `1.6`, and
  `timestamp(3) '2020-01-02 03:04:05.6789'` is `2020-01-02 03:04:05.679`, each on both
  engines (`char`'s blank padding is row 95's and `bit`'s `type "bit" is not supported`
  an unmodelled type; neither is this class). For `interval` and `nchar` it never
  starts, so 18.6 answers a **value** where pglet answers that `0A000`:
  `SELECT interval(3) '1 day'` is `1 day`, the modifier live rather than parsed and
  dropped (`interval(3) '1.23456 sec'` is `00:00:01.235`), and
  `SELECT nchar(3) 'ab'` is the padded `ab `. Pglet-stricter at that spelling rather than
  loud both ways. All measured on both engines; recorded, not closed.

  **What closing it *narrowed* elsewhere, unasked**: the same-type-cast elision class
  (row 120's no-op-typmod residual). Over a `real` column, `CREATE INDEX ix ON t
  ((f::float(1)))` printed `((f)::double precision)` at `pg_indexes.indexdef` — measured
  before the repair — where 18.6 elides the no-op to `btree (f)`; the cast target is
  now `real`, pglet's own elision
  fires, and the two are byte-identical. Measured at `indexdef` and
  `pg_get_constraintdef` in both directions — the no-op that elides on both engines and
  the genuine widening/narrowing that prints on both — and at `column_default`, where a
  cast over a *literal* has no column to be a no-op against and prints either way. The
  class is otherwise untouched.

  **The placement is also a statement-level error-precedence change, and it wins where
  the type-modifier refusal loses.** `ALTER TABLE zex ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS b
  float(0)` over an existing `b` is this `22023` on both engines — ahead of the
  column-existence check *and* ahead of the `IF NOT EXISTS` skip, which is a Postgres
  **success**. An `int4(3)` at that position loses to both, `typenameTypeMod` refusing
  after parse analysis has run them: `ALTER TABLE zex ADD COLUMN b int4(3)` is
  `42701 column "b" of relation "zex" already exists` on both engines, and the
  `IF NOT EXISTS` spelling of it **succeeds** on both — 18.6 raising its `skipping`
  notice, pglet silent. `ALTER TABLE nosuchtbl ADD COLUMN b
  float(0)` outranks `42P01` the same way, and `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS zex (a
  float(0))` over an existing `zex` outranks `42P07` and its skip. All measured on both
  engines; `ddl/float_precision_outranks_the_add_column_gates.sql` and
  `ddl/float_precision_outranks_a_missing_relation.sql` pin the first `float(0)` one and
  the `nosuchtbl` one.

  The fixtures that carry the *shape* rather than a value
  are `types/float_bare_word_is_still_a_column.sql` and
  `types/float_named_column_survives_the_commit.sql` (the restore controls) and
  `ddl/float_precision_sequence_type_zero_loud.sql` /
  `ddl/float_precision_identity_type_zero_loud.sql` (the two positions the parse-time
  placement buys). `SELECT float(-1)`'s message still parts
  (`expected a number, found number` against `syntax error at or near "-"`); the SQLSTATE
  agrees and `@expect-message` is opt-in.

  **What pins it.** The differential half is every `float_precision_*`-prefixed fixture across `types/`,
  `ddl/`, `information_schema/` and `copy/`; `float_precision_selection.rs` carries the
  out-of-window refusal loop, the dump round-trip and the store reopen beside those
  window edges; and `parser::expr` carries **two** unit tests for the commit, both
  directions proved by mutation.

- **95 · `char(n)` is `bpchar` there — padded, trailing-blank-insensitive, and 1042.**
  Here it is stored as `varchar`, and that is a type-system fact rather than a
  description one: `executor::type_resolution` collapses `CHAR(n)` / `CHARACTER(n)` onto
  `TypeOid::Varchar`, the catalog `Column` keeps only `varchar_length`, and `coerce`'s
  `apply_length_typmod` truncates-or-`22001` with no blank padding.

  Measured over `t(c CHAR(5))` holding `'ab'`, every row of the table in both directions
  — the **descriptions** first:

  | probe | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `information_schema.columns.data_type` | `character varying` | `character` |
  | `udt_name` | `varchar` | `bpchar` |
  | `pg_attribute.atttypid` | 1043 | 1042 |
  | declared OID of `SELECT c` | 1043 | 1042 |

  — and there is no `pg_type` row for `bpchar` 1042 or `_bpchar` 1014 at all. Then the
  **answers**:

  | probe | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT c = 'ab   '` | `f` | `t` |
  | `concat_ws('-', c, 'y')` | `ab-y` | `ab   -y` |
  | `PRIMARY KEY (c)` over a second row spelled `'ab   '` | accepted | `23505` |
  | `c LIKE 'ab'` | `t` | `f` |
  | `c LIKE 'ab   '` | `f` | `t` |
  | `c ~ '^ab '`, and `'ab'::char(4) ~ '^ab '`, and `$1::char(4) ~ '^ab '` bound `'ab'` | `f` | `t` |
  | `c !~ '^ab '` | `t` | `f` |
  | `octet_length(c)`, and `octet_length('ab'::char(4))` | 2 | 5, 4 |

  **`LIKE` diverges in both directions**, and that pair is the row's own correction: it
  was written as an agreeing neighbour on the reasoning that `LIKE` is not
  blank-insensitive, which is true of the *operator* and says nothing about the
  *operand* — 18.6 pads the stored value before matching, so a wildcard-free pattern
  matches the padded string and not the bare one, inverting both answers.
  `octet_length(c)` counts the stored bytes on both engines — `bpcharoctetlen` reads the
  raw datum, padding included — so it answers the unpadded 2 here. The **agreeing**
  neighbours are the ones that go through bpchar→text, which strips:

  | probe | both engines |
  | --- | --- |
  | `length(c)` | 2 |
  | `upper(c)` | `AB` |
  | `c::text` | `ab` |
  | `c \|\| 'x'` | `abx` |

  — and `GROUP BY` / `DISTINCT` fold the paddings together on both engines here only
  because pglet never pads. These agree only over a value stored **without** trailing
  blanks, as `'ab'` is: 18.6 strips the blanks a `char(n)` value holds wherever it reads it
  as `text`, and pglet stores and reads them, so over `c3 (c CHAR(3))` holding `'a '`,
  `length(c)` is 2 here and 1 there, `c || 'x'` is `a x` against `ax`, `md5(c)` is the
  digest of `a ` against that of `a`, and `left(c, 3)` and `substr(c, 1)` keep the blank
  there stripped (`md5('a '::char(3))` likewise). `octet_length(c)` is 2 here and 3 there,
  18.6 counting the stored datum.

  **Silent, and it writes**: the duplicate key is a uniqueness the DDL asked for and did
  not get. **Deferred by measurement, not by argument**, and the reason is the *answers*
  half. Padding on store plus a trailing-blank-insensitive comparator is not one change
  but a set that must agree with each other — the B-tree **index-key encoder** has to
  order the padded form the comparator calls equal or a unique index and a filter scan
  disagree, and `LIKE` has to keep seeing the padded value while `=` does not. Option
  (i), a `bpchar` bit on `Column`, fixes the four descriptions and none of the answers;
  option (ii), a real `TypeOid::Bpchar`, is a **persisted enum** so it is a store-magic
  bump (a `PGM*` roll) with the `pglet_core` layout pins, the text/binary/index-key
  codecs, the `pg_type` rows 1042/1014 and `array_of` beside it. And the parenless
  spellings are a third measured rule, and the **position** is inside it: at a column or
  cast position 18.6's bare `char` and `character` are `char(1)`
  (`length('abc'::char)` is 1) while bare `bpchar` is unbounded
  (`length('abc'::bpchar)` is 3); at a **typed constant** all three are unbounded there,
  `ConstCharacter` clearing the default `CharacterWithoutLength` installs. pglet
  reproduces that split (`docs/parser.md` § Known lexical / parse divergences, *A typed constant is a cast*), which
  **narrows** this row at the descriptions and **widens** it at the answers.

  The narrowing: `length(char 'ab')` is 2 on both engines now and the spurious `(1)` is
  gone from all four catalog renderings. What stands there is **not** uniformly the
  name. Measured over
  `CREATE TABLE d1 (c TEXT DEFAULT char 'ab', CHECK (c <> char 'zz'))` plus
  `CREATE INDEX d1_i ON d1 (c) WHERE c = char 'ab'`:

  | rendering | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `column_default` | `'ab'::character varying` | `'ab'::bpchar` |
  | `check_clause` | `(c <> 'zz'::character varying)` | `(c <> ('zz'::bpchar)::text)` |
  | `pg_get_constraintdef` | `CHECK ((c <> 'zz'::character varying))` | `CHECK ((c <> ('zz'::bpchar)::text))` |
  | `pg_indexes.indexdef` | `… WHERE (c = 'ab'::character varying)` | `… WHERE (c = ('ab'::bpchar)::text)` |

  Only `column_default` differs by the name alone; the other three differ by a whole
  extra **coercion node**, 18.6's parse analysis inserting the `bpchar→text` that
  pglet's fold makes unnecessary. That mechanism is older than the split; what is new is
  this enumeration of it. Beside the table stand the constant's declared 1043 against
  1042 and its unaliased output column `varchar` against `bpchar`.

  The widening reaches the **answers** half, at a position no row of the two tables
  above names. Truncating every bare `char` constant to one character discarded the
  trailing blanks before anything compared them; without the truncation they survive,
  and this row's two missing pieces — the `bpchar` comparator and the blank-stripping
  `bpchar→text` cast — decide the result. Every cell measured on both engines, with the
  **pre-split** column measured on a build whose `char` constant still takes the
  declared default:

  | probe | pglet pre-split | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | `char 'ab ' = char 'ab'` | `t` | `f` | `t` |
  | `char 'x ' = 'x'` | `t` | `f` | `t` |
  | `char 'a ' \|\| 'x'` | `ax` | `a x` | `ax` |
  | `CHECK (c <> char 'z ')` over an inserted `'z'` | `23514` | accepted, stores `z` | `23514` |
  | `length(char 'ab ')` | 1 | 3 | 2 |
  | `'[' \|\| char 'ab ' \|\| ']'` | `[a]` | `[ab ]` | `[ab]` |
  | `(char 'ab ')::text` | `a` | `ab ` | `ab` |
  | `length(char '   ')` | 1 | 3 | 0 |
  | `char '   ' = ''` | `f` | `f` | `t` |

  The first four rows **agreed before and diverge now** — the truncation was
  accidentally reproducing 18.6's blank-insensitivity — and the fourth of them
  **writes**, the same shape as the duplicate key above. The last five diverged before
  and diverge now. The pre-split column is here so each cell carries its own
  before-and-after. `octet_length(char 'ab ')` is 3 on both: the constant keeps its
  blanks here, and 18.6 counts the stored datum.

  **Rtrimming the constant's literal is not the fix**, and the polarity that agrees is
  the measurement that rules it out: `SELECT char 'ab   '` sends `ab   ` byte-identical
  on both engines (`od -c` on each: `a b sp sp sp \n`), and `octet_length(char 'ab ')`
  is 3 on 18.6. 18.6 **stores** the blanks and strips them per *reader*, and by more than
  one mechanism: the `bpchar` operators trim through `varchar.c`'s `bcTruelen`
  (`bpcharlen` and the comparisons are among its callers), while the `bpchar→text` cast
  is a different function in a different file — `pg_cast`'s `text(bpchar)` is
  `oracle_compat.c`'s `rtrim1`, a right-trim of spaces, and that file names neither
  `bcTruelen` nor the `bpchartruelen` it wraps. `bpcharoctetlen` trims nothing — it
  reads the raw datum size — which is why `octet_length` keeps its 3. Reproducing that
  is the comparator and the cast, this row's deferred store-magic work.
  `types/typed_constant_bare_char_keeps_its_trailing_blanks.sql` pins that agreeing
  polarity — the raw value and an equality against a text literal carrying the same
  blanks, both of which an rtrim would redden (measured, by making the rtrim) — beside
  `types/typed_constant_bare_char_carries_no_length.sql` on the blank-free literals. The
  divergent cells have no fixture, for this row's own reason — a
  faithful one would be **red because the engine is wrong**, which is a different fact
  from the duplicate key below, whose shape the harness cannot express at all.
  **No consumer pressure**: a grep over the spine's
  migrations, fuz_app's DDL and the three consumer trees finds no `char(n)` column, and
  the fuz spine's own shipped schema loads and snapshots with none — so what is at stake
  is the correctness of the type, not a live cross-backend diff.

  `catalog/char_column_truncates_an_over_wide_literal.sql` and
  `catalog/char_column_uncast_agrees.sql` are row 86's `"char"` fixtures, not this type's;
  nothing pins the divergent rows of the `t(c CHAR(5))` tables above, a faithful fixture
  being red.
  The duplicate-key member could not be a fixture at all, the harness having no
  `@expect-error`-where-pglet-accepts shape, and its binary leg would additionally need a
  `bpchar` (1042) arm in `pglet_tests`' `column_value_to_json` before a `char(n)` fixture
  could assert anything.

  **An index key is sized unpadded.** 18.6 stores a `char(n)` value blank-padded to `n` and
  sizes its index entry that way; `executor::index_row` sizes the stored `varchar` as
  written, and the catalog keeps only `varchar_length`, so the size gate cannot tell a
  `char(n)` column from a `varchar(n)` one. Over `i3 (a char(2700))` with `CREATE INDEX i3_i
  ON i3 (a)`: a 2 692-character value is `54000 index row size 2712 exceeds btree version 4
  maximum 2704 for index "i3_i"` on 18.6 and accepted here, reading back 2 692 characters; a
  2 693-character value is refused on both (measured). Silent, and it writes an entry 18.6
  refuses. No fixture: a faithful one is red.

- **94 · An enum literal carries the enum's name there and a `text` label here.** pglet
  stores an enum value as `Value::Text` and hangs the enum name off the *column*, so
  `operand_type` answers `text` for the column and the unknown resolves to it, rendering
  `'public'::text` where 18.6 renders `'public'::cell_visibility`.

  Silent, and narrower than it looks: the `DEFAULT` position is **closed for the spelling
  this mechanism reaches**, a bare literal — `render_column_default` holds the column, so
  the spine's `DEFAULT 'private'` on a `cell_visibility` column reads
  `'private'::cell_visibility`, pinned by
  `catalog/column_default_literal_takes_the_column_type_label.sql`. That arm is not reached
  by a **written** cast: `DEFAULT 'private'::cell_visibility` is not a literal default at
  all by the time anything renders it — the parser drops the enum name before the cook, so
  the stored tree is a `Cast` to `text` that goes to the deparser instead, and the position
  reads `'private'::text` again. That is row 104's mechanism, not this one's, and at this
  position it makes the database undumpable; row 104 carries it. What is open under *this*
  mechanism is a CHECK or index predicate comparing against an enum column, which the
  spine's schema does not do, and that comparison polarity is unpinned — a faithful fixture
  would be red.

  **What the enum member order added to it: the rendering is not replayable.** Measured
  over `r(id, k, m mood NOT NULL, CHECK (m < 'ok'))` under
  `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX r_u ON r (k) WHERE m > 'sad'`, pglet renders
  `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX r_u ON public.r USING btree (k) WHERE (m > 'sad'::text)` and
  `(m < 'ok'::text)` where 18.6 renders `::mood` in both. Replaying **pglet's own**
  rendering on 18.6 is `42883 operator does not exist: mood > text` (and `mood < text`
  for the CHECK); replaying it on pglet builds an identically-enforcing index, the `text`
  cast being inert here. So the cast is a label there and a no-op here, and a tool that
  round-trips a definition through 18.6 cannot use pglet's spelling. That is the **catalog**
  rendering and not the dump's: `deparse`'s Portable mode leaves the unknown literal bare,
  so the same two shapes dump unlabelled — measured over
  `ck(id, k, m mood NOT NULL, CHECK (m < 'happy'))` under
  `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ck_u ON ck (k) WHERE m > 'sad'`, `pglet_server dump` emits
  `WHERE (m > 'sad')` and `CHECK ((m < 'happy'))` and stock 18.6 replays the whole file.
  That is the control that bounds row 104's undumpable case to a *written* cast. It does
  not move the `silent?` cell: nothing is written wrongly and the local behaviour is
  unchanged.

- **104 · An enum's identity lives on the column and not in the value, and a cast drops
  it.** An enum value is a `Value::Text` and its `TypeOid` is `Text`, so nothing in the
  value says which enum it belongs to. The **column** does — `Column.enum_type`, carried
  through the executor on `ColumnDesc` — and one exhaustive walk (`executor::expr`'s
  `expr_enum_with`) carries it up from there: a node's enum is the unified enum of the
  operands its own result type is drawn from, so `ORDER BY m`, `WHERE m > 'sad'`,
  `min(m)`, `greatest(m, 'ok')` and `COALESCE(m, 'sad')` alike order by member position,
  as 18.6 does (`docs/enums.md`). A **cast's** identity is dropped where the parser reads
  the type name: a member literal's cast is built as the plain cast to `text`
  (`planner::build_enum_cast`), so `'happy'::mood` is byte-identical to `'happy'::text` in the
  plan and no walk can recover it, and any other operand's cast is the conversion
  `StringFunc::EnumIn` under that same `text` cast — which names the enum for its
  membership test and answers no enum to the walk, as a string function does. It is the walk's only **boundary** — its only arm that
  drops an identity 18.6 can see, as against the many arms whose result type simply is not
  their operands'. A scalar subquery was recorded here as a second one, "measured
  unreachable", on a measurement that covered the single `ORDER BY (SELECT …)` position;
  closed, and what is left of it is row 107.

  Measured on the native server against 18.6, over `mood AS ENUM ('sad','ok','happy')`
  and `tb(id, m mood)` holding `happy`, `sad`, `ok`: `SELECT 'happy'::mood > 'sad'` is `f`
  here and `t` there; `greatest('sad'::mood, 'ok'::mood)` is `sad` here and `ok` there,
  and the **one-cast** `greatest('sad'::mood, 'ok')` is the same pair, 18.6 resolving the
  bare literal to the cast's own `mood`; `SELECT id, m::text AS lbl FROM tb ORDER BY
  m::mood` answers `happy, ok, sad` here against `sad, ok, happy` there; and
  `min(m::mood)` / `max(m::mood)` answer `happy` / `sad` here against `sad` / `happy`
  there. Those are the ordering consumers the member-position rule moved —
  `< <= > >=`, `ORDER BY`, `MIN`/`MAX` and `GREATEST`/`LEAST` — each reached here by a
  cast rather than by row 114's `text` operand, and the controls beside them agree: over
  the uncast column, `ORDER BY m` and `min(m)` / `max(m)` are the member positions on
  both engines.

  **The sort key has to be spelled so it cannot bind an output column, and the alias is
  what decides which one it binds.** `SELECT id, m::text FROM tb ORDER BY m` sorts the
  **projected text** — `happy, ok, sad` on **both** engines, separating nothing — because
  the unaliased `m::text` is still *named* `m`; the same statement with `m::text AS lbl`
  sorts the enum column and is `sad, ok, happy` on both. The key that separates the two
  engines here is the cast itself, `ORDER BY m::mood`. Row 114 records the same trap at
  its merged column.

  **And it writes**, by the routes below, some of which outlive the statement.
  Over `wc(id, m mood)` holding the three labels,
  `DELETE FROM wc WHERE 'happy'::mood > 'sad'` is `DELETE 0` here and `DELETE 3` there, so
  all three rows stand against an emptied table; the per-row
  `DELETE FROM wd WHERE m::mood > 'ok'` is `DELETE 1` on **both** and destroys a different
  row — the `sad` one here, the `happy` one there; and
  `UPDATE wu SET m = greatest('sad'::mood, 'ok'::mood)` is `UPDATE 3` on both and stores
  `sad` on every row here against `ok` there. Those two report 18.6's own tag and differ
  only in what is on disk, with no error on either engine. The read under the second of
  those `DELETE`s answers a different **row set** where it stays a `SELECT`, which is the
  damage kind row 114 records: over `tw(id, m mood)` holding
  `(1,'sad')`, `(2,'ok')`, `(3,'happy')`, `SELECT id FROM tw WHERE m::mood > 'ok'` is the
  `sad` row `1` here against the `happy` row `3` there — one row on each engine, a
  different one.

  Then the routes that are **persisted, and that both engines accept at DDL** — which is
  where this family parts from row 114's, whose `CHECK` over `greatest(m, t)` is `42804`
  on 18.6. `CREATE TABLE ck3 (m mood NOT NULL, CHECK (m > greatest('sad'::mood,'ok'::mood)))`
  is `CREATE TABLE` on both, and the constraint then admits `ok` **and** `happy` here,
  refusing `sad` `23514`, where 18.6's admits `happy` alone and refuses both `ok` and `sad`
  under the same code — the erasure legible in the catalog itself, `pg_get_constraintdef`
  rendering `CHECK ((m > GREATEST('sad'::text, 'ok'::text)))` here against
  `'sad'::mood, 'ok'::mood` there. That rendering is row 94's class — an enum-typed operand
  printing with a `text` label — and shares only the label with it, not the mechanism: row
  94's sentence covers a bare literal resolving to the column's `text` OID, where these are
  written `::mood` casts the parser dropped before anything could render them. And
  `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX pix_u ON pix (k) WHERE m > greatest('sad'::mood,'ok'::mood)` is
  accepted on both, after which a second `(2,'ok')` is
  `23505 duplicate key value violates unique constraint "pix_u"` here and an ordinary row
  there, pglet's membership holding the `ok` rows its own predicate admits. An index **key**
  expression is the persisted position this row did not carry, and it takes a written cast
  the same way: `CREATE INDEX ktab2_k ON ktab2 ((greatest(m, 'ok'::mood)))` and the bare
  `CREATE INDEX ktab_k ON ktab ((m::mood))` are `CREATE INDEX` on both engines. The
  enumeration to read is `docs/ddl.md`'s render-probe list, which is **four** sites and not
  three — `cook_column_default` for a column `DEFAULT`, and `validate_stored_expr_renders`
  for a CHECK, an index predicate and each key part of an expression key, verified against
  `executor::ddl`'s `index_stored_exprs` and its two consumers — and every one of the four
  is somewhere a written cast persists.

  **A column `DEFAULT` is persisted the same way, and it is the position row 94 reads as
  closed.** `CREATE TABLE wdef (id INT, m mood NOT NULL DEFAULT greatest('sad'::mood,
  'ok'::mood))` is `CREATE TABLE` on both, and `INSERT INTO wdef (id) VALUES (1)` is
  `INSERT 0 1` on both and stores `sad` here against `ok` there — on every insert that omits
  the column, for the life of the table. Row 94 reads the `DEFAULT` position as closed, and
  it is closed for the spelling its mechanism reaches: `render_column_default`'s
  `ColumnDefault::Literal` arm hands `col.enum_type` to `render_catalog_string_const`, so a
  **bare** `DEFAULT 'happy'` reads `'happy'::mood` on both engines (measured). A **written**
  cast never reaches that arm — the parser drops the enum name before the cook, so the
  stored default is a general `Cast` expression and the deparser has no column to ask — and
  `DEFAULT 'happy'::mood` reads `'happy'::text` here against `'happy'::mood` there.

  **And that breaks the dump invariant**, at each of those four positions and not at the
  `DEFAULT` alone. Portable mode renders an unknown literal bare, so a bare-literal
  spelling at each of the four positions replays: over one `--data-dir` database carrying
  a `DEFAULT 'happy'`, a `CHECK (m < 'happy')`, a `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX … WHERE m > 'sad'`
  and an index key
  `((greatest(m, 'ok')))`, `pglet_server dump` emits each unlabelled and stock 18.6 takes
  the whole file, `ON_ERROR_STOP=1`, exit `0` — measured. What a written cast erased is in
  the **stored tree**, so Portable renders it faithfully as `::text` and 18.6 refuses each.
  Measured over a second database isolating each position in its own table — a cast in a
  `DEFAULT` fails its `CREATE TABLE` and masks anything else on the same table behind
  `relation … does not exist` — every statement below being pglet's own dump text:
  `m mood NOT NULL DEFAULT ('happy')::text` is `42804 column "m" is of type mood but default
  expression is of type text` (`cookDefault`, `heap.c`);
  `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ptab_u ON ptab (k) WHERE (m > ('sad')::text)` and
  `ALTER TABLE ctab ADD CONSTRAINT ctab_m_check CHECK ((m < ('happy')::text))` are
  `42883 operator does not exist: mood > text` and `mood < text`;
  `CREATE INDEX ktab2_k ON ktab2 ((greatest(m, ('ok')::text)))` is
  `42804 GREATEST types mood and text cannot be matched` — a `42804` at an **index key**,
  where the `DEFAULT`'s is a different message under the same code; and the bare-cast key
  `CREATE INDEX ktab_k ON ktab (((m)::text))` was a third code,
  `42P17 functions in index expression must be marked IMMUTABLE`, the enum-to-`text` cast
  being I/O-based where the `::mood` pglet erased was a no-op relabel. Neither direction of
  the position/code mapping this paragraph used to state survives that: `42804` lands at two
  different positions, and one position lands two different codes.

  **A cast of a non-literal operand no longer renders `::text`.** Since row 241's close, a
  cast to an enum whose operand is not a string literal is the conversion
  `StringFunc::EnumIn` under the `text` cast, carrying the enum's name, and it renders as
  the one cast written: `ktab_k` dumps as `CREATE INDEX ktab_k ON ktab (((m)::mood))`,
  which 18.6 restores (as `USING btree (m)`, measured, `ON_ERROR_STOP=1`), and a
  `CHECK (s::mood IS NOT NULL)` or a `DEFAULT ('ok'::text)::mood` dumps and restores the
  same way. What a **member literal**'s cast renders is unchanged — the parser still
  builds the plain `text` cast for one, so the `DEFAULT`, the partial predicate, the
  `CHECK` and the `greatest` key above render `::text` as measured. The comparison and
  ordering half of this row is unchanged for every operand: the conversion node answers
  no enum to the walk, as the cast did (`expr_enum_walk_tests`' `a_cast_is_the_boundary_and_stays_one`).

  **The restore is loud per statement and silent per process, and the loss is not confined
  to the refused statements.** A refused `CREATE TABLE` takes its own `COPY` block down with
  it, and psql, no longer in copy-in mode, re-reads the tab-separated data as SQL — which
  desynchronises the framing of the `COPY`s after it, all three of them here. Over the
  five-table database above at psql's default: the `DEFAULT` table's `CREATE TABLE` is
  refused, its `COPY` reports `relation "dtab" does not exist`, and `ktab`, `ktab2` and
  `ptab` then restore **empty** although their own `CREATE TABLE`s succeeded — 2 of 9 rows
  land, all of them the first table's. Each swallowed block runs to the next `;`, and for
  the last one that is the `ALTER TABLE … ADD CONSTRAINT`, so the CHECK never raises its own
  `42883` at all. Final state: four of five tables, no user CHECK constraint, no index, and
  **psql exits `0`**. Row 113 records the same loud-per-statement / silent-per-process shape
  from the other direction, a real `pg_dump` into pglet.

  That is the catalog part of `docs/sequences.md`'s dump invariant,
  *any catalog pglet's own accepted statements build must
  dump to something that loads into stock Postgres and back into pglet*, broken at
  its stock-Postgres leg: measured, replaying the cast-spelled dump into a fresh pglet
  restores the type, all five tables, all nine rows, the `('happy')::text` default (which
  then writes `happy`), the CHECK, the partial index and both expression-key indexes,
  reporting no error at any statement — so nothing on the
  pglet leg raises at accept, at dump or at reload. Recorded, not repaired: the fix is this
  row's *Closing either* widening plus a deparser able to spell the enum a `Cast` would then
  carry.

  **A column a cast feeds carries the erasure on, and it writes there too.** A FROM-item
  `unnest(ARRAY['ok'::mood])`, or a derived table over `SELECT 'ok'::mood AS m`, outputs a
  column 18.6 types `mood` and pglet types `text` with no enum, since the cast it is built
  from carried none. Read directly, through a derived table, or beside a window call, it
  compares by the label bytes. Measured on the native server's default build, in-memory
  storage, simple-query leg, against 18.6, over `te(m mood, k INT)` holding
  `('happy', 1)`: `SELECT u.m > 'sad' FROM te, unnest(ARRAY['ok'::mood]) AS u(m)` and
  `SELECT (SELECT u.m FROM unnest(ARRAY['ok'::mood]) AS u(m)) > 'sad'` are `f` here and `t`
  there; `DELETE FROM te WHERE (SELECT u.m FROM te t2, unnest(ARRAY['ok'::mood]) AS u(m)) >
  'sad'` deletes nothing here and the row there, `UPDATE te SET k = 2` under the same
  predicate changes nothing here and sets `k = 2` there, and the `DELETE` whose subquery
  reads `x.m` from `(SELECT b.m FROM te a, (SELECT 'ok'::mood AS m) b) x`, from the same
  derived table with a `row_number() OVER ()` beside `b.m`, or from
  `(SELECT u.m FROM te a, unnest(ARRAY['ok'::mood]) AS u(m)) x` deletes nothing here and the
  row there. Some of these answered as 18.6 does while a descriptor lookup lent them a
  same-named `mood` column's identity; row 158's bullet has those pairs. That lending read
  another relation's column and is not a repair of this row. The repair is the widening
  below, which the derived-table spellings need and the `unnest` ones need together with
  row 112, whose descriptor derives no enum from its array at all.

  No fixture holds any of it, a faithful one being red. The member-order
  rule itself is pinned, on the shapes 18.6 answers, by the `enum/*_member_position.sql`
  family; `enum/order_by_text_cast_is_lexical.sql` is a separate fixture — the glob does not
  match it, and the row names the two apart — and it is the control that a cast *away* from
  the enum is still label-byte ordered on both engines. `test_dump`'s round-trip does build
  an enum column, under the bare-literal `DEFAULT 'active'`, which is the dump control
  rather than a guard on the cast spelling. What a fixture cannot express — that the
  `Cast` arm answers `None` at all — is pinned by `executor::expr`'s
  `expr_enum_walk_tests::a_cast_is_the_boundary_and_stays_one`, so widening the walk here
  reddens something.

  **The other family this row used to carry is row 114**, and that family is now
  **closed**: an enum column beside a plain `text` side used to keep its identity and
  answer by the member positions where 18.6 refuses the statement, and the gates now read
  the identity and refuse it too. What is left of the contrast is this row's own node. The
  two shared a root — an enum **value** carries no identity — and what separates them is
  that row 114's pair has a *decidable* one on the column side while a written cast's is
  not: `x::mood` reaches the planner as a cast to `text`, indistinguishable from
  `x::text`, so the gate reads `EnumIdentity::Undecided` and falls back to the OID rule
  rather than refusing a pair 18.6 accepts. **Every measurement in this bullet still
  holds, and the mechanism the sentence above gave for them does not**: they hold because
  the cast's identity is undecidable, not because the OID is `Text`. **What decides whether 18.6 answers or refuses is the operand
  standing beside the cast, not which row a spelling is filed under.** This row's and row
  114's member lists do not separate them: 18.6 refuses some of what this row measures and
  accepts some of what that one does — row 114's `greatest(m, 'ok')` and
  `greatest(m, t::mood)` controls are identical on both engines. **The neighbours are stated
  as measured pairs below rather than as a rule over neighbour kinds**: 18.6's verdict,
  pglet's answer and pglet's *rule* each vary with the neighbour, and not together.

  Neighbours 18.6 **answers** beside, all `mood AS ENUM ('sad','ok','happy')`: a bare
  `unknown` literal, which it resolves to the cast's own enum
  (`pg_typeof(greatest('sad'::mood, 'ok'))` is `mood` there); a second cast to the **same**
  enum, which is already it; and no neighbour at all (`ORDER BY m::mood`, `min(m::mood)`),
  where there is nothing to decide. That is what the `CHECK` above turns on: created on both
  engines here against row 114's `42804` there.

  Neighbours 18.6 **refuses** beside, and here pglet's own answer splits in two. Over
  `u(id, m mood NOT NULL, t TEXT NOT NULL)` with `t = 'ok'` on all three rows, a `text` one:
  `SELECT 'happy'::mood > 'sad'::text` is `f` here and
  `42883 operator does not exist: mood > text` there;
  `SELECT greatest('sad'::mood, 'ok'::text)` is `sad` against
  `42804 GREATEST types mood and text cannot be matched`;
  `SELECT ARRAY['sad'::mood] < ARRAY['ok']` is `f` against
  `42883 operator does not exist: mood[] < text[]`; and `SELECT id FROM u WHERE m::mood > t`
  keeps row `1` against the first refusal again. Those four answer by the **label bytes** —
  the cast having erased what row 114's `m > t` keeps, so a reader carrying row
  114's member positions onto them names the wrong row. A neighbour carrying a **different
  enum** is refused there too, and answered here by that neighbour's member positions
  instead: over `m3 AS ENUM ('sad','happy','ok')` and `v(id, m mood, y m3)` holding
  `(1,'ok','sad')`, `(2,'ok','happy')`, `(3,'ok','ok')`,
  `SELECT id, ('ok'::mood > y) FROM v ORDER BY id` is `t, t, f` here — `m3`'s positions,
  where the label bytes give `f, t, f` — and `42883 operator does not exist: mood > m3`
  there; `greatest('sad'::mood, y)` is `sad, happy, ok`, `m3`'s positions again against the
  bytes' `sad, sad, sad`, and `42846 GREATEST could not convert type m3 to mood` there — the
  code row 114 carries only at its enum-**array** shape, and row 115's throughout. `unify_enum_pair`'s `(Some, None)` arm is why the two split:
  the cast's erased side yields to whatever the neighbour declares, so the label bytes are
  what is left only when **neither** side declares an enum. Two casts to two *different*
  enums is that case — `SELECT 'sad'::mood > 'ok'::m3` is `t` here and `42883` there — which
  is also why "a second cast is already it" holds only for a second cast to the same enum.

  **And they write**:
  `DELETE FROM ug WHERE m::mood > t` over the same three rows is `DELETE 1` here, destroying
  the `sad` row, against the refusal there, which leaves all three — a wrong **acceptance**
  that writes, where the write routes above are wrong answers to statements 18.6 accepts.
  `DELETE FROM vg WHERE 'ok'::mood > y` over `v`'s three rows is `DELETE 2` here, leaving
  `id 3` alone, against `42883` there, which leaves all three.
  Row 114's cells do not claim any of them: the spellings with no enum column
  anywhere fall outside it, `m::mood > t`, which has one, answers by the label bytes
  where that row's *pglet* cell says member positions, and the different-enum spellings have
  no `text` side at all. Row 115's does not either, since these carry a cast and it is
  written for the pair that carries none. They are this row's, at its
  boundaries with those two. All three families write.
  Closing either is one type-identity widening across the parser (this row's site), the
  scope's column map, `Expr::infer_type` and both declared-type walkers.

  **An index key expression is sized by its label behind a cast.** `executor::index_row`
  sizes an enum key part as 18.6 lays it out, four bytes, and learns that the part is an
  enum through the same `expr_enum_with` walk, so a written cast leaves it a `text` part
  sized by its label's bytes. Over `m4 AS ENUM ('b', 'abcdefgh')`, both measured on both
  engines: after `CREATE INDEX d1_i ON d1 (t, (CASE WHEN t <> '' THEN 'b'::m4 END))`, a
  2 689-character `t` is `54000 index row size 2712 exceeds btree version 4 maximum 2704 for
  index "d1_i"` on 18.6 and accepted here, 2 688 accepted on both — an entry 18.6 refuses,
  **written**; and after `CREATE INDEX d2_i ON d2 ((CASE WHEN t <> '' THEN 'abcdefgh'::m4
  END), t)`, a 2 681- and a 2 688-character `t` are accepted there and refused `2712` here.

  **Two constants compared after such a cast are compared as their labels**, the cast
  having carried no identity for either side: over `mood AS ENUM ('sad', 'ok', 'happy')`,
  `SELECT 'happy'::mood > 'sad'::mood` is `f` here and `t` there, and a branch that
  comparison picks is the other one — `SELECT a FROM u ORDER BY CASE WHEN 'happy'::mood >
  'sad'::mood THEN a ELSE -a END` sorts `2, 1` against `1, 2`, and the grouping spelling
  `… GROUP BY a ORDER BY CASE WHEN … THEN max(a) ELSE -max(a) END` the same now that it
  answers (row 89). Silent. A grouping query does not let that comparison decide which
  branch's **aggregates run** (`enum/agg_expr_enum_ordering_decider_keeps_aggregate_loud.sql`).

- **~~114~~ · Closed — A plain `text` operand cannot contradict the column's enum, and
  18.6 has neither an operator nor a common type for the pair.** The gates that answer
  both questions now read a type as 18.6's `pg_type` row rather than as an OID:
  `planner::common_type`'s `ResolvedType` is the OID **and** the enum identity beside
  it, and it is the currency of `select_common_type`, `common_type_step` and
  `comparison_legality` alike. Nothing was erased before and nothing is now — what was
  missing was the **representation**: a `mood` column's own `TypeOid` is `Text`, the
  identity riding on `ColumnDesc::enum_type`, so every gate read the pair as two
  `text`s and had nothing to gate on.

  **The category is what is modelled, and modelling the type identity instead would have
  given the wrong code.** 18.6's `select_common_type` raises its `42804` only when the
  two `typcategory`s differ; an enum is `E` where `text`/`varchar`/`name` are `S`, so
  that pair has no common type, while **two enums share `E`** — the fold gets past the
  category check and `coerce_to_common_type` is what fails, `42846`. Row 115 is that
  second pair and closes on the same change, under its own code. An enum **array** is a
  third answer again: `typcategory` `A` like every other array, its identity carried at
  the element, so `mood[]` beside `text[]` is a same-category conversion failure —
  `42846 COALESCE could not convert type text[] to mood[]`, measured on both engines.
  A refusal keyed on type identity rather than category collapses all three to one code;
  the sweep measured it, and `enum/two_enums_greatest_loud.sql`,
  `enum/two_enums_setop_loud.sql`, `enum/two_enums_array_element_loud.sql` and
  `enum/enum_array_vs_text_array_loud.sql` are what redden for it — the `42846` family,
  and only it.

  **What the identity travels through.** One derivation, `executor::expr`'s exhaustive
  `expr_enum_with`, instantiated a third time at plan time over the clause's namespace
  and a second time over the catalog (`PlannerScope::enum_identity`) — so the ordering
  sites, `ColumnDesc::enum_type` and these gates are one arm list rather than three that
  must agree. Its `Column` leaf needed a namespace that carries the identity, which is
  why `ColumnScope`'s relations hold `ResolvedType`s; its `Subquery` leaf is
  `subquery_enum_name`, which is what closes the branch shape that is no column at all
  (`COALESCE((SELECT m FROM em), tx)`). The doors that are no branch reader — the
  set operation, a FROM-clause `VALUES`, a CTE, the recursive-CTE check in the *parser*,
  and the two `JOIN … USING` merge readers — resolve from a `ColumnDesc` and take the
  identity through one `ResolvedType::of_column`.

  **`EnumIdentity` has a third state, and without it the repair over-refuses.** A
  written `x::mood` reaches the planner as a cast to **`text`**, the enum name being
  dropped where the parser reads the type (row 104), so `t::mood` and `t::text` are the
  same `Expr` — refusing both against an enum breaks `greatest(m, t::mood)`, which 18.6
  answers, while accepting both leaves `m = t::text` silent, which row 104 already
  records. Only the first is a *new* wrong answer, so such an operand is `Undecided` and
  the pair falls back to the OID rule. A bare string or `NULL` literal takes that state
  for an exact reason rather than a conservative one: it is 18.6's `unknown`, which
  adopts the position's type, enum included, so `m = 'ok'` and `COALESCE(m, 'sad')`
  resolve to `mood` there. Measured: deleting the third state reddens the
  pre-existing `enum/*_member_position` family wholesale, beside the accept-side controls
  written for it — stated as a class, since a count here stales with the next fixture
  added.

  **The coercion pass moved with the gate.** A fold that lands on an enum target writes
  no cast — `Expr::Cast` names a `TypeOid` and none names an enum, so the only cast the
  pass could write for a `mood` target is one to `text`, which is 18.6's *other* type;
  18.6 coerces the unknown-typed sibling to the enum instead, and the values are already
  `Value::Text`. That guard is belt whose brace is the third state: removing it reddens
  nothing measured — not the `enum/` corpus, not `enum_identity_gates`, not the `dump`
  text of a `CHECK (greatest(m, 'ok') > 'sad')`, a stored expression being stored *as
  written* and so never reaching the pass at all.

  **The gates' *reach* was a second question from their identity, and it was open.** A
  gate reader answers `None` for a computed operand deliberately — its verdict must not
  rest on a guess, and what that costs over a non-enum pair is row 65 — so a `mood` column
  whose sibling was `lower(s)` had its identity read by the exhaustive walk and then
  thrown away with the `None` the OID came back as. Measured, and **pre-existing**: the
  same answers on builds before and after the enum-identity gates, so the identity work
  neither introduced nor closed it. `DELETE FROM w WHERE m > lower(s)` took the row 18.6
  keeps by refusing; `UPDATE w SET m = greatest(m, lower(s))` rewrote a stored member; and
  a further eleven spellings answered — `COALESCE`, `CASE`'s `ELSE`, `IN`, `BETWEEN`, `IS
  DISTINCT FROM`, `nullif`, a concatenation, a `CASE` operand, a scalar subquery,
  `min(s)`, and `greatest(m, s || '')`. The repair puts the **complete** type walk behind
  the shallow reader and spends it only where the pair, or the branch set, names an enum;
  replacing the reader outright is measured green over the whole corpus and closes most of
  the row-65 shapes measured against it, which is row 65's close and not this one's.

  **Whether a non-enum verdict moved is a claim about this repair, not about agreement,
  and the way to test it is a build from before the repair. Over a comparison it did not
  move; over a branch set it did, toward 18.6.** A comparison pair is widened only where
  the widened *pair* names an enum, so a pair with no enum in it keeps the shallow
  reader's answer. A branch set is widened where the *set* names one, and then every
  branch the shallow reader cannot type is read through the complete walk — so a non-enum
  pair *inside* such a set is judged on types the shallow reader never gave. Over `w(id, m
  mood, s TEXT, n INT)` holding `(1, 'ok', 'zz', 3)`, both legs of the native server,
  against 18.6 and a build before the enum-identity gates:

  | spelling | before the identity gates | now, and 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `COALESCE(n + 0, lower(s), COALESCE(m,'ok'))` | a row, `3` | `42804 COALESCE types integer and text cannot be matched` |
  | `greatest(n + 0, lower(s), m)` / `least(…)` | a row | `42804 GREATEST` / `LEAST types integer and text …` |
  | `ARRAY[n + 0, lower(s), m]` | a row, `{3,zz,ok}` | `42804 ARRAY types integer and text …` |
  | `COALESCE(n + 0, s, m)`, `COALESCE(n + 0, 'x' \|\| s, m)`, `COALESCE(abs(n), lower(s), m)` | a row | `42804 COALESCE types integer and text …` |
  | `UPDATE w SET s = 'q' WHERE COALESCE(n + 0, lower(s), m) IS NOT NULL` | `UPDATE 1` | `42804 …` |

  Every moved verdict measured is 18.6's own, message included past pglet's `type error:`
  prefix, and one of them is a **write** that no longer happens. What decides whether a
  set moves is the untyped branch's sibling, not the enum: the same sets with a bare `n`
  in place of `n + 0` — `COALESCE(n, lower(s))`, `greatest(n, lower(s))`, each with an `m`
  branch appended, and `COALESCE(n, lower(s), COALESCE(m,'ok'))` — answer exactly as
  before the identity gates — consistent with row 65's second sub-case, where a concrete
  sibling lets the coercion pass cast an untyped branch to its type before the gate reads
  it. Three of those still disagree with 18.6 — `COALESCE(n, lower(s))`, `greatest(n,
  lower(s))` and the nested `COALESCE`, where pglet answers rows or its own `22P02` —
  which is row 65, and unpinned because a faithful fixture is red at each. A set naming no
  enum (`COALESCE(n + 0, lower(s))`) is unmoved too, rows on both builds against 18.6's
  `42804`. The DDL-time `CHECK` walk refused `COALESCE(n + 0, lower(s), m)` and its
  `greatest` twin before the identity gates already, measured. So row 65 is **narrower**
  than it was, not unmoved; no fixture or test pins the moved half.

  **The silent residuals still surviving are below.** Measured on the native server
  against 18.6 over
  `mood ('sad','ok','happy')`, `m3 ('sad','happy','ok')` and `w(id, m mood, y m3, s TEXT)`:

  - **~~An `ARRAY[…]` pair over an unresolved *literal* element~~ — closed, and with it
    the whole of the element rule.** `erases_enum_identity`'s array arm called an array
    *undecidable* when **any** element was one of its producers, and a bare string or
    `NULL` literal was one — where 18.6's `transformArrayExpr` folds the elements through
    `select_common_type` before anything outside the constructor sees the array, and an
    `unknown` element contributes nothing to that fold. So the arm now excludes them: an
    array's identity is the unification of its **typed** elements', which is what
    `executor::expr`'s `Expr::Array` arm computes — the erasure predicate beside it
    having been the one that read an unresolved element differently. What it cost, all measured on both engines: `ARRAY[m] < ARRAY['ok']`
    answered `t, f, f` against `42883 … mood[] < text[]`, and the `DELETE` spelling took a
    row; `COALESCE(ARRAY[m], ARRAY['ok'])` and its `greatest` twin answered against
    `42846 could not convert type text[] to mood[]`; and at `op ANY`/`op ALL` **one added
    literal re-opened the door the arm rule had just closed** — `m = ANY(ARRAY[s,'ok'])`,
    `ARRAY['ok',s]`, `ARRAY[s,NULL]` and `ARRAY[y,'ok']` each answered rows, at every
    operator (`=`, `<>`, `>`, `= ALL`), in a `DELETE` and an `UPDATE` predicate, and in a
    `CHECK` and a partial index that **recorded**. The accept side moves with it and is
    the reason it is its own decision: `ARRAY[m,'ok']` is now a named `mood[]` rather than
    an undecidable one, `ARRAY[y,'ok']` an `m3[]`, and an all-`unknown` array falls out of
    the same fold as the `text[]` it always had to be — so
    `array_element_resolved_type`'s own all-`unknown` special case is gone, the rule
    having one home rather than two. `enum/any_all_mixed_array_*`,
    `enum/array_pair_unknown_element_loud.sql` and
    `enum/array_pair_value_constructor_loud.sql` pin both polarities.

    A bare **column** element was never one of the arm's producers, so the pair spellings
    that carry one always agreed: `ARRAY[m] < ARRAY[y]` is `42883 … mood[] < m3[]` and
    `ARRAY[m] < ARRAY[s]` is `… mood[] < text[]` on both engines.

    **What the element rule does not reach is the `NULL` this engine casts itself.** A
    bare `NULL` beside a typed element arrives at the gate as `Cast { NULL → text }`,
    written by `unify_common_type_branches` over the `ARRAY` branches — the same node a
    user's `NULL::text` parses to, which 18.6 types `text` rather than `unknown`
    (`ARRAY[m, NULL::text]` is `42804 ARRAY types mood and text cannot be matched` there,
    where `ARRAY[m, NULL]` is `mood[]`). Both are read here as the pass's output, so
    `m = ANY(ARRAY[s, NULL])` refuses as 18.6 refuses it and `m = ANY(ARRAY[m, NULL::text])`
    answers where 18.6 refuses — row 104's under-refusal, which that spelling already had
    from the cast alone. A `NULL::varchar(3)` element is a `CastTypmod`, which the
    exclusion does not match, so it erases as before: `m = ANY(ARRAY[s, NULL::varchar(3)])`
    answers against `42883 … mood = text`, while its enum-element twin is
    `42804 ARRAY types mood and character varying cannot be matched` on both.
  - **~~`op ANY` / `op ALL`~~ — closed, and with it `IN (SELECT …)`, which was never on
    this list at all.** Both were recorded as the array arm's or as nothing, and the cause
    of each is upstream of any identity: **neither gate had an arm for either construct**,
    in `check_expr_node_semantics` or in `check_expr_node_operand_types`, so the
    comparison each implies was never asked of `comparison_legality`. The repair is stated
    as a property rather than as two more arms — *every position at which 18.6 resolves a
    comparison operator is a position the gates ask about* — and the enumeration is 18.6's
    own `transformExpr` dispatch: `transformAExprOp`, `transformAExprIn`,
    `transformAExprNullIf`, `transformCaseExpr`'s simple form,
    `transformAExprOpAny`/`transformAExprOpAll`, and `transformSubLink`'s ALL/ANY/ROWCOMPARE
    branch. `transformAExprDistinct` and `BETWEEN` reach the first of those here;
    `make_row_comparison_op`'s **multi**-column route reaches none, a row constructor being
    `42601` in this parser and an `IN (SELECT a, b)` its own `0A000` against 18.6's
    `42601 subquery has too many columns` — both loud, neither this row's.

    What each was: `m > ANY(ARRAY[y])` answered three rows against
    `42883 operator does not exist: mood > m3`, `m > ANY(ARRAY[s])` / `m > ALL(ARRAY[s])`
    three rows against `… mood > text`, and `m = ANY(ARRAY['ok'])` — **member** labels —
    answered where 18.6 refuses, `transformArrayExpr` having folded an all-`unknown`
    element set to `text` before the operator. `IN (SELECT …)` was the same family through
    a door with more spellings: the plain and `NOT IN` forms, a second enum
    (`SELECT y`), a derived table over a FROM-clause `VALUES`, a CTE, a correlated
    subquery, and a bare `SELECT 'ok'` whose column is `text` and not an adoptable
    `unknown`. The predicate is the same one a `DELETE` or `UPDATE` takes, and it was
    measured writing at six of those spellings — `DELETE FROM w WHERE m IN (SELECT s FROM
    w)` and its `NOT IN`, second-enum and derived-table forms, `UPDATE … SET s = 'hit'
    WHERE m IN (SELECT s FROM w)`, and `DELETE … WHERE m = ANY(ARRAY[s])` — each removing
    or rewriting what 18.6 keeps by refusing. The `op ANY` half also **persisted**:
    `CHECK (m = ANY(ARRAY[s]))` and a partial index over it were recorded here and refused
    there. Pre-existing:
    measured on a build before the enum-identity gates with the same answers, so the
    identity work neither introduced nor closed them.

    Two things the arms alone would have got wrong. The right-hand operand is **not a
    sibling `Expr`** at either position, so `one_sided_operand_pair` reads it through the
    one reader it has (`branch_subquery_type`, `array_element_resolved_type`) and falls it
    back to `None` — not to a shallower answer — where the widened pair names no enum,
    which is what keeps rows 60 and 65 unmoved. And the conversion runs **one way**: 18.6
    resolves that side to a concrete type before building the operator, so
    `m IN (SELECT 'ok')` and `m = ANY(ARRAY['ok'])` are `42883` while
    `'zzz' IN (SELECT m FROM w)` and `'zzz' = ANY(ARRAY[m])` are `22P02`. Narrowing the
    array arm was **not** part of this and closed separately, above.

    The accept side is what bounds the element rule, and it is keyed on the **elements**
    rather than on the node: `ARRAY['ok'::mood]` is an `Expr::Array` too, its identity
    `Undecided` for row 104's reason, and 18.6 types *that* array `mood[]` — so folding
    every `Expr::Array` to `text` refuses `m > ANY(ARRAY['ok'::mood])`, which
    `enum/any_all_scalar_side_member_position.sql`,
    `enum/any_all_cast_element_array_accepts.sql` and
    `enum/check_ddl_any_all_cast_element_accepts.sql` redden for — measured. Its
    *array*-side sibling (`'ok' > ANY(ARRAY[m])`) stays green under that mutation, the
    element there naming an enum outright, which is why the accept control has to be the
    cast spelling. What is left of the `op ANY` door is one cast producer:
    `m = ANY('{ok}'::text[])` answers where 18.6 is `42883 … mood = text`; it writes
    (`DELETE` removed a row) and persists (the `CHECK` over it was recorded), and it closes
    where row 104's cast residual does.

    The string side is the whole of this row's, not just its `text` column: at both new
    positions a **`varchar`** column, a `name`-typed session source (`current_user`) and a
    `$N` the client declared `varchar` are `42883 operator does not exist: mood = character
    varying` / `mood = name` on both engines, byte for byte.
  - **A sub-plan column the subquery reader cannot type, where 18.6 can — and it writes.**
    The `IN (SELECT …)` arm asks `branch_subquery_type`, which is *certain-or-defer*, and a
    deferral is no verdict at all. Two shapes were found by asking what the residual list
    above excludes, and both are 18.6's `42883 operator does not exist: mood = text`:
    `m IN (SELECT $1)`, whose target-list entry is an unbound parameter that 18.6's parse
    analysis resolves to `text` where `resolved_subquery_type_in` defers — as does
    `m IN (SELECT NULL)`, whose entry the type walk answers `None` for; and
    `m IN (SELECT * FROM unnest(ARRAY['ok','sad']))`, a wildcard over a **function scan** —
    `wildcard_column_type`'s `_` arm, the same deferral row 152(c) records at a
    `COALESCE` branch. `DELETE FROM w WHERE m IN (SELECT $1)` bound to a member removed the
    row 18.6 keeps by refusing. A **computed** column is not in this class:
    `m IN (SELECT lower(s) FROM w)`, `m IN (SELECT s || '' FROM w)` and
    `m = ANY(ARRAY[lower(s)])` are all `42883` on both engines, the complete walk reaching
    them. Its **accept** half was a separate defect and is closed
    **at this door and one construct out**: a projected expression carries no
    `ColumnDesc::enum_type` (row 107), and reading that `None` as *not an enum* refused
    `m IN (SELECT 'ok'::mood)`, `m IN (SELECT min(m) FROM w)`, a `GROUP BY` key and the
    three value constructors, each of which 18.6 answers and the `DELETE` spelling of
    which writes. At the door, the identity is derived from the projection itself, by the
    same exhaustive walk, and is three-valued where the descriptor's `Option` was not —
    `Undecided` where a cast erased it, which is what makes `m IN (SELECT 'ok'::mood)`
    answer rather than refuse.

    **That derivation reached the door's own entry and not the `ColumnDesc` the readers
    around it resolve through, and those readers refused the same shapes one level out.** A scalar-subquery *operand* (`m > (SELECT min(m) FROM w)`), and a **derived
    relation**'s computed column wherever a gate binds one — a derived table, a CTE, a
    `JOIN … ON`, an `UPDATE … FROM` source — were `42883` here against rows there, at
    `=`, `>`, `BETWEEN`, `COALESCE`, `greatest` and `= ANY(ARRAY[…])`, over projections
    `min(m)`, `COALESCE(m,'ok')` and `m … GROUP BY m` — each of them ordinary SQL, and the
    loudest thing this row's gates have done. It is row 107's close — one derivation on
    `Expr::to_column_desc`, upstream of those namespaces rather than in any of them — and
    the controls that keep it a decision are the passthrough and
    computed **`text`** projections beside it, which must stay loud where a blanket
    *defer* would accept them.
  - **An operand a cast leaves undecidable — and one of its producers writes.**
    **The four doors that read a cast disagree about it, and each pays the other's cost.**
    The plain operand position and the `IN (SELECT …)` sub-plan column read an undecidable
    identity as *fall back to the OID rule*, so they accept and **write**:
    `DELETE FROM w WHERE m = s::text` and `DELETE FROM w WHERE m IN (SELECT s::text FROM
    w)` each remove the row 18.6 keeps by refusing `42883 operator does not exist: mood =
    text` (the `NOT IN` twin removes the complement, and the `UPDATE` spelling rewrites a
    stored member). The scalar-subquery **operand** door and the **derived-relation**
    door read it as *no enum*, so they refuse — which is `wildcard_column_type`'s and
    `set_op_enum_identity`'s side of the same trade, the one that never leaves a write
    silent. What refusing costs is measured and is not nothing, at
    **both** of the cast's source shapes: over a typed source, `m = (SELECT s::mood FROM
    w)` and `t.m = v.z` over `(SELECT s::mood AS z FROM w) v`; over an unresolved literal,
    `m > (SELECT 'ok'::mood)` and `t.m > v.z` over `(SELECT 'ok'::mood AS z) v` — each
    `42883` here against rows there, and each one the `IN (SELECT …)` door answers,
    `m IN (SELECT 'ok'::mood)` being what that door's middle state was taken for.

    **No rule over the cast's *source* separates the two sides**, which is what a
    discriminator would have to do: `'ok'::mood` and `'zz'::text` are the same `Expr` over
    an unresolved literal, and `s::mood`, `m::mood` and `lower(s)::mood` are the same
    `Expr` as `s::text`, `m::text` and `lower(s)::text` over a typed one — measured on
    both engines, 18.6 answering the `::mood` spelling and refusing the `::text` one at each
    source shape put to it — a literal, a column, and an aggregate and a function call
    over one. So keying on *the source is a typed
    expression* closes seven `::text` members and opens three working-SQL `::mood`
    over-refusals while leaving the literal `::text` members open; it moves the defect
    rather than closing it. Closing it is row 104's — carrying the enum name on the cast
    node — and nothing short of that separates them. The write is locked, at the door that
    takes it, by `crates/pglet`'s `enum_identity_gates::the_in_subquery_cast_door_still_writes`,
    which asserts the rows it removes beside the two doors that refuse and the
    `m IN (SELECT 'ok'::mood)` accept the middle state buys.

    `m > s::text` is one row here against `42883 operator does not exist: mood > text`,
    and `m > y::mood` one row against 18.6's `42846 cannot cast type m3 to mood` — the
    cast's own failure, not an operator's. A `$N` the client declared **`text`** is the
    same node and so the same residual; one declared `varchar` is a cast to `varchar`,
    which is decidable, and is refused as 18.6 refuses it. **A cast to the enum itself is
    a fourth producer, and it is the one that writes.** `x::mood` parses to a cast to
    `text`, so it is `Undecided` like every other, and it defeats *both* halves of the
    gate — the operator/fold refusal and the literal's conversion: measured on both
    engines, `greatest(m::mood,'zzz')` answers `zzz, zzz, zzz`, `COALESCE(m::mood,'zzz')`
    and `m::mood > 'zzz'` answer, `COALESCE(NULL::m9,'zzz')` answers `zzz`, and
    `CREATE TABLE c5 (z mood, CHECK (z::mood <> 'zzz'))` plus

    two DDL statements, so the catalog pglet holds after them is one stock 18.6 refuses to
    build. So the residuals of this member are not all read-only, and closing it is row
    104's: carrying the enum name on the cast node.
    **One producer of that cast is pglet itself**:
    `type_scalar_subquery_branches` wraps a branch subquery in a cast to its own type, so
    `greatest(m, (SELECT s FROM w))` and `greatest(m, (SELECT 'zz'))` answer `OK` / `zz`
    here against `42804 GREATEST types mood and text cannot be matched` there — the
    ambiguity manufactured rather than written. The *other* direction, the subquery being
    the enum side, is closed and measured (`COALESCE((SELECT m FROM w), s)` is `42804` on
    both) — row 152(a). Closing the rest is row 104's: carrying the enum name on the cast
    node.
  - **~~The recursive-CTE term's fold~~ — closed.** The set-operation door converts its
    `unknown` entry against the enum the fold landed on, and the **recursive** term's fold
    now converts it too, after the fold as 18.6 does: `WITH RECURSIVE r(x) AS (SELECT m
    FROM w UNION ALL SELECT 'zzz' FROM r WHERE false) SELECT * FROM r` answered two rows
    here and is now 18.6's `22P02 invalid input value for enum mood: "zzz"`, while the
    member `'sad'` still answers. It had been read-only because pglet refused every write
    spelling measured over a `WITH RECURSIVE`; two of them now run — the statement-body
    `WITH RECURSIVE … INSERT INTO tx …` and a data-modifying CTE beside the recursive one —
    and the conversion closed with them, pinned on both the read and the write
    (`with_recursive_list/enum_recursive_term_non_member_literal_loud.sql` and its
    `_write_loud` twin).

    **The identity reaching this fold is what made the fold a hazard, and the `unknown`
    branch is carved out of it for that reason.** The fold reads the seed's descriptor,
    which now carries the enum, so a *typed* text recursive term is `42804` on both
    engines. An `unknown` one is not that: 18.6 converts it rather than folding it, so the
    **member** literal `… UNION ALL SELECT 'sad'` is two rows there — and reading the
    identity on that branch refused it, measured, trading this silent residual for a loud
    over-refusal. `check_recursive_shape` therefore folds an `unknown` entry by the OIDs
    alone, through the set operation's own `unknown_output_columns`, and converts it
    after the fold, which is what refuses `'zzz'` above.

    **The missing conversion is not this row's, and it is not silent outside the string
    category.** The same fold is `42804 UNION types <T> and text cannot be matched` at
    every non-string seed type measured, where 18.6 converts — an over-refusal for a
    convertible literal and the wrong code for one that is not. That is **row 156**, and
    what made this residual silent rather than loud was only that a `mood` seed and a
    string literal both read `text`, so the fold succeeded.

  - **~~A genuinely recursive CTE's rebuilt descriptors~~ — closed.** The door this row
    lists apart from a plain CTE, and the reason it is listed apart: a recursive CTE's
    relation is built by neither of the two producers that close the others.
    `parser::select`'s `recursive_cte_columns` **rebuilds** the seed's descriptors to
    apply the `name(cols)` list, and rebuilt them through `ColumnDesc::new`, which
    answers `None` whatever the seed derived — so the working table's column ordered by
    its **label bytes** (`happy, ok, sad` against `sad, ok, happy`), `WHERE z > 'ok'`
    selected the `sad` row where 18.6 selects `happy`, `min`/`max` were inverted, a
    non-member literal ranked after every member instead of `22P02`, and the comparisons
    with a real enum column measured — a scalar-subquery operand, a `JOIN … ON`, an `IN
    (SELECT …)`, an `EXISTS`, an `UPDATE … FROM` and the `DELETE`/`UPDATE` predicate —
    were each `42883 operator does not exist: mood > text`. Read-only then, pglet refusing
    every write spelling measured over a `WITH RECURSIVE`.

    **The two halves have different provenance, and re-measuring on a build before the
    enum-identity gates is what separated them.** The *silent* half is pre-existing and
    measured identical there — the order `happy, ok, sad`, the `sad` row for `z > 'ok'`,
    `min`/`max` as `happy | sad`, `(0 rows)` for a non-member literal. The `42883` is
    **not**: before those gates `m > (SELECT z FROM r)` answered, and answered as 18.6
    does, the *enum column* operand supplying the order the CTE column could not. The gate
    that refuses `enum <op> text` arrived inside this row's own close, and over a
    descriptor carrying no identity it read the pair as `mood > text` — so the loud half
    is a regression this row's gates introduced at this one door and the rebuild's repair
    removes. The plain-`WITH` spelling of every shape above was right before those gates
    and is right now, which is what makes the *recursion* the condition rather than the
    CTE. The rebuild carries the seed's identity field by field now, and deliberately
    keeps zeroing `table_oid`/`column_id`, which 18.6 also sends as `0` for a recursive
    CTE where it sends the base table's for a plain one — measured on a raw
    `RowDescription`, and the reason propagating the whole descriptor is the *wrong*
    repair. `docs/enums.md`.

  **An unknown literal that resolves to an enum is *converted*, not left alone.** 18.6's
  `coerce_type` runs the target's input function on the `Const`, and `enum_in` is the
  whole of a `22P02`; pglet holds an enum value as a `Value::Text`, so the conversion is
  the membership test and nothing else — and skipping it is not that coercion. Pre-existing, measured on
  builds before and after the enum-identity gates alike, and it **wrote**: `INSERT INTO tx
  SELECT greatest(m, 'zzz') FROM w` landed rows in a `text` column where 18.6 lands none
  (an enum *column* was already caught by the write path's own gate, which is why the text
  sink is the shape that matters), `DELETE FROM w WHERE m IN ('ok','zzz')` removed the
  rows 18.6 keeps, and a `CHECK (m > 'zzz')` or partial index over one was **persisted** —
  measured end to end: `deno task dump` emitted it, `psql -f` into stock 18.6 exited `0`,
  and the restored database held `pg_constraint` and `pg_indexes` empty where pglet holds
  both. The conversion now runs at the comparison positions, at the five
  `select_common_type` constructs, at the set-operation door, and at both
  persisted-expression doors, whose probe schema was being built without the catalog's
  enum member lists at all.

  **A value the client *binds* is the same conversion, and it was reaching none of
  those doors.** 18.6 resolves an **undeclared** `$N` at an enum position to that enum
  during parse analysis and runs `enum_in` on the bound value at `Bind`; pglet's
  plan-time gate sees an `Expr::Parameter`, which carries no label, so
  `unknown_literal_spelling` answered `None` and every one of the doors above waved it
  through. It **wrote**, and on the in-process host as well as the native server —
  removing the gate from either one reddens that host's own guard at the same shapes:
  `DELETE FROM w WHERE m < $1`
  bound to `'zzz'` removed all three rows where 18.6 keeps them, and
  `INSERT INTO tx SELECT greatest(m, $1)` landed three `zzz` where 18.6 lands none —
  and it answered `f, f, f` / `zzz` at the reads, against `22P02 invalid input value for
  enum mood: "zzz"` at every spelling there. The control that made it sharp is that a
  **member** value already resolved to the enum and ordered by its member positions, so
  the operand was decided and only the conversion was missing.

  What plan time can record is the **target**, not the conversion, so
  `planner::param_types` carries it (`ParamTargets`, the OID beside the enum identity —
  `ResolvedType`'s shape at the gates, for `ResolvedType`'s reason) and each host spends
  it at its own decode, where 18.6 spends it: the native server's `Bind` and
  `Database::execute_bound`, which the wasm bindings' `queryParams` runs through. One
  predicate under both and under the literal door alike (`enum_label_legality`), so a
  bound value and a spelled literal cannot come to be judged differently. Eval time was
  not an option and the discriminator is measured: 18.6 refuses over an **empty** table
  and inside a `WHERE false`, so nothing about the refusal depends on a row.

  **Its reach is the positions the target walk reaches, read off the plan-time gate's
  own arm list** — a comparison, a simple-`CASE` label, an `IN` item, `nullif`'s pair, an
  `op ANY`/`op ALL`'s array element, and the branch fold over `unification_branches`.
  Measured closed at all of them, plus `BETWEEN` and `IS DISTINCT FROM` (comparisons),
  `ARRAY[m, $1]` (a fold whose element set holds a typed enum), and the write-path targets
  that already refused (`INSERT … VALUES ($1)`, `UPDATE … SET m = $1`). `m > ANY(ARRAY[$1])`
  is **not** a gap: 18.6 resolves that all-`unknown` array to `text[]` and answers the
  operator's `42883`, which both engines now do. A `$N` the client **declared** `text` is
  untouched by design — it is planned as a cast and is the undecidable-operand residual,
  measured unmoved.

  **What stays open is a target a *plan* decides rather than a sibling `Expr`, and one
  half of it writes and persists.** This walk records a target it can read off a
  neighbouring expression; at two positions the enum is a sub-plan's column instead, which
  `expr_enum_with` answers `None` for by design and which the query-path gate reads through
  a second, `ColumnScope`-bound reader `planner::param_types` does not hold. So
  `$1 IN (SELECT m FROM w)` bound to a non-member answers here against 18.6's `22P02`, and
  it is **read-only at both spellings measured**: the `SELECT` answers no rows and
  `DELETE FROM w WHERE $1 NOT IN (SELECT m FROM w)` removes none, where 18.6 refuses each.
  The **set-operation** door
  (`SELECT m FROM w UNION ALL SELECT $1`), which `coerce_unknown_entry` gates for a
  *literal* and not for a bound value, rewrites the `$N` into a cast to `text` while the
  fold's enum target is discarded (`Plan::SetOp` carries plain `TypeOid`s), leaving nothing
  for this walk to read. Measured on the native server, `ms ('ok','sad','happy')`, `$1` =
  `'zzz'` undeclared: `DELETE FROM ws WHERE m IN (SELECT m FROM ws WHERE id=1 UNION ALL
  SELECT $1)` is `DELETE 1` here against `22P02` and all three rows kept there;
  `UPDATE wu SET m = t.m FROM (SELECT m FROM wu WHERE id=1 UNION ALL SELECT $1) t WHERE
  wu.id=2 AND t.m <> wu.m` **rewrites a stored member** (`ok` → `sad`) against `22P02` and
  nothing written; and `INSERT INTO tx SELECT m FROM (… UNION ALL SELECT $1) u` lands `zzz`
  in a `text` sink where 18.6 lands nothing. The **member** polarity agrees
  (`m IN (SELECT m FROM ws WHERE id=1 UNION ALL SELECT $1)` bound `'ok'` is one row on
  both), so it is the conversion that is missing and not the door. No spelling measured put
  a non-member label into an enum **column** — the write path's own gate caught
  `UPDATE … SET m = $1`, `INSERT … VALUES ($1)`, `INSERT … SELECT` over the set op and the
  CTE spelling — which is a sample and not a bound: the text sink is the shape that
  escapes, as it is for the literal door above.

  **Arms the DDL-time rulebook did not have**, found by re-deriving the arm list from the
  grammar rather than from the class's own statement: `check_expr_node_operand_types`
  matched no `InList`, no simple-`Case` and no `AnyAll`, where the plan-time walk matched
  the first two — so `CHECK (m IN (s))`, `CHECK (CASE m WHEN s THEN …))` and their
  non-member-literal spellings were **recorded** here and refused there, the same
  restore-short as above. The value probe beside that walk hid it for a pair whose operands
  differ in shape (`CHECK (i IN (s))` is its `42883`, measured) and could not for an enum,
  whose value is a `Value::Text` like the `text` it is being compared to.
  `CHECK (m = ANY(ARRAY[s]))` and `CREATE INDEX … WHERE m = ANY(ARRAY[s])` are the third
  arm's members, recorded here and refused there the same way. The `IN (SELECT …)` half of that pair has
  **no** DDL twin and needs none: both engines refuse a subquery in every
  persisted-expression context — measured at the `CHECK` and index-predicate spellings
  (`0A000 cannot use subquery in check constraint` / `… in index predicate`,
  byte-identical), and read for the rest off `transformSubLink`'s own per-`ParseExprKind`

  `parser::ddl`'s `reject_persisted_expr_constructs` and `executor::ddl`'s
  `check_default_expr_nodes` here. So no stored expression can carry one. One rulebook, two
  callers, and it was the caller's arm list that had gone short — re-derive it rather than
  inherit it, and from the grammar rather than from the twin.

  Everything else measured is closed with 18.6's own SQLSTATE, and at the operator
  positions with its message byte for byte: the comparisons in both orders and at every
  operator, `IN`, `BETWEEN`, `IS DISTINCT FROM`, a simple `CASE` label, `nullif`, the
  four value constructors, `min`/`max` feeding one, a bare scalar subquery feeding one,
  the set operation in both orders and under `UNION`/`INTERSECT`/`EXCEPT`, a FROM-clause
  `VALUES`, a CTE, a recursive CTE — the degraded (no-self-reference) one and the **genuinely**
  recursive one, the latter closed separately for the reason the bullet below gives — both `JOIN … USING` readers, a `varchar` column, a
  `name`-typed session source, and the DDL-time `CHECK` and partial index that used to
  persist and then fail to restore. What a **deeper** gate moved is error precedence, and
  that is row 154: it now outranks a later target-list item's unbound name, as 18.6's
  source order does, and it pre-empts the `42P01` of a missing relation, which 18.6's
  does not. The accept side is pinned beside it — an unresolved
  literal beside an enum, a cast to the enum, two columns of the *same* enum, an
  `ARRAY[…]` of a column and a literal, `m::text` beside a `text` column, and a `CHECK`
  plus partial index over an enum and a literal — because an over-refusal here is a
  worse defect than the one this closed.

  **What the answer was, at the two kinds of position.** Where an order decided it the
  answer was the **member positions** — `WHERE m > t` kept the `happy` row — and at `=`
  it was the label bytes; the write routes include an `UPDATE … SET m = greatest(m,t)`
  beside the `DELETE` predicate, the `INSERT … SELECT` source and the persisted `CHECK`
  or partial index above.

  **One more producer of the pass's own cast.** Beside the scalar-subquery branch and the
  `unknown` array element, the pass rewrites a **set operation's** branch column and a
  **`VALUES`** cell, and at those two doors the node's under-refusal becomes a loud
  **over-refusal** instead.

  **What the guard reaches, and why no fixture holds the bound-`$N` half.** The corpus
  side is the `enum/*_loud.sql` family, one per gate and per door for the identity, plus
  `enum/computed_text_operand_*` for the gates' reach, `enum/from_derived_table_*` /
  `enum/from_cte_*` / `enum/join_on_derived_table_*` /
  `enum/scalar_subquery_computed_*` / `enum/update_from_derived_table_*` /
  `enum/subquery_enclosing_column_*` for the identity at the derived-relation and
  scalar-subquery doors in both polarities (row 107), and `enum/non_member_literal_*` for
  the literal's conversion, the recursive-CTE **comparison** door's
  `enum/non_member_literal_recursive_cte_loud` among them (the recursive **term's fold**
  is held outside that prefix, by
  `with_recursive_list/enum_recursive_term_non_member_literal_loud`) — a prefix that also
  carries this row's two **precedence** fixtures (`…_outranks_a_later_binding_error` and
  `…_yields_to_an_earlier_binding_error`, row 154's) — with the `enum/*_accept*.sql` and
