  `enum/member_literal_*` controls beside them in the over-refusal polarity, plus
  `crates/pglet`'s `enum_identity_gates` for the rows a refused write leaves and the
  catalog a refused DDL does not. The bound-`$N` half has **no fixture, and what stands
  in the way is the harness's own type table**: 18.6 resolves such a parameter to the
  enum's own OID, `postgres-types`' blanket `ToSql for String` declines that OID (its
  `accepts` has no `Kind::Enum` arm), so the oracle leg errors
  `error serializing parameter 0` before it reaches a server — and `FixtureParamType` has
  no enum spelling to reach past it. Both are `pglet_tests`', and `SqlNumeric` is the
  precedent for changing them: a bespoke `ToSql` newtype whose `accepts` took
  `Kind::Enum` beside `TEXT` would bind on both legs. Until one exists it is guarded
  off-corpus, on both decode paths and through all three instruments that reach them —
  `enum_identity_gates` and the wasm suite for `Database::execute_bound`,
  `pglet_server`'s `handlers.rs` Bind test for the native server's, with
  `enum/bound_param_non_enum_control.sql` holding the non-enum polarity on the corpus.

- **~~115~~ · Closed — Two different enums cancel to no enum at all, and the comparison
  used to fall back to the label bytes.** `executor::expr::unify_enum_pair`'s
  `(Some(l), Some(r))` arm is `(l == r).then_some(l)`, so two *different* enums answer
  `None` — the same verdict as a pair carrying no enum at all — and nothing downstream
  was handed a member list to order by. That arm is unchanged and still right for the
  **ordering** question; what was missing is the gate above it, which now refuses the
  statement before any order is asked for. Row 114's repair is this one: the gates read
  a `ResolvedType`, and 18.6's answer for two enums falls out of modelling the
  `typcategory` rather than the type identity.

  **The code is the whole reason this is its own row, and the repair had to produce
  both.** `select_common_type` (`parse_coerce.c`) raises `42804` only when the two
  categories differ; two enums share `E`, so the fold succeeds, keeps the first branch's
  type, and `coerce_to_common_type` (`ERRCODE_CANNOT_COERCE`) then fails to convert the
  second — *could not convert type m3 to mood*. Measured on both engines over
  `mood ('sad','ok','happy')`, `m3 ('sad','happy','ok')` and
  `v(id, m mood, y m3)`: `greatest(m,y)` is `42846 GREATEST could not convert type m3 to
  mood`, `least`, `CASE` and `COALESCE` the same under their own construct words, the
  set operation `42846 UNION could not convert type m3 to mood`, and `ARRAY[m, y]` its
  `ARRAY` spelling — while the comparisons, `BETWEEN` and `nullif` take
  `42883 operator does not exist: mood > m3`, the operator refusal, `nullif` being an
  equality one constructor in. pglet now answers each with 18.6's code **and** its
  message. Where it used to answer, it answered by the label bytes — `f, t, f` for
  `m > y`, `sad, ok, ok` for `greatest(m,y)` — neither column's positions, and it
  **wrote**: `DELETE FROM vw WHERE m > y` destroyed the row 18.6 keeps by refusing, and
  a `CHECK (m > y)` or a partial index over it was persisted and then dumped to SQL
  stock 18.6 rejects while psql exited `0`.

  **The residuals are row 114's, over a second enum in place of the `text` side, and the
  list this used to give was wrong in both directions.** `ARRAY[m] < ARRAY[y]` is **not**
  one — it is `42883 operator does not exist: mood[] < m3[]` on both engines, measured,
  as `ARRAY[m] < ARRAY[s]` is `mood[] < text[]` on both: `erases_enum_identity`'s array
  arm declined only where an **element** was an unresolved literal (and now not even
  there — it declines where an element is one of its own producers, a text-shaped cast or
  a bound value), and a bare column is none of those, so the `ARRAY[…]` pair over two enum columns was never in this class and the
  fixture cited for it (`enum/two_enums_array_element_loud.sql`) pins `ARRAY[m, y]`, the
  fold, which is a different statement. Nor is the cause "an operand no plan-time reader
  types": both sides are typed. What is left is `m > y::mood`, which a written cast leaves
  undecidable and is 18.6's `42846 cannot cast type m3 to mood`, the cast's own failure
  rather than an operator error; it closes where row 114's cast residual does.
  `m > ANY(ARRAY[y])` was on this list and is **closed**, and so is a third member the
  list never named, `m IN (SELECT y FROM w)` — neither gate had an arm for either
  construct, so the comparison each implies was never asked, and neither gap was the array
  arm's or reached by narrowing it. Both wrote at their `DELETE` spellings. Row 114's
  bullet carries the arm-list rule they closed under.

  **What no test could be red for before is now a fixture.** The four unit arms that
  pin `unify_enum_pair`'s cancellation — `executor::expr`'s
  `expr_enum_walk_tests::two_different_enums_unify_to_nothing`,
  `a_subquery_unifies_with_its_siblings`, `an_array_takes_its_elements_unified_enum`,
  and `executor::helpers`'s
  `unified_enum_type_tests::two_different_enums_decline_rather_than_picking_a_side` —
  stand unchanged, because the ordering rule they pin is still the right one; the
  refusal simply sits above it. The differential guard is
  `enum/two_enums_{comparison,greatest,setop,array_element,delete_predicate}_loud.sql`,
  each carrying `@expect-message`, joined by `enum/in_subquery_two_enums_loud.sql` and
  `enum/any_all_two_enums_loud.sql` for the two constructs closed since, and
  `crates/pglet`'s `enum_identity_gates` asserts the rows a refused `DELETE` leaves and
  the catalog a refused `CHECK` does not write.

- **~~105~~ · Closed — the routes that put a non-member beside an enum column are
  refused. A label the enum does not hold still compares, and sorts after every member,
  where one is stored.** The record as it stood, then what closed it. The comparator
  ranks a label as `Ok(position)` for a member and
  `Err(label)` for one the type lacks, which orders every member below every non-member
  and non-members among themselves by their bytes. That is a **total order** — the
  requirement `sort_by` has and "members by position, the rest by bytes, interleaved"
  does not satisfy — and it cannot brick a readable table, which is the posture this repo
  already takes toward a dump whose sequence owner it cannot resolve. 18.6 offers no
  answer to copy: its enum datum *is* a validated `pg_enum.oid`, so a label its cache
  lacks is an internal `elog(ERROR, "enum value %u not found in cache for enum %s")` —
  `typcache.c`'s `enum_cmp_internal`, where `find_enumitem` came back NULL — rather than
  a modelled SQLSTATE.

  Two routes reach it and they diverge differently. A non-member written as a **cast** —
  over `mqt (m mq)` holding `a` and `b`, `WHERE m < 'bogus'::mq` — is `22P02 invalid input
  value for enum mq: "bogus"` on 18.6 and answers here: every row for `<`, `(0 rows)` for
  `>` (measured on the native server, the in-memory B+tree). That is the cast-membership
  edge, row 241, seen from the comparison side. The **bare** literal does not reach it:
  `WHERE m > 'bogus'`, `m < 'bogus'`, `'bogus' < m` and `m = 'bogus'` are that `22P02` on
  both engines, the literal converted to the other operand's enum (`docs/coercion.md` § What
  the gate reads; `enum/non_member_literal_comparison_loud.sql`).

  A **stored** non-member is the second, and it is an ordinary statement rather than the
  exotic one this row used to name: `ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN m <enum> DEFAULT
  '<non-member>'` back-fills the existing rows without validating, where 18.6 raises
  `22P02` at the `ALTER` — measured, and it writes. The cast spelling `DEFAULT 'q'::mq` and
  `NOT NULL DEFAULT 'q'` back-fill the same (measured, the in-memory B+tree and `--storage
  memory`), and `m > 'b'` then selects the row. Once stored, an `UPDATE` of another column
  keeps it (`UPDATE m5 SET i = 2` answers `UPDATE 1`), while one writing it again — `SET m
  = m`, `SET m = DEFAULT`, an `INSERT … SELECT m` into another enum column — is `22P02`.
  The `CREATE TABLE … DEFAULT '<non-member>'` spelling does not reach it (pglet accepts the
  DDL that 18.6 refuses, but every later `INSERT` taking the default is `22P02` through
  `validate_column`), nor does the `ADD COLUMN` over an empty table, for the same reason;
  `DROP TYPE` + re-`CREATE TYPE` with different members reaches it too (row 261). **No differential
  fixture can express any of them**: for the `ALTER` a faithful fixture is red, and for
  the `DROP TYPE` route 18.6 refuses the setup outright (`2BP01`).
  `engine_ddl`'s `test_enum_non_member_label_sorts_after_every_member` is what pins the
  *comparison* over such a row; the two write routes are unpinned.

  **What closed it.** The two routes recorded are refused where 18.6 refuses them. The **cast** is row
  241's close: `m < 'bogus'::mq` is `22P02` at plan time, whatever the rows
  (`enum/cast_non_member_compared_to_column_loud.sql`). The **stored** route is the column
  `DEFAULT`'s cook: a bare string literal into an enum column is converted by the enum's
  member list as the default is cooked, on `CREATE TABLE`, `SET DEFAULT` and `ADD COLUMN`
  alike, so `ADD COLUMN m mq DEFAULT 'bogus'` is `22P02` at the `ALTER` over a table holding
  a row and over an empty one, and back-fills nothing
  (`enum/bare_non_member_add_column_default_loud.sql`,
  `…_add_column_default_empty_table_loud.sql`, `bare_non_member_default_create_table_loud.sql`,
  `bare_non_member_set_default_loud.sql`); the cast spelling `DEFAULT 'bogus'::mq` is row
  241's (`enum/cast_non_member_add_column_default_loud.sql`). Measured on the native server
  against 18.6, each statement above answering 18.6's `22P02` and message; the embed's
  refused `ADD COLUMN` leaves no column (`enum_identity_gates`'
  `a_cast_to_the_enum_converts_where_18_6_converts`).

  A third family back-filled too, and it is the one the assignment gate is blind to: a
  default of another type — `DEFAULT 'q' || ''`, `lower('Q')`, `'q'::text`, `5`, `now()`,
  `current_date`, `gen_random_uuid()`, `nextval('s')`, `'q' || nextval('s')::text` — is
  `42804 column "m" is of type mq but default expression is of type …` on 18.6 (row 6's
  enum residual, recorded under row 47), and stored its text here: `q`, `5`, a timestamp,
  a date, a uuid, `1`, `q2`. The back-fill now tests every value it writes by the write
  path's own member test (`constraints::validate_enum_member`), and the cook tests the
  value it evaluates on the `ADD COLUMN` route, so each is refused before any row is
  written, over an empty table too where the cook evaluates the default — `22P02`, loud
  under the wrong code (measured; `enum_identity_gates` holds the list). A `nextval` in
  such a default has drawn from its sequence before the refusal, as any failed back-fill
  does. A **member** so typed (`DEFAULT 'a'::text`) still back-fills, a valid label under
  18.6's `42804`, and the `CREATE TABLE` / `SET DEFAULT` spellings are still accepted and
  refused at the first write taking the default — both row 6's.

  **The residual is the comparator arm, and it is reachable through one door.** A stored
  label the enum does not hold is what `DROP TYPE` + re-`CREATE TYPE` with other members
  leaves under a column (row 261, which 18.6 refuses `2BP01`, so no fixture can set it up),
  and there it still ranks after every member — the total order this bullet's opening
  describes, pinned by `engine_ddl`'s `test_enum_non_member_label_sorts_after_every_member`,
  which builds its state through that door. No other door is known: `COPY`, `INSERT`,
  `UPDATE` and `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` validate the member, pglet has no `ALTER TYPE`, a
  dump carries the rows its source held, and a fork copies them.

- **~~241~~ · Closed — a cast to an enum converts its operand where 18.6 does. Cast is
  not membership-validated was the edge.** The record as it stood:
  Measured on the native server (the
  in-memory B+tree and `--storage memory`, npm `pg`) against 18.6, over `mq AS ENUM ('a',
  'b')`: `SELECT 'q'::mq`, `SELECT CAST('q' AS mq)`, `SELECT 'q'::text::mq`, `SELECT
  'q'::mq::text` and `SELECT $1::mq` with `$1` bound to `q` answer `q`; `SELECT 'q'::mq =
  'q'::mq` and `SELECT 'q'::mq > 'a'::mq` answer `t`; over `mqt (m mq)` holding `a` and
  `b`, `DELETE FROM mqt WHERE 'q'::mq > 'a'::mq` answers `DELETE 2` and empties it, and
  `SELECT m FROM mqt WHERE m = 'q'::mq` answers no row; `INSERT INTO tt SELECT 'q'::mq`
  into a `text` column writes `q`. 18.6 answers `22P02 invalid input value for enum mq:
  "q"` to every one — its `enum_in` validates at the cast — and keeps both rows. The
  embedded `Database` answers the first three the same, on its three backends.
  `INSERT INTO mqt VALUES ('b') RETURNING 'q'::mq` answers `INSERT 1` returning `q` and
  keeps the row, which 18.6 refuses whole. The DDL that stores the cast is accepted where
  18.6 refuses it `22P02`: `CREATE TABLE md (i INT, m mq DEFAULT 'q'::mq)`, `ALTER TABLE
  md3 ALTER COLUMN m SET DEFAULT 'q'::mq`, `CREATE TABLE mc (m mq CHECK (m <> 'q'::mq))`,
  `ALTER TABLE mqt ADD CONSTRAINT ck9 CHECK (m <> 'q'::mq)`, and the index predicate and
  key expression `CREATE INDEX pq1 ON mqt (m) WHERE m <> 'q'::mq` and `CREATE INDEX pq2 ON
  mqt ((m = 'q'::mq))` each answer `CREATE`/`ALTER` (`pq2`'s `indexdef` renders the key
  `(m = 'q'::text)`).

  The writes into an enum column measured are refused on both engines, `22P02` here too:
  `INSERT … VALUES ('q')` and `VALUES ('q'::mq)`, `INSERT … SELECT 'q'::mq`, an `INSERT …
  SELECT` from a subquery's cast column, `UPDATE … SET m = 'q'::mq` and `SET m = 'q'`, an
  `UPDATE … FROM` a subquery's cast column, `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET m = 'q'::mq`, `COPY …
  FROM STDIN` carrying `q` (psql, the in-memory B+tree), and an `INSERT` taking a `CREATE
  TABLE` or `SET DEFAULT` default of `'q'::mq` (whose DDL 18.6 refused) — the write path
  validating the member. The measured exception is `ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN m mq DEFAULT
  'q'::mq` over a table holding a row: its back-fill stores `q` without that validation, as
  the bare `DEFAULT 'q'` does — row 105. The cast resolves to the label's text without
  checking membership (`docs/enums.md`, *Cast is not membership-validated*). A non-member
  compared against an enum column is row 105, and the enum identity a cast erases is row
  104. Silent, and it writes: the `DELETE`, the `text` insert, the `RETURNING` insert and
  the stored `DEFAULT`, `CHECK` and index expressions land where 18.6 refuses them. No
  fixture holds it — a
  faithful one is red.

  **What closed it.** The parser dropped the enum where it read a cast's type name, so the
  conversion had nothing to name. A cast whose target resolves to an enum now parses
  through one builder, `planner::build_enum_cast`, from the `::`, `CAST(… AS …)` and
  typed-constant (`mq 'q'`) spellings alike. A **member** string literal, and `NULL`,
  keep the plain cast to `text` they always were, so nothing that reads one moved — row
  104's erasure, the dump, index probes. Every other operand is the conversion
  `StringFunc::EnumIn` under that same cast, carrying the enum's name and its member
  labels, and it is decided where 18.6 decides it:

  - a **string literal** the enum does not hold, where every constant cast is decided —
    plan time (`validate_const_casts`) and the DDL walk over a `DEFAULT`, `CHECK`, index
    predicate or key (`check_expr_node_operand_types`) — so over zero rows, under `WHERE
    false`, in an untaken `CASE` branch and at `CREATE TABLE`;
  - an undeclared **`$N`** at `Bind`, through the enum target `ParamTargets::enums`
    already carried for a comparison, on both hosts (the corpus cannot drive it:
    `tests/README.md` § `-- @param`) — where the cast is the parameter's first
    type-fixing use in 18.6's parse-analysis order. 18.6 fixes an unspecified parameter
    at its first coercion (`SELECT`: `WITH`, `FROM`, the select list, `WHERE`, `HAVING`,
    `ORDER BY`, `GROUP BY`; `UPDATE`: `FROM`, `WHERE`, `RETURNING`, then `SET`; an
    `INSERT`'s row source before `ON CONFLICT`; a parent node's operands when the parent
    resolves; every statement's `WITH` list first, its queries in declaration order — or
    `TopologicalSort`'s under `RECURSIVE` — wherever the statement reads them, a read-only
    CTE inlined at a scalar subquery of the select list included), so after a `text` use
    the cast converts on the value: over no row
    `SELECT $1::text, $1::mq` binds `q` and `SELECT $1::mq, $1::text` refuses it at
    `Bind`, on both engines (`planner::param_types`' `first_fix` and
    `walk_with_query`; `params/enum_cast_param_order_*` for the accepts the corpus can
    bind, and
    `enum_identity_gates`' `a_cast_is_the_enum_target_only_where_it_fixes_the_parameter`
    and the server's Bind test for the refusals);
  - anything else — a column, a declared or `text`-cast parameter, `'q'::text`, an
    expression — on the value, at evaluation: over no row nothing is converted, as on
    18.6, and a `CHECK` converting a column refuses the write carrying the label. A
    `DEFAULT` holding such a conversion is accepted at `CREATE TABLE` and `SET DEFAULT`
    and raised by `ADD COLUMN`'s eager evaluation, 18.6's split — for a default that is
    not volatile (the last residual below).

  Measured against 18.6 on the native server, statement by statement over the whole
  record above plus the zero-row, untaken-branch, `RETURNING`, typed-constant, case-differing
  (`'SAD'::mood`), `varchar`-operand and `ADD COLUMN` spellings: each answers 18.6's code
  and message. The accepts are controls: a member converts at every spelling
  (`enum/cast_members_convert_at_every_spelling.sql`), and a `text` operand over no row
  answers `(0 rows)` on both (`enum/cast_text_operand_zero_rows_accepts.sql`,
  `enum/cast_column_zero_rows_accepts.sql`, `params/enum_cast_text_param_zero_rows_accepts.sql`),
  which a plan-time check of a non-literal would refuse. A persisted conversion renders
  as the one cast it is — `pg_get_constraintdef` answers `CHECK (((s)::mood IS NOT
  NULL))` and `column_default` `('q'::text)::mood`, 18.6's own strings
  (`enum/cast_column_check_renders_the_enum_cast.sql`,
  `enum/cast_text_operand_default_accepts.sql`), and the dump emits it, loading into both
  engines (`test_dump`'s `expr_probe`). Because such an expression names the type,
  `DROP TYPE` refuses it `2BP01` with 18.6's detail and hint, and `DROP TYPE … CASCADE`
  drops the constraint or clears the default and keeps the table and its rows, through
  the one DROP-time resolver (`executor::dependencies`' `DropTarget::Type`;
  `enum/drop_type_*`, and `enum_identity_gates`'
  `drop_type_refuses_an_expression_that_converts_to_it` for the catalog and a rolled-back
  cascade); without that the dump would name a type it no longer creates. An **index**
  holding the conversion is refused at `CREATE INDEX`, `42P17 functions in index
  {predicate,expression} must be marked IMMUTABLE`, 18.6's answer — after parse analysis
  and ahead of a bare key column, the index name and the `IF NOT EXISTS` skip, as
  `DefineIndex` orders them — unless the operand is already the enum, a relabel both
  engines accept (`enum/index_predicate_enum_conversion_loud.sql`,
  `enum/index_key_enum_conversion_loud.sql`, `enum/index_key_enum_relabel_accepts.sql`).
  Accepted, such an index dumped to a `CREATE INDEX` stock 18.6 refuses and gated writes
  on its frozen member list.

  **Residuals** — loud, but for the members marked **silently**:

  - **The statement position is every constant cast's.** The plan-time pass runs ahead of
    the range table and after the whole statement is read, so `SELECT 'q'::mq FROM nosuch`
    is `22P02` here and `42P01` on 18.6, and a later syntax error in the same statement
    loses to the `22P02` too — measured, and `SELECT 'x'::int FROM nosuch` is the same
    pair on this build and the one before it, so the enum cast joined a position rather
    than opening one. Within one expression the cast's pass also runs ahead of the
    comparison-literal gate: `WHERE m = 'zz' AND m = 'q'::mq` is `22P02` naming `q` here
    and `zz` on 18.6, which converts left to right — same code, other label.
  - **A constant 18.6 folds, under an `AND` / `OR` operand the left one decides.** Since
    row 172's close such an operand is not evaluated, so the guard idioms of hand-written
    SQL answer as on 18.6: `WHERE (s = '' OR st = s::mq)` over a row holding `''` counts
    it, `WHERE (s <> '' AND st = s::mq)` counts none, and `WHERE ($1 = '' OR st =
    $1::mq)` bound to `''` counts the row (`enum/guard_*`,
    `params/enum_cast_param_or_guard_empty_accepts.sql`, the npm adapter suite) — each
    `22P02` here between this row's close and that one. What remains is a conversion 18.6
    decides while planning: over an enum `('open', 'closed')` and a row holding `id = 1`,
    `WHERE id = 99 AND 'q'::text::e = 'open'` is `22P02` there, its planner folding the
    constant, and was here; it now counts no row, **silently**, the operand being a
    non-literal one converted on the value.
  - **A bound parameter 18.6 converts while planning.** With `$1` typed `text` by an
    earlier use, 18.6 converts `st = $1::mq` in a `WHERE` at planning — its selectivity
    estimate folds `enum_in` over the bound value — so `SELECT count(*) FROM e WHERE
    coalesce($1, 'x') = 'y' OR st = $1::mq` (and the `lower($1)` and `$1 || 'x'`
    spellings) bound to `q` over an empty `e` is `22P02` there, no `Bind` context; here
    the conversion is on the value, `22P02` where a row reaches the conversion and
    **silently** `0` where none does — over no row, or where an `AND` / `OR`'s left operand
    decides every row: `SELECT count(*) FROM t WHERE s = $1 AND m = $1::mq` bound to `zz`
    over two rows neither holding `zz` is `22P02` there and `0` here (measured).
    `WHERE id = $1 OR st = $1::mq` is 18.6's `42846 cannot cast type integer to mq`;
    here the cast types `$1` `text` (a cast outranks a comparison in pglet's inference,
    whatever the order), so over a row it is `42883 operator does not exist: integer =
    text` and over none it answers, **silently** (measured). A `$1::text` inside an
    **unreferenced** CTE is a use the plan does not carry — a read-only CTE is in the plan
    only where a reference inlines it — so there the cast still converts at `Bind`: `22P02`
    where 18.6 answers (`WITH a AS (SELECT $1::text AS v) SELECT $1::mq FROM t WHERE
    false`, measured), and so does a CTE read only from inside an unreferenced one (`WITH a
    AS (SELECT $1::text AS v), b AS (SELECT * FROM a) SELECT $1::mq FROM t WHERE false`
    bound `zz`: `22P02` at `Bind` here, `0` rows on 18.6, measured). And a conversion 18.6 never evaluates because the query above it
    reads no row of the relation that projects it is evaluated here, pglet materializing a
    derived relation's rows whatever the query above asks of them: `WITH a AS (SELECT
    $1::text AS v), b AS (SELECT $1::mq AS w) SELECT * FROM b, a WHERE false` bound to `zz`
    answers `(0 rows)` there and passes `Bind` here, then raises `22P02` as `b`'s one row
    is projected — as `SELECT * FROM (SELECT 1/((SELECT count(*) FROM t) - 2) AS w) b
    WHERE false` is `22012` here before and after this row's close, `(0 rows)` there, and
    the `WHERE t.id = 99` join spelling likewise (measured); the same statement over an
    empty relation answers on both. And a bare select-list `$1` ahead of `$1::mq`, which
    18.6 answers `42P08` (the parameter's types collide), is `22P02` at `Bind` here —
    loud both. (A `$1 IS NULL` ahead of the cast is `42P08` on both engines since row 57's
    close.)
  - **A source that is not a string** — `5::mq`, `true::mq`, another enum's column — is
    18.6's `42846 cannot cast type integer to mq` in parse analysis. Here it is raised on
    the value: the same code for a non-string value (`enum/cast_integer_source_loud.sql`),
    and **silently nothing** over no row; and for **another enum's** column, whose value is
    a label like a `text` one (row 104's erasure), a membership test — `22P02`, or,
    **silently**, the label passing where the target enum holds it too — against 18.6's
    `42846` (measured: over `m3 ('a','z')` holding `z`, `y::mq` is `22P02` here).
  - **What `DROP TYPE … CASCADE` does not reproduce.** A column declaring the enum is row
    261's: it survives the cascade here, which 18.6 drops. A **member literal**'s cast
    (`CHECK (s <> 'a'::mq::text)`) is a plain `text` cast here and names no type, so a
    bare `DROP TYPE` proceeds **silently** where 18.6 refuses it `2BP01` naming the
    constraint (measured). No `NOTICE: drop cascades to …` is sent, as for every cascade
    here, and with more than one dependent the `2BP01` omits the detail 18.6 fills with
    each of them, in its OIDs' order.
  - **An index over a conversion** is refused `42P17`, and three orders are not 18.6's:
    a mixed key `((s::mq), nosuchcol)` is `42703` here (the bare part is read in parse
    analysis — the pre-existing mixed-key residual `execute_create_index` records); a
    `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX … USING gin` with a converting predicate is `42P17` here and
    18.6's `0A000` for the unique GIN; and a predicate `s::mq = 'zz'` is `42P17` here and
    `22P02` there, the `'zz'` beside the cast not being converted here (row 104's
    erasure). Another enum's column converted in a key, `m2::mq`, is `42P17` here and
    `42846` there.
  - **A volatile default is evaluated eagerly over an empty table.** `ALTER TABLE e ADD
    COLUMN c TEXT DEFAULT (gen_random_uuid()::text)::mq` over no row is `22P02` here and
    accepted on 18.6, which evaluates a volatile default per row and so not at all. The
    mechanism is the cook's `ADD COLUMN` evaluation, which does not ask about
    volatility, and it predates the conversion: `ADD COLUMN c INT DEFAULT
    length(gen_random_uuid()::text)/0` over no row is `22012` here and accepted there
    (both measured). A stable operand (`('q'::text)::mq`) is `22P02` on both.
  - **`'{q}'::mq[]`** is `42704 type "mq" is not supported` here (the enum array is
    unbuilt, `docs/enums.md` § Deferred) against 18.6's `22P02`.

  The **bare** literal into an enum column outside a `DEFAULT` is not a cast and not this
  row's: `UPDATE t SET m = 'q' WHERE false`, `INSERT INTO t (m) SELECT 'q' FROM e` over an
  empty `e`, and an `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET m = 'q'` whose key is free are `22P02` on
  18.6 and succeed here — the first two writing nothing, the third inserting its row —
  row 5's unfolded conversion reached by an enum target (measured). Loud wherever a row
  reaches the conversion, through `validate_column`.

- **~~106~~ · Closed — a duplicate enum member label is refused, with 18.6's own
  sentence.** `CREATE TYPE dup AS ENUM ('a', 'a')` used to store both labels, and
  `SELECT enumlabel FROM pg_enum …` answered two `a` rows for a type that does not exist
  at all on 18.6. `execute_create_type` now walks the member list once, below the
  duplicate-**type** check so the two refusals keep 18.6's order (`42710` for the name,
  then the label's `23505`, measured), and above the OID read and the index rebuild, so
  a refused statement touches no catalog.

  **The repair's justification is not the one this bullet used to imply by omission.**
  It breaks no **ordering** — `enum_rank` is `order.iter().position(…)`, which takes the
  first match, so distinct labels take distinct ranks and the arm stays a total order
  and stays `Equal` ⟺ the labels are byte-equal; measured green on a duplicate-bearing
  list both before and after the gate
  (`executor::expr`'s `a_duplicated_label_keeps_the_comparator_a_total_order`, written
  as a **legacy-state** pin for exactly that reason). What it broke is the catalog —
  two `pg_enum` rows under one label, which makes `docs/enums.md`'s
  "one member is one label is one OID" premise locally false — and the **dump**:
  `CREATE TYPE dup AS ENUM ('a', 'a')` is the text `pglet::dump` emits, stock 18.6
  refuses it, and the whole export then fails to load, not just that type's.

  The gate closes the *producers*, not the state: a store written by an earlier build
  still holds such a type and still reads through the comparator arm above. Pinned by
  `enum/create_type_duplicate_label.sql` (`@expect-message`, so the refusal names 18.6's
  own index) with `enum/create_type_duplicate_type_name_beats_the_duplicate_label.sql`
  for the order and `enum/create_type_labels_are_case_sensitive.sql` as the accept-side
  control — a label is a string literal and is never folded, so `'A'` beside `'a'` stays
  two members.

- **~~107~~ · Closed — a projected expression's descriptor derives its enum, at the one
  site that builds one.** The walk asks its subquery leaf for the enum of the plan's
  **first output column** (`Plan::output_columns`), and a *derived relation*'s scope entry
  is the same descriptor read one construct over. The rule that closed —
  *A scalar subquery projecting an expression carries no enum* — was never only about a
  scalar subquery. A passthrough column always carried the
  identity — `Plan::project_output_columns`'s `find_input` propagates the whole descriptor
  — while a projected **expression** got `ColumnDesc::new`, no enum at all. So the leaf
  read `None`, and what that `None` cost depended on who was reading it.

  **The ordering readers took it for *order by the label bytes*.** Measured on the native
  server against 18.6 over `mood AS ENUM ('sad','ok','happy')`:
  `SELECT (SELECT min(m) FROM u) > 'sad'` and
  `SELECT (SELECT COALESCE(m,'sad') FROM u LIMIT 1) > 'sad'` were `f` here and `t` there,
  silently, and by the route the passthrough spelling writes through — a `DELETE` or
  `UPDATE` predicate takes the same comparison.

  **The identity *gates* took it for *not an enum*, and that refused ordinary SQL** — the
  cost that arrived with row 114's gates and is the reason this closed rather than staying
  a residual. Every namespace a gate reads a derived relation through is built from these
  descriptors, so `SELECT t.id FROM t, (SELECT min(m) AS z FROM u) v WHERE t.m = v.z` and
  its `>`, `BETWEEN`, `COALESCE`, `greatest` and `= ANY(ARRAY[…])` spellings, the CTE and
  `JOIN … ON` forms, an `UPDATE … FROM` source, a derived table projecting
  `COALESCE(m,'ok')` or `m … GROUP BY m`, and the scalar-subquery operand
  `t.m > (SELECT min(m) FROM u)` were each `42883 operator does not exist: mood > text`
  here against rows there, each of them ordinary SQL 18.6 answers.

  The repair is one derivation at `Expr::to_column_desc`, which is where a computed
  descriptor is built and the only site every one of those namespaces passes through —
  `build_desc_type_map`'s scope entries, `push_plan_relations`' `UPDATE … FROM` ones,
  `Plan::output_columns_scoped`'s relations, and `executor::subquery_enum_name` alike. It
  is skipped outright for a catalog holding no enum.

  **One shape is left.** The derivation's own subquery
  leaf **declines**, so a projection that *is* a scalar subquery carries none:
  `SELECT (SELECT (SELECT min(m) FROM u) FROM u) > 'sad'` is `f` here against `t` there,
  the same label-byte answer under the same silence, and a `DELETE` over that predicate
  removes the rows 18.6 leaves. Declining is a cost decision measured
  on both sides — this walk runs inside `Plan::output_columns`, where `infer_type` is
  already descending, so a descending leaf makes two descents per level: over a projecting
  nest on a release server, declining is flat (32 / 32 / 31 / 33 ms at depth
  12 / 16 / 18 / 20) where descending is 50 / 316 / 1165 / 4507 ms at the same four and
  ~17 s at depth 22, against 18.4's 39 ms (measured on 18.4), and the per-row shape does not separate them
  (76–80 ms either way over 20 000 rows). `crates/pglet`'s
  `enum_identity_gates::the_identity_derivation_does_not_re_enter_output_columns` is that
  bound's guard, red at 30 s under a descending leaf. The **no-FROM** spelling of the
  same nesting, `SELECT (SELECT (SELECT min(m) FROM u)) > 'sad'`, is the same shape: a
  `Plan::Values` derives an identity only from a column its record of enclosing references
  holds (row 159), so a correlated enum column under it — `SELECT id, (SELECT m) > 'sad'
  FROM u`, and the `DELETE`/`UPDATE` over that predicate — answers as 18.6 does.

  The **gate** side has neither, `enum_identity_in` asking `resolved_subquery_type_in`
  instead, which is also what reaches a projection naming an *enclosing* query's column —
  an answer no descriptor built under the sub-plan's own scope can carry
  (`enum/subquery_enclosing_column_projection_accepts`).

- **108 · A partial or expression-key index refuses every `DROP COLUMN` on its table.**
  pglet keys an index by resolved row *position* where 18.6 uses stable attnums, so a
  drop at or below a key column's position would silently re-point the key — and pglet
  never rebuilds an index on a column drop, so `executor::ddl`'s
  `index_affected_by_column_drop` refuses instead. For a plain index that gate is exact.
  For a **partial** index (`predicate.is_some()`) and for an **expression key**
  (`IndexKey::Exprs`) it is deliberately conservative: the stored `Expr` reads the row by
  position and the gate does not walk it, so *any* drop on that table is refused, and the
  conservative arms are also an over-rejection.

  Measured over `dcp(a, b, c)` under `CREATE INDEX dcp_pred ON dcp (a) WHERE c > 0`,
  `dce(a, b, c)` under `CREATE INDEX dce_expr ON dce ((a + c))`, and `dcq(a, b, c)` under
  `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX dcq_u ON dcq (a) WHERE a > 0`: `ALTER TABLE dcp DROP COLUMN b`,
  `ALTER TABLE dce DROP COLUMN b` and `ALTER TABLE dcq DROP COLUMN c` are each `0A000`
  here and `ALTER TABLE` on 18.6, which then still refuses the duplicate `dcq_u` would
  hold. In the first, the key is at position 0 — *before* the drop — so nothing the gate
  is named for is even at risk.

  Loud, so nothing is written and nothing is wrong; what it costs is a schema migration.
  Closing it needs a position walk over the stored predicate and key expressions plus an
  index rebuild on drop. What **is** closed
  is the message: the refusal used to assert *"keys on this column or one after it"* for
  all three shapes, which is false for two of them, and it now names the reason it found.

- **~~109~~ · Closed — A merged column's enum fold is pairwise, so a third branch revives a
  cancelled pair: no statement reaches the revival.** A set operation's output
  column and a `JOIN … USING` merge both take their enum from
  `executor::expr::unify_enum_pair`, whose `(Some(a), Some(b))` arm answers `None` for two
  *different* enums and whose `(Some, None)` arm reads a side carrying no enum as **no
  information**. Those two arms are right about a pair and wrong about a *chain*:
  `Plan::SetOp` and `Plan::Join` are binary, so a three-branch spelling folds the pair
  rule over an already-merged descriptor, where `None` no longer distinguishes "this side
  has no enum" from "this side cancelled one". Stickiness is what `unify_enum` adds for an
  expression *list* — its own doc calls it load-bearing, *the third operand must not
  revive the enum the first two cancelled* — and these two sites cannot inherit it,
  because the state they would have to carry has nowhere to live: `ColumnDesc::enum_type`
  is an `Option<String>`.

  What it answered before the close, measured on the native server against 18.6, over
  `mood AS ENUM ('sad','ok','happy')` and `weather AS ENUM ('sun','rain')` with three rows
  in each column: `SELECT m … UNION ALL SELECT w …` ordered `happy, ok, rain, sad, sun,
  sun` — the label bytes — and the same query with a third `UNION ALL SELECT m` branch
  ordered `sad, sad, ok, ok, happy, happy, rain, sun, sun`, `mood`'s member positions with
  the non-members ranked after them. Under `WHERE x > 'ok'` the three-branch spelling
  answered five rows the two-branch reading would not have selected. The `JOIN … USING`
  spelling did the same over two enums sharing labels: two-way answered `happy, ok`,
  three-way `ok, happy`, and three-way under `WHERE m > 'ok'` answered one row where the
  label bytes select none. 18.6 refuses **every** one of those six statements —
  `UNION could not convert type weather to mood` for the set operation and
  `operator does not exist: mood = weather` for the merge's equality — so no answer 18.6
  agreed with moved; what moved was which wrong answer pglet gave, and it moved with
  the branch count.

  **Closed without widening the descriptor.** Every chain that reaches this fold carries
  two *different* enums — the only pair `unify_enum_pair` cancels — and that pair is now
  refused **above** the fold, at the gates that decide whether two operands have an
  operator or a common type (row 115, the plain binary comparison over the same arm): two
  enums share `typcategory` `E`, so the set operation is `42846 UNION could not convert
  type weather to mood` and the merge's equality `42883 operator does not exist: mood =
  weather`, as on 18.6. Re-measured on the native server over `mood` and `weather` columns:
  the three-branch `UNION ALL` with its `ORDER BY`, and the same three branches under
  `WHERE x > 'ok'`, are `42846`; `tm a JOIN tw b USING (m) JOIN tm c USING (m)` is `42883
  operator does not exist: mood = weather`. The pairwise arms are unchanged, and the third
  state on `ColumnDesc::enum_type` this bullet once named as the close was not needed
  (`docs/enums.md`). `enum/two_enums_setop_loud.sql` pins the two-branch pair; no fixture
  drives three branches or a two-enum `USING` merge.

- **~~111~~ · Closed — the `ANY`/`ALL` walk read the scalar side only, and an enum can be
  on the other one.** `executor::expr`'s `Expr::AnyAll` arm resolved its member order from
  `operands_enum_order([left.as_ref()], …)` — the scalar operand — where the `BinaryOp`
  arm passes both of its. It now passes both too, and its gate asks
  `operand_can_be_enum` of both.

  **Widening the arm was never the binding constraint, which is why it is closed together
  with a wider class.** `expr_enum_with`'s `Expr::Array` arm answered `None`, justified as
  *an enum array having no column form here* — true of a **column** (`ms mood[]` is
  `type "mood" is not supported` on this engine, where 18.6 accepts the declaration) and
  saying nothing about an `ARRAY[…]` **expression**, which pglet builds, orders and writes
  through. With that arm blind, `ARRAY[m]` carried no identity for either operand list to
  find, so passing both changed nothing. Three readers had to move together: the walk's
  `Array` arm (its elements' unified enum), `values_compare_ordered`'s array arm (the same
  member list at every element, where it called the *unordered* `values_compare`), and
  `operand_can_be_enum` (which admits an array whose elements could be labels — otherwise
  the widened walk is never asked).

  Measured on the native server against 18.6 over `mood AS ENUM ('sad','ok','happy')` —
  pglet before, then both engines now. The `ANY`/`ALL` half, over `u(id, m)` holding one
  `'sad'` row: `SELECT ('ok' > ANY(ARRAY[m])) FROM u` was `f`, now `t` on both;
  `('ok' > ALL(ARRAY[m]))` the same; `SELECT id FROM u WHERE 'ok' > ANY(ARRAY[m])` was
  `(0 rows)`, now one row on both; `DELETE FROM u WHERE 'ok' > ANY(ARRAY[m])` was
  `DELETE 0` leaving the row, now `DELETE 1` on both. The `ARRAY[…]`-comparison half, over
  `t(id, m)` holding `happy/sad/ok`: `WHERE ARRAY[m] < ARRAY['ok'::mood]` answered row `1`
  and now answers `2` as 18.6 does; `WHERE ARRAY[m] > ARRAY['sad'::mood]` answered
  `(0 rows)` and now answers `1, 3`; `ORDER BY ARRAY[m]` answered the label bytes and now
  answers `sad, ok, happy`. **Three write paths were in it**, each silent:
  `DELETE FROM w WHERE ARRAY[m] < ARRAY['ok'::mood]` reported `DELETE 1` on both engines
  while destroying a different row; `CHECK (ARRAY[m] < ARRAY['ok'::mood])` admitted the
  opposite row set with no error on the row it took; and a
  `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX … WHERE ARRAY[m] > ARRAY['sad'::mood]` held a duplicate 18.6
  refuses with `23505`.

  The **control** is the scalar side, which agreed on both engines throughout and still
  does: `SELECT (m > ANY(ARRAY['ok'::mood])) FROM u` is `f` on both,
  `(m < ALL(ARRAY['ok'::mood]))` is `t` on both. The sibling positions measured beside the
  original also agreed — `BETWEEN` and `NOT BETWEEN` with the enum on a bound, `greatest`,
  `least`, `nullif` over a member label, a `COALESCE`-wrapped comparison, a `CASE`-returned
  enum, and an `IN` list.

  **The residual was not this row's, and it has since closed under row 114.** Which side
  18.6 has an operator for is decided by the **array's element type**:
  `m > ANY(ARRAY['ok'])` is `operator does not exist: mood > text` there, an all-`unknown`
  array typing as `text[]`, where pglet answered `f` — the same answer before and after
  this row's repair, since the scalar side always carried the enum. That was row 114's
  `enum <op> text` over-acceptance, one of the residuals that row left behind rather than
  something that closed with it, and it is now `42883` on both: the gates gained an
  `Expr::AnyAll` arm, and an array's identity is now the unification of its typed
  elements' — an `unknown` contributing nothing, as `transformArrayExpr`'s
  `select_common_type` does — so an all-`unknown` array is `text[]`. The
  array-against-array spelling of the same mismatch (`ARRAY[m] < ARRAY['ok']`,
  `mood[] < text[]` there) was a **different** gap — `erases_enum_identity`'s array arm,
  which called an array undecidable when any element was; the reader was not the reason,
  both sides being typed `text[]` by the widened one — and it closed with that arm, as did the
  **mixed** spelling one added element makes of the `ANY` form (`ARRAY[s,'ok']`, `ARRAY[y,'ok']`,
  `ARRAY[s,NULL]`), a mixed array taking its typed element's identity. The **branch** shape one constructor over is closed —
  `COALESCE(ARRAY[m], ARRAY[t])` is `42846 could not convert type text[] to mood[]` on both
  engines — because `concrete_branch_type` carries an `Expr::Array` arm.
  Separately, `'ok' > ANY (SELECT m FROM u)` is
  not a member at any width: pglet's parser refuses the subquery right-hand side outright
  (`42601 syntax error: expected an expression, found 'select'`), for every operand type,
  which is `eval_any_all`'s own array-only `TODO` and not an enum edge.

  What pins it is `ls tests/fixtures/enum/*array* tests/fixtures/enum/any_all_*` — read
  the directory rather than a count here — beside `executor::expr`'s
  `an_array_takes_its_elements_unified_enum`,
  `unnest_passes_its_operands_element_enum_through`,
  `arrays_compare_element_wise_against_the_same_member_order` and
  `the_gate_admits_an_array_whose_elements_could_be_enum_labels`.

  **Five separating mutations, measured, each reddening a different subset**: the `Array`
  arm back to `None` (ten fixtures, two unit tests — and this is the measurement behind
  *widening `AnyAll` was never the binding constraint*, since the widened arm is in place
  and the `ANY` fixtures still redden); the comparator's element call back to the
  unordered `values_compare` (seven fixtures, one unit test — and **not** the `ANY`
  ones, which compare scalar-against-element); the gate back to `Value::Text`-only (eight
  fixtures, one unit test); the `AnyAll` walk back to the scalar operand (the two
  array-side `ANY` fixtures, no unit test); and the `Unnest` arm back to `None`
  (`order_by_unnest_of_array_member_position` and one unit test). A sixth, the plausible
  wrong fix — the `Array` arm reading its **first** element instead of unifying — is
  caught by `order_by_array_mixed_elements_member_position` and by the walk test, and by
  nothing else.

- **112 · A FROM-item `unnest`'s column descriptor carries no enum.** `execute_unnest`
  builds each output column with `ColumnDesc::new(name, element_type)` and derives no
  enum, and `Plan::FunctionScan`'s `output_columns_scoped` — the other producer of the same
  descriptor — does the same. So a `WHERE`, `ORDER BY` or aggregate over that column reads
  `enum_type: None` and orders by the label bytes, even where the array expression feeding
  it does carry an enum.

  Only **one** spelling reaches it, and finding which is the whole of this row. A FROM-item
  `unnest` has no inner scope, so an enum can enter its array expression by exactly three
  routes and two of them are recorded elsewhere: a **cast**
  (`unnest(ARRAY['happy'::mood, …])`) carries no identity for any walk to find, which is
  row 104's boundary and not this descriptor; a **scalar subquery**
  (`unnest(ARRAY[(SELECT m …)])`) is `0A000 scalar subquery requires execution context` in
  that position, which is row 89's class. What is left is a **correlated column**, and it
  works: `FROM t, unnest(ARRAY[t.m])` is `42703` here, but the same reference inside a
  correlated subquery resolves.

  Measured on the native server against 18.6 over `mood AS ENUM ('sad','ok','happy')` and
  `t(id, m)` holding `happy/sad/ok`, pglet then 18.6:
  `SELECT id, (SELECT count(*) FROM unnest(ARRAY[t.m]) u WHERE u > 'ok') FROM t ORDER BY id`
  is `0, 1, 0` against `1, 0, 0`;
  `SELECT id, (SELECT min(u)::text FROM unnest(ARRAY[t.m,'ok'::mood]) u) FROM t ORDER BY id`
  is `happy, ok, ok` against `ok, sad, ok`; and
  `DELETE FROM w WHERE (SELECT count(*) FROM unnest(ARRAY[w.m]) u WHERE u > 'ok') = 1`
  reports **`DELETE 1` on both engines** while pglet destroys `sad` and 18.6 destroys
  `happy`. Silent, and the last one writes.

  Closing it needs the enum's **name** at that descriptor, and the channel that would have
  to carry one is `OuterFrame`, which carries member **orders** (`&[String]` borrowed from
  `Schema.enums`) and not names — as does every scope that fills one, which a
  `grep col_enums` over `executor/` enumerates (re-run it rather than reading a count here).

  And it would close the executor's half only. `Plan::FunctionScan`'s descriptor is built from
  `PlannerScope::none(schema)`, which cannot see an outer frame, and the planner derives an
  enum from a **descriptor pair** (`unified_enum_type`, for a set op and a `USING` merge)
  and from an *expression* only through `Expr::to_column_desc`'s shallow derivation
  (`PlannerScope::expr_enum_shallow`, row 107's close), which over `PlannerScope::none`
  has no outer frame to resolve `t.m` through. So the two producers of this one
  descriptor would disagree by construction (read in the source, not measured). No
  fixture holds it: a faithful one is red.

- **113 · Two refusals stand between a real `pg_dump` of an enum database and a restore,
  and closing either alone leaves the other.** Both are `42601`, they are raised at
  different parse positions, and each appears in an enum dump for its own reason:

  - `ALTER TYPE public.mood OWNER TO postgres` — `parser::ddl`'s `parse_alter` takes
    `SEQUENCE` and otherwise `expect_kw(Table)`, so an `ALTER` naming any other object is
    a syntax error there; both `ALTER TYPE …` and `ALTER SCHEMA …` report
    `syntax error: expected 'table', found identifier`, measured. What it refuses is the
    **kind**, not the qualifier or the `OWNER TO` tail: `ALTER TABLE public.r OWNER TO
    postgres` succeeds as a tolerated no-op and the unqualified
    `ALTER TYPE mood OWNER TO postgres` raises the same error, both measured too.
  - `m public.mood` in the column-type position — `parser::type_name`'s
    `expect_type_word` consumes exactly one bare identifier, so a qualified type name is
    `syntax error: expected ')', found '.'`. `parse_object_name` *does* take the
    qualifier, so `CREATE TYPE public.mood AS ENUM (…)` parses and the table declaring a
    column of the type then fails, taking its `COPY` block and its `PRIMARY KEY` with it.

  The second is **enum-shaped** because of what `format_type.c` qualifies: built-in OIDs are
  special-cased above the branch that calls `quote_qualified_identifier`, and `pg_dump`'s
  `search_path = ''` preamble makes every user type non-visible — so in a real dump
  `id integer` is bare and `m public.mood` is qualified. The first is enum-shaped for a
  blunter reason: a database with no user type has no user type to own.

  Measured end to end. `pg_dump` (18.6) of `r(id INT PRIMARY KEY, m mood NOT NULL)`
  holding two rows in a `CREATE DATABASE`-fresh database, replayed with `psql` into a
  release `pglet_server` on the default profile, in-memory B+tree, simple query, one
  server per run: with `ON_ERROR_STOP=1` psql exits **3** at the `ALTER TYPE` (dump line
  33) and stops there; at psql's default it exits **0** with four `ERROR` lines — the
  `ALTER TYPE`, the column type, `relation "r" does not exist` for the `COPY`, and a
  `syntax error at or near "1"` where psql, no longer in copy-in mode, re-reads the
  `COPY` data as SQL and swallows the trailing `ADD CONSTRAINT` into that statement — plus
  one psql-side diagnostic of its own, the `\.` terminator refused under the dump's
  `\restrict` preamble. The restored database holds the **type and no table at all**.
  *Loud per statement, silent per process.*

  **The control, and the bound that made three measurements of this row disagree.** The
  same table with a `TEXT` column, dumped from its own fresh database, restores **clean**:
  exit 0 and both rows, with and without `ON_ERROR_STOP`. Its dump carries neither
  statement — no user type to own, no qualified type name — so on a fresh database the
  `ON_ERROR_STOP` exit *is* the enum's. What varies underneath is a **third** refusal that
  may or may not be in the dump at all: `ALTER SCHEMA public OWNER TO postgres`, which
  `pg_dump` emits when `public` is owned by `postgres` and omits when it is owned by
  `pg_database_owner`. On this instance the `postgres` database has the first owner and a
  `CREATE DATABASE`-fresh one the second, and the dumps follow — the line is present in the
  `postgres` database's dump and absent from both fresh databases', measured, which also
  shifts every line number after the preamble. Dump the `postgres` database and the refusal
  is in the enum dump and the control alike, which is what hides the split.

  `docs/compatibility.md`'s *`pg_dump` plain-text restore* row records this; its former ✅ rested on
  `test_pg_dump`'s round-trip, whose schema builds no enum column. The pglet-**own**-dump
  half of the standing invariant is unaffected and holds: a `pglet_server dump` of the same
  database loads into 18.6 with the member order intact and back into pglet, where
  `ORDER BY m` agrees and a reloaded unique partial index still enforces membership by
  member position. Closing it takes **both** members — an `ALTER` dispatch that tolerates
  `ALTER TYPE … OWNER TO` as it already tolerates the `TABLE` spelling, and a parser change
  taking a schema qualifier in the type position — and neither finishes it alone: with only
  the second done (the dump edited to read `m mood`, replayed), psql's default restores the
  table and both rows while `ON_ERROR_STOP=1` still exits 3 at line 33.

- **93 · A rendered constant carries its output function's text there and its written
  text here.** `DEFAULT '{"a":1}'::jsonb` reads back `'{"a":1}'::jsonb`,
  `DEFAULT ' 2024-01-01 '::date` keeps its spaces, and `time DEFAULT '10:00'` reads
  `'10:00'::time without time zone`, where 18.6 prints `typoutput`'s text in each
  position. A `bytea` default is a member: `DEFAULT 'hello'` reads back `'hello'::bytea`
  and `DEFAULT '\xAB'` keeps its case, where 18.6 prints `'\x68656c6c6f'::bytea` and
  `'\xab'::bytea`.

  Silent, same schema-differ consumer. The types whose output *is* reproduced are `bool`,
  `int4`, `int2`, `int8` and `numeric` — for the first three the fold decides whether a
  label is printed at all, so it could not be skipped (`'007'::int4` reads `7`,
  `'t'::bool` reads `true`), and `int2`/`int8` fold under a label that is always printed
  (`'007'` on a `bigint` column reads `'7'::bigint`, `get_const_expr`'s `default:` arm) —
  all measured. **The fold is one implementation reached from every position**,
  `information_schema.columns.column_default` included; a second copy there labelled
  without folding, so `bool`/`int4`/`numeric` diverged at that one position while
  agreeing everywhere else. Closing the rest means evaluating the cast at render time,
  which the deparser is deliberately pure of. The folding types are pinned by
  `catalog/column_default_string_literal_folds_through_its_output_function.sql`, whose
  `@setup` carries both sides of the rule column by column; nothing pins the divergent
  ones, a faithful fixture being red.

- **92 · An index modifier 18.6 renders is dropped from `indexdef` here.** Four members,
  the fourth being the one the row first omitted: a per-key `ASC`/`DESC`, `NULLS FIRST`
  (`NULLS LAST` is the default and 18.6 prints neither it nor a `DESC` key's implied
  `NULLS FIRST`), an operator class (`text_pattern_ops`; under `USING gin`,
  `jsonb_path_ops` — `CREATE INDEX q ON t USING gin (j jsonb_path_ops)` renders `… USING
  gin (j)` here and `… USING gin (j jsonb_path_ops)` there, measured), and `NULLS NOT
  DISTINCT` *in `indexdef`*. Three of the four reach the fuz spine's own shipped schema —
  `idx_audit_log_seq (seq DESC)`, `idx_actor_name_lower (lower(name) text_pattern_ops)`,
  `idx_cell_grant_unique_role_scope … NULLS NOT DISTINCT`.

  Silent, and the first consumer is the schema **differ** — the rendering. Not a deparser
  question: the modifiers are not in the catalog `Index` at all, so closing it is a
  store-shape change (**two** new fields — a per-key sort spec and a per-key opclass;
  `nulls_not_distinct` is already a persisted `Index` field) before any renderer sees
  them.

  **The row's two mechanism claims were both wrong.** `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` is *not*
  discarded — it is persisted in `catalog::Index::nulls_not_distinct`, read by
  `executor::constraints`, and enforced per row identically to 18.6 on fresh state. What
  made the two-NULL-rows case succeed was row 26's missing index build, which needs no
  modifier at all and is now closed; with it,
  `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX u ON t (a) NULLS NOT DISTINCT` over two NULL rows is
  `23505 … Key (a)=(null) is duplicated.` on both engines, and the same statement over
  `NULLS DISTINCT` is created on both. Nothing pins the four renderings; the enforcement
  polarity is pinned per row by the `constraint/unique_index/nulls_not_distinct_*`
  fixtures and `test_nulls_not_distinct_index_enforced`, and at build time the
  `NULLS DISTINCT` accept is (`ddl/create_unique_index_over_distinct_keys_builds.sql`).

  **An index build reads the dropped direction too.** A build over rows holding more than
  one oversized entry names the one it loads first, which is the first in the key's order
  (`constraints::scan_index_build_sizes`), and a `DESC` key part is not there to read: over
  `i4 (a text)` holding `'a'` and `'b'` followed by 2 800 and 2 750 random characters,
  `CREATE INDEX i4_i ON i4 (a DESC)` is `54000 index row size 2768 …` on 18.6 — the `b` row,
  first descending — and `2816` here, the `a` row, first ascending (measured). The SQLSTATE
  and the index agree; the message reports another row's size. The same store-shape change
  closes it.

- **122 · An index's name and its table's go into `indexdef` raw.** `catalog::pg_catalog`'s
  `index_def` renders its **key columns** through `quote_ident` and then interpolates the
  two relation names around them with neither:
  `format!("CREATE {unique}INDEX {} ON public.{} USING {method} ({key})", index.name,
  index.table_name)`. 18.6's `pg_get_indexdef` runs `quote_identifier` over both.

  **Membership is 18.6's predicate, and pglet's own is not consulted at all.** Reading no
  predicate means pglet writes the stored spelling bare whatever it is, so the two
  renderings diverge at just the names 18.6 quotes — `ruleutils.c`'s `quote_identifier`
  quotes anything that is not `^[a-z_][a-z0-9_]*$`, and any keyword whose
  `ScanKeywordCategories` entry is not `UNRESERVED_KEYWORD`. That is **not**
  `is_safe_bare_ident`'s rule (row 85 (f)), and the table below carries a witness each
  way: `numeric` is a member though pglet's predicate would leave it bare, and `action`,
  which pglet's predicate quotes, is not a member at all. Measured over one relation
  per name, on a fresh server and a fresh database each, at the table-name position —
  and at the index-name position too for `Odd Ix`, `select`, `numeric` and `action`,
  which answer the same way there. The last column is what routing this rendering through
  `quote_ident` would produce, read off `::regclass` over the same names:

  | name | 18.6's `quote_identifier` | today's `indexdef` pair | through `quote_ident` |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | `Odd Tbl` / `Odd Ix` | `"Odd Tbl"` / `"Odd Ix"` | diverges | quoted — closes |
  | `OddTbl` | `"OddTbl"` | diverges | quoted — closes |
  | `select` | `"select"` | diverges | quoted — closes |
  | `position` | `"position"` | diverges | quoted — closes |
  | `left` | `"left"` | diverges | quoted — closes |
  | `numeric` | `"numeric"` | diverges | **bare — still diverges** |
  | `action` | `action` | **agrees** | **quoted — opens a divergence** |

  Measured on both engines, over `"Odd Tbl" (a INT, "action" INT)` carrying
  `CREATE INDEX "Odd Ix" ON "Odd Tbl" (a)` and
  `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX "select" ON "Odd Tbl" ("action")`, plus a
  `"Par Ent" (id INT PRIMARY KEY)` for the auto-named PK index:

  | index | pglet `indexdef` | 18.6 `indexdef` |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `"Odd Ix"` | `CREATE INDEX Odd Ix ON public.Odd Tbl USING btree (a)` | `CREATE INDEX "Odd Ix" ON public."Odd Tbl" USING btree (a)` |
  | `"select"` | `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX select ON public.Odd Tbl USING btree ("action")` | `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX "select" ON public."Odd Tbl" USING btree (action)` |
  | `"Par Ent_pkey"` (a PK's auto index) | `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX Par Ent_pkey ON public.Par Ent USING btree (id)` | `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX "Par Ent_pkey" ON public."Par Ent" USING btree (id)` |

  The second row is the one that shows both directions in one string: the **key column**
  is over-quoted (`"action"` here, bare `action` there — row 85 (f)'s keyword
  disagreement) while the **index name** is under-quoted (`select` here, `"select"`
  there).

  **What the bare rendering then costs is per-member.** Each of pglet's own renderings
  fed back to each engine, over a database holding the correctly-spelled relation:

  | pglet's rendering, replayed | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `CREATE INDEX Odd Ix ON public.Odd Tbl USING btree (a)` | `42601 syntax error: expected 'on', found identifier` | `42601 syntax error at or near "Ix"` |
  | `CREATE INDEX select ON public.t_plain USING btree (a)` | `42601 syntax error: expected a name, found 'on'` | `42601 syntax error at or near "select"` |
  | `CREATE INDEX ix_l2 ON public.left USING btree (a)` | `42601 syntax error: expected a name after '.', found 'using'` | **accepted** |
  | `CREATE INDEX ix_pos2 ON public.position USING btree (a)` | accepted | accepted |
  | `CREATE INDEX ix_num2 ON public.numeric USING btree (a)` | accepted | accepted |
  | `CREATE INDEX numeric ON public.t_plain2 USING btree (a)` | accepted | accepted |
  | `CREATE INDEX OddIx ON public.OddTbl USING btree (a)` | `42P01 relation "oddtbl" does not exist` | `42P01 relation "public.oddtbl" does not exist` |

  No one consequence covers the class. `42601` on both engines at the space-carrying pair
  and at the reserved `select`; a **different relation** at `OddTbl`, whose bare form
  parses on each and resolves the folded `oddtbl` — and where a folded twin does exist it
  indexes that twin instead, silently and on both (measured); **nothing at all** at
  `numeric` and `position`, where both grammars take the bare word for the relation it
  names, so what moved is only the spelling a schema differ compares; and at `left` the
  asymmetry runs the other way — text 18.6 parses and **pglet** does not, its own
  `42601` against 18.6's acceptance, the quoted `public."left"` being accepted here
  (measured), so the quotes are the whole of it.

  **It does not reach the dump, and that is a fact about a second copy rather than about
  this one.** `pglet::dump`'s `emit_create_index` builds the same statement and passes
  both names through `quote_ident` (`quote_ident(&index.name)`, `quote_ident(&table.name)`)
  — measured: a `--data-dir` database holding `"Odd Tbl"` and its two indexes dumps a
  script whose `CREATE INDEX` lines carry the quotes, and that script loads into a
  `CREATE DATABASE`-fresh stock 18.6 under `ON_ERROR_STOP=1` with psql exiting `0`, both
  indexes landing. So the dump-invariant is intact and the two renderers of one statement
  disagree, which is the seam this row records.
  `pg_get_constraintdef` is the other control and it agrees with 18.6: a FK's referenced
  table renders `REFERENCES "Par Ent"(id)` on both.

  **Nothing pins it.** The fixtures that read `indexdef` —
  `information_schema/pg_indexes_projection.sql`, `catalog/spine_snapshot_indexes.sql`,
  `catalog/spine_snapshot_cell_indexes_and_columns.sql`,
  `catalog/indexdef_bool_chain_is_n_ary.sql` — name their relations and indexes with
  words 18.6 leaves bare too, which is where the two renderings agree; a fixture over a
  name 18.6 quotes would be red, pglet's answer being the wrong one. Recorded rather than
  fixed — whether `index_def` should route both names through a predicate, and **whose**,
  is an engine decision, and the membership table above is why the second half of that
  question is not a detail: over those seven names pglet's own predicate closes five,
  leaves `numeric` open, and opens `action`, which agrees today. It is entangled with
  row 85 (f)'s question of whether the keyword half should become a category table,
  which is the same question read from the other end.

- **91 · A rendered `CASE` is indented over four lines there and one here.** pglet
  renders `CASE WHEN (a = 1) THEN 'y'::text ELSE 'n'::text END` on one line; 18.6 spreads
  it over four with a four-space indent, because `pg_get_expr` runs with
  `PRETTYFLAG_INDENT`.

  Silent, same schema-differ consumer as row 90. It is a formatting mode over the whole
  renderer, not a `CASE` rule: adopting it means reproducing `ruleutils.c`'s indent state
  machine, which also decides where a long boolean chain breaks. **Two content members
  were separate and are closed**: the branch results resolve their unknowns
  (`THEN 'y'::text`) and an ELSE-less `CASE` renders 18.6's implicit
  `ELSE NULL::<result type>` (`transformCaseExpr` supplies a NULL `defresult`) —
  measured at five result types and at both `CASE` forms, so what remains is whitespace.
  Nothing pins the layout, a faithful fixture being red; the contents are pinned by
  `deparse`'s `case_branch_unknowns_take_the_common_type`, which is a unit test
  **because** of this row — a differential fixture over any `CASE` is red on the
  indentation whatever the constants do.

- **90 · An implicit coercion under an operator is spelled there and not here.** The
  measured members are `CHECK (n > 1)` over a `numeric` column, `DEFAULT 2.5 * 2`,
  `a IN (1, 2.5)`, `a IN (1, 1000000000000)`, and a `varchar` operand's relabel
  (`v = 'x'`). A **top-level** implicit cast is hidden by `get_func_expr`'s
  `showimplicit` and so agrees by construction (`int8 DEFAULT 5::int4` reads `5` on both)
  — the divergence is the nested ones.

  Two more shapes were measured after the fix, both the *outer* cast alone:
  `v IN ('x','y')` over a `varchar(10)` reads
  `((v)::text = ANY ((ARRAY['x'::character varying, 'y'::character varying])::text[]))`
  there against pglet's
  `(v = ANY (ARRAY['x'::character varying, 'y'::character varying]))` — the elements
  agree, the relabel and the array cast do not — and `n = ANY (ARRAY[1, 2])` over a
  `numeric` column casts the **whole array** (`ANY ((ARRAY[1, 2])::numeric[])`) where the
  `IN` spelling of the same predicate casts each element
  (`ARRAY[(1)::numeric, (2)::numeric]`), so the two are not one rule even there. Two
  further measured members: a **typed `ANY` array** — `b = ANY (ARRAY[1,2]::int8[])` over
  a `bigint` column reads `(b = ANY (ARRAY[(1)::bigint, (2)::bigint]))` there against
  pglet's outer-cast form, and its `IN` spelling `b IN (1, 2)` reaches this row's own
  decline (the elements do not share the left operand's type) and falls back to the
  written `IN`; and `EXTRACT('year' FROM t) > 2000`, whose `(2000)::numeric` is the same
  widening under a special form.

  Silent, and the consumer is a schema **differ**, which reads the two as a changed
  constraint. **Not bounded** — the sentence that stood here said this class plus row 91
  and the `+5` fold were *all* that remained after a 34-shape `CHECK` and 45-shape
  `DEFAULT` sweep, and a 77-shape / 87-shape re-sweep found more: the two
  `COERCE_SQL_SYNTAX` spellings, the `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` node, the keyword function
  name, `concat_ws`'s and `date_part`'s declared `text` argument, the `CASE` branches'
  unknowns, and row 93's `jsonb` / `time` members — seven classes, of which all but the
  two `COERCE_SQL_SYNTAX` spellings are now closed. What is measured is what the sweeps
  covered; the count of shapes is the claim, never the absence of others. Closing this
  one means modelling `select_common_type` and the assignment-cast insertion at render
  time, over an IR that carries no coercion nodes. A faithful fixture would be red;
  `catalog/constraintdef_in_list_is_a_scalar_array_op.sql` pins the *uniform*-type
  polarity beside it, so the fallback path is exercised but its answer is not
  asserted.

- **89 · A subquery whose evaluation is lent no callback is `0A000`; an aggregate under
  an expression the grouping evaluates answers.** The row held two classes that shared a refusal, and the first
  is closed.

  **Closed — an aggregate under an `Expr` node a hand-listed aggregate walker had no arm
  for.** That walker evaluated what stood above an aggregate in a grouping query and sent
  every node it did not list to the scalar walk, which refused the aggregate below it:
  `round(avg(x), 2)`, `abs(sum(x))`, `upper(max(y))`, `concat('n=', count(*))`,
  `jsonb_build_object('n', count(*))`, `date_trunc('day', max(t))`, `extract(year FROM
  max(t))`, `greatest` / `least` / `nullif`, `IN`, `ARRAY[…]`, `CASE WHEN true THEN max(a)
  END`, `HAVING round(avg(b)) > 1`, `ORDER BY abs(sum(b))` and `abs(max(a)) … WHERE false`
  were each `0A000` where 18.6 answers. The grouping computes the aggregates and
  evaluates `HAVING`, the select list and its junk columns through the scalar walk itself,
  lending it each aggregate's value by node (`docs/scope.md` § A grouping query's
  aggregates are values the scalar walk reads by node), so the answers are 18.6's, declared
  types included on both legs (`select/agg_expr_*`, `enum/agg_expr_enum_member_order.sql`;
  `crates/pglet/tests/aggregate_walker_arms.rs` runs an aggregate under each `Expr`
  variant the walk evaluates an operand of, in the projection, an `ORDER BY` key and
  `HAVING`).

  **Which aggregates a group computes.** 18.6 computes every aggregate that survives its
  planner's constant folding, for every group. A grouping here drops an aggregate only
  with a branch dropped by a decider that is a constant **by its shape alone**, and
  computes the others before it evaluates the expression above them (in its own order,
  row 304). Those deciders are the literals `true`, `false` and `NULL`; a comparison of two
  integer or `numeric` literals; `NOT`, `AND`, `OR`, `IS [NOT] NULL` and `IS [NOT] TRUE |
  FALSE | UNKNOWN` over those; a simple `CASE` whose operand and arm value are such number
  literals; and, for a `COALESCE`, an earlier integer, `numeric` or boolean literal
  (`docs/scope.md`; `select/agg_expr_fold_*`). It evaluates nothing but those deciders
  while it collects the aggregates.

  **An aggregate over a column or a literal keeps its operand's type check where it is
  dropped, and where no group is computed.** 18.6 resolves an aggregate against its
  argument's type in parse analysis, before its planner folds anything. The collection
  refuses an aggregate that has no form for its operand's type before any group is
  formed, where it reads that type without evaluating anything: a column's **declared**
  type, a literal's, and — for a dropped aggregate, whose argument nothing evaluates — a
  cast's target, which is what a typed constant and a declared `$N` are. Over `o (a INT,
  b INT, t TEXT, j JSONB, bo BOOL)`: `SELECT true OR sum(t) > 0 FROM o`, its `HAVING` and
  `ORDER BY` spellings, `CASE WHEN false THEN max(j) END`, `coalesce(true, min(bo))`,
  `SELECT true OR sum(true) > 0 FROM o` and `SELECT sum(t) FROM o GROUP BY a HAVING
  count(*) > 5` are `42883` on both (`select/agg_expr_*operand_type*`). The `CASE`,
  `COALESCE` and no-group spellings answered before; and the refusal is raised ahead of
  the groups, so `SELECT sum(1/b), sum(t) FROM o` over a `b = 0` row and `SELECT sum(t)
  FROM o GROUP BY 1/b` are `42883` as on 18.6 where each was `22012`.

  **What that check costs, and does not reach** — each measured, none held by a fixture,
  a faithful one being red:

  - **It refuses on a declared type, and a declaration can be a guess** — loud where
    18.6 answers, in statements that form no group. A derived column that is a correlated
    scalar subquery is declared `text` here where 18.6 declares its type — `SELECT x FROM
    (SELECT (SELECT i4) AS x FROM o) s` is `25` against `23` on both legs, and `sum(x)`
    over it with a group was `42883` already, where 18.6 answers the sum: over `o (i4 INT, nu NUMERIC, f8 FLOAT8, iv
    INTERVAL, d DATE, ai4 INT[])`, `SELECT sum(x) FROM (SELECT (SELECT i4) AS x FROM o) s
    WHERE false GROUP BY x`, its `GROUP BY x HAVING false` and `avg` spellings, and the
    `(SELECT nu)`, `(SELECT f8)`, `(SELECT iv)`, `(SELECT d - d)` and `(SELECT unnest(ai4)
    LIMIT 1)` columns are `42883` here and no row there — no row here before. And an
    outer-level aggregate's qualified argument resolves to the inner relation's column of
    the same name (row 303): over `x (a INT, v INT)` holding a row and an empty `ye (a
    INT, v TEXT)`, `SELECT (SELECT sum(x.v) FROM ye GROUP BY ye.a) FROM x` is `42883
    function sum(text) does not exist` here and `NULL` there — `NULL` here before.
  - **`sum` / `avg` over `time`** is refused over no group too, where it answered no row
    as 18.6 does — row 307.
  - **An operand the check cannot type is judged where the aggregate is computed, so
    under a dropped branch, or over no group, not at all** — silent. A bare `$N`:
    `SELECT true OR sum($1) > 0 FROM o` bound an untyped `'5'` is `t` here and `42725`
    there (`42883` here before), and `SELECT a FROM o WHERE bo = $1 GROUP BY a HAVING true
    OR max($1) ORDER BY a` bound `'t'` answers where 18.6 and the earlier build are
    `42883`. `DEFAULT`: `SELECT true OR sum(DEFAULT) IS NULL FROM o` is `t` here and
    `42601` there, `42601` here before. A kept aggregate over a cast, a typed constant or
    a declared `$N` in a statement that forms no group, as before: over an empty `e (a
    INT, t TEXT)`, `SELECT sum(date '2020-01-01') FROM e GROUP BY a`, and the `max(uuid
    '…')`, `sum(bool 't')`, `sum(text 'abc')`, `max(NULL::bool)` and declared-`bool`
    `max($1)` spellings, answer no row where 18.6 is `42883`. A computed argument is the
    bullet below.
  - **A statement with no `FROM` is not a grouping here**: `SELECT true OR sum(true) > 0`
    is `t` and `SELECT CASE WHEN false THEN min(false) END` `NULL`, where 18.6 is `42883`
    — as before; the aggregate such a statement does evaluate is `0A000` (the last
    paragraph of this bullet).

  That closed silent and loud members the walker's per-node choices had made: `CASE
  WHEN a > 0 THEN 1 ELSE sum(1/b) END … GROUP BY a` over a `b = 0` row answered `1` per
  group and its `HAVING` spelling kept the groups, where 18.6 raises the untaken `sum`'s
  `22012`; `coalesce(max(a), sum(1/b))` answered `2` (row 172's `COALESCE` residual); a
  `CASE` decided by a stable call — `CASE WHEN current_user IS NOT NULL THEN 0 ELSE
  sum(1/b) END`, and the `now()`, `concat('a', 'b')` and `'…'::date::timestamptz`
  spellings — answered `0` where 18.6, which does not fold a stable decider, raises
  `22012`; and `true OR sum(1/b) > 0` and `HAVING false AND sum(1/b) > 0` raised `22012`
  where 18.6's planner drops the aggregate. A variadic over an aggregate types the
  aggregate as its siblings, so `greatest(sum(i), tx)` is 18.6's `42804` and
  `least(sum(i), 5)` is `bigint` (row 65's aggregate arm, which this would otherwise have
  turned from a refusal into an answer).

  **Residuals of the closed half**, each measured over `u (a INT, b INT)` holding `(1,
  10)` and `(2, 0)`; no fixture holds one, a faithful one being red:

  - **A decider 18.6 folds that is not a constant by its shape keeps every aggregate
    under it** — loud. Whether 18.6 folds a decider turns on the volatility of every
    function, operator and cast under it, on its types' collations and on the plan it
    builds, and nothing here models that: what is not on the list above keeps its
    branches, their aggregates are computed, and one that fails raises where 18.6,
    having dropped it, answers. The direction is the design — a decider taken for a
    constant that 18.6 does not fold would answer where 18.6 raises — so this class is
    loud by construction and its members are whatever 18.6 folds beyond the list. Each
    below is `22012` here, against the answer named:
    - a decider computed from constants: `CASE WHEN 7 % 2 = 1 THEN 0 ELSE sum(1/b) END`,
      and its `length('abc') = 3` and `1 + 1 = 2` spellings (`0`); `(7 % 2 = 1) OR
      sum(1/b) > 0` (`t`); `HAVING 7 % 2 = 1 OR sum(1/b) > 0` (the group); `ORDER BY CASE
      WHEN 7 % 2 = 1 THEN a ELSE sum(1/b) END` (the rows); `CASE 7 % 2 WHEN 1 THEN 0 ELSE
      sum(1/b) END` (`0`); `coalesce(1 + 1, sum(1/b))` (`2`) and `coalesce(abs(1),
      sum(1/b))` (`1`);
    - a bound `$N`, which 18.6 folds where it builds a custom plan — the plan psql's
      `\bind` gets — and not under `plan_cache_mode = force_generic_plan`, where it raises
      `22012` too: `CASE WHEN $1 THEN 0 ELSE sum(1/b) END` bound `true` (`0`),
      `coalesce($1::int, sum(1/b))` bound `1` (`1`), `$1::bool OR sum(1/b) > 0` bound
      `true` (`t`);
    - an `IN` list, which 18.6 builds as an `OR` of `=` comparisons and a `NOT IN` list
      as an `AND` of `<>` ones (`transformAExprIn`; row 88 has the shapes): an item
      holding a column — an aggregate's argument counts — is a comparison of its own,
      and the items holding none are gathered into one array where there are two or more
      of them, a lone one being its own comparison too. An arm of constants that decides
      the connective — an `=` that holds, a `<>` that does not — folds it, wherever the
      arm stands in the list, and the other arms' aggregates go with it: `1 IN (1,
      sum(1/b))`, `1 IN (2, 1, sum(1/b))` and `1 IN (sum(1/b), 1)` (`t`), and `1 NOT IN
      (1, sum(1/b))` (`f`). Where no arm decides 18.6 keeps the aggregate too — `1 IN
      (2, sum(1/b))` and `1 NOT IN (2, sum(1/b))` are `22012` on both, and so is `1 IN
      (count(*), 1, sum(1/b))`, whose `count(*)` holds no column and so makes the array
      one that is no constant;
    - a comparison of anything but two number literals: `CASE WHEN 'a' = 'a' THEN 0 ELSE
      sum(1/b) END`, and the `'a' < 'b'`, `greatest('a', 'b') = 'b'`, `'abc' LIKE 'a%'`,
      `'a' ~ 'a'`, `'2020-01-01'::date < '2021-01-01'::date`, `'happy'::mood =
      'happy'::mood`, `'happy'::mood > 'sad'::mood` and `'{"a":1}'::jsonb @> '{}'::jsonb`
      conditions (`0`); `(true > false) OR sum(1/b) > 0` (`t`); `CASE 'a' WHEN 'a' THEN 0
      ELSE sum(1/b) END`, `CASE true WHEN true …` and `CASE 'a  '::char(3) WHEN 'a' …`
      (`0`); `CASE WHEN upper('ß') = 'SS' THEN sum(1/b) ELSE 0 END` (`0` — `upper('ß')` is
      `ß` there and `SS` here, and the `THEN 0 ELSE sum(1/b)` spelling is `22012` on both);
    - a cast, a `NULL`'s included: `CASE WHEN NULL::bool THEN sum(1/b) ELSE 0 END`, `CASE
      WHEN 'f' THEN sum(1/b) ELSE 0 END` and `CASE WHEN 1::int8::int = 1 THEN 0 ELSE
      sum(1/b) END` (`0`); `(NULL::int IS NOT NULL) AND sum(1/b) > 0` (`f`);
      `coalesce('x', max(1/b)::text)` (`x`), `coalesce('1'::int, sum(1/b))` and
      `coalesce('1', sum(1/b))` (`1`);
    - a strict operator or function over a constant `NULL` (row 273's fold): `NULL::int +
      sum(1/b)`, `upper(NULL) || sum(1/b)::text`, `nullif(NULL, sum(1/b))`, `sum(1/b) IN
      (NULL::int)`, `NULL::int IN (1, sum(1/b))` and `NULL::int NOT IN (sum(1/b))`
      (`NULL`); `CASE 1 WHEN NULL THEN sum(1/b) ELSE 0 END` and `CASE WHEN NULL::int > 0
      THEN sum(1/b) ELSE 0 END` (`0`);
    - a deciding constant on the **right** of an `AND` / `OR`, which the scalar walk
      reaches after the operand holding the aggregate: `sum(1/b) > 0 OR true` (`t`) and
      `sum(1/b) > 0 AND false` (`f`).

    The `CASE`, `COALESCE` and `IN` members the hand-listed walker evaluated at all, it
    answered as 18.6 does: it computed an aggregate only where the expression above it
    read the value — which is also how it answered `0` for `CASE WHEN 'B' < 'a' THEN 0
    ELSE sum(1/b) END` and for `CASE WHEN upper('ß') = 'SS' THEN 0 ELSE sum(1/b) END`,
    where 18.6 raises `22012`. The `AND` / `OR` members were `22012` then too.
  - **A refusal that needs evaluation is not raised in a branch a certain decider
    drops** — silent, row 60's class. Nothing evaluates a dropped branch, so a type
    refusal pglet raises only at evaluation passes unseen there. Over `o (a INT, b INT, t
    TEXT)` holding two rows, one with `b = 0`:

    - the aggregate's argument, where its refusal is raised by evaluating it or its type

      18.6 raises the cast's: `SELECT true OR max(a::jsonb) IS NULL FROM o` is `42883`
      here and `42846` there — loud, and `42846` here before. Kept, `SELECT max(a::jsonb)
      FROM o` is `42846` on both
      (`select/agg_expr_kept_cast_refusal_outranks_operand_type_loud.sql`).

    A failing constant the walk does not reach beside a kept aggregate is row 60's too,
    with its measured members.
  - **`avg` over an integer whose type is not certain, under a function** — **silent**.
    Row 2's residual keeps such an `avg` `float8`, and a function over it now answers
    from that value: `SELECT round(avg(x)) FROM unnest(ARRAY[1, 4]) v(x)` is `2` here and
    `3` there (a `float8` `2.5` rounds to even), and so is the derived-table spelling
    `(SELECT (SELECT 1) AS x UNION ALL SELECT 4) v`; `round(avg(x) * 3)` over `1` and `2`
    is `4` against `5`; `GROUP BY g HAVING round(avg(x)) > 2` keeps no group where 18.6

    over the same `unnest` is `2` against `3`, by the cast's own rounding. The `VALUES`,
    computed derived-column and `UNION ALL` spellings this was measured over first are
    row 2's certain columns now, and answer 18.6's `3`.
  - **A `NULL` aggregate passes a type gate keyed on the value** — row 305.
  - **An aggregate in a position the grouping does not evaluate is still refused.** A
    window function's keys are the window executor's, and a set-returning `unnest` in a
    grouping query's projection is refused wherever it stands, so over `t (id INT, i INT)`
    `SELECT rank() OVER (ORDER BY sum(i)) FROM t GROUP BY id` and `SELECT
