    unnest(ARRAY[max(i)]) FROM t` are `0A000` here and answered there (measured). Loud and
    pglet-stricter — over a group. A grouped table that forms none never reaches the
    window's keys: over an empty `e (a INT, t TEXT)`, `SELECT rank() OVER (ORDER BY
    sum(a)) FROM e GROUP BY a` answers no row on both, and `… ORDER BY sum(t) …` answers
    no row here where 18.6 is `42883` — silent, the operand check not walking a window's
    keys, and as it was.
  - **The order a group's aggregates and expressions are evaluated in** is row 304.
  - **An unaliased `CASE` is named `case` here** where 18.6 names it after a named `ELSE`
    branch — `CASE WHEN 1 = 1 THEN 0 ELSE sum(1/b) END` is the column `sum` there; row
    277's naming residual, reached by more spellings now that the shape answers.

  **What the live class is keyed on is neither one message nor a countable set of SQL
  positions.** Three
  `Expr` arms carry a subquery — `Subquery`, `Exists`, `InSubquery` — and each raises
  `0A000` under its **own** message (`scalar subquery requires execution context`,
  `EXISTS subquery requires execution context`, `IN subquery requires execution context`)
  when the `SubqueryExec` its evaluation was lent holds `None` for that kind. **Derive
  membership from the code rather than from a list here**: `grep SubqueryExec::NONE` names
  the evaluations that lend none — today the three wrappers in `executor::expr`
  (`eval_expr`, `eval_expr_env`, `eval_expr_join`), two direct `eval_expr_full` calls in
  `executor::dml`, and the grouping's own `SubqueryExec { aggregate, ..SubqueryExec::NONE
  }` in `executor::query::aggregate`, which lends aggregate values and no sub-plan
  callback — and a SQL position is a member when its expression reaches one of them
  carrying a subquery. So a grouping query's expressions are members:
  `SELECT (SELECT 1) FROM t GROUP BY i` and `SELECT count(*) FROM t GROUP BY i HAVING
  max(i) > (SELECT 1)` are `0A000` here and answered there (measured). Re-run that grep instead of reading a count off this paragraph: the
  list that used to stand here went stale twice by the same predicate, two positions and
  then four.

  Samples rather than the extent, measured against 18.6 over
  `u(id INT PRIMARY KEY, m mood, flag BOOL, n INT)` holding one `'happy'` row — each
  `0A000` here and answered there. The stored label is load-bearing where a value is
  quoted below, and only there: measured on 18.6, `'happy'` sets `flag` to `t` and
  `'sad'` sets it to `f`. Carrying an enum: `ORDER BY (SELECT m …)`; a window's
  `ORDER BY (SELECT m …)` and its `PARTITION BY (SELECT m …)`; `DISTINCT ON ((SELECT m …))`;
  `HAVING min(m) > (SELECT m …)`; an `ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET flag = ((SELECT m …) >
  'ok')` (which sets `flag` to `t` there); and the plain `UPDATE u SET flag = ((SELECT m …)
  > 'ok')`. **Carrying none at all**: `GROUP BY (SELECT n …)`, `ORDER BY (SELECT n …)`,
  `INSERT INTO u VALUES (2, 'ok', false, (SELECT n …))`, `ORDER BY EXISTS (SELECT 1 …)` and
  `ORDER BY (n IN (SELECT n …))`. This class is a missing evaluation context and not an
  enum corner, which the enum-free half above is here to say: the paragraph it replaced
  reached it only through enum spellings, and a reader took the whole class for an
  enum-ordering residual.

  Some of it is recorded elsewhere and not re-derived here: the `UPDATE … SET` /
  `INSERT … VALUES` pair in row 47's
  assignment-cast sub-bullet, which reaches them from an unresolvable relation inside the
  subquery. Loud and pglet-stricter like the rest of the row, and unpinned for the same
  reason. One member answers instead of refusing: a `NULL` left operand of `IN (SELECT …)`
  is evaluated ahead of the refusal and answers `NULL`, wrongly over an empty set — row 274.

  **An aggregate in a `SELECT` with no `FROM` is refused.** `plan_select_no_from`
  (`parser/select.rs`) lowers a `SELECT` with no `FROM` to a one-row `Plan::Values` of its
  entries (a `ProjectUnnest` where an entry holds `unnest`) and builds no `Aggregate`
  node, so the scalar walk meets the aggregate with no value lent for it and refuses it
  — `0A000 aggregate function evaluated where no aggregation computes it`, the closed
  half's message by another road. 18.6 reads such a statement as an aggregate query over
  one row. The lowering is read from the code; the refusal and its controls are measured,
  on the native server (its two backends and the stripped build agreeing) and, where
  marked †, through the npm package as well, against 18.6:

  | statement | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT count(*)` †, `SELECT count(1)`, `SELECT count(DISTINCT 1)`, `SELECT max(1)` † | `0A000` | `1` |
  | `SELECT count(NULL)` | `0A000` | `0` |
  | `SELECT min(1), sum(1), avg(1)` | `0A000` | `1`, `1`, `1.00000000000000000000` |
  | `SELECT count(*) + 1` †, `SELECT COALESCE(max(1), 0)`, `SELECT CASE WHEN count(*) > 0 THEN 'y' ELSE 'n' END` | `0A000` | `2`; `1`; `y` |
  | `SELECT count(*) + $1` bound `1` † | `0A000` | `2` |
  | `SELECT count(*) ORDER BY 1`, `SELECT count(*) LIMIT 1` | `0A000` | `1` |
  | `SELECT (SELECT count(*))` †, `SELECT (SELECT (SELECT count(*)))` | `0A000` | `1` |
  | `SELECT x, (SELECT count(*)) FROM (VALUES (1), (2)) v(x)` | `0A000` | `1`, `1` and `2`, `1` |
  | `SELECT x FROM (VALUES (1), (2)) v(x) WHERE x = (SELECT count(*))` | `0A000` | `1` |
  | `SELECT EXISTS (SELECT count(*))`, `SELECT 1 IN (SELECT count(*))` | `0A000` | `t` |
  | `SELECT * FROM (SELECT count(*) AS n) s`, `WITH w AS (SELECT count(*) AS n) SELECT n FROM w` | `0A000` | `1` |
  | `SELECT count(*) UNION ALL SELECT 5` †, `SELECT 5 UNION ALL SELECT count(*)`, `SELECT count(*) INTERSECT SELECT 1` | `0A000` | `1`, `5`; `5`, `1`; `1` |
  | `INSERT INTO dt SELECT count(*)` †, `INSERT INTO dt SELECT max(7)` | `0A000`, no row written | `INSERT 0 1` |
  | over a `dt (n bigint)` holding rows: `SELECT n, (SELECT count(*)) FROM dt`, `SELECT n FROM dt WHERE EXISTS (SELECT count(*))`, `SELECT n FROM dt WHERE n = (SELECT max(1))`, `DELETE FROM dt WHERE n > (SELECT count(*))` | `0A000` | the rows; the `DELETE` removes its rows |
  | `SELECT count(*), unnest(ARRAY[1, 2])` | `0A000` | `1`, `1` and `1`, `2` |

  A window function over no `FROM` takes the same lowering and its own message: `SELECT
  row_number() OVER ()` † and `SELECT rank() OVER (ORDER BY 1)` are `0A000 window
  functions must be evaluated via Window plan executor` against `1`.

  The refusal is raised where the aggregate is evaluated, so a statement that does not
  evaluate it answers — 18.6's answer in each of these: `SELECT CASE WHEN false THEN
  count(*) ELSE 0 END` † is `0`, `SELECT true OR count(*) > 0` † `t`, `SELECT false AND
  count(*) > 0` `f` and `SELECT COALESCE(1, count(*))` `1`; and over an empty `de (n
  bigint)`, `SELECT n FROM de WHERE n = (SELECT count(*))` answers no row and `UPDATE de
  SET n = (SELECT count(*))` `UPDATE 0`. A `WHERE`, `GROUP BY` or `HAVING` after the
  select list is refused first, `42601`, by row 296: `SELECT count(*) WHERE false` † (`0`
  on 18.6), `SELECT count(*) HAVING true` and `SELECT 1 HAVING count(*) > 0` (`1`), and
  `SELECT count(*) GROUP BY 1` (`42803` there). In an `UPDATE … SET` and an `INSERT …
  VALUES` the subquery itself is refused first, by this row's other half.

  Controls: the same statements over a one-row `FROM` answer as 18.6 does — `SELECT
  count(*) FROM (SELECT 1) s` †, its `WHERE false` (`0`) and `HAVING true` spellings,
  `SELECT count(*) + 1 FROM (SELECT 1) s`, `SELECT max(1) FROM (VALUES (1)) v(x)` †,
  `SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT 1) s)`, `SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT 1) s UNION
  ALL SELECT 5`, `INSERT INTO dt SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT 1) s` † and `SELECT
  row_number() OVER () FROM (SELECT 1) s`. **Loud** — a refusal where 18.6 answers.
  Reach: ordinary — `SELECT count(*)` written as a probe, an `INSERT INTO t SELECT
  max(…)`. No fixture: a faithful one is red, and an `@expect-error` one passes on any
  error where 18.6 accepts.

- **304 · A grouping query computes a group's aggregates in its own order.** 18.6's
  `Agg` node advances **every** aggregate over each input row in turn — all of a hashed
  aggregation's groups before it projects any — and only then evaluates `HAVING` and the
  select list. pglet computes one aggregate over all of a group's rows before the next,
  computes a group's `HAVING` aggregates and evaluates its predicate before it computes the
  select list's, and evaluates one group's expressions before it computes the next group's
  aggregates (`executor::query::aggregate`'s `execute_aggregate`). So where two failures
  are present the first in pglet's order is raised, and where `HAVING` discards a group, a
  select-list aggregate that raises on 18.6 is never computed here. Measured over `u (a
  INT, b INT)` holding `(1, 10)` and `(2, 0)`: `SELECT sum(sqrt(b - 5)), sum(1/(b - 10))
  FROM u` is `2201F` here and `22012` there (the first row's division raises before the
  second row's `sqrt`); `SELECT sum(1/(b - 10)) FROM u HAVING sum(sqrt(b - 5)) > 0` is
  `2201F` here and `22012` there; `SELECT a/0 + sum(sqrt(b - 5)) FROM u GROUP BY a` is
  `22012` here and `2201F` under 18.6's hashed plan; and — the **silent** member —
  `SELECT sum(1/b) FROM u GROUP BY a HAVING count(*) > 5` is `(0 rows)` here and `22012`
  there. 18.6's own order is its plan's (a sorted aggregation projects each group as it
  completes), so no fixed order of pglet's reproduces it in general. Silent where `HAVING`
  discards the group, loud under another code otherwise. No fixture: a faithful one is
  red.

  **A refusal pglet raises only at evaluation loses to an aggregate's failure.** A type
  error 18.6 raises in parse analysis and pglet raises when the scalar walk evaluates the
  node is raised after that clause's aggregates are computed for the group, so a failing
  aggregate among them outranks it: `SELECT count(*) || 1, sum(1/b) FROM u` is
  `22012` here and `42883` there (and was `42883` here while the first item was evaluated
  before the second's aggregate was computed), and likewise `upper(count(*))`, `count(*)
  + 'x'` and `max(a) + max(t)` beside `sum(1/b)` — `42883` / `22P02` there, `22012` here.
  Loud, wrong code.

  **A failing constant loses to an aggregate's failure too, and `HAVING`'s to the select
  list's.** 18.6's planner folds the constants of the select list, then `HAVING`'s, before
  a row is read. Here a constant is evaluated by the scalar walk — after the group's
  aggregates are computed, `HAVING` ahead of the select list, and after the `WHERE` has
  run: `SELECT 1/0 + sum(sqrt(b - 5)) FROM u` is `2201F` here and `22012` there, and
  `SELECT 2147483647 + 1 > 0 OR sum(1/b) > 0 FROM u` `22012` against `22003` (each was
  18.6's code here while an expression was evaluated before the aggregates under it were
  computed); `SELECT sqrt(-1.0), sum(1/0 + a) FROM u` is `22012` against `2201F`, the
  aggregate's argument being evaluated per row ahead of the item beside it; `SELECT 1/0 +
  count(*) FROM u HAVING 2147483647 + 1 > 0` is `22003` against `22012`; and `SELECT 1/0 +
  sum(a) FROM u WHERE sqrt(b - 5.0) > 0` is `2201F` against `22012`, as the ungrouped
  `SELECT 1/0 + a FROM u WHERE sqrt(b - 5.0) > 0` is. Loud, wrong code. A constant the walk
  never reaches is not raised at all (row 60).

  **An operand-type refusal is raised ahead of a kept aggregate's refused cast, and the
  select list's ahead of `HAVING`'s — junk sort keys with the select list.** The
  collection refuses an operand type before any argument is evaluated (row 89), and a
  kept aggregate's cast is refused only as its argument is evaluated; 18.6 raises
  whichever stands first in its analysis order. Over `o (g INT, a INT, t TEXT, j JSONB, bo
  BOOL)`: `SELECT max(a::jsonb), sum(t) FROM o`, its `GROUP BY a` spelling, `SELECT
  count(a::uuid), sum(t) FROM o`, `SELECT count(a::uuid), true OR sum(t) > 0 FROM o`,
  `SELECT max(a::jsonb), CASE WHEN false THEN min(bo) END FROM o`, `SELECT max(a::jsonb)
  FROM o GROUP BY g ORDER BY sum(t)` and `SELECT g FROM o GROUP BY g HAVING max(a::jsonb)
  IS NULL ORDER BY sum(t)` are `42883` here and `42846` there — `42846` here before.
  Alone, `SELECT max(a::jsonb) FROM o` is `42846` on both. And 18.6 analyses `HAVING`
  ahead of `ORDER BY`, where a junk sort key rides in the select list here: `SELECT g FROM
  o GROUP BY g HAVING max(j) IS NULL ORDER BY sum(t)` is `42883` on both, reporting
  `max(jsonb)` there and `sum(text)` here. Loud, wrong code or message.

- **305 · A `NULL` passes a type gate keyed on the value.** 18.6 refuses an operand type
  in parse analysis, from the expression's declared type and whatever the rows. pglet
  raises most such refusals where it evaluates the node, from the **values** the
  evaluator is handed (`executor::expr` — the string and math function evaluators, the
  arithmetic one, a comparison's `comparison_legality` over `Value::type_oid`), and a
  `NULL` value carries no type: the evaluators measured below answer `NULL` for a `NULL`
  operand, their refusals never raised. So a `NULL` of a type the function or operator
  has no form for answers `NULL` where 18.6 refuses the call. The class is that
  mechanism, and its members are whatever is refused from values; measured, over `n (a TEXT)` holding one `NULL` row and
  an empty `e (a TEXT, t TEXT, f FLOAT8)`, each `NULL` here (or no group) and `42883`
  there unless another code is named:

  - a function: `SELECT abs(a) FROM n`, `SELECT sqrt(a) FROM n`, `SELECT abs(NULL::text)`,
    `SELECT upper(NULL::int)`; over an aggregate, `abs(max(t))`, `sqrt(max(t))`,
    `ceil(max(t))`, `sign(max(t))`, `length(sum(f))`, `upper(max(f))`, `replace(max(f),
    'a', 'b')`, `btrim(max(f))`, `strpos(max(f), 'x')`, `round(avg(f), 2)`,
    `isfinite(max(t))`, `date_trunc('day', max(a))`, `extract(year FROM max(t))` and
    `nullif(max(f), max(t))`, each `FROM e`, and `SELECT count(*) FROM e HAVING
    upper(max(f)) = 'X'`; and the call-spelled `md5`, `left`, `octet_length`, `substr`,
    `mod` and `power` the same way — `SELECT octet_length(NULL::int)`, `SELECT
    substr(NULL::int, 1)`, `SELECT mod(NULL::float8, 2)`, and over an empty `e2 (a TEXT, t
    TEXT, f FLOAT8)` no row for `SELECT md5(f) FROM e2`, `SELECT left(f, 1) FROM e2`,
    `SELECT mod(t, 2) FROM e2` and `SELECT power(t, 2) FROM e2`, each refused before any
    row there;
  - an operator: `SELECT a + 1 FROM n`, `SELECT NULL::float8 + NULL::text`, `SELECT
    -max(t) FROM e`, `SELECT max(f) + max(t) FROM e`, `SELECT max(t) LIKE max(f) FROM e`,
    `SELECT ARRAY[max(f)] || max(t) FROM e`;
  - a comparison whose operand the plan-time gate does not type: `SELECT max(f) = max(t)
    FROM e`, `SELECT max(f) = ANY(ARRAY['a']) FROM e`, `SELECT a = ANY(ARRAY[1]) FROM n`,
    `SELECT CASE max(f) WHEN max(t) THEN 1 END FROM e`, and `SELECT max(f) IN ('x', 'y')
    FROM e` (`22P02` there).

  Where the plan-time gate types both operands it refuses as 18.6 does — `SELECT f = t
  FROM e`, `SELECT a = 1 FROM n`, `SELECT a IN (1, 2) FROM n`, `SELECT nullif(a, 1) FROM
  n` and `SELECT NULL::float8 = NULL::text` are `42883` on both, and
  `greatest(max(f), max(t))` and `coalesce(max(f), max(t))` `42804` on both — and over a
  non-`NULL` value the eval-time gate fires. The members under an aggregate were `0A000`
  while an expression over an aggregate was not evaluated (row 89), save `max(f) =
  max(t)`, `max(f) + max(t)`, `-max(t)` and the `LIKE`, which answered then too. Silent —
  an answer where 18.6 refuses. No fixture: a faithful one is red.

- **307 · `sum` and `avg` over `time`: the aggregate has no form for a `time` operand.**
  18.6 registers no `sum(time)` or `avg(time)` either, and resolves the call through
  `time`'s implicit cast to `interval`, answering an `interval`.
  `planner::legality`'s `aggregate_legality` accepts the numeric family and `interval`
  for the two and models no implicit cast, so a `time` operand is refused. Over `o (g
  INT, tm TIME)` holding two rows of `01:02:03` in one group: `SELECT sum(tm) FROM o` is
  `42883` here and `02:04:06` there, and `avg(tm)` `42883` against `01:02:03`. The
  refusal is asked for the statement, ahead of every group and of an aggregate a certain
  decider drops (row 89), so it reaches statements that form no group, which answered as
  18.6 does while the check ran per computed group: over an empty `e (g INT, tm TIME)`,
  `SELECT sum(tm) FROM e GROUP BY g`, its `avg` and `sum(DISTINCT tm)` spellings, `SELECT
  count(*) FROM e GROUP BY g HAVING sum(tm) > '00:00'` and `SELECT g FROM e GROUP BY g
  ORDER BY avg(tm)` are `42883` here and no row there; over `o`, `SELECT g, sum(tm) FROM o
  GROUP BY g HAVING false` likewise, and `SELECT CASE WHEN false THEN sum(tm) END IS NULL
  FROM o GROUP BY g` is `42883` against `t`. `SELECT true OR sum(tm) IS NULL FROM o` is
  `42883` against `t`, as it was while a decided `OR` still computed its aggregate. The
  cast written out answers on both — `SELECT sum(tm::interval) FROM o` is `02:04:06` —
  and `min` / `max` over `time` agree. `isfinite(time)` is the sibling through the same
  cast (row 144). Loud — a refusal where 18.6 answers. Reach: ordinary. No fixture: a
  faithful one is red.

- **306 · `jsonb_build_object` renders a value it has no JSON kind for as its text
  output.** `executor::expr`'s `value_to_jsonb` maps a boolean, a number, a text and a
  `jsonb` value to their JSON kinds and every other value to a JSON **string** holding
  `value_to_text`'s rendering. 18.6's `datum_to_jsonb` renders a timestamp in ISO 8601
  (`JsonEncodeDateTime`) and an array as a JSON array of its elements, and the value
  here carries no declared type, so a `timestamptz` is rendered without its offset.
  Measured over `o (id INT, a INT, ts TIMESTAMPTZ, tm TIMESTAMP, d DATE)` holding `(2, 1,
  '2021-01-02 03:04:05+00', '2021-01-02 03:04:05', '2021-06-01')`, `TimeZone` `UTC`:
  `jsonb_build_object('ts', ts)` is `{"ts": "2021-01-02 03:04:05"}` here and `{"ts":
  "2021-01-02T03:04:05+00:00"}` there, and the `'…'::timestamptz` constant the same;
  `jsonb_build_object('tm', tm)` is `"2021-01-02 03:04:05"` against
  `"2021-01-02T03:04:05"`; `jsonb_build_object('a', ARRAY[a])` is `{"a": "{1}"}` against
  `{"a": [1]}`, and `ARRAY['x', 'y']` `"{x,y}"` against `["x", "y"]`. Under an aggregate
  — `jsonb_build_object('ts', max(ts))`, `jsonb_build_object('a', ARRAY[max(ts)])`, the
  second `{"a": "{\"2021-01-02 03:04:05\"}"}` against `{"a":
  ["2021-01-02T03:04:05+00:00"]}` — the same values are reached where the statement was
  `0A000` (row 89). The `date`, `time`, `interval`, `uuid`, number, boolean, text, `NULL`
  and `jsonb` values tried each rendered as 18.6 renders them; `to_jsonb` and
  `jsonb_build_array` are `0A000`.

  Other members of the same function, measured: a `float4` value is widened before it is
  rendered — `jsonb_build_object('x', f4)` over `1.1` is `{"x": 1.100000023841858}`
  against `{"x": 1.1}`, and `0.1::real + 0.2::real` `0.30000001192092896` against `0.3`
  (a `float8` `1.5` agrees); a `char(4)` value loses its padding, `"ab"` against `"ab  "`;
  and two are loud — `jsonb_build_object('x', 'Infinity'::numeric)` is `22P02` against
  `{"x": "Infinity"}`, and a key that is not text, `jsonb_build_object(1, 2)`, `42804`
  against `{"1": 2}`. Silent — another jsonb value, returned or stored — but for those
  two. Reach: ordinary. No fixture: a faithful one is red.

- **~~88~~ · Closed — an `IN` list is `= ANY (ARRAY[…])` there, in five shapes.** In a
  rendered stored expression — `pg_get_constraintdef`,
  `information_schema.check_constraints.check_clause`, `column_default` and
  `pg_indexes.indexdef` — pglet used to print the written spelling
  `CHECK ((a IN (1, 2, 3)))` where 18.6 prints `CHECK ((a = ANY (ARRAY[1, 2, 3])))`,
  which the fuz spine's own `cell_grant_level_check` read back as a changed constraint.

  That is **one shape among five** `transformAExprIn` builds, which is why the closure
  reproduces the transformation rather than the string: the array is built only for more
  than one element holding no column, `NOT IN` flips to `<> ALL` and an `AND` chain, a
  lone element is a plain comparison, a column element stays its own chain operand, and
  the array comes first with the column elements after it in list order.

  It is closed in `RenderMode::Catalog` **only** — a *rendering*, not a normalisation of
  the stored plan. Normalising would move every `InList` reader in the evaluator and the
  index-probe path, and would make the dump emit `= ANY (ARRAY[…])`, which re-parses to
  `Expr::AnyAll` and breaks the round-trip invariant a restored partial index depends on.
  **Live residual**: a list whose elements do not already share the left operand's type
  (`a IN (1, 2.5)`, `a IN (1, 1000000000000)`) falls back to the written `IN`, because
  18.6 wraps every operand in a `select_common_type` coercion pglet does not store — row
  90. `catalog/constraintdef_in_list_is_a_scalar_array_op.sql` pins all five shapes plus
  the `= ANY` polarity that already agreed,
  `catalog/check_clause_unknown_literal_takes_its_operand_type.sql` the second surface,
  and `catalog/spine_snapshot_cell_grant_shapes.sql` the spine's own constraint through
  the statement its snapshot issues.

- **87 · `oid` and `"char"` have comparison rules and no cast rows.** The positions are
  the common-type fold (`coalesce(conrelid, 0)`, `CASE … ELSE 0 END`,
  `greatest(conrelid, 0)`, `ARRAY[conrelid, 0]`), the assignment cast
  (`INSERT INTO snap (relid) SELECT conrelid`,
  `UPDATE snap SET relid = (SELECT conrelid …)`), and an aggregate's result type
  (`max(contype)`). The first two are **loud and pglet-stricter** — no row is written and
  no value is coerced — and the third is **silent**, a declared type over values that
  agree.

  Measured on 18.6's `pg_cast`: `int2`/`int4`/`int8 → oid` are implicit,
  `oid → int8`/`int4` assignment, `"char" → text` implicit,
  `text`/`char`/`varchar → "char"` assignment, `"char" ↔ int4` explicit-only. pglet has
  no `pg_cast` **table**; what it has is `planner::common_type`'s enumeration of the
  implicit rows (`implicitly_coercible`), which carries neither of these two — they are
  wired into the **category predicates** instead — `oid_comparable` and `is_string` (which holds
  `"char"` and `name`) — and those cover exactly the positions a category answers, so
  `contype LIKE 'n'`, `upper(contype)`, `conrelid > 100` and an assignment into a `text`
  column all behave; the concatenation position is where a category answer and 18.6 part,
  recorded at row 85(d) (measured: `INSERT INTO ttxt (t) SELECT conrelid` and its
  `contype` twin write on **both** engines, `assignment_compatible` accepting any source
  into a string target). What has no predicate is the *fold* and
  `assignment_compatible`'s **source** side, which is where a `pg_cast` row is the only
  thing that would answer. `is_numeric_family` excludes `oid` deliberately — putting it
  in would widen the arithmetic gate above it, which is the divergence this one is the
  price of.

  **The polarity that shows it is a *cast* question and not a *type* question**:
  `nullif(conrelid, 0)` **answers** `16384` here, because `NULLIF` resolves through `=`
  (which `oid_comparable` registers) rather than through the fold. Closing it is a design change,
  not a local fix: `oid` into `type_category`/`implicitly_coercible` with the asymmetry that
  makes `(int4, oid)` fold to `oid`, an `oid[]` type for the `ARRAY` member, and
  `assignment_legality` rows in both directions — each of which reaches the 441-pair
  assignment matrix and the arithmetic gate.
  `catalog/oid_in_a_common_type_fold_is_pglet_stricter.sql` and
  `catalog/oid_assigned_into_an_integer_column_is_pglet_stricter.sql` pin the two loud
  halves as `@expect-error`-where-18.6-accepts, so a future silent coercion reddens them,
  and `catalog/oid_comparison_still_resolves.sql` is the `nullif`-side control. Nothing
  pins the `max(contype)` declared type, the values agreeing.

- **86 · A `"char"` is one byte wide there and one character wide here.** 18.6's
  `charin` truncates to the first byte — `'é'::"char"` is the lone `\303`, which no Rust
  `String` can hold — so pglet truncates to the first **character** instead. And
  `'abcdef'::"char"` is `42601` here against 18.6's `a`: the type has no cast spelling,
  because bare `char` is SQL's `character` and taking it for `"char"` would mis-read
  every `CHAR(n)` column.

  Silent for the truncation, loud for the cast, and both bounded to a value no catalog
  `"char"` column carries. `virtual_tables.rs` declares **ten** of them — `relkind`,
  `relpersistence`, `attidentity`, `attgenerated`, `typtype`, `typcategory`, `contype`,
  `confupdtype`, `confdeltype`, `confmatchtype` — and every value either engine produced
  over the corpus's catalogs is one ASCII byte or empty, measured with `length` alone,
  `octet_length` being `0A000` here: a `length` of 0 or 1 is where the byte rule and the
  character rule agree exactly. The per-column figures move with the corpus's own DDL — a
  `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` column makes `attidentity` non-empty
  (`catalog/char_column_uncast_agrees.expected.json` records an `a` beside an empty one)
  — so re-derive them from the catalogs, not from this bullet, which is also how that
  list of ten was corrected from a written five. The *identity* this replaced was the one
  that mattered: `WHERE contype = 'nx'` matched every `'n'` row on 18.6 and **none**
  here.

- **85 · `::regclass` answers a name, not an OID, and consequences follow.** pglet
  answers the relation's **name**, rendered for an identifier position (`quote_ident`,
  (f)) and carried as `text`; 18.6's value is an OID that merely *prints* as the name. So
  what goes over the wire differs by format, and not only the declared type does:
  measured over `'"Odd"'::regclass`, the **text** format sends the same five bytes
  `"Odd"` from each, while the **binary** format sends 18.6's four OID bytes under 2205
  against pglet's five name bytes under 25.

  - **(a) The declared types differ.** A bare `<expr>::regclass` is declared `text` (25)
    where 18.6 declares `regclass` (2205), `$1::regclass` reports `ParameterDescription`
    OID 0 where 18.6 reports 2205, and an unaliased `'x'::regclass` over a **nameless**
    argument is named `?column?` where 18.6 names it `regclass`. What a **stack** of casts
    above it is named is row 117's. The parameter's OID 0 is not erased by an outer
    `::text`: `$1::regclass::text` reports it too.
  - **(b) The canonical `pg_catalog` idiom is loud here.**
    `WHERE conrelid = 'child'::regclass` is `42883 operator does not exist: integer = text`
    here and four rows there, because the two sides are an OID and a name rather than two
    OIDs.
  - **(c) A schema-qualified literal resolves only when the qualifier is `public`.**
    `'public.zz'::regclass` and `'"public".zz'::regclass` answer `zz`, while
    `'pg_catalog.pg_class'::regclass` and `'nosuchschema.zz'::regclass` are `42P01`
    **naming the whole literal** (`relation "pg_catalog.pg_class" does not exist`) — the
    qualifier is stripped for `public` and carried into the lookup otherwise, so a
    `pg_catalog` name never reaches the synthesized views, which are not catalog
    `Table`s.
  - **(d) Beside them, the concatenation concatenates.** `"char" \|\| text` concatenates
    here, and so does the `unknown` right-hand spelling, which answers what the explicit
    cast gives on 18.6:

    | spelling | pglet | 18.6 |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | `SELECT contype \|\| 'x' FROM pg_constraint` | `nx` over a `'n'` row | `42725 operator is not unique` |
    | `contype::text \|\| 'x'` | the same `nx` | `nx` |

  - **(e) A sequence is not one of the relations it searches.** After `CREATE SEQUENCE
    s1`, `SELECT 's1'::regclass` is `42P01 relation "s1" does not exist` here against
    `s1` there — while `nextval('s1')` on the same connection answers `1`, so the
    sequence plainly exists — and a `SERIAL` column's implicit `ser1_id_seq` answers the
    same way. `eval_regclass` reads `schema.tables` and then `schema.indexes`, in its OID
    arm and its name arm alike, and a sequence is in neither. That is consistent with
    pglet giving a sequence no `pg_class` row at all (no `relkind = 'S'`, `docs/compatibility.md`'s
    pg_catalog row), but it is a **second** reader of the same gap: closing the
    catalog side does not close this one unless this resolver moves with it.

  - **(f) The name is rendered for an identifier position, and the predicate is pglet's
    lexer's.** 18.6's `regclassout` (`utils/adt/regproc.c`) ends in
    `quote_qualified_identifier`, so a relation created as `"Odd"` prints as `"Odd"`.
    pglet answered the *stored bytes* until `eval_regclass` was routed through
    `lexer::quote_ident` — the one `fmtId`-style renderer here — in the OID arm and the
    name arm alike. What that closed is a **round trip**, not a rendering preference: the old bare `Odd` fed back to
    `'…'::regclass` folds to `odd` and is `42P01 relation "odd" does not exist` on both
    engines, so the value named nothing on either. Two residuals stand under it. The
    **keyword half** of the predicate is not 18.6's, in both directions: `quote_identifier`
    quotes a keyword whose `ScanKeywordCategories` entry is not `UNRESERVED_KEYWORD`,
    while `is_safe_bare_ident` asks whether *pglet's own lexer* reads the word as an
    `Identifier`. The instrument is `pg_get_keywords()` — create one relation per word and
    compare `'"<word>"'::regclass::text` against 18.6's `quote_ident(word)`. Measured
    members: `action`, `key`, `set` and `index` are `UNRESERVED_KEYWORD` and bare there,
    quoted here; `numeric`, `interval`, `user` and `window` are quoted there and bare here.
    The disagreement is wide rather than a handful, and a count of it would go stale
    against both the oracle's keyword table and pglet's lexer — re-run the sweep for its
    extent. **Part of it the routing made**, which is the argument for moving the
    predicate to a keyword-category table rather than refining it: `action`, `key`, `set`
    and `index` are `UNRESERVED_KEYWORD`, bare there, and were bare here too before
    `eval_regclass` was routed through the predicate — the stored-bytes answer agreed with
    18.6 at those four and the quoted one does not (measured on this tree and on a build
    of it with the two engine files reverted). The four beside them, `numeric`,
    `interval`, `user` and `window`, disagreed on both builds. What a disagreement there
    costs is smaller than the one it replaced, which is
    why it is a residual and not the same defect: `'"action"'::regclass::text` is
    `"action"` here and `action` there, and each spelling re-resolves to `action` on the
    engine that printed it (measured), where the old bare `Odd` named nothing on either.
    And **`InvalidOid` is not digits**: `regclassout` short-circuits OID 0 to `-` ahead of
    the catalog lookup, so
    `SELECT 0::regclass::text` is `-` there against `0` here, while an OID no relation
    holds prints its digits on both (`SELECT 99999::regclass::text` is `99999`).

  The `::regclass::text` spelling `fuz_app`'s `schema_introspect.ts` writes (its Rust
  twin joins `pg_class`) does not shield (c) or (e): `'pg_catalog.pg_class'::regclass::text`
  and `'s1'::regclass::text` are `42P01` here against `pg_class` and `s1` there. pglet's
  encoders carry no catalog, so a `regclass` *value* could be right in the text format or
  the binary one and not both; closing (b) would need either that value or a comparison
  arm resolving a name to an OID, which is a rule 18.6 does not have (its own is
  `oid = oid`).
  `catalog/regclass_resolves_a_relation_name.sql`,
  `catalog/regclass_unknown_relation_is_loud.sql` and
  `catalog/spine_snapshot_constraints_regclass.sql` pin the `::text` spelling and the
  name side's reject over a **table**; nothing pins (a), (e), or (c)'s divergent half.

- **~~118~~ · Closed — A non-bare `regclass` cast target is refused, where it used to answer.**
  `parser::expr`'s `parse_cast_target` decided on the **identifier** `regclass` and then
  discarded what `parse_type_name` returned; that reader consumes a trailing `[]` (one or
  more, with an optional dimension) *and* a `(…)` modifier as part of the name, so a
  suffix or a modifier was consumed into the name it discarded and the target built the
  node `'t'::regclass` builds. It decides on the **canonical type name** now —
  `regclass` exactly, or the target is not the model — and everything else routes to the
  same `executor::resolve_column_type` the non-intercept path uses, which answers
  `42704 type "regclass" is not supported`: the code the *column* form already gave, where
  18.6 accepts `a regclass` and `a regclass[]` as column types. Over a table named `t`,
  measured on both engines before and after:

  | spelling | pglet before | pglet now | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT 't'::regclass[]` | `t` | `42704` | `22P02 malformed array literal: "t"` |
  | `SELECT CAST('t' AS regclass[])` | `t` | `42704` | the same `22P02` |
  | `SELECT 't'::regclass[][]` | `t` | `42704` | the same `22P02` |
  | `SELECT 't'::regclass[3]` | `t` | `42704` | the same `22P02` |
  | `SELECT 't'::REGCLASS[]` | `t` | `42704` | the same `22P02` |
  | `SELECT 't'::regclass(3)` | `t` | `42704` | `42601 type modifier is not allowed for type "regclass"` |
  | `SELECT 't'::regclass(5,2)` | `t` | `42704` | the same `42601` |
  | `SELECT 't'::regclass(3)[]` | `t` | `42704` | `42601 … for type "regclass[]"` |
  | `SELECT 1::regclass[]` | `1` | `42704` | `42846 cannot cast type integer to regclass[]` |
  | `SELECT ('{t}'::regclass[])::text` | `42P01 relation "{t}" does not exist` | `42704` | `{t}` |

  **It wrote, and that is what closed.** Over `dw` holding `1, 2`,
  `DELETE FROM dw WHERE 't'::regclass[] = 't'` was `DELETE 2` here and left
  `count(*) = 0`, where 18.6 raises the `22P02` in parse analysis and keeps the rows;
  the same statement is `42704` now and the rows survive on the in-memory CoW-B+tree and
  on the double-meta store alike. Not every DML position took it: over that same `INT`
  column, `INSERT INTO dw VALUES ('t'::regclass[])` wrote nothing even then, answering
  `42804 … column "a" is of type integer but expression is of type text`.

  **The first residual is loud, and it is why no fixture holds the headline spellings.**
  For every row of the table above except the last, both engines refuse and their
  SQLSTATEs differ — so a faithful `@expect-error` over `'t'::regclass[]` compares `42704` against
  `22P02` and is red under `tests/README.md`'s rule. What the corpus *can* hold is that
  last row, where 18.6 **accepts**: `catalog/regclass_array_target_is_loud.sql` drives
  that spelling over a relation deliberately created under the literal's *own* spelling
  (`"{arr_qt}"`), so the swallowing reader answered a row there and "any pglet error
  passes" is a live assertion rather than a waiver. The
  SQLSTATE at each spelling above, the surviving rows, and the accept-side polarity are
  `crates/pglet/tests/regclass_cast_target.rs`.

  A **second** residual, and the modifier half of it is **closed**:
  `--coerce-unknown-types` routes the refused name through
  `planner::unsupported_type_oid`'s lenient arm, so `'t'::nosuchtype` becomes `'t'::text`
  under that flag and `DELETE FROM dw WHERE 't'::nosuchtype = 't'` is `DELETE 2` against
  18.6's `42704`, `count(*)` going 2 → 0 (measured). That is the flag's declared legacy
  posture rather than this spelling's, and the default is off. **`'t'::regclass(3)` no
  longer joins it**: row 119's modifier gate reads the *resolved* type, which under the
  flag is `text`, and `text` carries no modifier — so that `DELETE` is `42601` on both
  engines now and both rows survive (measured). The exemption that would re-open it was
  weighed and declined; `crates/pglet_sql/src/planner/unknown_types.rs`'s module doc
  carries the argument and `the_coerce_flag_does_not_exempt_the_modifier_gate`
  (`crates/pglet/tests/typmod_decomposition.rs`) pins both polarities. The *array*
  spelling stays loud under the flag anyway (`22P02`, the array reader refusing `'t'`).

  A **third**, and the branch created it: the array spelling now reaches
  `resolve_column_type`, where a user enum whose quoted name *is* the canonical spelling
  resolves. With `CREATE TYPE "regclass[]" AS ENUM ('a','b')` on an otherwise clean
  server, `SELECT 'a'::regclass[]` answered `a` and `SELECT 'zzz'::regclass[]` `zzz` on
  that branch; the resolver now decomposes the name before the enum lookup, so both are
  `42704 type "regclass" is not supported` here (measured), against 18.6's `22P02
  malformed array literal` for both. On a build of this tree
  with the branch's two engine files reverted, both were `42P01 relation "…" does not
  exist` — so the answer is the branch's and not a pre-existing one (measured on both
  builds and, for the `22P02`, on 18.6). Neither half of it is `regclass`'s own: an enum
  named `"int4[]"` shadows `int4[]` on the reverted build too (`SELECT 'zzz'::int4[]`
  answers `zzz` there, and `SELECT '{1,2}'::int4[]` the text `{1,2}`), and a non-member
  label cast to an ordinary enum answered there against 18.6's `22P02 invalid input value
  for enum` — the cast-membership edge, row 241, since closed. What the branch moved is that
  `regclass[]` now *reaches* that resolver at all.

  The **bare** name shadowed is a divergence of its own, and it is at the column rather
  than the cast: with `CREATE TYPE regclass AS ENUM ('a','b')`, `SELECT 'a'::regclass` is
  `42P01 relation "a" does not exist` here — the branch takes it, the enum invisible —
  and 18.6 answers the same `42P01`, resolving the builtin; but `CREATE TABLE z1 (a
  regclass)` declares that **enum**'s column here, so `INSERT INTO z1 VALUES ('a')`
  stores and reads back `a`, where 18.6 declares a builtin `regclass` column and the same
  `INSERT` is `42P01`. Silent, and it writes. Both engines accept the `CREATE TYPE`.

  **For a builtin pglet has a type for, the name is the builtin's wherever `resolve_type_name` reads it** — the column type, `::` / `CAST`, the typed constant and an undeclared `$N`'s cast.
  `resolve_type_name` asked the enum catalog first, so beside `CREATE TYPE int4 AS ENUM
  ('k')` a `c int4` column was the enum's (`INSERT … VALUES ('5')` refused `22P02`), and
  once a cast converted to the enum (row 241) `SELECT '5'::int4` was `22P02` and `SELECT
  5::int4` `42846` where 18.6 answers `5` — its search path puts `pg_catalog` first, and a
  keyword spelling (`integer`) names `pg_catalog`'s type outright. The resolver now asks the
  enum only for a name `type_oid_from_name` does not resolve, so each of `'5'::int4`,
  `CAST('6' AS int4)`, `int4 '7'`, `8::int4`, an undeclared `$1::int4` and the column
  answers 18.6's integer (`enum/builtin_named_enum_*`, `params/builtin_named_enum_param_cast`),
  and `'k'::int4` is the integer input's `22P02` on both. The `SERIAL` spellings are not
  among those names — 18.6 has no such type, and an enum named `serial` is the cast target
  there as here. What is left, each measured: 18.6 reaches the enum as `public.int4`
  (`'k'::public.int4` answers `k`), which is `42704 type "public" is not supported` here,
  pglet parsing no qualified type name; `DROP TYPE int4` drops the enum here and is
  `2BP01 cannot drop type integer because it is required by the database system` there,
  **silently**; a `serial` column beside an enum named `serial` declares the enum here
  (its sequence default then refused `22P02`), a `serial` column there; and a name 18.6's
  catalog holds that pglet has **no** type for still resolves to a same-named enum, as
  `regclass` does above — `'o'::oid` answers `o` and `'j'::json` `j` here, **silently**,
  against 18.6's `22P02` for each.

  The persisted-expression positions take the same `42704`, measured: a `CHECK`, a column
  `DEFAULT`, an index predicate and an index key over `'t'::regclass[]` each answer `type
  "regclass" is not supported` here against `22P02 malformed array literal: "t"` there.
  The refusal is the cast target's, not row 84's — the array spelling builds no
  `StringFunc::Regclass` node, so the render/eval probe that raises row 84's
  `0A000 … is not available in this context` is never reached; the *scalar*
  `'t'::regclass` at those same four positions is that `0A000` (and 18.6 accepts two of
  them and answers `22P02 invalid input syntax for type oid: "t"` at the two carrying a
  `= 't'` comparison, which is the comparison's coercion rather than the cast's). The
  column `DEFAULT`'s *sequence* route reaches a third reader again and refused it before
  this rule too — `parser::ddl`'s `parse_nextval_arg` reads one bare name after the cast
  token, so `DEFAULT nextval('ps'::regclass[])` is `42601 syntax error: expected ')',
  found '['` here against 18.6's `22P02`, and nothing persists.

  **Neighbouring spellings the branch does not reach**, each refused here where
  18.6 answers the relation name, measured over a table `t` on both engines:

  | spelling | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT regclass 't'` | `42704 type "regclass" is not supported` | `t` |
  | `SELECT 't'::"regclass"` | `42601 syntax error: expected a type name…` | `t` |
  | `SELECT 't'::pg_catalog.regclass` | `42704 type "pg_catalog" is not supported` | `t` |

  They belong here rather than under row 85 by that row's own test: each would stand if
  the two engines' `regclass` *values* agreed. The typed-constant one is a different
  reader — `parser::expr`'s `typed_constant_from` calls `executor::resolve_constant_type`
  directly and never routes through `parse_cast_target`, so the `regclass` model is absent
  from a position 18.6 reads as `CAST('t' AS regclass)`. The quoted one never reaches the
  branch either: `parser::type_name`'s `expect_type_word` takes a bare
  `TokenKind::Identifier` only, so the `"…"` token is refused before any type name is
  read — that reader's own doc is where the quoted-spelling rule lives, `regclass`
  included in it now. The schema-qualified one is `parse_type_name` reading `pg_catalog` as the type word;
  `planner::sequence_name_from_arg`'s doc carries it beside `nextval('s1'::regclass)`,
  which is pglet's `0A000` against 18.6's answer.

  A fourth spelling passes that same test and is **not** `regclass`'s alone, which is why
  it is not in the table above: 18.6's function-style coercion `regclass('t')` is
  `0A000 function not supported: regclass` here against `t` there, a refusal it shares
  with `int4(1)`, `text(1)`, `int8(1)`, `bool(1)`, `float8(1)` and
  `date('2020-01-01')` — row 121.

  The swallow was the intercept's and not the type-name reader's: over a type pglet does
  model, the suffix decides the target on both engines — `'1'::int[]` is refused `22P02` by
  each and `'{1,2}'::int[]` is `{1,2}` on each. The **modifier** half had a wider sibling this rule does not reach, because it
  lives in a different reader — row 119, closed since.

  It is not row 85 read one spelling wider, which is why it is its own row rather than
  another lettered consequence there. Row 85 is the row for what follows from `regclass`
  answering a **name** where 18.6 answers an **OID**; this divergence would have stood if
  those two values agreed, because 18.6 refuses `'t'::regclass[]` over exactly the
  argument its own scalar `::regclass` resolves.

- **~~119~~ · Closed — A type modifier on a type that carries none is swallowed.** It
  is refused now, `42601 type modifier is not allowed for type "…"` under 18.6's
  own sentence. Membership is the *type's* fact, `pg_type.typmodin <> 0`, measured on
  18.6 rather than reasoned from the spellings: `bpchar`, `varchar`, `numeric`, `time`,
  `timetz`, `timestamp`, `timestamptz` and `interval` carry one, and `bool`, `bytea`,
  `"char"`, `date`, `float4`, `float8`, `int2`, `int4`, `int8`, `json`, `jsonb`,
  `money`, `name`, `oid`, `regclass`, `text`, `uuid`, `xml` and every enum
  (`typtype = 'e'`) carry none. `pglet_core`'s `type_oid_carries_modifier` is that list,
  exhaustive over `TypeOid` so a new type must decide rather than join the refusing
  half by default, and `executor::type_resolution`'s `resolve_type_name` is the one gate
  reading it, entered as `resolve_column_type` or `resolve_constant_type` from each of its
  four call sites outside the resolver (the `::`/`CAST` pair, a column definition, `ADD
  COLUMN`, a typed constant — the last of which the refusal
  cannot reach **on the default route**, for a reason below). Each pair below measured
  on both engines, after the fix:

  | spelling | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT 1::int4(3)`, `::int2(3)`, `::int8(3)` | `42601`, naming `int4` / `int2` / `int8` | the same code, the same sentence |
  | `SELECT 1.5::float4(3)` / `::float8(3)` | the same, naming `float4` / `float8` | the same |
  | `SELECT true::bool(3)`, `'2020-01-01'::date(3)` | the same, naming `bool` / `date` | the same |
  | `SELECT 1::int4(5,2)` / `1::int4(-2)` | the same — the *presence* of a modifier is what is refused | the same |
  | `SELECT CAST(1 AS int4(3))` | the same | the same |
  | `CREATE TABLE t (a bool(3))`, `ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN c int4(7)` | the same | the same |
  | `CREATE TABLE t (a serial(3))` / `bigserial(3)` / `smallserial(3)` | the same, naming `integer` / `bigint` / `smallint` | the same |
  | `SELECT 'ok'::moodg(3)` and `CREATE TABLE (b moodg(3))`, live enum | the same, naming `moodg` | the same |
  | `SELECT 'x'::int4(3)` | the same — the refusal outranks the value's own `22P02` | the same |

  **The `serial` family names its rewritten integer type**, because 18.6's grammar has
  already turned `serial` into `integer` by the time parse analysis reads the modifier;
  pglet reads that name off the resolved `TypeOid` rather than off a second list of
  serial spellings. And the swallow's catalog effect is gone with it: `serial(3)` used
  to build a bare nullable `integer` — no sequence, no `NOT NULL`, no `DEFAULT`, so
  `INSERT … DEFAULT VALUES` stored NULL — and now no table is created at all.

  **The residual is where the refusal sits in the statement's error order**, and it is
  the class pglet's `42704` for an unsupported type already occupied rather than a new
  one. 18.6 resolves the relation first and reads the modifier in parse analysis. At a
  **cast** pglet still decides earlier, and that is the whole of what is left:

  | statement | pglet | 18.6 | the `42704` twin, unchanged |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT 1::int4(3) FROM nosuchtable` | `42601` | `42P01` | `SELECT 1::nosuchtype FROM nosuchtable` is `42704` / `42P01` |
  | `SELECT 'ab'::char(0) FROM nosuchtbl` | `22023` | `42P01` | the same twin, measured on both engines |
  | `SELECT nosuchcol, 'ab'::char(0) FROM t` — a **sibling column reference** | `22023` | `42703` | `SELECT nosuchcol, 'x'::nosuchtype FROM t` is `42704` / `42703` |

  The last two rows are row 124's arrival, not a second class: the carrier's `22023` is
  raised from the same `resolve_type_name` this `42601` is, so it sits at the same
  position and takes the same residual. Three verdicts, one ordering — and this row's own
  `42601` reaches the sibling-column width too (`SELECT nosuchcol, 1::int4(3) FROM t` is
  `42601` / `42703`, measured). That pair is this close's *arrival* at the ordering rather
  than an unchanged twin, which is why the last column above carries the `42704` instead.

  **The sibling-column member, at the width measured.** The split is by *position*, not by
  verdict, and the pattern it tracks — whether a column reference stands ahead of the cast
  in 18.6's transform order — is read off the measurements rather than from the source.
  Seven positions probed on both engines. Divergent (`22023` here, `42703` there):
  `SELECT nosuchcol, 'x'::char(0) FROM t`, `SELECT nosuchcol FROM t GROUP BY 'x'::char(0)`,
  `SELECT 1 FROM t WHERE nosuchcol AND 'x'::char(0) = 'y'`. Agreeing on the `22023`:
  `SELECT 'x'::char(0), nosuchcol FROM t`, `SELECT 'x'::char(0) FROM t WHERE nosuchcol`,
  `SELECT 'x'::char(0) FROM t ORDER BY nosuchcol`, and the cast's own **operand**
  `SELECT nosuchcol::char(0) FROM rtmc` — which is what
  `types/refused_typmod_beats_missing_column_loud.sql` pins. The remaining clause positions
  are **unswept**. The class is this residual's and not row 124's arrival: the `42704` twins
  in the table's last column diverge at the same position, measured, so what the carrier's
  `22023` did was land a third verdict on an ordering already visible there.

  **`ADD COLUMN` was two more rows of that table and is closed**, taking three
  pre-existing `42704` twins and three pre-existing identity `22023`s with it —
  `execute_alter_table_add_column` resolves the declared type **after** the relation
  lookup and the column-existence check, which is where 18.6 puts it
  (`check_for_column_name_collision` runs ahead of the `BuildDescForRelation` that
  resolves the type, and the comment between them in `tablecmds.c` says so). Ten pairs
  moved, each measured on both engines with fresh state per statement:

  | statement, over `ex (a INT)` | pglet before | pglet now, and 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `ADD COLUMN a int4(3)`, `a int4(3)[]`, `a nosuchtype` | `42601`, `42601`, `42704` | `42701 column "a" of relation "ex" already exists` |
  | `ADD COLUMN a text GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` | `22023` | the same `42701` |
  | `ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS a int4(3)` / `a nosuchtype` / `a text GENERATED …` | `42601` / `42704` / `22023` | a skip |
  | `ALTER TABLE nosuchtbl ADD COLUMN b int4(3)` / `b nosuchtype` / `b text GENERATED …` | `42601` / `42704` / `22023` | `42P01` |

  The polarity controls held, each measured on both engines: a genuinely new column
  still takes the type's verdict (`ADD COLUMN z int4(3)` is `42601`, `z nosuchtype`
  `42704`, `z text GENERATED …` `22023`, and `z varchar(3)[]` is accepted), and the type
  still outranks the identity check (`z nosuchtype GENERATED …` is `42704`,
  `z int4(3) GENERATED …` `42601`). **`ALTER TABLE IF EXISTS` is no control here**: the
  parser reads `IF` as the table name, so the statement is row 15's whole-statement
  no-op and this function is never called — `ALTER TABLE IF EXISTS ex ADD COLUMN z INT`
  over a live `ex` reports `ALTER TABLE` and adds nothing where 18.6 adds the column
  (measured), and the missing-table spelling matches 18.6 only in reporting success —
  18.6 gets there by noticing and skipping, with the `NOTICE` pglet does not send.
  **`CREATE TABLE` did not move and must not**: 18.6 is genuinely asymmetric between the
  two statements — its `tableElts` walk precedes even the `42P07`, so
  `CREATE TABLE ex (a int4(3))` over an existing `ex` is `42601` on both engines, while
  `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS ex (a int4(3))` and `… (a nosuchtype)` skip on both.

  Moving the modifier's gate alone would split a pair 18.6 raises from one call
  (`LookupTypeName` then `typenameTypeMod`), so the two travel together at every
  position — which is why the `ADD COLUMN` repair moved the `42704` and the `42601`
  in one step. What the same placement *gains* is measured too,
  each pair taken on both engines before and after: `SELECT 1::int4(3), 1/0` and
  `SELECT 1/0, 1::int4(3)` are `42601` on both where pglet answered `22012`,
  `SELECT 'x'::int4(3)` is `42601` on both where pglet answered `22P02`, and
  `CREATE TABLE p (a int4(3), b nosuchtype)` and
  `CREATE TABLE p (a int4(3), PRIMARY KEY (nosuch))` are `42601` on both where pglet
  answered about the *other* element (`42704`, `42703`). Six more were **silent**
  before — `SELECT 1::int4(3) FROM t` over an existing `t`,
  `INSERT INTO t VALUES (1::int4(3))`, `UPDATE t SET x = 1::int4(3)`,
  `SELECT x FROM t WHERE x = 1::int4(3)`,
  `CREATE TABLE p (a INT CHECK (a::int4(3) > 0))` and
  `CREATE TABLE p (a INT DEFAULT 1::int4(3))` were each accepted here against 18.6's
  `42601`, and `CREATE INDEX ix ON t ((x::int4(3)))` persisted the stored expression on
  top of that. The gate runs **after** an `IF NOT EXISTS` skip on `CREATE TABLE` —
  measured, both engines skip — which is where 18.6 puts it.

  A fourth pair moved from silent to loud without agreeing: the `SERIAL` family is not a
  cast-target type name on 18.6, so `SELECT 1::serial(3)` is its `42704` against this
  `42601` — pglet's own `SELECT 1::serial` answers `1` there against the same `42704`,
  which is the gap the modifier rides on.

  **The second residual is a type pglet does not model.** `SELECT 1::name(3)`,
  `::oid(3)`, `::money(3)`, `::regclass(3)`, `::xml(3)` and `::point(3)` are
  `42704 type "…" is not supported` here against 18.6's `42601 type modifier is not
  allowed for type "…"` (each re-measured), because the name
  resolves on 18.6 and does not here — the gate runs after resolution, as
  `typenameTypeMod` does, so pglet cannot reach the modifier's verdict for a type it has
  no entry for. `1::nosuchtype(3)` is `42704` on **both**. Closing these six needs the
  `pg_type` typname table `parser::type_name`'s `expect_type_word` already records pglet
  as lacking; each is loud either way.

  **`json(3)` is not one of them, and that same prescription would make it worse.**
  18.6's answer there is a bare `42601 syntax error at or near "("` — `json` is a
  `COL_NAME_KEYWORD` (`kwlist.h`) whose type production takes no `opt_type_modifiers`,
  so 18.6's refusal takes the *shape* the group below has rather than the six above's,
  and giving it the typmod sentence would move it off that shape. It does not join that
  group in **agreeing**, though: what diverges is the **cast** position, where `parse_scalar_type_name`'s `json` arm answers pglet's
  `42704 type "json" is not supported` against that syntax error; at a **column**
  definition `CREATE TABLE jt (a json(3))` is `42601` on both. Both measured.

  **Where it still stops, unchanged.** `1::int(3)`, `::integer(3)`, `::smallint(3)`,
  `::bigint(3)`, `::real(3)`, `::boolean(3)` and `::double precision(3)` are `42601` on
  each engine and must stay so — 18.6's grammar gives those keyword spellings no
  `opt_type_modifiers` production, so its refusal is a bare `syntax error at or near
  "("` and giving them the typmod message would move them off its shape. `'x'::text(3)`,
  `1::jsonb(3)`, `'\x11'::bytea(3)` and a `uuid(3)` cast are `42601` on each too, under
  pglet's own wording, their arms returning before the `(`; over a value that fails its
  own input parse the value error still wins there (`'x'::bytea(3)` is `22023`,
  `'a'::uuid(3)` is `22P02`, each against 18.6's `42601`). The **typed-constant**
  position does not reach the arm **on the default route**: `int4` is not one of
  `is_multiword_type_lead`'s words, so `SELECT int4(3) '1'` falls to the function-call
  path for pglet's own `0A000 function not supported: int4` against 18.6's `42601`
  (`bool(3) 't'` and `date(3) '2020-01-01'` read the same), while the modifier-less
  `SELECT int4 '1'` is `1` on both. **Under `--coerce-unknown-types` it does reach it**,
  at three `is_multiword_type_lead` words whose base pglet does not model and whose
  modifier `passthrough_type` keeps: `bpchar(3) 'ab'`, `bit(3) '1'` and `varbit(3) '1'`
  resolve to `text` under the flag and are this `42601` against 18.6's `ab `, `100` and
  `1` (measured). `timetz` is the fourth unmodelled word of that list, and it **joined** them when row
  123 moved the temporal precisions off the reader that discarded a modifier: the canonical name now keeps the
  `(3)`, so under the flag `timetz(3) '01:02:03'`, `'01:02:03'::timetz(3)` and
  `time(3) with time zone '01:02:03'` are each this `42601` against 18.6's
  `01:02:03+00`, where the discarded modifier used to let the flag answer `01:02:03` as
  text (measured, both engines, before and after). The modifier-less
  `timetz '01:02:03'` still answers `01:02:03` under the flag. All of it is the coerce
  fork's own divergence, argued in `planner::unknown_types`'s module doc. Two positions do not resolve a declared type at
  all, so the gate is unreachable there rather than outranked:
  `CREATE`/`ALTER SEQUENCE … AS <type>` and a column identity clause's
  `( AS <type> )` discard what
  `parse_type_name` returns, so `CREATE SEQUENCE sq1 AS int4(3)`, `… AS varchar(3)` and
  `… AS nosuchtype(3)` are each an accepted `CREATE SEQUENCE` here against 18.6's
  `42601` / `22023` / `42704`, and each of five identity `( AS <type> )` spellings
  measured is accepted here against 18.6's blanket
  `42601 conflicting or redundant options` — each measured on both engines, and the
  dropped `AS` clause's divergence (row 260) rather than this row's.
  `'ab'::varchar(1)` is `a` and `1.234::numeric(4,1)`
  is `1.2` on each engine — two modifiers those types do carry, honoured as before — and
  `FLOAT(n)` is row 116's, a modifier 18.6 **accepts** and reads as a *type selector*,
  so it never reaches this gate: `float(1)` resolves as `real` and `float8(1)` — the
  spelling that names the type — is this `42601`.

  **What guards it.** Ten `types/typmod_not_allowed_*` fixtures — the `::` and
  `CAST(… AS …)` forms, the two-part modifier, `date`, `float8`, a column definition,
  `ADD COLUMN`, `serial`, an enum, and the value-error precedence — each carrying
  `@expect-message`, so the sentence is locked and not only the SQLSTATE. The **order**
  has four of its own: `types/typmod_add_column_loses_to_column_exists.sql` and
  `types/typmod_add_column_loses_to_missing_table.sql` pin the two `ADD COLUMN` refusals
  (`@expect-message` too), `types/typmod_add_column_if_not_exists_skips.sql` pins the
  skip as a *value* fixture — a regression raises inside its `@setup` and reddens —
  and `types/typmod_create_table_if_not_exists_skips.sql` pins the polarity on the other
  statement, which nothing else in the corpus spelled.
  Beside them `crates/pglet/tests/typmod_decomposition.rs` holds the position list,
  the polarity controls and the `--coerce-unknown-types` decision, and `pglet_core`'s
  `membership_matches_pg_type_typmodin` pins the list above. The residuals are pinned by
  nothing: the surviving cast-position pair needs a fix, not a fixture, and the
  unmodelled types would be red under the rule that a shared error must share its
  SQLSTATE.

- **~~120~~ · Closed — A modifier the canonical type name keeps cancels the `[]` beside it.**
  A `[]` now makes the modifier the **element's** rather than a reason to
  lose either the modifier or the array. `executor::type_resolution`'s
  `decompose_type_name` is the one split — the `[]` comes off first, then the `(` — and
  the modifier is judged and captured at the element's width, which is 18.6's own shape:
  `LookupTypeName` resolves `varchar(3)[]` to `_varchar` before `typenameTypeMod` reads
  the modifier, and `_varchar.typmodin` is `varchartypmodin` (measured, as `_int4`'s is
  0). The old reader split on `(` first, so the `[]` rode away inside the discarded tail
  and the name resolved to the **scalar** element, with `parse_length_typmod` /
  `parse_numeric_typmod` then declining the `)[]`-terminated string too — the cap lost
  with the array. Measured on both engines, after the fix:

  | read position — the `::` and `CAST(… AS …)` spellings answered alike at each member | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT '{abcdefg,xy}'::varchar(3)[]`, and `::character varying(3)[]` | `{abc,xy}` | `{abc,xy}` |
  | `SELECT '{1.25,2.5}'::numeric(4,1)[]`, and the `decimal` / `dec` spellings | `{1.3,2.5}` | `{1.3,2.5}` |
  | `SELECT '{1 day}'::interval(3)[]` | `{"1 day"}` | `{"1 day"}` |
  | `SELECT '{abcdefg,xy}'::char[]` — the element's default `char(1)` survives the `[]` | `{a,x}` | `{a,x}` |
  | `SELECT 1::int4(3)[]`, `'{1}'::int2(3)[]`, `'{1.5}'::float8(3)[]`, `'{t}'::bool(3)[]`, `'{2020-01-01}'::date(3)[]` | `42601 … for type "int4[]"` and so on | the same code, the same sentence |
  | `SELECT ARRAY[1]::int4(3)[]`, `ARRAY[true]::bool(3)[]` | the same `42601` | the same |
  | `SELECT 1::numeric(4,1)[]` | `42846 cannot cast type integer to numeric[]` | the same |
  | `SELECT 'ok'::moodg(3)[]`, live enum | `42601 … for type "moodg[]"` | the same |

  | column position — a column definition and `ADD COLUMN` answered alike at each member | pglet `information_schema` | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `a varchar(3)[]` | `ARRAY`, udt `_varchar`, `character_maximum_length` NULL | the same |
  | `a numeric(4,1)[]` | `ARRAY`, udt `_numeric`, `numeric_precision`/`_scale` NULL | the same |
  | `a interval(3)[]` | `ARRAY`, udt `_interval` | the same |
  | `a bool(3)[]`, `a int4(3)[]`, `a date(3)[]` | `42601 … for type "bool[]"` and so on | the same |

  **The catalog reports the column and the cap rides on `atttypmod`.**
  `information_schema.columns.character_maximum_length` answers NULL for an array column
  even though the column has a cap, because the view describes the column's type and no
  array type has a character length — the fact 18.6 sends is
  `pg_attribute.atttypmod`, and pglet's is now `7` for a `varchar(3)[]` column, the same
  value the scalar `varchar(3)` beside it reports and the same 18.6 sends. That reader
  is a **member** of this row rather than a downstream effect: it reads the very field
  the modifier is captured into, and left ungated it would have reported the element's
  length where 18.6 reports NULL.

  **And it wrote.** The four writes the swallow allowed are each 18.6's answer now,
  measured on both engines over `va (a varchar(3)[])`, `nu (a numeric(4,1)[])` and
  `iv (a interval(3)[])` with fresh state per row:

  | write | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `INSERT INTO va VALUES ('{abcdefg,xy}')` | `22001 value too long for type character varying(3)` | the same |
  | `INSERT INTO nu VALUES (1.25)` | `42804 column "a" is of type numeric[] but expression is of type numeric` | the same |
  | `INSERT INTO nu VALUES ('{1.25,2.5}')` | `INSERT 0 1`, reads back `{1.3,2.5}` | the same |
  | `INSERT INTO iv VALUES ('{1 day}')` | `INSERT 0 1`, reads back `{"1 day"}` | the same |

  Enforcement is **element-wise and context-aware**, one `executor::coerce::apply_typmod`
  reached from the store finalizer (`is_explicit = false`, so a non-blank over-run is
  `22001`) and from `Expr::CastTypmod` (`is_explicit = true`, so the cast truncates) —
  18.6's `ArrayCoerceExpr`, which runs the element cast per element.

  **What is left under this number belongs to other rows.** `'{abcdefg,xy}'::char(3)[]`
  is `{abc,xy}` here against `{abc,"xy "}` there, and a `char(3)[]` column's udt is
  `_varchar` against `_bpchar` — pglet folds `char` onto `TypeOid::Varchar` and models no
  bpchar blank-padding, row 95's divergence, which is why the guard for the bare
  `char[]` spelling uses values the padding cannot reach. `'{1.23456 secs}'::interval(3)[]` was
  `{00:00:01.23456}` here against `{00:00:01.235}` there — an interval's precision
  discarded rather than applied, in the scalar position as much as under the `[]`, which
  is the third arm of the decompose rule; it is **row 123**, and closed.
  `serial(3)[]` is `42601` here against 18.6's
  `0A000 array of serial is not implemented`: 18.6 refuses an array of serial before it
  reads any modifier, and the modifier-less `serial[]` builds an `ARRAY` / `_int4` column
  here against that same `0A000` there (measured; row 177), so what diverges is that gap and not
  the modifier. A modifier-less `moodg[]` stays
  `42704` here against an accepted column there — pglet models no array of enum — while
  `moodg(3)[]` agrees, the base being an enum the catalog holds. And a **bare scalar
  assigned to an array column** is the array reader's `22P02` on both for the
  text-shaped cases (`'abcdefg'` into a `varchar(3)[]`, `'1 day'` into an
  `interval(3)[]`), as over a plain `varchar[]` / `interval[]` column with no modifier
  anywhere. The numeric-shaped case is `42804` on both.

  **The discard-the-modifier arm was never a member.** When this row closed, `timestamp`,
  `timestamptz`, `time`, `timetz` and `float` all discarded the modifier in the parser,
  so `timestamp(3)[]` reached `type_name_to_oid` as `timestamp[]` and built the array
  both engines build, before that fix and after it. Row 123 has since moved the four
  temporal spellings onto the kept-modifier path — `timestamp(3)[]` now decomposes here
  exactly as `varchar(3)[]` does, and enforces element-wise — and row 116 moved `float`,
  the last one, onto a third path: its modifier *selects* the type, so `float(1)[]` is
  `real[]` here as there and no modifier survives the decomposition at all.
  `timetz(3)[]` is
  `42704 type "time with time zone" is not supported` here against 18.6's `ARRAY` —
  `TIMETZ`'s standing gap, which the `(3)` and the `[]` only ride on, and the
  modifier-less `timetz[]` answers the same way.

  **The arms that read no `(` at all** reach neither this row nor row 119's: `int`,
  `integer`, `smallint`, `bigint`, `real`, `boolean`, `json`, `double precision`, `text`,
  `bytea`, `jsonb` and `uuid` leave the `(` for the caller, so at a **column definition**
  each is pglet's `42601 syntax error … found '('` against 18.6's own `42601` —
  `syntax error at or near "("` at `int`, `integer`, `smallint`, `bigint`, `real`,
  `boolean`, `json` and `double precision`, and
  `type modifier is not allowed for type "…[]"` at `text`, `bytea`, `jsonb` and `uuid`.
  At the **cast** position two of them answer elsewhere, both still loud, and each under
  a rule already written down: `SELECT '{}'::json(3)[]` is pglet's
  `42704 type "json" is not supported`, the position split `parse_scalar_type_name`'s
  `json` arm states, against 18.6's `42601`; `SELECT 'x'::bytea(3)[]` is `42601` on
  both, pglet's the syntax error at the `(`.

  **The readers — and the one the first derivation missed.**
  `resolve_type_name`'s call sites outside its own module, through its two entry points,
  are `executor::ddl`'s `execute_create_table` and `execute_alter_table_add_column` and
  `parser::expr`'s `resolve_type_with_typmod` (which serves the `::` and `CAST(… AS …)`
  positions alike), all through `resolve_column_type`, and `typed_constant_from`, through
  `resolve_constant_type`. The two tables above drive the two DDL sites and
  `resolve_type_with_typmod`. `typed_constant_from` cannot spell an array at all —
  `parse_scalar_type_name` consumes no `[]` — so
  `SELECT varchar(3)[] '{abcdefg,xy}'` is pglet's own
  `0A000 function not supported: varchar` (the row 121 shape) against 18.6's
  `42601 syntax error at or near "["`, loud on each; 18.6's own
  `doc/src/sgml/syntax.sgml`, § Constants of Other Types, says the `type 'string'` form
  does not work for array types. Beyond those four, the captured modifier itself has
  **six** readers: `ResolvedColumnType::typmod` (which routes the cast into
  `Expr::CastTypmod`), `information_schema.columns`, `Column::pg_type_modifier` (the
  `atttypmod` and the `RowDescription`'s `type_modifier`), `dump`'s `column_type_sql`,
  the store finalizer, and `deparse`'s `render_cast` — via `cast_type_spelling`, the
  one type-with-modifier renderer the four Catalog surfaces and the dump's expression
  text share. Three needed code the first time — the catalog width gated on the scalar
  type, the dump's suffix, the finalizer's variant guards dropped — and `render_cast`
  needed it too and was **missed**, because the list was derived by grepping
  `numeric_typmod` / `varchar_length` and that reader touches neither: it reads the
  `Typmod` the first of the six built. It printed **two** wrong spellings, one per
  `RenderMode`: `varchar[](3)` at the four dump statement kinds, the dump rendering in
  `Portable` whose name function is `type_oid_sql`, and `character varying[](3)` at the
  five catalog positions, which take `catalog_type_name` — SQL neither engine re-parses
  either way, `42601` on each (measured) — until the
  suffix rule reached it. *Re-derive a reader list by the thing itself, not by the field
  the first hop happened to use.* The two that needed no code answer differently anyway,
  because the field they read now holds the element's modifier for an array column;
  each of those two was measured rather than assumed.

  **What guards it.** Eleven `array/typmod_*` fixtures — the four cast members, the
  refused group, the scalar-into-array cast, the two column stores, the
  scalar-assignment refusal, the catalog shape and the `atttypmod` — plus
  `array/plain_no_typmod_unaffected.sql` as the polarity control. Three more cover the
  **Catalog rendering**, the position the first pass shipped broken and had no fixture
  at: `array/typmod_catalog_render_constraintdef.sql` (`pg_get_constraintdef` and
  `information_schema.check_constraints.check_clause` together),
  `array/typmod_catalog_render_column_default.sql`, and
  `array/typmod_catalog_render_index_predicate.sql` — the index *key* position is
  deliberately absent, 18.6 eliding a no-op typmod cast there that pglet keeps, at the
  scalar spelling as much as the array one. The Portable half is
  `dump::render_expr_round_trips_to_the_identical_variant`, over two new
  `ROUND_TRIP_CORPUS` lines; what *requires* those lines is
  `round_trip_corpus_covers_every_renderable_form`, whose discriminant (`expr_node`)
  now splits `CastTypmod` on array-ness, so a scalar corpus line can no longer stand in
  for an array render arm. Measured on the pre-fix shape: with array-ness out of the
  key, the renderer bug left **both** tests green. `crates/pglet/tests/typmod_decomposition.rs` holds what a fixture cannot: the
  dump renders `varchar(3)[]` with the modifier inside the suffix and **reloads** to a
  column that is still an array and still caps its elements (rendering it at the
  column's width would emit a scalar `varchar(3)`, valid SQL that reloads a different
  table), and the cap survives a double-meta store reopen.

- **~~123~~ · Closed — A modifier the type does carry is kept, clamped and enforced.**
  This is the third arm of the decompose rule rows 119 and 120 opened
  (`docs/coercion.md` § A canonical type name decomposes once): a `(…)` on a type that
  carries none is refused (119), a `[]` makes the modifier the element's (120), and a
  modifier the type *does* carry is now applied rather than thrown away — through
  `executor::coerce::apply_typmod`, rounding half away from zero about the value's internal
  zero, at a cast as at a write (`'…05.6789'::timestamp(3)` kept four fractional digits
  before). Six types carry
  one; `varchar`/`char` and `numeric` were already enforced, and the four with a
  **sub-second precision** were not — `timestamp`, `timestamptz` and `time` had it
  discarded in `parser::type_name` before the resolver ever saw it, and
  `interval` carried it into the canonical name and lost it at a resolver that captured
  only `numeric` and `varchar` widths.

  **It wrote**, at every write path, over
  `t (id int PRIMARY KEY, a timestamp(3), b time(3), c interval(3), d timestamptz(3))`
  with fresh state per row. Each line measured on both engines before the fix and again
  after it; the "now" column is byte-identical to 18.6's on every one:

  | write | was | 18.6, and now | 
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `INSERT` of `'2020-01-02 03:04:05.6789'` / `'03:04:05.6789'` / `'1.23456 secs'` | stored **whole** | `…05.679` · `03:04:05.679` · `00:00:01.235` |
  | `UPDATE t SET a = '1999-12-31 23:59:59.9995'` | `…59.9995` | `…59.999` |
  | `COPY t FROM STDIN` (text) and `COPY t TO STDOUT` | whole | rounded on both sides |
  | `ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET a = EXCLUDED.a` with `'…05.9999'` | `…05.9999` | `2020-01-02 03:04:06` |
  | `ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN e timestamp(3) DEFAULT '…05.6789'` (back-fill) | whole | `…05.679` |
  | `CREATE TABLE u (a timestamp(3) DEFAULT '…05.6789')` + `INSERT … DEFAULT VALUES` | whole | `…05.679` |
  | `INSERT … RETURNING a` | whole | `…05.679` |
  | a bound `$1` `timestamptz` over the extended protocol | whole | rounded |

  So the column kept a precision its declared type does not have, and every later read
  of it was that value — row 116's own words for the `FLOAT(n)` sibling, which is **not**
  a member and closed by a different rule: `float`'s modifier *selects* the type rather
  than being one the type carries, so it is spent on the decision rather than applied.

  **Two Rust guards stand behind that write and behind the array encoding**, because the
  Rust suite reached neither: deleting `coerce_column_value`'s store-time rounding block,
  or making `Column::pg_type_modifier` read the column's own OID where it reads the
  element's, each left `cargo test` over `pglet`, `pglet_sql`, `pglet_core` and
  `pglet_storage` green — measured with these two guards skipped, against the `varchar`
  equivalent whose deletion reddens two tests in that same file.
  `crates/pglet/tests/typmod_decomposition.rs` now holds a store-and-reopen guard beside
  the `varchar` one it is modelled on, and an `atttypmod` guard whose `interval(3)[]`
  column is the one position that element derivation decides; each was watched go red
  under its own mutation and green again after it. The differential harness caught both
  all along, measured: the first reddens **eight** `precision_*` fixtures in
  `test:fixtures` and both `copy/` ones in `test:copy`; the second reddens
  `catalog/precision_atttypmod.sql` and the dump round-trip's `atttypmod` probe. So what
  moved is what `test:rust` can see.

  `pglet_core::types::precision`'s own rounding tests sit under those, and the fixture
  side is stated as the `precision_*` prefix rather than as a count and a directory
  list, which rot without reddening anything.

  **The read positions moved with them**, each measured on both engines and each now
  agreeing: `'…05.6789'::timestamp(3)` / `::timestamptz(3)` / `::time(3)` /
  `'1.23456 secs'::interval(3)`, the `CAST(… AS …)` spelling of each, the typed constants
  `timestamp(3) '…'` / `timestamptz(3) '…'` / `time(3) '…'`, the two-word
  `::timestamp(3) without time zone` / `with time zone`, the array spellings
  `'{…}'::timestamp(3)[]` / `::interval(3)[]` / `::time(3)[]`, `interval(0)` over
  `'1 day 1.5 secs'`, and `timestamp(0)` over `…05.6789` / `…05.5` / `…05.4999999`.

  **The rounding rule is 18.6's `Adjust*ForTypmod`, and the trap is its sign.**
  `AdjustTimestampForTypmod` (`timestamp.c`), `AdjustTimeForTypmod` (`date.c`) and
  `AdjustIntervalForTypmod`'s sub-second half add half a scale and truncate toward zero,
  branching on the value's **internal** representation — microseconds since
  **2000-01-01** for a timestamp, since midnight for a `time`, the `micros` field for an
  interval. pglet has that arithmetic once
  (`pglet_core::types::round_micros_to_precision`) with one wrapper per carrier.
  Measured on 18.6, and the third column is what a naive half-up on the wall-clock
  fraction would have given:

  | statement | 18.6, and now pglet | a naive half-up |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `'1999-12-31 23:59:59.9995'::timestamp(3)` | `1999-12-31 23:59:59.999` | `2000-01-01 00:00:00` |
  | `'2000-01-01 00:00:00.0005'::timestamp(3)` | `2000-01-01 00:00:00.001` | same |
  | `'1969-07-20 20:17:40.0005'::timestamp(3)` | `1969-07-20 20:17:40` | `…40.001` |
  | `'1999-12-31 23:59:59.9995'::timestamptz(3)` | `1999-12-31 23:59:59.999+00` | `2000-01-01 …` |

  Ties go **away from zero**, not to even — `'00:00:00.0005'::time(3)` is `.001`,
  `.0015` is `.002`, `.0025` is `.003` (half-to-even would give `.002`), and
  `'-0.0005 secs'::interval(3)` is `-00:00:00.001` with `-0.0015` at `-00:00:00.002`.
  An **interval** rounds only its `micros`: months and days are a *range* spec's
  business, so `'1 day 1.5 secs'::interval(0)` is `1 day 00:00:02` on both. A `time`
  carry is **not** wrapped — `'23:59:59.9999'::time(3)` is `24:00:00` on both.

  **Three decisions are the type's, not the spelling's**, and each was a place the
  modifier could still have been lost. The **clamp**: `p > 6` records as `6`, which is
  what `anytimestamp_typmodin` does — 18.6 warns and accepts, and `timestamp(9)` /
  `timestamp(2147483647)` both land on `atttypmod = 6` and `datetime_precision = 6`
  (measured). `6` is therefore a **captured** modifier whose rounding is a no-op, not the
  `None` a bare `timestamp` carries, whose `atttypmod` is `-1`. The **grammar** is a
  single `Iconst` (`TIMESTAMP '(' Iconst ')' opt_timezone`,
  `ConstInterval '(' Iconst ')'`), so `timestamp(3,1)`, `timestamp(3.5)`,
  `timestamp(-1)`, `timestamp(99999999999999)` and their four `interval` spellings are
  `42601` on both engines. **All but `timestamp(-1)`** were accepted-and-discarded here
  before, measured before the repair at all eight: `interval`'s four rode
  `passthrough_type`'s comma list, which took a sign and a decimal point as readily as a
  comma, and `timestamp`'s other three rode a reader that validated a number and
  then discarded it — the same one `float` used, and the last arm to lose it (row 116). `timestamp(-1)` alone was already `42601`, its reader taking an
  *unsigned* number. The messages differ — pglet names the token where 18.6 points at
  it — but `@expect-error` compares the SQLSTATE. And the
  **canonical spelling carries the precision last**: `decompose_type_name` cuts on the
  first `(`, so 18.6's own mid-name `time(3) with time zone` would decompose to base
  `time` and build a `time(3)` column out of a type this engine refuses. It is spelled
  `time with time zone(3)`, and `timetz(3)`, `timetz`, `time(3) with time zone` and
  `time with time zone` are one `42704 type "time with time zone" is not supported`
  (all four measured, against four accepted `timetz` values there — `TIMETZ`'s standing
  gap, which the `(3)` only rides on).

  **The catalog reports three different facts about the same modifier.**
  `pg_attribute.atttypmod` is the bare `p` for `timestamp`/`timestamptz`/`time` and
  `(INTERVAL_FULL_RANGE << 16) | p` for `interval`, whose typmod packs a range mask
  beside the precision — measured over a fourteen-column table, both engines answering
  `3 · 2 · 1 · 2147418116 · -1 · -1 · -1 · 9 · 262149 · 3 · 2147418115 · 6 · -1 · -1`
  across `timestamp(3)`, `timestamptz(2)`, `time(1)`, `interval(4)`, bare `timestamp`,
  `date`, `int`, `varchar(5)`, `numeric(4,1)`, `timestamp(3)[]`, `interval(3)[]`,
  `timestamp(9)`, bare `time` and bare `interval`. The array columns report the
  **element's**, on the same terms row 120's `varchar(3)[]` reports `7`.
  `information_schema.columns.datetime_precision` is the second fact and a **different
  one**: it describes the *type*, so a bare `timestamp` is `6` where its `atttypmod` is
  `-1`, a `date` is `0` though it carries no modifier at all, and an array column is
  **NULL** — the same split `character_maximum_length` takes, and the reason this reader
  gates on the scalar `TypeOid` rather than on the field being set. pglet had no
  `datetime_precision` column at all before (`column "datetime_precision" does not
  exist`). The third is the **wire**: `RowDescription.type_modifier` for a *column* now
  carries exactly the `atttypmod` above, at each of those fourteen columns — the same
  values in the same order on both engines, read off the `RowDescription` field itself —
  so this paragraph holds one vector rather than a second to keep in step with it. For an
  **expression** both engines still disagree and always did: `a::timestamp(3)`,
  `'ab'::varchar(3)` and `1.5::numeric(4,1)` send `-1 · -1 · -1` here against 18.6's
  `3 · 7 · 262149`, which is `docs/declared_types.md`'s limit.
