  **The dump carries it**, and the instrument that proves so is a write rather than a
  read. `pglet::dump`'s `column_type_sql` emits `timestamp(3)` / `timestamptz(2)` /
  `time(1)` / `interval(4)` and the `timestamp(3)[]` / `interval(3)[]` spellings — a form
  stock 18.6 also accepts — where it emitted the bare name before, silently dropping the
  rounding a restore should re-apply. A dump of a nine-column table plus rows loads under
  `ON_ERROR_STOP=1` into stock 18.6 **and** back into pglet with identical
  `data_type` / `udt_name` / `datetime_precision` and identical rows. The rows alone
  cannot see the defect: the source's values are **already rounded**, so a dump that lost
  the `(p)` restores every one of them byte-identically — which is why `test_dump`'s
  probe inserts a fresh four-fractional-digit literal through the *restored* catalog and
  reads it back, and why mutating `column_type_sql` to drop the precision reddens both
  restore legs on exactly that line (the harness reports the first differing select per
  leg, so what the mutation shows is which line fails first, not that no other would).
  **A write probe is still not enough for one pair**: a `p = 6` rounding is the identity,
  so a mutation dropping the precision *only* at `p == 6` writes the same microseconds
  and reads back the same `datetime_precision` (`6` for a bare `timestamp` too) — it left
  `test_dump` and `cargo test` green, measured. `pg_attribute.atttypmod` (`-1` against
  `6`) is the one observable that separates the pair, so the round-trip reads it too, and
  that mutation now reddens both legs. On the `pg_dump` side the same blindness
  has a different remedy: pg_dump's `COPY` data is already rounded too, so that
  round-trip compares `datetime_precision` as well as the rows, and its `CREATE TABLE`
  is where 18.6's **mid-name** spelling (`ts timestamp(3) without time zone`) arrives as
  SQL pglet has to read back.

  **The residual is a rounding overflow, and it is loud.**
  `'9999-12-31 23:59:59.9999'::timestamp(3)` carries into year 10000, which 18.6
  represents (`10000-01-01 00:00:00`) and pglet's `OffsetDateTime` does not
  (`'10000-01-01'::timestamp` is already an error here). It raises
  `22008 timestamp out of range` — `ERRCODE_DATETIME_VALUE_OUT_OF_RANGE`, the code 18.6
  itself spends when a timestamp leaves its range — rather than silently keeping the
  unrounded value. Pglet-stricter, so `types/precision_rounding_overflow_loud.sql` holds
  it as an `@expect-error` 18.6 accepts.

  **What the fix widened is a *rendering*, and it is `render_cast`'s.** 18.6's
  `coerce_type` drops a cast whose type **and** typmod both match the operand's;
  `render_cast` keeps every typmod'd cast. Before this row's fix a temporal cast carried
  no typmod, so `a::timestamp(3)` over an `a timestamp(3)` column was elided on **both**
  engines; now pglet prints `((a)::timestamp(3) without time zone = a)` where 18.6 prints
  `(a = a)`, and `btree (((a)::timestamp(3) without time zone))` where 18.6 prints
  `btree (a)` — measured on both engines at `pg_get_constraintdef`, `check_clause` and
  `indexdef`'s key and predicate. The same change moved four spellings the other way: a
  cast whose `p` differs from the column's (`a::timestamp(6)`, `b::timestamptz(1)`,
  `c::time(1)`, `d::interval(1)`) is a node 18.6 keeps, and each now prints
  byte-identically where **all four** were elided before, which is what
  `catalog/precision_catalog_render_constraintdef.sql` locks. The mirror is unchanged and
  pre-existing: `a::timestamp` over an `a timestamp(3)` column is elided here and kept
  there. This is row 120's own bullet's "no-op typmod cast" residual reaching two more
  type families; closing it needs the **operand's** typmod, which `LeafScope` does not
  carry, and it is deliberately out of scope.

  **Two neighbours measured while closing this and left open.** A `DEFAULT` literal's
  *recording* diverges, and what decides it is **which of two things gets rendered**:
  18.6's `pg_get_expr` prints the coerced `Const`'s **value**, through the type's output
  function, where pglet prints the **literal as written** — for the types pglet prints
  verbatim, which is row 93's rule and its scope. Within that bucket the two can coincide
  only where pglet's source text is already what that output function produces — an
  agreement that is the *literal's* property and not the engine's — and that condition is
  necessary rather than sufficient: an **`interval(p)`** column's **label** diverges on
  top of it (`'00:00:01.235'::interval` here against `'00:00:01.235'::interval(3)` there,
  measured with the literal already spelled in output form). That exception is the
  *modifier*'s and not the type's — a **bare** `interval` column agrees outright at the
  same literal and at `'1 day 02:03:04'`, both reading `'…'::interval` on each engine —
  for the `INTERVALOID` reason stated below. It is **not** a rule about all types:
  `deparse::render_catalog_string_const` reproduces the output function itself for
  `bool`, `int2`, `int4`, `int8` and `numeric`, so `bool DEFAULT 'yes'` / `'on'` / `'1'` /
  `'TRUE'` / `'t'`, `int DEFAULT '007'` / `'+7'`, `smallint DEFAULT '007'` and
  `numeric DEFAULT '+1.5'` / `'0001.5'` each agree on both engines from a source text that
  is nothing like the output form — ten measured lines, against the verbatim-bucket
  control `date DEFAULT '2020-1-2'`, which reads `'2020-1-2'::date` here and
  `'2020-01-02'::date` there. (18.6's `bool` arm is not `boolout` either: `get_const_expr`
  special-cases `BOOLOID` to `true`/`false` where `boolout` gives `t`.) Over the
  four canonical spellings — `a timestamp(3) DEFAULT '2020-01-02 03:04:05.6789'`,
  `b timestamptz(3)` with the same literal, `c time(3) DEFAULT '03:04:05.6789'`,
  `d interval(3) DEFAULT '1.23456 secs'` — `information_schema.columns.column_default`
  agrees at **two**: `a` and `c` read their own text back on both engines; `b` reads
  `'2020-01-02 03:04:05.6789+00'::timestamp with time zone` on 18.6 against pglet's
  offsetless string, because `timestamptz_out` appends the offset a bare spelling omits;
  and `d` diverges on **two** axes, because `coerce_type` passes the typmod to the input
  function for `INTERVALOID` alone (`parse_coerce.c` says so in as many words), so 18.6
  records `'00:00:01.235'::interval(3)` against `'1.23456 secs'::interval` here —
  divergent in the value **and** in the label.

  **`a` and `c` are not safe there, they are lucky.** Respell either literal in any other
  form both engines accept and it diverges too, measured: `timestamp(3) DEFAULT
  '2020-01-02T03:04:05.6789'` and `DEFAULT '2020-01-02 03:04:05.6789+00'` each read the
  plain `'2020-01-02 03:04:05.6789'::timestamp without time zone` on 18.6, against the
  `T` and the `+00` kept verbatim here, and `time(3) DEFAULT '3:4:5.6789'` reads
  `'03:04:05.6789'` there against `'3:4:5.6789'` here. It runs the other way too:
  `timestamptz(3) DEFAULT '2020-01-02 03:04:05.6789+00'` — the literal spelled *in* the
  output form — agrees byte for byte, which is the spelling
  `information_schema/precision_column_default_literal.sql` carries so that its
  `timestamptz` column can stand beside its `timestamp` and `time` ones rather than being
  omitted for being red. Every line above was re-measured and is
  pre-existing, unchanged by this row: the *stored* value rounds either way, which
  `ddl/precision_default_values_insert.sql` pins. pglet's **array text encoder** dropped a
  `timestamptz` element's `+00` offset — `'{2020-01-02 03:04:05.6}'::timestamptz[]` was
  `{"2020-01-02 03:04:05.6"}` here against `{"2020-01-02 03:04:05.6+00"}` there, with the
  scalar column agreeing, which made it the column-type-aware text encoder not reaching an
  array's elements and not this row's. It reaches them now, at the declared element type
  (`docs/temporal.md` § `timestamptz` text encoding).

- **~~124~~ · Closed — A modifier the type itself refuses.** `typenameTypeMod` refuses on its own
  account and then **delegates**: row 119's `42601` when `typmodin == InvalidOid`, and
  otherwise a *call* to the typmodin, which can refuse the value it is handed. pglet had
  only the first. Calling that pair "two refusals" understates it: 18.6's own half has a
  further reachable arm, `type modifiers must be simple constants or identifiers`, which a
  signed or computed component earns (`1.5::numeric(+5)` is that message there —
  `LOCATION: typenameTypeMod, parse_type.c:407`, measured — against pglet's
  `42601 expected a number, found number`, and `numeric(+5) '1'` is it against pglet's
  `0A000`). The delegation is the shape; a total is not part of the rule.
  `parse_length_typmod` and `parse_numeric_typmod` each answered `None` for a modifier
  they declined, and `resolve_type_name` read that `None` as **no cap** — so the type
  resolved unconstrained where 18.6 refuses the spelling outright. Both readers now return
  a `Result`, and the `Option` that means *no modifier was spelled* is
  `TypeNameParts::modifier`, a different one a hop earlier.

  **The class is the `(…)`'s, not `char`'s**, and bounding it to a character length is how
  it stayed open through row 119's and row 120's closes: the `numeric` modifier is the same
  site, the same silence and the same mechanism, and it carries members no length can reach.
  The members, by the layer that decides each — the pglet column measured on a pre-close
  build, the 18.6 column on the live instance, cell by cell:

  | spelling | pglet was | 18.6 | layer |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | `'ab'::char(0)`, `character(0)`, and the column/`ADD COLUMN`/typed-constant spellings | `ab` | `22023 length for type char must be at least 1` | `anychar_typmodin` |
  | `'ab'::varchar(0)`, `character varying(0)` | `ab` | `22023 length for type varchar must be at least 1` | `anychar_typmodin` |
  | `'ab'::char(10485761)`, `char(20000000)`, `varchar(10485761)` | `ab` | `22023 length for type {char,varchar} cannot exceed 10485760` | `anychar_typmodin` |
  | `'{ab}'::char(0)[]` | `{ab}` | the element's `22023`, naming `char` | `anychar_typmodin` |
  | `'abcd'::char(3.5)` | `abcd` | `42601 syntax error at or near "3.5"` | the grammar's `Iconst` |
  | `'abcd'::char(2147483648)`, `char(99999999999999999999)` | `abcd` | `42601`, naming the number | the grammar's `Iconst` |
  | `1.5::numeric(0)`, `decimal(0)`, `numeric(-1)`, `numeric(1001)`, `numeric(2147483647)` | `1.5` | `22023 NUMERIC precision <p> must be between 1 and 1000` | `numerictypmodin`'s `make_numeric_typmod_safe` |
  | `1.5::numeric(5,1001)` | a coincidental `22003 numeric out of range` | `22023 NUMERIC scale 1001 must be between -1000 and 1000` | `numerictypmodin`'s `make_numeric_typmod_safe` |
  | `1.5::numeric(5,-1001)` | `0` | `22023 NUMERIC scale -1001 must be between -1000 and 1000` | `numerictypmodin`'s `make_numeric_typmod_safe` |
  | `1.5::numeric(5,2,3)`, `numeric(5,2,3,4)` | `1.50` — the surplus components dropped and the second **applied** | `22023 invalid NUMERIC type modifier` | `numerictypmodin`'s arity count |
  | `1.5::numeric(2147483648)`, `numeric(5,2147483648)` | `1.5` | `22003 value "2147483648" is out of range for type integer` | `ArrayGetIntegerTypmods` |
  | `1.5::numeric(1.5)`, `numeric(5,1.5)` | `1.5` | `22P02 invalid input syntax for type integer: "1.5"` | `ArrayGetIntegerTypmods` |

  **The positions.** The class holds at `::` and at the `CAST(… AS …)` spelling of it, at a
  column definition, at `ADD COLUMN`, under a `[]`, and inside a persisted expression; the
  typed constant is a position too, and its own verdict is the restored-cursor split below.

  **It wrote.** `CREATE TABLE q (c CHAR(0)); INSERT INTO q VALUES ('abcdef')` reported
  `INSERT 0 1` and `SELECT c, length(c) FROM q` answered `abcdef|6`, where 18.6 has no
  table to insert into; `ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN c CHAR(0)` landed the same column on an
  existing table. And the arity member wrote a **value**: `1.5::numeric(5,2,3)` rounded to
  `1.50` under a scale that exists only because a spelling 18.6 refuses as a whole was
  half-honoured.

  **Two grammar layers, and the weaker window was the reason a refusal alone would not
  have been enough.** A character length **as the `character` keyword spells it** is
  `CharacterWithLength: character '(' Iconst ')'`
  and an `ICONST` is an unsigned integer that fits `int32`, so at that spelling a
  fractional or out-of-`int32` length is refused *in the grammar* and never reaches a
  type's modifier reader — where the `bpchar` spelling's does reach one, the residual
  below. `parser::type_name` read it through `expect_number_text`, which proves neither —
  so adding the `22023` without moving the window would have answered
  `length for type char must be at least 1` to `char(3.5)`, naming a bound that has nothing
  to do with it. The length window now routes through the one `opt_precision` the
  `ConstDatetime`, `ConstInterval` and `opt_float` windows already used; `numeric` is
  deliberately not one of them (`opt_type_modifiers` is an `expr_list`), which is why that
  family can answer `22003`/`22P02` and can spell a negative precision where
  `char(-1)` is `42601` on both engines. It is the one *carrier*'s window here that reaches
  the coercion, which is a fact about pglet's grammar rather than a uniqueness 18.6 shares —
  the residual below.

  **The order inside one modifier reader is part of the contract**, measured on 18.6 rather
  than inferred — and on the instance it is **one function's**, `numerictypmodin`: the
  arity `22023`'s `LOCATION` is that function (`numeric.c:1365`), and the two range checks'
  is the `make_numeric_typmod_safe` it calls (`numeric.c:1333` the precision, `1338` the
  scale), the same precision line for `numeric(0)` and `numeric(0,1001)` — both arity
  branches share the one check. It coerces every component to `int4` *before* the count
  selects a branch, and the range check tests the precision before the scale; the
  one-component branch has no scale to reach. Three pairs
  separate the steps — `numeric(5,2,1.5)` is the coercion's `22P02` and not the arity's
  `22023`, `numeric(0,1.5)` the coercion's and not the precision's, `numeric(0,1001)` the
  precision's and not the scale's — and a whole-pass reordering keeps every single refusal
  right while answering the wrong one at all three.

  **Where the refusal runs needed no decision**, and that is the argument for the position
  rather than a convenience: it is `resolve_type_name`'s, beside and after row 119's
  `42601`, so it inherits that gate's measured error order rather than earning one.
  `CREATE TABLE`'s left-to-right column walk (`CREATE TABLE g (a char(0), b nosuchtype)` is
  the length's and the mirror is `42704`), ahead of the `42P07` for an existing relation,
  behind the `IF NOT EXISTS` skip; and on `ADD COLUMN` behind the relation lookup, the
  column-existence check and that statement's own skip. Each of those pairs was
  re-measured on both engines for the `22023`, and each carries its own fixture —
  inheriting the order is not inheriting the evidence.

  It inherits the **residual** too: at a cast pglet decides
  the declared type before 18.6 reads the relation, so
  `SELECT 'ab'::char(0) FROM nosuchtbl` is the `22023` here against `42P01` there, which is
  the position `SELECT 'ab'::nosuchtype FROM nosuchtbl` (`42704` against `42P01`) and
  `SELECT 1::int4(3) FROM nosuchtable` (`42601` against `42P01`) already diverge at — a
  cell on row 119's first residual, not a class of its own.

  **Residuals, by whose they are.** Some are another rule's, two are a *message* rather
  than a verdict, and the last this close *moved*. The two
  positions that resolve a type name
  and **discard** it are untouched, the gate being at `typenameTypeMod`'s position:
  `CREATE SEQUENCE s AS varchar(0)` is accepted here against
  `22023 length for type varchar must be at least 1` (which beats even 18.6's own
  `sequence type must be smallint, integer, or bigint`), and an identity column's
  `(AS char(0))` against `42601 conflicting or redundant options` — both measured, both the
  dropped-`AS`-clause divergence, row 260's (row 116 records only its in-range `FLOAT(n)`
  spellings). The `22003`'s **sentence** is pglet's own
  `integer out of range` against 18.6's `value "…" is out of range for type integer` — the
  integer-input path's wording, not this position's. The SQLSTATE agrees *here* and off
  this position it does not: `'2147483648'::int` is `22P02` here against `22003` there,
  `'99999'::int2` and `'9223372036854775808'::int8` the same, all measured. That wider
  class is row 324. The grammar `42601`'s **message** is
  pglet's own, and differs at every spelling measured in this window rather than only where
  the payload does: `char(3.5)`, `char(2147483648)`, `char(99999999999999999999)` and
  `char(0.0)` each answer
  `syntax error: type modifier must be an integer that fits int4, found "…"` here against
  `syntax error at or near "…"` there, and a signed length (`char(-1)`, `char(+3)`, either
  family) answers `expected a number, found number` against 18.6's quoting of the sign —
  all measured. The lexer's *decoded* payload is one difference among those and not the
  whole of it: `'ab'::char(0xFFFFFFFF)` is `found "4294967295"` here against
  `syntax error at or near "0xFFFFFFFF"` there. Same SQLSTATE throughout, and no fixture at
  this window carries `@expect-message`, so nothing gates it — the two message residuals,
  neither of them a verdict.

  **The `expr_list` window is not `numeric`'s alone on 18.6, where pglet reaches it at
  `numeric` alone — so a spelling that bypasses a dedicated `Iconst` production is a
  residual of this row's whole layer table.**
  The `Iconst` productions narrow a *named* set of spellings and
  not a set of types: `GenericType: type_function_name opt_type_modifiers` gives the
  `expr_list` to any type name none of them captures, and `BitWithLength` is a keyword
  production that is an `expr_list` itself. A quoted type name is an `IDENT`, hence a
  `type_function_name`, so by the grammar any carrier has a spelling that reaches the
  coercion — that generalization is the productions' shape rather than a sweep. Measured on
  the oracle, `(1.5)` answering
  `22P02 invalid input syntax for type integer: "1.5"` at each: `bpchar`, `timestamptz`,
  `varbit` unquoted; `"varchar"`, `"bpchar"`, `"timestamp"`, `"time"`, `"timetz"`,
  `"interval"`, `"numeric"` quoted; and `bit varying(1.5)`. `'ab'::bpchar(2147483648)` is
  the `22003` and `'ab'::bpchar(0)` is `anychar_typmodin`'s
  `length for type char must be at least 1` — this row's own verdict at a spelling no
  `Iconst` narrows. pglet answers none of those, by three refusals: `42704` for a type it
  does not model (`bpchar`, `bit`, `varbit`), `42601` for a quoted type name — the rule
  `parser::type_name`'s `expect_type_word` doc carries, that reader taking a bare
  `TokenKind::Identifier` only — and its own `42601` where
  `opt_precision` does read the spelling (`timestamptz(1.5)`, `timetz(1.5)`). Row 119's
  second residual is the `42704`'s other half and cannot hold these three: its pairing is
  pglet's `42704` against 18.6's `42601`, which 18.6 answers only where the type carries no
  typmodin — and `bpchar`, `bit` and `varbit` all carry one where its `name`, `oid`,
  `money`, `regclass`, `xml` and `point` carry none (`pg_type.typmodin`, measured). Loud
  either way, in both directions; closing any of it needs the `pg_type` typname table
  `expect_type_word` already records pglet as lacking. The **rest** of 18.6's carrier ×
  spelling grid is unswept — only the spellings named above were probed, and only at `::`.

  And at a **typed constant** a refused
  number answers a third way, by a **mechanism** rather than at a list of spellings:
  `try_typed_constant` reads a multi-word type name *speculatively* and
  `commits_on_open_paren` is `float` alone, so at every other carrier lead word a `(…)` that
  fails the reader's own window **restores** the speculation and the window falls to the
  function-call path. What answers then is the restored cursor's — `0A000 function not
  supported: <word>` where the lead word is the whole spelling, and a `42601` of `SELECT`'s
  own grammar where it is not. That is the property; the membership follows from it, and it
  is not a property of `char`:

  | typed constant | pglet | 18.6 | in the class because |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | `char(3.5) 'ab'`, `char(2147483648) 'ab'`, `char(99999999999999999999) 'ab'` | `0A000 function not supported: char` | `42601` | **moved in by this close** — the length window became `opt_precision`'s one `Iconst`; all three were a silent `ab` before |
  | the same three spelled `character(…)` / `varchar(…)` | the same, naming `character` / `varchar` | `42601` | the same, the lead word still being the whole spelling |
  | the same three spelled `character varying(…)` | `42601 syntax error: expected ';' or end of input, found '('` | `42601` | the same, except the restored cursor leaves `varying` behind and the statement dies in `SELECT`'s grammar — **the one member whose SQLSTATE agrees** |
  | `char(-1) 'ab'`, `char(5,2) 'ab'`, and those two at each of the other three spellings | the same `0A000` / `42601` split | `42601` | **pre-existing** — `expect_number_text` refused a sign and a comma too |
  | `numeric(+5) '1'` | `0A000 function not supported: numeric` | `42601 type modifiers must be simple constants or identifiers` | **pre-existing** — a **leading `+`** is what `numeric`'s reader refuses (a leading `-` it reads and carries, which is how `numeric(5,-2)` works); its window is otherwise a bare number text the resolver judges |
  | `timestamp(3.5) '…'`, `timestamp(-1) '…'`, `time(3.5) '…'` | the same `0A000`, naming `timestamp` / `time` | `42601` | **pre-existing**, measured on the pre-close binary too — their `(p)` is the same `opt_precision` |

  Three near neighbours are **outside** it, each for its own reason, and they are why the
  bound is the property and not a spelling family. `numeric` / `decimal` / `dec` **agree
  with 18.6's SQLSTATE** at every number shape their reader accepts — `numeric(3.5) '1'` is
  `22P02`, `numeric(2147483648) '1'` `22003`, `numeric(-1) '1'` the `22023`, on both engines
  — so the family most of this close's members come from is the one the restore barely
  reaches. `float` **commits**, so its own verdict survives the window (row 116's close).
  And `interval`'s speculation never starts (`parse_primary_inner` reads its literal ahead
  of the window) while `bit` is `42704` for a type pglet does not model. Widening the commit
  set is row 116's to decide.

  **What pins it.** Every `refused_typmod_*`-prefixed fixture under `types/`, with the
  ordering pairs and the `window_ends` / `window_ends_bpchar` / `window_ends_column`
  polarity fixtures among them; `executor::type_resolution`'s unit tests for the
  per-member verdicts, the internal type name, the window's inclusive ends and the
  non-carrier polarity list; `parser::expr`'s `a_character_length_is_one_iconst`; and
  `crates/pglet/tests/typmod_decomposition.rs` for what no fixture can see — the
  **catalog** a refused `CREATE TABLE` / `ADD COLUMN` must not leave.

  `docs/coercion.md` § A modifier the type refuses carries the rule,
  `docs/parser.md` the `Iconst` window and the typed constant's share,
  `docs/numeric.md` § Known gaps the `numeric` neighbours.


- **121 · A function-style type coercion is not a cast pglet reads.** 18.6 takes
  `typename(expr)` as a third cast spelling beside `::` and `CAST(… AS …)`, and its own
  documentation gives the mechanism: the form "is in fact just a function call" to the
  conversion function `pg_proc` registers under the type's name
  (`doc/src/sgml/syntax.sgml`, § Type Casts). pglet's grammar has no such spelling, so
  the name falls to `planner::expr`'s `build_call`, whose default arm answers
  `0A000 function not supported: <name>`. Measured on both engines, over a table `t`:

  | spelling | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT regclass('t')` | `0A000 function not supported: regclass` | `t` |
  | `SELECT int4(1)` | the same, naming `int4` | `1` |
  | `SELECT text(1)` | the same, naming `text` | `1` |
  | `SELECT int8(1)` | the same, naming `int8` | `1` |
  | `SELECT bool(1)` | the same, naming `bool` | `t` |
  | `SELECT float8(1)` | the same, naming `float8` | `1` |
  | `SELECT date('2020-01-01')` | the same, naming `date` | `2020-01-01` |
  | `SELECT "varchar"('ab')` | the same, naming `varchar` | `ab` |
  | `SELECT "numeric"(1)` | the same, naming `numeric` | `1` |
  | `SELECT varchar('ab')` — unquoted | the same, naming `varchar` | `42601 syntax error at or near "'ab'"` |
  | `SELECT numeric(1)` — unquoted | the same, naming `numeric` | `42601 syntax error`, the token it names being whatever follows the `)` |

  The two **unquoted** rows are 18.6 refusing a spelling of its own, not declining the
  coercion: double-quote the name and it answers each, as the two rows above them record,
  while pglet's `0A000` is the same message quoted and unquoted at every name in the
  table. So `varchar` and `numeric` are two more type names in this class rather than its
  edge, and `pg_proc` on the oracle says so as well: it carries
  `varchar(character varying, integer, boolean)` and `varchar(name)`, and eight `numeric`
  arms including `numeric(integer)`. 18.6's § Type Casts calls the double-quote
  requirement a syntactic conflict and names `interval`, `time` and `timestamp` in that
  paragraph; it does not name these two, which the oracle refuses unquoted all the same.
  Both halves are a fix's, then: answering the double-quoted spelling as the coercion it
  is, and refusing the unquoted one, where 18.6's grammar has already read the name as a
  type. Following that pointer lands elsewhere again and not here: double-quoted, all
  three answer `42883` at an integer argument on the oracle —
  `function interval(integer) does not exist`, and the same naming `time` and
  `timestamp` — against pglet's `0A000` at each, so both engines refuse. All three are in
  `pg_proc` under their own names and none of their arms takes a lone integer, so what is
  missing there is an argument type and not the name.

  **The unquoted `numeric` message is the probe's, not the statement's.** The parse gets
  as far as a complete type name and stops at whatever comes next, so one statement has
  three messages: `SELECT numeric(1)` is `syntax error at end of input`,
  `SELECT numeric(1);` is `at or near ";"`, and `SELECT numeric(1) AS x;` is
  `at or near "AS"`. Quote a message from this member and quote the framing with it.
  `SELECT varchar('ab')` names `'ab'` under all three framings, its argument not being
  the integer the length production takes — `SELECT varchar(3)` is `at end of input` and
  `SELECT varchar(3) AS x;` is `at or near "AS"`, the same shape as `numeric`.

  **Why its own row.** It is not row 45's: that row's members are loud under the *wrong
  code* where 18.6 refuses too, and wherever 18.6 **answers** here the polarity is a
  false refusal rather than a miscoded one; the two unquoted rows, where 18.6 refuses as
  well, are what the paragraph above accounts for. It is not row 85's, by row 85's own
  test — `regclass('t')` would still be refused here if the two engines' `regclass` values
  agreed, since pglet reads the spelling as a function call and `regclass` is not one of
  `build_call`'s names. And it is not row 118's,
  whose subject is the cast *target* the `regclass` intercept reads: a reader triaging
  `int4(1)` would not search a `regclass` row for it. What row 118 carries is the
  pointer, from its neighbouring-spellings table.

  **Nothing guards it, deliberately.** An `@expect-error` fixture over
  `SELECT regclass('t')` would be **green** — 18.6 accepts, so `tests/README.md`'s rule
  lets any pglet error pass — and what it would lock is the over-rejection itself, which
  is the thing to close rather than to pin. Row 118's unpinned neighbouring spellings are
  unpinned for the same reason. The name side is a member of the open unimplemented-
  function set `docs/compatibility.md`'s *Scalar string + misc functions* row states; what is this
  row's is that the names are 18.6's **type** names, so the statement a user wrote was a
  cast and the error it met names a function.

- **156 · A recursive term's bare string literal is folded against the seed's type, not
  converted to it.** The three neighbouring doors measured beside it — the plain set
  operation, the non-recursive CTE and the degraded `WITH RECURSIVE` — all *convert* it,
  running the target type's input function over the literal, and `check_recursive_shape`
  instead hands the pair to `select_common_type`. Where the two
  types have no common type that is a refusal, and it is the wrong answer twice over.
  Measured over `s8(i INT, d DATE, tz TIMESTAMPTZ, b BOOL, ia INT[], j JSONB, u UUID,
  n NUMERIC, m mood, t TEXT)`, each as
  `WITH RECURSIVE r(a) AS (SELECT <col> FROM s8 UNION ALL SELECT <literal> FROM r WHERE
  false) SELECT a FROM r`:

  | seed | literal | 18.6 | pglet |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | `i` | `'7'` | one row, `1` | `42804 UNION types integer and text cannot be matched` |
  | `d` | `'2021-02-03'` | one row, `2020-01-01` | `42804 … date and text …` |
  | `tz` | `'2021-02-03 00:00:00+00'` | one row | `42804 … timestamp with time zone and text …` |
  | `b` | `'true'` | one row, `t` | `42804 … boolean and text …` |
  | `ia` | `'{2}'` | one row, `{1}` | `42804 … integer[] and text …` |
  | `j` | `'{}'` | one row, `{}` | `42804 … jsonb and text …` |
  | `u` | a uuid | one row | `42804 … uuid and text …` |
  | `n` | `'2.5'` | one row, `1.5` | `42804 … numeric and text …` |
  | `i` | `'x'` | `22P02 invalid input syntax for type integer: "x"` | the same `42804` |
  | `d` | `'x'` | `22007 invalid input syntax for type date: "x"` | the same `42804` |

  So the over-refusal and the wrong-code halves are **one** mechanism seen through a
  convertible literal and a non-convertible one: at these seeds pglet reaches no
  conversion — it runs one only after a fold that succeeds, which is the enum's — so it
  can reach neither answer.

  **A bare `NULL` is not a member, measured.** `… UNION ALL SELECT NULL FROM r WHERE
  false` over an `int` seed and over a `date` seed answers one row, declared `23` / `1082`
  at typmod `-1`, on **both** engines — identical. It never reaches the fold: a bare
  `NULL` has no inferable type, so `recursive_term_inferred_types` answers `None` and the
  column is skipped whole. The two unresolved literals part company at that skip, and a
  row written over "an unresolved literal" would be false at half its own class.

  **The controls say it is the recursive fold and nothing wider.** The plain set operation
  (`SELECT i FROM s9 UNION ALL SELECT '7'`), the non-recursive CTE over the same body, and
  the **degraded** `WITH RECURSIVE` — `RECURSIVE` written with no self-reference, which
  both engines silently treat as an ordinary `UNION` — all three answer `1, 7` on both
  engines and both raise `22P02` on `'x'`. Only the genuinely-recursive term, which is the
  one door whose descriptors `recursive_cte_columns` rebuilds, diverges.

  **Its silent face, over an enum seed, is closed.** Over a `mood` seed the two sides
  both read `text`, so the fold *succeeds*, and `check_recursive_shape` then converts the
  literal as the set-operation door does: `… UNION ALL SELECT 'zzz'` is `22P02 invalid
  input value for enum mood: "zzz"` on both engines, where it answered rows here. The
  enum identity still stays out of the fold itself — reading it there refused the
  **member** literal `'sad'` that 18.6 accepts, measured. At every seed type above the
  fold refuses first, so no conversion is reached and the class stays loud.

  **It predates the enum identity.** Before the enum-identity gates the fold was
  `select_common_type(&[Some(nr), Some(got.type_oid)], "UNION")` over two bare `TypeOid`s,
  which gives `integer` against `text` the same `42804`; the enum identity and the
  `unknown` carve-out that later joined it changed which pairs reach the fold, not what
  the fold does to this one.

  **No fixture can hold it**: pglet refuses where 18.6 answers, so a faithful value
  fixture is red, and an `@expect-error` one over the non-convertible literal would be
  red too: `@expect-error` compares the code, and the codes differ.

- **155 · A computed column's type modifier is `-1` in every `RowDescription`.** `ColumnDesc::new` defaults
  `type_modifier` to `-1`, and the sites that write anything else are the two
  base-table-column ones (`planner::plan`'s `table_columns_desc`, `executor::helpers`'s
  `table_column_descs`) plus the recursive-CTE pair (`parser::select`'s
  `recursive_cte_columns` and the fold its caller writes over that list); every other
  site either mints the default or copies a descriptor one of those built. So a column no
  copy reaches carries the default, whatever the SQL says about its width. A base-table
  column projected directly is excluded, and the `Describe`-leg arms are row 11's. Three families are
  measured, and they are different kinds of loss:

  - **An explicit cast.** `'x'::varchar(7)` · `1::numeric(8,3)` · `'…'::timestamp(3)` ·
    `'…'::time(3)` · `'…'::interval(3)` describe as `11 · 524295 · 3 · 3 · 2147418115` on
    18.6 and `-1` at every one here, on **both** legs — the modifier is applied to the
    *value* (the cast really does truncate and round) and simply never reaches the
    descriptor. A `float(n)` cast is **not** in the family: its modifier is spent
    selecting the type, so `0.1::float(1)` is `real` and `0.1::float(30)` is `double
    precision`, both `-1`, on 18.6 and here alike.
  - **A value constructor.** 18.6's `exprTypmod` gives a `CaseExpr`, `CoalesceExpr` or
    `MinMaxExpr` its arms' modifier when every arm agrees on type *and* modifier
    (`nodeFuncs.c`, "if all the alternatives agree on type/typmod, return that typmod,
    else use -1"), so `COALESCE(v, v)` over a `varchar(5)` is `9` there and `-1` here.
    `NULLIF` **is** in it — `exprTypmod`'s `T_NullIfExpr` arm returns the first
    argument's — and it is the type, not the arm, that decides whether the modifier
    survives: `NULLIF(n, n)` over a `numeric(6,2)` describes as `1700 / 393222` on 18.6,
    while `NULLIF(v, v)` over a `varchar(5)` describes as `25 / -1`, the `=` resolution
    having made the result `text`. Both measured over the wire; `-1` here at each.
  - **A column two sources unify or a subquery passes up.** 18.6 keeps the sources'
    modifier where they agree — `select_common_typmod` for a set operation, the joined
    column for a `JOIN … USING` merge, the inner column for a scalar subquery — and pglet
    builds each with `ColumnDesc::new`. Over `t(v VARCHAR(5), n NUMERIC(6,2))` and
    `t2(v VARCHAR(5), n NUMERIC(6,2))`, both legs: `SELECT v FROM t UNION ALL SELECT v
    FROM t2` (and `UNION`, `INTERSECT`, the `numeric` spelling) is `9` / `393222` on 18.6
    and `-1` here; `SELECT v FROM t JOIN t2 USING (v)` is `9` there — with `t`'s
    provenance for an inner, left or right join, none for a full one — and `-1` with no
    provenance here, `SELECT * … USING (v, n)` likewise for both merged columns; and
    `SELECT (SELECT n FROM t LIMIT 1)` is `393222` there, `-1` here, bare or under a derived
    table. Where the sources disagree (`varchar(5)` beside `varchar(3)` or `varchar(8)`)
    both engines send `-1`, which is why a probe with disagreeing sources reads as
    agreement.

  **It is a metadata divergence that also blocks a refusal**, which is the part worth
  carrying. A recursive CTE's declared modifier is resolved by `select_common_typmod`
  rather than compared against 18.6's `42804`, *because* of this row: raising was
  implemented and measured against the oracle first, and refused a whole family of
  statements 18.6 answers — a cast to the seed's *own* width (`a::varchar(5)`,
  `'xy'::varchar(5)`, `1.5::numeric(6,2)`) and a value constructor over the working-table
  column (`CASE`, `COALESCE`, `GREATEST`, `NULLIF`, a scalar subquery) — each of which
  18.6 declares at the seed's own modifier. A gate over a value
  this engine cannot read lands wrong in both directions; closing this row is what makes
  that comparison 18.6's **at the terms pglet reads as `-1`**. Those are the recursive
  CTE's residuals that ride on this cause: a **seed** spelled as a cast (`SELECT
  'ab'::varchar(5) UNION ALL SELECT 'abcdefgh'::varchar(8) FROM r …`) leaves the pair
  looking modifier-free on both sides and is accepted here against 18.6's `42804`, and the
  family above is declared `-1` here against the modifier 18.6 declares. They are not
  every over-acceptance the recursive CTE has: a recursive term that reads a **base
  column** with a different modifier — a `VARCHAR(8)` column beside a `VARCHAR(5)` seed,
  a `TIMESTAMP(3)` one beside a `TIMESTAMPTZ(3)` seed — is read exactly, declares `-1`,
  and is accepted against 18.6's `42804` with nothing in this row missing. That subset
  needs a refusal rather than this row's repair, resting on the premise that a modifier
  pglet reads is the column's own — which row 158 falsified until it closed. Both subsets
  are in `docs/declared_types.md` § A recursive CTE's declared modifier.

  **No fixture can hold any of it.** Neither differential leg compares a type modifier —
  `tests/README.md` § Declared column types states the harness half — so the whole row is
  invisible to the corpus by construction, and what pins the one place the value is now
  *decided* is `crates/pglet/tests/cte_column_list.rs`.
- **117 · A stack of casts is named after its innermost cast here and its outermost
  there.** Measured against 18.6, with no `regclass` anywhere: `SELECT '1'::int::text`
  is a column named `int4` here against `text` there, `SELECT 1::int::text` the same, and
  `SELECT '1'::varchar::text` is `varchar` against `text`. Stacking another cast moves
  18.6 and not pglet — `'1'::int::text::varchar` is `int4` here against `varchar` there.
  The **values** agree byte for byte; what diverges is the `RowDescription` column name.

  The mechanism is `planner::expr`'s `cast_output_name`, which decides "nameless" by
  testing `inner.output_name() == "?column?"`, where 18.6's `FigureColnameInternal`
  (`parse_target.c`) decides on a *strength*: a cast over a strength-≤ 1 argument
  substitutes its own type name and **returns 1**, so the cast above it substitutes in
  turn. pglet's inner cast emits a real-looking name (`int4`), which the cast above then
  passes through as if a column had supplied it. The controls bound the rule: a single
  cast agrees (`'1'::int` is `int4` on both) and a **named** operand agrees under a stack
  (`a::int::text` and `a::int::text::varchar` are both `a` on both engines) — 18.6's
  strength-2 arm, which pglet's pass-through does match. Which *other* node kinds
  `cast_output_name` mis-scores as named is unswept.

  Nothing pins it, and a faithful fixture would be **red**: the harness keys each
  compared row by its column name, so this divergence is exactly what it compares.
  `tests/fixtures/types/cast_unaliased_column_names.sql` covers the single-cast shape
  only. Row 85's (a) records the neighbouring `regclass` naming divergence, and
  `catalog/regclass_output_column_name.sql` is green over the **one** cast standing above
  its `regclass`; a second one falls to this row — `'zz'::regclass::text::varchar` is
  `text` here against `varchar` there.

- **84 · A catalog-reading expression cannot be stored.** `pg_get_constraintdef` or
  `::regclass` inside a CHECK, an index predicate or an index key is
  `0A000 … is not available in this context`, refused at DDL time by the render/eval
  probe, where 18.6 accepts and stores it.

  Loud, deliberate, and the boundary is exactly the stored-expression one: every **query
  and DML** position answers — `SELECT`, `INSERT … VALUES`, `INSERT … SELECT`,
  `UPDATE … SET`, `UPDATE`/`DELETE … WHERE`, `RETURNING` on all three, and
  `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`'s `SET` and `WHERE` — the catalog being lent at
  `execute_plan_node`, at `eval_expr_subquery_with`, and per-evaluation at the three DML
  sites that also hold `&mut schema.sequences`. It was **not** that boundary when this
  row was written: only the first seam lent, so all five DML positions were `0A000` while
  the identical expression in a `SELECT` answered. What keeps the refusal at DDL is that
  the write path's evaluation environment has no catalog either, so accepting would
  persist an expression that fails `0A000` on **every insert**.

  It is also why `pglet::dump`'s `ROUND_TRIP_CORPUS` cannot reach the two, and why their
  deparse arms are pinned by a direct unit test instead — `deparse`'s
  `catalog_reading_string_fns_render_to_their_written_form`, beside
  `NOT_STORABLE_STRING_FUNCS`, which keeps the corpus's completeness check failing for
  any *new* `StringFunc` until someone classifies it. The DML positions are pinned by
  `catalog/regclass_in_dml_positions.sql` and `catalog/regclass_in_returning.sql`.

- **83 · An unmodelled catalog column is refused rather than bound as an empty one.**
  Over a relation pglet models completely, a catalog column 18.6 declares and pglet does
  not model is `42703` — the relation binds exhaustively — where 18.6 answers the column,
  usually NULL or a vector. The twelve measured are `pg_constraint`'s `conbin`,
  `conpfeqop`, `conppeqop`, `conffeqop`, `confdelsetcols` and `conexclop`, and
  `pg_index`'s `indkey`, `indcollation`, `indclass`, `indoption`, `indexprs` and
  `indpred`.

  **Loud, and deliberately over-refusing.** The alternative is what stood before: any
  name at all, invented or real, bound as a zero-row `text` column, so
  `SELECT zzz FROM pg_constraint` answered `(0 rows)` where 18.6 raises `42703`.
  Modelling them is not a matter of declaring a type — `indkey` is 18.6's `int2vector`
  (space-separated text, lower bound 0), which declaring `int2[]` would get wrong on both
  counts, and the other five need an opclass/collation model or a `pg_node_tree`
  renderer. **Guarded** by `catalog/unmodelled_column_is_loud_*.sql` — five zero-row
  rejects, the shape only the plan-time gate can refuse — plus
  `unmodelled_column_over_populated_relation.sql` for the executor's own per-row arm, and
  `modelled_column_binds_on_every_complete_relation.sql` as the accept polarity.

- **82 · A sequence has no `pg_class` row, and `public`'s namespace OID is a constant.**
  pglet emits no `relkind = 'S'` row at all, where 18.6 carries one row per sequence, and
  reports `public` as OID 2200 always, where 18.6's is per-database — 2200 only where the
  schema was never dropped and recreated. Silent both ways: a client counting relations
  sees fewer than there are, and one joining on a hardcoded 2200 agrees with pglet by
  accident.

  The sequence row is **omitted rather than invented**: pglet's `Sequence` record carries
  no OID, and a derived one would either collide with a relation's or change under DDL.
  `information_schema.sequences` needs none and is complete.
  `catalog/pg_class_index_rows.sql` projects the `r` and `i` rows and would go red if an
  `S` row appeared with a wrong shape; nothing pins the absence itself.

- **81 · A synthesized `pg_constraint.oid` is stable only inside the statement that
  reads it.** pglet stores no constraint OID — and one of the five kinds (`NOT NULL`) is
  a `Column.nullable` bit rather than a record, so no persisted field could name it — so
  `pg_constraint.oid` and `pg_enum.oid` are synthesized from a reserved band's base plus
  the object's position in the catalog-wide enumeration. Adding or dropping a constraint
  that sorts **before** it in that enumeration shifts it; one added after it does not.
  18.6's OID is stable for the object's lifetime.

  A consumer that reads the OID and uses it in the same statement —
  `pg_get_constraintdef(c.oid)`, which is what both real consumers write — cannot see the
  difference; one that caches it across DDL resolves to a different constraint. **No
  fixture**: an OID is a catalog identity and the two engines' never agree, so the corpus
  compares `oid <> 0` polarities instead, and `catalog/pg_get_constraintdef_shapes.sql`
  proves the OID a row carries resolves to that row's own definition — which is the
  property the consumers need.

- **~~157~~ · Closed — a later CTE's read of a recursive one was counted as its own
  self-reference, and the list was resolved in declaration order.** Every CTE of a `WITH
  RECURSIVE` list went through `parse_recursive_cte_body`, which counted a FROM reference as
  a self-reference whenever the entry it resolved to was a `Plan::CteScan` — the entry's
  kind, which an earlier genuinely recursive CTE's entry is too. Confirmed by mutation on
  the pre-repair engine: excluding already-resolved recursive CTEs from that test made
  `q AS (SELECT * FROM r)`, its `UNION`-branch spelling and its `IN (SELECT n FROM r)`
  spelling answer, and left a later *genuinely* recursive `q` on the separate
  one-recursive-CTE limit.

  The repair resolves the list the way `transformWithClause` does, with a token pre-scan
  standing in for the raw parse tree (`parser::with_recursive`): each body's
  range-variable names give the dependencies, `TopologicalSort`'s swap order resolves a
  forward reference, a cycle of more than one item is 18.6's `0A000`, the well-formedness
  verdicts run before any body is analysed, and a CTE that does not name itself is parsed
  as an ordinary CTE. A self-reference is keyed on the name being defined, and every
  recursive CTE is an entry of the `Plan::With`, materialized in order with the entries
  before it bound. Measured against 18.6, each of the old members answers as it does there:
  `q AS (SELECT * FROM r)` and its filtered, aggregated, derived-table, scalar-subquery,
  `IN`, `EXISTS` and `UNION`-branch spellings, a third CTE reading `q`, two later CTEs
  reading `r`, an `INSERT … SELECT` statement body, and a later recursive CTE whose seed
  reads `r`; so do a forward reference, two independent recursive CTEs, a recursive term
  reading an earlier recursive CTE, a three-deep chain declared in reverse, a recursive
  CTE beside a data-modifying one that reads it, and mutual recursion's `0A000`.

  **One member had been silent.** `WITH RECURSIVE q AS (SELECT * FROM s), s AS (SELECT 5
  AS x) SELECT * FROM q` over a base table `s` read the table's rows, where 18.6 reads the
  CTE: the later name was not registered yet, so the reference fell through to the
  relation (`forward_reference_shadows_a_table`).

  **A recursive seed reading a later recursive CTE was `42883 operator does not exist: text
  < integer`**, not the `42P19` of its neighbours: the later name fell through to a relation
  the catalog lacks, the working table typed that relation's column `text`, and the
  recursive term's `m < 13` was judged against it — row 154's class, reached through a
  recursive CTE. It answers now because the name resolves.

  The repair moved some precedence answers, all measured against 18.6: a well-formedness
  verdict now outranks an earlier item's analysis error, and the cycle `0A000` outranks
  one, as 18.6 has both; what it cannot reproduce of the raw parse is row 80's. What the
  repair leaves includes rows 80, 160, 161 and 162. And a CTE that does not name itself now
  parses as it does under a plain `WITH`, so under `WITH RECURSIVE` it carries whatever an
  ordinary CTE body carries there — row 30's `FOR UPDATE OF <a CTE>` member, for one, whose
  direct spelling in a list body the old parse refused `42601` and that now answers; nested
  in a derived table inside a list body it already answered before the repair. Row 167's clause
  stacking is another where the CTE's own body is the parenthesized query, a spelling the
  old parse refused `42601` and that now reads, and under a data-modifying statement writes,
  silently; nested deeper in such a body, in a derived table, the stacking was already
  reached before the repair.

- **160 · A data-modifying CTE's write is visible to the rest of its statement.** pglet
  runs a `WITH`'s data-modifying CTEs in order, then the body, against one storage, so
  every other part of the statement reads the rows the write left, where 18.6 runs every
  part against the snapshot taken before the statement and sees the write only through the
  CTE's own `RETURNING` rows. The snapshot is what 18.6 **reads**; what a data-modifying CTE
  writes depends on the order its writers run in as well, since one skips a row a writer run
  earlier in the statement already changed — so two writers of one row do not both take it,
  and which one does is row 162's order. Measured over `s` holding two rows, each statement
  inside a block rolled back: `WITH w AS (INSERT INTO s VALUES (9) RETURNING x) SELECT count(*) FROM
  s` is `3` here and `2` there; an ordinary CTE, `q AS (SELECT count(*) AS c FROM s)`,
  the same, declared before `w` or after it, since it runs inside the body; and a later
  data-modifying CTE, `v AS (INSERT INTO u SELECT x FROM s RETURNING
  x)`, **writes** three rows into `u` where 18.6 writes two. These are the plain-`WITH`
  members, and each answered the same way before `WITH RECURSIVE` lists took
  data-modifying CTEs.

  The write a reader sees includes what a foreign key's action writes: pglet runs the
  actions when the data-modifying statement finishes, and 18.6 runs them once the whole
  statement has. Measured over `p` holding `1, 2` and `c(pid REFERENCES p ON DELETE CASCADE
  ON UPDATE CASCADE)` holding `1, 2`: `WITH a AS (INSERT INTO p VALUES (1, 5) ON CONFLICT
  (id) DO UPDATE SET id = 9 RETURNING id) SELECT pid FROM c ORDER BY 1` is `2, 9` here and
  `1, 2` there, and `WITH a AS (UPDATE p SET id = 9 WHERE id = 1 RETURNING id)` before the
  same body the same; `WITH a AS (DELETE FROM p WHERE id = 1 RETURNING id) SELECT count(*)
  FROM c` is `1` against `2`. Beside the upsert, a later data-modifying CTE `b AS (INSERT
  INTO lg SELECT pid FROM c)` **stores** `2, 9` where 18.6 stores `1, 2`.

  For the readers below, the statement is refused `0A000` in the parse, before anything
  runs (`Parser::wrap_with_ctes`):

  - a body that **writes** — `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, or a sequence function — beside a
    data-modifying CTE, under either spelling of `WITH`. Measured, `WITH w AS (INSERT INTO s
    VALUES (9) RETURNING x) DELETE FROM s WHERE x = 9` deleted the inserted row where 18.6
    deletes none, and its `UPDATE` and `INSERT … SELECT` twins wrote from three rows where
    18.6 reads two. The refusal is keyed on the body writing, not on what it reads, so one
    beside a CTE on an unrelated table is refused too (it also stands in for the order row
    162 records), and so is one reading only the CTE's `RETURNING` rows — the move-rows
    `WITH w AS (DELETE FROM s … RETURNING x) INSERT INTO other SELECT x FROM w`, which 18.6
    runs, and which was loud before `WITH RECURSIVE` lists took data-modifying CTEs as well,
    from the executor;
  - a **recursive** CTE resolved after a data-modifying one — measured, `w AS (INSERT INTO s
    VALUES (9) RETURNING x), r(n) AS (SELECT x FROM s UNION ALL …)` counted the inserted row
    where 18.6 does not — and so is one that reads only `w`'s `RETURNING` rows, which would
    be right: the refusal is keyed on the order, not on what the recursive CTE reads
    (`data_modifying_then_recursive_loud`). A recursive CTE resolved **before** the write
    runs first and reads what 18.6 reads;
  - under `WITH RECURSIVE`, a second data-modifying CTE (row 162), and a body naming a table
    the data-modifying CTE can write — directly, or through an ordinary CTE it reads — its
    target, or a table a foreign key's `CASCADE` or `SET NULL` writes from a written one: on
    a delete, or on an update that assigns a referenced column, an `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO
    UPDATE`'s included, carried on through the referencing table's own keys
    (`recursive_list_body_reads_*_loud`). A `NO ACTION` or `RESTRICT` key writes nothing and
    neither does a plain `INSERT`, so those reads answer
    (`recursive_list_body_reads_a_table_an_insert_references`,
    `…_a_no_action_delete_references`); the write such a key forbids is refused, `23503` /
    `23001`, an `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`'s included — save a key an `ON DELETE SET NULL` action
    nulls, which pglet writes (row 163). The reach is decided per table, never per row: an
    update of a referenced column that no referencing row matches is refused too, where 18.6
    answers, and so is one that assigns the column its own value — `UPDATE p SET id = id`, or
    `… ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET id = p.id` — which changes no key and fires no action
    there. Which tables a body names is counted where the parser binds each one, so an
    ordinary CTE's tables count at every reference that inlines it.

  Refused in the parse, the statement is refused ahead of the data-modifying CTE's own
  execution error, which 18.6 raises. Measured under a plain `WITH`: `WITH w AS (INSERT INTO
  s VALUES (1/0) RETURNING x) DELETE FROM s WHERE x = 9` is `0A000` here and `22012` there,
  and a duplicate key or a null in a `NOT NULL` column inside the CTE, `23505` / `23502`
  there, is `0A000` here too; under `WITH RECURSIVE` the refusal of a second
  data-modifying CTE outranks a `23505` the same way. The refusal sits ahead of the entries
  because one raised after an entry has run leaves that entry's write on `--storage
  memory`, which has no statement rollback: measured, an executor-side refusal of the
  `DELETE` twin above raised its error there and left the inserted row in `s`.

- **161 · A `WITH RECURSIVE` query 18.6 answers is refused, or one it refuses is refused
  under another code.** Measured against 18.6, each answering there unless its item says
  otherwise:

  - a non-recursive term that is itself a set operation — `r(n) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL
    SELECT 2 UNION ALL SELECT n+1 FROM r WHERE n<3)` is `42P19 recursive query "r" does not
    have the form non-recursive-term UNION [ALL] recursive-term` here, five rows there: the
    recursive path parses a two-term body only;
  - a recursive CTE 18.6 skips — unreferenced — or stops early — read under a `LIMIT`. pglet
    materializes every recursive CTE, evaluated to its fixed point before the body runs, so
    one that does not terminate (`WITH RECURSIVE r(n) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n+1 FROM
    r) SELECT 1`, and `… SELECT n FROM r LIMIT 3`) is `54000 recursive query "r" exceeded the
    maximum of 100000 iterations` here, and an unreferenced one whose evaluation raises
    (`… UNION ALL SELECT n/(n-1) FROM r WHERE n<3) SELECT 1`) raises its error, `22012`;
  - - a body leading with a parenthesized query that holds its whole `UNION`, followed by a
    clause over it that `insertSelectOptions` merges into it without refusal — `r(n) AS
    ((SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n+1 FROM r WHERE n<3) FOR READ ONLY)`. The pre-scan reaches no
    self-reference verdict for such a body, and the parse takes the whole parenthesized query
    for the non-recursive term, so its self-reference resolves against the placeholder's
    untyped columns and the parse raises — `42883` here, `42804` for `SELECT n FROM r WHERE
    false`. Under `ORDER BY`, `OFFSET`, `LIMIT` or `FOR UPDATE` 18.6 refuses too, `0A000 … in
    a recursive query is not implemented`, so there the code is the divergence. A body the
    parentheses enclose whole, with nothing after them, is read inside them and answers.
    A clause `insertSelectOptions` refuses beside the parenthesized query's own is not a
    member: `((SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n+1 FROM r WHERE n<3) FETCH FIRST ROWS WITH TIES)`
    and `((SELECT n FROM r LIMIT 1) LIMIT 2)` are `42601` on both engines, with 18.6's
    message (`recursive_body_*_repeated_loud`);
  - a clause over the recursive query that 18.6's grammar reads and pglet's reader of those
    clauses does not — `ORDER BY n USING OPERATOR(pg_catalog.<)`, and a sort operator pglet's
    lexer refuses (`USING ~<~`) — is `42601` here and `0A000 ORDER BY in a recursive query is
    not implemented` there.

  Each is loud and each predates the dependency-order repair; a faithful fixture is red.

- **162 · A plain `WITH`'s data-modifying CTEs write in declaration order.** pglet runs
  them in the order the list declares them, each to completion, before the body. 18.6's
  executor is pull-driven: it runs a data-modifying CTE a reader reads when that reader
  first pulls a row from it, and every one still unfinished once the statement's own query
  is done in `ExecPostprocessPlan`, over `es_auxmodifytables` — a list
  `ExecInitModifyTable` builds with `lcons`, so in the reverse of the order the CTEs were
  initialized. Every writer reads the statement's snapshot, and one that finds a row a
  writer run before it already changed skips it. So the divergence is the **execution
  order** itself, seen wherever it decides what two writers write or return — on the same
  rows, or through a shared sequence — and a repair has to reproduce that order, or refuse
  wherever two writers could meet; one keyed on sequences alone leaves the rows. Measured over `s` holding `1`
  and `2`: `WITH a AS (DELETE FROM s WHERE x = 1 RETURNING x), b AS (DELETE FROM s WHERE x =
  1 RETURNING x) SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM b), (SELECT count(*) FROM a)` is `1|0` there,
  `b` pulled first and `a` skipping the row `b` deleted, and `0|1` here; with the reads the
  other way round both answer `1|0`. And over `t (id SERIAL, v TEXT)`:

  - `WITH p AS (INSERT INTO t (v) VALUES ('p') RETURNING id), q AS (INSERT INTO t (v) VALUES
    ('q') RETURNING id) SELECT 1` gives `p` serial 1 here and `q` serial 1 there;
  - the same list under `SELECT * FROM q, p` gives `q` serial 1 there and `p` serial 1
    here;
  - `s0 AS (INSERT … VALUES ('s') …), p AS (INSERT … SELECT 'p' FROM s0 …), q AS (INSERT …
    SELECT 'q' FROM s0 …) SELECT 1` gives `s`, `p`, `q` serials 1, 2, 3 here and `s`, `q`,
    `p` there — `q` runs first at the end, and pulls `s0` as it starts.

  Each answered the same way before `WITH RECURSIVE` lists took data-modifying CTEs. Under
  `WITH RECURSIVE` the resolved order is `TopologicalSort`'s rather than the declaration's,
  and a second data-modifying CTE is refused `0A000` rather than run in an order that could
  differ — measured for two unrelated inserts (18.6 serial 1 to the second), for two CTEs
  reading a third (`s`, `p`, `q` there, where declaring `s0` last reorders the sort), and for
  two tables whose defaults share a sequence. A body that writes beside a data-modifying CTE
  is refused under either spelling (row 160), which covers its order against them too.

- **163 · A key an `ON DELETE SET NULL` action nulls does not enter the `ON UPDATE`
  worklist.** `plan_delete_cascade` records the `SET NULL` edit and checks the nulled row — its
  NOT NULL, its `CHECK` and each index entry — but it hands the nulled row to no
  `ON UPDATE` pass, so a foreign key referencing the nulled column is never asked. 18.6
  runs the `SET NULL` as an `UPDATE` of the child, which fires the referencing key's
  `ON UPDATE` action like any other. The `ON UPDATE` cascade is transitive among `ON
  UPDATE` actions only (`FkTriggerQueue`); this is the edge where an `ON DELETE`
  action should start one. Measured over `p(id PK)`, `c(id PK, pid INT UNIQUE REFERENCES
  p ON DELETE SET NULL)`, `g(cp REFERENCES c(pid) …)`, `c` = `(10, 1)`, `g` = `(1)`:
  `DELETE FROM p WHERE id = 1` is `23503` on 18.6 with `g` `NO ACTION` (and with `ON DELETE
  CASCADE`, whose `ON UPDATE` is `NO ACTION`), `23001` with `ON UPDATE RESTRICT`, and sets
  `g.cp` to NULL with `ON UPDATE CASCADE` or `SET NULL`; here each deletes the row, nulls
  `c.pid` and leaves `g.cp = 1`. The plain `WITH` data-modifying CTE spelling writes the
  same. The control agrees: `UPDATE c SET pid = NULL WHERE id = 10` is `23503` on both
  engines, the `UPDATE` path running the worklist.

- **164 · A data-modifying statement's `RETURNING` subquery reads the statement's own
  write.** The `RETURNING` projection runs over storage the statement has already
  changed, where 18.6 evaluates it against the snapshot the statement started from, so a
  subquery there that reads the written table sees the write. Measured over `p` holding
  two rows: `DELETE FROM p WHERE id = 1 RETURNING (SELECT count(*) FROM p)` is `1` here and
  `2` there; `INSERT INTO p VALUES (3, 3) RETURNING (SELECT count(*) FROM p)` `3` against
  `2`; `UPDATE p SET v = 10 WHERE id = 1 RETURNING (SELECT sum(v) FROM p)` `12` against
  `3`, and its `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` twin the same; a correlated `RETURNING (SELECT
  count(*) FROM p p2 WHERE p2.id = p.id)` on the `DELETE` `0` against `1`. A table a plain
  `UPDATE`'s or `DELETE`'s foreign-key action writes reads the same way, those two running
  their actions before the projection: with `c(pid REFERENCES p ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE
  CASCADE)` holding `1` and `2`, `DELETE FROM p WHERE id = 1 RETURNING (SELECT count(*) FROM
  c)` is `1` against `2`, and the `UPDATE` moving key `1` to `9` returns `max(pid)` `9`
  against `2`. The `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` moving the same key projects its `RETURNING`
  before its actions run, and returns `2` on both engines. The value is a read the client receives, and under a plain `WITH` it is also a
  write's source: `WITH w AS (DELETE FROM p WHERE id = 1 RETURNING (SELECT count(*) FROM p)
  AS n), v AS (INSERT INTO q SELECT n FROM w RETURNING n) SELECT * FROM v` stores `1` in `q`
  where 18.6 stores `2`. Under `WITH RECURSIVE` it stays a read: the data-modifying CTE
  carries the same wrong value into the body (`WITH RECURSIVE w AS (DELETE … RETURNING
  (SELECT count(*) FROM p) AS n) SELECT * FROM w` is `1` against `2`), while a second
  data-modifying CTE and a body that writes are refused `0A000` (row 160) — measured, both
  spellings above that write under a plain `WITH` are refused there.

- **~~165~~ · Closed — a row a statement rewrote was never repointed by another rewritten
  row's `ON UPDATE CASCADE`, nor nulled by its `ON UPDATE SET NULL`; the residual is a
  referencing row its own transaction wrote.** The `ON UPDATE` plan put every row the
  statement itself rewrote in its `visited` set before it walked any child, and a cascade
  skipped a child `visited` held — so over a self-referencing key a rewritten row whose new
  image still referenced a key another rewritten row moved kept that old key: a **durable
  orphan** where it was written while the row it referenced still held the key, and `23503`
  where it was written after, its own key being checked as it was written. The actions now
  run as 18.6's after-row triggers do — each written row's actions, then its own key checks,
  queued as the row is written and fired in order once the statement's rows are written
  (`executor::dml`'s `FkTriggerQueue`) — so a rewritten row is a child like any other, and a
  check of a version an action has since rewritten is skipped, as 18.6's `SnapshotSelf` test
  skips it. Measured over `p(id INT PRIMARY KEY, par INT
  REFERENCES p ON UPDATE CASCADE)`, rows inserted `1`, `3`, `2` and then `UPDATE p SET par =
  2 WHERE id = 3`, each statement its own transaction: `UPDATE p SET id = id + 10 WHERE id IN
  (2, 3)` leaves `(13, 12)` on both engines, and so does the insertion order `1`, `2`, `3`;
  over a `p` with a `v` column, `UPDATE p SET id = CASE WHEN id = 2 THEN 12 ELSE id END, v =
  1 WHERE id IN (2, 3)` leaves `(3, 12)` on both; and `INSERT INTO p VALUES (3, 0), (2, 0) ON
  CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET id = p.id + 10` leaves `(13, 12)` on both. Under `ON UPDATE SET
  NULL` the same statements leave `(13, NULL)`, `(3, NULL)` and `(13, NULL)` on both. A
  self-referencing hierarchy whose every row moves, `(1, NULL), (2, 1), (3, 2)` and `UPDATE h
  SET id = id + 10`, leaves `(11, NULL), (12, 11), (13, 12)` on both, and was `23503` here
  before. An `ON UPDATE RESTRICT` key is `23001` on both engines in both orders.

  **The residual: a referencing row an earlier statement of its transaction wrote.** 18.6
  fires a row's own key check on `UPDATE` even where the key is unchanged when the
  transaction running the `UPDATE` wrote the row (`RI_FKey_fk_upd_check_required`), and
  queues it with that row, ahead of the action a later row's move fires — so where the
  referencing row is written first, the check finds the key already moved and refuses
  `23503`. pglet knows a row the statement itself wrote, and checks every key of one an
  action rewrites, but not a row an earlier statement of the block wrote, so it queues no
  check of that row's unchanged key and repoints or nulls it. Measured with the table, its rows and the statement in one block: over the rows
  inserted `1`, `3`, `2`, the `id + 10` statement, the `v = 1` spelling and the upsert are
  each `23503` on 18.6 and leave `(13, 12)`, `(3, 12)` and `(13, 12)` here — `(13, NULL)`,
  `(3, NULL)` and `(13, NULL)` under `SET NULL`; over the rows inserted `1`, `2`, `3` both
  engines leave `(13, 12)` (`(13, NULL)`); and with the rows committed before the block opens,
  the `id + 10` statement leaves `(13, 12)` (`(13, NULL)`) on both. The same holds without a
  self-rewritten row: over `t3 (id int PRIMARY KEY, par int, v int)` holding `(2, 1, 0), (1,
  NULL, 0)`, its `par` key added `ON UPDATE CASCADE` after the rows, `UPDATE t3 SET v = 1, id
  = CASE id WHEN 1 THEN 10 ELSE id END` in the block that created them is `23503` on 18.6
  and leaves `(2, 10)` here, and both leave `(2, 10)` with the rows committed before it
  (`fk/update_unchanged_key_not_checked_before_later_cascade.sql`). Nor does it need a
  self-referencing key: a cycle of tables reaches it. Over `a (k int PRIMARY KEY, b int, v
  int)` holding `(1, NULL, 0), (2, NULL, 0)` and `b (k int PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES a ON
  UPDATE CASCADE)` holding `1`, then `UPDATE a SET b = 1 WHERE k = 2` and `a`'s key `(b)
  REFERENCES b ON UPDATE CASCADE` added, `UPDATE a SET v = 1, k = CASE k WHEN 1 THEN 10 ELSE
  k END` in the block that ran all of it is `23503` on 18.6, naming `a_b_fkey`, and leaves
  `a` holding `(2, 10, 1), (10, NULL, 1)` and `b` holding `10` here; run in autocommit, both
  engines leave that. The three-table cycle of
  `fk/update_cascade_rewritten_row_not_written_before_checks_changed_key_only.sql`, run in
  one block, is `23503` on 18.6 and accepted here, which is why that fixture is `@no-txn`.
  **Silent** — a statement
  18.6 refuses runs, though what it leaves holds its foreign keys. No fixture holds it: the
  harness's isolating block is itself the transaction that writes a fixture's rows, which is
  why the closed members' referencing-row-first fixtures run under `@no-txn`. The upsert's
  other row order, `VALUES (2, 0), (3, 0)`, is row 166's: `23503` here, `(13, 12)` on 18.6.

- **166 · A row's own foreign key is checked as the row is written, where 18.6 queues the
  check beside the statement's actions.** The `INSERT` and `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` paths
  run the written row's child-side check, `enforce_foreign_keys`, at the write. 18.6 queues
  it as an after-row trigger beside the rows' actions and fires the queue in order once the
  statement's plan has run, skipping a queued check whose row an action has since rewritten
  (`RI_FKey_check`'s `SnapshotSelf` test). An `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` over a table some
  foreign key references queues each row's check as well, in its place beside the rows'
  actions (`executor::dml`'s `FkTriggerQueue`), so a key the written row's own check
  accepts the queued check can still refuse, where 18.6 refuses it; a key the written row's
  own check refuses stays refused. Over a self-referencing key that leaves one direction.
  Measured over `p(id INT PRIMARY KEY, par INT REFERENCES p ON UPDATE CASCADE)` holding `(1,
  NULL)`: `INSERT INTO p VALUES (1, NULL), (4, 1) ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET id = 10` is
  refused `23503` here, key `1` having moved before `(4, 1)` is written, where 18.6 accepts
  and leaves `(4, 10), (10, NULL)`, the action rewriting row `4` before its check runs. The
  other order, `(4, 1), (1, NULL)`, is `23503` on both engines, the queued check of `(4, 1)`
  running ahead of the action that moves key `1`
  (`fk/upsert_self_ref_inserted_row_checked_before_later_move_loud.sql`). `ON UPDATE SET
  NULL` and `ON UPDATE RESTRICT` reach it too, over the same table with `par INT REFERENCES
  p ON UPDATE SET NULL` or `… ON UPDATE RESTRICT`: `(4, 1)` second is `23503` here, where
  18.6 accepts and leaves `(4, NULL), (10, NULL)` under `SET NULL` and refuses `23001` under
  `RESTRICT`; `(4, 1)` first is `23503` on both engines under both. A row the `DO UPDATE`
  rewrites is a member the same way: over the `CASCADE` table holding `(1, NULL), (2, NULL)`,
  `INSERT INTO p VALUES (1, 0), (2, 0) ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET par = CASE WHEN p.id =
  2 THEN 1 ELSE p.par END, id = CASE WHEN p.id = 1 THEN 10 ELSE p.id END` is `23503` here and
  accepted there, leaving `(2, 10), (10, NULL)`, and with the `VALUES` rows the other way
  round both engines refuse `23503`
  (`fk/upsert_rewritten_row_checked_before_later_move_loud.sql`). A plain `UPDATE` is not a member: it queues each row's actions and then its
  own key checks, and fires them once its rows are written, as 18.6 does (`FkTriggerQueue`,
  `fk/update_self_ref_*_reference_before_move_loud.sql`, `fk/update_own_key_before_later_row_*`).
  Over `u1c (id int, p int REFERENCES q1p, a text
  CHECK (length(a) < 5), u int UNIQUE, n int NOT NULL)` holding `(1, 1, 'x', 1, 0), (2, 1,
  'y', 2, 0)`, `UPDATE u1c SET p = CASE WHEN id = 1 THEN 99 ELSE p END, a = CASE WHEN id = 2
  THEN 'toolong' ELSE a END` is `23514` on both engines, and its `u = … 1` and `n = … NULL`
  spellings `23505` and `23502` on both (measured). An ordinary
  multi-row `INSERT` is one too: over `c (p int REFERENCES p(id), a text)` with an index on
  `a`, `INSERT INTO c VALUES (99, 'x'), (NULL, '<3 000 characters>')` is `23503` here, the
  first row's key checked as it is written, and `54000` on 18.6, whose queued check runs
  after the second row's oversized index entry is refused (measured). The later row's other
  refusals are members the same way, over `q1c (p int REFERENCES q1p, a text CHECK
  (length(a) < 5), u int UNIQUE)` with `q1p` holding `1`: `INSERT INTO q1c VALUES (99, 'x',
  1), (NULL, 'toolong', 2)` is `23503` here and `23514` on 18.6, `(99, 'x', 1), (NULL, 'y', 1)`
  is `23503` here and `23505` there, and over `q2c (p int REFERENCES q1p, n int NOT NULL)`,
  `(99, 1), (NULL, NULL)` is `23503` here and `23502` there (each measured). Where no later
  row fails, `(99, 'x', 1), (NULL, NULL, 2), (NULL, 'y', 3)`, both engines answer `23503`.
  A multi-row `INSERT` that writes a row before the row it references is one too, and the
  plainest: over `t (id int PRIMARY KEY, par int REFERENCES t)`, `INSERT INTO t VALUES (2,
  1), (1, NULL)` is `23503` here and accepted on 18.6, whose queued check of `(2, 1)` runs
  once `(1, NULL)` is written (measured).

  **A row that references its own key is a member with no second row**, and the plainest
  of all: the check runs before the row is stored, so the key it references is not yet
  there. Over `o (k int PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES o ON UPDATE CASCADE)`, `INSERT INTO o VALUES
  (1)` — a root that is its own parent, a primary key that is its own foreign key — is
  `23503` here and accepted on 18.6; over `i (k int PRIMARY KEY, par int REFERENCES i)`,
  `INSERT INTO i VALUES (1, 1)` is the same split. The upsert reaches it on both of its
  paths, over `o2 (k int PRIMARY KEY, v int)` holding `(102, 0), (110, 0)` with `FOREIGN KEY
  (k) REFERENCES o2 ON UPDATE CASCADE`: `INSERT INTO o2 VALUES (5, 0) ON CONFLICT (k) DO
  UPDATE SET k = 50`, which conflicts with nothing and inserts `(5, 0)`, and `INSERT INTO o2
  VALUES (110, 0) ON CONFLICT (k) DO UPDATE SET k = 50`, whose rewritten row references its
  own new key, are each `23503` here and accepted on 18.6 (each measured). A plain `UPDATE`
  of such a row is not a member (`fk/update_self_ref_row_is_its_own_parent.sql`, which
  builds its row by `UPDATE`).

- **198 · The actions on the foreign keys referencing one table fire in an order of pglet's
  own.** 18.6 fires a row's triggers in trigger-name order, and an action trigger is named
  `RI_ConstraintTrigger_a_<oid>` after its own OID, minted when its key is created, so the
  actions fire in the order the keys were created while those OIDs have one number of
  digits; across a digit boundary the name order is not the numeric one
  (`RI_ConstraintTrigger_a_100000000` sorts before `RI_ConstraintTrigger_a_99999999`). That
  last is read from the source (`trigger.c`'s `RelationBuildTriggers`, which reads the
  triggers through `TriggerRelidNameIndexId`, and `CreateTriggerFiringOn`'s `"%s_%u"`), not
  measured: the oracle's OID counter is nowhere near a boundary. pglet keeps no creation
  stamp on a foreign key. An `UPDATE`'s queue orders them by the
  referencing table's OID and then the key's place in that table's list
  (`executor::dml`'s `referencing_fks_on_update`), which is creation order wherever each key
  was declared with its table; a `DELETE`'s plan walks `Schema::referencing_foreign_keys`
  as the catalog holds it, by table name. Measured over `p (k int PRIMARY KEY)` referenced
  `ON UPDATE RESTRICT ON DELETE RESTRICT` by `zc` and then `ac`, each holding `1`: `DELETE
  FROM p` names `ac_k_fkey` here and `zc_k_fkey` there, and `UPDATE p SET k = 2` names
  `zc_k_fkey` on both. With `ac2` created before `zc2` but its key added by `ALTER TABLE`
  after `zc2`'s, `UPDATE p2 SET k = 2` and `DELETE FROM p2` both name `ac2_k_fkey` here and
  `zc2_k_fkey` there. The order moves more than a name: over `t (id int PRIMARY KEY, xp int,
  par int)` and `p (k int PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES t ON UPDATE CASCADE)`, `t`'s keys `par
  REFERENCES t` and `xp REFERENCES p`, both `ON UPDATE CASCADE`, added by `ALTER TABLE`
  after `p`'s, over `t` holding `(1, NULL, NULL), (2, NULL, 1)` and `p` holding `1`, `UPDATE
  t SET id = CASE id WHEN 1 THEN 10 ELSE id END, xp = CASE id WHEN 2 THEN 1 ELSE xp END` is
  accepted there, leaving `(2, 10, 10)`, and `23503` here: 18.6 moves `p`'s key before it
  repoints the second row's `par`, so `p`'s repoint of `xp` is queued ahead of the rewritten
  row's check, and pglet the other way round. Loud in every member measured — the wrong
  constraint named, or a refusal of a statement 18.6 runs. No fixture holds the members: a
  faithful one is red.

- **199 · A referenced key is "changed" when its value is, where 18.6 asks whether its bytes
  are.** 18.6 queues a parent-side action only when the referenced key changed, and on the
  referenced side it compares the old and new keys' stored images, not their `=`
  (`ri_KeysEqual`'s `datum_image_eq`, so that a change that "looks" different reaches the
  children). pglet compares by value (`executor::dml`'s `key_tuples_equal`), so a key moved
  to a value `=` calls equal and whose bytes differ — a `numeric` whose value stays and
  whose display scale changes — fires nothing. Measured over `p (k numeric
  PRIMARY KEY)` holding `1.0`, referenced `ON UPDATE CASCADE` by `c` holding `1.0`: `UPDATE
  p SET k = 1.00` leaves `c` at `1.0` here and `1.00` there; and with an `ON UPDATE
  RESTRICT` child `r` holding `1.0` beside it, `UPDATE p SET k = 1.000` is accepted here and
  `23001` there. `interval` is a member the same way, its `=` comparing the span a value
  totals and its image keeping the fields: over `pi (k interval PRIMARY KEY)` holding `'1
  day'`, referenced `ON UPDATE CASCADE` by `ci` holding `'1 day'`, `UPDATE pi SET k = '24
  hours'` leaves `ci` at `1 day` here and `24:00:00` there; over `pr` the same, referenced
  `ON UPDATE RESTRICT` by `cr` holding `'1 day'`, it is accepted here and `23001` there.
  A `jsonb` key is a member through a number inside it: over `xp (tenant int, payload
  jsonb, PRIMARY KEY (tenant, payload))` holding `(1, '{"k":1}')`, referenced `ON UPDATE
  CASCADE` by a child holding `(1, '{"k":1.0}')`, `UPDATE xp SET payload = '{"k":1.00}'`
  leaves the child at `{"k": 1.0}` here and `{"k": 1.00}` there, on both build profiles.
  A float key is a member through the sign of zero, `0 = -0` being true and the two images
  differing: over `p (k float8 PRIMARY KEY)` holding `0`, referenced `ON UPDATE RESTRICT`
  by a child holding `0`, `UPDATE p SET k = '-0'` is `UPDATE 1` here, leaving `-0`, and
  `23001` there, and a `real` key answers the same way; with `ON UPDATE CASCADE` the child
  keeps `0` here and reads `-0` there; with no action declared the statement is `UPDATE 1`
  on both (measured through the npm package and the native server, both build profiles).
  **Silent** — a child value 18.6 rewrites is left, and a statement 18.6 refuses runs. The
  members are the `numeric` scale, `interval`, `jsonb` and float-zero ones measured; which
  other types' images differ where their `=` does not was not enumerated. No fixture: a faithful one is
  red.

- **200 · An action's conversion is refused over a key no child row references, where 18.6
  refuses it only while the action's plan is a custom one.** 18.6 runs an `ON UPDATE
  CASCADE` as `UPDATE ONLY child SET col = $1 WHERE $2 = col` through SPI, over a plan it
  keeps per constraint for the session. `plancache.c`'s `choose_custom_plan` builds a custom
  plan, the bound key a constant in it (`spi.c`'s `PARAM_FLAG_CONST`), for each of the first
  five executions, and may take a generic plan after. A custom plan folds the assignment
  conversion of `$1` to the child column when the action is planned, so a refused
  conversion refuses the statement though no row matches; a generic plan converts only for
  a row it rewrites. pglet converts once per action event ahead of the lookup
  (`executor::dml`'s `action_assigned_values`) — the custom-plan answer, at every firing.
  Measured over `pv (k varchar(10) PRIMARY KEY)` and `cv (id int PRIMARY KEY, pk
  varchar(3) REFERENCES pv ON UPDATE CASCADE)`, no row of `cv` referencing the moved key:
  an `UPDATE` moving a key of `pv` to `'abcdef'` is `22001 value too long for type character
  varying(3)` on both engines as the constraint's first firing and as its fifth, after four
  moves of the key in the same session; after five, as its sixth, it is accepted on 18.6
  and `22001` here. At the ninth firing, over a key a row of `cv` references, it is `22001`
  on both.

  **Each row one statement moves is a firing of its own, so no session history is
  needed.** Over `pv` holding `'a'` to `'g'` and `'j'`, with `cv`'s one row referencing
  `'j'`, `UPDATE pv SET k = CASE k WHEN 'f' THEN 'ffffff' ELSE k || 'z' END WHERE k IN ('a',
  'b', 'c', 'd', 'e', 'f')` — six keys moved, the sixth to a value too long for `cv`'s column
  — is `UPDATE 6` on 18.6 and `22001` here, in a fresh session and inside `BEGIN … ROLLBACK`
  alike; an `int2` child of an `int` key, the sixth of six moved keys going to `40000`, is
  `UPDATE 6` there and `22003 smallint out of range` here. The controls, `22001` on both:
  five keys moved with the fifth refused, and six moved with the first refused. **A firing
  whose conversion is refused is not counted**: over a fresh pair of tables of the same
  shape, after four moves, a fifth refused `22001` on both, and then a move of another key no
  child row references to `'ffffff'` is `22001` on both as well — the fifth counted firing,
