  not the sixth. Each measured.

  Loud — a refusal of a statement 18.6 runs, once that key's action has fired five times in
  the session, the rows of the statement itself included. The switch at the sixth firing was
  measured on these shapes alone; the choice is a cost comparison, so another shape may keep
  its custom plan longer. No fixture: a faithful one is red, whether its setup spends the
  five firings or its one `UPDATE` does — the one-statement shape measured inside the
  harness's `BEGIN … ROLLBACK`.

- **~~201~~ · Closed — a statement overwrote pages the last durable slot's tree reaches before
  its own slot was durable.** A commit is durable once its meta slot is written and fsynced
  (`double_meta.rs`'s `save_state`), and a reopen adopts the newest valid slot, so every page
  that slot's tree reaches has to stay as it was until a newer slot is durable. Read in the
  source: `CowBtree::try_gc` frees a superseded page once its `freed_version` is below the
  oldest active snapshot's version, or below the **in-memory** current version when no snapshot
  is active — nothing in it knows which version is durable. A statement can publish several
  versions before its `save_state`: a DDL statement's eager wrapper batch, the commit's own
  batch, and `commit_metadata`'s catalog batch (`persist_catalog_if_changed`) are three
  `apply_batch` calls, and `commit_transaction`'s `release_snapshot` runs `try_gc` between them
  once 100 pages are pending (`vacuum_threshold`). The pages an earlier batch superseded are
  the durable version's, they go back on the free list, and the next batch writes over them.

  Measured before the repair, debug builds, through `crates/pglet/tests/durability.rs`'s DDL
  workload (`t` and 40 rows, `big0` and twelve 60 000-character rows, `DROP TABLE big0`,
  `CREATE TABLE big1`, …): the durable-window check found one write — to page 198, issued by
  `CREATE TABLE big1` — to a page the durable slot's tree reaches. The power-loss image a
  kill leaves there (every issued write landed) reopens with no error and matches no
  acknowledged commit: `information_schema.tables` lists `big1` and `SELECT * FROM big1`
  answers `relation "big1" does not exist`. A real process running `Database::open` over a
  file on tmpfs, `DROP TABLE big0` then `CREATE TABLE big1`, killed with `SIGKILL` at 60
  delays swept over the `CREATE`'s own 414 µs: 4 of 60 reopens adopted that same state.
  A second measurement on the same shape, a release build: 7 of 120 kills left
  `t` reading 0 of its 40 acknowledged rows, with no error, and in other images of the class
  `recover` overflowed its stack (row 205).

  **The failed-commit member.** When the meta-slot write fails, the older slot stays the
  durable one while the in-memory tree has moved past it, so the same rule frees its pages to
  every later statement. Measured with the slot write failing (injected) under `DELETE FROM
  big0` of the twelve long rows: nine writes of the `INSERT` after it landed on pages the
  still-durable slot reaches.

  The native server did not reproduce it in 1 510 kill-9 cycles and 250
  in-statement kills; a scratch trace put its GC at the start of each statement, which keeps
  the window under the threshold — a timing, not a rule (measured, and the placement read from a
  trace). The OPFS store (`PgletBtreePersistent`) runs the same `CowBtree` and
  `DoubleMetaStore` and was not measured. Four records said the opposite: `docs/storage.md`
  (§ File Layout and § Crash Recovery), `btree/CLAUDE.md` and `double_meta.rs`'s module doc
  each said the pages a committed slot references are never overwritten in place.

  **The repair.** `CowBtree::try_gc` bounds its threshold by the store's durable version
  (`PageStore::durable_version`), which `DoubleMetaStore` takes from the adopted slot at
  open and moves only once a `save_state`'s fsync returns — so a failed slot write leaves
  it, and the older slot's pages held. Every host runs that one core. Measured after: the
  durable-window check finds no write over three workloads and after the failed commit;
  the DDL power-loss sweep and 60 `SIGKILL`s of the embedding process adopt only
  acknowledged states. Red on revert, and on a pin one version late, a pin applied only
  while a snapshot is open, and the durable version moved before the fsync (the last
  reddens only the failed-commit check). The residual is row 207: a recovered free list
  that itself names a durable page hands it out. Since row 208's repair a failed slot write
  also fails the store, so no statement follows it until a reopen; the pin is the durable
  slot's **tree** version, and a guard runs it with the slot counter both ahead of that
  version and behind it (`the_pin_is_the_tree_version_not_the_slot_counter`).

- **~~202~~ · Closed — a power-loss image could adopt a slot whose free-list chain page was from
  an earlier commit.** Read in the source: `persist_freelist` writes the new free list into the chain pages
  the alternate slot's previous generation held, and `save_state` writes the slot, both before
  the one `sync` that makes them durable. A device may land the writes issued between two
  syncs in any subset, so the slot can land while a chain page does not; the page it names then
  still holds the list from two commits back, checksum-valid, its ids all below
  `next_page_id`, so `read_freelist_chain` accepts it. Measured before the repair with
  `pglet_testing::power_loss` over a 40-step mixed workload, seeds 1, 3, 4 and 6: 16 to 40
  images per seed, 113 in all, recovered a free list naming live pages (seed 1, boundary 251,
  the slot landing alone: pages 133, 134 and 136). In 72 of the 113, a table created,
  filled with long rows and dropped after the reopen changed rows it did not write, with no
  error. A second harness
  measured the root on it, and the next `INSERT`, over its seed-1 image at boundary 538, died
  with `memory allocation of 6442450944 bytes failed` under `ulimit -v 4G` and grew past
  28 GiB resident without one; the site is row 205's. A kill -9 cannot reach this: the page
  cache holds every issued write (inferred). `save_state`'s comment ("a torn
  chain under a valid slot degrades the free-list gracefully") and `read_freelist_chain`'s
  ("never corruption") said otherwise; a torn page fails its checksum, a stale one did not.

  **The repair** (store magic `PGMR`, v27). The slot records the head chain page's
  checksum (`freelist_crc`) and each chain body its successor's, so `read_freelist_chain`
  stops at a page whose checksum is not the one recorded for it. A per-page version stamp
  was not enough: a retried save of the same slot reuses the same page ids and the same
  version, so a page left by the failed attempt would match. Measured after: none of the
  images of `durability.rs`'s mixed sweep (seed 4, 30 steps — 18 of its images recover a
  live page with the check removed) recovers a live page, and a unit test puts the stale
  page at the head and at the tail. The cost is a leak — the ids past the stale page, and the
  chain pages after it — and a stale page whose CRC32 matches by chance is not caught
  (inferred, about one in 2^32).

- **~~203~~ · Closed — pages superseded but not yet collected when a store closed were leaked for
  good.**
  Read in the source: a superseded page waits in `CowBtree`'s in-memory `pending_gc` until no
  snapshot can reach it and 100 are pending, and only a freed page is written into the
  persisted free list; nothing at open reclaims a page that is neither. Measured before
  the repair: after `durability.rs`'s DDL workload and a clean drop, a reopen accounts for 101
  of 202 allocated pages as neither live, free, nor a free-list chain page. Another probe
  measured 6 to 143 such pages per clean drop and a kill loop that grew a file to 63 MB over
  at most 78 live rows. Space, not data: no row is wrong.

  **The repair.** Every save logs the pages the tree has superseded and not freed, apart
  from the free list: the tree hands the save its pending set (`CowBtree::save_state`), the
  slot carries the log's newest entries — at most 240 — and a floor, the oldest version still
  pending, below which a logged page has been freed since; a save past 240 entries spills them
  into chain pages written once, linked in front of the older ones and released once both
  slots' floors pass them. A reopen takes every logged entry at or past the adopted slot's
  floor as free. The first form of the repair wrote these pages into the free list itself,
  which every save rewrites whole, so with a snapshot held — an idle open block — every
  commit rewrote every page superseded since. Measured (release, `MemBlockIo` under
  `CountingBlockIo`, 2 000 rows, one `UPDATE` a commit, a second connection holding `BEGIN;
  SELECT count(*)`, the last 200 commits): that form wrote 198 494 bytes and 49.4 writes per
  commit after 4 000 commits and 742 853 bytes and 182.3 writes after 16 000, where the base
  wrote 18 430 and 5.5 (22 526 and 6.5 with no snapshot held); with the log, 20 472 bytes and
  5.5 writes after 4 000 and 20 522 and 5.5 after 16 000, against 23 400 and 6.5 with no
  snapshot held — each figure re-measured with that probe, the log's on the tree that keeps
  an empty chain page unwritten (below). A save whose free list
  needed fewer chain pages than its slot's old chain held put the surplus on the in-memory
  free list only, so a close before another save left it named by nothing (2 such pages
  measured; 0 after); the surplus is now listed in the chain being
  written, and a page kept with no id left for it is written empty. Written empty at every
  save, that page cost a page write each commit while the list stayed empty — with a
  snapshot held the list empties, and the probe above read 24 568 bytes and 6.5 writes after
  4 000 commits; a save whose list is empty and whose slot's one chain page already lists
  nothing now leaves that page as it is, so only the first save into each slot after the
  list empties writes it (`a_save_with_nothing_to_list_writes_no_chain_page`). The open-time cost, over
  a store of 100 000 rows of 200 characters, half deleted, 11 343 free ids (median
  of 21 opens, three runs each): 125–153 µs before any of these store repairs, 372–392 µs with the
  first form of this one (row 202's chain checksum and row 207's open-time check beside it),
  302–320 µs now. Timed by phase now: the active slot's chain walk 97–151 µs, row
  207's check 139–157 µs; the alternate slot's retired log is read at its next save, not at
  open (it held 46 pages here). Measured after: every allocated page of four workloads,
  thirty create-fill-drop cycles among them, is live, free or a chain page after a clean
  close, and after every kill and no-write image the power-loss sweeps build. After a fallback
  open — the newer slot torn — the pages only that slot's previous save named are named by
  nothing, for good: its free-list chain pages, and the retired-log pages its walk read past
  the adopted slot's. Measured (debug, `MemBlockIo`, 600 rows, a block held open on a second
  connection over N one-statement range `UPDATE`s, then committed, then the next save torn):
  4 pages leaked after N = 150 — the torn slot's three-page
  retired chain, read page by page, and one page beside the adopted slot's chain page, read
  as the torn slot's free-list chain — and 15 after N = 600, so the count
  grows with how long the snapshot was held; with one more save between the commit and the
  tear, 2 and 7; none of them came back over 50 more commits. Not repaired: only the torn
  slot named those pages and its bytes are gone, so reclaiming them needs the adopted slot to
  record the other slot's pages — a change to what a slot persists, not to the release rule.

  A save that stops between its chain-page writes and its slot write leaks too, for good.
  Measured with each
  slot's chain printed (debug, `MemBlockIo`, a probe over a
  churned store whose two slots each name a one-page chain, the active slot `[141]` and the
  alternate `[142]`; an autocommit `INSERT` writes its batch, the data `fsync`, one chain
  page, then the slot): with the slot write refused, and with the chain page's write
  landing and then refused, the store fails as it should, the image's alternate chain walks
  to nothing, and it audits `leaked = [142]`; after twelve reopens of three commits each,
  `142` is still named by nothing. A sweep over the refusal's positions reports `leaked = 1` in each of its
  76 cells whose refusal landed there. A kill between the two writes leaves the same image
  (inferred: the page cache holds the chain write). Read in the source: `persist_freelist`
  rewrites every page of the alternate slot's old chain it keeps — the head always, a
  non-empty old chain keeping at least one page, except one page that already lists
  nothing with nothing to list, left as it is — and lists the rest only in the chain it
  writes; the next open walks the old chain from its head, whose checksum no longer
  matches, so the walk holds nothing, and the whole old chain is in no chain, no list and
  no tree (a multi-page old chain read, not measured). Space, not data.

  Not repaired, by choice, though a local fix exists: take the new chain's pages off the
  free list and rewrite only the old chain's last page, which the walk then reaches and
  holds although its checksum no longer matches. Tried, it reddens seven of `double_meta.rs`'s unit tests, each pinning the old placement
  rather than finding a defect of it — each of the seven measured, and its message read against its test: chain pages fresh from `next_page_id`, a free list's exact size
  across reopens, an allocation served from the free list, a setup that overwrites the
  pages the old placement makes a chain (under the attempt, ids past the file's end), and
  a crafted list that names
  the id the attempt makes the chain page, so the reopen correctly recovers `[3]` where the
  pin wants `[3, 4]`. Under it the whole-engine durability,
  server and crash tests are green (measured); whether it closes the leak is not measured, the
  probe reaching no chain write under its placement. Its cost is why it is not landed: the
  page its walk stops at is rewritten at the slot's next save, which for a crafted slot
  naming a live page with a wrong checksum is that live page — widening row 207's trust, for
  a leak of one chain's pages (read, not measured).

- **~~204~~ · Closed — a crash while a store was being created left a file every open refused.** Read in the
  source: a new store is `set_len` to the 128 KiB of the two meta slots, then slot A is
  written, then one `sync`. Measured before the repair: the power-loss image where the `set_len`
  lands and slot A's write does not is a 128 KiB zero file, and open answers `double-meta:
  both meta slots are invalid (unrecoverable corruption)` on every start, though the store
  never acknowledged anything. A store that acknowledged a commit that wrote a page cannot
  look like this: data pages sit past the slots, and the store never shrinks its file.

  **The repair.** With no valid slot, open creates the store afresh when the file is no
  longer than the two slots and every byte of it is zero — what `set_len` without the
  slot write leaves — and refuses anything else, so a foreign or damaged small file is not
  overwritten, and a store that held a page is refused even with both slots zeroed.

- **~~205~~ · Closed — a B+tree page that names an ancestor as its child made a walk
  unbounded.** Read in
  the source: `find_leaf_from` and `find_leaf_with_path_ws` loop down child pointers with no
  bound, and `collect_range` recurses through them; only the overflow-chain walk
  (`walk_chain`) bounds itself. Measured before the repair: row 202's seed-1 image
  whose next `INSERT` asked for 6 GiB, rerun with a temporary panic once
  `find_leaf_with_path_ws`'s path passed 100 000 entries — it fired at page 56, the path of
  an `INSERT`'s commit batch, so the allocation is that `Vec` doubling past 2^28 entries
  (6 442 450 944 bytes is 2^28 × 24; that 24 is a path element's size is inferred). The
  other members are earlier measurements: a crafted internal page pointing at the root made a
  point read loop until killed, and in row 201's
  images `BtreeStorageWrapper::recover` overflowed its stack in 4 of 8 runs.
  The wasm build shares the walkers and was not measured.

  **The repair.** `find_leaf_from`, `find_leaf_with_path_ws` and `collect_range` each keep
  the pages the walk has entered and refuse a page reached twice as
  `PageStoreError::CorruptTree`, so no walk visits more pages than the store holds, and
  `collect_range` walks from its own stack rather than recursing. Measured after: a page
  naming the root is refused by a point read, a scan and an insert; a child two pages name
  is refused by a scan; a 60 000-deep chain of pages is walked. With the check removed
  from the write descent, the unit test grew past the 8 GiB cap of its scope and was
  killed; from the point read, it looped until killed.

- **~~206~~ · Closed — a batch that failed after allocating page ids leaked them.** Read in the source:
  `apply_batch` returns an I/O error from `put_batch`, from the data `flush`, or from a chain
  walk inside the batch without returning `ws.created` to the free list — only the
  `Overfull` refusal does — and the next successful commit persists a `next_page_id` past
  them. A leak, not corruption: no root reaches those ids.

  **The repair.** Every error after the working set exists — a refused change, any
  `put_batch` error, a failed flush — returns the batch's fresh ids to the free list.
  Measured with the fix reverted: an `INSERT` failing at its `fsync`, one failing at its
  second page write, then one that succeeds, left pages neither live nor free after a
  reopen. A refused write the file store survives (row 208) hands them back there too:
  `durability.rs`'s `a_failed_batch_leaks_no_page` commits after one, closes, and finds
  every allocated page live, free or a chain page.

- **207 · The recovered free list is trusted not to hold live ids.** Read in
  the source: `read_freelist_chain` appends every id a checksum-valid chain page lists, below
  `next_page_id`, with no check for an id listed twice or one the adopted tree reaches;
  `allocate` then hands each out. A well-formed store does not write either. A crafted image
  can, since the page checksum vouches for the bytes and not for what they claim — the same
  gap row 202's stale page falls through. Not measured.

  **Narrowed.** Open now drops an id listed twice and an id that is one of either slot's
  chain pages (`a_recovered_free_list_hands_each_id_out_once`). An id the adopted tree
  reaches is still trusted: telling needs a walk of the whole tree at open, which the
  startup budget rules out. Row 202's repair makes a chain page from another commit
  stop the walk, so what is left is a page the slot's own commit wrote wrong.

- **~~208~~ · Closed — a commit whose durable write fails still took effect.** Read in the source: every
  host publishes a commit in memory before it writes the meta slot — the embed
  `Database::publish_autocommit`, the explicit `COMMIT` (`TransactionSession::commit`) and
  the native server's `Connection::publish_autocommit` each run `storage.commit` (its
  `apply_batch` publishes the new root to every reader) and only then `save_state`. A
  `save_state` error is returned to the client, nothing takes the published root back, and
  the next successful `save_state` writes the current root, which holds it. Measured before
  the repair, a debug build, over `MemBlockIo` with the slot write failing (injected) for one
  statement: an autocommit `INSERT` answers `auto-commit persist failed …`, yet the same
  connection and another one both read its row, and a reopen before the next commit does not;
  a block whose `COMMIT` fails goes aborted, the client's `ROLLBACK` answers `ROLLBACK`, and
  the row is still read by both connections; a `CREATE TABLE u` whose slot write fails
  answers the error and `SELECT count(*) FROM u` then answers `0`; after one more successful
  `INSERT`, a reopen holds every one of them. The server path was read, not run. What makes
  it reachable is a write or `fsync` the device refuses — a full disk, an I/O error, an OPFS
  quota — none of which was measured on a real device.

  Silent: the client that saw the error, or that rolled the block back, has the write
  anyway. No fixture can drive it — the harness has no way to fail a write. The one guard
  that fails a slot write (`durability.rs`'s `a_failed_commit_leaves_the_durable_slot_protected`)
  runs two statements after the failure and requires them to succeed; it checks which pages
  they write, not what any connection reads.

  **The repair.** A write or `fsync` the device refuses fails the store: `DoubleMetaStore`
  records the first one (`WriteFailure`) and refuses every later read, write and save,
  since the tree may hold a published commit the store can no longer make durable and a
  refused slot write or `fsync` may have landed. The statement meeting it answers `58030`
  (`Error::DurableWriteFailed`; `Error::DurableWriteUnconfirmed`, whose message says the
  outcome is unknown until a reopen, for a refused slot write or the `fsync` after it, and
  for a block's `COMMIT` — healthy or aborted — once a save has made a catalog change of the
  block's durable — row 211);
  `Database`'s entry check answers every later call `57P02`
  (`Error::DatabaseMustBeReopened`), and the native server ends each connection at its next
  message with `FATAL 57P02` and refuses a new one `FATAL 57P03`, reading the record
  without its storage lock. A reopen reads the durable slot alone. The shape follows 18.6
  (the PostgreSQL source): a failed WAL write or flush is `PANIC` with `errcode_for_file_access`,
  every other backend is told `57P02` and ended, and a new connection is refused `57P03`
  until recovery; unpublishing the root instead was rejected, since a lock-free reader may
  already hold it. Four DDL sites that ignore their storage call's error
  (`storage.create_table`, `drop_table` twice, `add_column`) now pass this one through —
  without that, a `CREATE TABLE` meeting a refused page write answered `57P02` instead of
  `58030`. Measured after, over `MemBlockIo`: each of an autocommit `INSERT`, a block's
  `COMMIT` and a `CREATE TABLE`, under a failed slot write, page write and `fsync`,
  answers `58030`; a read on that connection and on another, a `ROLLBACK`, a write and
  `Database::sync` then answer `57P02`; and a reopen holds the pre-failure rows and no
  `u`. The OPFS store runs the same `DoubleMetaStore` and was not run.

  **Narrowed: a refusal the statement can drop no longer fails the store.** The repair
  failed it on every refused write, and four of the nine cells of its guard pinned that as
  the requirement (an autocommit write and a `COMMIT`, each under a refused page write and
  a refused `fsync`; the two `CREATE TABLE` cells under those faults are ones the narrowed
  rule still fails, for the catalog): a write refused before anything was published — the
  one batch of an autocommit write or of a `COMMIT`, at a page write or its data `fsync` — publishes
  nothing (`apply_batch` refuses before `publish_root`), yet the statement answered `58030`
  and the store `57P02` until a reopen, where the engine before the repair served on (its
  own guard committed after such a refusal), and 18.6 answers a data file it cannot extend with an `ERROR`
  (`mdextend`, `53100` for `ENOSPC`) and serves on. Now the store answers a refused page
  write or data `fsync` as `WriteRefused` and the tree decides
  (`CowBtree::settle_refusal`): the batch is dropped, its ids handed back, and the store
  serves on when its caller says the batch is the whole of what it did — the wrapper's
  commit of a transaction that did no DDL there, from a block or from an autocommit
  statement of no catalog-writing kind (`pglet::autocommit_is_discardable`; a sequence
  advance is not one). A block whose `COMMIT` meets it ends rolled back,
  its catalog changes taken back by the rollback, which restores the block whole; a
  rollback whose save of what it restored is refused fails the store. Anything else fails the store as before: a
  refusal of a batch no commit issued (a DDL statement's eager build, a save's catalog
  batch), one in an autocommit statement
  of a catalog-writing kind (the change is live in the session and the autocommit path cannot take it back —
  measured, a `CREATE TABLE` refused at its first write, before anything published, and a
  `TRUNCATE … RESTART IDENTITY` refused at its commit), one in a block holding a table or
  index it created or dropped at the storage layer (measured, a `DROP TABLE`), and every
  refused save. The statement's
  SQLSTATE is now the OS error's, as `errcode_for_file_access` gives it: `53100` for
  `ENOSPC` (`std::io::ErrorKind::StorageFull`), `58030` for any other. Measured over
  `MemBlockIo`, a debug build: five insert shapes — a one-row and a multi-page autocommit
  `INSERT`, one into a `SERIAL` table, and the one-row and the `SERIAL` insert committed
  from a block —
  under a refused first to fourth data write, `fsync` and full disk: 19 cells refused
  before anything published, each answering its code, the rows gone, no page leaked after
  a later commit and a close; 4 refused after a batch published (the `SERIAL` insert's
  catalog batch after its rows), each failing the store; the rest completed. The residual
  is the catalog case, and the code where the OS error carries no kind: the OPFS
  `BlockIo` builds every error as `Other` (read), so a quota there answers `58030`, and
  18.6's other `errcode_for_file_access` classes (`42501`, `53000`, `53200`, and its
  default, `XX000`, for any errno it does not name — `EFBIG`, `EDQUOT`; read, `elog.c`) are
  not split out.

  **Another connection's unsaved DDL no longer decides.** As first narrowed, the tree also
  refused to drop a batch while any version past the durable one was published — a belt
  under the callers' conditions — so on the server one client's open block holding a
  `CREATE TABLE` or `CREATE INDEX` (its eager batch published, unsaved) turned another
  client's unrelated full-disk `INSERT` into `53100` then `57P02` on every connection
  (measured twice before the change; a `CREATE SEQUENCE`,
  which publishes nothing, did not). The belt
  is gone: whether a refusal fails the store is the refused statement's own effects. Before
  removing it, measured with it removed (debug, `MemBlockIo`): 44 statement
  shapes and four more under three faults, all 102 served cells clean — the dump (sequence
  counters aside), eleven
  reads and the storage index count unchanged across the refusal, a later commit reading the
  same live and after a reopen, the image auditing clean — including the shapes where the refused block had
  itself published and only the belt failed the store: a `CREATE INDEX`, a `CREATE TABLE …
  PRIMARY KEY` and an `ADD … UNIQUE`, each undone by a `ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT` before the
  `COMMIT` (the undo sheds the index; the table's directory entry stays in the tree at an id
  recovery skips, as after a successful `COMMIT`); and a block re-creating an enum
  a column still declares, whose eager index rebuild the rollback re-derives — there, under
  the faults driven, each of which keeps failing once armed, the rollback's own
  rebuild met the same refusal and failed the store. So no shape driven depended on the belt
  for a clean answer. After: the server cells serve on, the block's `COMMIT` succeeds, and a
  reopen holds its DDL and the one earlier row. The enum block had one more cell, measured
  twice (debug, `MemBlockIo`):
  under a **one-shot** refusal —
  any of the `COMMIT`'s first five data writes, or its data `fsync` — the rollback's rebuild
  succeeds and the block is dropped, the store serving and every read, the dump and a reopen
  after three later commits clean; that cell the belt alone had failed. Under a full disk at
  any of the first four data writes, or a data `fsync` that keeps failing, the store fails and a reopen reads the
  database as before `BEGIN` — an over-refusal of the residual's kind, since 18.6 answers a
  data file it cannot extend with an `ERROR`. The same holds, measured here, for a block whose
  `COMMIT` is refused after another connection saved its DDL (row 211): its rollback saves
  the restored catalog, and a save refused by a fault that persists fails the store,
  answering that the `COMMIT`'s outcome is unknown.

  **The server recovers by itself.** Read in the source before: after a failure,
  `handle_message` answered every message on every connection `FATAL 57P02` and every
  startup `FATAL 57P03`, and nothing reopened the store or exited, so the process kept
  running and refusing — a supervisor restarting on failure saw a live process, and 18.6,
  whose postmaster ends every backend, runs crash recovery and accepts again
  (`restart_after_crash`, on by default), needs no operator. Now the server holds the state
  new connections are served from (`server::Server`), and the next connection it accepts
  after a failure is served from the store reopened from its durable slot; each connection
  still on the failed store ends at its next message, and the data-dir lock, which the
  server rather than a state holds, is held throughout. In the process rather than by an
  exit: the failed store refuses every page write, save and tree-page read before touching
  the file, a connection never leaves the state it started on, and a restart would read
  the file through the same kernel page cache. A tree-page read that passed that check
  just before the failure was recorded read the file afterwards unchecked: measured
  (debug, `MemBlockIo`), an index lookup whose page read
  was held while the store failed and a store reopened over the bytes rewrote that page
  answered no rows, no error, where the table held one — 1 of 32 gated reads. The read
  now checks the failure again once its bytes are read, before any of them is used;
  the new store exists only after the record, so a read that sees its bytes sees the
  record (inferred from the order, not from a memory-model argument over a real file).
  Measured after, each cold read gated in turn: an index lookup, a primary-key lookup and
  a scan embedded (32 reads) and an index lookup and a scan on the server's read path (31)
  each answer `57P02`. Measured over a loopback socket (`serve`, `MemBlockIo`):
  after a refused slot write, a reconnect reads exactly the durable rows and writes
  durably, the failed connection and an idle one in a block each answer their next query
  `FATAL 57P02` and close, and a second attempt on the data-dir lock fails before and after
  the reopen; a reopen that fails refuses that startup `57P03` and the next one is served. An
  idle connection learns of the failure at its next message, where 18.6 ends it at once.

  **An over-refusal: a commit whose only write is the catalog.** Measured (debug,
  `MemBlockIo`, a full disk armed just before the commit): a block's `COMMIT` whose block ran
  only a `CREATE SEQUENCE`, an `ALTER SEQUENCE … START WITH`, a `CREATE INDEX`, a `CREATE
  TABLE`, a `SELECT nextval` — alone or before a `CREATE SEQUENCE` — and an autocommit
  `SELECT nextval` each answer `53100` (`DurableWriteFailed`) and fail the store, a reopen
  holding none of it; the same `CREATE SEQUENCE` behind an `INSERT` in the block, and a
  block of one `SERIAL` insert, answer `WriteRefused` and serve on; an empty block and one
  of `SELECT 1` commit. Read in the source: with no staged rows the commit publishes
  nothing, so its first write is the save's catalog batch (`persist_catalog_if_changed`),
  which no caller can drop, and its refusal fails the store; with rows, the rows' batch is
  refused first, where the commit can drop it, and the block is rolled back instead. An
  in-place counter advance changes the catalog's bytes, so a lone `nextval` takes the same
  road. The refused catalog batch published nothing, so by this row's own rule — whether a
  refusal fails the store is decided by the refused statement's own effects — the commit
  could be dropped as the one with an `INSERT` in front is: this is an over-refusal, not a
  write that took effect. Its widest member is the autocommit `nextval`: a full disk fails
  the store at the first one. A rollback that leaves a counter advanced takes the same road,
  its counter save (row 214) being a catalog-only write: a `ROLLBACK` after a `nextval`,
  or an aborted block's `COMMIT`, under a full disk answers `53100` and fails the store
  (measured). Not repaired.

  **A refused save is answered as an unknown outcome.** Measured before the change (debug,
  `MemBlockIo`, the meta `fsync` refused after the slot's bytes were written, as a failed
  writeback leaves them in the page cache): an autocommit `INSERT` and a block's `COMMIT`
  each answered `58030` "could not make the statement durable", and a reopen served the row
  — a client that retried it would have written it twice (inferred). Now a refusal at the
  slot write or the `fsync` after it answers `Error::DurableWriteUnconfirmed`, same SQLSTATE,
  whose message says whether the statement persists is unknown until a reopen; the definite
  `DurableWriteFailed` is left to refusals before any slot naming the statement's writes was
  written — measured, a `SERIAL` insert whose catalog batch is refused after its rows, which
  the reopen does not hold — and not after a save that made part of it durable: a block's
  `COMMIT` whose refusal fails the store after a save that wrote a catalog change of the
  block's answers the unknown outcome too, the `COMMIT` of an aborted block, which 18.6
  converts to a rollback, included — and so does one whose durable catalog holds a change
  another connection committed during the block, nothing of the block durable (row 211). It is still an `ERROR` on its connection, where 18.6's `PANIC`
  ends the connection; the server ends it at its next message (`57P02`).

- **209 · A delete that empties a B+tree leaf leaves the empty leaf in the tree.** Read in the
  source: `cow_delete_leaf_ws` removes the entry and writes the leaf back whatever it holds,
  and no path removes an empty leaf from its parent or merges it into a sibling (the write
  path's own comment: "simplified: no rebalancing"). A row's key
  is its table id and a row id that only grows, and a dropped table's id is not reused, so in
  the workloads measured no later write lands in an emptied leaf's key range. Measured on the
  file store (debug, after the retired-log repair), a clean close audited: 100 cycles of
  `CREATE TABLE x`, 20 rows of 300 characters, then `DROP TABLE x` — or `DELETE FROM x`, or
  `TRUNCATE x`, over a table created once — each leave 201 leaves of which 200 are empty, and
  no page leaked; a queue of 200-character rows, 3 000 inserts each deleting the row 100
  back, leaves 333 leaves of which 322 are empty. Measured earlier, 300 drop cycles left 600
  of 601 leaves empty, and a queue keeping 10 rows none — its rows fit one leaf, the one leaf
  it holds at close, which is why it once read as
  a batch-only shape. About 4 KiB of file per emptied leaf, the space of the per-test create-and-drop
  fixture pattern, and the in-memory store holds the same pages in memory (inferred: one
  tree code for both stores, not run).

  Silent, as space: no row is wrong. Not repaired: removing an empty leaf means removing
  its separator from the parent and handling a parent left with its first child alone, up
  to the root — a change to the tree's structure beyond the batch that empties the leaf.
  No guard.

- **167 · A parenthesized query's own clauses are applied before the clauses written after
  it, where 18.6 merges the two.** `gram.y`'s `insertSelectOptions` moves an `ORDER BY`,
  `OFFSET` or `LIMIT` written after a parenthesized query into that query, which then
  sorts, offsets and limits once, in that order. pglet merges only its record of which
  clauses are present (`QueryClauses::merge`, which refuses a clause both halves carry, as
  18.6 does) and plans the parenthesized query with its own clauses, then the later clauses
  over its output (`plan_set_op_order_limit`). The two agree where the later clause runs
  after the earlier one in 18.6's order anyway — measured, a `LIMIT` after an `OFFSET` or an
  `ORDER BY`, and an `OFFSET` after an `ORDER BY` — and disagree where 18.6 runs it first: an
  `OFFSET` after a `LIMIT`, and an `ORDER BY` after a `LIMIT` or an `OFFSET`. Measured over
  `s` holding `1` to `5`, inserted in that order: `(SELECT x FROM s ORDER BY x LIMIT 3)
  OFFSET 1` is `2, 3` here and `2, 3, 4` there; `(… LIMIT 1) OFFSET 1` is no row against
  `2`; `(SELECT x FROM s LIMIT 3) ORDER BY x DESC` is `3, 2, 1` against `5, 4, 3`; and
  `(SELECT x FROM s OFFSET 3) ORDER BY x DESC` is `5, 4` against `2, 1`; a set operation
  inside the parentheses the same, `(SELECT x FROM s UNION ALL SELECT x FROM s LIMIT 3)
  OFFSET 1` `2, 3` against `2, 3, 4`. A clause the parenthesized query already carries is
  `42601` on both engines. It writes: `WITH c
  AS ((SELECT x FROM s ORDER BY x LIMIT 3) OFFSET 1) DELETE FROM s WHERE x IN (SELECT x FROM
  c)` is `DELETE 2` here and `DELETE 3` there, and `INSERT INTO s SELECT * FROM ((SELECT x
  FROM s LIMIT 3) ORDER BY x DESC) q` copies `1, 2, 3` where 18.6 copies `3, 4, 5`. The
  `WITH RECURSIVE` spelling of a CTE that does not name itself carries it too (row 157):
  `WITH RECURSIVE c2 AS ((SELECT x FROM s ORDER BY x LIMIT 3) OFFSET 1) DELETE FROM s WHERE
  x IN (SELECT x FROM c2)` is `DELETE 2` here and `DELETE 3` there, and `SELECT * FROM c2`
  under the same list is `2, 3` against `2, 3, 4`. Before row 157's repair both statements
  were `42601` here, so the repair turned a loud refusal into a silent read and a silent
  write. Nested in a derived table inside such a CTE the stacking was already silent before
  the repair: `WITH RECURSIVE c2 AS (SELECT * FROM ((SELECT x FROM s LIMIT 3) ORDER BY x
  DESC) q) SELECT * FROM c2` was `3, 2, 1` here then and is now, against `5, 4, 3`. An
  `ORDER BY` key the parenthesized query does not project binds against that query's output
  here and against its tables there, and that half needs no `LIMIT` or `OFFSET` inside the
  parentheses: the same arm plans a parenthesized query that carries no clause of its own
  first and sorts its output after. Over `t(a, b)` holding `(1, 2), (2, 1)` and `tgt`
  holding `1` and `2`, `(SELECT a FROM t) ORDER BY b` and `(SELECT a FROM t LIMIT 5) ORDER
  BY b` are each `42703` here where 18.6 answers `2, 1`, and so are `SELECT * FROM
  ((SELECT a FROM t) ORDER BY b) q`, `INSERT INTO tgt SELECT * FROM ((SELECT a FROM t)
  ORDER BY b) q`, which 18.6 runs and inserts two rows, and `WITH c AS ((SELECT a FROM t
  LIMIT 5) ORDER BY b) DELETE FROM tgt WHERE a IN (SELECT a FROM c)` and its spelling
  without the `LIMIT`, which 18.6 runs. A key the query projects agrees: `(SELECT a FROM
  t) ORDER BY a DESC` is `2, 1` on both. In a CTE the
  statement never reads, the key is not bound here, so the same CTE beside `DELETE FROM tgt
  WHERE a = 1` runs on both engines; a key neither engine can bind there is row 30's.

- **168 · A plain `UPDATE`'s or `DELETE`'s foreign-key action raises ahead of its
  `RETURNING`.** `execute_update` runs its `ON UPDATE` actions (`FkTriggerQueue`) once its
  rows are written, and `execute_delete` plans its `ON DELETE` actions
  (`plan_delete_cascade`) before it removes a row, and both project `RETURNING` last, so a
  refusal an action raises — a `NO ACTION` key's `23503`, a `RESTRICT` key's `23001`, a `SET
  NULL` into a `NOT NULL` column's `23502` — comes ahead of the `RETURNING` projection, and
  an error the projection would raise is never reached. 18.6 projects
  `RETURNING` for each row as it writes it and fires the actions once the statement's plan
  has run. Measured over `p(id INT PRIMARY KEY, v INT)` holding `(1, 1), (2, 2)` and a
  child `c` holding `1` and `2`: with `c(pid INT REFERENCES p)`, `UPDATE p SET id = 9 WHERE
  id = 1 RETURNING 1/(id - 9)`, the child's own key in `UPDATE c SET pid = 99 WHERE pid = 1
  RETURNING 1/(pid - 99)`, and `DELETE FROM p WHERE id = 1 RETURNING 1/(id - 1)` are
  `23503` here and `22012` there; with `ON UPDATE RESTRICT ON DELETE RESTRICT`, `23001` for
  each against `22012`; with `pid INT NOT NULL REFERENCES p ON UPDATE SET NULL ON DELETE SET
  NULL`, `23502` for each against `22012`. A data-modifying CTE carries it: `WITH w AS
  (UPDATE p SET id = 9 WHERE id = 1 RETURNING 1/(id - 9)) SELECT * FROM w` and its `DELETE`
  twin give the same pair over each of the three children. Each engine refuses the
  statement; only the code differs. Each divisor reads the row it projects, so 18.6 cannot
  fold it: `UPDATE p SET id = 9 WHERE false RETURNING 1/(id - 9)` and `DELETE FROM p WHERE
  false RETURNING 1/(id - 1)` return no row on both engines. A constant divisor says
  nothing about the order — 18.6 folds `1/0` at plan time (row 60's `1/0` member), so
  `UPDATE p SET id = 9 WHERE false RETURNING 1/0` is `22012` there over no row and returns
  no row here. What the projection reads when no action refuses is
  row 164's. The `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` spelling runs its actions after its `RETURNING`:
  `INSERT INTO p VALUES (1, 0) ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET id = 9 RETURNING 1/(p.id -
  9)` is `22012` on both engines over each of the three children. Where the second error is
  a later row's own constraint rather than an action, the order is row 170's.

- **170 · A written row's own checks, a foreign key's included, run before any `RETURNING`
  is projected.** `execute_insert` and `execute_update` check and write every row the
  statement touches and then project `RETURNING` over the collected rows
  (`finish_returning`). 18.6 checks and writes a row and projects its `RETURNING` before it
  takes the next row (`nodeModifyTable.c`), so an earlier row's projection error is raised
  before a later row is checked. Measured over `p(id INT PRIMARY KEY, v INT CHECK (v <
  100))` holding `(1, 1), (2, 2)`: `UPDATE p SET v = v * 60 WHERE id IN (1, 2) RETURNING
  1/(id - 1)` is `23514` here and `22012` there, and so are `INSERT INTO p VALUES (1, 0),
  (2, 0) ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET v = p.v * 60 RETURNING 1/(p.id - 1)`, `INSERT INTO p
  VALUES (3, 1), (4, 200) RETURNING 1/(id - 3)` and `WITH w AS (UPDATE p SET v = v * 60
  WHERE id IN (1, 2) RETURNING 1/(id - 1)) SELECT * FROM w`. With `v INT NOT NULL` in place
  of the `CHECK`, `UPDATE p SET v = CASE WHEN id = 2 THEN NULL ELSE v END WHERE id IN (1, 2)
  RETURNING 1/(id - 1)` and `INSERT INTO p VALUES (3, 1), (4, NULL) RETURNING 1/(id - 3)`
  are `23502` against `22012`, and `INSERT INTO p VALUES (3, 1), (3, 2) RETURNING 1/(id -
  3)` is `23505` against `22012`. Two controls answer `23514` on both engines: `UPDATE p SET
  v = v * 60 WHERE id IN (1, 2) RETURNING 1/(id - 2)`, whose divisor fails on the row whose
  `CHECK` fails, and `INSERT INTO p VALUES (3, 200), (4, 1) RETURNING 1/(id - 4)`, whose
  first row fails its `CHECK`. A foreign key the written row references reaches further,
  because 18.6 queues that check until the statement's plan has run (row 166) while pglet
  runs it as the row is written. Over `p(id INT PRIMARY KEY, v INT)` holding `(1, 1), (2,
  2)` and `c(pid INT REFERENCES p, x INT)` holding `(1, 10)`, `INSERT INTO c VALUES (99, 0)
  RETURNING 1/(pid - 99)` — one row, no key `99` in `p` — is `23503` here and `22012` there,
  and so are `INSERT INTO c VALUES (1, 0), (99, 0) RETURNING 1/(pid - 1)` and `UPDATE c SET
  pid = 99 WHERE x = 10 RETURNING 1/(pid - 99)`; over `c2(id INT PRIMARY KEY, pid INT
  REFERENCES p)` holding `(1, 1)`, `INSERT INTO c2 VALUES (1, 0) ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE
  SET pid = 99 RETURNING 1/(c2.pid - 99)` is the same pair. Each engine refuses the
  statement; only the code differs. Row 168 is the foreign-key action's counterpart, whose
  refusal comes from a plan run before any row is written.

- **80 · pglet has no raw-parse phase to hang the `WITH` scan on, so its walk raises
  eagerly.** 18.6 raw-parses the whole statement, then scans the list for duplicate names,
  then analyses each body; pglet's walk parses, plans and checks each declaration in turn,
  and fires the deferred duplicate and arity verdicts once the list has parsed.

  **Under a plain `WITH`**, measured against 18.6: a body error pglet raises at plan time
  pre-empts a later duplicate — `WITH c AS (SELECT nosuchcol FROM t), c AS (SELECT 1)
  SELECT 1` is `42703` here and `42712` there — and an earlier item's arity error —
  `WITH c(a,b) AS (SELECT 1), q AS (SELECT nosuch FROM t) SELECT 1` is `42703` here and
  `42P10` there; and a deferred verdict pre-empts the statement body's syntax error —
  `WITH c AS (SELECT 1), c AS (SELECT 2) SELECT FROM FROM` is `42712` here and
  `WITH c(a,b) AS (SELECT 1) SELECT FROM FROM` `42P10`, where 18.6 is `42601` for both.

  **Under `WITH RECURSIVE` the list is read by a token pre-scan first, and a failure to
  resolve it is re-parsed** (`parser::with_recursive`): a recorded duplicate, then an arity
  verdict an item resolved before the failing one recorded, outrank the failure, and the
  first syntax error the re-parse reaches — each body in declaration order, then the
  statement body — outranks all of it; a deferred verdict takes the same re-parse. So
  `recursive_cte_columns`'s eager arity check, which still runs as a self-referencing item
  parses, no longer decides the statement's error against a later body's syntax error, a
  duplicate or an earlier item's arity error (`syntax_error_outranks_an_eager_arity_loud`,
  `duplicate_outranks_an_eager_arity_loud`, `earlier_arity_error_outranks_a_later_eager_one_loud`),
  and each plain-`WITH` member above answers 18.6's code under `RECURSIVE`. What the
  re-parse does not reach is a syntax error behind a non-syntax error: `WITH RECURSIVE a AS
  (SELECT * FROM b), b AS (SELECT * FROM a), c AS (SELECT (SELECT nosuch FROM t) FROM t
  WHERE FROM) SELECT 1`, and the same scalar subquery ahead of `WHERE FROM` in the
  statement body, are `0A000 mutual recursion …` here and `42601` there. And the
  self-reference verdicts a set operation inside a recursive term decides — `… within
  INTERSECT`, `… within EXCEPT` — are judged as that body parses, so they follow the
  analysis of every body resolved before it, where 18.6 judges every item before analysing
  any: `WITH RECURSIVE a AS (SELECT nosuch FROM t1), r(n) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL (SELECT n+1
  FROM r WHERE n<3 EXCEPT ALL SELECT 9)) SELECT 1` is `42703` here and `42P19` there, and
  declared the other way round answers `42P19` on both.

  **A token pre-pass alone is a net loss**, measured: hoisting the duplicate scan ahead of
  the bodies answers `42712` to `WITH c AS (SELECT FROM FROM), c AS (SELECT 1)` where 18.6
  is `42601`, since no token scan can tell a well-formed body from a malformed one. That
  is why the recursive path re-parses for the syntax error rather than trusting its scan,
  and why the plain path keeps its walk.

- **~~79~~ · Closed — The `WITH` duplicate scan runs before the arity checks and after the bodies'
  syntax.** 18.6 fires both verdicts only after the whole list has parsed, duplicate
  first (`transformWithClause` before `analyzeCTE`), so a duplicate query name whose first
  *declaration* fails its own arity check is `42712` there:
  `WITH c(a,b) AS (SELECT 1), c AS (SELECT 2)` reported that `42P10` here and now reports
  18.6's `42712`. A body's own **syntax** error still outranks both, which is exactly what an
  eager duplicate scan breaks: one answered `42712` to
  `WITH c AS (SELECT 1), c AS (SELECT FROM FROM)` where 18.6 is `42601`. Both verdicts now
  land where 18.6 puts them; row 80 records the eager sites that remain.

- **78 · A FROM item takes no column-alias list.** `FROM t AS k(y)` over a base table,
  `FROM (SELECT …) AS k(y)` over a derived table and `FROM c AS k(y)` over a CTE reference are
  each `42601` here, where 18.6 renames the columns positionally, exactly as a CTE's own
  `name(cols)` list does — and answers
  `42P10 table "k" has 2 columns available but 3 columns specified` to a list longer than the
  item's column count. Only two FROM shapes parse a list here at all,
  `( VALUES … ) AS k(…)` and `unnest(…) AS k(…)`.

  **One gap, two faces.** The plan-time binding gate runs before the end-of-input check, so
  the `42601` is masked whenever the projection also names a column the list would have
  created: `SELECT y FROM t AS k(y)` is `42703 "y"` and `SELECT * FROM t AS k(y)` is the
  `42601`. No `@expect-error` fixture can hold either face, pglet refusing where 18.6 answers;
  the routes that do parse a list are pinned by
  `select/unnest_alias_column_list_too_long_loud.sql`,
  `generate_series/alias_list_too_long_loud.sql` and the `VALUES` route's own arity check.

- **77 · 18.6's other wrong-kind wordings, and the `D` pglet invents for two of them.**
  `validate_relation_kind` answers `42809 cannot open relation "x"` plus
  `This operation is not supported for {indexes,sequences}.` in `D` for every wrong-kind
  route. That is 18.6's own wording for the scan and DML-on-an-**index** routes, and those
  two are pinned as agreeing by `error_fields/open_wrong_kind_detail.sql` and
  `error_fields/drop_wrong_kind_hint.sql`. Four other routes reach the same answer and do
  **not** diverge alike:

  - **(a) `REFERENCES <a sequence>`** and its `ALTER TABLE … ADD FOREIGN KEY` spelling: 18.6
    says `referenced relation "x" is not a table`, with **no `D`**.
  - **(b) `INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE` on a sequence**: 18.6 says `cannot change sequence "x"`,
    with **no `D`**. Measured as the harness's own **superuser** `postgres`; a non-superuser
    — the sequence's own owner included, since a sequence carries no INSERT/DELETE ACL bit —
    gets `42501 permission denied for sequence x` from `aclcheck_error` instead, which is not
    what this corpus compares against.
  - **(c) `ALTER TABLE <an index or sequence>`**: 18.6 says
    `ALTER action ADD COLUMN cannot be performed on relation "x"` **plus the same `D`** pglet
    sends, so there the `D` agrees byte-for-byte and `M` alone diverges. No fixture, and no
    field to compare.
  - **(d) `SELECT * FROM <a sequence>`**: 18.6 answers the sequence's three columns and pglet
    is `42809 cannot open relation`. No fixture.

  The SQLSTATE agrees on every route, so what is recorded is a message divergence: on (a) and
  (b) both `M` and `D` — pglet sending a `D` the oracle omits, an invention by this file's own
  rule — and on (c) `M` alone. Five fixtures carry a justified `-- @no-error-fields:` naming
  18.6's actual wording for their route
  (`sequences/{references,sequence_insert,sequence_update,sequence_delete,add_constraint_references}_*`),
  so (a) and (b) are recorded rather than silenced.

- **76 · Structured error fields still omitted, and the harness scores the omission as
  agreement.** `Error::wire_fields` fills what pglet can fill truthfully and sends nothing
  where it cannot, which is the declared posture (`docs/errors.md`); what that costs is a
  driver reading `undefined` where 18.6 hands it a value. Measured, field by field:

  - **`P`, on a position-bearing SQLSTATE `Error::position` has no arm for** — `42P01`,
    `42703`, `42883`, `22P02`, `42702`, `42804`, `42803`, `42P02` and the
    `0A000 cannot use subquery in check constraint` route, all measured; a **`42701` route**
    — a `PRIMARY KEY`/`UNIQUE` key list naming a column twice, where 18.6's `P` is the
    `Constraint` node's own location (`parser_errposition(cxt->pstate, constraint->location)`
    in `transformIndexConstraint`): the `CONSTRAINT` keyword where one is declared and the
    `PRIMARY`/`UNIQUE` keyword otherwise (`P=24` at
    `CREATE TABLE t (a int, PRIMARY KEY (a, a))`, `P=20` at
    `ALTER TABLE tt ADD CONSTRAINT c UNIQUE (a, a)`), measured at `CREATE TABLE` and
    `ALTER TABLE … ADD`, `PRIMARY KEY` and `UNIQUE`, each named and unnamed. `42701` is
    **not** the predicate there: each `42701` route measured beside it sends no `P` on either
    engine — a repeated column name at `CREATE TABLE` (`MergeAttributes`), a system column
    name at `CREATE TABLE` (`CheckAttributeNamesTypes`) and at `ADD COLUMN`
    (`check_for_column_name_collision`) — as does the foreign key referenced-list repeat's
    `42830` (`transformFkeyCheckAttrs`). This list also holds an **unrecognized type
    name** — `42704` at each caller of `executor::type_resolution`'s `resolve_type_name`
    (`1::nosuchtype`, `nosuchtype 'x'`, `CREATE TABLE … (a nosuchtype)`,
    `ADD COLUMN … nosuchtype`, `CAST(1 AS nosuchtype)`, and the `nosuchtype[]` spelling of
    each but the typed constant, whose grammar takes no `[]` — `nosuchtype[] 'x'` is
    `42601` on both engines) — and a **carrier's type-modifier refusal** (row 124), which
    it gained by that row's measurement and which arrives under the `22023` itself
    (`'ab'::char(0)`, `1.5::numeric(0)`) and under the `int4` coercion of a `numeric`
    component ahead of it, `22003` at `1.5::numeric(2147483648)` and `22P02` at
    `1::numeric(1.5)`. Every one of those `42704`s, and each modifier refusal beside them,
    carries a caret on 18.6 and no `P` here, measured.
    What pglet *does* fill is `Error::position`'s own arms — the `42601`s that carry a token, and `opt_float`'s two
    `22023`s — and that match is the enumeration to re-read rather than this list, which
    grows only by measurement. `Plan` and `Expr` carry no spans, so there is no offset to
    send — which is the `42701` member's reason too, its key list reaching `executor::ddl`'s
    `validate_key_columns` on a `UniqueConstraint` that carries no location. That reason does
    not reach the unrecognized type name or the carrier's modifier refusal:
    `resolve_type_name` takes a type *name* and no span, and two of its four callers are
    the **parser** (`parser::expr`'s cast target and typed constant), where a cursor is in
    hand, so the omission there is the resolver's signature, not the tree's. The SQLSTATE is the
    predicate in neither direction — `opt_float`'s two share the `22023` and fill a `P`,
    and the list's own `22P02` is a **value's** input function's (`'x'::int`), the same
    `Error` variant raised from a value's conversion rather than from a name's resolution.
    This list also holds the **`22025`** of a Unicode escape given too few hex digits
    inside an `E'…'` — measured at the four-digit form given two digits, the eight-digit
    form given seven, and a two-digit form after a pending first surrogate, the three
    spellings `docs/parser.md` § A string literal is assembled in 18.6's units names under *Residuals*, each sent as `SELECT E'…'` — where 18.6's
    `{xeunicodefail}` sends a caret at the escape (`P` `10`, `10` and `16`) and pglet sends none:
    `Error::InvalidUnicodeEscape` is a unit variant, so no position rides it out.
  - **`H`, the near-name hint, on `42703`'s two `errorMissingColumn` routes**, and the
    escape hint on that `22025` — `{xeunicodefail}`'s `errhint`, naming the two escape
    forms, sent by 18.6 at each of the three spellings and by pglet at none, measured; and
    `op_error`'s no-match hint on a `42883` (`No operator matches the given name and argument
    types. You might need to add explicit type casts.`), sent by 18.6 at
    `SELECT 'a' IN ('a') LIKE 'a'` and by pglet at none, measured (row 185).
  - **The `D`+`W` pair on a jsonb `22P02`**, where 18.6 sends `Token "bad" is invalid.` and
    `JSON data, line 1: {bad`: pglet's JSON parser surfaces no failing token.
  - **The `D`, `W` and `P` on a jsonb `22P05`**, the code-point-zero escape inside a jsonb
    string. 18.6 sends a `D` saying the escape cannot be converted to text, the `W`
    `JSON data, line 1: …` and a `P` (`8` at `SELECT '<that string>'::jsonb`), and pglet
    sends none of the three, `Error::UnsupportedUnicodeEscape` being a unit variant —
    measured over a raw wire client on both engines.
  - **The `W` (CONTEXT) on COPY's and a bound parameter's errors**, a field `wire_fields`
    never builds. Measured over a raw wire client on both engines, 18.6 sending each and
    pglet none: `COPY ct, line 1` on a `22021` in COPY's raw input, at an illegal byte and
    at a NUL; `COPY ct, line 1: "<the line>"` on a `22021` in a de-escaped field, at an
    escaped NUL and at an escaped illegal byte; that form on a
    `22P04 extra data after last expected column`, at line 1 and at line 2; and
    `unnamed portal parameter $1` on a text-format bound parameter's `22021`, at a NUL and
    at an illegal byte; and that same `unnamed portal parameter $1` on a **binary**-format
    `jsonb` parameter's version-byte `XX000` (row 138), where 18.6 sends
    `[SVCMWFLR]` and pglet `[SVCM]`.
  - **The `D` on a `numeric` `22003`** —
    `A field with precision 3, scale 1 must round to an absolute value less than 10^2.`,
    sent under 18.6's `numeric field overflow` message rather than pglet's
    `numeric out of range`. The overflow site does not carry the typmod.
  - **The `D` on a non-`CASCADE` `DROP SCHEMA public` over a non-empty schema.** 18.6 lists
    every dependent on its own newline-separated line (`table t depends on schema public`
    times N, measured) and pglet sends none, because `DependentObjectsExist` is raised from a
    schema-emptiness test rather than from an enumeration — there is no list to render.
  - **The `D` on a `CREATE TYPE … AS ENUM` repeated label.** The refusal stands in for a
    collision on 18.6's own catalog index, so 18.6 sends
    `Key (enumtypid, enumlabel)=(<oid>, b) already exists.` beside `s`/`t`/`n` and pglet
    sends `n` alone — raw-wire measured on both engines. The `enumtypid` is a live OID, so
    what is comparable across runs is the field's presence rather than its value. `s`/`t`
    is the declared posture there (pglet's single `IMPLICIT_SCHEMA` would answer `public`
    where 18.6 answers `pg_catalog`) and the `D` is a **gap**: the refusal is
    `Error::UniqueViolation` with `key: None`, so no detail payload is built at all, and the
    payload that would carry the key description carries the relation with it —
    `docs/enums.md` § An enum's labels are a set.

  No fixture can hold any of it by construction: `ErrorFields::divergences` scores pglet's
  omission as agreement, which is exactly what makes the class invisible here rather than
  red.

- **75 · The word is reserved in expression position and unreserved in every name position — a
  state neither engine has.** 18.6 admits none of the eleven in a name position — none is a
  valid `ColId` there — so `CREATE TABLE t (user TEXT)`, `INSERT INTO q (user) VALUES (…)` and
  `UPDATE q SET user = …` are each `42601 syntax error at or near "user"` there — the last two
  measured over `CREATE TABLE q ("user" TEXT, id INT)`, a table 18.6 itself accepts. pglet
  reads the word only where an expression can begin, so all three name positions take it, and
  the eleven `SqlValueFunction` spellings behave alike: `current_date`, `current_time`,
  `current_timestamp`, `localtime`, `localtimestamp`, `current_user`, `session_user`, `user`,
  `current_role`, `current_catalog` and `current_schema`.

  What the acceptance costs is a column that cannot be read by the name it was created with.
  `SELECT user FROM t` answers the role, `WHERE user = <a stored value>` matches nothing and
  `ORDER BY user` orders by a constant; only `"user"` reaches the column, while the `INSERT`
  column list and the `SET` target still write it, being name positions — so the statement that
  fills the column and the statement that reads it disagree about what the bare word means,
  with no error at either. Every statement succeeds, which is what makes the class silent.

- **74 · A bare string literal is `text` here and `unknown` there, so the two-argument session
  functions split.** 18.6 leaves an unquoted literal `unknown` until a signature claims it, and
  both of these signatures take a `boolean`: `current_setting('search_path','x')` is
  `22P02 invalid input syntax for type boolean: "x"` — the literal reaching the boolean input
  function and failing on its *value* — while `current_schemas('t')` **answers**
  `{pg_catalog,public}`, `'t'` being a boolean spelling that input function accepts. pglet
  types the literal `text` where it reads it, so both are `42883` before either value is looked
  at. Loud and pglet-stricter, and the split is why no fixture holds it: 18.6 accepts one of
  the two, so an `@expect-error` over the pair would pin them as though they agreed. Row 54's
  band is the wider statement.

- **73 · pglet models no roles, so `SET ROLE` and `SET SESSION AUTHORIZATION` cannot move the
  session identity.** That identity is the startup packet's claim, echoed: `current_user` and
  `session_user` both answer the role the client connected as, and neither statement is
  refused: each is an accepted no-op of row 67's GUC-echo family. 18.6 assumes the named role
  instead, so `current_user` moves and `session_user` does not, and the two stay apart for the
  rest of the session. Silent: the two spellings agree here whatever was set, which is what
  makes `session/session_user_identity.sql` a guard on the *post*-`SET` state rather than on
  the rule, since it asserts the two agree, which is true here for a reason 18.6 does not
  share.

- **70 · `set_config` reads its setting name as a literal.** The `search_path` decider
  (row 43) is reached from the `set_config` arm at **plan** time, where the setting name
  is an `Expr`. pglet does not constant-fold before lowering, so a computed name —
  `set_config('search' || '_path', 'nosuch', false)`,
  `set_config(lower('SEARCH_PATH'), …)`, `set_config($1, …)` — cannot be proved not to
  be `search_path`, and is **refused** (`0A000`) rather than echoed. A *cast* around a
  literal is not in that set: `'search_path'::text` and `CAST(… AS text)` are peeled to
  the literal, because the cast decides the argument's type and this gate reads its
  value. They used to join the computed names, which made the two spellings of one valid
  request disagree — the parser folds `set_config(('search_path'), …)`'s parentheses away
  and that one always worked. 18.6 accepts all of
  them, so this is a pglet-stricter over-refusal; echoing them instead reproduced row
  43's silent-wrong end to end, which is why the refusal is the posture. Two neighbours
  ride the same plan-time placement and are the rest of this row: a checked GUC's
  **value** that is not a literal is refused too (`set_config('search_path', $1, false)`
  is `0A000` at `Parse`, even for `'public'` — the one shape a driver would
  parameterise, and it displaced a pre-existing `08P01` from the discarded name
  argument), and the gate fires over expressions 18.6 never evaluates: `SELECT
  set_config('search_path','nosuch',false) … WHERE false`, a never-taken `CASE` arm, and
  a `DEFAULT` / `CHECK` at `CREATE TABLE` are all `0A000` here and succeed there. That
  last group is CLAUDE.md's "a gate standing in for *no* Postgres error" class; all of
  it is loud, and all of it closes at once if the check ever moves to eval time — which
  would mean giving `set_config` a real runtime node instead of the `Expr::Alias` its
  measured walker pins depend on.
- **44 · Absent-but-fail-loud surface (generic suites).** These fail loud (correct-or-loud
  holds) but are undocumented as gaps, so a broad generic Postgres suite hits them:
  **`generate_series`** beyond its integer `FROM` item (row 321), most aggregates
  (`array_agg`/`string_agg`/`bool_and`/`bool_or`/`jsonb_agg`/`FILTER`/ordered-set),
  window offset/frame functions (`lag`/`lead`/`ntile`/frames), part of the `func-info`
  surface — `pg_typeof`, `format_type` and `to_regclass` are `0A000`, while `version()`,
  `current_user` and `current_setting` **answer** (measured on the native server:
  `PostgreSQL 18.6 (pglet) on x86_64-linux, 64-bit` and `18.6`) — most jsonb/array
  helper functions (`array_append`, `array_prepend` and `array_length` among those measured
  `0A000`), datetime constructors (`make_*`/`age`/`OVERLAPS`), `to_char` on
  non-timestamp types,
  row-constructor comparison, `ANY/ALL(subquery)`, `SIMILAR TO`,
  `BETWEEN SYMMETRIC`, `TABLE t`, `FETCH FIRST … ROWS ONLY`, `COLLATE`,
  `ARRAY(SELECT …)`, `B'…'`/`X'…'` bit-string literals, `MERGE`,
  `CREATE TABLE … AS SELECT`. The **SQL typed-constant grammar** and
  **`IS [NOT] TRUE/FALSE/UNKNOWN`** were members and are not any more
  ([docs/parser.md](docs/parser.md) § Known lexical / parse divergences).

  **A bare `VALUES` is a member, and its two spellings answer differently.** As a statement
  `VALUES (1,2)` is `0A000`, and as a CTE body `WITH c AS (VALUES (1,2)) …` is `42601`, so a
  `VALUES` relation is reachable here only as a derived table — `FROM (VALUES …) k`, the
  supported way `cte/column_list_values_source.sql` reaches it.

  **The calls a migrator or `pg_dump` makes first are members.** `pg_advisory_lock`,
  `pg_advisory_unlock`, `pg_try_advisory_lock`, `pg_is_in_recovery` and `pg_sleep` each answer
  `0A000 not implemented: function not supported: <name>` (measured on the native server).
  kysely 0.28.8's `Migrator` is no longer stopped: the calls its introspector's `getTables`
  query and its migration lock make — `col_description`, `quote_ident`,
  `pg_get_serial_sequence`, `has_schema_privilege`, `nspname !~ $1` over `'^pg_'`,
  `pg_advisory_xact_lock` — answer (rows 250, 251, 252), and it migrates unstubbed on the npm
  package and on the native server. `pg_dump` cannot read a pglet server: its query `SELECT
  pg_catalog.pg_is_in_recovery()` is refused and it exits `1`; a pglet store's export is
  `pglet_server dump`.

- **~~225~~ · Closed — An `INSERT` whose row length disagrees with its target list answers
  18.6's `42601`, not `22000`; a loud residual stands.** Measured before the repair on the native server against 18.6, over
  `ar1 (i int)` and `ar2 (a int, b int)`:
  - `INSERT INTO ar1 VALUES (1, 2)` and `INSERT INTO ar1 SELECT 1, 2`: `22000 execution
    error: INSERT has 2 expressions but table "ar1" has 1 columns`; 18.6 `42601 INSERT has
    more expressions than target columns`.
  - `INSERT INTO ar1 (i) VALUES (1, 2)` and `INSERT INTO ar1 (i) VALUES (DEFAULT, 1)`:
    `22000 … INSERT has 2 expressions but 1 target columns`; 18.6 the same `42601`.
  - `INSERT INTO ar2 (a, b) VALUES (1)`: `22000 … INSERT has 1 expressions but 2 target
    columns`, and `INSERT INTO ar2 (a, b) SELECT 1`: `22000 … INSERT has 2 target columns
    but the source query produces 1`; 18.6 `42601 INSERT has more target columns than
    expressions` to both.
  - `INSERT INTO ar1 VALUES (1), (2, 3)`: `22000 … INSERT has 2 expressions but table "ar1"
    has 1 columns`; 18.6 `42601 VALUES lists must all be the same length`. Under a column
    list, `INSERT INTO ar2 (a, b) VALUES (1, 2), (3)` is `22000 … INSERT has 1 expressions but
    2 target columns`. With no column list and every row within the table's width, a list
    of different lengths is accepted instead — row 226.
  - The control, `INSERT INTO ar2 VALUES (1)` — a short row with no column list — is `INSERT
    0 1` on both.

  Read in the source: the planner's arity checks (`planner/dml.rs`) raised
  `Error::Execution`, whose SQLSTATE is `22000`. Loud, under the wrong code.

  **What closed it.** The checks raise 18.6's three sentences as `42601`, with no `P` (a
  lowered row carries no spans): `row_length_refusal` for a `VALUES` list — each row's
  length against the first row's, then against the target list, a row shorter than an
  explicit column list refused and one shorter than the table without a list defaulted —
  and `insert_select_target_indices` for an `INSERT … SELECT` source, longer or shorter
  than its column list. Measured after the repair against 18.6 on the native server: each
  statement above answers 18.6's code and sentence, and a row's own cells are resolved
  before its length is compared, so a cell verdict pglet reaches at plan time wins —
  `INSERT INTO t (a, b) VALUES (COALESCE(1, 'x'::text), 2, 3)` is the cell's `42804` on
  both; one it reaches only at execution loses (row 226's residual). An `INSERT … SELECT`
  source's arity is compared ahead of the source's assignment gate and its relation
  resolution, so a source error pglet reaches after it loses too — `INSERT INTO t SELECT
  nosuch, 1, 2` is `42703` on 18.6 and `42601` here, also row 226's residual, where the
  class and its measured members are recorded. `@expect-message` fixtures hold the sentences
  (`insert/insert_*more_*_loud.sql`, `insert/values_lists_length_under_a_column_list_loud.sql`,
  `insert/values_lists_length_yields_to_a_long_first_row_loud.sql`), and the order row 226
  records is that row's.

- **~~226~~ · Closed — A `VALUES` list of different row lengths with no column list is
  refused, where it was accepted with each short row padded with defaults.** Measured
  before the repair on the native server, over `f8a (a INT, b INT
  DEFAULT 7)`: `INSERT INTO f8a VALUES (1, 2), (3)` answers `INSERT 0 2` and stores `1|2`
  and `3|7`; so do `VALUES (4), (5, 6)` (`4|7`, `5|6`) and `VALUES (8), (9, DEFAULT)`, and
  the list with `RETURNING a, b`, which answers `16|17` and `18|7`, and with `ON CONFLICT DO
  NOTHING`. Over `f8b (a INT, b INT NOT NULL)`, `INSERT INTO f8b VALUES (1, 2), (3)` is
  `23502` on `b`. 18.6 refuses such a list in parse analysis, row by row in list order
  (read, not run): `transformInsertStmt`'s one loop over the lists transforms a row,
  compares its length with the first row's — `42601 VALUES lists must all be the same
  length` where they differ — and then takes that same row through `transformInsertRow`
  (the target-list arity check and the assignment coercion) before it reads the next. So a
  row ahead of the first mismatched one meets the target list first, and an error there —
  a first row longer than the table, or a value its column cannot take — is the one 18.6
  answers: which error wins is decided per row, not by a pass over the whole list. Here
  each short row is padded as a one-row `INSERT` would be: the no-column-list arm of the
  planner's arity check (`planner/dml.rs`) refuses only a row longer than the table and
  fills the rest with `DEFAULT`, row by row.
  Under a column list, or with a row longer than the table, the list is refused, under the
  wrong code — row 225. A `VALUES` list in `FROM` answers `42601 VALUES lists must all be
  the same length` here, alone (`SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1, 2), (3)) v`) and as an `INSERT …
  SELECT` source. Silent, and it wrote.

  **What closed it.** `planner::dml`'s `lower_insert_rows` lowers the rows one at a time in
  list order, each whole before the next — its cells resolved, its length against the first
  row's, its length against the target list, each cell's assignment — and the
  `GENERATED ALWAYS` guard, a rewriter check in 18.6, after every row. Which row is refused is
  known from the parsed lengths before any cell is lowered (`row_length_refusal`), and two
  verdicts 18.6 reaches in parse analysis and pglet only as the executor stores a row are
  put through a probe for the rows up to it: a column reference anywhere in a cell
  (`probe_bare_names`, the refused row's own cells included), and a bare string literal's
  input conversion with its enum membership (`probe_literal_input`, the rows before it,
  without the column's length or precision modifier, which 18.6 applies in the planner —
  save `interval`'s, which 18.6 applies at input and the probe does not, a residual member
  below).
  With no refusal nothing is probed. Measured after the repair against 18.6 on the native
  server, each answering as 18.6 does: the statements above are `42601`, `RETURNING` and
  `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` forms included, a list whose rows share one short length is
  padded on both, and the error an earlier row raises wins — `VALUES (1, 'x'), (2)` is
  `22P02`, an enum label the enum lacks `22P02`, `VALUES (1, nosuch + 1), (2)` and
  `VALUES (1, 2), (nosuch)` `42703` — while `VALUES (1, 2), ('x')`, `VALUES (1, 2), (2),
  (3, 'x')`, an over-long `varchar(3)` literal, `1 / 0`, a `GENERATED ALWAYS` value and a
  first row's `DEFAULT` over a `SERIAL` (which then draws nothing) all lose to the
  refusal. The fixtures are `insert/values_lists_*.sql`, and the sequence is
  `crates/pglet/tests/on_conflict_row_affected_twice.rs`'s.

  **Residual, loud: an error pglet reaches only after the length comparison.** 18.6
  transforms a `VALUES` row's cells before it compares the row's length
  (`transformInsertStmt`'s loop runs `transformExpressionList` ahead of the `VALUES lists`
  check, and `transformInsertRow` after both), and an `INSERT … SELECT` source whole before
  its arity (`transformStmt` over the source, then `transformInsertRow`). pglet compares a
  row's length at plan time, after resolving its cells and the probe above, ahead of the
  verdicts it reaches only as the executor stores the row; and an `INSERT … SELECT`
  source's arity ahead of the source's assignment gate and its relation resolution (row
  225's closure). So an error 18.6 raises in a cell's or a source's parse analysis, and
  pglet only after that comparison — in any row up to and including the refused one, a
  one-row `INSERT` included — is answered by the `42601` refusal here. Measured on the npm
  package against 18.6, over `t (a INT, b INT)` and `u (x INT)`; each cell reads 18.6's
  code, then pglet's, then pglet's before the repair — every one already a wrong code:
  - a row ahead of the refused one: `VALUES (1 + '1x', 1), (2)` `22P02` / `42601` /
    `42804`; `VALUES (count(*), 1), (2)` `42803 aggregate functions are not allowed in
    VALUES` / `42601` / `0A000`; over `tj (a INTERVAL(0), b INT)`, `VALUES
    ('2562047788:00:54.4', 1), (2)` `22008 interval out of range` / `42601` / `42804` —
    the literal's input under `interval`'s precision, which 18.6 applies at input and the
    probe does not.
  - the refused row's own cells: `VALUES (1, 2), (1 + '1x')` `22P02` / `42601` / `42804`;
    `VALUES (1, 2), ((SELECT 1 FROM nosuch))` `42P01` / `42601` / `0A000`; `VALUES (1, 2),
    (count(*))` `42803` / `42601` / `0A000`; `VALUES (1, 2), (3, 4, 1 + '1x')` `22P02` /
    `42601` / `22000`.
  - a one-row `INSERT`: `INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES (1 + '1x', 2)` and `INSERT INTO t VALUES
    (1 + '1x', 2, 3)` `22P02` / `42601` / `22000`; `INSERT INTO t (a, b) VALUES (count(*))`
    `42803` / `42601` / `22000`.
  - an `INSERT … SELECT` source: `INSERT INTO t SELECT nosuch, 1, 2` and `INSERT INTO t (a,
    b) SELECT nosuch` `42703`; `INSERT INTO t SELECT 1 + true, 1, 2` and `INSERT INTO t
    SELECT x + true, 1, 2 FROM u` `42883`; `INSERT INTO t SELECT 1 + '1x', 2, 3` `22P02`;
    `INSERT INTO t (a) SELECT 1, 2 FROM nosuch` and `INSERT INTO t (a, b) SELECT x FROM
    nosuch` `42P01` — each `42601` here and `22000` before.

  The members are examples of the mechanism, not its extent. A verdict pglet reaches before
  the comparison wins on both: a source's bare name bound against its `FROM` — `INSERT
  INTO t SELECT nosuch, 1, 2 FROM u`, `INSERT INTO t SELECT 1, 2, 3 FROM u WHERE nosuch` and
  `INSERT INTO t SELECT count(*), 1, 2 FROM u GROUP BY nosuch` are `42703` on both — a
  comparison pglet types at plan time, in either clause — `INSERT INTO t (a) SELECT x, x
  FROM u WHERE x = true` and `INSERT INTO t SELECT x = true, 1, 2 FROM u` are `42883` on
  both, `… WHERE x = 'abc'` behind three expressions `22P02` — and a cell pglet gates at
  plan time, as row 225's closure measures. The clause does not decide the side; the
  operator does. An operator pglet resolves only at eval is a member in the `WHERE` as in
  the target list: `INSERT INTO t SELECT 1, 2, 3 FROM u WHERE x = 1 + true` is `42883` on
  18.6 and `42601` here, as `SELECT x + true, 1, 2 FROM u` is. So are a `WHERE`'s scalar
  subquery over an unknown relation (`WHERE x = (SELECT 1 FROM nosuch)`, `42P01`) and its
  array literal (`WHERE x = ANY('{1,x}')`, `22P02`). The same
  class stands against pglet's other plan-time verdicts, with no length refusal involved: `VALUES (1, 'x'), (2, true)` is the first
  row's `22P02` on 18.6 and the second row's `42804` here (`docs/names.md` § What the
  refusals do not carry records the class for the `SET`-list gate).

- **99 · Whatever the `CREATE` / `DROP` dispatch does not name falls through to one
  `0A000`, and the code a consumer meets is not the one the docs attribute.** State the
  set by the arm, not by a list: `parse_create` (`crates/pglet_sql/src/parser/ddl.rs`)
  tests the token after `CREATE` for `TABLE`, `UNIQUE`/`INDEX`, `SEQUENCE`, `TYPE`,
  `SCHEMA` and `EXTENSION`, and everything else raises `0A000 not implemented: only CREATE
  TABLE / INDEX / SEQUENCE / TYPE / SCHEMA / EXTENSION are supported`; `parse_drop` is a
  second dispatch with its own arms — `SCHEMA` and `EXTENSION` first, then `TABLE`,
  `INDEX`, `SEQUENCE`, `TYPE` — and its message names five of those six. Measured members,
  every one `0A000` on the native server: `CREATE DOMAIN`; `DROP DOMAIN`, and
  `DROP DOMAIN IF EXISTS` identically, because the arm is chosen before the `IF EXISTS`
  tail is read; `CREATE VIEW`, `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW`, `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW`,
  `CREATE TEMP VIEW`; `DROP VIEW`, `DROP VIEW IF EXISTS`, `DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW`;
  `DROP TRIGGER`; `DROP FUNCTION`. The arm keys on the **token**, not on the object kind,
  so `CREATE TEMP TABLE` is a member too — refused by a message that says `CREATE TABLE`
  is supported. A column declared with a domain's name is a *separate* refusal from the
  type resolver, `42704 type "pos" is not supported`. `PLAN.md` § Non-goals lists `domain`
  among the types absent by omission and attributes `42704` to it, which is that usage
  code and not the DDL statement's `0A000` — `docs/compatibility.md` carries the DDL row.
  Nothing is silently accepted, so this is a documentation edge; it earns a row because a
  real consumer's migration issues `CREATE DOMAIN`, and because the `VIEW` spellings ride
  the same two arms; row 15 records the `IF EXISTS` members of that set from the other
  side (a `NOTICE` + skip on Postgres, `0A000` here).

  The `VIEW` members of that set are the plain spelling and the `OR REPLACE`, `MATERIALIZED`
  and `TEMP` ones, and a column declared with a domain's name is a separate `42704` from the
  type resolver rather than either dispatch's `0A000`.
- **45 · Wrong-SQLSTATE-class (fail-loud, safe, but breaks `@expect-error` trust).** An
  absent function → `0A000` not `42883`; a wrong arity through `math_call` /
  `single_arg` / `binary_call` (`abs(1,2)`, `round(1,2,3)`, `lower('a','b')`,
  `starts_with('a')`) → `0A000` where 18.6 is uniformly `42883` — the
  `string_call`/`variadic_call` arities (`upper('a','b')`) already answer `42883` and
  are the control, so the arity-refusal *spelling* is per-helper and unifying it is a
  behavior change per family (`planner/expr.rs`'s `arity_error` doc names the seam); a
  **wildcard argument to a name 18.6 gives no
  zero-argument signature** — `build_call`'s generic `{name}(*) not supported` arm — →
  `0A000` where 18.6 is `42883 function upper() does not exist`, measured for `upper(*)`,
  `sum(*)`, `concat(*)` and `concat_ws(*)` (the last two variadic with a one-argument
