  minimum, so they carry no niladic entry either and stay on the generic arm, which is
  correct behaviourally and diverges only in the code): a `*` contributes no argument, so
  `func_get_detail` fails to resolve a zero-argument signature before the `agg_star`
  check is reached, and the names that *do* carry one take that check's `42809` instead
  and agree — the five niladic impure builtins the oracle models, plus
  `jsonb_build_object`, which is the only such name below `build_call`'s niladic block
  (measured over every name that match holds; see the *Niladic impure builtins refuse
  their arguments* bullet). Two neighbours of the class are worth separating from it, and
  the first splits where the naive reading says it does not. The names that are
  **grammar** rather than functions on 18.6 are all `42601` there — `coalesce(*)`,
  `greatest(*)`, `least(*)`, `nullif(*)`, `substring(*)`, `trim(*)` — but pglet answers
  them **two** ways, so only four of the six are divergences: the first four are `0A000`
  here, while `substring(*)` and `trim(*)` **agree at `42601`**, refused by pglet's own
  grammar because it too gives those two a production of their own with no `*` in it.
  (Measured on both; that pair is what keeps "the grammar names diverge" from being
  written as a sixfold universal.) And a name 18.6 resolves niladically that pglet **does
  not model at all** — `random(*)`, `42809` there against `0A000` here — is the
  absent-function divergence wearing this shape rather than a missing arm. A scalar subquery returning >1 row → `0A000`
  (no `21000` cardinality-violation variant exists); a window function in `WHERE` →
  `0A000` not `42P20`; an
  `Error::Execution → 22000` catch-all masks several specific codes
  (`42704`/`42601`/`42703`/`22023`); and an **ambiguous bare column compared against an
  unparseable literal** reports the coercion failure instead of the ambiguity —
  `SELECT ja.t FROM ja JOIN jb ON ja.id = jb.id WHERE id = 'abc'` is pglet `22P02` where
  PG is `42702`, because the plan-time constant cast is validated before the executor
  reaches the ambiguous name. A `USING`-merged name beside a third relation carrying it is
  the same pair beside an aggregate too: `SELECT max(n) > 'x' FROM ja JOIN jb USING (n), jc`
  is `22P02` here and `42702` there, the merged name binding before the level's other
  claimants are counted (`ColumnScope::binding_bare`). Both fail loud; only the code (and
  which fault the message names) diverges. **A `Debug` type spelling reaching a client's message is a class, not
  a place** (a producer live at HEAD: `SELECT 2 ^ 'q'` and its `%` twin answer
  `42883 operator does not exist: Some(Int4) ^ Some(Text)` — an `Option<TypeOid>` rendered
  by `Debug` in `executor/expr/arithmetic.rs`'s modulo and power arms — where 18.6 is
  `22P02`), and the sentence here — "the one place a `Debug` rendering reaches a user" —
  was false when it was written as well as after the fix it now outlives. **This is the
  class's one enumeration and it counts *producers*, not message spellings** — cite it
  rather than re-counting: `validate_btree_key_type`'s own comment and
  `the_container_key_refusal_names_its_type_in_sql` are the two homes repaired against it
  here, and one producer prints more than one spelling. The producers
  **closed**: `Error::TypeCoercion`'s two fields, built with `format!("{:?}", …)` over
  `Option<TypeOid>` / `TypeOid` at `executor/coerce.rs`'s unsupported-conversion arm, so
  a client read `cannot cast type Some(Int8) to Bool` (now `format_type`'s spelling
  through `sql_type_name`); and `executor/ddl.rs`'s `validate_btree_key_type`, whose
  `format!("{col_type:?}")` made `CREATE INDEX` over a `jsonb` or `text[]` column read
  `data type Jsonb` / `data type TextArray has no default operator class for a B-tree
  index` (now `data type jsonb` / `data type text[]`); and the index-key *encoder*'s array
  arm in `pglet_core`, whose `format!("{:?}[]", element_type)` made a write refused by a
  container-keyed index read `data type Text[] …` — the arm keys an array now and raises
  nothing (row 25); and `executor/expr/`'s `function … does not exist for argument type`
  arms (`lower`, `sqrt`, `sign`, `length`, the string and integer argument readers,
  `extract`/`date_part`, `date_trunc`, `concat_ws`), which printed `Some(Int4)` and now print
  the display name (`integer`) — still not 18.6's `function lower(integer) does not exist`
  wording. Live producers: `abs`, `ceil`/`floor` and `round`/`trunc`'s "requires a numeric
  argument, got …" (read, not run); and, measured through the npm package against 18.6,
  `executor/sequence.rs`'s `setval` value check, `42804 type error: setval() requires an
  integer value, got Some(Text)` (row 266); and the modulo arm above over a `real`, `SELECT
  1.5::real % 2` answering `42883 operator does not exist: Some(Float4) % Some(Int4)` where
  18.6 names `real % integer`. This bullet is that producer's
  record: `PLAN.md`, which this line used to name, carries no mention of the leak (grepped
  for `Debug` and for the message text). Each is a
  message-quality edge only — the SQLSTATE is right and the statement is refused.
- **47 · A column `DEFAULT` is an expression, and its verdicts are positional within that
  expression *and* at Postgres's own statement position.** The rule — the capability, the
  cook's position at `AddRelationNewConstraints`, the statement-level precedence measured
  from both sides, the eager `ADD COLUMN` arm, the `b_expr` mode and the closed
  `ColumnDefault` arms — is `docs/ddl.md` § A column `DEFAULT` is an expression the
  executor cooks, and the DDL-time coercion rule is `docs/coercion.md` § Which coercion
  runs at DDL time is a precise rule. This row is what still diverges.
  - **That row of the precedence contract is now satisfied rather than untestable.** 18.6
    reports `42701` for a duplicate column ahead of the cook, and pglet's
    `CREATE TABLE` duplicate-column gate is in — at `MergeAttributes`'s position, which
    is above the cook and below the column types and the index constraints. The
    statement that used to be accepted with `information_schema.columns` listing `a`
    twice is `ddl/create_table_duplicate_column_name.sql`; the ordering **against the
    cook** is measured off-corpus, no fixture's `CREATE TABLE` both repeating a column
    name and carrying a `DEFAULT`. The `ALTER … ADD COLUMN` spelling was reproduced
    throughout.
  - **The DDL-time coercion rule leaves one divergence of its own.** Of the divergences
    this list used to carry, two are gone: `DEFAULT 1` into `BOOL` at `42846` against
    `42804`, with its `DEFAULT
    true`-into-`INT` twin (see the next bullet), and `'x' || 'y'` into `INT`, which was
    `22P02` here against 18.6's `42804`. One remains:
    `5 + 'x'` is `42804` here against `22P02` there, pglet's operand gate answering before
    any literal is coerced.
  - **A cast whose operand is not an `unknown` literal is refused at `CREATE TABLE` when the
    type's input function refuses the text, where 18.6 refuses it per row.** The cook probe
    evaluates the default and returns an input-function code (`is_cook_time_error`'s `22P02`,
    `22007`, `22008` and `22009`) whatever the cast's operand was; 18.6 raises those at
    `CREATE TABLE` only where the input function runs on an `unknown` literal during parse
    analysis, and defers a cast over an operand that already has a type — a typed constant
    (`'x'::text`, `text 'x'`) as well as a computed value — to the write. Measured, each
    `CREATE TABLE` accepted on 18.6 and its omitted-column `INSERT` refused there:

    | `DEFAULT` | 18.6, at the `INSERT` | pglet, at `CREATE TABLE` |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | `('2000-01-01 00:00:00+' \|\| '16')::timestamptz` | `22009` | `22009` |
    | `'2000-01-01 00:00:00+16'::text::timestamptz`, `text '2000-01-01 00:00:00+16'::timestamptz` | `22009` | `22009` |
    | `('1' \|\| 'x')::int` | `22P02` | `22P02` |
    | `'x'::text::int`, `('x'::varchar)::int`, `'x'::varchar(3)::int`, `CAST(CAST('x' AS text) AS int)`, `text 'x'::int`, `$$x$$::text::int` | `22P02` | `22P02` |
    | `'x'::text::int::int8` into `INT8` | `22P02` | `22P02` |
    | `length(('1' \|\| 'x')::int::text)` into `INT` | `22P02` | `22P02` |
    | `('not' \|\| 'auuid')::uuid`, `'notauuid'::text::uuid` | `22P02` | `22P02` |
    | `('2026-13-' \|\| '01')::date`, `'2026-13-01'::text::date` | `22008 date/time field value out of range` | `22008 date out of range` |
    | `('zz' \|\| 'z')::timestamp`, `'zzz'::text::timestamp` | `22007` | `22P02` (row 96) |

    The controls, measured on both: a cast straight over an `unknown` literal the input
    function refuses is refused at `CREATE TABLE` — the bare literal (`DEFAULT 'x'` into `INT`,
    `DEFAULT '2000-01-01 00:00:00+16'` into `TIMESTAMPTZ`), `'x'::int`, `CAST('x' AS int)`,
    `('x')::int`, `int '5x'`, `timestamptz '2000-01-01 00:00:00+16'`, and the inner cast of
    `'5x'::int4::int8`; a cast over a typed operand that succeeds (`('1' || '2')::int`,
    `'5'::text::int`) is accepted; and `ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN` carrying `'x'::text::int` or
    `('1' || 'x')::int` over an empty table is refused at the `ALTER`. So what decides the verdict
    is whether the operand of the cast that refuses is an `unknown` literal, not the code: the
    bare-literal arm reads the same `is_cook_time_error`, so dropping an input-function code
    from it would accept the bare literal 18.6 refuses. Loud — a table 18.6 creates is refused
    — and unpinned.
  - **The opposite direction: a cast straight over an `unknown` literal that sits in a branch
    the cook does not take is accepted here where 18.6 refuses it at the DDL statement.** 18.6
    runs the input function on such a literal during parse analysis, wherever in the
    expression it stands (`coerce_type` folds it into a constant); pglet's cook probe evaluates the default, and evaluation reaches
    only the branches it takes. Measured, each refused on 18.6 at the statement named and
    accepted here — the first, third, fourth and fifth then writing the taken branch's value
    at an omitted-column `INSERT`:

    | statement | 18.6 |
    | --- | --- |
    | `CREATE TABLE r (a int DEFAULT CASE WHEN false THEN 'x'::int ELSE 1 END)` | `22P02` |
    | `CREATE TABLE r (a int DEFAULT CASE WHEN true THEN 1 ELSE 'x'::int END)` | `22P02` |
    | `CREATE TABLE r (a int DEFAULT coalesce(1, 'x'::int))` | `22P02` |
    | `CREATE TABLE r (a timestamptz DEFAULT CASE WHEN false THEN '2000-01-01 00:00:00+16'::timestamptz END)` | `22009` |
    | `ALTER TABLE r ALTER COLUMN a SET DEFAULT CASE WHEN false THEN 'x'::int ELSE 1 END` | `22P02` |
    | `ALTER TABLE r ADD COLUMN a int DEFAULT CASE WHEN false THEN 'x'::int ELSE 1 END` | `22P02` |

    The control, on both: `CASE WHEN false THEN 'x'::text::int ELSE 1 END` — the same branch
    over a typed operand — is accepted. **This is not only an over-accept: it breaks the dump
    invariant.** A database holding the first, third and fourth tables dumps with exit `0`;
    the dump renders the refused cast (`('x')::integer`), and `psql -f` of it into 18.6 exits
    `0` with each such `CREATE TABLE` refused — the codes above. The loss does not stop at
    those tables, and it is not one `COPY` failing per refused table: the first refused table's
    `COPY` fails `42P01` on the missing relation, and the data lines behind it then sit in
    psql's query buffer, so the next `COPY` statement is sent joined to them and fails as a
    `42601` syntax error, its own data lines taking the one after it down the same way — the
    COPY framing desync row 104 records. Measured with six tables in dump order, `a1` (the first
    `DEFAULT` above), `b2`, `c3` (the `timestamptz` one), `d4`, `e5` (the `coalesce` one) and
    `f6`, each holding one row: 18.6 creates `b2`, `d4` and `f6`; `a1`'s and `e5`'s `COPY`s
    fail on the missing relation; `b2`'s, `c3`'s and `f6`'s are syntax errors; and `b2` and
    `f6` restore **empty**. `d4` loads its row, and the desync ends there — `e5`'s `COPY` is a
    `42P01` again — because `c3`'s data line starts `\N`, which psql reads as a backslash
    command (`invalid command \N`) rather than buffering it, so the buffer is empty when
    `d4`'s `COPY` arrives.

    So the verdict turns on the cast's operand, and on
    *where* the input function runs rather than on whether evaluation reaches it: a repair
    that keeps the probe for the bullet above must also reach a cast over an
    `unknown` literal in a branch evaluation does not take, which evaluating the default cannot do.
    Unpinned.
  - **The message still diverges in the three ways the cook's own doc comment names** —
    `Error::Type`'s `type error: ` prefix, `expression` where 18.6's default route says
    `default expression`, and `bigint` where 18.6 names an integer literal `integer`.
  - **What the 456-shape sweep's 30 remaining divergences are**, all measured: 13 are the

    pglet has not implemented). The later 540-shape `ADD COLUMN` sweep's two

    `ADD COLUMN x BYTEA DEFAULT 'abc'` — accepted there and `22023 invalid hexadecimal

    **invalid label**, `e vis DEFAULT 'zz'`, was accepted here and `22P02` at DDL on
    18.6, and it is `22P02` at the DDL now on `CREATE TABLE`, `SET DEFAULT` and `ADD
    COLUMN` alike, over an empty table too — the cook converts an unknown literal into an

    `crates/pglet/tests/assignment_cast_verdicts.rs`'s
    `a_missing_relation_in_a_set_subquery_keeps_the_execution_verdict` asserts the

    *client* declares is not checked

    `UPDATE 0` where 18.6 says `42P01` — the same hole a well-typed right-hand side

    column-`DEFAULT` position's classifier reads.

    fastidiousness: `pglet::dump` renders every persisted expression through one

    `42703` here — a plain column in that list is resolved by `DefineIndex`, so only the
    parenthesized expression is transformed early — measured in both key orders, so it is

    family, at both index positions, and is recorded with its CHECK twin in row 51's
    bullet. Running
    18.6's argument transform in pglet's *parser* closes them as a side effect and moves
    every unquantified table-route verdict in front of itself doing it (row 51), which is
    why they are recorded here: the repair is the transform on this route's own lowering,
    ahead of the name conflict and the `IF NOT EXISTS` skip and behind the `42P01`.

    `CHECK (count(*) > 0 AND (SELECT true))` is `42803` and
    `CHECK (row_number() OVER () > 0 AND (SELECT true))` is `42P20`, both `0A000` here;

  A `nextval` inside an untaken branch of a default is drawn anyway —
  `substitute_nextval` walks the whole tree before `eval_expr` decides which arm is live
  — so `CASE WHEN false THEN nextval('s') ELSE 0 END` leaves the counter at 2 after two
  inserts against 18.6's 1, and `coalesce(1, nextval('s'))` at 1 against 0: **values
  agree on both engines, only the counters diverge**, and closing it means drawing
  lazily inside the evaluator. `draw_nextval` is a sequences-map-only lookup, so a
  `DEFAULT nextval('<a table>')` reaching a write would answer `42P01` where
  `init_sequence` says `42809` — unreachable through the engine's own accepted DDL now
  that all three registration sites gate the kind, and unfixed because the catalog is not
  reachable from that signature (four callers pass `&mut schema.sequences`).

  The rest, each measured and none of them pinned: pglet's parse-time absent-function
  refusal beats every
  positional verdict (`DEFAULT (count(*) + nosuchfunc(1))` is 18.6's `42803` and pglet's
  `0A000 function not supported`), and row 48's close added its niladic-arity and wildcard
  refusals to that same parse-time class (`DEFAULT (now(1))` beside a `nosuchtype` column
  is `42883` here against 18.6's `42704`, tabulated in row 48's bullet);
  `nextval('s'::regclass)` is recognized bare and pglet's own
  `0A000 not implemented: nextval() requires a string-literal sequence name`
  parenthesized (18.6 accepts both); `DEFAULT nextval('<no such sequence>')` auto-mints
  the sequence where 18.6 is `42P01` at DDL, and `nextval('<a table>')` is `42809` at DDL where 18.6 defers it to
  the first write — both pre-existing properties of the bare spelling that the expression
  spelling now shares rather than escaping; and `COPY`'s **input** path reads each field
  through the target type's input function rather than an assignment cast, so
  `COPY cb (b) FROM STDIN` over `cb(b BOOL)` takes `1`/`0`/`t`/`f`/`true`/`false`
  byte-identically to 18.6 (measured on both) while every *expression* route — the DDL
  cook, all four DML assignment sites, `COPY`'s default resolution and `resolve_default`
  — refuses the pair `42804`.

  **A NULL cast to another type than the column's is stored as no default.** `c bigint
  DEFAULT NULL::int` and `f numeric DEFAULT NULL::int` read back a NULL `column_default`
  here and `NULL::integer` on 18.6, where `d int DEFAULT NULL::int` and `e bigint DEFAULT
  NULL::bigint` are no default on both; an `INSERT` that omits the column stores NULL on
  both. Silent in the catalog, and wherever a default's presence is read: `ALTER COLUMN c
  ADD GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` over `c bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT NULL::int` is accepted
  here and `55000 column "c" of relation … already has a default value` there. Measured on
  both backends.

  **A NULL cast again to the type it already has is stored as a default.** `c int DEFAULT
  NULL::int::int`, `d bigint DEFAULT (NULL::bigint)::int8` and `t text DEFAULT
  NULL::text::text` read back `NULL::integer`, `NULL::bigint` and `NULL::text` here and a
  NULL `column_default` on 18.6; `ALTER COLUMN c SET DEFAULT NULL::int::int` likewise.
  `without_null_default` (`parser/ddl.rs`) looks through one cast over a bare `NULL` and
  keeps anything deeper. Silent in the catalog, and loud where a default's presence is
  read: `ALTER COLUMN c ADD GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` over `c int NOT NULL DEFAULT
  NULL::int::int` is `55000 column "c" of relation … already has a default value` here
  and accepted there, and after `ALTER COLUMN c DROP DEFAULT` it is accepted on both.
  Measured on both backends.

  Beyond the fixtures the row names (`ddl/default_*`,
  `ddl/alter_column_set_default_*`, `ddl/add_column_default_*`),
  `crates/pglet/tests/column_default_verdicts.rs`
  holds the rules two refusals sharing `0A000` make unpinnable by fixture, `crates/pglet`'s
  `a_refused_column_default_*` the DDL atomicity (its divide-by-zero-interval row is the
  one that separates the render probe from the eval probe), `dump::tests`'s
  `a_database_with_any_accepted_expression_default_dumps` the render invariant from the
  reader's side, and `test_dump`'s `expr_minted_host` the sequence a default's own
  registration mints.

- **48 · Niladic impure builtins refuse their arguments — closed, and it took two checks
  rather than one.** `planner/expr.rs`'s `build_call` used to route `now` /
  `transaction_timestamp` / `statement_timestamp` / `clock_timestamp` onto their own
  `BuiltinFn` arms, and `gen_random_uuid` / `uuid_generate_v4` onto
  `BuiltinFn::RandomUuid`, **by name alone** — the argument list was parsed and then
  discarded ("arguments ignored", as the comment said). (The four `now`-family names
  once shared one arm; splitting them changed *which* builtin a discarded-argument call
  resolved to, not that it resolved.) Postgres resolves a function by name *and*
  argument types, so each of those spellings named a function that does not exist
  there. Measured on both engines before the close: `SELECT now(1)`,
  `clock_timestamp(1)`, `statement_timestamp(1)`, `transaction_timestamp(1)`,
  `gen_random_uuid(1)`, `uuid_generate_v4(1)`, `now(NULL)`, `now('zzz', 42)` and the
  quoted `"now"(1)` were each `42883 function now(integer) does not exist` (and its
  siblings) there and each answered an ordinary timestamp / UUID here. **Engine-wide**,
  since `build_call` is the one site a function call is built at, and **silent**: the
  wrong answer was a plausible value. It was the silent twin of the
  *Wrong-SQLSTATE-class* row's absent function, which is loud in the other direction
  (`0A000` here against `42883` there); what separated them is that this name resolves.
  Through the column-`DEFAULT` bullet's general-grammar path it was a **DDL
  over-acceptance** too: `CREATE TABLE t (a INT, b TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT (now(1)))` was
  accepted — the column defined, `information_schema.columns.column_default` reading
  the argument-less spelling of whichever builtin the name resolved to (so
  `(clock_timestamp(1))` read `clock_timestamp()`; the discarded arguments were never
  rendered) — and an `INSERT` omitting the column backfilled a real timestamp. **Every
  persisted-expression site reached it by the same grammar**, and the repo's own
  enumeration of those is four rather than the two an `ALTER … ADD COLUMN` twin
  suggests: a column `DEFAULT` (both the `CREATE TABLE` and the
  `ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN … DEFAULT (clock_timestamp(1))` route), a `CHECK`
  (`CHECK (now(1) > now())`), an index **key part**
  (`CREATE INDEX … ON t ((t > now(1)))`) and an index **predicate**
  (`CREATE INDEX … ON t (a) WHERE t > now(1)`) — the same four the render probe runs at,
  which is where the list comes from. The three non-`DEFAULT` ones each stored an
  expression naming a signature 18.6 has no function for; all four are `42883` on both
  engines now, measured, and all four are fixtured.
  The gate is `niladic_call`, at that one call site, and it is **two checks whose
  order is 18.6's own**. A wildcard spelling parses to `wildcard = true` with an
  **empty** `args`, so an arity-only guard passes `now(*)` straight through — and 18.6
  answers it differently, not identically: `ParseFuncOrColumn` runs `func_get_detail`
  first and a `*` contributes no argument, so a name carrying a zero-argument entry
  reaches the `agg_star` arm and is
  `42809 now(*) specified, but now is not an aggregate function` while a non-empty list
  fails resolution ahead of that (`now(DISTINCT 1)` is `42883`, the `DISTINCT`'s own
  aggregate-ness check never reached). So the wildcard is judged first, as
  `Error::NotAnAggregate`, and everything else as `Error::UndefinedFunction` — measured
  identical on both engines for `now(*)` and `gen_random_uuid(*)`. **That arm is reached
  only because the name resolves**, which is what keeps it off the generic wildcard
  refusal beside it: `upper(*)` and `sum(*)` are `42883 function upper() does not exist`
  on 18.6, since neither `upper()` nor `sum()` exists — pglet answers `0A000` there, a
  separate pre-existing loud divergence recorded in the *Wrong-SQLSTATE-class* bullet.
  **The shape the gate took was already in the same `match`**: the sequence arms below
  these route through `sequence_call`, which range-checks the arity and raises
  `Error::UndefinedFunction`, so `DEFAULT (nextval('s', 1))` is
  `42883 nextval() expects 1 to 1 argument(s)` here against 18.6's
  `42883 function nextval(unknown, integer) does not exist`. Adopting it inherits that
  family's residuals exactly, which is the control that identifies them as the family's
  rather than this gate's — **three, each loud with the wrong code, each measured on
  both engines, and each with its `nextval('s', 1)` twin answering the same way**:

  | statement | 18.6 | pglet |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT now(1) FROM nosuchtable` | `42P01` (the range table resolves first) | `42883` |
  | `CREATE TABLE t2 (a INT DEFAULT (now(1)), b nosuchtype)` | `42704` (column types resolve in the `tableElts` walk, ahead of default cooking) | `42883` |
  | `SELECT now(nosuchcol)` | `42703` (arguments resolve before the function lookup) | `42883` |

  All three are the recorded *"pglet's absent-function refusal is raised while parsing
  and so pre-empts every positional verdict"* class from the column-`DEFAULT` bullet
  above, not a new one: pglet raises this verdict in the **parser**, which stands ahead
  of every executor gate and ahead of the relation resolution the executor does. A
  faithful fixture for any of them would be red, so they are recorded and not pinned.
  Beside those three, further residuals — **named rather than counted**, since a count
  is the form that goes stale, and split by whether the close created them. **Three stand
  unchanged.** The **bare** `DEFAULT` spelling is loud for a different reason and keeps
  its own code — `DEFAULT now(1)` is `42601 syntax error: expected ')'` from the
  token-level classifier's `eat_empty_call`, which demands an *empty* list and so answers
  ahead of `build_call`, where 18.6 says `42883`. **The classifier's one argument-taking
  arm has the same gap** and it belongs beside this rather than with row 51, which only
  measured it: `parse_nextval_arg` reads exactly one argument and expects `)`, so
  `DEFAULT nextval('r4s', 1)` is `42601 expected ')' found ','` here against
  `42883 function nextval(unknown, integer) does not exist` there, `DEFAULT nextval()` is
  `42601` against `42883`, and the set-quantifier spellings of both diverge identically —
  an *arity* verdict the route does not render, not the modifier's. Every parenthesized
  twin is `42883` on **both**, that spelling leaving the classifier for `build_call`'s
  arity check, which is the control that identifies the classifier here too.
  `DEFAULT now(*)` and its
  `ALTER TABLE … ALTER COLUMN … SET DEFAULT now(*)` twin are the same classifier's
  `42601` against 18.6's `42809` — `eat_empty_call` again, the exact sibling of the
  `DEFAULT now(1)` residual and the same cause rather than a second one; measured on the
  pre-close build, the `42601` stood there before this close too, so the close neither
  created nor moved it. The **parenthesized** `DEFAULT (now(*))` leaves the classifier
  and agrees at `42809`, which is the control identifying the classifier rather than the
  clause. And `uuid_generate_v4` is **not**
  pinnable in its argument-less spelling: the oracle carries no `uuid-ossp` extension, so
  `uuid_generate_v4()` is `42883` there and answers here — a pre-existing **silent**
  divergence the
  gate neither opened nor closed, and the reason only the `uuid_generate_v4(1)` spelling
  (`42883` on both, for different reasons) has a fixture. **One the close created**,
  an improvement rather than a regression — a loud wrong code standing where a
  silent answer stood — measured on both engines:

  - `SELECT uuid_generate_v4(*)` is pglet's `42809` against 18.6's
    `42883 function uuid_generate_v4() does not exist` — the same missing-extension
    carve-out as the argument-less spelling above, one spelling over, and the reason the
    `docs/compatibility.md` sentence about these names' `pg_proc` status covers five of the six rather than
    all. **Kept deliberately**: pglet models the function as existing, and `42809` is
    what a Postgres *with* `uuid-ossp` installed answers, so matching the oracle here
    would mean encoding the oracle's missing extension into the engine. Its sibling
    `gen_random_uuid(*)` is the fixtured half of the pair for exactly that reason.

  A second one this close created — `SELECT now(DISTINCT *)`, pglet's `42809` against
  18.6's `42601` — is **gone**, and so is the silent member beside it,
  `SELECT count(DISTINCT *)`, which answered a count here where 18.6 is that same
  `42601`. Both were the one cause wearing two faces: pglet's parser accepted a
  combination `gram.y` has no production for and handed `wildcard = true` on to
  `build_call`, which judged the wildcard and never saw the `DISTINCT`. The set-quantifier
  close (row 51) reproduces the grammar bound in the parser, ahead of that dispatch, so
  both spellings are `42601` on both engines now.

  **Two more stand unchanged, and they are this family's members of a class recorded
  under row 51** — a syntax error *later* in the statement text beating a verdict pglet
  raises mid-parse, because 18.6's bison scans the whole statement before parse analysis
  runs. `SELECT now(1) FROM` is `42601` there against pglet's `42883`, and
  `SELECT now(*) FROM` is `42601` there against pglet's `42809`; the controls that
  identify it as position are under row 51's bullet, where the class is stated once.

  Guarded by 18 differential fixtures, and the members are the enumeration: ten
  argument-list spellings under `functions/niladic_*` — the six names one apiece
  (`uuid_generate_v4(1)` included), plus the multi-argument `now('zzz', 42)`, the
  `NULL`-argument `now(NULL)`, the quoted `"now"(1)` and a `WHERE` position — two `f(*)`
  spellings (`functions/niladic_now_star_not_an_aggregate_loud.sql` and its
  `gen_random_uuid` twin), `functions/jsonb_build_object_star_not_an_aggregate_loud.sql` for the arm that
  proves the `f(*)` rule keys on the signature rather than on this family, and five
  fixtures covering the four persisted-expression sites — the column `DEFAULT` site by
  both its fixtured routes, with the third route,
  `ALTER TABLE … ALTER COLUMN … SET DEFAULT (now(1))`, measured agreeing `42883` on both
  engines and deliberately unfixtured — `ddl/niladic_arg_column_default_loud.sql`,
  `ddl/add_column_niladic_arg_default_loud.sql`, `ddl/niladic_arg_check_loud.sql`,
  `ddl/niladic_arg_index_expr_loud.sql` and `ddl/niladic_arg_index_predicate_loud.sql` —
  and by `crates/pglet/tests/column_default_verdicts.rs`'s
  `a_niladic_builtins_arguments_are_refused`, which holds what a differential fixture
  cannot: the refusal's own **message** text (`expects 0 to 0 argument`, and that
  `uuid_generate_v4(1)` names the spelled function rather than the `gen_random_uuid` its
  `BuiltinFn` is shared with — two names, one variant), the two non-`42883` codes this
  clause produces (`42601` for the bare `DEFAULT now(1)`, a residual against 18.6's
  `42883`; `42809` for the parenthesized `DEFAULT (now(*))`, which agrees with it), the
  sequence-family control `(nextval('s', 1))`, and the argument-less spellings still
  building their defaults. The **three precedence
  residuals tabulated above are recorded and pinned nowhere** — each needs a live
  comparison against 18.6 to mean anything, and a faithful fixture for any of them is
  red. No store bump: the change refuses SQL text
  that used to be accepted, and adds no persisted shape — `Error` is not serialized,
  and every catalog record a pre-gate build wrote still decodes and renders (a
  persisted `ColumnDefault::Now` is the argument-less builtin either way, since the
  arguments were never stored).


  The pre-close `DEFAULT` route in the spellings the table row named: the column was
  defined, `column_default` read the *argument-less* spelling of whichever builtin the
  name resolved to, and an omitting `INSERT` backfilled a real value. Its
  `SET DEFAULT now(*)` spelling measures with the bare `DEFAULT now(*)` one above, both
  the classifier's `42601` against 18.6's `42809`. The 18 fixtures cover the four
  persisted-expression sites over five routes — the column `DEFAULT` by its `CREATE TABLE`
  and `ADD COLUMN` routes, then the CHECK, the index key part and the index predicate. The
  one residual the close created is a loud improvement on a silent answer:
  `uuid_generate_v4(*)` is pglet's `42809` against the extension-less oracle's `42883`.

- **50 · A sequence function in a stored expression is refused everywhere, and 18.6
  accepts it at the CHECK sites.** `nextval` / `currval` / `setval` inside a CHECK
  predicate, an index partial predicate or an index key part is
  `0A000 nextval() is only supported as a top-level SELECT expression (and in INSERT … VALUES)`
  here — the parser's position gate, raised before any persistence question is asked.
  18.6 **accepts** the CHECK spelling and persists it, the acceptance measured at
  `CREATE TABLE`, `ALTER TABLE … ADD CONSTRAINT … CHECK` and `ADD COLUMN` alike and the
  persisted row read back on the first (`CHECK ((nextval('s'::regclass) > 0))`); `currval`
  and `setval` behave identically on both engines at every one of them. The two **index**
  positions it refuses `42P17`, `nextval` not being IMMUTABLE.

  Unpinned, and it will stay so: a faithful fixture would be red at the CHECK sites and
  would compare two different SQLSTATEs at the index ones. **Distinct from row 49 and
  from the deparser**: an `Expr::SequenceFn` **renders**, so this is not a dump-outage
  gate but the same `0A000` the bare-`SELECT`-position rule raises everywhere else, and
  closing it is the sequence-position work rather than the render work. The sibling
  recorded in row 47 — a `currval`/`setval` in a column `DEFAULT` being `0A000` here
  where 18.6 accepts — is this rule at the fourth site, where plain `nextval` is the one
  spelling both engines take.

- **49 · An interval literal in a stored expression cannot render, so it is refused at
  DDL.** The parser carries an `INTERVAL '…'` literal as an `Expr::Bound`, for which the
  deparser has no source spelling, so `executor::ddl`'s `validate_stored_expr_renders`
  answers `0A000` at every stored-expression position — a CHECK predicate, an index
  partial predicate, an index key part. 18.6 accepts the literal at all of them; an index
  position there additionally requires IMMUTABLE (`42P17`), which is why the index
  fixtures probe an `INTERVAL` column rather than `now()`.

  **The refusal stands in for a whole-database dump outage**, which is what it buys.
  Before it, `CREATE TABLE ck1 (t TIMESTAMPTZ, CHECK (t > now() - interval '1 day'))` was
  accepted at all five CHECK routes and `CREATE INDEX … ((iv + interval '1 day'))` /
  `… WHERE iv > interval '1 day'` at both index positions, each making
  `pglet_server dump` exit 1 for the **whole** database.

  **Statement position is closed at all seven spellings — the five CHECK ones over three
  call sites, the two index ones over one — and by the same rule at each**: the probe
  stands in for no 18.6 error, so it runs after every gate that stands in for one and
  immediately before the statement's first catalog write. `validate_check_exprs_render`
  is a whole-statement pass on the three CHECK routes; `validate_index_exprs_render` runs
  after the name conflict and the `IF NOT EXISTS` skip on the two index ones. Ten
  arrangements were measured diverging while the probe rode inside the per-constraint
  cook, and all ten agree now: a taken constraint-index name (`42P07`) and a missing FK
  parent (`42P01`) on `CREATE TABLE` in **both** source orders, a later duplicate CHECK
  name (`42710`) there, the duplicate name (`42710`) and the existing-row violation
  (`23514`) on `ALTER TABLE … ADD CONSTRAINT … CHECK`, and the duplicate name, the
  missing FK parent and the backfill violation on `ADD COLUMN`. Of the three kinds a
  `CREATE TABLE` can put in either order, only the duplicate name was order-sensitive —
  it shares the cook-then-name loop, so writing the duplicate first already agreed —
  while the constraint-index and FK kinds diverged whichever order they were written in,
  the whole CHECK loop standing ahead of them. The reverse arrangements are not a control:
  measured, two of the three kinds diverge in either order.

  **One residual, and it is the state rather than the producers**: the persisted shape is
  unchanged, so the gate carried no store-magic bump of its own, and a database a pre-gate
  build wrote still holds its interval CHECK, reopens, reads and writes, and still cannot
  dump — loudly, which is the property pinned rather than the absence. (The magic has since
  moved for other reasons; `docs/storage.md` § Store versioning is where the
  current value lives.)

  Beyond the five site fixtures the row names, the closed statement positions are pinned
  by `ddl/create_table_interval_check_yields_to_taken_index_name.sql`,
  `…_to_missing_fk_parent.sql`, `…_to_dup_check_name.sql`,
  `ddl/alter_add_check_dup_name_beats_interval_check.sql` and
  `ddl/add_column_interval_check_yields_to_backfill_violation.sql` — ordinary
  differential `@expect-error` fixtures whose SQLSTATEs now **match** 18.6's, which is a
  stronger pin than the pglet-stricter kind.
  `ddl/create_table_dup_check_name_beats_interval_check.sql` is the already-agreeing half
  of the one order-sensitive pair and is only worth keeping beside its reverse;
  `ddl/create_index_if_not_exists_skips_over_unrenderable_key.sql` pins the index
  placement; `dump::tests`'s `a_database_with_any_accepted_stored_expression_dumps` pins
  the invariant from the reader's side, and
  `a_legacy_stored_expression_that_cannot_render_fails_the_dump_loudly` the legacy-store
  residual, which is the only unpinned one left.

- **51 · A function-call set quantifier is 18.6's, both keywords — closed, and the grammar
  half was the silent one.** The rule, its grammar derivation and what pins it are
  `docs/parser.md` § A function-call set quantifier is 18.6's, both keywords; this row is
  the measured record and the residuals. pglet parsed the modifier, carried it to
  `build_call` as a `distinct` flag, and every arm but the aggregates dropped it. Measured
  on both engines before the close: `SELECT upper(DISTINCT 'a')` answered `A` here and is

  worse than a wrong value: a `nextval` advance is non-transactional, so the divergence
  outlived the failed statement and any rollback around it. **Silent** throughout — a
  plausible value, and no error channel anywhere; the persisted-expression sites stored
  the call with the modifier stripped, so `column_default` and the dump rendered
  something the user never wrote.

  rather than one. Against 18.6's `42601` for the whole cross-product {`DISTINCT`, `ALL`}
  × {`)`, `*`} × {ordinary call, window call}, four spellings **answered rows** here —

  `row_number(DISTINCT *) OVER ()`, the last two because the window fork then read neither

  cell: `upper(DISTINCT)` was `42883` and `upper(DISTINCT *)` was `0A000`. `ALL` was the
