  load). pglet's own restore of the same script reports no error at all — the tables those
  expressions sit on are necessarily empty, which is the same condition that made the DDL
  silent. That is the catalog part of `docs/sequences.md`'s dump invariant, *any catalog
  pglet's own accepted statements build must dump to something that loads into stock
  Postgres and back into pglet*, violated by pre-existing accepted DDL rather than by anything the close did.
  Their sites are `executor::ddl`'s `check_stored_expr_nodes`
  and the `set_config` arm, and that is where the repair belongs — a constant cast is not
  the value-dependent outcome `validate_stored_expr`'s probe filter is written for, and an
  arm that discards an argument still has to validate it. The **typmod'd** cast spelling is
  the same class through the same routes, silent before the close and today:
  `set_config('abc'::numeric(5,2), 'y', false)` answers `y`, and
  `CHECK (concat('abc'::numeric(5,2)) = 'A')` is accepted over an empty table at
  `CREATE TABLE` and at `ADD CONSTRAINT` (`22P02` on 18.6 either way, and `22P02` here over
  one row); their `::numeric` controls behave identically — which is what says
  the gap is the *site's* and not the cast node's.
  Residuals, each measured on both engines on the closed build. **Two more the close
  created**, beside the `DEFAULT` column reference recorded above, all loud, all the
  recorded *"pglet's parse-time refusal pre-empts every positional verdict"* class rather
  than a new one: `SELECT upper(DISTINCT 1)` is
  18.6's `42883 function upper(integer) does not exist` and pglet's `42809` (the operand
  type is an eval-time gate here, a later phase than the modifier) — as is
  `SELECT upper(DISTINCT '12345'::numeric(3,1))`, the same divergence reached through a
  typmod'd cast whose *input conversion succeeds*, which is what leaves an argument typed
  `numeric` for a signature 18.6 has no `upper` for — and
  `SELECT upper(DISTINCT nosuchcol) FROM pun` / `SELECT upper(DISTINCT a::text) FROM
  nosuch_table` are 18.6's `42703` / `42P01` — it transforms the arguments and the range
  table before `ParseFuncOrColumn` — against pglet's `42809`. **One more at the quoted
  grammar names**, and it replaces a silent answer: `SELECT "coalesce"(DISTINCT 1, 2)` is
  `42883` on 18.6 (a quoted name is a `pg_proc` lookup and `pg_proc` holds no `coalesce`)
  against pglet's `42601`, where it used to answer `1` — the recorded quoted-name class,
  since pglet's function table does not record which of its names `pg_proc` holds.
  **And one closed as a bonus**: `SELECT "substring"(DISTINCT 'abcdef', 2)` answered
  `bcdef` here against 18.6's `42809` and now agrees — `substring` is a grammar name
  *and* a `pg_proc` entry there, so only its quoted spelling reaches this verdict, which
  is why it is deliberately absent from `grammar_only_name`.
  **The three siblings of the same `ParseFuncOrColumn` block are loud divergences of their
  own**, unclosed because pglet's grammar has none of the three productions and none is
  fixturable — an `@expect-error` compares the codes. `upper('a' ORDER BY 1)`,
  `upper('a') FILTER (WHERE true)` and `upper('a') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY 1)` are 18.6's
  `42809 ORDER BY specified, …` / `42809 FILTER specified, …` / `42883` and `42601` here,
  as is `concat('a') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY 'b')` against
  `42809 WITHIN GROUP specified, …`. `FILTER` had no record *as a
  sibling of this block* (the missing `FILTER` grammar is listed in the
  absent-but-fail-loud surface above, which is the other claim — `count(*) FILTER (WHERE
  true)` answers `1` there and is `42601` here),
  and `Error::NotAnAggregate`'s doc had all three the other way up ("each is
  `42601` — measured on both engines"), which is what a claim inherits when the pglet half
  is measured and the 18.6 half is assumed. The `ORDER BY` sibling has a **FROM-route**
  member too: `FROM unnest(ARRAY[1,2] ORDER BY 1)` is `42809 ORDER BY specified, but
  unnest is not an aggregate function` there against `42601` here, and its `DISTINCT`
  spelling `FROM unnest(DISTINCT ARRAY[1,2] ORDER BY 1)` is 18.6's `42809` for the
  *quantifier* — the modifier is judged before the sort clause — against the same `42601`
  here.
  **A whole class of residual sits above all of those and is not this gate's to fix**:
  18.6's bison scans the entire statement before parse analysis runs, so a syntax error
  *later* in the text beats a verdict this gate raises. pglet raises `build_call`'s
  verdicts inside the parser, mid-statement, so it answers the verdict instead —
  `SELECT upper(DISTINCT 'a') FROM`, `SELECT upper(DISTINCT 'a') FROM rv1 WHERE` and
  `SELECT nextval(DISTINCT 'rq_seq') FROM` are `42601` on 18.6 against `42809` here, and
  row 48's own members `SELECT now(1) FROM` and `SELECT now(*) FROM` are the same class
  at `42883`/`42809`. The FROM-clause route contributes members at both of its codes:
  `SELECT * FROM unnest(DISTINCT ARRAY[1,2]) AS u(x) WHERE` is `42809` here and the
  multi-array spelling `42883`, both `42601` there (and any later syntax error does it —
  `ORDER BY` measured the same). A syntax error *inside* the call's
  parens is **not** this class and does agree — `FROM unnest(DISTINCT ARRAY[1,2] junk)`
  is `42601` on both — because pglet's own `expect(RParen)` meets that token before the
  verdict is rendered, which is where `build_call` has always sat and where the FROM
  route's verdict sits too now, having been raised above the paren before that.
  The argument transform contributes only its **quantified** spelling, because it is
  gated on a written quantifier: `SELECT upper(DISTINCT 'a'::int) FROM;` is `42601` on
  18.6 and `22P02` here — this class's member for that spelling, at the transform's code
  rather than the quantifier's `42809` (before the close the modifier was dropped and the
  statement was `42601` on both, which is what the close replaced), while
  the unquantified `SELECT upper('a'::int) FROM;` is `42601` on both, as before the close. A *trailing* token is in neither spelling's class and the pair says
  why: `SELECT upper('a'::int) junk` parses on both (`junk` is a column alias), so it is
  `22P02` on both, and its `DISTINCT` spelling is `22P02`
  on both.
  Two controls identify the open class as *position* rather than as the gate: an
  **earlier** syntax error wins on both engines (`SELECT , upper(DISTINCT 'a')` is
  `42601` on both), and so does a gate whose own verdict is already a syntax error
  (`SELECT coalesce(DISTINCT 1,2) FROM`, `42601` on both). This is the parse-time-precedence
  class `docs/ddl.md` § Which error wins is part of the contract records, which **closed**
  for a column `DEFAULT`'s own verdicts because they moved out of the parser; moving these
  would reorder them against every executor gate, so they are recorded rather than fixed.
  Teaching `ALL` **widens existing silent families, and what matters is which ones rather
  than how many** — this sentence has been written as "one" and as "two" and been wrong
  both times, so it enumerates and does not count. Because the keyword is dropped,
  `f(ALL args)` is exactly as right or wrong as `f(args)`, which is the whole mechanism:
  every family whose members answer wrongly gains their `ALL` spellings, each `42601`
  before — loud, with the wrong code. The list came from sweeping every name the dispatch
  models against 18.6's `pg_proc` and re-measuring each, so it is an enumeration and not
  a proof: a family that sweep missed is a member by the same mechanism.
  **And the sweep's shape bounds it in a particular direction**: it ranges over `pg_proc`
  *names*, so it can only reach a family keyed to a name. A family keyed to a **route** is
  structurally outside it, and one was found afterwards by reading the route instead — the
  DDL `DEFAULT` classifier's missing argument transform, the classifier family above. So read
  "each `42601` before" as true of every member, and the enumeration itself as bounded by
  names rather than by routes.
  **Row 53's**: `count(ALL a, b)`, `sum(ALL a, b)`,
  `row_number(ALL 1) OVER ()`, `rank(ALL a) OVER (…)` and `dense_rank(ALL a) OVER (…)`.
  **The GUC-echo tolerance below**: `set_config(ALL 'x', 'y', false)` answers `y` here
  against 18.6's `42704 unrecognized configuration parameter "x"` — the *unquantified*
  `set_config('x', 'y', false)` is the same pair, and `set_config(ALL 'x.y', 'z', false)`
  answers `z` on **both** engines, which is the control that identifies the family as the
  GUC name rather than the keyword. **And the unresolved schema qualifier on a function
  call** — the widest of them, because the qualifier is stripped before dispatch and so
  every modeled name is a member: `SELECT public.upper(ALL 'a')` answers `A` here against
  `42883 function public.upper(unknown) does not exist`, with the other qualifiers, the
  other names and the persisted-`DEFAULT` route measuring the same way. Its members, its
  controls and its polarities live in the foreign-schema-qualifier bullet above, since
  that record owns the family and this widening only reached it; the one thing worth
  carrying at this end is that the same family's `DISTINCT` spellings moved the *other*
  way — `public.upper(DISTINCT 'a')` answered `A` before and is `42809` now, loud against
  18.6's `42883` — so a reader should not take the mechanism as uniformly worsening.
  **And the DDL `DEFAULT` classifier's missing argument transform** — the family the name
  sweep could not reach, since it is keyed to a route: `DEFAULT nextval(ALL 'x'::int)` is
  accepted here and mints `x` where 18.6 is `22P02`, at all three `DEFAULT` positions, its
  `DISTINCT` sibling and its unquantified twin recorded with it in the classifier paragraph
  above. One
  family was **genuinely new** and is why this needed a second pass: `pg_proc` holds
  `btrim` and not `trim`, so a quoted `SELECT "trim"(ALL ' x ')` — which leaves
  `parse_trim`'s keyword route for the ordinary dispatch — **answered `x`** against
  18.6's `42883 function trim(unknown) does not exist`. Adding `trim` to
  `grammar_only_name` makes both quoted spellings `42601`: loud, still 18.6's `42883` on
  the other side, and the same posture the four bare grammar names already carry. It does
  not close the unquantified `SELECT "trim"(' x ')`, which still answers `x` — that is
  the recorded quoted-name class, and closing it means recording which of pglet's names
  `pg_proc` holds.
  The per-name sweep the fixtures stand for, the silent members, and every statement 18.6
  answers with a *skip* are recorded rather than pinned: an `@expect-error` over a
  statement 18.6 accepts passes on any pglet error at all.
  Two spellings name the class where a one-line row cannot: `upper(DISTINCT 'a')` for the
  ordinary call, and `nextval(DISTINCT 's')` for the sequence arm, whose pre-close answer
  advanced the counter.


  Two members of the *later-syntax-error* class come from row 55's plan-time `unnest` gate
  rather than from this one, one in each direction, and both are measured and recorded
  there: pglet's own `LIMIT 'x'` / `OFFSET 'x'` grammar bound pre-empts that gate where
  18.6 raises `42883`, and the gate pre-empts pglet's own trailing-token error, because
  `parser::parse` plans each statement before checking for one. Whoever moves either
  verdict re-measures the pair.

- **~~52~~ · Closed — `concat()` is the arity arm row 48 did not reach.** `concat` is
  variadic with a **one**-argument minimum on Postgres, so `SELECT concat()` is
  `42883 function concat() does not exist` there; pglet's `build_call` built an
  `Expr::VariadicFn` from whatever list it was handed and answered the empty string.
  Measured on both. It is the same family as row 48 — a modeled name whose argument list
  is not checked against the signature — and the same shape of fix: `concat` is the one
  arm in `build_call`'s variadic group that range-checks **nothing**. Every neighbour
  range-checks, though only one is right on both axes: `concat_ws()` is `42883` on both
  engines; `greatest()`, `least()` and `nullif(1)` refuse `42883` here against 18.6's
  `42601` — grammar names there, so the code diverges while the direction does not;
  `coalesce()` refuses with pglet's own `0A000` against the same `42601`; and
  `jsonb_build_object` checks parity — `42804` here against 18.6's `22023`, its empty
  call a legitimate `{}` on both engines.
  `concat_ws()` measured `42883` on both is the discriminating control: same group,
  same shape, and it is the arity check that separates them. **Silent**: `''` is a
  plausible value and a caller concatenating a computed list would not notice.
  A second member of the same shape sits at a route that never touches `build_call`, and
  it carries no row of its own: `SELECT * FROM unnest() AS u(x)` is
  `42883 function unnest() does not exist` on 18.6 and a zero-row, zero-column `SELECT 0`
  here, because `parse_unnest_table` builds a `Plan::FunctionScan` from whatever array list it
  is handed and range-checks nothing either. Measured on both, and untouched by the
  set-quantifier close (row 51) — that close's grammar bound reaches only the
  *quantified* spelling of an empty argument list. (Measured again before the repair, the
  `AS u(x)` spelling had come to answer `42P10 table "u" has 0 columns available but 1
  columns specified` — the alias-count check reading the empty relation — and the
  unaliased spelling the zero-column relation.)

  **What closed it.** `concat` takes `variadic_call`'s one-argument minimum, as
  `concat_ws` does, and `parse_unnest_table` refuses an empty array list
  `42883 function unnest() does not exist` once its closing paren is read. Measured after
  the repair against 18.6: `SELECT concat()` and `SELECT * FROM unnest() AS u(x)` are
  `42883` on both, and `concat('a')` / `concat(NULL)` answer `a` / the empty string on
  both. Both refusals are raised as the call is parsed, so they join row 51's
  *later-syntax-error* class, as `build_call`'s other arity refusals already stood in it —
  and two of its measured members **agreed before the repair**, when the empty list went
  on to fail where 18.6 does: `SELECT concat() FROM nosuch` is `42883` here against `42P01`
  (`42P01` before), and `SELECT concat() FROM t WHERE 1 +` `42883` against `42601` (`42601`
  before); `SELECT * FROM unnest() AS u(x) WHERE` is `42883` against `42601` (`42P10`
  before). Each loud on both sides. Guards: `functions/concat_no_arguments_loud.sql`, the
  control `functions/concat_one_argument.sql`, `functions/unnest_from_no_arguments_loud.sql`.

- **~~53~~ · Closed — Row 48's class at the two sites its close did not reach — the
  aggregate arm and the window route.** Both dropped an over-long argument list instead
  of failing resolution: the aggregate arm took `args.into_iter().next()`, and
  `parse_window_over` read neither `args` nor the quantifier at all. Measured on both engines: `count(a, b)`,
  `sum(a, b)` and `count(DISTINCT a, b)` answer here where 18.6 is
  `42883 function count(integer, integer) does not exist`; `row_number(1) OVER ()` and
  `row_number(DISTINCT 1) OVER ()` answer rows against the same code for `row_number`;
  `rank(a) OVER (ORDER BY a)` and `dense_rank(DISTINCT a) OVER (ORDER BY a)` answer rows
  against `42809 WITHIN GROUP is required for ordered-set aggregate rank`. **Silent**,
  and the `DISTINCT`-spelled members are decided by the *argument* there rather than by
  the quantifier — which is why the set-quantifier close (row 51) leaves them silent
  rather than closing them, and why teaching `ALL` added each member's `ALL` spelling to
  the list: `count(ALL a, b)`, `sum(ALL a, b)`, `row_number(ALL 1) OVER ()`,
  `rank(ALL a) OVER (ORDER BY a)` and `dense_rank(ALL a) OVER (ORDER BY a)`, all measured
  answering here against the same three codes. The control the fix must keep:
  `SELECT row_number(*) OVER () FROM t` answers on **both** engines — the `FROM` is
  load-bearing in the control, since the no-FROM spelling is pglet's separate
  `0A000 window functions must be evaluated via Window plan executor` against a row
  there.


  The window half's members are the bare spellings as well as the quantified ones:
  `dense_rank(a) OVER (ORDER BY a)` stands beside the `DISTINCT` and `ALL` spellings named
  above. And the control's `FROM` is load-bearing, the no-FROM spelling being a separate
  `0A000` here.

  **What closed it.** The aggregate arm destructures exactly one argument and refuses any
  other count `42883` — save `count()`, which resolves the zero-argument aggregate
  `count(*)` is and is refused `42809 count(*) must be used to call a parameterless
  aggregate function` (`Error::ParameterlessAggregateWithoutStar`); `count()`, `sum()`,
  `avg()`, `min()` and `max()` were all pglet's own `0A000` before. The window route
  judges its argument list once the `OVER` clause is read
  (`planner::refuse_window_arguments`): `row_number` over any argument is `42883`, and
  `rank` / `dense_rank` over any are `42809 WITHIN GROUP is required for ordered-set
  aggregate …` (`Error::WithinGroupRequired`); a `*` contributes no argument, and a written
  quantifier brings only the constant-cast transform ahead of the verdict, as at
  `build_call`. Measured after the repair against 18.6, each agreeing in code, and the
  `42809`s in message too: every member above over an empty table, `count()`, `sum()`,
  `max(a, b, a)`, `rank(a, b) OVER (ORDER BY a)`, `rank(1) OVER ()` and `row_number(1)
  OVER ()` with no `FROM`, `row_number(DISTINCT 'a'::int) OVER ()` (`22P02`),
  `row_number(1) OVER (PARTITION BY nosuch)` (`42883` — the call resolves before the
  window's keys bind), and the controls `row_number(*)`, `rank(*)` and `dense_rank(*)`
  `OVER (…)`, which answer on both.

  **What it inherits, and the answers it moved away.** The refusal is raised as the call
  is parsed, so every error 18.6 meets first in parse analysis loses to it — row 51's
  *later-syntax-error* class, which `build_call`'s other arity refusals already stood in.
  Four members were measured after the repair, and three of them **agreed before it**,
  when the extra argument was dropped and the statement went on to fail where 18.6 does:
  `SELECT count(nosuch, 1) FROM t` and `SELECT nosuch, count(a, b) FROM t` are `42883`
  here against 18.6's `42703` (both `42703` here before), `SELECT count(a, b) FROM nosuch`
  `42883` against `42P01` (`42P01` before), and `SELECT row_number(nosuch) OVER () FROM t`
  `42883` against `42703` (a row before). Each is loud on both sides. Guards: the
  `functions/aggregate_*_arguments_loud.sql` and `functions/aggregate_*_empty_list_loud.sql`
  fixtures, the `functions/window_*_loud.sql` fixtures and the control
  `functions/window_star_argument.sql`.

- **300 · A `DO` body's parse-time refusals escape its own `EXCEPTION` handler.**
  `parser::plpgsql`'s `parse_do_inner` parses the whole body, every statement of every
  block, when the `DO` statement itself is parsed, and a refusal pglet raises while
  parsing is the `DO`'s error. 18.6's PL/pgSQL compiles the body's syntax up front too —
  so a syntax error escapes the handler on both engines (`INSERT INTO dz VALUES (11, 1 +)`
  inside `BEGIN … EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS …` is `42601` on both, measured) — but it runs
  each statement's **parse analysis** only when the statement executes, inside the block,
  so an analysis error there is caught. The members are therefore pglet's refusals that 18.6
  raises in analysis, which include `build_call`'s argument-count refusals and the window
  and aggregate ones rows 52 and 53 added. Measured over `dz (a int, b text)`, each body
  `BEGIN <stmt>; EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN INSERT INTO dz VALUES (<n>, 'caught'); END`,
  against 18.6 (which answers `DO` and writes the `caught` row for each):
  `INSERT INTO dz VALUES (1, concat())` and `INSERT INTO dz SELECT 5, count(a, a)::text
  FROM dz` are `42883` out of the `DO` here, nothing written, over any contents of `dz`.
  The build before rows 52 and 53 closed answered them by what `dz` held, each measured
  from a fresh `dz` with no earlier block run over it: the `concat()` member wrote `1|`
  (**silent**); the `count(a, a)` member wrote `5|0` over an empty `dz` and `5|1` over one
  holding a row (**silent**); and `INSERT INTO dz SELECT 9, row_number(1) OVER ()::text
  FROM dz` answered `DO` with nothing written over an empty `dz`, and over one holding a
  row reached an execution error the handler caught. `INSERT INTO dz VALUES (3,
  upper('a', 'b'))` is `42883` here, as it was before them.

  A typed constant's **input conversion** is the same kind of member, pglet converting it
  while it parses where 18.6 converts it in the statement's analysis:
  `INSERT INTO dz VALUES (1, '1e39'::real::text)` is `22003` out of the `DO` here — at
  the build before row 149 closed it wrote `1|Infinity` (**silent**) — and `INSERT INTO dz
  VALUES (3, 'zzz'::int::text)` is `22P02` out of the `DO` on both builds; 18.6 runs the
  handler for each. The controls are what pglet converts or binds at execution: `INSERT
  INTO dz VALUES (5, 1e400::float8::text)` (a `numeric` constant's cast) and `INSERT INTO
  dz VALUES (7, nosuch)` (a missing column) are caught on both engines — the first written
  as `5|Infinity` by the build before row 149's close. Loud wherever it is reached. No fixture: 18.6's answer is the handler's row, which pglet does not reach.

- **301 · A typed constant that fails its input conversion is accepted in a stored
  expression.** 18.6 converts a typed constant (`'1e39'::real`, `'zzz'::int`) in parse
  analysis, so a `CHECK`, an index predicate or an index key expression holding one that
  its type's input function refuses is refused by the DDL itself. pglet's stored-expression
  gate (`executor::ddl`'s `validate_stored_expr`) does not convert it there: the
  representative-row probe reaches the conversion and fails on it, and its match keeps only
  `UndefinedFunction` / `NotImplemented`, so the input error is **discarded by kind** and
  the DDL is accepted — after which every write that evaluates the expression is refused,
  a `NULL` one included, since the constant is converted before the comparison is decided.
  The class was first recorded as a residual of row 51's quantifier close (`CHECK
  (upper('a'::int) = 'A')` at its five spellings and both index positions, and the year-0
  date member), where its routes and its row-count condition are stated; row 149's close
  added a member that **moved**: a float input past its range, which the build before it
  answered as `±Infinity` and stored.

  Measured on both engines over empty tables, each refused by the DDL on 18.6 and accepted
  here: `CREATE TABLE fr1 (r real CHECK (r < '1e39'::real))` (`22003` there), after which
  `INSERT INTO fr1 VALUES (1)` and `… (NULL)` are each `22003` here — at the build before
  row 149's close both rows were stored, the check comparing against `Infinity`;
  `CREATE INDEX fr5_i ON fr5 (r) WHERE r < '1e39'::real` and `CREATE INDEX fr5_j ON fr5
  ((r + '1e39'::real))` (`22003` there), after which `INSERT INTO fr5 VALUES (1)` is
  `22003` here and `INSERT 0 1` there; and `CREATE TABLE fz (a int CHECK (a < 'zzz'::int))`
  and `CHECK (a < '99999999999'::int)` (`22P02` and `22003` there), after which every
  `INSERT` is `22P02` here, on both builds.

  **The column `DEFAULT` is a separate gate, and it is not total either.**
  `executor::ddl`'s `cook_column_default` refuses a default whose probe raises an
  input-function code, matched by SQLSTATE (`is_cook_time_error`), so `CREATE TABLE fd2 (a
  int DEFAULT 'zzz'::int)` is `22P02` on both engines and `DEFAULT '99999999999'::int` is
  refused on both (`22P02` here, `22003` there). `22003` is outside that set, deliberately
  — `(2147483648)::int` is accepted by 18.6's DDL and refused per row — and a float input's
  range refusal carries `22003` too, so `CREATE TABLE fd (r real DEFAULT '1e39'::real)` and
  `DEFAULT '1e309'::float8` are accepted here and `22003` on 18.6, every defaulted
  `INSERT` then `22003` here. The build before row 149's close accepted the same DDL and
  stored `Infinity` through it.

  **The dump carries the accepted expression to a restore that drops it.** Over a
  `--data-dir` store holding `CREATE TABLE fq (k int, r real, CHECK (k < 5 OR r <
  '1e39'::real))` and the row `(1, 1)` — written, the `OR` deciding at `k < 5` — `pglet_server
  dump` exits `0` and emits `ALTER TABLE fq ADD CONSTRAINT fq_check CHECK (((k < 5) OR (r <
  ('1e39')::real)))`; `psql -f` of that script into 18.6 reports `22003` on that statement
  and exits `0`, leaving the table and its row and no constraint. Measured. Reach:
  ordinary for a `CHECK` or partial index written with such a constant. No fixture: 18.6's
  refusal is the DDL's, which an `@expect-error` scores as agreement with any pglet error,
  and the accept here is the divergence.
- **96 · A malformed timestamp / timestamptz spelling answers `22P02`.** DATE and TIME
  split malformed input from an out-of-range field the way the repo `CLAUDE.md` says the
  temporal family does — `'zzz'::date` is `22007`, `'2026-13-01'::date` is `22008`,
  `'zzz'::time` is `22007`, `'25:00:00'::time` is `22008`, all four agreeing with 18.6. The
  timestamp types split them as well, their reader following 18.6's field loop
  (`docs/temporal.md` § Reading a timestamp spelling), but spend a different code on the
  malformed half: `'zzz'::timestamp` is `22P02 invalid input syntax for type timestamp`
  here against `22007` there, and `timestamptz` answers the same way. The malformed half
  was measured on all five routes a timestamp literal reaches — `TIMESTAMP '…'`,
  `::timestamp`, `CAST(… AS timestamp)`, a column `DEFAULT` and an `INSERT` — with no
  route splitting.

  **The out-of-range half agrees.** A time of day, a year 0, a month or a day out of range
  is 18.6's own `22008 date/time field value out of range: "…"`, message and all —
  `'2024-13-01 00:00:00'::timestamp`, `'2000-06-30 23:59:60.5'::timestamp` and
  `'0000-02-30 12:00:00'::timestamp`, measured, and pinned by
  `types/timestamp_month_13_loud.sql`, `types/timestamp_second_60_fraction_past_midnight_loud.sql`,
  `types/timestamp_year_zero_field_loud.sql` and their siblings; 18.6 adds a `DateStyle`
  hint to the month and day-range sentence that pglet does not send. A numeric offset out
  of range is 18.6's `22009` where 18.6's field loop reads it: after a time of day written
  before it (`'2000-01-01 25:00:00+16'::timestamptz` is `22008` on both), ahead of one
  written after it (`'+16 2000-01-01 25:00:00'::timestamptz` is `22009` on both), and in a
  signed year whose digits 18.6 reads as an offset (`'+2026-06-15 12:00:00'::timestamp` is
  `22009` on both).

  **What the malformed half holds**, each measured: a spelling 18.6 also refuses as
  malformed — `'zzz 00:00:00+16'::timestamptz`, `'2000-01-01-12:34:56'::timestamp`,
  `'+0001-01-01 12:00:00'::timestamp` (its offset field in range and not read whole) and
  `'2000-01-01 00:00:00+05.5'::timestamptz` — and a spelling 18.6 reads through a field kind
  the reader does not model, where 18.6 answers a value or another code: a month name, a
  named zone, a POSIX zone with a daylight-saving part, a run-together `hhmmss`
  (`docs/temporal.md` lists them). The `date` cast of a timestamp spelling is DATE's own
  reader and answers `22007`: `'2024-01-01 00:00'::date` is `22007` here and `2024-01-01`
  on 18.6. A consumer reaches it: drizzle's `date({mode: 'date'})` column binds a `Date`
  as `toISOString()`, and `'2024-06-15T00:00:00.000Z'::date` is `22007` here and `2024-06-15`
  on 18.6 (measured; `tests-web/npm/drizzle_test.ts` pins pglet's `22007`).

  Loud at every member, so nothing is silent; what it costs is a client that branches on
  the SQLSTATE class, and a fixture — an `@expect-error` over a malformed timestamp literal
  compares `22P02` against `22007` and fails, so this half is pinned by the unit tests in
  `types::text` instead.

- **142 · A date or timestamp outside pglet's domain is refused.** pglet's `date`,
  `timestamp` and `timestamptz` values are `0001-01-01` through `9999-12-31`, a
  `timestamptz` read in UTC (`docs/temporal.md` § The date and timestamp domain). 18.6's
  range is wider on both sides and prints the years before 1 with ` BC`, so where a
  statement's value falls between the two ranges, 18.6 answers it and pglet refuses. The
  refusal is `22008` with 18.6's own sentence for a value leaving its range —
  `date out of range` for a `date` result, `timestamp out of range` for a `timestamp` or
  `timestamptz` one — at each producer that section's table names. Measured on both
  engines:

  | statement | 18.6 | pglet |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `'0001-01-01'::date - 1` | `0001-12-31 BC` | `22008 date out of range` |
  | `'9999-12-31'::date + 1` | `10000-01-01` | `22008 date out of range` |
  | `'0001-01-01'::date - interval '1 day'` | `0001-12-31 00:00:00 BC` | `22008 timestamp out of range` |
  | `timestamp '0001-01-01 00:00:00' - interval '1 microsecond'` | `0001-12-31 23:59:59.999999 BC` | `22008 timestamp out of range` |
  | `date '9999-12-31' + time '24:00'` | `10000-01-01 00:00:00` | `22008 timestamp out of range` |
  | `timestamptz '0001-01-01 03:00:00+05'` | `0001-12-31 22:00:00+00 BC` | `22008 timestamp out of range` |
  | `timestamptz '9999-12-31 23:00:00-05'` | `10000-01-01 04:00:00+00` | `22008 timestamp out of range` |
  | `'9999-12-31 23:59:59.9999999'::timestamp` | `10000-01-01 00:00:00` | `22008 timestamp out of range` |
  | `date_trunc('decade', timestamp '0005-06-01')` | `0001-01-01 00:00:00 BC` | `22008 timestamp out of range` |
  | `'10000-01-01'::date` | `10000-01-01` | `22008 date out of range` |

  The two `timestamptz` literals are the pair that shows the instant is read in UTC and
  not as written, and `'0001-01-01 04:59:59.9999995+05'::timestamptz` — below the edge in
  UTC until the rounding carries it onto `0001-01-01 00:00:00+00` — is a value on both
  engines, which is what places the check after the rounding. Without the domain, the
  upper `timestamptz` literal panicked inside `time`'s `to_offset`, which under the release
  profile's `panic = "abort"` ends the server process; and the lower rows were silent
  values, `0000-12-31` and its neighbours, which a dump carries into a `COPY` 18.6 refuses
  while `psql -f` exits `0`.

  **A timestamp literal's five-digit year lands here too**, and so does a carry out of
  year 9999: `'10000-01-01 00:00:00'::timestamp` and `'9999-12-31 23:59:60'::timestamp` are
  `22008 timestamp out of range` here against 18.6's `10000-01-01 00:00:00`, while
  `'10000-01-01 00:00:00+05'::timestamptz`, whose UTC reading is inside the domain, is
  `9999-12-31 19:00:00+00` on both, each measured. The rounding carry of a `(p)` modifier is
  this refusal under row 123's residual.

  **At `Bind`, the refusal costs what row 139's reader verdicts cost.** A binary `date`,
  `timestamp` or `timestamptz` parameter outside the domain but inside 18.6's range — a
  year before 1 or a year past 9999 — is
  `22008` here, raised inside the reader and so ahead of the leftover check: given a
  trailing byte, 18.6 answers `22P03 incorrect binary data format in bind parameter 1`
  and pglet this `22008`, measured at a year-0 `date` and `timestamp`. The `infinity` /
  `-infinity` sentinels are values on both engines, not members (row 139). Outside 18.6's range the two agree — measured without a tail at both ends
  of `date`, `timestamp` and `timestamptz`, and with one below a `date`'s range and past a
  `timestamp`'s. And a refusal
  at `Bind` fails an open block where 18.6's accepted value leaves it healthy — measured
  with a year-0 binary `date` bound between two inserts and a `COMMIT`, which keeps both
  rows on 18.6 and neither here, as row 139 measured for a `timestamp` in year 20029.

  **A store written without the domain is not opened, and its rows would still be
  refused.** Every such store carries a store magic older than `PGMO`, which reopen refuses.
  Measured, by a build that opened one, over one holding a year-0 `date`, `timestamp` and `timestamptz`: each renders as
  stored, while a cast building a new value from one, an `INSERT … SELECT` of one and an
  `UPDATE` assigning one back are refused `22008`, and the export refuses with `22008` too
  rather than emit the `COPY` line a restore loses (`dump::temporal_restore_failure`, asked
  by the dump's row walk and guarded by `crates/pglet/tests/temporal_domain.rs`); it refuses
  a timestamp stored at a non-UTC offset, whose text would reload as a different instant,
  with `22000 cannot dump a timestamp stored at UTC offset …`. An
  `UPDATE` that does not assign the column rewrites the row with the value as stored. No
  18.6 statement corresponds, so these refusals are the dump invariant holding rather than a
  divergence of this row. **The walk asks stored rows only**: an older store's — refused at
  open now —
  `DEFAULT '0000-12-31'`, `CHECK (d <> date '0000-12-31')` or partial-index
  `WHERE d > date '0000-12-31'` dumps at exit `0` and restores into 18.6 short, also at exit
  `0` — measured, with what each loses in `docs/temporal.md` — and a `CHECK` or partial
  index carrying such a constant is still accepted over an empty table here (row 51).

  **Why no fixture holds the code.** 18.6 answers every statement above, so an
  `@expect-error` fixture passes on any pglet error. `types/date_minus_int_below_year_one_refused.sql`,
  `types/date_trunc_decade_below_year_ten_refused.sql` and
  `types/timestamptz_offset_past_year_9999_refused.sql` hold that pglet refuses, and the
  last reddens on a dropped connection too; the code is pinned under `cargo test` by the
  tests the row names.

  **A foreign-key action's conversion is a producer, and it needs no row.** An `ON UPDATE
  CASCADE` converts the parent's new key to the referencing column once per firing, ahead of
  the lookup of the rows it rewrites (`executor::dml`'s `action_assigned_values`, row 200),
  so a key whose `(p)` rounding into the child carries past year 9999 refuses the parent's
  `UPDATE` though no child row takes the carried value, where 18.6's action matches no row
  and the statement stands. Measured on both engines over `p1 (k timestamp PRIMARY KEY)`
  holding `2020-01-01` and `2021-01-01`, referenced `ON UPDATE CASCADE` by `c1 (id int
  PRIMARY KEY, pk timestamp(0))` holding one row at `2020-01-01`: `UPDATE p1 SET k =
  '9999-12-31 23:59:59.9' WHERE k = '2021-01-01'` is `UPDATE 1` there, the parent holding the
  unrounded value, and `22008 timestamp out of range` here; so is a `timestamptz(1)` child of a
  `timestamptz` key moved to `'9999-12-31 23:59:59.99+00'`, with no child row at all. With a
  child row both refuse, with different codes: moving `p1`'s `2020-01-01` to `'9999-12-31
  23:59:59.7'` is `23503` there, its detail `Key (pk)=(10000-01-01 00:00:00) is not present in
  table "p1".` — the repointed child holding the carried value, which no parent row does —
  and `22008` here, and the `timestamptz(1)` child's is the same pair (`Key
  (pk)=(10000-01-01 00:00:00+00)`). An `ON UPDATE SET NULL` child assigns a NULL, which no
  rounding reaches: the childless `timestamptz(1)` move under a `SET NULL` child alone is
  `UPDATE 1` on both. No fixture holds the childless member — 18.6 runs the statement, so a
  faithful fixture is red and an `@expect-error` one passes on any pglet error — nor the code
  of the other, where a faithful `@expect-error` fixture is red on `23503`.

- **143 · An interval at 18.6's infinity field triple is a finite value here.** 18.6 reads
  an `interval` whose months, days and microseconds are all at their maximum
  (`2147483647`, `2147483647`, `9223372036854775807`) as `infinity`, and all at their
  minimum as `-infinity` (`INTERVAL_IS_NOEND` / `INTERVAL_IS_NOBEGIN`). `PgInterval` has no
  infinity. Its binary receive arm refuses either triple (`22007`,
  `docs/param_binding.md`); the text inputs below do not. Writing `<max>` for
  `interval '2147483647 mons 2147483647 days 2562047788:00:54.775807'`, measured on both
  engines, 18.6 at `TimeZone` UTC:

  | statement | 18.6 | pglet |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `<max>::text` | `infinity` | `178956970 years 7 mons 2147483647 days 2562047788:00:54.775807` |
  | `interval '-2147483648 mons -2147483648 days -9223372036854775808 microseconds'::text` | `-infinity` | `-178956970 years -8 mons -2147483648 days -2562047788:00:54.775808` |
  | `interval '2147483647 mons 2147483647 days 2562047788:00:54.775806' + interval '1 microsecond'` | `22008 interval out of range` | the `<max>` value |
  | `interval '-2147483648 mons -2147483648 days -2562047788:00:54.775807' - interval '1 microsecond'` | `22008 interval out of range` | the minimum triple |
  | `- interval '-2147483647 mons -2147483647 days -2562047788:00:54.775807'` | `22008 interval out of range` | the `<max>` value |
  | `timestamp '2000-01-01' - interval '-2147483647 mons -2147483647 days -2562047788:00:54.775807'` | `22008 interval out of range` | `22008 timestamp out of range` |
  | `timestamp '2000-01-01' + <max>` | `infinity` | `22008 timestamp out of range` |
  | `timestamp '-infinity' + <max>`, `timestamp 'infinity' - <max>` | `22008 timestamp out of range` | `-infinity`, `infinity` |
  | `timestamp 'infinity' - <min>`, `timestamptz 'infinity' - <min>`, `timestamp '2000-01-01' - <min>`, `<min>` being the second row's interval | `infinity` | `22008 interval out of range` |
  | `timestamp '-infinity' - <min>` | `22008 timestamp out of range` | `22008 interval out of range` |
  | `timestamp 'infinity' + <min>` | `22008 timestamp out of range` | `infinity` |
  | `timestamp '2000-01-01' + <min>`, `timestamp '2000-01-01' - <max>` | `-infinity` | `22008 timestamp out of range` |
  | `<max> - <max>` | `22008 interval out of range` | `00:00:00` |
  | `<max> / 2` | `infinity` | `89478485 years 3 mons 1073741838 days 1281023906:00:27.387904` |
  | `<max> * 1` | `infinity` | `22008 interval out of range` |
  | `'2147483647 mons 2147483647 days 2562047788:00:54.775807'::interval(3)` | `infinity` | `22008 interval out of range` |
  | `time '00:00' + <max>` | `22008 cannot add infinite interval to time` | `04:00:54.775807` |
  | `extract(epoch from <max>)` | `Infinity` | `5842218453753654.775807` |
  | `sum` / `max` over one `<max>` row | `infinity` | the `<max>` value |
  | `avg` over one `<max>` row | `infinity` | `22008 interval out of range` |

  The `date` and `timestamptz` twins of the `timestamp` rows answer as those rows do —
  measured at each statement of each row that names `<max>` or `<min>` beside a
  `timestamp`. Beside those rows, `<min>` added to `-infinity` leaves it unchanged on both
  engines, measured at each of the three types.
  The `<max>` triple reaches both engines from the verbose spelling with `years` and
  `hours`, the ISO-8601 `P178956970Y7M2147483647DT2562047788H54.775807S`, the SQL-standard
  `178956970-7 2147483647 2562047788:00:54.775807`, a `CAST`, an array literal's element,
  an `INSERT`, a `COPY FROM` field and a text-format bound parameter — `infinity` on 18.6
  and the finite value here at each — and a string the wasm host binds is the finite value
  too. A stored `<max>` value dumps as its finite text, and `psql -f` loads that dump into
  18.6 at exit `0` as `infinity`.

  **A stored minimum triple loses its table on restore.** Stored from
  `interval '-2147483648 mons -2147483648 days -2562047788:00:54.775807' - interval '1 microsecond'`
  beside two ordinary rows, it dumps as
  `-178956970 years -8 mons -2147483648 days -2562047788:00:54.775808`, text 18.6 and pglet
  each refuse `22007`. The export exits `0`; `psql -f` into 18.6, and into a pglet B+tree
  server, exits `0` with that table's `COPY` refused and the table empty — the two ordinary
  rows lost with it — while a table dumped after it loads. The text is unreadable because
  of its microseconds field, not the triple: `-2562047788:00:54.775808` alone, and
  `-2147483648 days -2562047788:00:54.775808`, are values both engines hold and neither
  reads back, and 18.6's own `pg_dump` round trip loses a table holding either one the same
  way; a stored `-2147483648 days`, `-178956970 years -8 mons`, or the two together, reads
  back on both. So the minimum triple's loss is pglet's alone: 18.6 holds it
  as `-infinity`, and its `pg_dump` round trip restores that row and its neighbours.

  **Why no fixture.** Where pglet answers and 18.6 answers otherwise or refuses, a faithful
  fixture is red; where pglet refuses and 18.6 answers, `@expect-error` passes on any error.
  At the `timestamp - interval` negation row and its twins both engines refuse `22008`, and
  the divergence is the message (`interval out of range` there, `timestamp out of range`
  here): an `@expect-error` fixture is green on the shared code and holds nothing of it,
  and one with `@expect-message` is red.

- **144 · `isfinite` checks its argument's type at eval, after a NULL has answered.**
  `StringFunc::IsFinite` is a strict string function: `eval_string_fn` answers NULL for a
  NULL argument before any arm runs, and the `IsFinite` arm refuses a value that is not a
  `date` or a `timestamp` with `42883` only when one reaches it. 18.6 resolves the call
  against its four overloads (`date`, `timestamp`, `timestamptz`, `interval`) before any row
  is read. Measured on both engines, `cls (i INT)`:

  | statement | 18.6 | pglet |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT isfinite(NULL)` | `42725 function isfinite(unknown) is not unique` | one NULL row |
  | `SELECT isfinite(NULL::text)` | `42883` | one NULL row |
  | `SELECT isfinite(i) FROM cls`, `cls` empty | `42883` | no rows |
  | `SELECT isfinite(i) FROM cls`, `cls` holding one NULL | `42883` | one NULL row |
  | `SELECT isfinite(i) FROM cls`, `cls` holding a NULL and a `1` | `42883` | `42883` |
  | `SELECT isfinite(interval '1 day')` | `t` | `42883` |
  | `SELECT isfinite(time '01:00')` | `t` | `42883` |

  `isfinite(NULL::timestamp)` is NULL on both. The `time` member reaches 18.6's `interval`
  overload through the implicit `time → interval` cast (`pg_cast`'s `castcontext` is `i`);
  pglet models no `interval` overload, `PgInterval` having no infinity (row 143). Only a
  **non-NULL** `interval` or `time` parts the engines: `isfinite(NULL::interval)` and
  `isfinite(NULL::time)` are NULL on both, and over a `time` or an `interval` column the
  call answers no rows on an empty table and one NULL on a table holding one NULL, on both
  — so the late type check costs nothing there, and a plan-time gate refusing those two
  types would refuse what 18.6 answers.

  A bare `NULL` is not a type with no overload: it is `unknown`, which more than one of
  the four overloads could take, so 18.6 refuses the call as ambiguous (`42725`) rather
  than as missing. An untyped literal is `unknown` too — `isfinite('infinity')`,
  `isfinite('1 day')` and `isfinite('2000-01-01')` are each `42725` on 18.6 — and each is
  `42883` here, with the `IsFinite` arm's own message, the literal reaching it as a
  value that is neither a `date` nor a timestamp.

  **The silent members are not particular to `isfinite`.** `upper(i)` and
  `date_trunc('day', i)` over the same `cls` answer as `isfinite(i)` does at each of its
  three rows above, against 18.6's `42883` at each. What they share is the strict string
  function's NULL check standing ahead of its argument's type check at eval, where 18.6's
  refusal does not depend on any row.

  **Why no fixture.** At the silent members pglet answers where 18.6 refuses, so a faithful
  fixture is red; at `interval` and `time` 18.6 answers, so `@expect-error` passes on any
  error.

- **~~145~~ · Closed — a bare `$N` whose type the client declared has that type as a
  result column.** A client that declared a parameter's type at `Parse` and projected the
  parameter used to get a column typed `text`: the output-type walks gave an
  `Expr::Parameter` no type and neither was handed the statement's parameter types, so a
  `timestamptz` rendered without `+00`, and in binary results the declared type's bytes
  arrived under `25`. Under an operator the column took the other operand's type
  (`$1 + 1` declared `int8` was `23`), under `ARRAY[$1]` `text[]`, under `abs` and `round`
  `701`, under `date_trunc` a `timestamptz` became `1114`. A bare `$N` whose type the client
  declared is now read as a typed operand from the parser on — the mechanism, and why the
  value itself was wrong beside a typed sibling, is row 146's bullet. The measured members —
  the bare and binary-result ones at `int4`, `int8`, `bool`, `float8`, `jsonb`, `date`,
  `numeric`, `timestamp`, `uuid`, `bytea`, `int4[]`, `timestamptz` and `timestamptz[]`,
  `COALESCE($1, NULL)`, `CASE WHEN true THEN $1 END`, a derived table, `unnest($1)`,
  `concat`, `concat_ws`, `::text` and `||` over a `timestamptz`, and the operator and
  function members with their `int4`, `int2`, `int8` and `text` controls — were re-measured
  on both engines over a raw extended-protocol client, text and binary results: each agrees
  with 18.6 in the `ParameterDescription`, the statement and portal descriptors, and the
  value. Pinned by `params/declared_bare_param_result_column_type.sql`,
  `params/declared_numeric_function_result_type.sql` and
  `params/declared_timestamptz_result_type.sql` through `Describe`, and by
  `engine_declared_params.rs` over the executor's result columns too — the walk the
  simple-query descriptor and the column-type-aware text encoder read, which no bound
  fixture reaches.

- **~~146~~ · Closed — a declared `$N` has its declared type in parse analysis.** A client
  that declared a parameter's type at `Parse` and put the parameter in a `COALESCE`, a
  `CASE`, `greatest`/`least`, `nullif` or an `ARRAY[…]` beside an operand the lowering types
  used to get the parameter converted to that operand's type: `coalesce($1, 1)` declared
  `numeric` and bound `1.5` answered `integer` `2`, `int8` `5000000000` was
  `22003`, a `boolean` `t` answered `1` where 18.6 refuses `42804`, an `INSERT` stored the
  converted value, and `DELETE … WHERE n = coalesce($1, 0)` over rows `1.5` and `2` removed
  the `2` row. The server planned through `parse_single`, which is given no parameter
  types, and `infer_param_types` read the declared ones only over the finished plan.

  18.6's `exec_parse_message` seeds the parameter-type array `variable_paramref_hook`
  reads with the Parse message's OIDs (`parse_param.c`), so a declared `$N` is a `Param` of
  that type from its first reference, and `select_common_type` resolves the construct over
  it. The native server's `Parse` now plans through
  `parser::parse_single_with_param_types`, which reads a declared `$N` as
  `Expr::Cast { Parameter, <type> }` — the shape a written `$N::<type>` lowers to, so the
  coercion pass, the branch-unification gate and both declared-type walkers see a typed
  operand through the arms they already carry, and the bound value, decoded as the declared
  type, is not converted. A re-plan after DDL is handed the declared types again, at
  `Describe` and at `Execute`. An undeclared parameter is still a bare `Expr::Parameter`;
  where its inference reads a sibling's type it now reads the declared one, as on 18.6 —
  `$1 = $2` with only `$1` declared `numeric` describes `{numeric,numeric}` and answers
  `t`, where it was `42883 operator does not exist: numeric = text`. A string literal beside
  a declared `$N` resolves to the declared type at a comparison (`$1 = '1.50'`), through the
  comparison coercion's cast anchor, which also serves a written `x::numeric = '1.50'`, and
  in a common-type construct. Neither reaches every construct — the residuals below.
  Each statement above and each measured member beside it — `CASE` in either branch,
  `greatest`/`least`/`nullif`, `ARRAY[$1, 1]`, the `int8` overflow shapes, the `date` and
  `text` refusals and the undeclared and wider-sibling controls — agrees on both engines
  in both result formats, as do the write shapes.

  **A declared `$N` is still an index probe.** The cast wrapper is not a bare parameter, and
  index selection declined it at first: a point read over a 100 000-row `INT` primary key
  measured about 0.05 ms undeclared and about 19 ms declared `int4`. `is_row_independent`
  admits a `Cast` directly over a `$N`, and `probe_key_value` exact-or-declines the cast's
  result as it does a bare parameter's; `planner::tests`'s
  `a_parameter_the_client_declared_is_a_probe` pins the plan shape, which no differential
  fixture can see.

  **Residuals.** Each measured against 18.6 over a raw extended-protocol client; the full
  statements are `docs/param_binding.md` § A declared type is part of parse analysis.

  - A declared OID pglet does not model is collapsed to no declaration by the wire decoder
    (row 43), so it reaches no analysis: `coalesce($1, 1)` declared `point` and bound
    `(1,2)` is `22P02` here against 18.6's `42804`.
  - `LIMIT` and `OFFSET` read the `$N` token without the expression parser, so the
    declaration is not seen there: `LIMIT $1` declared `text` is `22000` at `Execute`
    against 18.6's `42804` at `Parse`, and declared `numeric` bound `1` is `22000` where
    18.6 answers. Loud.
  - An undeclared sibling is described `0` and refused at `Execute` where pglet's inference
    has no rule for the construct: with `$1` declared `int4`, `nullif($1, $2)` and
    `CASE $1 WHEN $2 …` (`42883`), `$1 + $2`, `$1 - $2`, `$1 * $2` (`42804`), all
    `{int4,int4}` and answered on 18.6; `$2 IN ($1)` with `$1` declared `numeric`
    (`42883`); and over an `INT` column `a IN ($1, $2)` with `$1` declared `numeric`
    describes `$2` as `int4` against 18.6's `numeric`, so binding `1.0`, `1.5` is `22P02`
    where 18.6 answers the row. Loud.
  - A string literal beside a declared `$N` is not resolved at `$1 IN ('1')` and
    `nullif($1, '1.5')` (`42883`), `$1 = ANY('{1,2}')` (`0A000`) or `$1 + '2'` (`42804`),
    where 18.6 answers; the written `1::int4 IN ('1')`, `nullif(1.5::numeric, '1.5')`,
    `1::int4 = ANY('{1,2}')` and `1::int4 + '2'` refuse identically, so these belong to the
    literal resolution rather than to the declaration (row 262 records the `IN` and arithmetic members; the
    `nullif` and `ANY` members refuse beside a plain column as well — `nullif(n, '1.5')` `42883`, `a = ANY('{1,2}')`
    `0A000` — so they are outside its class and recorded only here). Loud.
  - A declared **`text`** beside an enum column orders by the label bytes, and it writes.
    The declared `varchar` spelling beside it is now refused as 18.6 refuses it: a cast to
    `varchar` is an identity the gate can decide, where a cast to `text` is the node a
    written `x::mood` also produces and so is not. Row 114's bullet, where both are
    recorded, and row 104 for the cast node itself. The fixture harness reaches this
  class through `-- @param-declared` (`tests/README.md`): the `params/declared_*` fixtures
  hold each construct, the `42804` refusals with the SQLSTATE matched, the `DELETE`,
  `INSERT` and `UPDATE` write shapes, and `params/declared_coalesce_undeclared_control.sql`
  the undeclared polarity.

- **148 · One parameter deduced two types.** Postgres deduces one type per parameter
  across the whole statement and refuses a statement whose positions deduce two;
  `docs/compatibility.md` records the missing unification as a gap in the parameter-inference section.
  Measured on the native server against 18.6 over a raw extended-protocol client, `$1`
  undeclared at `Parse` and bound `5` as text, over `tgt (i int, t text)`:

  | statement | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT $1, $1 UNION SELECT 5, 'a'` | `ParameterDescription` `[23]`, rows `(5, 5)` and `(5, a)` | `42P08 inconsistent types deduced for parameter $1` at `Parse` |
  | `INSERT INTO tgt (i, t) SELECT $1, $1 UNION SELECT 5, 'a'` | accepted, both rows written | `42P08` at `Parse`, nothing written |
  | `INSERT INTO tgt (i, t) VALUES ($1, $1)` | accepted, the row written | `42P08` at `Parse` |
  | `UPDATE tgt SET i = $1, t = $1` | accepted | `42P08` at `Parse` |
  | `SELECT * FROM (VALUES ($1, $1), (5, 'a')) v` | rows `(5, 5)` and `(5, a)` | `42P08` at `Parse` |
  | `SELECT $1 = 1, $1 = 'a'::text` | `42883 operator does not exist: integer = text` at `Execute`, after a `ParameterDescription` of `[23]` | the same `42883` at `Parse` |

  The class does not depend on the set operation or the `VALUES` list: the `INSERT …
  VALUES` and `UPDATE` members name neither.

  **Where the second deduction is an operator, whether pglet refuses follows the rows and
  the plan.** 18.6 refuses `SELECT 1 FROM u WHERE id = $1 AND t = $1` over `u (id uuid, t
  text)` at `Parse`, `42883 operator does not exist: text = uuid`. Here the answers below fit an operator gate
  that runs where a row is evaluated or an index probe is built (inferred from them, not
  read from the code). Measured through the npm
  package and the native server on both build profiles, `$1` bound a uuid's text: over an
  empty `u` with no index, `(0 rows)` on each; with `id` a `PRIMARY KEY` and the table
  empty, `42883 … uuid = text` on the accelerated build and `(0 rows)` on the stripped one;
  over one row whose `id` is the bound value, `42883` on each — `text = uuid`, as on 18.6,
  save the accelerated build over the `PRIMARY KEY`, which names `uuid = text`; and over
  one row whose `id` is another value, the empty-table answers again — `(0 rows)` on each
  with no index, and with the `PRIMARY KEY` `42883` accelerated and `(0 rows)` stripped.
  The members where no row passes `id = $1` are **silent** — the empty table is one case —
  and the indexed ones are a build-profile divergence (`docs/indexes.md` § Build profiles).

- **~~149~~ · Closed — Out of range for a float type.** 18.6's `float4in` / `float8in` refuse a decimal
  whose value overflows the type, or underflows it to zero, with `22003 "<input>" is out of
  range for type real` (`double precision`). pglet read the text through
  `executor::coerce`'s `parse_float`, a `str::parse` with no range check (read from the
  code), so the value saturated. Measured on the native server against 18.6, in sequence
  over one `tt (r real)`, empty at the start:

  | statement | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT '1e39'::real` / `'-1e39'::real` | `Infinity` / `-Infinity` | `22003` |
  | `SELECT '1e-50'::real` | `0` | `22003` |
  | `SELECT '1e309'::float8` | `Infinity` | `22003` |
  | `INSERT INTO tt (r) VALUES ('1e39')` | `INSERT 0 1`, `Infinity` stored | `22003` |
  | `SELECT r FROM tt UNION SELECT '1e39'` | a row `Infinity` | `22003` |
  | `INSERT INTO tt (r) SELECT '1e39' UNION SELECT r FROM tt` | `INSERT 0 1` | `22003` |
  | `INSERT INTO tt (r) SELECT x FROM (VALUES (1::real), ('1e39')) v(x)` | `INSERT 0 2` | `22003` |

  The `numeric`-to-`real` cast is half a member: it refuses an overflow itself
  (`1e39::numeric::real` is `22003 real out of range` here, the code agreeing and the
  message not), and `1e-50::numeric::real` is `0` here and `22003` there.
  The `numeric`-to-`double precision` conversion does not refuse: `SELECT 1e400::numeric::float8`, `SELECT
  1e400::float8` and `INSERT INTO t (x) VALUES (1e400)` over a `float8` column answer `Infinity` here and `22003`
  there, and a foreign key reads the saturated value — over `pf (k float8 PRIMARY KEY)` holding `'Infinity'` and `cf
  (k numeric REFERENCES pf)`, `INSERT INTO cf VALUES (1e400)` is accepted here and `22003` there.

  **What closed it.** One reader, `pglet_core::types`' `parse_float4_text` /
  `parse_float8_text` (the `float_input` module), is `float4in_internal` /
  `float8in_internal`: it delimits the number `strtod` would read — a sign, then
  `infinity` / `inf` / `nan` in any case, or a decimal — converts it with one correctly
  rounded step to the target width, refuses an overflow or a nonzero value that rounds to
  zero `22003` naming the number as read (a subnormal is in range), and only then refuses
  trailing text `22P02`, the order `float.c` takes, so `'1e39x'::real` is the range error
  on both. Whitespace is C's `isspace` set, so a no-break space is no longer trimmed: a
  no-break space (U+00A0) ahead of `1`, cast to `float8`, answered `1` here before the
  repair and is `22P02` on both now.
  `coerce_value`'s text arms and both `numeric` arms read through it — the `numeric` value
  rendered by its `numeric_out` text first, as `numeric_float4` / `numeric_float8` do — so
  the `numeric`-to-`real` refusal now carries 18.6's message, digits and all. Measured
  after the repair against 18.6, each agreeing in code and message: every row of the table
  above, `' 1e39 '::real`, `'1e39x'::real`, `'2e-324'::float8`, `'3.4028236e38'::real`,
  `1e39::numeric::real`, `1e-50::numeric::real`, `1e400::numeric::float8`,
  `1e400::float8`, `INSERT INTO t (x) VALUES (1e400)` over a `float8` column, `ARRAY['1e39']::real[]`
  and `'{1e39}'::real[]`; and the controls `'1e-40'::real`, `'4e-324'::float8`,
  `'0e-999'::float8`, `'-0'::float8`, `'Infinity'`, `'-inf'`, `'+inf'`, `'INFINITY'`, `'NaN'`
  and `'-nan'`, which answer on both.

  **Residuals.** A `numeric` operand beside a float in an operator is converted by
  `executor::expr`'s `value_to_f64_opt`, which does not refuse: `SELECT 1e400 > 1::float8`
  is `t` here and `SELECT 1e400 * 1::float8` `Infinity`, both `22003` on 18.6, which casts
  the `numeric` to `double precision` through the same `float8in` — **silent**, measured,
  and it **writes** and filters: over `fj (d float8)` holding `1` and `0`, `UPDATE fj SET d =
  d + 1e400 WHERE d = 1` stores `Infinity` here, and `SELECT d FROM fj WHERE d = 1e-400`
  matches the `0` row, each `22003` on 18.6. A foreign key reads its child value the
  same way: over `pf (k float8 PRIMARY KEY)` holding `'Infinity'` and `0` and `cf (k numeric
  REFERENCES pf)`, `INSERT INTO cf VALUES (1e400)` and `… (1e-400)` are `23503` here — the
  probe finding no parent — against 18.6's `22003`, whose check casts the child to
  `float8` (both were accepted at the build before this close). And the `double
  precision`-to-`real` cast refuses its overflow but not its underflow:
  `'1e-50'::float8::real` is `0` here and `22003 value out of range: underflow` on 18.6
  (`'1e39'::float8::real` is `22003` on both, the message pglet's own) — pre-existing,
  measured.
  Two spellings glibc's `strtod` reads and this reader refuses `22P02` are loud the other
  way: a hexadecimal float (`'0x1A'::float8` is `26` on 18.6) and a NaN with a payload
  (`'nan(123)'::float8` is `NaN` there). A `real` column's `IN` list keeps the timing
  row 280 records: a constant past the range, or one that underflows, is refused when a
  row's evaluation reaches it, so over an empty table `x IN (0.1, 1e-50)` answers here and
  is `22003` there. Guards: the `types/float4_input_*`, `types/float8_input_*` (the
  no-break space's `types/float8_input_no_break_space_loud.sql` among them),
  `types/float_input_*` and `types/numeric_to_*` fixtures, and `float_input`'s unit tests.

- **150 · A claimed parameter in an INSERT source.** In an `INSERT … SELECT` source,
  `planner::dml`'s `target_list_source_types` reads a bare undeclared `$N` as
  `AssignmentSource::Opaque`, which a sort, grouping, `DISTINCT` or window key naming the
  entry leaves unresolved (read from the code), so the assignment gate never sees `text`.
  18.6 resolves such a parameter to `text` as it resolves a constant. Measured on the
  native server against 18.6, `$1` undeclared at `Parse` and bound `t`, over `s (n int)`
  holding one row and `t (b bool)`:

  | statement | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `INSERT INTO t (b) SELECT $1 FROM s ORDER BY 1` | accepted, the row written | `42804 column "b" is of type boolean but expression is of type text` at `Parse` |
  | the same with `ORDER BY $1`, with `GROUP BY 1`, and as `SELECT DISTINCT $1 FROM s` | accepted, the row written | `42804` at `Parse` |
  | `INSERT INTO t (b) SELECT $1 FROM s` — no key (the control) | accepted, the row written; `ParameterDescription` `[16]` | accepted, `ParameterDescription` `[16]` |

  Over `tgt (bo bool, b bigint)`, `INSERT INTO tgt (bo, b) SELECT $1, row_number() OVER
  (PARTITION BY $1) FROM s` and `SELECT DISTINCT ON ($1) $1, 1 FROM s` are accepted here
  and `42804` there as well.

  **The target column's type decides whether there is a divergence at all, and the bound is
  the string family rather than `text`.** 18.6 resolves the parameter to `text`, and an
  assignment from `text` is legal to `text`, `varchar(n)` and `char(n)` — so the same
  `ORDER BY 1` statement into a `v varchar(5)` or a `c char(3)` column is **accepted on
  both engines**, and an over-long one is `22001 value too long for
  type character varying(5)` on both. Into `varchar(5)` the stored value agrees too; into
  `char(3)` only the *acceptance* does — 18.6 stores the blank-padded `'ab '` under
  declared `1042` where pglet stores `'ab'` under `1043`, which is pglet modelling no
  `bpchar` rather than anything this row's parameter does. `bool`, `int`, `numeric` and
  `date` are the measured divergent members. A set operation's side reads the same `$N` as `unknown`
  instead, so the set-operation spellings of these keys are refused on both engines.

- **151 · A VALUES cell naming an enclosing column.** `planner::query`'s
  `unify_values_columns` types a FROM-clause `VALUES` list's cells as the list is parsed,
  against no relation (read from the code), so a cell naming an enclosing query's column
  contributes no type and an `unknown` constant beside it makes the column `text` — where
  18.6 types the column by the enclosing column and converts the constant. A set
  operation's side naming an enclosing column is typed by the statement's **second**
  parse, from the types the correlated re-walk recorded (`docs/scope.md` § A pending
  set-op column's type is never read); this list is not. Measured on the native server against 18.6 over `tt (i int)`
  holding `7`:

  | statement | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT (SELECT x FROM (VALUES (i), ('7')) s(x) LIMIT 1) FROM tt` | `7`, declared `text` | `7`, declared `integer` |
  | `SELECT count(*) FROM tt WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM (VALUES (i), ('07')) s(x) GROUP BY x HAVING count(*) = 2)` | `0` | `1` |
  | the same predicate as `DELETE FROM tt WHERE EXISTS (…)` | `DELETE 0` | `DELETE 1` |

- **153 · Which record is borrowed from is order-dependent.** A set-op node built inside
  a subquery leaves a column naming an enclosing level pending; the correlated re-walk
  records what it unified that column with, and the statement is parsed a second time from
  those records (`docs/scope.md` § A pending set-op column's type is never read). A node
  the re-walk never *reached* — a `SELECT DISTINCT` sort key the rewrite matched to an
  equal target entry and discarded — has no record of its own and takes the hints of a
  node built equal to it. `Plan` equality is blind to the enclosing level a correlated
  name resolves at, so two nodes spelled alike whose bare `i` binds at different levels
  compare equal, and `hinted.iter().find` takes the **first** of them in build order —
  which is decided by the order the entries are written in.

  Measured on the native server against 18.6 over `pp (i INT)` holding `8` and
  `qq (i TEXT)` holding `'7'`, on both wire formats:

  | statement | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT DISTINCT (SELECT i EXCEPT SELECT '7') AS z, (SELECT (SELECT i EXCEPT SELECT '7') FROM qq) AS y FROM pp ORDER BY (SELECT i EXCEPT SELECT '7')` | `8`, NULL under `23`, `25` | the same |
  | the same two entries **swapped** | `42P10 for SELECT DISTINCT, ORDER BY expressions must appear in select list` | NULL, `8` under `25`, `23` |

  The refusal is the key's orphan borrowing the **nested** entry's hints rather than its
  own: the second parse then builds the key unlike the entry it must match, the match
  misses, the key survives into the plan, and `SELECT DISTINCT`'s own gate raises — an
  error `parse_statement` returns from `parse_statement_once` before the `unresolved`
  check is reached at all.

  **What a reader should build from this is not a second refusal.** 18.6 answers both
  orders, so the answering one is the behaviour to keep: what has to move is the match —
  a record must not be borrowed across a level the two nodes resolve differently, which
  means the equality the borrow keys on has to carry what `Plan` equality drops. Refusing
  the first order too would make the pair consistent and both halves wrong.

  Nothing pins either half. The answering order is unpinned, and the refusing one is
  **writable** and unwritten — an `@expect-error` whose recorded shape is 18.6's success
  passes on any pglet error, the shape row 87's two fixtures wear.
  `select/set_op_outer_column_distinct_sort_key_repeats_it.sql` is the control beside it:
  one pending node written twice at **one** level, which both engines answer.

- **260 · The sequence `AS` clause is read and discarded.** `CREATE SEQUENCE … AS <type>`,
  `ALTER SEQUENCE … AS <type>` and an identity column's `GENERATED … AS IDENTITY ( AS <type>
  … )` option read a type name and discard it (`Plan::CreateSequence`'s doc), so a refusal
  18.6 raises only once it has resolved the type never runs here, and a type 18.6 accepts
  does not bound the counter. Measured through the npm package against 18.6:

  | statement | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `CREATE SEQUENCE sq1 AS int4(3)` | `CREATE` | `42601 type modifier is not allowed for type "int4"` |
  | `CREATE SEQUENCE sq2 AS varchar(3)`, and `AS text`, `AS numeric`, `AS FLOAT(1)` | `CREATE` | `22023 sequence type must be smallint, integer, or bigint` |
  | `CREATE SEQUENCE sq3 AS nosuchtype(3)` | `CREATE` | `42704 type "nosuchtype" does not exist` |
  | `CREATE SEQUENCE sq4 AS varchar(0)` | `CREATE` | `22023 length for type varchar must be at least 1` |
  | `ALTER SEQUENCE sq8 AS varchar(3)`, and `AS text` | `ALTER` | `22023 sequence type must be smallint, integer, or bigint` |
  | `CREATE TABLE ti (a int GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY (AS char(0)))`, and `(AS bigint)`, `(AS text START WITH 5)` | `CREATE` | `42601 conflicting or redundant options` |
  | `CREATE SEQUENCE s AS smallint START WITH 32767`, then two `nextval('s')` | `32767`, `32768` | `32767`, then `2200H nextval: reached maximum value of sequence "s" (32767)` |
  | `CREATE SEQUENCE sq7 AS smallint`, then `setval('sq7', 40000)` | `40000` | `22003 setval: value 40000 is out of bounds for sequence "sq7" (1..32767)` |
  | `CREATE SEQUENCE s2 AS integer`, then `setval('s2', 3000000000)` | `3000000000` | `22003 … (1..2147483647)` |

  After `CREATE SEQUENCE sq7 AS smallint`, `information_schema.sequences` answers
  `data_type` `bigint` and `maximum_value` `9223372036854775807` here, `smallint` and
  `32767` there; `ALTER SEQUENCE sq8 AS smallint` answers `ALTER` on both. The refusals
  18.6's grammar raises while it reads the type name are raised here too — `AS FLOAT(0)`
  and `AS FLOAT(54)` `22023`, `AS timestamp(3,1)` and `AS interval(-1)` `42601`, per
  `Plan::CreateSequence`'s doc. Rows 116, 119 and 124 name members of this clause among
  their residuals; row 215 records the other sequence options discarded beside it.
  **Silent**: DDL 18.6 refuses runs, and a counter runs past its declared type's range.
  Reach: ordinary — plain DDL through the npm package. No fixture: a faithful one is red.

- **261 · `DROP TYPE` does not look for a dependent column.** 18.6 refuses `DROP TYPE` of an
  enum a column still declares — `2BP01 cannot drop type mood because other objects depend
  on it` — and `DROP TYPE … CASCADE` drops the column with it. pglet drops the type either
  way and keeps the column. Measured through the npm package against 18.6, over `CREATE
  TYPE mood AS ENUM ('a', 'b'); CREATE TABLE t (m mood); INSERT INTO t VALUES ('a')`:

  | statement, in order | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `DROP TYPE mood` | `DROP` | `2BP01` |
  | `SELECT m::text FROM t` | `a` | `a` |
  | `INSERT INTO t VALUES ('zz')` | `22000 execution error: enum type "mood" not found in catalog` | `22P02 invalid input value for enum mood: "zz"` |
  | `CREATE TYPE mood AS ENUM ('x')` | `CREATE` | `42710 type "mood" already exists` |
  | `INSERT INTO t VALUES ('x')` | `INSERT 0 1` | `22P02 invalid input value for enum mood: "x"` |

  With `CASCADE`, over `t (id INT, m mood)` holding `(1, 'a')`, both answer `DROP`; `SELECT *`
  then answers `1 | a` here, `m` declared `text` (`25`), and `1` alone on 18.6, whose column
  is gone. **Silent, and it writes**: the column outlives its type, and a same-named type
  created later governs the old column with its own member list, its own order and its own
  labels. Rows 105, 110 and 242 reach their states through this route, each noting that 18.6
  refuses the setup; row 248's bullet records what the orphaned column costs the dump.
  `planner/legality.rs` and `docs/enums.md` name the gap where their rules meet it. Reach:
  ordinary — a migration dropping an enum type before the column that uses it. No fixture: a
  faithful `@expect-error` over the `DROP TYPE` is red, pglet answering where 18.6 refuses.

- **262 · A bare string literal stays `text` beside an operand the plan-time pass does not
  type.** 18.6 resolves an `unknown` literal from the operator and its other operand's type,
  so `(SELECT max(ts) FROM t) > '2023-01-01'` reads the literal as `timestamptz` and `a +
  '1'` reads it as `integer`. pglet resolves it in the plan-time pass
  (`planner/coercion.rs`), against only the operand forms that pass can type, and each
  construct has its own list — read from the code, and measured by member rather than
  exhaustively. Under a comparison operator (`IS [NOT] DISTINCT FROM` included, and
  `BETWEEN`, which reaches the gate as two of them), `coerce_comparison_operands` resolves
  it beside a column, an explicit cast (a declared `$N` included), a non-string literal or
  an aggregate whose type is certain as written (`docs/coercion.md` § Where the plan-time
  coercion pass reaches) — so `max(a) = '1'` and `HAVING max(ts) > '2023-01-01'` answer on
  both engines, while one over a guessed argument (`avg(x) = '0.3'` over an
  `unnest(ARRAY[…])` column) or over an argument naming an enclosing query's column

  in an `IN` list, `resolve_in_list_items` resolves it beside a column alone; a simple
  `CASE`'s label is resolved against what `concrete_branch_type` types, a column, a cast, a

  pattern as `bytea` and answers (measured through the npm package; `bytea` is the member
  measured, not a bound). A bound `$N` is typed off its sibling there, so `b LIKE $1` reaches the
  unimplemented `bytea ~~ bytea` instead, `0A000`, as `b LIKE 'ab%'::bytea` does. Beside any other operand
  the literal stays `text`, and where that operand is not text the operand gate refuses the

  for the last line's columns:

  | statement | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |

  | `SELECT 1 IN ('1', '2')`, and `a::int IN ('1', '2')`, `CASE abs(a) WHEN '1' …` | `42883 … integer = text` | `t` / `y` |
  | `SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM p) = '1'`, and a `uuid`, `boolean`, `jsonb`, `numeric` or `date` subquery beside its literal | `42883 … bigint = text` (each with its type) | `t` |
  | `SELECT 1 FROM p WHERE (SELECT max(ts) FROM p) > '2023-01-01'` | `42883 … timestamp without time zone > text` | the row |
  | `SELECT now() > '2023-01-01'`, and `date_trunc('day', ts)` beside it | `42883 … timestamp without time zone > text` | `t` |
  | `SELECT abs(a) = '1'`, and `coalesce(a, 0)`, `(a + 0)`, `length(t)`, `CASE WHEN true THEN a END` | `42883 … integer = text` | `t` |

  | `SELECT d -> 'a' = '1'` | `42883 … jsonb = text` | `t` |
  | `SELECT a + '1'`, and `'1' + a`, `a * '2'`, `(SELECT a FROM p) + '1'`, `'1' + 1`, `2 * '3'`, `1::int + '1'`, and a `bigint`, `numeric` or `float8` column beside a literal | `42804 type error: operator + requires numeric operands` (each with its operator) | each answers |

  `(SELECT a FROM p) = 1`, `(SELECT a FROM p) = $1` bound `'1'`, `a = '1'`, a derived-table
  column's `x = '1'`, `a IN ('1', '2')`, `a::int = '1'`, `a::int BETWEEN '0' AND '2'`, `CASE
  a::int WHEN '1' …`, `(SELECT t FROM p) = 'x'` over a `text` result, `arr @> '{1}'`, `(d ->
  'a') @> '1'`, `jsonb_build_object('a', 1) @> '{"a":1}'` and `(SELECT d FROM p) ? 'a'`. Casting the literal —
  `'2023-01-01'::timestamptz`, `'1'::int`, `'{"a":1}'::jsonb` — answers as 18.6 does on
  every member tried, and is the workaround. Where 18.6's reading of the literal fails, both
  refuse under different codes: `ts - '1 day'` is `42804` here and `22007` there, and `1 +
  'a'` is row 268's. The aggregate members are reached under more nodes now that an
  aggregate under an expression is evaluated (row 89): `max(d) IN ('2022-01-02')` and
  `nullif(max(d), '2022-01-02')` are `42883` here and answered there, where each was
  `0A000`; `CASE max(a) WHEN '1' …` answers on both.

  second argument resolved beside nothing (above).

  The comparison, `IN` and arithmetic refusals are raised from the values, so over no

  arithmetic ones among them do — as 18.6 does where it can read the literal: over an empty `e0 (i4 INT, ts

  ordinary SQL — a timestamp bound written as a literal beside `now()` or an aggregate

  fixture: a faithful one is red; `jsonb/containment_expression_operands.sql` holds the

- **263 · A foreign key with no referenced column list, to a parent with no primary key, is

  `REFERENCES p2(a)` is `CREATE` on both, and `REFERENCES p(a)` is `42830` on both. Loud, a

  `@expect-error` compares the SQLSTATE and a faithful one is red.

- **264 · `lower`, `upper` and `ILIKE` fold Unicode case by the full mapping, context rules
  included.** pglet's value functions fold through Rust's `to_lowercase` / `to_uppercase`

  can turn one character into several and reads the characters around one; 18.6 on a
  libc-provider UTF-8 database folds one character at a time (`towlower` / `towupper`, read
  from the source, not run). They part wherever the two mappings differ, and the members
  below are examples of that, not its list: a character whose full lowercase or uppercase is
  longer than one character — LATIN CAPITAL LETTER I WITH DOT ABOVE, written `İ` below,
  lowercases to two characters here (an `i` and a combining dot above) and to a bare `i`
  there; LATIN SMALL LETTER SHARP S, LATIN SMALL LIGATURE FI and LATIN SMALL LETTER N
  PRECEDED BY APOSTROPHE each uppercase to two characters here and are left unchanged there
  — and a rule that reads context: a GREEK CAPITAL LETTER SIGMA ending a word lowercases to
  GREEK SMALL LETTER FINAL SIGMA here and to GREEK SMALL LETTER SIGMA there. Measured through
  the npm package against 18.6 (database `en_US.UTF-8`, libc):

  | statement | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT 'İstanbul' ILIKE 'istanbul'` | `f` | `t` |
  | `SELECT 'istanbul' ILIKE 'İstanbul'` | `f` | `t` |
  | `SELECT length(lower('İ'))` | `2` | `1` |
  | `SELECT lower('İ') = 'i'` | `f` | `t` |
  | `SELECT upper('straße')`, and its `length` | `STRASSE`, `7` | `STRAßE`, `6` |
  | `SELECT upper('ﬁ')`, over the ligature | `FI` | the ligature unchanged |
  | `SELECT lower('ΑΣ') = 'ασ'`, capital alpha and sigma against small alpha and sigma | `f`, the fold ending in a final sigma | `t` |
  | `SELECT 'ΑΣ' ILIKE 'ας'`, the pattern ending in a final sigma | `t` | `f` |

  The controls agree on both: `SELECT upper('i') = 'İ'` is `f`, a lone capital sigma
  lowercases to the plain small sigma, and `SELECT 'STRASSE' ILIKE 'straße'` is `f`.
  **Silent**: a wrong boolean, and a `WHERE lower(name) = …` or `ILIKE` filter that drops a
  row 18.6 keeps. The reference is the oracle's provider and encoding: an ICU-provider
  database could answer otherwise. The name fold is not this row's: it is ASCII-only here,
  and 18.6's depends on the database encoding, not the provider (`docs/compatibility.md`'s
  identifier case-folding row). `docs/compatibility.md`'s `ILIKE` row states the full-mapping
  fold. Reach: ordinary SQL, data-dependent. No fixture: a faithful one is red.

- **265 · A draw a column `DEFAULT` makes does not set `currval`.** pglet's `currval` answers

  back the id just drawn — `INSERT …; SELECT currval('<table>_id_seq')` — is refused.
  `docs/compatibility.md`'s sequences details record it. Reach: ordinary. No fixture: a faithful one is
  red; `sequences/currval_after_nextval.sql` is the explicit-draw control.

  `sequences/from_bearing_nested.sql` and `sequences/nested_position.sql` pin the position

- **267 · The sequence-name reader raises ahead of 18.6's overload resolution and

  | `SELECT setval('noschema.sq', NULL::text)` | `42P01 relation "noschema.sq" does not exist` | `42883` |
  | `SELECT nextval('a.b.c')` | `42601 syntax error: improper qualified name (too many dotted names): a.b.c` | `0A000 cross-database references are not implemented: "a.b.c"` |
  | `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS tb (a INT DEFAULT nextval('s x'))` | `42602` | `CREATE`, the skip |
  | `ALTER TABLE IF EXISTS nosuch ADD COLUMN b INT DEFAULT nextval('s x')` | `42602` | `ALTER`, the skip |

  where 18.6 skips. `docs/compatibility.md`'s sequences details state why the gate is not moved — closing it
  means moving name resolution later on the DDL and the expression paths, a precedence change

  | `SELECT true + 'a'`, and `'a' + true`, `true - 'a'` | `42804 type error: operator + requires numeric operands` (each with its operator) | `42883 operator does not exist: boolean + unknown` / `unknown + boolean` / `boolean - unknown` |

  | `SELECT 1 + 'a'`, and `'a' - 1` | `42804 … operator + requires numeric operands` | `22P02 invalid input syntax for type integer: "a"` |

- **269 · An unaliased scalar subquery or `$N` is named `?column?` / `$N`, not 18.6's name.**

  over `p (a INT)` holding `1`:

  | statement | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM p)` | `?column?` | `count` |
  | `SELECT (SELECT a FROM p)` | `?column?` | `a` |
  | `UPDATE p SET a = 2 RETURNING (SELECT count(*) FROM p)` | `?column?` | `count` |
  | `SELECT $1`, bound `'x'` | `$1` | `?column?` |
  | `SELECT $1::int`, bound `'3'` | `$1` | `int4` |
  | `SELECT NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM p)` | `exists` | `?column?` |

  FROM p) + 0` (`?column?`), `SELECT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM p)` (`exists`), `SELECT $1 AS v`
  (`v`), `SELECT $1 + 1` (`?column?`), `SELECT NOT (SELECT true)` (`?column?`), and a subquery whose own column 18.6 names
  `?column?` — `SELECT (SELECT 1)`, `SELECT (SELECT a + 1 FROM p)`. **Silent** (metadata): the `RowDescription` name differs, and through the npm
  package or `pg` a result row is an object keyed by that name, so `rows[0].count` is
  `undefined` here. Row 117 is the stacked-cast member of the naming rule, and struck row
