  fixture: the harness keys each compared row by its column name, so a faithful one is red.

- **270 · The wasm bindings, and so the npm package, take one statement per call.** Every
  `PgletBtree` entry point the npm adapter reaches — `query`, `exec`, `queryParams` — runs
  through `Database::execute_bound`, which raw-parses the text and refuses more than one
  statement, `42601 syntax error: expected 1 statement, got 2`, running none of them. A `pg`
  client sending the same string with no parameters uses the simple `Query` protocol, where
  18.6 runs each statement in turn. Measured against 18.6 over node-postgres:
  `db.query('SELECT 1; SELECT 2')`, `db.query('CREATE TABLE t (a INT); INSERT INTO t VALUES
  (1)')` and `db.query("SET TIME ZONE 'UTC'; SELECT 1")` are that `42601` here and run both
  statements there; the raw binding's `query`, `exec` and `queryParams` refuse the same way. A
  trailing `;` is one statement on both. With parameters the engines agree on the code: `SELECT
  1; SELECT $1::int` is `42601` here and `42601 cannot insert multiple commands into a
  prepared statement` there. Loud: the whole string is refused, so nothing is half applied,
  and a migration or seed file handed over as one string must be split by the caller. The
  native server and `Database::execute` split a simple query into its statements, so rows
  68, 175, 176 and 250's multi-statement members cannot reach the npm package.
  Reach: ordinary. No test found that sends one through the wasm or npm suites.

- **271 · A correlated `IN (SELECT …)` runs its sub-plan to its end before any comparison.**
  The sub-plan's rows are collected whole (`executor::query::correlated`'s
  `execute_in_subquery`) and compared after; 18.6's `ExecScanSubPlan`, which runs a
  correlated sub-plan it keeps as a sub-plan, stops at the first row the left operand
  matches. Measured over `rz (a int)` holding `2` and `0` and `t1 (x int)` holding `1`:
  `SELECT x IN (SELECT 2/a FROM rz WHERE x IS NOT NULL) FROM t1` is `22012` here and `t`
  there. The same stop decides which of two errors is raised: `SELECT (1/(x-x)) IN (SELECT
  CASE WHEN a = 2 THEN a ELSE (a::text || 'z')::int END FROM rz WHERE x IS NOT NULL) FROM
  t1` is `22P02` here — the second sub-plan row's — and `22012` there, 18.6 evaluating the
  operand at the first row. It was `22012` here too before row 180's repair, which moved
  the sub-plan ahead of the operand. The engines agree where 18.6's plan reads the whole
  sub-plan first: `SELECT x IN (SELECT 2/a FROM rz) FROM t1`, a hashed sub-plan, and
  `DELETE FROM d2 WHERE x IN (SELECT 2/a FROM rz WHERE d2.x IS NOT NULL)` are `22012` on
  both. A join 18.6 makes of a `WHERE … IN (SELECT …)` can instead hash the outer
  relation, and an empty hash never reads the sub-plan: over `tn (x int, y int)` holding
  `(NULL, 0)` and `r (a int)` holding `1`, never analyzed, `SELECT count(*) FROM tn WHERE x
  IN (SELECT 1/(a-a) FROM r WHERE tn.y = 0)` — and the `DELETE` over the same `WHERE` — is
  `0` there and `22012` here, `0` here before row 180's repair, whose `NULL` shortcut
  skipped the sub-plan; analyzed, 18.6 plans a nested-loop semi-join and raises too. Which plan 18.6 takes is
  its planner's choice, so the member set is not a list of spellings. Loud — a refusal
  where 18.6 answers, or the other engine's code. No fixture: a faithful one is red.

- **272 · An `IN` list is evaluated item by item, not as 18.6's array first.**
  `transformAExprIn` gathers the items that name no column of the list's own query level
  and, when there are two or more of them and their common type has an array type, builds
  one array of them, compared before the
  items that do name one (row 88's shapes); the array's elements are all evaluated before
  any comparison. `eval_in_list_node` evaluates each item in list order and stops at the
  first match. Measured over `r (a int)` holding `1`, and `t1 (x int, y int)` holding `(1,
  0)`: `SELECT x IN (1, (SELECT 1/(a-a) FROM r)) FROM t1` and `x IN (1, 2, (SELECT 1/(a-a)
  FROM r))` are `t` here and `22012` there, and `DELETE FROM d1 WHERE x IN (1, (SELECT
  1/(a-a) FROM r))` over `d1` holding `1` deletes the row here and refuses there. With a
  `NULL` operand every item is evaluated on both engines, and the order decides which
  error: `SELECT x IN (1/y, 5, (SELECT (a::text || 'z')::int FROM r)) FROM tn` over `(NULL,
  0)` is `22012` here and `22P02` there. Controls agreeing on both: `x IN (1, 1/y)` over
  `(1, 0)` is `t` — one item names no column, so there is no array — and `x IN (1/y, 1)` is
  `22012`. Silent — an answer, and a write, where 18.6 refuses. No fixture: a faithful one
  is red.

- **273 · A strict operator over a constant `NULL` still evaluates its other operand.**
  18.6's `eval_const_expressions` replaces a call of a strict function or operator that has
  a constant-`NULL` input by a `NULL` constant while planning, "even if there are other
  inputs that aren't constant", so the other input is never evaluated; pglet evaluates
  both operands. Measured over `tn (x int, y int)` holding `(NULL, 0)`: `SELECT NULL::int =
  1/y FROM tn`, `SELECT NULL::int + 1/y FROM tn` and `SELECT NULL::int IN (1, 1/y) FROM tn`

  comparison there) are `22012` here and `NULL` there. A bound `$N` is such a constant in a
  custom plan, which is every unnamed-statement query a `pg` client sends: bound `NULL`,
  `SELECT count(*) FROM tn WHERE $1 IN (x, 1/y)` counts `0` there and is `22012` here, and
  so is `$1::int = 1/y`; under a generic plan 18.6 raises `22012` too. The same operand
  held in a column is not folded, and `SELECT x IN (1, 1/y) FROM tn` is `22012` on both; a
  scalar subquery beside the constant is folded like any operand — `SELECT NULL::int =
  (SELECT 1/(a-a) FROM r)` is `22012` here and `NULL` there — but an `IN` list's items
  gathered into 18.6's array (row 272) are not: `NULL::int IN (1, (SELECT 1/(a-a) FROM r))`
  is `22012` on both. The same fold removes an **aggregate** from a grouping query there,
  and a grouping here computes it (row 89's residuals): over `u (a INT, b INT)` holding

  there. So is `SELECT NULL::int IN (1/(count(*) - 2)) FROM u` — a one-item list is a
  plain `=`, folded — which was `NULL` here, 18.6's answer, while an `IN` item holding
  an aggregate was skipped under a `NULL` operand (row 274). Loud —
  a refusal where 18.6 answers. No fixture: a faithful one is red.

- **274 · A `NULL` operand of `IN (SELECT …)` answers `NULL` where the sub-plan cannot run.**

  `false` for `IN` and `true` for `NOT IN` — row 180's rule, which a position with a
  callback follows. Measured over `t (x int)` holding `NULL`, `r (a int)` holding `1` and
  `2`, and `e (a int)` empty: `SELECT x IN (SELECT a FROM e) FROM t GROUP BY x` is `NULL`
  here and `f` there (the ungrouped projection is `f` on both); `SELECT count(*) FROM t

  `0` there; `UPDATE w SET v = CASE WHEN v NOT IN (SELECT a FROM e) THEN 7 ELSE 8 END` over

  FROM e))::int` stores `NULL` here and `1` there; and over `u` holding `(6, NULL)`, `INSERT INTO u VALUES (6, NULL) ON CONFLICT
  (id) DO UPDATE SET v = 7 WHERE excluded.v NOT IN (SELECT a FROM e)` leaves `v` `NULL`
  here and sets it to `7` there. The same positions skip an `IN` list item the walk cannot
  evaluate under a `NULL` operand, where 18.6 evaluates it: `SELECT x FROM t GROUP BY x
  HAVING x IN (1, (SELECT 1/(a-a) FROM r LIMIT 1))` is `(0 rows)` here and `22012` there,
  and `UPDATE w SET v = (v IN (1, (SELECT 1/(a-a) FROM r LIMIT 1)))::int` stores `NULL`
  here where 18.6 raises `22012`. Every position skips an item that holds a window

  skipped too: over `t` holding `(NULL, 0)` as `(x, y)`, `SELECT x IN (1, CASE WHEN false
  THEN row_number() OVER () ELSE 1/y END) FROM t` is `NULL` here and `22012` there. An
  item holding an aggregate was skipped the same way and no longer is where a grouping
  lends the walk its aggregates' values: `SELECT x IN (1, CASE WHEN false THEN max(x)
  ELSE 1/y END) FROM t GROUP BY x, y` answered `NULL` and is `22012` on both

  is row 89's missing evaluation context. Silent — an answer, a stored value, and a filter
  deciding which rows a statement keeps or a write moves. No fixture: a faithful one is red.

- **275 · A written foreign-key column list of the wrong length is refused in the parser.**

  further members (18.6's arity `42830`, pglet's `0A000`). 18.6 raises it in

  `42704`, a constraint name a `CHECK` already took `42710`, `CREATE TABLE p (…)` over the
  existing `p` `42P07`, and `y int int` written after the key `42601`; `ALTER TABLE nosucht
  ADD FOREIGN KEY (x) REFERENCES p (id, t)` `42P01`, `ALTER TABLE c3 ADD FOREIGN KEY (x,

- **~~277~~ · Closed — An unnamed `CREATE INDEX` was a syntax error.** `CREATE TABLE f (x
  float8); CREATE INDEX ON f (x)` was `42601 syntax error: expected a name, found identifier`
  where 18.6 answers `CREATE INDEX` and names the index `f_x_idx` — the parser read a relation
  name where `gram.y`'s `IndexStmt` reads an `opt_single_name`. **Loud**; reach: ordinary, a
  hand-written migration's `CREATE INDEX ON users (email)`. (The `float8` key of that first example was row 25's when this closed, and is no longer:
  the index is built under 18.6's name and `INSERT INTO f VALUES (1.5)` then answers `INSERT 0 1`
  on both engines.)

  **What closed it.** The parser takes the name as optional in the plain production and
  leaves it required behind `IF NOT EXISTS`, as `gram.y` spells the two apart: `CREATE INDEX
  IF NOT EXISTS ON t (a)` is `42601` on both engines
  (`ddl/create_index_unnamed_if_not_exists_loud.sql`), and a quoted `"on"` is still a name
  (`ddl/create_index_named_on_is_still_a_name.sql`). `Plan::CreateIndex` carries the name as
  declared-or-nothing and `execute_create_index` chooses an absent one where it tests a
  declared one — after the statement's other gates, so a missing table is `42P01` and a
  missing key column `42703` as with a name
  (`ddl/create_index_unnamed_missing_{table,column}_loud.sql`), and ahead of the build. The
  name is 18.6's `ChooseIndexName` for an index that is no
  constraint's (`executor::ddl`'s `choose_index_name`): the table's name, the key parts' names
  joined by `_`, and the label `idx` — for a `UNIQUE` index too, `key` being a constraint's
  label (`ddl/create_index_unnamed_unique.sql`). A bare column's part is its own name, in key
  order; an expression's is the name a `SELECT` gives it as an output column, with `expr`
  where a `SELECT` says `?column?`; and a part whose name the key already holds takes a digit
  of its own (`a, a` is `a_a1`). The whole is cut to 63 bytes as `makeObjectName` cuts it —
  the label never, the longer of the two names a byte at a time, each cut landing on a
  character boundary — and a taken relation name moves a digit onto the label (`idx1`, `idx2`)
  and cuts again around it. What it steps around is the relation namespace — a table, an
  index, a sequence — and not a constraint's name or a type's
  (`ddl/create_index_unnamed_ignores_constraint_and_type_names.sql`). Measured against 18.6
  statement by statement through the npm package — the fixtures' shapes, a `DO` body, a
  block rolled back and a `ROLLBACK TO`, and a build that fails and leaves its name free
  (`crates/pglet/tests/unnamed_index.rs` holds those three) — and the naming shapes through
  the native server as well. The chosen name is the catalog's: the dump writes it and a
  reopened store holds it.

  One chooser stands behind both engine-chosen relation names now (`choose_relation_name`),
  so a `SERIAL` or identity column's sequence name is cut the same way: over 40-byte table and
  column names `pg_get_serial_sequence` answers the 63-byte name 18.6 answers, and `CREATE
  TABLE … (<c> SERIAL, <c>x SERIAL)` whose two names meet after the cut is `42P07` on both
  (`sequences/serial_long_name*.sql`).

  **Residual — silent.** An expression part's name is `Expr::output_name`'s, so it differs
  where pglet names an output column differently, and the index name with it. Measured, each
  alone on a fresh `o (a int, t text, "?column?" int)`: `CREATE INDEX ON o (('1'::int::text))`
  is `o_int4_idx` here and `o_text_idx` there (row 117's cast stack); `CREATE INDEX ON o
  ((CASE WHEN a > 0 THEN 1 ELSE a END))` is `o_case_idx` here and `o_a_idx` there, and its
  `ELSE lower(t)::int` spelling `o_case_idx` against `o_lower_idx` — 18.6 names a `CASE` after
  a named `ELSE` branch, and `SELECT CASE WHEN a > 0 THEN 1 ELSE a END FROM o` is the column
  `case` here and `a` there; and a cast over a column that is itself named `?column?`,
  `CREATE INDEX ON o ((("?column?")::bigint))`, is `o_int8_idx` here and `o_?column?_idx`
  there. Two more mechanisms, measured over `t (a int, b text, c int)`: a cast over a nameless `CASE` takes the
  type's name there and stays `case` here (`((CASE WHEN a > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 2 END)::text)` is `t_text_idx` there and
  `t_case_idx` here), and a `char` cast of a constant is named `bpchar` there and `varchar` here (`(('x'::char(3)))` is
  `t_bpchar_idx` there and `t_varchar_idx` here). The members are examples of the class, not its extent. No fixture: a
  faithful one is red.

- **~~278~~ · Closed — A constraint's chosen name was not cut.** `ConstraintNames`' two

  catalog name, and 18.6 truncates an identifier it reads to 63 bytes, so two chosen names
  that shared their first 63 bytes arrived as one: over that table with a second `CHECK (e…
  > 1)` and a second foreign key on `c…f`, the dump restored into 18.6 with `psql` exiting
  `0` and one `UNIQUE` and one `FOREIGN KEY` of six constraints present — measured on the
  build before the repair.

  **What closed it.** Neither minter formats a name any more: each hands the table's name, a
  second name and a label to `executor::ddl`'s `choose_name`, the digit loop the implicit
  sequence and the unnamed index already went through (row 277), over
  `catalog::make_object_name`, the one cut. The second name is absent for a `PRIMARY KEY`
  and for a `CHECK` reading no single column, a `UNIQUE`'s key columns joined in key order,
  a `FOREIGN KEY`'s referencing columns, a single-column `CHECK`'s column; the digit goes on
  the label and the name is cut again around it; the namespace each kind steps around is
  unchanged. Measured against 18.6, name for name, through the native server and
  statement by statement through the npm package: every kind at `CREATE TABLE` (column- and
  table-level), `ADD COLUMN`'s inline constraints, `ADD PRIMARY KEY` / `ADD UNIQUE` / `ADD
  CHECK` / `ADD FOREIGN KEY`, multi-column keys written out of the table's column order,
  quoted mixed-case and multibyte names cut inside a character, names meeting after the cut
  within a statement, across statements and across two tables, a declared name holding the
  cut candidate, and a rolled-back block and a `ROLLBACK TO` giving the names back
  (`ddl/constraint_auto_name_cut_*`; the three `*_violation_names_it` fixtures hold the
  message and the constraint-name field). The table above now dumps to a script 18.6
  restores whole, and `pg_dump` of that restore loads back into pglet under the same names,
  measured; `test_dump`'s `long_chosen_*` tables hold the dump's two restore legs, and

  same cut (`ddl/not_null_constraint_name_is_cut.sql`). A name that fits in 63 bytes is

  **Residual — silent.** Three members, each measured.
  *A `NOT NULL`'s name takes no digit.* pglet stores no record for a `NOT NULL`, so its

  `s_a_not_null1` there for the `NOT NULL` and `s_a_not_null` for both rows here — that one

- **~~279~~ · Closed — a string read as `bytea` was read as hex whatever its prefix.**
  18.6's `byteain` reads a string that starts `\x` as hex and anything else in the escape
  format — the bytes of the text, a `\\` or a `\ooo` octal escape apart. pglet's reader
  trimmed the string's surrounding whitespace, stripped a leading `\x` **or `\X`** and read
  what was left as hex digits either way, so `'abcd'` stored the two bytes `\xabcd` with no
  error and `WHERE b = 'abcd'` matched the row holding them.

  **What closed it.** `executor::coerce`'s `parse_bytea` is `byteain`'s two formats, and it
  is the one reader `coerce_value` gives a `text` value headed for `bytea`:

  - the **hex format** behind a lowercase `\x` at the string's first byte: pairs of hex
    digits in either case, with a space, a tab, a newline or a carriage return skipped
    where a pair would start. A character that is no hex digit is
    `22023 invalid hexadecimal digit: "…"` — whitespace between the two digits of a pair,
    a vertical tab and a form feed included — and a digit left without its pair is
    `22023 invalid hexadecimal data: odd number of digits`, the first of the two found
    winning;
  - the **escape format** otherwise: each byte of the text is itself, a non-ASCII
    character its UTF-8 bytes, `\\` one backslash, and `\ooo` — three octal digits, the
    first `0` to `3` — the byte of that value. A backslash before anything else, or ending
    the string, is `22P02`. Nothing is trimmed.

  Measured against 18.6 on the native server, which agrees with it on each cell:

  | input read as `bytea` | 18.6, and pglet now |
  | --- | --- |
  | `'abcd'`, `'abc'`, `'hello'`, `'x6162'` | the text's bytes — `\x61626364`, `\x616263`, `\x68656c6c6f`, `\x7836313632` |
  | `''`, `' '`, `'  abcd '` | `\x`, `\x20`, `\x20206162636420` |
  | `'\141\142'`, `'\000\377'`, `'a\\b'`, `'\\x6162'` | `\x6162`, `\x00ff`, `\x615c62`, `\x5c7836313632` |
  | `'\x'`, `'\x6162'`, `'\xDeadBEEF'`, `'\x6162 63'`, `'\x 61  62 '` | `\x`, `\x6162`, `\xdeadbeef`, `\x616263`, `\x6162` |
  | `'\X6162'`, `' \x6162'`, `'a\b'`, `'ab\'`, `'\400'`, `'\12'`, `'\128'` | `22P02 invalid input syntax for type bytea` |
  | `'\x616'`, `'\xzz'`, `'\x6 162'`, `'\x61 6 '` | `22023` |
  | `E'\\001'`, `'\001'` | `\x01` — the reader is handed `\001` by both spellings |
  | `'\\001'`, `E'\\\\001'` | `\x5c303031` — the reader is handed `\\001` by both |

  The doors measured, each answering as 18.6 does: a `::bytea` cast and `CAST`, the typed
  constant `bytea '…'`, a `text` or `varchar` column, a concatenation and a bound `text`
  parameter cast to `bytea`, an `INSERT … VALUES` cell, an `INSERT … SELECT` source, an
  `UPDATE … SET`, an `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`, a `DEFAULT` declared by `CREATE TABLE`,
  `ADD COLUMN` and `SET DEFAULT` (its accepted strings; the residual below is its refused
  ones), a comparison and an `IN` list beside a `bytea` column,
  scanned and through a primary key's index, a `bytea[]` literal's elements and an
  `ARRAY[…]::bytea[]` constructor's, a `COPY … FROM` field, a text-format `$N` on the
  native server, and a JS string bound to a `bytea` column or under `$1::bytea` on the
  npm package — where a byte view (a `Buffer`, any typed array, a `DataView`) is the bytes
  of its window and passes through no reader, an object that is neither a view nor an
  array is refused `22023` rather than read through its JSON spelling (node-postgres sends
  that spelling and 18.6 stores its bytes: `{}` for an `ArrayBuffer`), and a string
  element of a JS array bound to `bytea[]` is read as a string bound on its own is. `'\X6162'` and `' \x6162'` were over-accepts and are refused now.

  **The array reader moved with it.** An unquoted element of an array literal kept a
  backslash as a character where 18.6's `ReadArrayToken` takes the next character as it
  is, so `'{\\x6162}'::bytea[]` handed the element reader `\\x6162`: `22023` under the hex
  reading, and the six characters `\x6162` under the escape format, where 18.6 stores the
  two bytes. The array reader reads the escape now — an escaped character is copied,
  does not end the element, is not trailing whitespace and keeps the element from being
  `NULL` — which moved `text[]` too: `'{a\\b}'` is the element `a\b` and `'{a\,b}'` one
  element, as on 18.6. A backslash ending the literal's body in an unquoted element
  (`'{a\}'`, `'{1\}'::int4[]`) is `22P02` on both, behind the input error of an element read before it:
  `'{\\x616,a\}'::bytea[]` is the first element's `22023` on both, 18.6 converting each
  element as it reads it. The reader's grammar is 18.6's as a whole (rows 283 and 294): a
  literal 18.6's array reader refuses is `22P02` here too.

  **The store magic moved with it** (`PGMU`, `docs/storage.md` § Store versioning). A
  stored expression is kept as written and read anew, so on a store an earlier build wrote
  a `bytea` default string gave later rows other bytes, a row a
  `CHECK (b <> 'cafe'::bytea)` admitted was refused by that check at its next `UPDATE`,
  and a unique partial index `WHERE b = 'cafe'::bytea` accepted a second row beside a
  stored one its predicate now selects — measured on the native server over such a store
  before the magic moved. An array literal with a backslash in an unquoted element is a
  stored expression of the same kind. That store is refused at open now, as stale.

  **Residuals, measured.** A `22P02` raised here reads
  `invalid input syntax for type bytea: "…"`, quoting the string, where 18.6's message
  stops at the type name; the code agrees. A string `DEFAULT` on a `bytea` column is
  rendered as written by the catalog views (`'hello'::bytea`) where 18.6 prints its
  output function's text (`'\x68656c6c6f'::bytea`) — row 93's rule, of which it is a
  member. And a raw NUL inside the literal, through an in-process door, is one of the
  text's bytes now (row 133). A default the **hex** format refuses is not refused where it
  is declared: `CREATE TABLE d (b bytea DEFAULT '\x616')` and `ALTER TABLE … ALTER COLUMN b
  SET DEFAULT '\x616'` are accepted here and `22023` there, and each `INSERT` that takes
  the default is `22023` here — loud, accept-then-unwritable; `ADD COLUMN … DEFAULT
  '\x616'` is `22023` on both, and a default the escape format refuses (`'\X61'`) is
  `22P02` at each of the three statements on both. The same holds under a cast or a typed
  constant (`'\x616'::bytea`, `bytea '\x616'`) and for a `bytea[]` default
  (`'{\\x616}'`). The DDL gate reads an input function's refusal by its code
  (`ddl.rs`'s `is_cook_time_error`), `22023` is not among those codes, and it is also the
  code of a refusal 18.6 raises per row: `split_part('a,b', ',', 0)` and
  `date_trunc('bogus', now())` are accepted as defaults on both and `22023` at the
  `INSERT`.

  Guards: `types/bytea_input_*.sql` — value fixtures per door and one `@expect-error`
  fixture per refusal — `copy/bytea_input_formats_from.sql` and
  `copy/bytea_input_uppercase_prefix_from_loud.sql`,
  `array/unquoted_element_backslash_escape.sql` and the
  `array/unquoted_element_trailing_backslash*_loud.sql` fixtures, `pglet`'s
  `a_store_written_under_the_earlier_bytea_reading_is_rejected`, `coerce.rs`'s
  `bytea_input_is_hex_behind_its_prefix_and_the_escape_format_otherwise` and
  `bytea_hex_refusals_carry_18_6s_messages`, `pglet_server`'s
  `a_text_format_bytea_parameter_is_read_by_the_input_function`, the npm suite's
  `a string bound to a bytea parameter is read as PostgreSQL reads it`, and the dump
  round-trip's `bytea_probe` table, whose string defaults are read again by the restored
  catalog on each engine.

- ~~**280 · An `IN` list is compared at the type 18.6 gives it.**~~ **Closed class, silent
  residual.** 18.6's `transformAExprIn` gathers the items that name no column of their query
  level and, when there are two or more, asks `select_common_type` for one type over the left
  operand and those items, converts each to it and compares through one array operator; a
  single such item, and an item that names a column, is an ordinary `=`. pglet compared item
  by item, each pair resolved as that `=` would be, and the two differ where the common type
  is not the type a pair compares at: beside a `real` left operand a numeric constant is
  converted to `real` in the list and compared as `double precision` in the pair, where
  `real` `0.1` and the constant `0.1` are not equal — `x IN (0.1, 1.5)` missed the `0.1` row,
  `NOT IN` kept it, and a `DELETE` or `UPDATE` through either wrote accordingly.

  **What closed it.** The plan-time pass asks for that type (`planner/coercion.rs`,
  `in_list_array_type`) where every operand's type is certain by construction, read off the
  statement as written: the left operand is a plain reference to a column of a base table at
  the list's own query level, and each of two or more items is a constant the parser typed by
  its spelling — a numeric, string, boolean or `NULL` literal, or a cast written directly
  over one. A string literal and a `NULL` are 18.6's `unknown` and take the type without
  choosing it. A string literal is then read as the common type rather than the column's, and
  an item of another type is cast to it where it is `real` or `double precision` — the
  conversions that round. Measured against 18.6 through the native server on both build
  profiles and both storage backends and through the npm package, over `real`, `double
  precision`, `numeric`, `integer`, `bigint` and `smallint` columns: `x IN (0.1, 1.5)`, `NOT
  IN`, a `NULL` item, integer constants beside `real` (`x IN (16777217, 5)` finds `16777216`),
  a `real` or `double precision` constant beside an `integer`, `bigint` or `numeric` column,
  `i IN ('1.0', 2.5)` (the string is `numeric`; it was `22P02`), and the `SELECT` list,
  `WHERE`, `CASE`, `GROUP BY`, `HAVING`, `JOIN … ON`, `RETURNING`, `UPDATE … SET`, `INSERT …
  SELECT` and `ON CONFLICT … DO UPDATE … WHERE` positions. `tests/fixtures/in_list/` pins a
  member of each and the accept-side controls beside them — a single item, one constant
  beside a column, a list whose `double precision` item makes `0.1` not match, a list with
  no common type (`42883` for its first operator-less item).

  **Residual — a list outside those shapes is compared item by item, as before.** A type the
  pass would have to infer is one 18.6 can read differently, and a list converted on a wrong
  reading matches rows 18.6's does not, so nothing is converted on an inferred type: not
  under a left operand that is an expression, a constant, a scalar subquery, or a column of
  anything but a base table at the list's own level — nor a column of an `UPDATE … FROM`
  source, base table or not, whose relations that statement's scope registers without their
  kind — and not beside an item that is a
  column, a subquery, a parameter or a computed expression; nor in a stored expression,
  which no coercion pass runs over. Measured over `r (id INT, x REAL, d FLOAT8)` holding
  `(1, 0.1, 0.1)`, `(2, 1.5, 1.5)` and `(3, 16777216, 16777216)`:

  | statement | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `CREATE TABLE c (id INT, x REAL CHECK (x IN (0.1, 1.5)))`, then `INSERT INTO c VALUES (1, 0.1)` | `23514` | inserts |
  | `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON r2 (id) WHERE x IN (0.1, 1.5)`, then a second `(1, 0.1)` | inserts | `23505` |
  | `CREATE TABLE df (id INT, f BOOL DEFAULT (0.1::real IN (0.1, 9)))`, then `INSERT INTO df (id) VALUES (1) RETURNING f` | `f` | `t` |
  | `SELECT id FROM r WHERE x IN (0.1, 7, d)` | `2`, `3` | `1`, `2`, `3` |
  | `SELECT id FROM r WHERE x IN ((SELECT 0.1), 1.5)` | `2` | `1`, `2` |
  | `SELECT id FROM r WHERE x IN (0.05 + 0.05, 1.5)` | `2` | `1`, `2` |
  | `SELECT id, (SELECT count(*) FROM r q WHERE q.x IN (0.1, o.x)) FROM r o` | `1`, `1`, `1` | `1`, `2`, `2` |
  | `SELECT id FROM r WHERE abs(x) IN (0.1, 1.5)` | `2` | `1`, `2` |
  | `SELECT max(f4) IN (0.3, 0.5) FROM r1`, `r1.f4` a `real` holding `0.3` and a `NULL` | `f` | `t` |
  | `SELECT (SELECT x FROM r WHERE id = 1) IN (0.1, 1.5)` | `f` | `t` |
  | `SELECT 0.1::real IN (0.1, 1.5)` | `f` | `t` |
  | `SELECT id FROM (SELECT id, x AS y FROM r) v WHERE y IN (0.1, 1.5)`, and the same through a `WITH` query | `2` | `1`, `2` |
  | `SELECT o.id FROM r o WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM r q WHERE q.id = 2 AND o.x IN (0.1, 1.5))` | `2` | `1`, `2` |
  | `UPDATE t SET … FROM r WHERE t.id = r.id AND r.x IN (0.1, 1.5)`, `t` holding ids `1` to `3` | `UPDATE 1` | `UPDATE 2` |
  | `SELECT id FROM r WHERE x IN ($1, 0.1)`, `$1` bound `7`, and `x IN ($1::real, 0.1)` | no row | `1` |
  | `UPDATE r SET d = $1 WHERE x IN ($1, 0.1) RETURNING id`, `$1` bound `5` | `UPDATE 0` | `1` |
  | `SELECT id FROM r WHERE id < $1 AND x IN ($1 + 0, 0.1)`, `$1` bound `5` | no row | `1` |
  | `SELECT id FROM r WHERE id IN ($1, 2.5)`, the type `$1` is reported at | `integer` | `numeric` |

  A stored expression — a `CHECK`, a column `DEFAULT`, a partial-index predicate, an
  expression index's key — is stored and evaluated as written, so its list is compared item
  by item: the `CHECK` refuses the row 18.6 takes, and the partial index leaves it out, so a
  unique one admits the duplicate. A query over such a table is typed as above, so it does
  not spell the stored predicate and is answered by a scan. An item that names a column is
  counted by 18.6 as a constant by the *level* of the columns it names — one naming only an
  enclosing query's column joins the array, as the correlated count shows — which this pass
  does not read.

  The left operand and the computed items are where a guess costs most, and where 18.6's own
  list is `double precision` the item-by-item answer is its answer: `x * (SELECT 1) IN (0.1,
  0.3)`, `q.x * o.b IN (0.1, 0.3)` with `o.b` the enclosing query's `bigint` column, a column
  a derived table computes as `COALESCE(x + 0::float8, 1.5::real)` and `x IN
  (COALESCE(5::float8 + 0, 1), 0.1)` find no `0.1` row on both engines — this engine reads
  each of those operands as `real` or `integer` (`SELECT COALESCE(1.5::float8 + 0, 1)`
  answers `2`, declared `integer`), and a list converted on that reading found the row.

  A parameter is the same case. 18.6 counts one an earlier-analysed use has typed as an item
  of that type, so `d < $1 AND x IN ($1, 0.1)` is a `double precision` list there and finds
  no `0.1` row, as here, while `x IN ($1, 0.1)` alone is a `real` one and finds it — and
  where the list is planned the parameter's type is not yet known, at any depth of an item
  (`$1 + 0`, `COALESCE($1, 1)`) or under a cast. A `$N` item is reported at the left
  operand's type, where 18.6 reports the list's common type; inside a branch construct
  beside a typed sibling it is reported at the sibling's, so `d < $1 AND x IN (COALESCE($1,
  1), 0.1)` describes `integer` where 18.6 describes `double precision`. Over a `numeric`
  column `n` holding `0.1`, `x < $1 AND n IN ($1, 0.1)` bound `5` finds the row where 18.6's
  list is `real` and does not, and over an `integer` column `n < $1 AND i IN ($1, '0.1', 7)`
  is `22P02` where 18.6 reads the string as `numeric`.

  Casting each constant to the column's type answers as 18.6 does in every residual member
  tried — `x IN ($1, 0.1::real)` bound `7`, alone and behind `d < $1`, and `abs(x) IN
  (0.1::real, 1.5::real)`. In the lists that are converted, the conversion itself can differ:
  a constant past the type's range, or one that underflows it (row 149's reader), is
  refused when a row's evaluation reaches the item, where 18.6 refuses the statement as it
  plans it — `x IN (0.1, 1e39)` and `x IN (0.1, 1e-50)` are `22003` on both over a row
  holding `1.5`, and answer here over an empty table or a row the `0.1` already matched. **Silent, and it writes** — a `CHECK` over an `IN` list is the loud member
  (`23514`), and one over a `NOT IN` list is silent the other way: `CHECK (x NOT IN (0.1, 1.5))`
  takes the `0.1` row 18.6 refuses. Reach: ordinary for a
  `real` column's `CHECK … IN` list of decimal constants, and for a `real` column's list
  holding a parameter. No fixture for a member that differs: a faithful one is red. Row 272 is the same node's evaluation order, unchanged.

- **281 · An `ARRAY[…]` constructor is typed by its elements' value where an operator reads
  it, and a value carries no `timestamptz`, `varchar` or `name`.** The declared type of
  `SELECT ARRAY['…'::timestamptz]` is 18.6's (`timestamptz[]`, and `varchar[]`, `name[]`
  for the other two), but the operand type the `@>` / `<@` / `=` gate compares is taken
  from the built value, whose element type is the family's base — `timestamp`, `text`.
  Measured over `a (tsa timestamptz[], va varchar[], ta text[])` holding one row, through
  the npm package and the native server, both build profiles agreeing:

  | statement | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `WHERE tsa @> ARRAY['2024-01-01 00:00:00+00'::timestamptz]`, and `=`, `<@`, and `@> ARRAY[$1::timestamptz]` | `42883 operator does not exist: timestamp with time zone[] @> timestamp without time zone[]` | the row |
  | `WHERE va @> ARRAY['a'::varchar]`, and `=`, and `@> ARRAY[$1::varchar]` | `42883 … character varying[] @> text[]` | the row |
  | `WHERE ta @> ARRAY['a'::varchar]`, and `=` | the row | `42883 … text[] @> character varying[]` |
  | `WHERE ta @> ARRAY[current_user]` | no row | `42883 … text[] @> name[]` |
  | `SELECT ARRAY['a'::varchar] = ARRAY['a'::text]` | `t` | `42883 … character varying[] = text[]` |
  | `SELECT ARRAY['2024-01-01 00:00:00+00'::timestamptz] = ARRAY['2024-01-01 00:00:00+00'::timestamp]` | `t` | `42883 … timestamp with time zone[] = timestamp without time zone[]` |

  Controls answering alike on both: the constructor under a cast to the column's type
  (`ARRAY[…]::timestamptz[]`, `::varchar[]`), a scalar `= ANY (tsa)`, `va @> ARRAY['a']`
  and `va @> ARRAY['a'::text]` (`42883` on both), `tsa @> ARRAY[…::timestamp]` (`42883`
  on both), a same-typed pair of constructors compared with `=`, and an `UPDATE … SET tsa =
  ARRAY[…::timestamptz]`. Loud where 18.6 answers — cast the constructor; **silent, and it
  writes**, where 18.6 refuses, a predicate answering over a pair it has no operator for:
  `DELETE FROM a WHERE ta @> ARRAY['a'::varchar]` removes the row here and is `42883` there. Reach: ordinary.
  Row 25's bullet carries what the same typing costs a GIN probe. No fixture: a faithful
  one is red in each direction.

- **282 · A constructor under an array cast is resolved before the cast is applied.** For
  `ARRAY[…]::T[]`, 18.6's `transformArrayExpr` is handed the cast's array type and converts
  each element to its element type, so a bare literal there is read as `T`. pglet resolves
  the constructor by itself first — a bare literal beside a typed element is read as that
  element's type (`docs/compatibility.md`'s Arrays row) — and casts the built array after. Measured
  through the npm package and the native server, both build profiles agreeing:

  | statement | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT ARRAY['NaN', 0]::float8[]`, `ARRAY[0, 'NaN']::float8[]` | `22P02 invalid input syntax for type integer: "NaN"` | `{NaN,0}`, `{0,NaN}` |
  | `SELECT ARRAY['x', 0]::text[]`, and `'t'`, `'2024-01-01'` for the literal | `22P02 … integer: "x"` | `{x,0}` |
  | `SELECT ARRAY['1.5', 1]::numeric[]`, `::float8[]`, `ARRAY['Infinity', 1]::numeric[]` | `22P02 … integer: "1.5"` | `{1.5,1}`, `{Infinity,1}` |
  | `SELECT ARRAY['01', 0]::text[]`, and `'+1'`, `' 1'` for the literal | `{1,0}` | `{01,0}`, `{+1,0}`, `{" 1",0}` |
  | `SELECT ARRAY['007', 1]::varchar[]` | `{7,1}` | `{007,1}` |

  Controls answering alike on both: `ARRAY['1', 0]::text[]`, `ARRAY['1', 0]::float8[]`,
  `ARRAY['1', 2]::numeric[]`, `ARRAY['NaN', 0.5]::float8[]`, `ARRAY['NaN'::float8, 0]`,
  and the uncast `ARRAY['NaN', 0]` (`22P02` on both). Loud for a literal that does not read
  as its sibling's type; **silent** for one that does and whose text the reading changes —
  a leading zero, sign or space is gone. Reach: ordinary. No fixture: a faithful one is
  red.

- **283 · A nested array literal is refused where 18.6 builds a multidimensional array.**
  Arrays are one-dimensional here (`docs/arrays.md`), and both spellings say so: the
  constructor `ARRAY[ARRAY['a','b']]` and the literal `'{{a,b}}'` are
  `0A000 multidimensional arrays are not supported`. The literal was once split at its
  commas — `'{{a,b}}'::text[]` the two elements `{a` and `b}`, silently, and stored. The
  reader (`executor::array_parse`) now walks a nested literal as 18.6's `ReadArrayStr`
  does — elements converted as they are read, sub-array lengths compared — and refuses it
  at the end, so what 18.6 refuses keeps 18.6's answer and only what 18.6 accepts takes
  the `0A000`. Measured through the npm package and the native server:

  | statement | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT '{{a,b}}'::text[]`, `'{{a},{b}}'`, `'{{{a}}}'`, `'{{"a","b"}}'`, `'{{a,NULL}}'` — and as `varchar[]`, `bytea[]`, `int4[]`, `int8[]`, `numeric[]`, `float8[]`, `bool[]`, `uuid[]`, `jsonb[]`, `date[]`, `time[]`, `timestamptz[]`, `interval[]` with that type's elements | `0A000` | the multidimensional array |
  | that string bound under `$1::text[]`, or given to a `text[]` column by `INSERT`, `UPDATE` or `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` | `0A000`; nothing is stored | accepted |
  | `SELECT '{"a":{"b":1}}'::jsonb #> '{{a,b}}'` — the path operand | `0A000` | `1`: the path is read flattened |
  | `SELECT '{{}}'::text[]`, `'{{},{}}'::int[]` — no element at all | `{}` | `{}` |
  | `SELECT '{{1,2},{3}}'::int[]`, `'{a,{b}}'::text[]`, `'{{a},b}'::text[]`, `'{{a}{b}}'::text[]` | `22P02` | `22P02` |
  | `SELECT '{{x}}'::date[]` — an element its type refuses | `22007`, the element's | `22007` |
  | `SELECT '{{{{{{{a}}}}}}}'::text[]` — a seventh level | `0A000` | `54000 number of array dimensions exceeds the maximum allowed (6)` |
  | `SELECT '[1:2]={a,b}'::text[]`, `'[0:1]={a,b}'`, `'[1:1][1:1]={{a}}'` — explicit bounds | `22P02`, as for any literal that does not open with a brace | `{a,b}`, `[0:1]={a,b}`, `{{a}}` |

  Loud in every cell that differs. Through the npm package a nested **JS array** bound to
  an array parameter is the same `0A000`, whatever the element type, where node-postgres
  sends the nested literal; an element ahead of it that its type refuses answers first. Reach: ordinary — a hand-written two-dimensional literal; the
  npm README lists it.

- **284 · `CREATE INDEX` accepts spellings 18.6's grammar refuses.** Each measured through
  the npm package and the native server, both build profiles agreeing, over `t (id INT
  PRIMARY KEY, a INT, b TEXT, j JSONB, ar INT[])`; 18.6 answers `42601` unless said:

  | statement | pglet |
  | --- | --- |
  | `CREATE INDEX public.zq ON t (a)`, and `"public".zq`, `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX public.zq …`, `IF NOT EXISTS public.zq` | builds `zq` — the qualifier is stripped (row 28 holds the other qualifiers, `42P01` here) |
  | `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS CONCURRENTLY ON t (a)`, and the `UNIQUE` spelling | builds an index named `concurrently` |
  | `CREATE INDEX q ON t (t.a)`, `(zz.a)` naming another table, `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX q ON t (t.a)` | builds; `pg_indexes.indexdef` renders the key `(t.a)`, text 18.6's grammar refuses in turn; the unique one enforces |
  | `CREATE INDEX q ON t (t.ar)`, `(t.j)` | builds a B-tree over the container column that row 25 refuses as `(ar)`; an `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` after it, and `=` and `@>` reads over the column, answer as on 18.6 |
  | `CREATE INDEX q ON t (a + 1)`, `(a::text)`, `((a) + 1)`, `((b)::text)` — an expression key without its own parentheses | builds; the last is rendered `(b)` |
  | `CREATE INDEX q ON t ((NULL))`, `(('x'))` — a key of unknown type; 18.6: `42704 data type unknown has no default operator class for access method "btree"` | builds, rendered `(NULL)`, `('x')` |

  `gram.y`'s `index_elem` takes a column name, a function call or a parenthesized
  expression, and its index name is an unqualified `name`; `IF NOT EXISTS` must follow
  `CONCURRENTLY` and be followed by a name. Controls agreeing on both: `CREATE INDEX
  CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS ON t (a)` and `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS ON t (a)` are
  `42601`, `CREATE INDEX q ON t (public.t.a)` is refused on both (`0A000` here), and
  `((1))`, `((NULL::int))`, `((a))` build on both. The grammar errs the other way at one
  spelling measured: `CREATE INDEX if ON t (a)` is `42601 … expected 'not'` here and an
  index named `if` there.

  **What the dump makes of them**, measured on the native server's `dump` restored into
  18.6: the qualified keys are written `((t.a))` and `((t.ar))`, which 18.6 loads as plain
  `btree (a)` and `btree (ar)`; `((b)::text)` as `(((b)::text))`, loaded as `btree (b)`;
  the index named `concurrently` as `CREATE INDEX concurrently ON t (a)`, which 18.6 reads
  as the keyword and builds under the name it chooses, `t_a_idx`; and `((NULL))` is
  refused there `42704`, psql exiting `0` with that index missing. **Silent** — a statement
  18.6 refuses runs. Reach: ordinary for the spellings a hand-written migration can carry;
  the dump is the native server's. No fixture: pglet accepts where 18.6 errors.

- **285 · `CREATE INDEX` builds over a function 18.6 does not mark `IMMUTABLE`.** 18.6
  requires every function in an index expression or predicate to be `IMMUTABLE` (`42P17
  functions in index expression must be marked IMMUTABLE`, `… index predicate …`). pglet
  builds the index for each function measured below. Measured through the npm
  package and the native server, both build profiles agreeing, over `t (id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  a INT, b TEXT, ts TIMESTAMPTZ)`, each `42P17` on 18.6 and built here: the keys
  `((now()))`, `((current_user))`, `((CURRENT_DATE))`, `((gen_random_uuid()))`,
  `((clock_timestamp()))`, `(concat(b, 'x'))`, `(concat_ws(',', b, b))`, `(to_char(ts,

  CURRENT_TIMESTAMP))`, and the predicates `WHERE now() > '2020-01-01'::timestamptz`,
  `WHERE gen_random_uuid() IS NOT NULL` and `WHERE current_user = 'x'`. Refused on both,
  under different codes: `(to_char(a, '999'))` over an integer is `0A000`
  here, and `((ts + interval '1 day'))` is `0A000` here (row 49). Controls built on both:
  `(lower(b))`, `((a::text))`, `((b || 'x'))`. A conversion **to** an enum is refused `42P17` on both — `((b::vis))`,
  `((CAST(b AS vis)))` and `WHERE b::vis = 'a'` over a `text` `b` (`docs/enums.md`) — and so
  is a call of the `VOLATILE` `random()`, `((a + random()))` and `WHERE random() < 0.5`
  (`functions/random_index_*_loud`) — while
  the conversion from one, `((m::text))` over an enum column, builds here and is `42P17`
  there. **Silent**: the index is
  built over a value that moves, and the native server's dump writes a `CREATE INDEX` 18.6
  refuses — measured for `((now()))`, psql exiting `0` with the index missing. Reach:
  ordinary. No fixture: pglet accepts where 18.6
  errors.

- **286 · `column_default` writes a sequence's name bare inside the literal.** 18.6 renders
  a `nextval` default's argument as a `regclass` constant, whose output quotes the name as
  an identifier where it needs it. pglet's `information_schema.columns.column_default`
  writes the stored name as it is. Measured through the npm package and the native server,
  both build profiles agreeing:

  | table | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `CREATE TABLE "Up" (id serial)` | `nextval('Up_id_seq'::regclass)` | `nextval('"Up_id_seq"'::regclass)` |
  | `CREATE TABLE "sp ace" (id serial)` | `nextval('sp ace_id_seq'::regclass)` | `nextval('"sp ace_id_seq"'::regclass)` |
  | `CREATE TABLE "tablé" (id serial)` | `nextval('tablé_id_seq'::regclass)` | `nextval('"tablé_id_seq"'::regclass)` |
  | `id int DEFAULT nextval('"séq"')` over such a sequence | `nextval('séq'::regclass)` | `nextval('"séq"'::regclass)` |

  A name needing no quotes (`plain_id_seq`) renders alike, `pg_get_serial_sequence`
  answers the quoted name on both, and the native server's dump writes the quoted name
  inside the literal, a script 18.6 restores to its own rendering (measured). Silent — a
  rendering, read by a schema differ or an introspecting ORM; the text is not one 18.6
  reads back as the same relation (`docs/sequences.md`). Reach: ordinary for a quoted
  mixed-case table with a `serial` column. No fixture: a faithful one is red.

- **287 · Under `OVERRIDING USER VALUE` the identity column's cell is replaced before it is
  read.** 18.6 analyses the whole `VALUES` row and then discards the identity column's
  value for the sequence's. pglet's `planner::dml`'s `apply_identity_rules` swaps the cell
  for `DEFAULT` while the row is lowered, and the members below are what that leaves
  unread.
  Measured over `g (id INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY, k TEXT)` and the `BY DEFAULT`
  twin `d`, through the npm package and the native server, both build profiles agreeing
  unless said:

  | statement | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `INSERT INTO g (k, id) OVERRIDING USER VALUE VALUES ('a', 'notanint')`, and over `d`, and `INSERT INTO d (id) OVERRIDING USER VALUE VALUES ('x')` | `INSERT 0 1` | `22P02 invalid input syntax for type integer` |
  | `… VALUES ('a', nosuchcol)` | `INSERT 0 1` | `42703` |
  | `… VALUES ('a', nextval('nosuchseq'))` | `INSERT 0 1` | `42P01` |
  | `… VALUES ($1, $2)`, two values bound | npm: `INSERT 0 1`; native server: `08P01 bind message supplies 2 parameters, but prepared statement "" requires 1` | `INSERT 0 1` |
  | `… VALUES ($1, $2)`, `$2` bound `'notanint'` | npm: `INSERT 0 1` | `22P02` |
  | `INSERT INTO d OVERRIDING USER VALUE SELECT $1::int, $2::int` | `0A000 … OVERRIDING USER VALUE for an identity column in INSERT … SELECT is not supported` | `INSERT 0 1` |

  Agreeing on both: a cell of another type family is `42804` (`'x'::text`, `true`), the
  in-range and out-of-range integer constants and `1/0` are discarded unevaluated, a
  parameter list whose identity cell comes first (`(id, k) … VALUES ($1, $2)`) binds, and
  without the clause `VALUES ('a', 'notanint')` over `d` is `22P02` (over `g` it is `428C9`
  here and `22P02` there). **Silent** for the unread cell
  — a statement 18.6 refuses writes a row; loud for the dropped parameter, which a client
  meets at `Bind`, and for the `SELECT` source. Reach: ordinary for the unread-cell
  lines; native server for the parameter. No fixture: a faithful one is red.

- **288 · A parameter no rule types is decoded by its JS runtime type through the wasm
  binding.** Where pglet's inference has no rule for a `$N`'s position it reports OID `0`,
  and the wasm binding then decodes the bound value by what the JS value is — a `number`
  as an integer or a float (`docs/param_binding.md` § Deferred / known gaps). The value
  therefore reaches an operator 18.6 could not resolve, or a function under another
  argument type. Measured through the npm package against 18.6 and the native server, a JS
  `number` bound:

  | statement | npm | native server, both profiles | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT -$1 AS n`, bound `5` (and `1.5`) | `-5` (`-1.5`), described `text` | `0A000 … negation not supported for type: Text("5")` | `42725 operator is not unique: - unknown` |
  | `SELECT -$1 = -5 AS n`, bound `5` | `t` | `0A000` | `42725` |
  | `SELECT abs($1) AS n`, bound `-5` | `5`, described `text` | `0A000 … abs() requires a numeric argument` | `5`, `double precision` |
  | `SELECT $1 + 1 AS n`, bound `2 ** 63` | `9.223372036854776e+18`, described `integer` | `42804` | `22003 … out of range for type integer` |

  The same statements bound a JS **string** (`'5'`) or a `bigint` are `0A000` through the
  npm package too, and `-$1::int` answers `-5` on each. Bound `null`, `SELECT -$1` answers
  `NULL` through the npm package and the native server alike, where 18.6 is `42725`. **Silent** through the npm package
  — an answer where 18.6 refuses, or a value described under a type 18.6 does not give
  it; the native server, which decodes an untyped parameter as text, is loud for each bound
  number. Reach:
  ordinary for the npm package. The npm README's *Known differences* names the `2 ** 63`
  member. No fixture: a faithful one is red, and the fixture harness binds wire text and
  binary values rather than JS ones.
  A **byte view** at such a position is decoded as text — its bytes read as characters,
  `22021` where they are not UTF-8 — which is 18.6's answer wherever 18.6 answers
  (`SELECT coalesce($1, $2)`). Where the untyped expression is assigned to a column
  — `INSERT INTO t (b) VALUES (coalesce($1, $2))`, `VALUES (CASE WHEN $2 THEN $1 END)` —
  18.6 refuses the statement (`42804`, the expression being `text`) and pglet converts the
  text to the column's type, as it does for a bound string: into a `bytea` column the
  view's bytes are read by `bytea`'s text input, so `Buffer.from('a\\\\b')` stores `a\b` and
  `Buffer.from('\\x4142')` stores `AB`, and into a `jsonb` column `Buffer.from('{"a":1}')`
  stores the object. **Silent**, at a statement 18.6 refuses. `UPDATE t SET b =
  coalesce($1, $2)` types both parameters `bytea` and stores the bytes.

  **`nullif`'s second argument is such a position, and there the value handed back is
  the first argument under another type.** 18.6 resolves `nullif(n, $1)` as `n = $1`
  and types the parameter from `n`; here, beside each number column measured, a `$N`
  standing as `nullif`'s second argument or under arithmetic there (row 54) is left
  untyped — the native server reads it as text and refuses — so the binding decodes a JS
  number by what it is, a fraction as a `double precision`. `eval_nullif`
  (`executor/expr/string_fn.rs`) then returns its first argument at the type `nullif_result_type` gives for the two
  **values** it was handed: a `numeric` or a `bigint` beside a `double precision` has no
  `=` of its own, so the first argument is converted to `double precision`, as 18.6
  converts it where the second argument is written as one (`nullif(price, 1.5::float8)`
  is `701` on both). The plan had declared the first argument's own type. Through the npm
  package the cell is then a JS `number` where a `numeric` cell is a string and a
  `bigint` cell a JS `bigint`, the digits past a `double precision`'s are gone, and
  stored to a `numeric` column the value is the float's fifteen digits. The reading of
  `eval_nullif` is from the code and agrees with the cast controls below; no build
  isolated it.

  Measured over `p (id int, price numeric, qty int, w real, f float8, b bigint, t text)`
  holding `(1, 1.5, 3, 0.1, 0.25, 30, 'a')`, `(3, 19.99, 7, 1.5, 2.5, 70, 'b')` and `(5,
  0.1234567890123456789, 9, 2.5, 3.5, 9007199254740993, 'c')`, in `id` order, a JS
  `number` bound through the npm package, the same
  value sent by `pg` to the native server (both profiles and both backends, which agree)
  and to 18.6; a declared type and the row values, a JS number written bare and a string
  quoted:

  | statement, bound | npm | native server | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT nullif(price, price * $1) FROM p`, `0.1` (and `price + $1`, `price - $1`, `price / $1`, `0.5`) | `1700`: `1.5`, `19.99`, `0.12345678901234568` | `42804 operator * requires numeric operands`, the operator named | `1700`: `'1.5'`, `'19.99'`, `'0.1234567890123456789'` |
  | `SELECT nullif(price, $1) FROM p`, `1.5` | `1700`: `NULL`, `19.99`, `0.12345678901234568` | `42883 operator does not exist: numeric = text` | `1700`: `NULL`, `'19.99'`, `'0.1234567890123456789'` |
  | `SELECT nullif(b, b * $1) FROM p` and `nullif(b, $1)`, `0.5` | `20`: `30`, `70`, `9007199254740992` | `42804`; `42883 … bigint = text` | `22P02 invalid input syntax for type bigint: "0.5"` |
  | `SELECT nullif(qty, qty * $1) FROM p` and `nullif(qty, $1)`, `0.5` | `23`: `3`, `7`, `9` | `42804`; `42883 … integer = text` | `22P02 invalid input syntax for type integer: "0.5"` |
  | `SELECT nullif(w, $1) FROM p`, `0.1` | `700`: `0.1`, `1.5`, `2.5` — compared as `double precision` | `42883 … real = text` | `700`: `NULL`, `1.5`, `2.5` — compared as `real` |
  | `SELECT nullif(t, $1) FROM p`, `0.5` | `42883 operator does not exist: text = double precision` | `a`, `b`, `c` | `a`, `b`, `c` |
  | `SELECT nullif(price, price * $1) + 1 FROM p`, `0.1` | `1700`: `2.5`, `20.99`, `1.1234567890123457` | `42804` | `1700`: `'2.5'`, `'20.99'`, `'1.1234567890123456789'` |
  | `SELECT COALESCE(nullif(price, price * $1), 0) FROM p`, `0.1` | `23`: `2`, `20`, `0` | `42804` | `1700`: `'1.5'`, `'19.99'`, `'0.1234567890123456789'` |
  | `SELECT sum(nullif(price, price * $1)) FROM p`, `0.1` | `0A000 sum() argument declared as numeric holds a value of type double precision` | `42804` | `'21.6134567890123456789'` |
  | `INSERT INTO sinkn SELECT id, nullif(price, price * $1) FROM p`, `0.1`, into `sinkn (id int, n numeric)` | stores `1.5`, `19.99`, `0.123456789012346` | `42804` | stores `1.5`, `19.99`, `0.1234567890123456789` |
  | `UPDATE p SET price = nullif(price, price * $1) WHERE id = 5`, `0.1` | `price` becomes `0.123456789012346` | `42804` | `price` unchanged |

  The unknown arithmetic as the **first** argument takes the other reading, the pass
  casting it to its sibling's type (row 65): `nullif(price * $1, price)` bound `0.1` is
  `1700` over strings, the product a float's digits (row 54), and `nullif(price * $1,
  0)` is `23` over `NULL`, `2`, `NULL` against 18.6's `1700` `0.15`, `1.999`,
  `0.01234567890123456789`.

  Controls, each agreeing with 18.6 through the npm package: a whole number bound, which
  decodes as a `bigint` — `nullif(price, price * $1)` and `nullif(price, $1)` bound `2`
  hand back the `numeric` strings, `nullif(b, b * $1)` bound `2` the JS `bigint`s; `null`
  bound; a cast parameter — `nullif(price, price * $1::numeric)` and `nullif(price,
  $1::numeric)` are `numeric`, and `nullif(price, price * $1::float8)` is `701` on both;
  the parameter as the **first** argument, which the second types (`nullif($1, price)`);
  a `double precision` first argument, a float either way (`nullif(f, $1)`, `nullif(f, f
  * $1)`); and the spellings with no parameter — `nullif(price, price * 0.1)` `1700`,
  `nullif(price, f)` and `nullif(price, f + 0)` `701`. The other folds over the same
  pair, the unknown arithmetic a later branch — `COALESCE(price, price * $1)`, `greatest`,
  `least`, a `CASE` and `ARRAY[price, price * $1]` bound a fraction — hand back
  `numeric` strings, the type 18.6 declares; where the product is what they hand back
  its digits are a float's (row 54) — `least(price, price * $1)` bound `0.1` is
  `'0.0123456789012346'` for the last row against 18.6's `0.01234567890123456789`.
  **Silent, and it writes**; loud at `sum`, and for the `text` column. Reach: ordinary
  for the npm package — a discount or a ratio bound as a JS number. No fixture, for the
  reason above.

  **A `$N` compared with, or added to, a column of a relation the catalog does not hold is
  such a position** — a FROM-clause `generate_series` or `unnest` item, a derived table:
  the inference resolves a column through the catalog and the FROM-alias map, neither of
  which holds those relations (`planner/param_types.rs`). Measured through the npm package,
  the native server under a text `Bind`, and 18.6:

  | statement | npm | native server | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT g FROM generate_series(1, 5) g WHERE g > $1`, bound `3` | `4`, `5` | `42883 operator does not exist: integer > text` | `4`, `5` |
  | the same, bound `3.5` | `4`, `5` | `42883` | `22P02` at `Bind` |
  | the same, bound the string `'3'` | `42883` | `42883` | `4`, `5` |
  | `SELECT g + $1 AS s FROM generate_series(1, 3) g`, bound `1` | `2`, `3`, `4` as JS `bigint`s under an `integer` (`23`) field | `42804` | `2`, `3`, `4`, `integer` |
  | the same, bound `1.5` | `2.5`, `3.5`, `4.5` under the same `integer` field | `42804` | `22P02` at `Bind` |
  | `SELECT x + $1 AS s FROM (SELECT 1 AS x) d`, bound `1.5` | `2.5` under an `integer` field | not measured | `22P02` |
  | `SELECT u FROM unnest(ARRAY[1,2]) u WHERE u = $1`, bound `2` | `2` | `42883` | `2` |
  | `SELECT x FROM (SELECT 1 AS x) s WHERE x = $1`, bound `1` / the string `'1'` | `1` / `42883` | `42883` | `1` / `1` |

  Silent through the npm package at the fractional bound and where the values are another
  type than the field declares (`bigint` and `double precision` values under `integer`);
  loud elsewhere. The controls `… WHERE g > $1::int` and a bound parameter **as** a
  `generate_series` argument (`generate_series(1, $1)`, typed by the overload) agree with
  18.6 on each door.

- **289 · A referential action written twice is accepted, the later action kept.**
  `gram.y`'s `key_actions` takes at most one `ON DELETE` and one `ON UPDATE`, in either
  order; a second of either is `42601 syntax error at or near "DELETE"` (`"UPDATE"`; `"ON"` where
  the other clause stands between the two) on 18.6. pglet's reader takes the clauses as they come. Measured through the npm package
  and the native server, both build profiles agreeing, over `p (k INT PRIMARY KEY)`, each
  `42601` on 18.6 and accepted here, `pg_constraint` then holding the later action:
  `CREATE TABLE c1 (k INT REFERENCES p ON DELETE CASCADE ON DELETE SET NULL)`
  (`confdeltype` `n`), `… ON DELETE SET NULL ON DELETE CASCADE` (`c` — a `DELETE FROM p`
  then removes the child row), `… ON UPDATE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE`, the table-level
  `FOREIGN KEY (k) REFERENCES p ON DELETE CASCADE ON DELETE RESTRICT` (`r`), a repeat
  split by the other clause (`ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE ON DELETE SET NULL`),
  `ALTER TABLE c ADD CONSTRAINT f FOREIGN KEY (k) REFERENCES p ON DELETE CASCADE ON DELETE
  SET NULL`, and `ALTER TABLE c ADD COLUMN k2 INT REFERENCES p ON UPDATE SET NULL ON UPDATE
  CASCADE`. The control `ON UPDATE CASCADE ON DELETE SET NULL` builds alike on both.
  **Silent** — a statement 18.6 refuses builds a constraint, under the action written
  last. Reach: ordinary DDL holding the slip. No fixture: pglet accepts where 18.6 errors.

- **290 · pglet holds no record for a `NOT NULL`, so a declared constraint can take the name
  18.6 gives one.** 18.6 stores each `NOT NULL` as a `pg_constraint` row named
  `<table>_<column>_not_null`, minted through `ChooseConstraintName` so that it steps
  around the statement's declared names, and refuses a later constraint of a taken name.
  pglet renders that row where `pg_constraint` is read (row 278's residual) and its name
  pool does not hold it. Measured through the npm package and the native server, both
  build profiles agreeing:

  | statement | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `CREATE TABLE s (a INT NOT NULL, CONSTRAINT s_a_not_null CHECK (a > 0))`, and with the `CHECK` at the column, and with the `NOT NULL` added later by `SET NOT NULL` | accepted; the `CHECK` and the `NOT NULL` both read `s_a_not_null` | accepted; the `NOT NULL` is `s_a_not_null1` |
  | `CREATE TABLE s2 (a INT NOT NULL)`, then `ALTER TABLE s2 ADD CONSTRAINT s2_a_not_null CHECK (a > 0)` | `ALTER TABLE` | `42710 constraint "s2_a_not_null" for relation "s2" already exists` |
  | `CREATE TABLE s3 (a INT NOT NULL, CONSTRAINT s3_a_not_null UNIQUE (a))` | accepted | `42710` |
  | `CREATE TABLE s9 (a INT NOT NULL, b INT CONSTRAINT s9_a_not_null REFERENCES s8)` | accepted | `42710` |
  | `CREATE TABLE s5 (a INT CONSTRAINT nn NOT NULL, CONSTRAINT nn CHECK (a > 0))` | accepted | `23505 … "pg_constraint_conrelid_contypid_conname_index"` |
  | `CREATE TABLE s5 (a INT CONSTRAINT nn NOT NULL)` — a declared `NOT NULL` name, read back from `pg_constraint` | `s5_a_not_null` | `nn` |

  The first line is accepted on both and costs a dump: the native server's dump of `s`
  writes `ALTER TABLE s ADD CONSTRAINT s_a_not_null CHECK ((a > 0))` after a `CREATE TABLE`
  at which 18.6 has already minted that name for the `NOT NULL`, so the restore answers
  `42710`, psql exits `0`, and the table stands without its `CHECK` (measured) — the
  database-state invariant `docs/sequences.md` states, broken by short names. **Silent** —
  a lost constraint on the first line, an accept where 18.6 refuses on the lines after it,
  and another name read back on the last.
  Reach: ordinary for the DDL through the npm package, which has no dump; the dump is the
  native server's. No fixture: a faithful one is red.

- **291 · An identifier is kept whole, where 18.6 cuts it to 63 bytes.** 18.6 truncates each
  identifier to `NAMEDATALEN - 1` bytes where the scanner reads it, under `NOTICE 42622
  identifier "…" will be truncated to "…"`; pglet kept each name measured here whole (`docs/parser.md` § Known
  lexical / parse divergences holds the message-size consequences). Measured through the
  npm package and the native server, both build profiles agreeing, with `<c>` a 63-byte
  name and `<d>` a 70-byte one:

  | statement | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `CREATE TABLE <d>a (v INT)`, then `CREATE TABLE <d>b (v INT)` | two tables | the second is `42P07` |
  | after those, `CREATE SEQUENCE <d>sa`, `CREATE INDEX <d>ia ON lt (x)`, `CREATE TYPE <d>ea AS ENUM ('a')` | each built | `42P07`, `42P07`, `42710` — the cut name is the first table's |
  | `CREATE TABLE two (<d>a INT, <d>b INT)` | two columns | `42701 column "<d>" specified more than once` |
  | `SELECT <c>zz FROM lt`, `lt` holding a column `<c>` | `42703` | answers |
  | `SELECT count(*) FROM <d>zzz`, a table `<d>a` existing | `42P01` | answers |
  | `INSERT INTO lt (<c>, <c>q) VALUES (1, 2)` | `42703` | `42701` |
  | `SELECT 1 AS <d>a` | the column is named the 71 bytes | named the first 63 |

  Constraint names are row 278's residual, and an `application_name` row 258. The native
  server's dump of the two tables, each holding a row, and of `two` restores into 18.6
  with psql exiting `0` and one table of the three present (measured). **Silent** where
  two names 18.6 would merge both stand; loud for a reference longer than the name it

- **~~292~~ · Closed — The `now()` family read the clock at each call.** 18.6 fixes `now()`,
  `transaction_timestamp()` and `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` at the transaction's start and
  `statement_timestamp()` at the statement's, so two reads inside one statement are one
  value. pglet modelled neither clock and read the host's where the call was evaluated;
  through the wasm binding that clock stepped a microsecond forward at each read. Measured through the npm
  package and the native server, both build profiles, on the build before the repair:

  | statement | npm | native server | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT now() = now()`, and `now() >= now()`, `now() BETWEEN now() AND now()`, `now() = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`, `now() = transaction_timestamp()`, `now() = statement_timestamp()`, `LOCALTIMESTAMP = LOCALTIMESTAMP` | `f` | `f` in each run measured | `t` |
  | `SELECT count(*) FROM n WHERE now() = now()`, `n` holding 3000 rows | `0` | some of the rows — `512` on one build's run, `233` on the other's | `3000` |
  | `SELECT now() - now()` | `-00:00:00.000001` | `-00:00:00.000003` | `00:00:00` |
  | `CREATE TABLE e (id int, created timestamptz DEFAULT now(), updated timestamptz DEFAULT now())`, one row inserted, `SELECT created = updated FROM e` | `f` | `f` | `t` |
  | `INSERT INTO n VALUES (1, now(), now())`, and the `UPDATE n SET a = now(), b = now()` spelling, then `a = b` | `f` | `f` | `t` |
  | a 3000-row `INSERT` under `DEFAULT now()`, `INSERT … SELECT id, now()`, `UPDATE m SET ts = now()` — the distinct stamps written | `3000` | `3000` | `1` |
  | inside one `BEGIN`, four `INSERT`s writing `now()`, `now()`, `transaction_timestamp()`, `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` — the distinct stamps | `4` | `4` | `1` |

  **Silent, and it wrote.** Reach: ordinary — a test asserting `created_at = updated_at` on
  a fresh row, or reading back the rows one statement or one transaction stamped by their
  shared time.

  **What closed it.** The family reads one of three clocks, by spelling
  (`pglet_sql::builtins`, `docs/temporal.md` § The transaction and statement clocks): the
  transaction's start for `now()`, `transaction_timestamp()`, `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`,
  `LOCALTIMESTAMP`, `CURRENT_DATE`, `CURRENT_TIME` and `LOCALTIME`; the statement's for
  `statement_timestamp()`; the wall clock, at the call, for `clock_timestamp()` — 18.6's
  assignment, measured there spelling by spelling inside a block opened before a
  `pg_sleep`. A host marks each statement's arrival, an open block carries its start in its
  connection's settings, and the two read sites — the expression evaluator's builtin arm and
  a column `DEFAULT`'s — read those instants. Each cell of the table above now answers 18.6's
  value through the npm package and through the native server — the B+tree and the memory
  backend, and the stripped build — as does each relation the row recorded as agreeing
  (`now() <= now()`, `now() < clock_timestamp()` — on wasm until the reads of one
  millisecond of the JS clock tie, where the two are equal (`docs/temporal.md` § The
  transaction and statement clocks) — `now() > now()` for no row, `x = x` over a
  derived `now()`, `ts <= now()` for each stamp an earlier statement wrote). The
  differential fixtures hold the relations — the index-probe one on both build profiles in the gate set, the
  rest on the stripped build where that pass is run by hand: the
  select list, a predicate over many rows, the defaults of a multi-row `INSERT` and an
  `INSERT … SELECT`, `UPDATE … SET` and `SET … = DEFAULT`, `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`,
  `RETURNING`, a `CHECK`, a CTE and a subquery, a `DO` body, an `ADD COLUMN` back-fill, a
  `COPY`'s defaults, a statement with bound parameters, an index probe's constant, and — in a
  fixture that drives its own transactions — a block, a savepoint and `ROLLBACK TO` inside
  it, the autocommit statements after it and a second block. The boundaries a fixture cannot
  drive are tests on each host: an aborted block, a second connection served by the same
  thread, one message carrying several statements, a prepared statement executed twice, and
  on wasm the count of reads of the JS clock a statement makes.

  **The residuals, silent**, are the extended protocol's and, on wasm, the tie: from the
  five-hundredth read of one millisecond of the JS clock the reads answer one instant, so
  two statements' stamps are equal and `now() < clock_timestamp()` is `f`
  (`docs/temporal.md`, same section; reach: ordinary under a test runner's frozen clock).
  The extended protocol's: 18.6 starts the implicit transaction
  at the first message after a `Sync` and stamps the statement again at each `Bind` and
  `Execute`; pglet takes both instants where it executes. Measured:

  | statement | npm | native server | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | outside a block, `SELECT now() = statement_timestamp()` sent with the extended protocol (`psql`'s `\bind`; a parameter through node-postgres) | `t` | `t` | `f` — `now() <= statement_timestamp()` is `t` on each |
  | outside a block, a bound `INSERT` into a table defaulting one column to `now()` and one to `statement_timestamp()`, then the two compared | equal | equal | different |
  | three bound `INSERT`s in one `psql` pipeline, under `DEFAULT now()` and `DEFAULT statement_timestamp()` — the distinct `now()` stamps, and statement stamps | not reachable: one statement a call | `3`, `3` | `1`, `3` |

  The simple protocol agrees on each: outside a block `now() = statement_timestamp()` is `t`,
  and two `INSERT`s sent as one message write one `now()` and one `statement_timestamp()`.
  Reach: ordinary for the first two rows — a parameterized statement that compares the two
  clocks — and server-only for the pipeline. No fixture: a faithful one is red, and the
  first row's `@text` twin (`functions/clock_autocommit_statement_is_its_transaction`) is the
  simple-protocol control.

- **293 · An untyped side of `||` beside an operand whose type has a `||` of its own stays
  `text`, where 18.6 reads it as that type.** 18.6 resolves an `unknown` operand of `||` to
  the other operand's type wherever that type carries a `||` of its own — `bytea || bytea`,
  `jsonb || jsonb`, the array forms — so `'abcd'::bytea || 'ef'` is `byteacat` over two
  `bytea`s and `j || '{"x": 1}'` merges two `jsonb` objects. pglet has the text forms of
  `||` only (`planner::legality`'s `concat_legality`), and nothing reads the untyped side
  off its sibling: a string literal reaches that rule as `text`, and a bare `$N` is typed
  `text` by parameter inference's `||` arm whatever the other operand
  (`planner/param_types.rs`). The other side is then stringified — or, for an array, the
  pair has no text form and is refused. The members below are the types measured, not a
  bound on the class: a type that gains a `||` of its own here joins it. Row 262 is the same
  literal-stays-`text` reading at other operators and constructs — the comparisons, `IN`,
  containment, arithmetic and `LIKE` among them. Measured over `t (j JSONB, b BYTEA, a
  INT[], s TEXT)` holding `('{"k": 1}', 'abcd', '{1,2}', 'x')`, on the native server and the
  npm package, which agree:

  | statement | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT 'abcd'::bytea \|\| 'ef'` | the `text` `\x61626364ef` | the `bytea` `\x616263646566` |
  | `SELECT 'ef' \|\| 'abcd'::bytea` | the `text` `ef\x61626364` | the `bytea` `\x656661626364` |
  | `SELECT '\xabcd'::bytea \|\| '\x'` | the `text` `\xabcd\x` | the `bytea` `\xabcd` |
  | `SELECT 'abcd'::bytea \|\| '\q'` | the `text` `\x61626364\q` | `22P02` |
  | `SELECT substr('\x0102'::bytea, 1, 1) \|\| 'x'` | the `text` `\x01x` | the `bytea` `\x0178` |
  | `SELECT b \|\| $1`, a string or a `Buffer` bound | the `text` `\x61626364ef` | the `bytea` `\x616263646566` |
  | `SELECT … WHERE b \|\| 'ef' = 'abcdef'` | no row | the row |
  | `UPDATE t SET b = b \|\| 'ef'` | `42804` | appends the two bytes |
  | `SELECT … WHERE b \|\| 'ef' = b` | `42883` | answers |
  | `SELECT j \|\| '{"x": 1}'`, and `'{"x": 1}' \|\| j` | the `text` `{"k": 1}{"x": 1}` (`{"x": 1}{"k": 1}`) | the `jsonb` `{"k": 1, "x": 1}` |
  | `SELECT j \|\| '[1]'` | the `text` `{"k": 1}[1]` | the `jsonb` `[{"k": 1}, 1]` |
  | `SELECT j \|\| 'x'` | the `text` `{"k": 1}x` | `22P02` |
  | `SELECT j \|\| $1`, `'{"x": 1}'` bound | the `text` `{"k": 1}{"x": 1}` | the `jsonb` `{"k": 1, "x": 1}` |
  | `SELECT … WHERE j \|\| '{"x": 1}' = '{"k": 1, "x": 1}'`, and `j \|\| $1 = $2` | no row | the row |
  | `DELETE FROM t WHERE j \|\| '{"x": 1}' = '{"k": 1, "x": 1}'` | `DELETE 0` | `DELETE 1` |
  | `UPDATE t SET s = j \|\| '{"x": 1}'` | writes `{"k": 1}{"x": 1}` | writes `{"k": 1, "x": 1}` |
  | `UPDATE t SET j = j \|\| '{"x": 1}'`, and `j \|\| $1` | `42804` | merges |
  | `SELECT … WHERE j \|\| '{"x": 1}' = j`, and `… @> '{"x": 1}'` | `42883` | answers |
  | `SELECT a \|\| '{9}'`, `a \|\| $1`, and in a `WHERE` or an `UPDATE t SET a =` | `42883 operator does not exist: integer[] \|\| text` | `{1,2,9}` |
  | `SELECT '{9}' \|\| a` | `42883 … text \|\| integer[]` | `{9,1,2}` |

  The result column is declared `text` (OID 25) here and the other operand's type there, so
  through the npm package a `bytea` cell is a string where node-postgres gives a `Buffer`,
  and a `jsonb` cell a string where it gives an object. Controls that agree: an explicit
  `text` side — `'abcd'::bytea || 'ef'::text`, `j || '{"x": 1}'::text`, and `b || s` or `j
  || s` over the `text` column — is the joined text on both. A bare `NULL` is an untyped
  side too: `b || NULL` and `j || NULL` are NULL on both engines but declared `text` here
  and `bytea` / `jsonb` there, and `UPDATE t SET b = b || NULL` is `42804` where 18.6 writes
  the NULL. With the untyped side written as the operand's own type (`'ef'::bytea`, `'{"x":
  1}'::jsonb`, `ARRAY[9]`) the pair is the `0A000` of the unimplemented `bytea || bytea`,
  `jsonb || jsonb` and array `||` — for an `ARRAY[…]` operand, once a row is evaluated.
  **Silent** in a select list, where the result is written to a `text` column, and in a
  comparison with a literal or a parameter, which compares the joined text — so a `DELETE`
  or an `UPDATE` filtered that way writes; and read as text where 18.6 has no reading of the
  result, so `j || '{"x": 1}' LIKE '%x%'` and `length(j || '{"x": 1}')` answer where 18.6 is
  `42883`; loud into a `bytea` or `jsonb` column (`42804`), in a comparison with an operand
  of the other's type (`42883`) or under `@>` / `<@`, and beside an array at every position
  — `0A000` rather than `42883` over a `text[]`, whose element type is the literal's, and
  only once a row is evaluated where the array is an `ARRAY[…]` constructor. Reach: ordinary
  — the `jsonb` merge idiom `data || '{…}'` in a seed, a query or a filter, and a test
  joining a `bytea` to a quoted string. No fixture: a faithful one is red.

- **294 · Narrowed — the array reader's grammar is 18.6's; the element readers still trim a Unicode space.**
  The array-literal reader split the body at its commas with no state for *where* an
  element may start or end, and tested whitespace by Unicode's `White_Space`, so it read
  what 18.6's `ReadArrayStr` refuses — `'{a,,b}'::text[]` three elements, `'{a{b}'` one
  element keeping the brace — and trimmed a no-break space off an element, silently, for a
  `text[]`, `varchar[]` or `bytea[]` target.

  **What closed that.** `executor::array_parse` is 18.6's two functions: a token reader
  (`read_array_token`, its `ReadArrayToken`) and the walk that says where a token may
  stand (`parse_array_literal`, its `ReadArrayStr`), with 18.6's `scanner_isspace` set as
  the only whitespace. Each element is converted as it is read. Measured on a cast
  literal, a bound string, the column doors (`INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`,
  a `DEFAULT`) and the jsonb path operand, through the native server and the npm package:

  | array literal | pglet and 18.6 |
  | --- | --- |
  | `'{a,,b}'`, `'{a,}'`, `'{,a}'`, `'{,}'`, `'{a, ,b}'`, `'{NULL,}'`, `'{"a",}'` | `22P02`, whatever the element type |
  | `'{a{b}'`, `'{a}b}'`, `'{a"b}'`, `'{"a"b}'`, `'{"a}'`, `'{a}x'`, `'{a'`, `'a'` | `22P02` |
  | `'{a<U+00A0>}'::text[]`, `'{<U+00A0>a}'` | the element keeps the space |
  | `'<U+00A0>{a}'`, `'{a}<U+00A0>'`, `'{"a"<U+00A0>}'` | `22P02` |
  | `'{x}2024-01-02}'::date[]`, `'{x,,01:00}'::time[]` — a refused element ahead of the structural error | `22007`, the element's |
  | `'{2024-01-01,,x}'::date[]`, `'{x{}'::date[]`, `'{x'::date[]`, `'{"x"y}'::date[]` — the structural error first, or inside the element | `22P02` |

  Guards: the `array/literal_*.sql` fixtures, `jsonb/path_malformed_array_literal_loud.sql`
  and `array_parse.rs`'s unit tests. A stored expression holding such a literal reads
  differently, which the `PGMU` store magic already covers (row 279).

  **What remains** is not the array reader's. The scalar text readers for the integer
  types, `numeric`, `float4`, `float8`, `uuid`, `date`, `time` and `interval` trim their
  input with `str::trim`, which drops Unicode `White_Space`, where 18.6's input functions
  skip ASCII whitespace at most. So `'1<U+00A0>'::int` is `1` here and `22P02`
  there, and an array element handed to such a reader with the space still on it —
  `'{1<U+00A0>}'::int[]`, `'{<U+00A0>2024-01-01}'::date[]` — is read where 18.6
  refuses it: `22P02`, or `22007` for `date`, `time` and `interval`. Measured with
  U+00A0, U+0085 and U+2003, leading and trailing, as a scalar and as an element; with a
  structural error later in the literal the array reader's `22P02` is then the answer here and
  the element's own code there (`'{<U+00A0>2024-01-01,}'::date[]`: `22P02`, `22007`). `uuid`
  trims ASCII whitespace as well (`' 0000…'::uuid` is read here, `22P02` there), which an
  escaped or a quoted space reaches through an array (`'{\ 0000…}'::uuid[]`). `bool` and
  `jsonb` refuse the space on both, the timestamp types refuse it with row 96's code, and
  `text`, `varchar` and `bytea` keep it on both. The types above are the ones measured,
  not the class's bounds. Two renderings also differ: a `22P02` from the array reader
  reads `invalid input syntax for type array: "…"` where 18.6's reads
  `malformed array literal: "…"`, and on output an element holding a Unicode space is
  quoted where 18.6 prints it bare (`docs/arrays.md`). **Silent, and it writes.** Reach:
  ordinary — a number pasted with a no-break space. No fixture: a faithful one is red.

- **295 · A parameter run straight into a character that can start an identifier is two
  tokens, where 18.6's scanner refuses it.** 18.6's scanner has a rule for a parameter
  followed with no space by an identifier (`scan.l`'s `param_junk`,
  `\${decdigit}+{identifier}`) and refuses the statement `42601 trailing junk after
  parameter` as it scans, before any of it is analysed. pglet's
  lexer reads no trailing junk after a parameter: `scan_dollar` (`lexer/core.rs`) ends the
  `$N` token at its last digit, and the character after it starts the next token. Measured
  through the native embed's `Database::execute_bound`, the wasm bindings' `queryParams`
  (the npm package's path) and the native server's extended protocol (psql's `\bind`), the
  three agreeing, against 18.6 over the extended protocol:

  | statement | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT $1abc`, `$1` bound to `5` | one row, its column named `abc`, holding `5` | `42601 trailing junk after parameter at or near "$1abc"` |
  | `SELECT $1<U+00E9>`, `$1` bound to `5` | one row, its column named `<U+00E9>` | `42601 trailing junk after parameter at or near "$1<U+00E9>"` |
  | `SELECT x FROM (VALUES (1)) v(x) WHERE $1or true`, `$1` bound to `f` | one row, `1` | `42601 trailing junk after parameter at or near "$1or"` |
  | `SELECT $1abc` with no parameters — the simple-query protocol, `Database::execute`, the wasm `query` | `22000 execution error: bind message supplies 0 parameters, but statement requires $1` | `42601 trailing junk after parameter at or near "$1abc"` |

  Control: `SELECT $1 abc`, `$1` bound to `5`, answers one row, its column named `abc`
  holding `5`, on both. **Silent** with parameters — an answer where 18.6 refuses; loud,
  under the wrong code, without them. Reach: ordinary — a parameter typed against the word
  after it. Row 171's bullet names `SELECT <chain>, $1abc` among its deep-chain members. No
  fixture: a faithful one is red.

- **296 · A `SELECT` with no `FROM` ends before its `WHERE`, `GROUP BY` and `HAVING`.**
  `parse_select_leaf` (`parser/select.rs`) ends a select with no `FROM` before its `WHERE`,
  `GROUP BY` or `HAVING` and returns the leaf, so the clause keyword is what the statement's
  end-of-input check meets next. `ORDER BY` and `LIMIT` are read past the leaf and agree.
  Measured through the native server (simple query) and the wasm bindings' `query` (the
  npm package's path), the two agreeing, against 18.6:

  | statement | pglet | 18.6 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `SELECT 1 WHERE true` | `42601 syntax error: expected ';' or end of input, found 'where'` | one row, `1` |
  | `SELECT 1 WHERE false` | `42601 syntax error: expected ';' or end of input, found 'where'` | zero rows |
  | `SELECT 1 GROUP BY 1` | `42601 syntax error: expected ';' or end of input, found 'group'` | one row, `1` |
  | `SELECT 1 HAVING true` | `42601 syntax error: expected ';' or end of input, found 'having'` | one row, `1` |

  Controls: `SELECT 1 ORDER BY 1` and `SELECT 1 LIMIT 1` answer one row, `1`, on both
  engines and both pglet legs, and `SELECT 1 FROM (VALUES (1)) v(x) WHERE true` on 18.6
  and the native server. **Loud** — a refusal where 18.6 answers, never
  a wrong answer. Reach: ordinary — a guard row written as `SELECT 1 WHERE <condition>`. No
  fixture: a faithful one is red, and an `@expect-error` one passes on any error where 18.6
  accepts.

- **297 · A plain aggregate beside a `DISTINCT` one keeps input order where 18.6 presorts
  the aggregate input.** 18.6's planner (`adjust_group_pathkeys_for_groupagg`, under the
  default `enable_presorted_aggregate`) appends a `DISTINCT` aggregate's sort to the
  grouping's pathkeys and, where the plan takes that sorted path, sorts the node's input
